Innovation Ranking Criteria

Papers are ranked from most to least innovative by a composite score from 0 to 100. Each paper is scored on six dimensions: (1) novelty, (2) scientific rigor, (3) non-obviousness, (4) completeness, (5) resilience, and (6) practical impact. The composite is a weighted average of the six scores under one of three weight profiles (empirical, theoretical, or systems), chosen per paper. Each paper includes a justification explaining its placement.

≥75 Highly Innovative
≥60 Innovative
≥40 Moderately Innovative
≥20 Incremental
<20 Routine

#1 — Highly Innovative (85)

FESOM2. 8 in single precision: climate fidelity over six decades and performance on CPUs and GPUs

SK Cheedela, NV Koldunov, S Danilov, J Streffing… · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a single-precision (32-bit default working precision) implementation of the global ocean–sea-ice model FESOM2, with a conservative tracer-update scheme that eliminates precision-induced heat and salt drift over 60-year climate hindcasts. - Why it's important: Ocean models are memory-bandwidth-bound and run for decades of simulated time on expensive HPC systems, so halving the bytes moved per value translates directly into ~35% more climate throughput and 40–43% less GPU memory — but only if rounding errors do not silently corrupt multi-decadal heat and salt budgets. - How it does it: The core trick is accumulating tracer tendencies and layer thicknesses in 64 bits and applying compensated (Kahan-style) summation to the thickness-weighted tracer update, carrying each step's rounding remainder into the next, so that flux cancellation between control volumes survives 32-bit storage of the state. - The good: The evaluation is unusually honest and controlled: with the fix, the single-minus-double heat-content difference (≤1.5 ZJ over 60 years) is within the chaos-spread of two double-precision runs, internal heat residual is 7.3×10⁻⁶ W m⁻², and the paper demonstrates the fix also in a coupled model (AWI-ESM3) and against an independent C++/Kokkos implementation. - The missing: The climate-fidelity validation covers only one mesh at nominal 1° resolution and 60 years; eddy-rich/kilometre-scale configurations, century-scale conservation, passive tracers, and the biogeochemistry model (REcoM) remain untested, and the small residual surface-salt uptake in single precision is not explained. - Read it or not: Essential reading for anyone building or porting Earth-system models to reduced precision or GPU hardware; specialists outside climate/numerical-model development can skip it, as the insights (stagnation of small increments, conservative updates, budget-based validation) are specific to that setting.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile (with a strong systems component — a released model version). Rigor (92) is exceptional: every headline number is paired with a double-precision control, the failed first implementation is fully documented, budgets are closed to ~10⁻¹⁰ of content, timing runs are repeated with reported medians, and code, commits, meshes, and data are archived on Zenodo. Novelty (78) is high — first multi-decadal heat/salt-budget evaluation of a fully single-precision ocean–sea-ice model plus a genuinely new conservative tracer-update scheme — while Non-Obviousness (80) captures the key insight that increment bias, not just update rounding, must be addressed (compensated summation alone demonstrably fails), plus the novel use of an independent implementation's precision sensitivity as a bug detector that found two real defects. Completeness (85) benefits from direct, non-minimizing acknowledgment of the 60-year/one-mesh validation scope and the unexplained residual salt uptake. Resilience (88) reflects claims carefully bounded to tested configurations with a reusable, falsifiable validation protocol. Impact (88) reflects the released FESOM2.8 build, the Kokkos port, and a validation methodology transferable to any reduced-precision climate model. Weighted composite: 0.20*78 + 0.25*92 + 0.15*80 + 0.15*85 + 0.15*88 + 0.10*88 = 85.

Problem & Motivation: Global ocean–sea-ice models compute in 64-bit arithmetic even though discretization and forcing errors exceed 32-bit rounding error (~10⁻⁷ relative) by orders of magnitude. Because ocean-model kernels are memory-bandwidth-bound, storing fields in 32 bits halves memory traffic and roughly doubles usable throughput — a lever that matters as 64-bit arithmetic stagnates on modern hardware (Blackwell Ultra cut it to ~1.2 TFLOP s⁻¹ per GPU). Numerical weather prediction already runs single precision operationally (ECMWF IFS: ~40% cost reduction, no skill loss), but ocean models have lagged because a rounding bias invisible in a days-long forecast can accumulate over decades of heat and salt integration; prior ocean evaluations covered days to a few years, and the only multi-decadal evidence (Nakano et al. 2025, land-surface studies) showed real drift. No prior work had evaluated the heat and salt budgets of a fully single-precision ocean–sea-ice model over multiple decades, traced the drift to its source, or removed it. Key Idea: The key insight is that the fatal precision error in an ocean model is not chaotic round-off divergence (harmless) but a biased numerical source or sink created when small flux increments are rounded either during computation from large background values or when added to a large stored state (stagnation: at S≈35 psu, adjacent 32-bit values are 3.8×10⁻⁶ psu apart, so smaller increments are lost). The fix — the paper's technical contribution — is a conservative update in three parts: (1) accumulate tracer tendencies in 64 bits so fluxes cancel between adjacent control volumes, (2) store layer thicknesses in 64 bits so volume is not corrupted, and (3) compute the new state in 64 bits, round to 32 bits, and carry the thickness-weighted rounding remainder into the next update (compensated summation applied to tracer content). This keeps the entire prognostic state and operators in 32 bits — capturing the full memory-bandwidth gain, unlike NEMO 4.2's single-precision build which keeps the state in 64 bits — at ≤8% runtime cost. Methodology: The implementation is a model-wide precision parameter (kind WP) set by a build option, with targeted 64-bit exceptions: time-mean output accumulation, global budget reductions, conjugate-gradient solver scalars and z*-coordinate matrix updates (accumulated in a 64-bit copy, rounded once per step), and the conservative tracer/thickness updates above. A runtime option stores salinity as S−35 psu (reviving a MOM3 practice), which reduced drift 32× before the fix and is a no-op after. Validation uses 60-year CORE-II hindcasts (1948–2007) on the CORE2 mesh (126,858 surface vertices, 47 layers, nominal 1°, 900 s timestep — deliberately half the production timestep, making the small-increment problem harder), with daily-recorded global volume/heat/salt budgets. The judging criterion is established port-validation methodology: single-vs-double differences are compared against double-vs-double differences from round-off or a 2×10⁻⁴ K initial-temperature perturbation. The failure of the first implementation (salt loss 1.2×10⁻⁴ psu yr⁻¹, 129 ZJ heat deficit) was isolated via controlled 20-year and 9-month experiments that ruled out surface fluxes, global sums, solver, and decomposition, then traced to the tracer update. Performance is measured as strong scaling on four meshes (CORE2 to NG5, 7.4×10⁶ vertices, ~5 km) up to 512 CPU nodes / 128 A100 GPUs, for both the Fortran model and an independent C++/Kokkos implementation; a precision-sensitivity comparison (relative L2 distances against a 5-member perturbed-initialization baseline) tests whether two implementations respond identically to reduced precision. Finally, four coupled AWI-ESM3 pre-industrial 60-year integrations repeat the budget test with a freely evolving atmosphere. Key Results: With conservative updates, single precision over 60 years differs from double precision by ≤1.5 ZJ in heat content (vs 1.0 ZJ between the double-precision controls; the naive implementation lost 129 ZJ), 0.47×10⁻⁶ psu in volume-mean salinity (14× the control but 14,000× smaller than before), SST RMS 0.0046 °C vs 0.0040 °C control (0.7% of the model's HadISST1 error), Arctic/Antarctic sea-ice volume and area ≤0.2% (control 0.07%), and internal heat residual 7.3×10⁻⁶ W m⁻². In the coupled model, the precision-dependent part of the internal heat residual is 5.3×10⁻⁷ W m⁻², and all climate differences sit within the coupled chaos spread (heat content drifts up to 54 ZJ between near-identical runs). Performance: 1.35× speedup end-to-end on the 60-year hindcasts (52→70 simulated years/day), up to 1.66× for Fortran on CPUs (falling to 1.02× at 4096 processes on CORE2), 1.40–1.64× retained on eddying meshes up to 64 nodes, 1.05–1.27× for Kokkos on A100 GPUs, 40–43% device memory reduction (NG5: 21.6 vs 35.9 GiB per GPU), with component speedups matching the memory-bound diagnosis (tracers 1.85×, sea ice 1.14×). The implementation comparison found Kokkos precision effects 0.65–0.83× Fortran's for global T/S and exposed two real bugs (uninitialized Adams–Bashforth history; Redi/GM increments added directly to the state). Baselines are appropriate and current (double-precision self-controls, perturbed-twin methodology from port validation). Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (first multi-decadal heat/salt-budget evaluation of a fully single-precision ocean–sea-ice model, with the drift traced and removed) plus NEW METHOD (the conservative tracer-update scheme combining 64-bit tendency/thickness accumulation with compensated state updates, keeping the full prognostic state in 32 bits) plus NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (released FESOM2.8 single-precision build with coupled support). The compensated summation and reference-salinity ideas are standard (Kahan 1965; MOM3 1999), and the validation methodology is borrowed from port validation; the genuinely novel parts are the demonstration that increment bias — not just update rounding — must be addressed (compensated summation alone fails), and the use of an independent implementation's precision sensitivity as a bug-detection instrument. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong. Controlled experiments isolate each suspected drift source; every headline climate number is paired with a double-precision control; ablations show compensated summation alone is insufficient while the full conservative updates suffice. Timing runs are repeated in mirrored order (median 0.3% difference), implementation-comparison ratios carry propagated uncertainties (e.g., 0.76±0.08), and budgets are closed to 1.8×10⁻¹⁰ (single) / 1.8×10⁻¹⁵ (double) of content. Code is public (github.com/FESOM/fesom2, GPL v3; Kokkos version under Apache 2.0), specific commits and PRs are cited, and all configurations, scripts, meshes, and derived data are archived on Zenodo (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24014072, 10.5281/zenodo.24015804); raw 1.3 TB output is retained but only on request. Methodological caveats the paper itself flags: scaling points at 256/512 nodes on DARS/NG5 come from an earlier code version with absolute double-precision times differing −22 to +30% between campaigns; throughput figures are projections that exclude output; a few incomplete jobs were salvaged. The remaining salinity drift (14× control) is admitted as unexplained. No significance testing is performed on the climate comparisons, though the perturbed-twin framing makes formal tests largely unnecessary. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a strong SYSTEMS component — a released model version). - Practical: Yes — it runs on standard CPU clusters (DKRZ Levante, AMD EPYC) and commodity NVIDIA GPUs, and is already released as FESOM 2.8.0+. - Efficient: Strictly favorable: 1.35× faster end-to-end for ≤8% overhead in the update scheme, 40–43% less GPU memory; CVMix-coupled configurations gain less since that library stays in double precision. - Effective: For its stated purpose (climate integrations at ~1°, prescribed forcing and coupled), the evidence — budget closure plus twin-run equivalence over 60 years — is directly on target, not a proxy, though the residual surface salt uptake is unexplained. - Scalable: Only partially tested: scaling is measured to 512 nodes / 128 GPUs and kilometre-scale meshes, but climate fidelity is validated at one resolution and 60 years; the authors show the small-increment problem worsens with shorter timesteps, so kilometre-scale safety is claimed only as a hypothesis. Delivers a concrete software artifact (model release, archived data, Kokkos port), not just a paper. Strengths: - The conservative tracer-update scheme is a genuine, transferable numerical-design contribution: it demonstrates empirically that compensated summation of the update alone fails because the increments themselves are biased, and that 64-bit tendency/thickness accumulation is the necessary complement — a non-obvious decomposition of where precision must live. - The two acceptance criteria (no numerical source/sink in conserved quantities beyond control spread; climate differences far below model-vs-observation error, trajectory divergence permitted) give the field a reusable, falsifiable validation protocol, and the paper shows budgets expose drift within one model year versus decades for field-based checks. - The independent-implementation precision-sensitivity comparison is a clever and apparently new verification tool: it detected two real bugs (one affecting double precision too) that double-precision verification had missed. - Transparency is exemplary: the failed first implementation is documented in full with its own controls, and each result is mapped to a specific code revision. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that the conservative updates are validated only over 60 years at nominal 1° resolution; eddy-rich and kilometre-scale configurations (shorter timesteps, stronger intrinsic variability that can mask precision errors), century-scale conservation, and passive tracers are untested; REcoM biogeochemistry and CVMix remain double precision, excluding carbon-cycle configurations; the mechanism of the small residual surface-salt uptake is unidentified; the coupled test is intrinsically weak because chaos noise (54 ZJ) swamps the signal; a fixed domain decomposition is required for isolating precision effects; and reduced precision pushes the model into the latency-dominated regime earlier, shrinking speedup at large process counts. This is direct, non-minimizing confrontation of limitations — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the acknowledged limitations: (1) the entire climate-fidelity validation rests on a single mesh (CORE2) and single forcing dataset; a second mesh or forcing would strengthen the external claim considerably; (2) the main implementation-comparison (Sect. 6) uses the Kokkos version without conservative updates, so the cross-implementation agreement partially measures a defect the final code fixes — the comparison does not validate the fixed configuration across implementations; (3) the unexplained surface salt uptake is bounded only at this configuration, and its extrapolation to passive-tracer or carbon-cycle budgets (which the authors themselves propose as the sensitivity metric) is unquantified; (4) coupled sea-ice volume differences of −22% (Arctic) and +5% (Antarctic) between single and double precision are reported in Table D1 but not discussed — they are similar to the perturbed-twin values (−26%, +13%), yet this equivalence is asserted rather than statistically supported given the acknowledged noise; (5) no wall-clock cost is reported for the 8% overhead at the kilometre-scale meshes where the small-increment problem is worst, so the cost–benefit at the configurations the paper most wants to enable is unmeasured. Bottom Line: This is the reference work for anyone converting an ocean or climate model to single precision — rigorous, self-critical, with a validated fix and a reusable validation protocol — and there is no comparable study covering multi-decadal budget fidelity; read it before attempting any reduced-precision climate integration.

#2 — Highly Innovative (85)

PAC Learning with Multiple Correct Answers

S Hanneke, F Mansouri, AF Pour, A Shaeiri, K Wang · arxiv.org · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds a PAC learning theory for tasks where each input has up to ℓ correct labels and predicting any one of them suffices, giving complete learnability characterizations under three feedback models (full label sets, bandit feedback, and single demonstrated labels) for finite and countable label spaces, in both realizable and agnostic settings. - Why it's important: Supervised fine-tuning and learning-from-demonstration pipelines (e.g., training on one accepted proof or one correct program per prompt) train on exactly the one-correct-label feedback studied here, and the paper shows this feedback can be qualitatively and quantitatively harder than the full feedback that classical multiclass theory assumes. - How it does it: The core move is a reduction: learning from demonstrations of a class H is equivalent to full-set learning of the intersection class I_{ℓ+1}(H) (intersections of at most ℓ+1 hypotheses), plus a new "packed dimension" that replaces the DS dimension for countable label spaces, all built on a transductive potential argument that counts products of minimal empty-intersection label families. - The good: The characterizations are if-and-only-if theorems with matching upper and lower bounds: demonstrations provably require eO(ε^{-ℓ}) samples and Theorem C exhibits classes where this exponent ℓ is unavoidable, even when the same class is learnable from eO(1/ε) full-set examples or a single bandit answer. - The missing: The learners rely on finite covers of size exp(O_ℓ(d log(nk))) with no computational-complexity analysis, the worst-case ε^{-ℓ} rate is not tight for every class (only in the worst case over classes of a given dimension), and whether finiteness of the joint DS dimension of the intersection class is necessary for countable label spaces is left open by the authors. - Read it or not: Learning theorists working on multiclass learnability, partial concept classes, or the statistical theory of learning from demonstrations should read it in full; practitioners doing SFT/RLHF-style training can skip the proofs but should absorb the demonstration-vs-full-set separation and the ε^{-ℓ} lower bound.
Why this rank
Scored using Theoretical profile. Novelty (90) is the top contributor: a NEW PROBLEM (PAC learnability with multiple correct answers under three feedback models) with NEW FORMULATIONS (intersection-class reduction, packed dimension) that no prior work covers. Rigor (85) is strong — ~100 pages of complete proofs, iff characterizations with matching ε^{-ℓ} lower bounds, explicit small separating constructions — though AI-assisted proofs without independent verification and partial overlap with prior work temper it slightly. Non-Obviousness (88) is high: the demonstrations-harder-than-bandit separation (Example 15) genuinely inverts practitioner intuition. Completeness (85) and Resilience (85) benefit from direct acknowledgment of worst-case caveats, open problems, and LLM assistance. Impact (55) is conceptual only — exponential-size covers make the learners non-algorithmic. Weighted composite: 0.25*90 + 0.20*85 + 0.25*88 + 0.10*85 + 0.15*85 + 0.05*55 = 86, rounded to 85 after the preprint/AI-verification discount.

Problem & Motivation: In classical multiclass PAC learning a prediction is correct only if it equals the single target label, and learnability is characterized by the Natarajan dimension (finite label spaces) and the DS dimension (general label spaces). Many real tasks violate this singleton-label assumption: a theorem admits many valid proofs, a specification many correct programs, a chess position several winning moves, and SFT data consists of one correct output per prompt. The paper asks which hypothesis classes are PAC learnable when each example carries a set of at most ℓ correct labels, under three feedback regimes that practice actually provides: full sets (the whole correct-label set), bandit feedback (a checker says yes/no to a proposed label), and demonstrations (one correct label drawn by an unknown demonstrator). Prior multiclass theory (Natarajan, DS dimension, work of Brukhim et al. 2022) does not answer this, and prior statistical work on learning from demonstrations (Joshi et al.) covers only finite reward classes with inverse-linear accuracy dependence, which this paper shows can be exponentially optimistic. Key Idea: The single load-bearing insight is that demonstrations are governed not by the hypothesis class H itself but by its intersection class I_{ℓ+1}(H): since any family of correct-label sets of size ≤ ℓ with empty intersection is witnessed by at most ℓ+1 members (Lemma 8), a label in the intersection of ℓ+1 hypotheses is a valid demonstration for all of them, so learnability from demonstrations is equivalent to full-set learnability of I_{ℓ+1}(H). The quantitative loss comes from a minimax argument: if the best label at an input is wrong with probability ν, then ℓ+1 independently drawn candidates conflict there with probability at least ν^ℓ, which is exactly where the ε^{-ℓ} sample-complexity exponent — and the matching lower-bound construction on the grid [n]^ℓ — comes from. Methodology: The paper is pure learning theory: definitions, dimensions, and proofs, with no empirical component. The pipeline for each upper bound starts from a transductive rule on a known pool of n inputs that keeps a version space of partial patterns and predicts labels whose sub-potentials retain more than an ℓ/(ℓ+1) fraction of a potential Φ(W) counting realized products of minimal empty-intersection families; a mistake multiplies Φ(W) by at most ℓ/(ℓ+1), giving O_ℓ(d log(nk)) mistakes for d = d∩_N(H). Because this rule is conservative, its run is determined by its O(d log(nk)) mistake positions, which yields a finite cover of H on any pool of size (1+nqk)^{M_d(n)}; exponential weights over this cover give agnostic full-set learners, elimination/expert algorithms give bandit learners (with an extra factor k from uniform random queries and unbiased loss estimates in the agnostic case), and leave-one-out plus confidence-amplification arguments convert expected-risk bounds to PAC bounds. For one-correct-label feedback, the reduction retains candidates consistent with demonstrations on a random half-split, uses families of label vectors with an intersection property (built from compression descriptions for infinite label spaces), and applies the minimax conflict argument. For countable label spaces, a weak one-inclusion learner based on the packed dimension d∩_{pack,γ} (weighted lists where disjoint conflict blocks of ≤ ℓ+1 patterns cover a γ fraction in every direction) is boosted via multiplicative weights — with threshold 1/(ℓ+1) playing the role of 1/2 in binary boosting — and converted to a sample compression scheme. Lower bounds come from DS witnesses and product witnesses drawn at random from shattered inputs. Critical design decisions: the ℓ+1 truncation of intersections (justified by Lemma 8 and shown non-restrictive via Corollary 58), the coverage parameter γ < 1/(ℓ+1) (justified by the plurality-vote Lemma 11), and the collapsed-class construction Ĥ for the agnostic demonstration characterization (justified by an explicit indistinguishability obstruction on a single input). Key Results: Seven main theorems (A–G), summarized in Table 1. Theorem A: for finite label spaces of size k, full-set and bandit learnability (realizable and agnostic) are each equivalent to finiteness of the generalized Natarajan dimension d∩_N(H) or joint DS dimension, with m_full = O_ℓ((1/ε)(d log((d+1)(k+1)/ε) + log²(1/δ))), optimal in d/ε up to logarithmic factors for d ≥ 2 (Proposition 23), and bandit rates carrying an extra factor k. Theorem B: realizable learnability from demonstrations is equivalent to d∩_N(I_{ℓ+1}(H)) < ∞, with m_one = O_ℓ((d+1)/ε^ℓ · log²((d+2)(k+1)/ε) · log(1/δ)); Example 15 gives a three-label class with d∩_N = 1 learnable from a single full-set example or a single bandit answer that is not learnable from any number of demonstrations. Theorem C: a matching lower bound m_one(ε, 1/8) > d/(4·(32(ℓ+1)ε)^ℓ), so the ε^{-ℓ} exponent is necessary in the worst case (a factor ε^{-(ℓ-1)} worse than full-set feedback). Theorem D: for countable label spaces and ℓ ≥ 2, the packed dimension characterizes full-set learnability, while the joint DS dimension is neither necessary nor sufficient (two explicit separating classes, one with d∩_DS = 1 unlearnable, one with d∩_DS = ∞ learnable). Theorem E: demonstrations reduce to the packed dimension of I_{ℓ+1}(H), with sufficient conditions via d∩_DS or d_pair bounded by O(D log(D+2)). Theorem F: for nondegenerate classes, agnostic learnability from demonstrations holds iff d∩_DS(Ĥ) < ∞ and H is locally compatible; nondegeneracy cannot be dropped (a three-set class on one input with all four intersection dimensions equal to 1 is not agnostically learnable). Theorem G: without a uniform bound ℓ, no parameter with finite witnesses characterizes learnability. All results are worst-case theory; there are no datasets or benchmarks. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM (PAC learnability of multi-label targets under three feedback models, extending multiclass theory), NEW FORMULATION (the intersection-class reduction I_{ℓ+1}(H), the packed dimension, the collapsed class Ĥ with local compatibility), NEW METHOD (the product-counting transductive potential argument and the packing-based weak learner with threshold 1/(ℓ+1)), and NEW EMPIRICAL-FINDING-equivalent theoretical findings (the demonstrations-harder-than-bandit separation, the realizable/agnostic split under demonstrations, and the impossibility Theorem G). Genuine novelty is high: the packed dimension and the ε^{-ℓ} exponent are not combinations of known techniques; the finite-label full-set machinery is a competent extension of the halving/one-inclusion graph toolkit, and the qualitative part of Theorem A for realizable full-set learning is also derivable from prior work (BBCB+25, Appendix C), as the authors state. Rigor & Reproducibility: As theory, rigor rests on proof completeness, and the paper provides it: roughly 100 pages of detailed proofs across Sections 7–15 plus appendices, with explicit inequalities (Lemma 17's product-counting bound, the minimax conflict argument), matching upper and lower bounds up to logarithmic factors in the finite-label regimes, and explicit handling of measurability for standard Borel instance spaces (Appendix E). Every claim I checked against its stated proof sketch is internally consistent, and separations are witnessed by explicit small constructions (Examples 12–15) rather than existence arguments. There are no error bars, seeds, or code (none is applicable); no software, dataset, or model artifact is released. Methodological caution: the quantitative part of Theorem A's realizable full-set result overlaps with [BBCB+25] (acknowledged in a footnote), the ε^{-ℓ} lower bound is worst-case over classes of a given dimension and the authors are careful to say so, and the AI Statement discloses that all results beyond Theorem A and the writing were developed with the help of Claude and ChatGPT — a transparency positive, though it places extra weight on the authors' verification of the AI-assisted proofs. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: THEORETICAL — proofs and characterizations with no primary experimental claim. Sound: Assumptions (partial hypotheses, countable/standard-Borel instance spaces, uniform ℓ bound, nondegeneracy for the agnostic demonstration theorem) are stated explicitly, and proofs including the obstruction cases are given in full. General: Results hold for finite and countable label spaces, partial classes, and both realizable and agnostic settings, with the notable restrictions that Theorem F requires nondegeneracy and everything requires a uniform ℓ; the general-instance-space extension needs regularity assumptions. Tight: Upper and lower bounds match up to logarithmic factors in the finite-label full-set case and in the ε^{-ℓ} exponent for demonstrations; some questions remain genuinely open (necessity of d∩_DS(I_{ℓ+1}(H)) for countable Y; scale-sensitive characterizations for finite but unbounded label sets), so the characterization program is not complete. Implementable: The learners are constructive (explicit transductive rule, exponential weights, compression), but they enumerate covers of size (1+nqk)^{M_d(n)} with no runtime or memory analysis, so an efficient algorithmic instantiation is unaddressed. Deliverable: paper form plus reusable proof techniques (the product-counting potential and the packed dimension); no software artifact. Strengths: - Complete iff characterizations rather than one-sided bounds: each feedback model's learnability is pinned to a combinatorial dimension, with matching lower bounds up to log factors — the strongest form of result in this genre. - The demonstrations-vs-bandit separation is genuinely surprising and practically pointed: a class identifiable from one bandit query (Example 15) is unlearnable from unlimited demonstrations, directly challenging the intuition that demonstrations (a positive label) are always at least as informative as a yes/no check. - The ε^{-ℓ} lower bound (Theorem C) is matched to the minimax conflict mechanism (ν^ℓ), an unusually tight theory-explanation loop: the hard construction's empty-intersection probability (ℓ+1)^ℓ/n^ℓ exactly mirrors the quantity the upper bound loses a root on. - The impossibility result (Theorem G) is a substantive negative: it shows the uniform ℓ bound is not a convenience but a necessity for any finite-witness dimension characterization, via an explicit block construction rather than set-theoretic pathologies. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state: (i) the worst-case ε^{-ℓ} bound is a statement about the worst class of a given dimension — some classes with the same dimension are learnable from O((d+log(1/δ))/ε) demonstrations (Remark 44); (ii) two open problems — whether finiteness of d∩_DS(I_{ℓ+1}(H)) is necessary for countable label spaces, and whether a family of scale-sensitive parameters with finite witnesses characterizes learnability for finite but unbounded correct-label sets; (iii) finiteness of the joint DS dimension fails as a characterization in both directions once ℓ ≥ 2, which they treat as motivation for the packed dimension rather than as a limitation of their framework; and (iv) the AI Statement disclosing LLM assistance. They confront limitations directly, particularly by flagging which qualitative results are derivable from prior work. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No computational-complexity treatment anywhere: the covers have size (1+nqk)^{M_d(n)} where M_d(n) grows like d log(nk), and the reduction's candidate-retention step may consider infinitely many hypotheses abstracted away by label-vector families; the characterizations are information-theoretic, and a practitioner cannot currently run these learners on nontrivial classes. - The agnostic-from-demonstrations characterization (Theorem F) holds only for nondegenerate classes, and the degenerate obstruction is exhibited on a single-input class; how commonly nondegeneracy fails in structured classes over large instance spaces, and what the right characterization for degenerate classes is, are not explored. - The impossibility result in the scale-sensitive part of Theorem G requires relabeling-invariant parameters and permits infinite correct-label sets; the authors acknowledge the finite-sets case remains open, but the framing of "no dimension characterizes learnability" is slightly stronger than what is proven at that level of generality. - The sample-complexity upper bounds hide dependence on γ and ℓ, and the bandit agnostic rate carries a √k factor; for moderate k these constants could dominate, and no comparison against the empirical performance of naive baselines (e.g., ERM on demonstrated labels) is offered — acceptable for a theory paper but worth noting for the ranker's practical-impact dimension. - Beyond the disclosed LLM assistance, the paper does not report any independent verification process for the AI-assisted proofs; given the volume of material, residual error risk is nonzero, though the presence of full proofs permits checking. Bottom Line: This is the definitive foundational treatment of PAC learning with multiple correct answers and is essential reading for learning theorists — its intersection-class reduction, packed dimension, and demonstration hardness results have no existing alternative covering the same ground — though its impact on practice is currently conceptual rather than algorithmic.

Keel: A Verified In-Kernel Proof Checker for Proof Carrying BPF

Y Cai, TC Chang, S Nagarakatte · arxiv.org · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds Keel, a formally verified in-kernel proof checker in Lean 4 (compiled to runtime-free C via a deep embedding called EmbC) that replaces the unverified ~5,000-line C checker of the eBPF Certificate Framework (BCF) while accepting the same binary certificates. - Why it's important: In BCF/Proof-Carrying BPF, an untrusted user-space SMT refutation certificate convinces the Linux eBPF verifier to accept programs its abstract domains cannot prove safe, so a single bug in the in-kernel checker lets an attacker load arbitrary unsafe kernel code — and the authors found 13 such bugs (some exploitable to accept forged certificates for unsafe programs). - How it does it: Keel separates a pure functional certificate checker in Lean (proved sound against bit-vector semantics, with rewrite rules stored as data so a single meta-theorem covers all 164 table entries) from an EmbC implementation proved to refine that specification without undefined behavior or leaks, with amortized-potential proofs of linear time and memory budgets. - The good: Formalization of BCF's checker uncovered 13 previously unknown bugs — including silently unchecked proof steps (7.2% of steps on BCF's own evaluation corpus) and an unsound rewrite (products wrapping in 8 bits: 64·2 wraps to −128) with a demonstrated 13-step forged certificate that BCF accepts for every formula while Keel rejects it — plus Keel is 1.3× faster in-kernel and never crashed or hung on 64 million fuzzed certificates. - The missing: Evaluation covers BCF's own object-file corpus (1,588 files, 1,891 certificates) on one server under Linux 6.19 in QEMU; there is no independent security audit of the trusted printer, EmbC semantics, or kernel API contracts, and no evidence of upstream Linux acceptance of the ~6.6K-line generated C checker. - Read it or not: Worth reading in full if you work on verified systems code, proof-carrying code, or eBPF verifier internals; skimmable if you only want the bug taxonomy in Table 1 and the wrap-around rewrite case study.

Problem & Motivation: The Linux eBPF verifier uses non-relational abstract domains (intervals plus tristate numbers), so it rejects safe programs whose safety depends on inter-register relations — e.g., a program writing two stack traces into an 800-byte buffer where the verifier cannot recover the invariant offset + size = 800 and deduces a write up to byte 1600. BCF and Proof-Carrying BPF fix this with selective proof-carrying code: when a safety check C fails under path condition P, the verifier emits a refinement condition φ = P ∧ ¬C and accepts the program if an untrusted user-supplied cvc5 certificate refutes φ. All trust then concentrates in the in-kernel checker — approximately 5,000 lines of C in BCF — where any bug compromises kernel security. Nobody had formalized that checker; this paper does, and the formalization immediately pays off by exposing 13 exploitable or latent bugs. Key Idea: The core insight is a three-layer factoring of the trusted-checker problem: (1) soundness of the checking machinery is decoupled from soundness of individual rewrite rules by storing all 164 rewrites as data in a typed pattern language, so one generic meta-theorem (Lemma 4.7) covers any table of per-entry identity proofs — new rules need only a standalone Lean lemma, not re-verification of the checker; (2) the C implementation is written in EmbC, a deeply embedded C fragment in Lean with typed-cell memory and a non-deterministic kernel-API oracle, forcing every proof to handle allocation failure, copy errors, and pending signals on every path; and (3) denial-of-service resistance is proved by making resource budgets (two counters initialized linearly in input size, decremented before every input-dependent operation) the potential functions of a machine-checked amortized analysis, which eliminates the need for hash-load-factor or DAG-shape invariants. Methodology: The pipeline has three layers. (1) Functional specification (§4): checkLean processes a certificate π = (term pool Π_π, steps s_0..s_{n−1}) over 50 proof rules (42 structural — refl/symm/trans/cong, Boolean, resolution; 7 computational — evaluate, poly_norm, bitblast, etc.; 1 table-driven rewrite), maintaining the invariant Δ ⊆ Cn(φ); Theorem 4.4 proves acceptance implies φ unsatisfiable under bit-vector semantics. Rewrite entries in a pattern language with typed parameters, width/overflow guards, and side conditions are checked by one generic routine whose soundness (Lemma 4.7) reduces to per-entry validity (Lemma 4.8, 164 entries). (2) EmbC implementation (§5): ~6,616 lines of C across 174 functions, using a flat u32 array pool with topological (DAG) ordering, open-addressing hash table for canonical term indices (making term equality a single integer comparison), a conclusions array, in-place mark-and-slide compaction of dead terms, and a last-citation scan for liveness. State correspondence (Definition 5.3) leaves dynamic term indices unconstrained so compaction is transparent to the rule proofs; a four-layer argument (footprint invariant, per-rule refinement, compaction soundness, single-step simulation) yields Theorem 5.4 (no stuck states, caller memory preserved, all allocations freed, accept only when checkLean accepts). EmbC semantics are validated against CompCert Clight (in Lean via Clean) by forward/backward simulations with UB reflection (Theorem 5.2). (3) Resource bounds (§6): work and mem counters as potentials give Theorem 6.3, T ≤ R·W_T(B) = O(B) and M ≤ W_M(B) = O(B). A 268-line trusted printer emits the C; key design decisions — data-driven rewrite table (well justified by the extensibility measurements), canonical-hash equality (justified empirically by the speedup), and metered budgets (justified: removing counters only saves 2%) — are each individually ablated. Key Results: (1) Bug discovery: 13 bugs in BCF's checker (Table 1): 1 unchecked-step bug where rewrite 0/poly_norm accepts any equation (7.2% of certificate steps on BCF's 361-object-file evaluation are unchecked), 6 unsound rule semantics (including the rewrite 73/74 multiplication wrap-around, exploited via a 13-step forged certificate accepted by a BCF-patched kernel even for φ = ⊤), 4 missing-check unsoundnesses, and 3 memory-safety errors (out-of-bounds stack write in absorb, null-pointer reads). (2) Compatibility: on 1,588 real-world object files (Calico, Cilium, Inspektor Gadget, BCC), Keel and BCF agree on all verdicts (1,226 load, 362 reject); on 1,891 certificates both accept 1,522, and Keel additionally accepts 16 valid certificates BCF rejects (BCF's constant evaluator lacks some operators). No certificate exhausts a budget. (3) Performance: in-kernel, 1.3× faster than BCF overall; 2.0× on the slowest 1.4% of certificates (median 5.4 KB: 55 µs vs 110 µs); 3.4× at 16–32 KB; outside the kernel 3.6× per-certificate average and 8.1× on the largest (5.6 MB). Memory is slightly worse: 13 KB vs 10 KB peak at the median certificate, 9.54 MB vs 8.48 MB on the largest. (4) Ablations: without compaction, peak grows to 28.9 MB; compaction actually saves 4% time (cache locality); removing counters saves 2%. (5) Extensibility: 13 new cvc5 rewrites added in 633 lines of Lean (median 35 per rule), zero C changes, only two lines for the refinement connection. (6) Fuzzing: 64 million mutated certificates, no crash, hang, or leak. Proof effort: refinement proof 52,398 lines of Lean; cost proof 12,863 lines. Baselines are current and directly relevant (BCF is the SOSP '25 system Keel replaces); scale is realistic kernel-corpus scale plus one large stress certificate, not massive scale. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, with a NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the 13-bug security assessment of BCF's checker). The genuinely novel elements are the Extensible-rewrite-table-as-data design with a single soundness meta-theorem, the EmbC deep embedding with kernel-API oracles under which total safety is proved, and the machine-checked linear resource bounds for kernel code. The constituent techniques — deep embedding à la Bedrock2/Fiat-Crypto, CompCert-style simulations, Tarjan-style potentials, PCC — are standard and honestly credited; the contribution is their combination to produce the first verified, runtime-free C checker for SMT refutation certificates deployable in the Linux kernel. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and targeted (compaction on/off, counters on/off, each with verdict-equivalence checked on all 1,891 certificates). All theorems are machine-checked in Lean depending only on three standard axioms (plus two Clight-model axioms for external functions and inline assembly). The evaluation uses the adversary's own corpus (BCF's repository), 1,891 classified certificates, and 64M fuzzed inputs for differential testing; forged certificates are demonstrated in an actual kernel. Code is publicly released (github.com/rutgers-apl/keel). Methodological concerns: the EmbC-to-Clight correspondence assumes the kernel builtin contracts in Clight exactly match EmbC's API specifications, and the printer and C compiler remain trusted and unvalidated by execution testing beyond the differential fuzzing (which does exercise the printed C against BCF's checker — a partial mitigation). Timing is single-server (AMD EPYC 7302P, QEMU VMs); no error bars or repeated-run variance are reported for the timing figures, though medians over certificate classes partially blunt this. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a built, kernel-deployable tool with machine-checked proofs) — with a strong THEORETICAL component. - Practical: Yes — it emits standalone runtime-free C that links into Linux 6.19 with no Lean runtime, targeting commodity x86 servers. - Efficient: Faster than the incumbent (1.3× total, up to 8.1× on large certificates) at the cost of ~30–50% more peak memory (13 KB vs 10 KB median); proof effort was large but is a one-time cost. - Effective: The evidence shows it solves the stated problem — accepts everything BCF accepts on real corpora, rejects BCF's demonstrably forged certificates, and is provably sound — though real-world adoption by kernel maintainers is untested. - Scalable: The O(B) time/memory bound is proved for all inputs, so asymptotic scaling is established formally rather than claimed; empirically it was tested up to 5.6 MB certificates with graceful behavior, but 10×–100× beyond that is untested in practice. The work delivers a concrete software artifact: open-source Lean development, EmbC framework, generated C checker, and evaluation scripts. Strengths: - The bug discovery is a genuine, high-value empirical finding: 13 bugs including a provably exploitable unsound rewrite (bit-vector product wrap-around missing the W ≥ w + w′ side condition) with an end-to-end forged-certificate attack demonstrated in a running kernel — direct evidence that formalization of security-critical checkers pays for itself. - The rewrite-table-as-data design with Lemma 4.7 is a real architectural contribution: it converts a per-change re-verification problem (which would make a verified checker unmaintainable in the kernel) into per-entry standalone identity proofs, and the authors quantify the extension cost (35 lines of Lean per rule, no C changes). - The resource-bounds proof technique — using the runtime budget counters directly as amortized potentials, thereby needing no hash-distribution or DAG-shape invariants — is a clean trick that decouples worst-case guarantees from data-structure-specific reasoning. - The evaluation is honest and ablated: the authors report where Keel is worse (memory) and measure precisely what each kernel-serving design decision costs (4% time saving from compaction, 2% from counters), rather than only headline numbers. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The threat model section explicitly enumerates the trusted computing base: the eBPF verifier constructing φ, the bit-vector semantics formalization, EmbC semantics, kernel API specifications, the EmbC-to-C printer, and the C compiler. The authors frame Keel as "a first step" toward verified core infrastructure and acknowledge that rejection (e.g., on budget exhaustion or kernel API failure) sacrifices precision, never safety. They confront the discovered BCF bugs directly with a per-bug table and case study rather than minimizing them — a credibility positive. The Clight correspondence theorem's assumptions (kernel builtins behave exactly per contract; all reachable states fit 64-bit representations) are stated explicitly in Theorem 5.2. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The kernel API contracts (Table 2) are assumptions about Linux behavior, not verified properties of the actual kernel implementations; a divergence between, say, kvrealloc's real semantics and its contract would void the safety guarantee in ways the paper does not empirically probe. - The trusted printer (268 lines) and the C compiler are in the TCB with no translation-validation or post-printer checking described; a printer bug silently reintroduces the exact class of bug Keel exists to prevent. Differential fuzzing against BCF mitigates but does not close this. - No adversarial evaluation by anyone other than the authors: the 64M fuzzed certificates were generated by the authors' own mutator against their own checker; there is no third-party red-team attempt against Keel's TCB. - Security of the verifier-side glue (how φ is communicated and matched, the compare function) is proved, but the paper does not discuss denial-of-service interaction between Keel and the verifier's certificate-request mechanism (e.g., an attacker forcing repeated proof generation to burn user-space SMT time) — arguably out of scope but unaddressed. - No error bars or seed variance on the timing measurements; single-machine, QEMU-based timings may not reflect bare-metal or other architectures. - Upstream Linux acceptance, maintainability by non-authors, and integration friction (the checker is built for one kernel version, 6.19) are untested. Bottom Line: This is the strongest available replacement for BCF's checker — anyone deploying or building on proof-carrying eBPF should adopt or at least study Keel, since it strictly dominates the incumbent on soundness, speed, and extensibility, with the open question being whether its trusted printer and kernel-API contracts survive community scrutiny rather than whether the approach works.

FINCOSMOS: An Open-World Evaluation Paradigm for Agents in Finance (20 ▲ )

Yupeng Cao, Xueqing Peng, Lingfei Qian, Haohang Li, Yangyang Yu, Anke Xu, Wenbo Cao, Yan Wang, Yuechen Jiang, Yuyan Wang, Zhuohan Xie, Yankai Chen, Zehan Li, Jimin Huang, Xue Liu, Jian-Yun Nie, Sophia Ananiadou · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 11 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces FinCosmos, an open-world benchmark and evaluation paradigm that grades financial agents on multi-turn sessions where the user's intent is hidden, the agent must self-source all Web data, and the agent must keep its own backtest point-in-time under a data cutoff — with acceptance decided by 15 programmatic veto checks rather than reference answers or user satisfaction. - Why it's important: Financial agents fail silently — an unrequested strategy, unverified data, or a look-ahead backtest produces a report as convincing as a correct one, and existing benchmarks close the intent, the data, or the timeline, thereby removing these failures instead of measuring them. - How it does it: Hidden strategy specifications are sampled from a compositional grammar (~3.8M strategies across six strategy components), an LLM user simulator reveals the spec only when asked, and an evaluator combines program checks (data provenance, point-in-time correctness, independent recomputation of reported metrics from the delivered trade log) with an LLM judge for semantics, accepting a session only when the user signs off and no veto fails. - The good: Across 150 sessions from four coding agents, zero sessions are accepted, and the paper shows this is not a grading artifact — user sign-off alone would pass 23% of sessions and an LLM judge alone 11%, yet every one of those sessions fails a program check, while two human experts attribute 88.33% of failures to the agents (judge-expert agreement κ = 0.87). - The missing: The benchmark covers only ten frozen tasks with three sessions per agent over long-only U.S. equity strategies with a single data API (Financial Modeling Prep), and the simulator, LLM judge, and one evaluated agent all come from the same model family. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or evaluate LLM agents for finance or agentic benchmark design — the reference-free, program-verified grading scheme and the silent-failure analysis are directly reusable; skip it if you need finance-domain model comparisons, since the task coverage is too narrow for leaderboards beyond the ten frozen tasks.

Non-Obviousness (85) is anchored by the silent-failure finding — sign-off and LLM-judge grading both count broken deliveries as successes and reorder agents — which generalizes beyond finance. Problem & Motivation: Language agents increasingly work for real users on the open Web, and finance is the domain where trusting them is hardest and errors cost the most. Three uncertainties make financial work genuinely open-world: the task intent lives in the user's head and surfaces only through questioning; the data lives on the Web, not in the model; and correctness is point-in-time, so today's data carries the future into the past. Each uncertainty produces a silent failure — nothing crashes and the report looks as convincing as a correct one. The authors argue that every existing benchmark closes at least one of these three channels: QA benchmarks (FinQA, FinanceBench, FinBen) hand over curated data with fully specified questions; strategy benchmarks (BacktestBench, AlphaForgeBench) provide explicit specifications and data; simulated-user benchmarks (τ-bench and successors) hide intent but work over closed databases and grade against a target state; trading benchmarks (InvestorBench, AMA) score realized returns without requiring the agent to build and verify its own backtest. No prior benchmark simultaneously opens intent, data, and time while verifying the deliverable itself. Key Idea: Grade the delivery, not an answer: because a financial task needs only a hidden specification and no reference result, the evaluation can (a) sample unlimited hidden strategies from a compositional grammar, (b) reveal them only through a simulated user under a strict disclosure policy, and (c) verify the delivered artifact with programs that recompute every reported metric from the delivered trade log, check point-in-time correctness against a fixed cutoff, and match the delivered strategy against the hidden spec — so a polished report cannot hide a leaky or irreproducible backtest. Methodology: FinCosmos has three components. (1) A Strategy Generator samples one option for each of six strategy components (stock selection, market timing, portfolio construction, risk control, execution, transaction cost) from a grammar with coherence rules, yielding ~3.8M strategies before parameters are drawn; each option carries a difficulty weight, and seeded sampling makes tasks reproducible and renewable. (2) A User Simulator (Claude Opus 4.8) plays one of three personas holding the hidden belief as plain-language convictions; a disclosure policy (formalized as S_t \ S_{t−1} ⊆ Q(a_t), Equation 2) ensures the user states only what the agent asks about or proposes, and a program validates every simulator decision before it is sent, so the simulator can close a session only when every core goal is met with cited evidence. (3) An Evaluator grades 45 dimensions in seven categories (data, strategy, backtest, assessment, UX, cost, process transparency) on a 0–4 anchored scale; programs grade 17 dimensions, an LLM judge 19, both 6. The pre-veto quality Q (Equation 3) weights the five scored categories equally; 15 veto dimensions (point-in-time strictness, per-component strategy fidelity, independent recomputation, verifier audit, process completeness, ambiguity, grounded conclusions, conversation experience, internal leak) gate acceptance: Score = Q · pass, AC = pass · 1[satisfied] · 1[grading complete]. Critical design decisions: (i) leak-free feedback (scores without reasons for data/strategy categories, so the hidden spec is not revealed across attempts) — justified as necessary for a renewable leaderboard; (ii) the LLM grade is bounded by program counterparts where both exist (s_j = min(s_LLM, s_P)) — a sensible anti-hallucination guard; (iii) execution logs can fail checks but never pass them — a deliberate conservative choice. Agents run up to six 300-second turns in a sandbox with a 247-API Financial Modeling Prep MCP server; the deliverable (messages plus files) is what is graded. Key Results: On ten frozen tasks with three sessions per agent (150 sessions total), no session is accepted for any agent, so pass^k = 0 for all agents. Pre-veto quality (0–100): Codex 37.2 [95% CI 30.6–43.3], Claude Code 37.1 [27.8–45.0] (not significantly different, p = 0.99), Gemini CLI 22.2, Kimi Code 22.3, bare Claude Opus 5.5 without tools 20.2 [18.8–21.5] — the tool-less model is statistically indistinguishable from Gemini CLI and Kimi Code (p ≥ 0.44). The simulated user signed off in 23% of sessions (35/150), and all 35 fail at least one program veto; 29 of 35 delivered no trade log or no prices, so reported returns cannot be rebuilt, and in the 5 sessions where the program could rebuild them, none matched the report. Grading by the four LLM-judged vetoes alone would accept 17 of these 35 (11% acceptance) and would reorder the agents. Along the workflow (of 120 agent sessions): 25 deliver the user's strategy, 15 in sequence also keep data within the cutoff, 14 also avoid look-ahead, and 0 deliver trades reproducing reported returns. Agents elicit only 54–64% of unstated spec details and mismatch 66–83% of details never stated; clarification coverage correlates with quality (Spearman ρ = 0.25, p = 0.007). Quality falls with task difficulty (ρ = −0.24, p = 0.007). Cost: Codex reads 3.2M input tokens/session; Claude Code costs $2.24/session at API prices. Two paid financial experts (independent of the authors' team) attribute 88.33% of failed sessions to the agent, 5% to the simulator, 7% to the evaluator; the LLM judge agrees with them at κ = 0.87 (expert-expert κ = 0.93). In a learning experiment, a Claude Code + persistent-memory agent reaches acceptance on all ten tasks after a median of 34.5 sessions per task (range 12–132; 506 total), with median failed vetoes per session falling from 8.0 (first session) to 2.6 (last five before acceptance). Scale: standard benchmark scale, not stress-scale; all tasks are U.S. equity. Novelty Classification: NEW BENCHMARK/NEW PROBLEM formulation: the genuinely novel contributions are (1) the first evaluation setting that keeps intent, data, and timeline simultaneously open for financial agents, and (2) reference-free, program-verified grading of an executed deliverable (independent recomputation from the trade log, point-in-time vetoes on agent-built backtests) with a grammar-based renewable task generator. The constituent techniques — LLM user simulators (τ-bench), programmatic verification, Web-based agent environments, leakage-aware backtesting — are each established; the combination, the disclosure-policy formalization, and the veto-gated acceptance rule are what is new. The silent-failure finding (sign-off and LLM-judge grading both count broken deliveries as successes) is a NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING with value beyond finance. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong for a benchmark paper. Ablations of the grading rule exist: the paper recomputes acceptance under three graders (sign-off, LLM-judged vetoes, all vetoes) and shows the choice changes both the pass rate (23% → 11% → 0%) and the agent ranking, with significance tests (Fisher's exact, paired permutation with Holm–Bonferroni correction) and 95% bootstrap CIs over tasks. The simulator decision validator runs on every turn; two failed gradings were rerun. Human validation is real but modest: two paid experts, 60 stratified sessions, one calibration set of 30, independent annotation with discussion-based resolution, κ reported. Every score is stored with evaluator version and scoring-code hash. Code, task generator, evaluator, rubric, and a live leaderboard are released (leaderboard.fincosmos.com.co). Concerns: only 10 tasks and 3 sessions per agent, so CIs are wide and several agent contrasts do not survive correction (e.g., Claude Code vs. bare model, adjusted p = 0.10); the simulator, the LLM judge, and Claude Code share the Claude model family (acknowledged); the single data provider (Financial Modeling Prep) is a potential bottleneck; and two near-catch-all completeness vetoes (3.7, 3.8) fail in 119–120/120 sessions and do not separate agents, which the authors themselves flag — the 0% acceptance headline is partly an artifact of these strict checks, though removing them still yields only 2/150 accepted sessions. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a benchmark system with an executed evaluation campaign). Practical: Yes — agents run in sandboxes on standard cloud/CLI harnesses, and even the learning experiment used API-priced sessions under ~$3 each, so replication is feasible on commercially available hardware. Efficient: Sessions cost 0.89–3.51M tokens and $0.80–$2.24 (API-equivalent), but 70% of agent turns hit the 300-second limit, so wall-clock is the binding cost, and the learning experiment needed up to 132 sessions for one task. Effective: The evidence shows the evaluator does what it claims — it catches silent failures that sign-off and LLM judging miss, and the learning loop works — but whether program checks prove figures are real is limited by what the agent chooses to deliver (the authors admit programs cannot prove every figure is genuine). Scalable: Untested beyond ten tasks and U.S. long-only equity; the grammar's ~3.8M strategy space suggests task renewal is feasible, but grader reliability at 10× the session count, other asset classes, and adversarial leaderboard users are only claimed, not measured. The work delivers a software artifact: released benchmark, generator, evaluator, and a live leaderboard with leak-free feedback; whether the harness itself is fully open-sourced is not stated in the text beyond the leaderboard URL. Strengths: - The acceptance rule is anchored in program-verifiable invariants (point-in-time row checks, signal-before-fill ordering, independent recomputation of every reported metric within fixed tolerances), which removes the reference-answer dependence that makes most interactive-agent benchmarks gameable and stale. - The silent-failure analysis is a genuinely valuable empirical result: it quantifies precisely how much grading-by-satisfaction (23%) and grading-by-LLM-judge (11%) overcount success relative to program-verified acceptance (0%), and shows the choice of grader reorders the agents — relevant far beyond finance. - The disclosure policy is formalized (Equation 2) and measured rather than assumed: the evaluator extracts S from user turns with a phrase matcher plus LLM check, and elicitation metrics (clarification coverage, assumption rate) are computed from that measurement. - The human validation is well-designed for credibility: annotators independent of the builders, masking of agent names, a staged protocol (simulator fidelity before seeing automatic grades), and failure attribution showing 88% of failures are the agents', not the benchmark's. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: the benchmark freezes only ten tasks with three sessions per agent; the grammar covers only long-only U.S. equity strategies with a fixed-cost model; the simulator, judge, and one evaluated agent come from the same model family (Claude), with program checks and expert annotation limiting but not removing this risk; 70% of turns hit the 300-second cap, so longer turns may change results; program checks cannot prove every figure is real; and feedback scores could leak information about the hidden strategy across attempts, so leaderboard results should come from frozen agents. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section and is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Single data vendor: the Financial Modeling Prep MCP server is the sole sanctioned data channel, so "self-sourced Web data" is really self-sourced from one API; data-provenance and source-diversity dimensions are effectively graded within one vendor's coverage, and results may not transfer to agents using alternative sources. - The learning experiment has no control: 506 practice sessions against the same frozen tasks means the agent could partially memorize task-specific quirks of the evaluator, and the paper offers no held-out-task generalization test of what the memory learned. - Two vetoes (verifier audit 3.7, process completeness 3.8) fail in ~100% of sessions, meaning the 0% headline rests partly on checks no agent can currently pass; the paper handles this honestly (the counterfactual without them gives 2/150 accepted) but the rubric's sensitivity calibration is under-analyzed. - Simulator fidelity is validated on only 60 of 150 sessions by two annotators, and simulator quality is known to shift with the underlying model and with assistant strength (which the related-work section itself cites) — a single simulator-model configuration is a narrow validity check. - No wall-clock or cost-controlled comparison: quality differences between agents are not normalized for tokens or turns, so it is unclear whether Codex's edge over Gemini CLI reflects capability or budget (Codex reads ~3× the tokens of Claude Code). - The 300-second turn limit interacts with the 70% cutoff rate — an unexamined confound for cross-agent comparison, since agents with slower tooling are penalized non-uniformly. Bottom Line: This is the most credible attempt yet to measure whether financial agents can be trusted with real, underspecified work — the program-verified, reference-free grading scheme and the silent-failure quantification alone justify a read by anyone building agentic benchmarks or deploying agents on consequential deliverables, despite the narrow ten-task, single-vendor, single-model-family evaluation.

Screen Before You Add: Reducing Candidate Inference in Model Ensembles

D Mambelli, A Rozza, S Motta · vault.dcog.com · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a certified screening procedure that decides whether a candidate model should join a convex ensemble while querying the candidate on only a subset of the annotated screening set, built on an exact residual-alignment characterization of when the candidate can improve the population-optimal aggregate under squared or multiclass Brier loss. - Why it's important: Continuously released foundation models force practitioners maintaining LLM ensembles to re-screen candidates, and full screening-set inference is wasteful and expensive when the candidate ultimately adds no value — the paper shows every tested model hurts at least one of 15 tasks, so the reject decision is real and frequent. - How it does it: The core move is a projection argument: the candidate improves the population-optimal convex ensemble if and only if its prediction change is positively aligned with the incumbent ensemble's residual, which enables a residual-informed stratified query path and an optimistic quadratic program (joint over unobserved predictions and refitted weights) that certifies safe early rejection. - The good: On two LLM panels (120 and 60 cases over 12 models and 15 task families), certified QP rejection saves 21–23% of candidate calls while maintaining 100% screening accuracy, with QP stopping overhead of only ~0.34% of the avoided inference time, and no incorrect early rejections were observed. - The missing: The certified target is agreement with a full-screening-set refit decision, and that reference itself predicts held-out usefulness only 83–89% of the time, so the paper's certificate guarantees fidelity to a proxy, not to realized gains; LLM panels are small (15 task clusters, 4 purposive new candidates) and posterior rejection lacks any calibration guarantee. - Read it or not: Read it if you maintain model pools or LLM ensembles and need a principled, cost-aware candidate-evaluation protocol with provable rejection safety; skip it if you only need routing or benchmark-subset selection, since it does not address per-input routing and its theory is restricted to convex aggregation under squared/Brier loss.
