Problem & Motivation: Teams operating model ensembles or multi-LLM systems face a recurring screening decision: a new model appears (the paper cites the rapid release cadence of foundation models), and someone must decide whether adding it improves the ensemble. The natural test — fit aggregation weights with and without the candidate on an annotated screening set and compare losses — requires inference from the candidate on the entire screening set. For expensive models this cost is paid even when the candidate adds nothing. The paper shows empirically (Table 1: 12 LLMs, 15 task families) that standalone benchmark scores do not settle the question: the best standalone model (Falcon-H1, 79.98% accuracy) still hurts 3 tasks, and weaker models can help. An oracle that knew held-out outcomes could skip 40.0–93.3% of candidate calls. Prior approaches do not address this exact gap: routing methods select per input, active-testing methods estimate risk from fewer labels but assume labels are the missing quantity, whereas here labels and incumbent predictions are cached and the candidate's outputs are what is missing. Key Idea: Under population-optimal convex aggregation with squared loss, the candidate b improves the optimal incumbent ensemble f_A if and only if the inner product of the incumbent residual r_A = μ − f_A and the candidate direction d_b = b − f*_A is positive (Theorem 1); disagreement orthogonal to the residual cannot help regardless of refitting. This geometric criterion converts the screening question into estimating one scalar alignment statistic from a small number of queried candidate outputs, and the completion-box structure of unobserved predictions supports a convex QP that jointly optimizes over the most favorable unobserved predictions and refitted weights to certify rejection when even the best completion cannot reach the required (1% relative) gain (Theorem 2, with a corollary that this QP rejects earliest among all zero-error rules on the same query path). Methodology: The pipeline has three phases. (1) Population theory: the screening criterion is derived via L2(P_X) projection onto the convex hull of incumbent predictors, using R(f) = E[Var(Y|X)] + ||μ − f||²; the multiclass Brier case reduces to the same geometry on one-hot targets in the probability simplex. An identity c_b = (R(f_A) − R(b) + q_b)/2 connects alignment to standalone quality and disagreement, explaining why standalone scores are insufficient. (2) Query path: before any candidate call, alignment-contribution envelopes [ℓ_i, u_i] are computed from cached residuals and known prediction bounds; rows are sorted into four strata by envelope width and queried with a stabilized (half proportional, half range-based) Neyman-style allocation, executed by a greedy integer scheduler; queried rows get post-stratification weights so the weighted empirical risk is unbiased. (3) Stopping:* at checkpoints (0, every 32, and each budget), an optimistic QP over a completion box — formulated with the perspective substitution t = βv so constraints stay linear — is solved with SLSQP, and rejection is certified only via an explicit solver-independent weak-dual lower bound (Proposition 5) with a floating-point cushion; if no certificate fires by budget B, a weighted refit decides by the 1% relative-gain fallback. A posterior-scenario extension (Bayesian linear model for regression deviations; normal–inverse-gamma models in centered-log-ratio coordinates for LLMs, 512 draws per checkpoint, 99% Clopper–Pearson upper bound below δ) trades the safety guarantee for earlier rejection. Critical design decisions: one-sided rejection only (early acceptance is a max–min problem they explicitly decline to solve — well-justified); using the loose coordinate box [0,1]ᴷ instead of the probability simplex for Brier (safe but delays rejection — acknowledged); the equal-mix stabilized allocation (justified by Proposition 3 plus empirical variance diagnostics). Assumptions are stated: unregularized convex aggregation, finite prediction bounds, squared/Brier loss; extension beyond population optimality to finite-sample transfer is handled by a separate held-out split rather than a theory claim. Key Results: Regression: 1,400 cases (35 OpenML-CTR23 datasets × 4 candidate families × 10 seeds, screening sets 129–3,000 rows). Certified QP saves 28.5% of calls at 99.89% screening accuracy (4.5 points beyond the 24.0% from the budget cap alone); posterior scenarios reach 63.4% savings but accuracy drops to 92.73%. LLM panels: unseen-task (120 cases) and unseen-model (60 cases), 192-row screening sets, 12 quantized open-weight LLMs (Qwen3 4B through Apertus 8B). QP saves 21.42–23.03% of calls at 100% screening accuracy versus 11–13% for the alignment-completion certified baseline at equal accuracy; posterior scenarios raise savings to ~36.6–37.2% with under one percentage point accuracy loss (δ = 0.05). Both residual-aware samplers beat uniform sampling at fixed budgets by 2.9–3.3 pp (regression) and 6.5–7.8 pp (LLM) screening accuracy at 64 calls. Held-out agreement of the reference decision with a 1% held-out usefulness label: 89.29% (regression), 85.00% (unseen tasks), 83.33% (unseen models). QP relative overhead 0.34% (break-even 0.286 ms/call vs. 83.45 ms mean Qwen3 inference). Baselines compared: uniform sampling, incumbent-loss stratification, alignment-completion certificate, two-negative stability heuristic — all implemented by the authors; no external active-testing or tinyBenchmarks-style baseline is run on this task. Scale is standard (hundreds of calls), not stress-scale; baselines are purpose-built rather than established external methods. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW METHOD, with a NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING component (the Table 1 demonstration that standalone quality does not predict ensemble value across 12 LLMs). The genuinely new elements are the exact iff residual-alignment characterization of candidate value under weight reoptimization (Theorem 1) and the completion-box optimistic QP that certifies rejection valid under full ensemble refitting (Theorem 2). The supporting machinery is a standard combination of known ideas — Cochran-style stratified allocation, Neyman allocation, safe-screening logic from ℓ1 methods, and Hoeffding-races-style early stopping — which the authors themselves explicitly credit rather than claim as new (Propositions 2–3 are presented as applications of established sampling results). Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough: a row-assignment placebo isolating residual-aware assignment (+4.19 pp in regression, CI excluding zero; LLM intervals cross zero), a proportional-strata control showing most variance reduction comes from unequal allocation (60–64% reduction vs. 1–8% for proportional strata within the same strata), a scalar-mixture baseline, and a standalone-QP reference point. Uncertainty is handled with 10 nested paths per case and 5,000 paired hierarchical bootstrap draws with 95% intervals; the authors honestly flag that LLM intervals rest on only 15 independent task clusters and that the four new candidates are a purposive set, so no population-level family claim is supported. No public code or data URL is printed in the provided text, though Appendix D.6 describes manifests binding configurations, repository revisions, prediction shards, and SHA-256 hashes, and admits that timing logs were not retained in independently reproducible form. Methodological concerns: the certified target is a finite-set refit decision developed and evaluated on the same panels (though held-out evaluation is kept strictly separate from querying, which the authors are careful about); benchmark contamination in LLM pretraining is acknowledged as unremovable; the posterior threshold δ was swept post hoc on the same frozen paths rather than chosen on an independent validation panel; and the LLM certificate uses the loose [0,1] coordinate box rather than the simplex, so its completeness is weaker than the theory could deliver. Overall this is a high-rigor paper with unusually candid internal controls. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS-flavored artifact — a screening policy with measured overhead). - Practical: Yes — the stopping machinery runs on a laptop-class machine (Apple M5 Pro, single-thread BLAS, SLSQP), and the inference side uses quantized GGUF models via llama.cpp. - Efficient: Very — QP overhead is 0.34% of avoided Qwen3 inference time (break-even 0.286 ms vs. 83.45 ms per call, a 292× margin), posterior scenarios ~3.7% (~26.8× margin). - Effective: For the stated target — reproducing the full-screening-set decision — the evidence is strong (100% LLM screening accuracy, zero observed incorrect early rejections); for actually improving held-out performance, the evidence is indirect because the reference decision itself matches held-out usefulness only 83–89% of the time. - Scalable: Not tested beyond ~3,000-row screening sets and 12 models; QP cost is O(I(dm + m³)) per checkpoint, so scaling to very large model pools or multiclass coordinate counts is claimed plausible but not demonstrated, and 10–100× screening sets are unexamined. The work delivers a method with detailed implementation specifications (solver tolerances, dual witnesses, numerical cushions) and provenance manifests, but no public release URL is stated in the provided text, so the software artifact's availability cannot be confirmed. Strengths: - Theorem 1 is a clean, exact, and checkable characterization (an iff, not a heuristic) that also yields the interpretable identity c_b = (R(f*_A) − R(b) + q_b)/2, which directly explains why standalone benchmark scores cannot determine ensemble value — a genuinely useful conceptual contribution beyond the algorithm. - Theorem 2 plus Corollary 1 establish not just safety but completeness/earliest-rejection optimality among zero-error rules on a fixed path, and the implementation certifies via a solver-independent weak-dual bound (Proposition 5) rather than trusting the solver's objective value — a level of numerical-care rigor rarely seen. - The evaluation separates two questions that papers in this space routinely conflate: fidelity to the full-screening-set decision (measured directly, 100% on LLMs) and whether that decision predicts held-out usefulness (measured separately at 83–89%, and honestly reported as not repairable by the certificate). - The mechanism diagnostics (exact design-variance ratios in Table 2, the assignment placebo in Table 9) verify that the proposed allocation's benefit comes from where queries go, not from stratum formation alone — moving the ablation from plausible to demonstrated. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that: certification is one-sided (no safe early acceptance; the max–min acceptance problem is explicitly left open, Appendix C.1); the certificate is conservative because it must consider arbitrarily favorable completions; the posterior extension carries no guarantee on the actual false-rejection rate (the Clopper–Pearson bound controls only simulation error, not model misspecification, and δ was swept post hoc); the coordinate-box QP forgoes simplex constraints, delaying rejection; Proposition 2 shows no fixed nonproportional allocation dominates uniform sampling in general; benchmark contamination cannot be ruled out; 13 of 60 model-panel held-out labels flip on a sensitivity split; the model-family test reuses the task surface from the task-family experiment; and the timing provenance is historical and not independently reproducible. This is a paper that confronts limitations directly rather than minimizing them — a substantial credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The 1% relative-gain threshold (γ = 0.01) is fixed throughout with no sensitivity analysis on the primary screening-accuracy metric; conclusions might differ at 0.1% or 5% thresholds. - No comparison against external sample-efficient evaluation baselines (e.g., tinyBenchmarks-style psychometric subsets or active-testing estimators) adapted to this setting — all baselines are author-built variants of the proposed machinery. - The theory covers unregularized convex aggregation only; practitioners typically use regularized or accuracy-weighted aggregation, and the certificate's safety does not transfer to those settings, a restriction not surfaced as a practical limitation. - LLM panels are small and clustered: 15 task families and only 4 new-family candidates, all purposive; per-candidate savings range from 4.44% to 32.89% (Table/Figures), so headline panel-level averages hide high candidate-level variance that the design cannot attach uncertainty to. - The end-to-end value chain is never closed: the certificate guarantees fidelity to a reference that itself matches held-out usefulness at only 83–89% (useful-candidate recall 75–81% on LLM panels), yet no experiment measures the operational question of whether the screened pipeline's final held-out performance differs from a always-full-evaluation pipeline. - For Brier loss the implementation uses the loose coordinate box rather than the simplex constraints the theory explicitly supports (the paper notes adding them is easy), leaving an untested middle ground between the cheap alignment bound and the implemented QP. Bottom Line: A practitioner maintaining weighted LLM or model ensembles should read this: it supplies the first certified, overhead-negligible protocol for skipping most of the cost of deciding whether a new model earns a place in an ensemble, with unusually honest accounting of what the guarantee does and does not cover — its main caveats (small panels, proxy-target fidelity, convex-aggregation restriction) narrow the scope but do not undercut the core contribution.

Flide: Accelerating Decision Inference with Exact State Forking (31 ▲ )

Bobo Li, Jiajia Song, Hao Fei, Wynne Hsu, Mong Li Lee · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 10 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds Flide, an inference engine for decision models (Jev-style single-token categorical classifiers) that runs a shared state and all of its questions as one flattened token stream, answering queries up to 9.5× faster than vLLM and SGLang while provably reproducing the exact standalone computation of every question. - Why it's important: Decision models are being deployed on every routed request and agent action with strict probability thresholds, and existing generation-oriented engines either waste GPU cycles recomputing shared prefixes or corrupt output probabilities with delimiter tokens — flipping up to 29% of categorical decisions in the authors' measurements. - How it does it: ForkAttention keeps the request tree as GPU-resident metadata over one flat stream: full-attention layers apply a visibility mask (same request, own trunk or branch only), while recurrent Gated DeltaNet layers execute in two calls so each question resumes from the exact recurrent state S_P of its trunk — combined with length-bucketed CUDA graphs keyed on stream length rather than request structure. - The good: The ablation (Table 5) cleanly isolates each component's contribution — removing state forking inflates multi-question QuALITY latency by more than an order of magnitude, removing CUDA graphs adds 8.5× latency on short inputs — and the fidelity evaluation shows Flide stays closest to a float32 reference in total variation distance on every workload. - The missing: All experiments run on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU with models up to 27B parameters; there is no multi-GPU evaluation, no measurement of the checkpoint memory footprint at high concurrency, and the exactness guarantee is proven only in exact arithmetic with floating-point behavior checked empirically rather than bounded. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or operate serving infrastructure for classification-style LLM workloads (routing, judging, agent decision gates) — this is the first system to make multi-question prefill-only requests both exact and CUDA-graph-replayable; skip it if you only serve autoregressive generation workloads.

Problem & Motivation: LLM-based decision engines (request routing, response evaluation, agent step selection) emit probability distributions over discrete choices rather than generated text, and are invoked with long shared context (a conversation, an article, an agent trajectory) queried by many short questions. Current serving engines are a poor fit in two ways. First, efficiency: vLLM and SGLang treat each question as an independent sequence, so a request with 18 questions per state (QuALITY) recomputes or re-restores a ~5,800-token state per question; on hybrid architectures, recurrent-state caches restore only at block boundaries, so tokens past the last block are recomputed for every question. Second, correctness: SGLang's multi-item scoring (MIS) appends a delimiter token before each question to share context in one pass, but the delimiter enters every question's input and shifts its output distribution — the authors measure MIS diverging from a float32 reference roughly 12× more than Flide in total variation and flipping up to 29% of thresholded decisions. A third aggravator is floating-point nondeterminism: batch composition changes reduction order, so the same question can receive different answers under different server loads, which matters when thresholds gate downstream actions. Key Idea: Separate the logical structure of a decision request (a tree: shared state trunk, question branches) from its physical execution (one flat token stream), encoding the tree entirely in GPU-resident metadata. The non-obvious move is handling recurrent Gated DeltaNet layers, where a mask cannot isolate sibling branches because a single recurrent state folds all prior tokens: Flide runs each GDN layer in two calls over the stream — first over all state segments to produce each request's S_P, then over all question segments, with each question continuing from its own request's S_P via an index (no copying) — so every branch computes exactly what it would compute alone, within a single forward pass. Methodology: The system has four stages. (1) ForkAttention: a request r = (s, q₁,…,qₙ) is flattened as s⁽¹⁾|s⁽²⁾|…|q₁⁽¹⁾|… with per-token metadata (request index j, branch index c, position t); full-attention layers apply the visibility rule j_y=j_x, c_y∈{0,c_x}, t_y≤t_x (plus a sliding-window variant), and positional indices continue from P so rotary embeddings match the standalone prompt. GDN layers use the two-call scheme described above; the causal convolution reads predecessors via an index so a question's first tokens see its state's last tokens. (2) Flat-graph execution: all round-composition variables (segment lengths, positional indices, key ranges, state indices) live in device buffers, so captured CUDA graphs are indexed only by stream capacity T and a small family of graphs serves arbitrary request mixes; padding occurs only at the stream tail. (3) Selective readout: the final layer's MLP runs only at each question's last-token row. (4) Incremental state forking: float32 GDN states and convolution windows are checkpointed at an internal position m during the same pass, with attention KV stored before m, letting growing agent histories resume without recomputation. Correctness is stated as Proposition 1 (each question's hidden states equal its standalone computation in exact arithmetic) proved by induction over layers. An optional batch-invariant mode fixes reduction orders for bitwise determinism. Critical design decisions: two-call GDN execution (well-justified — masks provably cannot separate branches in a recurrent state), graphs keyed on stream length rather than request shape (well-justified by the ablation showing over one-third throughput loss without it), and checkpoint placement at m slightly before the state end to exclude mutable trailing tokens (plausible but heuristic; no sensitivity analysis of m placement). Key Results: All experiments on one NVIDIA H200, bfloat16 with CUDA graphs. Models: Qwen3.5 (0.8B–27B) and Gemma 4 (E2B–31B). Workloads: RACE, QuALITY, MultiRC, and a 679-request Decision Index sample, spanning 1 to 47.6 questions per state (mean). Baselines: current major releases of vLLM (0.32.x) and SGLang (0.5.21) via decision endpoints, SGLang MIS, and vllm-jev with its RadixFlow scheduler on dedicated Open-Jev models. Headlines: up to 9.5× lower latency and 8.5× higher throughput than the best baseline on multi-question workloads; 12.7× over vLLM at 64 questions on one ~2,000-token state; 4.4–7.2× the steps/second of the strongest baseline on replayed SWE-agent trajectories (states up to 16k+ tokens), with marginal per-step cost of ~1 ms per 1,000 history tokens. Even with one question per state, single-request latency drops up to 3.2× on Qwen3.5-0.8B, attributed to the flat-graph replay versus heavier generation front ends. Fidelity: Flide's top answer agrees with a float32 reference most often on every workload averaged over model sizes, flipping at most 2.3% of decisions versus up to 29% for MIS; stability under 64 clients degrades at most 0.2% (vLLM up to 3.2%). Bitwise-invariant mode costs ≤10% throughput versus the 34% reported for SGLang's batch-invariant kernels. Against vllm-jev on Open-Jev models, roughly 3× speedup on short inputs and up to 1.7× on long prompts. The workload scale is standard (sub-thousands of requests per workload), not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL with a NEW METHOD component. The genuinely novel elements are (a) exact state forking of recurrent Gated DeltaNet layers within a single forward pass — prior hybrid serving (Marconi, RadixFlow) materializes recurrent states only at block boundaries or in a separate prefill phase — and (b) CUDA-graph replay over variable request trees via graphs indexed on stream length with all structure in GPU metadata. Tree attention masks and prefix caching are existing ideas; the combination applied to prefill-only, multi-question decision workloads, plus the checkpoint-resume mechanism for growing agent states, is the new contribution. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong. An ablation (Table 5) removes each of the four components on Qwen3.5-4B and shows each contributes a distinct, quantified cost. Proposition 1 comes with a proof (Appendix A), and a test ladder (Appendix G) checks kernels against a PyTorch reference and full forwards against a float64 reference on every engine change. Latency is reported as medians with P99 tails across concurrency levels 1–64. No error bars, seed counts, or significance tests are reported for the throughput comparisons, though the workload descriptions specify repeated sends (four times, twice for some workloads). The batch-invariant mode's cost is measured (≤10%), not merely claimed. Code is released at https://github.com/OmniJev/flide with a project page at https://flide.org; workloads are built from public datasets with fixed seeds and construction scripts in the release. Methodological concerns: (1) the MIS baseline runs without CUDA graphs and CPU-side GDN metadata — partly inherent to the approach but inflating the gap; (2) the authors tuned the vLLM comparison across two builds and report the faster, which is fair but shows the baselines needed care; (3) the "exactness" claim is proven only in exact arithmetic, with floating-point conformance enforced by empirical tests rather than analysis. Baselines are current and reasonably strong; a tree-attention system like DeFT is cited but not directly compared. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a built engine, evaluated by benchmark deployment on real hardware). - Practical: Runs on a single commercially available NVIDIA H200 with open-source code and shipped pre-compiled Triton kernel bundles (server start ~35 s versus 181 s without the bundle), so deployment friction is low. - Efficient: At 64 clients on the Decision Index, Flide converts 71–91% GPU busy time into 68k useful tokens/s versus 32–46k for vLLM/SGLang, and peaks at 18.8 GiB (versus 131.7–135.3 GiB for the defaults) — though the memory comparison is partly an artifact of KV-cache sizing settings, which the authors acknowledge by capping baselines at 10% of the card and showing the lead holds. - Effective: The evidence covers both the efficiency target (speedups across six workloads, four datasets, ten model sizes) and the correctness target (TV distance to a float32 reference, decision flip rates, bitwise tests on 626 questions), so the system demonstrably solves the stated problem, not just a proxy. - Scalable: Only claimed beyond one GPU — the paper tests up to 27B/31B models on one card and 64 concurrent clients; multi-GPU tensor parallelism, very large context states exceeding a graph's capacity (handled by splitting across replays, unquantified in cost), and heterogeneous request loads are untested. The work delivers a concrete software artifact (an open-source serving engine with HTTP front ends, decision endpoints, multimodal state support, and a listed roster of ~27 supported third-party decision models), not merely a paper. Strengths: - The two-call Gated DeltaNet forking scheme is a real technical contribution: it achieves token-exact branch isolation in recurrent layers where masking is impossible, which no published hybrid serving system does within a single pass. - Encoding request-tree structure purely in GPU-resident metadata so that length-bucketed CUDA graphs replay arbitrary request mixes is a clean solution to the shape-variability problem that typically forces eager execution or padding for structured workloads. - The evaluation distinguishes the two failure modes of prior engines independently — throughput (Tables 3, 6) and probability fidelity (Tables 4, 11, Figure 4) — and the delimiter-perturbation analysis (MIS shifting TV distance ~12× and flipping up to 29% of decisions) is a genuinely useful empirical finding for anyone using multi-item scoring in production. - The correctness test ladder (kernel-level, float64-referenced forward, bitwise checks on every change) is unusually disciplined for a systems paper and substantiates the exactness claims beyond the proof alone. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that exactness holds only in exact arithmetic, with floating-point differences held to rounding level and verified by tests rather than proven; that a round exceeding the largest graph's capacity splits along request boundaries (with an individual oversized request falling back to non-graph execution); that the bitwise-invariant mode costs up to 10% throughput; and that the checkpoint position m is placed heuristically "slightly before the end of a state" to dodge mutable trailing tokens. They confront limitations directly where they exist — notably measuring and publishing the invariant mode's cost and the memory settings behind the baseline peak-memory comparison — which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Single-GPU evaluation only; nothing measures behavior under tensor or pipeline parallelism, which is how models at and above this size are typically deployed. - No sensitivity analysis of checkpoint placement m; the heuristic could interact badly with conversation templates that mutate early state tokens. - The comparison against MIS reports it without CUDA graphs; a variant with graphs for the dense parts (even if the GDN branch metadata stays CPU-side) would sharpen the attribution of MIS's latency penalty to the delimiter versus the execution mode. - The exactness proposition assumes the state "never attends to a question" (strictly causal); bidirectional or two-way-reading backbones are handled by per-model workarounds in Appendix H (some falling back to per-question sequences), which limits the generality of the core guarantee — the paper mentions this only in passing in the model table. - Throughput comparisons lack variance estimates or seed-level reporting; medians over repeated sends mitigate this, but no confidence intervals are given. - The paper does not report end-to-end cost of the checkpoint memory (float32 states per checkpoint per layer) at high concurrency — a potential memory-pressure point for long agent histories that is not quantified. Bottom Line: A practitioner serving classification-gated LLM decisions — routing, judging, agent control — gains something concrete and immediately usable here, since Flide is the first open engine that makes multi-question shared-state workloads both an order of magnitude faster and numerically exact, and no published alternative covers that combination.

How Much Training-Inference Mismatch Can On-Policy Distillation Tolerate? (11 ▲ )

Cong Yu, Ziting Wang, Songlin Jiang, Sitong Zhang, Chengliang Chai, Youhe Jiang, Eiko Yoneki, Tuo Shi · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 10 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a measurement methodology — a common mismatch metric (per-token KL in nats/token), an empirical "mismatch budget," and a minutes-long pre-training admission check — that quantifies how much rollout-engine mismatch on-policy distillation (OPD) absorbs before training quality degrades. - Why it's important: Rollout generation consumes up to 76% of each OPD training step, and the standard speedups (FP8/FP4 quantization, asynchronous stale-weight rollouts) silently inject a train–inference gap that collapses RL training; knowing OPD's tolerance lets practitioners buy memory and speed without destabilizing post-training. - How it does it: It expresses every mismatch source (numerics, quantization, staleness, injected weight noise) on one KL scale, brackets the failure transition with pre-registered pass/fail training runs, and screens new engines by re-scoring a handful of their tokens under the standard BF16 engine. - The good: The headline result is clean and quantified: on a 7B student, OPD preserves quality at mismatch levels over 200× the standard engine's (passing ≤ 0.184 nats/token, failing ≈ 0.39), while REINFORCE and GRPO break at ~12× and ~60× under the same engines — and all eight pre-registered admission-check predictions matched observed training outcomes. - The missing: The budget bracket is calibrated for one 7B student–teacher pair on math with one run per configuration; no run lands inside the bracket, the 1.5B student's budget is never located, and both the mismatch magnitude and its quality impact proved strongly model-dependent, limiting transfer of the numbers. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or operate on-policy post-training systems (RLHF or OPD pipelines choosing rollout precision/asynchrony) — it is the first direct measurement of OPD's mismatch tolerance and yields immediately actionable recipes; skip it if you only consume finished models.

Problem & Motivation: Teams running on-policy distillation pay for rollout generation, which dominates step time (76% on the 7B student), so production systems quantize the rollout engine (FP8/NVFP4 weights, activations, KV cache) and let generation run ahead of training on stale weights. Both speedups mean the student trains on responses sampled from a model that is not exactly itself — the same train–inference mismatch that collapses RL post-training. RL practitioners have developed expensive remedies (bitwise-matched kernels, per-token importance corrections), and recent OPD pipelines import them without evidence that OPD needs them. Prior OPD studies kept the engine fixed or studied staleness alone, so no common scale existed to compare mismatch sources, and checking whether an engine is safe previously required a full 5.5–6-hour training run on eight GPUs. Key Idea: The core move is to put all mismatch sources on one measurable scale — the mean per-token KL divergence between the rollout engine's and the trainer's next-token distributions over the engine's visited prefixes (nats/token) — and then empirically bracket the level at which OPD's training quality degrades (the "mismatch budget"), so that cheap quantization and asynchrony can be treated as a spendable resource against that budget. A secondary insight explains the tolerance: in OPD the advantage vanishes at the teacher regardless of which engine samples, so matching the teacher remains a stationary point under any fixed engine, whereas in RL a constant reward leaves a residual R·δ bias that accumulates. Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) Measurement: at each training step, mismatch d_n is the average of log q(y_t|y_<t) − log p_θ(y_t|y_<t) over the engine's sampled tokens, an estimate of KL(q‖p_θ); a run's level D(c) averages this over 200 steps (standard vLLM BF16 engine: 0.0008 nats/token). (2) Budget characterization: the student is trained with 16+ rollout configurations on the 7B pair — three production quantization recipes (NVIDIA Model Optimizer FP8, emulated NVFP4, vLLM FP8 KV cache), each with and without the first layer's KV cache in BF16; staleness of k ∈ {1,2,4,8} versions via verl's fully asynchronous mode; fixed-direction Gaussian weight noise at four σ levels; and FP8+staleness combinations. Quality is judged by a pre-registered primary rule: relative change Δ(c) in mean held-out KL to the teacher on 530 problems (AIME24 + MATH-500) with a 20% threshold plus a problem-paired bootstrap test; accuracy on AIME24/25/AMC23 is a secondary check. The empirical budget B_emp(τ) is the bracket [max passing D, min failing D]. (3) Admission check: a candidate engine generates 32 responses offline, the standard engine re-scores the same tokens, and the estimate D̂(c) is admitted if α·D̂(c) < L (margin α = 1.5, pilot-derived line L = 0.41 nats/token). The mechanism analysis includes a closed-form gradient probe showing the mismatch-induced gradient bias gz_bias = δ⊙A − p_θ(δ⊤A) vanishes at the teacher, a proof that with fixed engine q the expected OPD gradient equals that of ½E_q[(log p_θ − log p_T)²], and a decomposition of update error into per-token error T (which corrections address) and prefix shift S (which they cannot). Critical design decisions: pre-registration of all pass/fail rules (well justified, unusually rigorous for a systems paper); use of weight noise as a controlled mismatch dial (justified by agreement with quantization results on the common scale); and evaluation of all checkpoints with the standard engine rather than the training engine (sound, avoids confounding). Key Results: On the 7B DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B student with Skywork-OR1-Math-7B teacher: all twelve configurations with D(c) ≤ 0.184 nats/token (>200× the standard engine's 0.0008) pass with held-out KL change between −5.0% and +6.4%; both runs at D ≈ 0.39 fail with Δ ≈ +23%, giving bracket [0.184, 0.39]; every-layer FP8/NVFP4 runs (D = 0.56–0.68) fail with Δ = +54% to +60% and lose 3–5 accuracy points. Staleness up to 8 versions yields only D = 0.0028. Under the same engines, REINFORCE breaks at ~12× and GRPO at ~60× the standard mismatch (REINFORCE lost 21–63 accuracy points; GRPO broke on 2 of 3 engines); score centering rescued both RL methods (+61.0 and +16.5 accuracy points) but did not help OPD. Mismatch is model-dependent: every-layer FP8 on Llama-3.2-3B gives D ≈ 0.01 and passes, while the 1.5B student fails catastrophically at similar nominal mismatch (Δ = +420% to +479%, ~11 accuracy points). The first layer's KV cache accounts for 93–99% of FP8-cache mismatch on the 7B student, with first-layer keys alone carrying 82.5% [73.7, 91.4]. Efficiency: asynchrony raises throughput 1.62× (saturating at k = 4); FP8 KV cache provides ≥1.93× BF16's KV-token capacity; FP8 + k = 8 staleness reaches the synchronous run's final held-out KL 1.62× sooner (3.69 vs 5.98 hours) with final accuracy 60.5% vs 61.5%. The admission check made 8/8 correct pre-registered predictions, screening six configurations in 24 minutes on one GPU. Prefix shift grows 5.3× from passing to failing noise versus 2.1× for per-token error; whole-response reweighting to reach prefix shift would need ~10²⁷ responses per effective sample. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the first quantified tolerance bracket for OPD under train–inference mismatch, and the demonstration that OPD's tolerance profile diverges sharply from RL's) plus a NEW METHOD at modest scale (the admission check — an offline, minutes-cost screening procedure — and the budget-calibration methodology). The individual ingredients are standard: per-token KL divergence, bootstrap significance tests, existing quantization recipes (vLLM FP8 cache, NVIDIA Model Optimizer), and verl's asynchronous mode. The genuine novelty is the unifying mismatch scale that makes bit-width and staleness-version configurations commensurable, plus the empirical bracket and the prefix-shift error decomposition explaining why per-token corrections inherited from RL cannot fix OPD's failure mode. The mechanistic analysis (stationarity of the teacher under any fixed engine; the ½E_q[(log p_θ − log p_T)²] identity) is a competent derivation of previously implicit structure rather than a new theoretical framework. Rigor & Reproducibility: This is among the more rigorous measurement studies one will see in this area. All pass/fail rules, quality thresholds, and admission decisions were pre-registered in dated, append-only plans before the runs they evaluate (App. B), and the authors candidly document every decision made with data in hand (App. B.7), including several post-hoc additions. Statistical treatment is careful: 95% problem-paired bootstrap intervals for all quality verdicts, a sensitivity analysis showing the bracket [0.184, 0.39] is stable for threshold lines from 6.35% to 23.28%. Ablations are present and informative: per-tensor quantization probes isolating first-layer keys, gradient probes, correction ablations, and a fixed-prefix error split. Code is public at https://github.com/benyucong/train-inference-mismatch-opd/. The main weakness is one run per configuration (four configurations run twice, with 1.0–1.5% repeat variation), which the authors flag — verdicts are provisional, and intervals resample problems, not seeds. One secondary concern: the admission line L = 0.41 derived from a pilot proved too high in practice (in-training mismatch exceeded the 1.5× margin at 1.56–1.68×), a self-identified calibration failure the authors handle honestly. A Qwen3-4B experiment was abandoned because plain OPD failed its sanity check on that pair, so model coverage is three pairs from two families. This is a preprint (arXiv 2611.11450), not peer-reviewed. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a measurement study with systems benchmarking on real hardware; no theoretical-only claim). Practical: Yes — all experiments run on commercially available NVIDIA GH200 GPUs with stock vLLM 0.19.1 and verl; the admission check needs one GPU and no teacher or trainer. Efficient: The deliverable itself is an efficiency tool — FP8 rollouts cut generation time (1.27× updates/hour at the training batch) and the FP8 cache yields 1.93× KV capacity, with combined FP8 + staleness reaching quality targets 1.62× sooner; however, real-kernel speedups fell below the authors' own pre-registered 1.15–1.30× thresholds at several batch sizes, and FP8's speed benefit largely vanishes when generation is off the critical path. Effective: The evidence supports the quality-preservation claim within the tested budget on the 7B pair (all in-budget runs finish within 0.5% of the standard run's held-out KL), but the budget is a per-student empirical bracket, not a portable guarantee — the 1.5B student's failure at nominally similar mismatch proves this. Scalability: Untested beyond 7B students, 200 training steps, and 8 GPUs; the authors claim no scaling and correctly decline to. The work delivers a concrete software artifact (code for engines, offline estimation, probes, and evaluation) plus a reusable calibration procedure; pre-registered plans and logs are promised after review. Strengths: (1) A genuinely useful reframing: treating mismatch as a spendable budget measured on a common KL scale converts an intractable engineering question ("is this engine safe?") into a two-number bracket and a cheap screening test, with the admission check's 8/8 pre-registered prediction record as direct validation. (2) The OPD-vs-RL contrast is well designed and consequential — REINFORCE breaking at ~12× while OPD passes at >200× under identical engines, with the mechanism traced to the advantage structure, gives practitioners a principled reason to drop expensive RL-style corrections from OPD pipelines. (3) The localization finding (first-layer KV cache keys carrying 93–99% of FP8-cache mismatch, explained via key-projection bias and missing QK normalization) is a concrete, actionable, and mechanistically explained result. (4) Methodological hygiene exceeds field norms: pre-registered rules, honest documentation of data-informed decisions, threshold sensitivity analysis, and a self-reported pilot calibration failure. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The limitations appendix is thorough and direct (a credibility positive): one run per configuration with provisional verdicts; the budget is specific to the 7B student and quality rule, with the teacher being an RL fine-tune of the student (a far-apart pair may have a smaller budget); the 1.5B budget never located and the Llama evaluation insensitive to KL rises below 14–20%; runs capped at 200 steps on GH200; NVFP4 emulated (quality only, no speed numbers); single-run speed and memory benchmarks with the memory credit (5.7%) barely passing its own 5% bar; staleness limit not located (all stale runs ≤ 0.005 nats/token); GRPO and REINFORCE never passed the learning test, so RL is compared on failure, not learning gains; and open mechanism questions (why noise at 0.39 fails only by step 200, why corrections and positive offsets behave as they do). Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the acknowledged limits: (1) No run exists inside the budget bracket — the gap between the highest passing (0.184) and lowest failing (0.39) level is untested, so the bracket's width and the shape of the quality-mismatch curve near failure are unknown, and the admission boundary (0.27) sits in this untested region by the authors' own admission. (2) The domain is exclusively math reasoning with a teacher that is a fine-tune of the student — the tolerance result may depend critically on the small student–teacher gap, and no evidence exists for general-instruction, code, or agentic distillation. (3) The RL comparison uses recipes that never demonstrated learning (the learning test was dropped after both methods failed it), so "RL breaks where OPD holds" is established only for failure modes on a weak RL setup at 1.5B–7B scale, not for production RL runs that actually improve. (4) 200 steps is short relative to real post-training runs; the authors note one verdict flipped between steps 100 and 200, and mismatch effects grow late in training (error-to-update ratio 0.93 → 1.88), so longer runs could shift the bracket. (5) The prefix-shift analysis and 10²⁷ effective-sample estimate are population calculations at the untrained student on fixed prefixes; whether S dominates in trained models under quantization (not just injected noise) is only partially explored. (6) Single-seed dynamics: with engine nondeterminism and one rollout seed per configuration, a 20% quality threshold sits only ~13× above the observed 1.5% run-to-run spread in the worst case, so borderline verdicts carry real seed risk. Bottom Line: For anyone operating or designing on-policy post-training infrastructure, this is worth reading in full — it replaces folklore about rollout quantization and asynchrony with a calibrated, pre-registered measurement, its FP8-with-BF16-first-layer recipe and admission check are immediately usable, and although the specific numbers are student-specific, no stronger alternative currently covers this ground.

#8 — Highly Innovative (80)

SafeStart: Mitigating the Overlooked Safety Cost of Active Expert Reduction in MoE LLM Serving

EB Potraghloo, S Shokoufa, S Azizi, A Fayyazi… · arxiv.org · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper shows that expert-reduction methods used to speed up MoE LLM serving (top-k truncation, top-p routing, threshold skipping, layer-wise allocation) silently weaken refusal of harmful requests, and introduces SafeStart, a vLLM patch that runs all experts for the prompt and first 8 generated tokens and a reduced budget afterwards, restoring refusal while keeping most of the speedup. - Why it's important: Serving operators adopt expert reduction as a one-line configuration change validated only on accuracy benchmarks; this work shows that at a recommended operating point, harmful compliance under a jailbreak rises by up to 18.4 percentage points while MMLU drops by at most 1.8 points, so accuracy-only validation is dangerously misleading for production safety. - How it does it: The core move is a position-dependent expert budget — the empirical discovery that the refusal change arises almost entirely in prefill and the first few generated tokens (92 of 101 safe-to-harmful flips on Qwen1.5-MoE diverge at the first token), so protecting only that opening with full experts recovers refusal at nearly no latency cost, implemented via a fused Triton kernel and sentinel expert IDs in vLLM 0.11.0. - The good: The statistical discipline is exceptional for a safety paper: paired exact McNemar tests with Holm correction, noise-floor reruns (max drift 2.75 pp across 84 comparisons), two automated judges plus blinded human annotation (587 responses, κ=0.933), and a pre-registered held-out analysis of 889 requests fixed before generation. - The missing: The effect is significant at the confirmatory operating point on only 3 of 9 models; SafeStart fails its own pre-registered non-inferiority test on DeepSeek-V2-Lite on the held-out set (+2.6 pp, 90% CI upper bound 4.37 pp above the +3 pp margin), and templates that dictate the opening words bypass the defense (+12.5 pp residual on Ling-lite under prefix injection). - Read it or not: Read it if you deploy or build inference-time optimizations for MoE models — it is a directly actionable negative result plus a practical fix; skip it if you work on training-time alignment or do not touch serving systems, since the scope is confined to inference-time expert reduction on models up to 57B parameters.

Problem & Motivation: Operators serving open-weight MoE LLMs (Qwen, DeepSeek, OLMoE, GPT-OSS, etc.) increasingly enable expert-reduction methods — uniform top-k truncation in vLLM and llama.cpp, dynamic per-token skipping, top-p routing, batch-level expert sharing — because a prior study recommends keeping roughly two-thirds of selected experts for 1.2–1.7× decode throughput. These methods are validated on accuracy, perplexity, or reasoning benchmarks. Prior work on MoE safety studied experts deliberately removed or steered for their link to refusal, and separate work showed KV-cache compression and speculative decoding can also degrade safety, but no prior work tests reduction at its published operating points for refusal inside a real serving engine, locates where the refusal change arises, and repairs it there while retaining the speedup. The threat model is realistic: a user without weight, routing, or configuration access submits harmful requests (optionally jailbreak-wrapped) to a model served with an accuracy-validated reduction enabled. Key Idea: The key insight is temporal localization: the safety-relevant computation is concentrated in the prompt and the first generated tokens, so expert reduction applied uniformly across all positions pays its safety cost entirely at the start while buying speed mostly later. Therefore, run the full expert budget only for prefill and the first N=8 generated tokens and the reduced budget for everything after — the opening decides refusal, the long tail decides latency. A supporting mechanistic finding is that truncation shifts the final prompt token's hidden state along the refusal direction (in the sense of Arditi et al. 2024) toward the harmless side, and that both lost expert identity and lost gate mass contribute, in model-dependent proportions. Methodology: The paper runs a paired evaluation in vLLM 0.11.0 on one RTX A6000 across nine MoE models (1.3B–57B active params), 472 harmful prompts (HarmBench test split + StrongREJECT) in three framings (plain, refusal suppression, prefix injection) plus two robustness templates, greedy decoding. Each modified condition is compared prompt-by-prompt against the unmodified model; ASR is the share of responses labeled harmful by Llama Guard 3 (HarmBench classifier as second judge, two blinded human annotators on 587 stratified responses), analyzed with exact McNemar tests, Tango intervals, Holm correction over a confirmatory family (7 models × 3 framings at k′=⌈2k/3⌉), and rerun-based noise floors. Speed is measured as offline decode time at batch sizes 1–256 and online time-per-output-token under Poisson arrivals, with the speedup explained by counting distinct expert weight reads per decode step (profiled kernel times predict GPU time saved within 2.4 points). SafeStart is a ~160-line Python/Triton runtime patch: (1) a GPU buffer marks tokens at position ≥ P−1+N read by captured CUDA graphs; (2) a fused Triton kernel per MoE layer replaces out-of-budget slots with a sentinel expert of weight zero for marked tokens, supporting top-k′, top-p, and threshold rules; (3) vLLM's expert map routes the sentinel to −1 so the grouped GEMM skips those weights. The rule depends on output position, staying correct under preemption and prefix-cache hits. Critical design decisions: N=8 chosen from evaluation-prompt sweeps then confirmed on held-out data (N=1 already removes the increase on evaluation prompts but removes only 81% vs. 90% held-out); giving up truncation's prefill saving (TTFT within 1% of original); gate-mass vs. expert-identity decomposition via controlled ablations (mass-restored, attenuation-only, swap). All choices are well justified with explicit statistics, though the confirmatory family and ±3 pp equivalence margin were fixed only after the first two models ran — disclosed by the authors. Key Results: At the confirmatory point k′=⌈2k/3⌉ under refusal suppression: truncation decode speedup is 15–28% at batch size 8 on six timed models but at most 5% at batch size 128 on four of them, because at larger batches the GPU reads nearly all expert weights anyway. ASR rises significantly (Holm-adjusted) on three models: +18.4 pp on Qwen1.5-MoE (46.6→65.0%; human labels +13.6 pp for clearly harmful, +17.0 pp counting partial), +9.5 pp on OLMoE, +6.6 pp on DeepSeek-V2-Lite; MMLU drops ≤1.8 points and GSM8K ≤3.5. Top-p routing raises ASR by up to +30.1 pp (Qwen1.5); threshold skipping does not rise significantly at matched budget. Removing half the experts raises ASR by up to +36.0 pp (OLMoE). SafeStart (N=8) brings the change to −0.6/+0.6/+1.3 pp on the three affected models (each significantly below truncation, p<0.005), keeps 85–104% of truncation's offline decode speedup at batch sizes 8 and 32, and at half the experts decodes 38–44% faster than the original at batch size 8 while scoring 3.6–3.9 GSM8K points above truncation. On the pre-registered 889-request held-out set, truncation raises ASR by 5.8–21.4 pp and SafeStart leaves 0.6–2.6 pp, non-inferior at the +3 pp margin on two of three models. The overhead of the patch with no experts removed is ≤1.9% offline and ≤2.4% online (median time per output token). Convergent evidence on reimplemented LExI (layer-wise allocation) and ACE (per-token skipping): SafeStart moves ASR toward the original model in every reported configuration (e.g., LExI on DeepSeek-V2-Lite 67.0%→53.3% vs. 51.3% original). A control (Qwen1.5 4-bit GPTQ checkpoint losing more accuracy) shows the safety regression is not a generic accuracy artifact. Baselines are current methods at their own recommended operating points; scale is single-GPU standard scale, not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (expert reduction at accuracy-validated operating points degrades refusal in a model-, template-, and method-dependent way, invisible to accuracy and over-refusal tests) + NEW METHOD and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (SafeStart, a position-dependent expert budget implemented as a vLLM engine patch with a fused budget kernel). The genuinely novel elements are the paired, noise-calibrated audit across nine models and the temporal localization of the refusal change to prefill plus first tokens, with the refusal-direction mediation analysis. The mitigation itself — spend more compute where it matters — is a straightforward consequence of that localization; the engineering (sentinel experts through vLLM's expert map, CUDA-graph-compatible masking) is competent execution of known serving techniques rather than a new algorithmic idea. Rigor & Reproducibility: This is among the more statistically careful papers in the LLM-safety genre: paired exact McNemar tests with pre-specified Holm correction, Tango intervals, a ±3 pp equivalence margin, four shuffled-order reruns establishing a 2.75 pp noise floor, label-churn analysis showing zero net change can hide real churn, two judges with quantified sensitivity/specificity against human labels (Llama Guard 3 specificity only ~66% — honestly reported), 587 human-labeled responses at κ=0.933, two held-out models added after the test family was fixed, and a second held-out set of 889 requests with the analysis script SHA-256-hashed and dated before generation. Ablations are extensive (gate-mass controls, protection-length sweep N∈{0..64}, emulation vs. engine, batch-size bound B). Not yet released: the paper promises public release of the harness, patch, prompt identifiers, labels, and hashes ("will release"), with raw outputs on request only; no repo URL is given in the text. Concerns: the confirmatory family and margin were fixed after two models had run (disclosed, with the restricted five-model analysis reported); the primary judge counts partial answers as harmful (mitigated by human verification); all timing is on one A6000 where vLLM has no tuned fused-MoE config, so absolute speedups may differ on production hardware; several headline settings are exploratory rather than confirmatory. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL with a SYSTEMS artifact (a built, measured vLLM patch). - Practical: Yes — runs on a single 48 GB RTX A6000 with vLLM 0.11.0 and ~160 lines of patch code, no extra model or second pass, though not yet tested with quantized MoE kernels or expert parallelism. - Efficient: Keeps ≥85% of truncation's offline decode speedup at batch sizes 8–32 and 38–44% absolute speedup at half the experts; patch overhead ≤2.4% online with nothing truncated; but only 60–65% of truncation's online gain is kept on Qwen1.5 (partly because truncation shortens answers, inflating its apparent gain). - Effective: It demonstrably restores refusal at the tested budgets on the three affected models (residual −2.1 to +2.6 pp), but fails non-inferiority on DeepSeek-V2-Lite held-out and is bypassed by opening-dictating templates, so it solves the measured problem for non-adaptive attacks only. - Scalable: Tested to batch 256 and 57B parameters; truncation's benefit itself collapses at batch 128 (≤3.9% of decode time), so the patch disables itself above a configurable bound; multi-GPU, expert-parallel, multi-turn (prefix-cache key interaction), and larger-model behavior are claimed-needing-future-work, not measured. Delivers a software artifact (vLLM runtime patch with fused Triton kernel, evaluation harness) plus a reusable audit methodology; release is promised but not confirmed in the text. Strengths: - A genuinely important negative result with practical stakes: a configuration change operators can make in one line (vLLM's `num_experts_per_tok`) silently raises attack success rate by up to 18.4 pp while every standard validation metric stays flat — and the paper shows the effect is not explained by generic accuracy loss (GPTQ control) nor visible on XSTest over-refusal. - The temporal-localization finding is a real, transferable insight: divergence analysis (92/101 flips at token 1), early-truncation and SafeStart-N=1 interventions, and refusal-direction mediation together establish where and why refusal breaks, not just that it breaks. - Statistical hygiene far above field norms: paired designs, pre-specified test families, noise floors from reruns, judge-error quantification against blinded humans, and a pre-registered held-out analysis — the paper reports its own failed non-inferiority test rather than hiding it. - The speedup is mechanistically explained (expert weight reads predict profiled GPU time saved within 2.4 points), which yields the actionable corollary that reduction only pays at small batch sizes and should be disabled above a bound. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: human labels cover only 587 responses from two models and the primary judge counts partial answers as harmful; opening-dictating or task-displacing templates bypass SafeStart (quantified: +12.5 pp residual on Ling-lite prefix injection) and no adaptive attacks are tested; on held-out DeepSeek-MoE-16B the first token does not carry the increase; models cap at 57B parameters and timings use one A6000 with default kernel settings; the patch is single-turn, excludes quantized MoE kernels and expert parallelism, and multi-turn serving needs the budget in the prefix-cache key; the confirmatory family and equivalence margin were fixed after the first two models ran. They also correctly note Llama Guard 3's low specificity (~66%). This is direct, quantified confrontation with limitations — a strong credibility signal. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Generality is thinner than the abstract implies: only 3 of 9 models show a significant increase at the confirmatory point, and two renormalizing models (Moonlight, Qwen3 at sane budgets) get safer under truncation — the paper gives a gate-mass hypothesis but no predictive model of which models are vulnerable, so a practitioner cannot tell in advance whether their model is at risk without running the audit. - No adaptive threat model: an attacker who knows SafeStart is enabled can shift the harmful content past token N (the distractor-template residual +5.1 pp on Qwen1.5 points this way); the defense protects the model's own opening, which is a fundamental structural limit acknowledged but not stress-tested with a purpose-built attack. - Hardware generality of the speedup claims is unestablished: vLLM reports no tuned fused-MoE configuration for the A6000, so the 15–28% decode gains (and SafeStart's retained share) could shift materially on H100/production fleet hardware where expert kernels are better tuned and the memory-bound regime differs. - The LExI and ACE comparisons use author reimplementations/ports on models those methods do not officially support, with LExI's runtime with protection never measured — these are supporting evidence, not validated reproductions of the third-party systems. - Batch-level expert-sharing methods (XShare, Lynx, SERE), explicitly named in the related work and arguably the next deployment wave, are not evaluated at all for safety. - Code is promised, not yet released at this preprint's writing; reproducibility currently rests on the paper's unusually detailed appendix. Bottom Line: Any practitioner enabling expert reduction, expert pruning, or adaptive expert skipping on MoE models in production should read this paper and adopt both its audit (test refusal per model and budget, not accuracy) and its patch pattern, because it is the only work that quantifies, locates, and cheaply repairs this specific safety regression — while remaining aware that the fix is bypassable by opening-manipulating attacks and validated only at single-GPU scale on a minority of affected models.

Problem & Motivation: Operators in regulated industries — a bank under MiFID II, a broker-dealer under FINRA suitability rules, a deployer under EU AI Act Article 50 — need to know whether a specific system satisfies their codified obligations. Existing behavioral benchmarks fix their dimension taxonomy in advance (hallucination, sycophancy, toxicity, over-refusal), which makes them comparable across systems but structurally silent on any particular rulebook, because those obligation sets appear in no benchmark's taxonomy. The authors frame the gap as a missing conditioning rather than a missing dimension. A secondary, related problem the paper foregrounds: once dimensions come from a runtime-supplied policy, conclusions can be moved by the corpus, by which obligations are admitted, and by the judge — so a policy-conditioned instrument owes its users a measured operating characteristic, which the authors argue no concurrent policy-grounded benchmark (MAC-Bench, CompliBench, JourneyBench) reports. Key Idea: Treat the policy corpus as a swappable argument to the metric suite, and make measurement honesty a first-class output: the substantive novelty is not the metrics themselves but a published five-criterion admission test (construct, independence, sensitivity, discrimination, attribution) that each reported quantity must pass — where the attribution criterion (A5) explicitly measures how far a reading moves when the judge changes and labels absolute levels with their panel range. A third design element makes cross-vendor claims interpretable: including target models with no authorship relationship to either specification converts the document-difficulty confound into a measured baseline. Methodology: The pipeline is: (1) corpus construction — 11 public documents across five registers (vendor specification, conduct regulation, analytical guidance, AI-transparency statute, acceptable-use policy) yield 1,003 extracted obligations with verbatim spans; severity is read from modal verbs (HARD from must/shall, SOFT from should; weights 5.0/1.5, swept exhaustively since the parameter space is one-dimensional); (2) bindability funnel — three judges from three providers decide whether an AI system could comply/violate an obligation in a single response or tool call: 1,003 → 489 majority-bindable → 309 unanimous → 260 high-confidence → 231 non-mixed; 401 majority-bindable rules survive a scope exclusion (88 rules withheld for requiring prohibited content), of which 397 enter the frozen probe set; (3) probe generation — k=4 probes per rule in fixed order (direct, scenario, boundary, adversarial), sha256-hashed and frozen so every target answers the identical exam; (4) scoring — a pinned judge (claude-opus-4-5) returns COMPLIANT/MARGINAL/VIOLATION/NA (0/0.5/1/excluded) per probe; CAS = 1 − Σwᵢv̄ᵢ/Σwᵢ; CRMΔ = CAS(L0) − CAS(L3) with a break-point distribution; (5) validation — a 60-item blinded calibration against one domain expert measures admission precision and extraction fidelity, and 2,672 stored records are re-scored under two swap judges (Gemini and GPT-family) with zero target re-queries, enabled by retaining the rendered judge prompt and raw response for every record. Critical design decisions: severity from modal verbs (crude but auditable; ordering invariant through 7× weight ratio); probe set frozen once (enables attribution re-scoring and identical exams); profile reporting rather than a scalar composite (justified by A2 independence plus a 10,000-vector weight sweep showing invariant ordering). All decisions are explicitly justified, mostly quantitatively. Key Results: Across 397 probed rules and 8 target models from 4 providers: (1) admission precision is 94.4% (vendor specification), 66.7% (conduct regulation), 50.0% (analytical guidance) against blinded human judgment; extraction fidelity is 94.6% on 56 span-bearing items; (2) judge-swap: a single target's absolute CAS spans up to 0.216 across three judges (Gemma 2 9B), but ordering is invariant (Kendall τ = +1.000 between swap judges, +0.905 vs primary; the one inversion separates targets 0.02 apart); (3) headline finding — GPT-4o violates 70.7% of the hard constraints binding it in OpenAI's own Model Spec at the rule level (36.2% at probe level, 58/160), vs 0.0% (Haiku) and 9.1% (Sonnet) of their Constitution's hard constraints; the asymmetry holds under all three judges (GPT-4o: 22.5–42.5%); (4) own-specification advantage is not resolved from zero (+3.8/+2.5/−2.7 points against the no-relationship arm mean, all intervals containing zero); GPT-4o scores 12.3 points higher on Anthropic's Constitution than on its own vendor's spec — the same margin as Llama 3.1 8B, which has no stake in either — so apparent self-privileging is document difficulty; (5) age control: gpt-5.5 (postdating the Model Spec) still violates 31.7% of its own vendor's hard constraints vs 22.0–23.2% for unaffiliated models, closing only half the gap; (6) CRM separates targets CAS does not: GPT-4o degrades 0.213 under adversarial framing while the Claude models are flat (−0.007/−0.029); (7) register effects are large: within-target CAS spread up to 24.7 points (GPT-4o: 0.708 vendor spec vs 0.461 statute) and compliance does not track capability rankings (compact Haiku beats frontier GPT-4o and Gemini Flash by 14–18 points on the Model Spec). The admission-rate result — vendor specifications admit at 68.0% vs 25.4% for conduct regulation, robust to precision correction — is a finding in its own right: vendor-published specs are the densest actionable source of agent-binding obligations. Baselines are the strongest available contemporaneous comparisons (frontier models, frontier judges, a concurrent-work related-work section citing 2026 benchmarks); the evaluation is at standard, not stress, scale (1,588 probe-response pairs per arm, ~4,000 probe-response pairs total across arms). Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW METHOD, with a NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING component. Genuinely novel: taking the policy corpus as a runtime argument (structural customizability rather than a claim), the metric admission test with measured attribution, and the first measurement of frontier models against the behavioral specifications their own vendors publish, with a no-relationship difficulty-baseline design. The individual components — LLM-as-judge, structured behavioral probes (CheckList-style), multi-judge panels, bootstrap intervals — are standard techniques competently combined in a new setting; the paper says so itself. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and unusually honest: severity-weight sweep (ordering invariant through 7×, first inversions only at 10–20× on overlapping intervals), conservative-set re-computation on the 231-rule non-mixed funnel stage, judge-panel swap over 2,672 records, pre-stated hypotheses (admission rates and cross-vendor hypotheses written into analysis code before runs, though the authors candidly state these are not timestamped registrations). Confidence intervals (Wilson and paired bootstrap over rules) and a Fisher exact test (p = 0.008) are reported; temperature 0 with pinned decoding substitutes for multi-seed variance, and the authors state this choice explicitly. The artifact is publicly released (Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22064759, per-file SHA-256 manifest) and every reported quantity is recomputable from stored records without querying a target — a strong reproducibility property. Methodological concerns: the calibration rests on 60 items from a single annotator (precision estimates, not agreement statistics); the primary judge is an Anthropic model grading Anthropic targets (the self-preference objection is directly tested and found small, ≤0.045 relative movement, but the panel is only three frontier judges); a Gemini 2.5 Pro arm was abandoned after quota exhaustion (rationally excluded, records retained); this is an arXiv preprint accepted to a NeurIPS 2026 workshop, not peer-reviewed in the main track. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a measurement instrument run on commercial API models, plus a released artifact). - Practical: Yes — targets are commercial API models plus two locally run 8–9B models; the pipeline needs a frontier judge and API access, no custom hardware. - Efficient: A full pass costs Nk target calls per target and NkT judge calls (N=397, k=4: 1,588 target probes and ~6,300 judge calls per target); judge calls dominate and judge swaps cost judge calls only, since admission and probe generation are one-time. - Effective: The evidence shows the instrument measures compliance ordering on the retained region of a policy reliably, but absolute levels are judge-dependent (±0.06–0.22) and results are over the criterion's retained region, not the specification in full — a well-quantified proxy, honestly labeled. - Scalable: Not tested at 10× scale; the authors note the corpus is amortized across targets but say nothing about behavior at 10,000+ obligations or in the 10,000-target fleet scenario the discussion gestures at. The work delivers a real software/metric artifact (suite, corpus, frozen probe set, judge records, annotation instrument, analysis scripts) at the stated DOI; BIV's deterministic Tier-A extractor is specified and constructible from the released artifact but not shipped as a measured result. Strengths: - The attribution criterion (A5) with judge-swap re-scoring of stored records is a real methodological contribution: it converts the usual silent LLM-judge dependence into a measured operating characteristic (ordering invariant, level moves up to 0.216), and the paper declines to claim judge-invariance for differenced quantities like CRMΔ where the panel cannot establish it. - The cross-vendor design — using three authorship-unrelated arms to measure document difficulty before subtracting it — is the right experimental logic and yields the sharpest result: apparent own-specification privilege for Claude models and anti-privilege for GPT-4o both collapse once difficulty is removed. - Honest reporting at every seam: an admission test that excluded one of the suite's own quantities (break-point as an independent metric), a measured-and-admitted failure of A5 on absolute levels, qualifier-shedding bias shown to inflate violations in the direction against the authors' convenience, and pre-stated predictions that missed (Article 50 admission at 39.3% vs the registered 60–90%) and are reported as a finding rather than dropped. - The register-level admission-rate finding (vendor specs at 68.0% vs regulation at 25.4%, robust to calibration correction, with a mechanistic explanation via descriptive-prose vs statutory-duty phrasing) is a non-obvious empirical result with governance implications independent of the metrics. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly and at length — a credibility positive. Explicitly acknowledged: calibration rests on 60 blinded items from one domain expert (precision is not agreement); admission precision degrades from 94.4% to 50.0% across registers; extraction sheds qualifiers, inflating measured violation (direction stated); absolute CAS fails the A5 level threshold under judge swap (6–15 points on weaker arms, up to 0.216 on Gemma 2 9B); the document-difficulty baseline comes from three arms that do not agree closely; BIV and BDI are specified but not measured; pre-stated predictions are released with a provenance note but are not verifiable timestamped registrations; the panel is three frontier judges from major providers and bounds nothing about other judge types; the Gemini 2.5 Pro arm does not exist (quota exhaustion, error rows retained); results measure base models, not assembled agent systems. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The headline GPT-4o number is a vendor-antagonistic claim measured by a single Anthropic judge; the judge-swap subsample contains only 40 hard-constraint probes for GPT-4o and 27 each for the Claude models, and the authors themselves note the panel-subsample intervals are wide — the claimed 1.9× asymmetry rests on modest cell counts even though it is direction-stable across judges. - Compliance probes are generated by LLMs and scored by LLM judges against LLM-extracted rules; the calibration validates extraction fidelity and admission precision, but there is no human validation that the probes (especially boundary and adversarial framings) faithfully exercise the admitted obligation — the one pipeline stage between the two validated stages that goes unmeasured. - Severity classification from modal verbs is binary and read from the source span; a spec that phrases a hard requirement as "we expect" would be down-weighted to SOFT, and the paper does not measure misclassification of this mapping (the conservative-direction argument covers soft-assignment of ambiguous cases but not systematic misreads). - Temperature 0 gives one sample per probe; response-level nondeterminism under pinned decoding is asserted to be small but never measured (the authors even note they excluded a judge over unpinned-decoding concerns while never reporting the measured decoding instability their setup rationale alludes to). - Small strata undermine several per-register claims: the AUP register has 11 rules and the statute 19, so the 24.7-point register-spread figure and per-register bootstrap intervals for non-vendor registers are thin; the "register uniformity" axis in Figure 4 inherits this. - No comparison against the closest concurrent systems (MAC-Bench, CompliBench) even on shared capability, so the claimed unit-of-analysis advantage (obligation vs trajectory) is argued, not benchmarked. Bottom Line: A practitioner building compliance or audit infrastructure for LLMs should read this — the policy-as-argument interface, the admission test, and the measured judge-sensitivity band are immediately reusable, and the vendor-spec finding matters to anyone relying on published model specifications — with the caveat that the headline cross-vendor numbers are directionally trustworthy but quantitatively fragile, and the whole edifice is LLM-judged end to end, preprint-stage, and unvalidated on probes.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces OPAL-Bench, a threshold-free, polymorph-aware benchmark with species-aware SE(3) alignment and nine geometric and physical distance metrics that re-evaluates 7 CSP and 2 SICSP crystal structure prediction methods as separate tasks, plus OPAL-CSP, an SE(3)-equivariant flow-matching baseline. - Why it's important: Current CSP evaluation relies on tolerance-sensitive metrics (Match Rate) and subset-dependent RMSE that produce contradictory method rankings, penalize correct predictions of unlisted polymorphs, and ignore physical plausibility — so reported progress in generative materials discovery is partly an artifact of the evaluation protocol. - How it does it: Each prediction is scored by its metric-specific minimum distance to all known polymorphs of the same composition, after an alternating Hungarian-assignment/gradient-refinement SE(3) alignment with infinite cost for cross-species matches, and physical metrics (formation energy via a 3-model MLIP ensemble, SOAP, XRD Wasserstein, density) are computed without alignment. - The good: The empirical demonstration that Match Rate rankings flip across 571 tolerance configurations (reversal rates up to 22.1%) and that geometric and physical quality are only weakly correlated (Spearman ρ mostly 0.06–0.44, near zero for density and XRD) are quantified, reproduced across datasets, and directly justify the redesign. - The missing: OPAL-CSP's per-dataset hyperparameters were selected with OPAL-Bench in view while baselines ran at released configurations, and all training used a single seed (42), so the flagship baseline's favorable showing lacks variance controls and symmetric tuning. - Read it or not: Anyone training or reviewing generative crystal structure models should adopt or at least read this, since it changes which comparisons are legitimate; readers outside CSP can skip it.
