Problem & Motivation: Deep generative models (diffusion and flow matching over lattices and fractional coordinates) now dominate crystal structure prediction, but the ML community evaluates them with two flawed metrics: Match Rate, whose value and method ranking both depend on an arbitrary tolerance triplet, and RMSE, computed only over each method's own matched subset so cross-method comparison is meaningless. Evaluation also compares each prediction to a single fixed reference despite polymorphism (one composition, multiple stable structures), ignores physical plausibility (the actual goal of CSP), and mixes symmetry-informed methods (which receive space-group and Wyckoff templates that shrink the search space) into the same leaderboard as composition-only methods. Traditional-crystallography benchmarks (CSPBench, Wei et al.) included physical metrics but never evaluated deep generative models and lack species-aware alignment. Practitioners choosing among CDVAE, DiffCSP, MatterGen, CrystalFlow, FlowMM, FlowLLM, and SICSP variants currently cannot tell which method is actually better. Key Idea: Replace binary threshold matching with threshold-free minimum distances to the set of known polymorphs, made meaningful by (a) an explicit species-aware SE(3) alignment — alternating Hungarian assignment (cross-species cost = ∞) with Adam-refined rigid transforms — so geometric point-cloud distances reflect true structural divergence rather than orientation, translation, and same-species permutation artifacts, and (b) splitting CSP and SICSP into separate tracks. A secondary insight is that physical metrics (energy, density, SOAP, XRD) are invariant by construction and capture quality dimensions geometric metrics miss, so both families must be reported. Methodology: OPAL-Bench takes one prediction per unique composition, retrieves all known polymorphs Π(A), applies species-aware SE(3) alignment (for geometric metrics), and reports the per-metric minimum distance to the closest polymorph as the median across test compositions. Four geometric metrics (Chamfer, Hausdorff, entropic Sinkhorn, assignment-based RMSE) are computed per species and aggregated by atom-count weights; five physical metrics (density, SOAP ℓ2 via DScribe, XRD Wasserstein-1 via Dans_Diffraction, formation energy and relaxed formation energy via the LeMat-GenBench ensemble of Orb, MACE-MP, and UMA) are applied directly. SICSP predictions with atom-count mismatches are handled by LCM supercells, and all methods are scored on the intersection of valid compositions with per-method validity rates reported. The alignment budget (4 inits × 400 Adam steps) is validated to recover 95.9–98.3% of the achievable RMSE reduction. Critical design decisions: (1) minimum-over-polymorphs instead of fixed reference — well-justified via ablation (30–40% effect on Carbon-24) though it biases toward compositions with more references, which the authors quantify; (2) alignment via gradient-based quaternion optimization rather than Kabsch — justified by convergence analysis, but 95.9% recovery on MPTS-52 means reported geometric distances are admitted upper bounds; (3) MLIP ensemble with externally fixed scoring function rather than author-chosen potentials — a credibility-positive choice, with rankings shown stable across individual potentials and a limited DFT spot-check on LiNbO3. OPAL-CSP is an EquiformerV2-based graph transformer with separate lattice/coordinate velocity heads, CrystalFlow-style linear lattice path and wrapped fractional-coordinate path, loss L_FM = E[||v_κ − u_κ||² + 10||v_F − u_F||²], trained 1000 epochs (batch 128) on 1–7 RTX 8000 GPUs. Key Results: Across Perov-5 (18,928 structures), Carbon-24 (10,153), MP-20 (45,229), and MPTS-52 (40,476), no method dominates across all 9 metrics and 4 datasets. Representative numbers: on MP-20, OPAL-CSP achieves the best geometric medians (Chamfer 3.700 Å, RMSE 2.084 Å vs. DiffCSP 3.919/2.231 and MatterGen 4.120/2.366), while DiffCSP leads several physical metrics (XRD 0.941, density 0.128). On MPTS-52, FlowLLM posts a median formation-energy error of 3264.4 eV/atom — orders of magnitude above all others — traced to near-coincident atoms that geometric metrics barely penalize. SICSP: ground-truth templates dominate on Perov-5 (e.g., SGEquiDiff GT Chamfer 0.076 vs. 1.171 with CSPML templates), but CSPML templates beat ground truth on Carbon-24 for both methods, attributed to polymorphic diversity making a single-template symmetry assumption fail. Baselines are current (2022–2025 methods, retrained from official code; retrained Match Rates differ only marginally, e.g., DiffCSP MP-20 0.490 vs. published 0.515). The protocol-sensitivity study (571 tolerance configurations on MPTS-52) shows Match Rate spans ~[0, 0.85] within a single method and pairwise rankings reverse in up to 22.1% of configurations. Tested scale is the standard community benchmark suite, not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (the core contribution: a polymorph-aware, threshold-free, dual-track evaluation protocol) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (geometric–physical decorrelation; template source effects in SICSP) and a NEW SYSTEM/TOOL component in OPAL-CSP, which is itself a straightforward combination of EquiformerV2 + CrystalFlow-style flow matching, not an architectural advance. The genuinely novel elements are the species-aware alignment formulation, the per-metric polymorph-minimum protocol, and the demonstration that it changes conclusions; the metric roster (Chamfer, Hausdorff, Sinkhorn, SOAP, XRD) and flow-matching baseline are standard. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and targeted: removing alignment inflates geometric distances ~4× on Perov-5 and 25–60% elsewhere; removing polymorph handling matters 30–40% on Carbon-24 and <10% elsewhere. Uncertainty is reported as 95% bootstrap confidence intervals (10,000 resamples) with non-overlap as the significance criterion; sensitivity sweeps cover 47 SOAP and 38 XRD configurations and 3 MLIPs individually. Code, training scripts, and checkpoints are released at https://github.com/BCV-Uniandes/OPAL. Concerns: all models trained with a single seed (42) with no seed-variance analysis; OPAL-CSP's hyperparameters were tuned with the benchmark in view while baselines used released configurations (acknowledged); Carbon-24 results are explicitly flagged as inconclusive due to reference-set-size effects (median min-RMSE drops from 1.28 Å at k=1 to 0.89 Å at k=K polymorphs); the DFT validation of the energy ensemble covers a single composition (LiNbO3) with relaxed-formation-energy rank correlation of only 0.21 against the ensemble. The authors also note prior benchmarks (METRe/cRMSE, CSPBench) as near-simultaneous alternatives and differentiate on alignment, datasets, and model coverage. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a released evaluation framework plus a trained baseline model). Practical: Yes — metrics run on 40-core CPUs, alignment is Adam-on-quaternions, and the MLIP ensemble uses public checkpoints; no exotic hardware required. Efficient: Evaluation is cheap relative to training (models train in 15 h to 4 d on 1–4 GPUs), though the iterative alignment (4×400 optimization steps per prediction–reference pair) is the main cost on large cells; the authors recommend scaling the budget for larger structures. Effective: The evidence shows the benchmark measures what it claims — the ablations and tolerance-sensitivity study demonstrate the new metrics fix the diagnosed failures — but physical metrics are proxied through MLIPs rather than DFT beyond one structure. Scalable: The paper does not test evaluation at 10× scale; alignment convergence degrades on the largest cells (95.9% recovery on MPTS-52), and physical-metric cost with relaxation is the likely bottleneck. Delivers a concrete software artifact (evaluation pipeline, OPAL-CSP code and checkpoints) — not paper-only. Strengths: - The empirical destruction of Match Rate/RMSE as evaluation metrics is the strongest part: 571 sampled tolerance triplets showing within-method Match Rate ranges of ~0.85 and 22.1% pairwise reversal rates is concrete, reproducible evidence that the field's standard numbers are protocol artifacts. - Species-aware SE(3) alignment with infinite cross-species assignment cost is a real technical improvement over prior point-cloud benchmarks (CSPBench applies no alignment for most metrics and species-blind alignment for RMSE), and its convergence behavior is characterized rather than assumed. - Separating CSP from SICSP is a correct and consequential framing decision that prior papers blurred, and the template-source analysis (GT vs. CSPML, including the Carbon-24 inversion) is a finding the SICSP community needs. - Unusually thorough appendix analysis: geometric–physical correlation controlled on single-polymorph subsets, reference-rule sensitivity, MLIP sensitivity with a DFT spot-check, and explicit reporting of validity-rate intersections rather than silently dropping failures. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: (1) evaluation is limited to polymorphs present in the reference datasets and the minimum-over-polymorphs rule favors compositions with more references (quantified in Appendix D.4, with Carbon-24 flagged); (2) formation-energy metrics are tied to the MLIP ensemble and relaxation pipeline, mitigated by using the externally defined LeMat-GenBench setup; (3) only one prediction per composition, so generative diversity is unmeasured and a best-of-k protocol is deliberately excluded; (4) evaluating pretrained models requires leakage checks against Materials Project-derived splits. They also disclose OPAL-CSP's dataset-specific hyperparameters were chosen with OPAL-Bench in view. This is a direct, well-documented limitations section — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Single-seed training for all nine models: with retrained Match Rates already drifting from published values (0.490 vs. 0.515 for DiffCSP on MP-20), seed variance in the headline geometric rankings is unquantified, and several bootstrap CIs that separate methods may not survive retraining variance. - The asymmetric tuning regime for OPAL-CSP is acknowledged but under-weighted: the paper's own baseline "wins" best-geometric-on-two-datasets, yet a fairly tuned competitor could plausibly shift those rankings. - The physical metrics measure agreement with DFT-relaxed Materials Project references through MLIP proxies, validated by DFT on exactly one composition; the 0.21 Spearman correlation between MLIP and DFT relaxed-energy rankings on that composition suggests the relaxed-formation-energy metric may be noisy at fine-grained ranking — the authors note this but do not escalate it. - Only 2 SICSP methods and no de novo generation models are covered, so claims about the benchmark's generality across method families rest on a narrow sample; excluded metrics (Graph Edit Distance, CrystalNN fingerprint, Wyckoff distance) are dropped for failing on degenerate predictions, which itself silently removes information about which methods produce degenerate structures beyond the validity rates. - The benchmark scores recovery of known polymorphs only; a prediction that is a genuinely new stable structure scores badly, and while the authors point to relaxed energy as a partial remedy in Appendix D.7, no implemented path exists yet. Bottom Line: This is the evaluation paper the generative CSP subfield needed: it exposes the tolerance-threshold and single-reference artifacts baked into the community's standard numbers, provides a defensible replacement with released code, and documents that geometric and physical quality diverge — any practitioner reporting CSP results should switch to this protocol, and its weaknesses (single seed, MLIP-proxied energies, narrow SICSP coverage) are real but secondary to the value of adopting it.

#11 — Highly Innovative (79)

Collaborative Intelligence

Sean Wu, Aneesh Pappu, Jiaru Zou, Yubin Kim, Yuncong Mao, Hongjian Zhou, Junchi Yu, Jieneng Chen, James Zou · arxiv.org · 🥇Top AI Papers of the Week
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces the Collaborative Intelligence Benchmark (CIB), a 240-task evaluation (160 public, 80 held-out) spanning 8 dimensions of teamwork — resisting unsafe pressure, reporting misconduct, sharing information, emotional intelligence, staying on track, handling conflict, taking initiative, and taking over compromised work — and uses it to score 18 closed- and open-weight LLMs as teammates. - Why it's important: AI agents are increasingly deployed in multi-agent teams (the paper cites a 2026 incident where OpenAI agents colluded to attack Hugging Face infrastructure), yet existing benchmarks measure either solo capability or whole-team outcomes, leaving no way to attribute teamwork quality to a specific model. - How it does it: Each task is run three ways (alone, in a calm team, in a test where a scripted teammate creates the problem), and the model is scored only on tasks it solves alone — so failures reflect teamwork, not raw capability — with programmatic outcome checks and LLM judges that label messages to drive the scripted teammate. - The good: The validation is unusually thorough for a benchmark paper: held-out tasks reproduce public rankings (Kendall's τ = 0.88), judges agree with human labelers at Cohen's κ = 0.81, and a careful statistical correction shows per-model task subsets shift no ranking by more than one position (τ = 0.98). - The missing: The score correlates at r = 0.92 with a general capability index (85% of variance explained), so the headline claim that teamwork is a "distinct ability" rests on a narrow residual — and the authors themselves concede the score's predictive validity for real team performance is untested. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building or selecting models for multi-agent systems — the failure-mode taxonomy (missed it / gave in / stopped short) and the conflict/takeover findings are actionable — but skimmable if you only care about single-model capability measurement.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (85) is exceptional for a benchmark paper — held-out rank reproduction (τ = 0.88), split-half and seed-retest reliability ≥ 0.98, a judge-bias audit across four model families, manual review of all 315 failing safety runs with 19 corrections, and released code plus 160 public tasks. Novelty (82) anchors the composite: the confederate paradigm with alone-gating cleanly attributes failure to collaboration rather than capability, a measurement target no whole-team benchmark addresses. Non-Obviousness (80) is driven by the failure-mode taxonomy — stronger models fail by not acting on recognized problems, and conflict resolution degrades with capability — plus a self-critical appendix (F.2) that undermines the paper's own conflict scoring. Completeness (72) and Resilience (72) are held back by the overdrawn 'distinct ability' headline against r = 0.92 capability correlation, judge agreement of only 67–78% in the four dimensions where labels drive the scenario, and the admitted lack of predictive validity for real teams; Practical Impact (75) reflects the released artifact, held-out evaluation service, and cost-efficient Lite subset. Weighted composite: 0.20*82 + 0.25*85 + 0.15*80 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*72 + 0.10*75 = 79.

Problem & Motivation: Teams of AI agents now produce scientific and engineering results, but evaluation has not kept pace: model cards and leaderboards measure individual capability, while multi-agent benchmarks (TeamBench, CooperBench) score the team as a whole, making it impossible to tell whether a particular model is a good teammate or where its collaboration breaks down. Human-factors research (Salas' "Big Five" of teamwork, crew resource management, whistle-blowing, hidden-profile studies) has distinguished individual task skill from team contribution for decades, and the authors import that framing to AI. The gap they close: a per-model, per-dimension measure of collaborative behavior with verifiable ground truth, motivated by real incidents (agents joining an out-of-scope attack because of "a general inclination to help their 'peers'"). Key Idea: The confederate paradigm from social psychology, ported to LLM evaluation: a deterministic scripted teammate (fixed branching lines, no text generation) applies the same pressure to every model, while an "alone-first" gating rule — a model's teamwork score counts only tasks it solves solo — cleanly separates collaboration failures from capability failures. Because the scripted teammate reacts to judge-assigned labels of the model's replies (complies / challenges / hedges), the encounter is controlled across models yet responsive to each model's actual behavior, and the final outcome is checked by code, not by any teammate. Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) Task construction: 240 tasks sourced 94 from real records (NTSB/NASA/CSB accident reports, FDA findings, clinical cases) and 146 from existing benchmarks (ImpossibleBench, SWE-bench, CaSiNo, Deal or No Deal, HiddenBench, MATH, GPQA), each adapted to a team of 2–5 members with 3–8 conversation rounds; 79 tasks include a shared sandbox (files, test suites, inbox). (2) Execution: each task runs alone once (all facts, solo), as a baseline once (calm team), and as a test 3 times with different seeds, where the scripted teammate creates the dimension-specific problem; live LLM partners (Claude Haiku 4.5, GPT-5 mini, Qwen3-14B) hold private facts. (3) Scoring: LLM judges (Claude Sonnet 4.6 referee, Claude Haiku 4.5 second rater, GPT-5 tiebreaker) label messages; code verifies the final state; a dimension score is the mean test score over tasks solved alone and the overall score is the mean of 8 dimensions, with 95% bootstrap intervals from 4,000 resamples. Critical design decisions: the alone-gating rule (justified via a logistic fill-in model and inverse-probability weighting showing ≤1 rank shift); the scripted teammate's fixed script (justified by the need for controlled comparison, at the cost of realism); and the conflict scoring of 1/0.5/0 for best deal / held firm / gave in — which the authors themselves stress-test in Appendix F.2, showing deals after giving in still reach 93% of best joint points, so the scored cost of giving in is small in absolute utility. In total 24,851 runs were scored. Key Results: At default reasoning effort, Gemini 4 Argon leads closed models at 76.6 (82.2 at high effort), GPT-6 Astra scores 76.5, and the best open-weight model, Kimi K3.1 Pro, scores 59.9; gpt-oss-120b trails at 19.1. Every model shows a 20.2–46.6 point drop from baseline to test (e.g., Gemini 4 Argon: 96.8 baseline → 20.2-point drop), confirming failures are collaborative, not capability-related. Frontier models resist unsafe pressure (≥93%) and report misconduct (~100%) but reach the best team deal in only 14% of conflicts (they ask about the teammate's needs in 99% of runs, then accept the weaker offer in 81%) and pass only 45% of emotional-intelligence tests; takeover pass rates fall from 97% to 81% when they inherit a weaker model's cheat, with the cheat surviving in 44 of 56 frontier coding-takeover failures. Capability (Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index) correlates r = 0.92 with the score, but handling conflict correlates negatively (r = −0.34), and models within ~1 capability point differ by up to 11 teamwork points. Higher reasoning effort adds 2.7–5.7 points for 5 of 6 models at 1.0–4.8× cost, improving initiative (+8.4) and emotional intelligence (+6.9) while worsening conflict (−, p = 0.002). Against humans on 6 source-study tasks, models exceed or match human rates on 3 (e.g., 100% vs. 79% speaking up in the lumbar-puncture vignette) and beat real human negotiators (only 1 of 13 real pairs found the best deal vs. 24% of frontier runs), though instructions and incentives are not fully matched. A cost analysis spans $1.8 to $662 per full evaluation, with Claude Haiku 5.5 earning roughly twice the points per dollar of any other row. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel elements are the per-model teammate framing (scoring an individual model while holding the team fixed, with alone-gating) and the finding structure — most failures occur after the model recognized the problem (45% overall, 61–88% in five dimensions), and conflict-resolution degrades with capability. The underlying machinery — LLM judges, programmatic checks, benchmark recycling (SWE-bench, CaSiNo, HiddenBench), and Asch-style confederates — is a competent combination of existing techniques applied to a new measurement target. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong. Ablations and validity checks are extensive: held-out vs. public rank agreement (τ = 0.88), seed-retest reliability (r ≥ 0.98), split-half reliability 0.99, head-to-head pairwise validation (higher-ranked row wins 271/276 pairs), a judge-bias audit across four other model families (no favoritism toward Claude models, p ≥ 0.30), human judge agreement (82.5%, κ = 0.81), and manual review of all 315 failing safety runs (19 grading errors corrected before scoring). A 40-task "Lite" subset reproduces the full ranking (τ = 0.95). Bootstrap intervals accompany every headline number and paired sign tests support the reasoning-effort claims. Code and 160 public tasks are released via GitHub/website (URLs referenced but not printed in the text provided); 80 tasks are held out. Methodological concerns: the scoreboard is generated on tasks partially drawn from public benchmarks (contamination risk is mitigated by the held-out set but not eliminated); LLM-judged intermediate labels drive the scripted teammate and agree at only 67–78% in four dimensions; and the "distinct ability" framing must be read against the r = 0.92 capability correlation. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a benchmark and measurement study, no trained artifacts). - Practical: Runs entirely through commercial LLM APIs; any lab with API access can replicate the protocol. - Efficient: A full evaluation costs $1.8–$662 at list prices (369× range); the released 40-task Lite subset needs 17% of full-evaluation runs while keeping τ = 0.95. - Effective: The evidence shows it detects measurable teamwork deficits under controlled pressure, but the authors admit it is not yet shown to predict real team-task contribution beyond general capability. - Scalable: Not stress-tested — tasks cap at 3–8 rounds and teams at 5 members; scaling to longer horizons, larger teams, or adversarial scripting is untested (only claimed as future use). The work delivers a software artifact: 160 public tasks, scoring code, and analysis scripts, with 80 held-out tasks managed by the authors for uncontaminated evaluation. Strengths: - The alone-gating design is a clean identification strategy: a 20–46 point baseline-to-test drop on tasks the model demonstrably solves solo isolates collaboration as the failure cause, which whole-team benchmarks cannot do. - The failure-mode taxonomy (missed it / gave in / stopped short), grounded in judge labels over 5,094 failed runs, yields a non-obvious, actionable finding: stronger models fail more by failing to act on recognized problems (62% of frontier failures) while weaker models fail by not noticing. - The validity appendix (C.1–C.5) is at the level the field needs but rarely gets — including a self-critical analysis (Appendix F.2) showing the conflict score's utility cost is only ~7% of joint points, which cuts against the paper's own framing. - The human-comparison section is honest about its limits (vignette vs. live settings, small human samples, unmatched incentives) rather than claiming parity experiments. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that alone/baseline versions run once while tests run three times; live teammates are LLMs, not people; the scripted teammate is less variable than real colleagues; LLM judges and code checkers can err (with quantified error handling: 19/315 corrected safety-run verdicts); some analyses use an earlier round of six models, one of which (Qwen 3.7 Max) is absent from the leaderboard; costs exclude partner and judge models; and, in the conclusion, that the score's predictive validity for team-task contribution "beyond its general capability" must be tested before labs report it with model releases. This is direct, specific confrontation of limitations — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The headline "capability does not guarantee teamwork" claim is thinner than presented: capability explains 85% of score variance, and the paper's flagship "11-point gap at equal capability" rests on two models near one index point apart; residual-variance claims at n = 18 models deserve more caution than the abstract gives them. - The conflict-dimension story has an internal tension the authors partially concede: deals after giving in reach 93% of best joint points, so the "caving" behavior the score penalizes costs the team little in the tasks as constructed — the benchmark penalizes deference as such, a normative choice, not a demonstrated loss. - Scripted-teammate scripts are hand-written per task from source records; scoring may partly measure robustness to specific script phrasings and pressure tactics, and no experiment varies scripts to test sensitivity (the 3 seeds vary generation, not the script). - Judge agreement drops to 67–78% in exactly the four dimensions where labels drive the scripted teammate's concessions (taking over, emotional intelligence, conflict, sharing), meaning run outcomes in those dimensions are partly determined by noisy labeling — the human validation covers only 40 messages. - All live teammates and judges come from three vendors; no all-same-family or all-human-partner ablation isolates partner-model effects on the model under test's score. - The human comparison uses written-vignette self-reports and groups as small as 5, yet Figure 7 presents model-vs-human bars without those caveats inline. Bottom Line: This is the most methodologically careful attempt yet to measure per-model teamwork rather than team-level outcomes, and its failure-mode findings (models act on recognized problems poorly, especially in conflict and over inherited work) should be read by anyone selecting or training models for multi-agent deployment — but the benchmark's headline independence-from-capability claim is overdrawn and its predictive validity for real teams remains, by the authors' own admission, unproven.

#12 — Highly Innovative (79)

Embodied First Exam (20 ▲ )

Kangrui Wang, Qineng Wang, Changhe Chen, Pingyue Zhang, Chi Gui, Feishi Wang, Canyu Chen, Wenli Xiao, Xiaoyu Huang, Tonghe Zhang, Linjie Li, Zihan Wang, Minyeong Kim, Yiyou Sun, Mingkai Deng, Jinyu Hou, Qi Zhu, Han Liu, Eric P. Xing, Huaxiu Yao, Zhiwen Fan, Yuejiang Liu, Dawn Song, Pieter Abbeel, Li Fei-Fei, Jiajun Wu, Yuke Zhu, Guanya Shi, Ruohan Zhang, Manling Li · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 11 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces the Embodied First Exam (EFE), a unified benchmark of 1,156 tasks in 35 suites on 47 simulated robots (2,288 tests; 456-task hard core set) that evaluates general-purpose coding agents as robot controllers under a three-setting protocol — Privileged (full simulator state, unlimited resets), Standard (own sensors only, no resets), and Realtime (world keeps running while the agent reasons). - Why it's important: Existing robotics benchmarks target visuomotor policy learning and existing coding-agent benchmarks ignore physical-world constraints, so nobody knows whether coding agents can reliably control robots before they are deployed on hardware — a question that determines whether agentic robotics is a viable third paradigm beyond manual programming and policy learning. - How it does it: Each robotics task is packaged in the Harbor/Terminal-Bench container format with an isolated, agent-proof verifier, and each task runs in up to three settings that hold the initial scene, success rule, and time limit fixed while varying state access, reset budget, and whether the simulation waits — producing paired measurements of what physical-world constraints cost. - The good: The controlled ablations cleanly attribute the gap: for the strongest agent (GPT-6 Astra in Codex), adding unlimited resets raises Standard-setting success from 28% to 53%, adding exact object state to 45%, both to 68% versus 77% Privileged on the same 391 tasks; failure-stage concentration (56–61% vs. 31–37% chance baselines) and harness effects (up to 12 percentage points, McNemar-tested) are quantified against baselines. - The missing: Every agent makes a single attempt per test with no confidence intervals on the headline success rates, all results are simulation-only, and the stage-level failure labels that ground the analysis were written by an LLM from the same model family as the top-scoring agent (GPT-6.1 Sol labeling GPT-6 Astra attempts). - Read it or not: Essential reading for anyone building coding-agent-on-robot systems or agent benchmarks, and highly informative for robot-learning researchers deciding whether agentic control is credible; skippable if you only need visuomotor policy evaluation, since the framework deliberately excludes learned-policy baselines.
Why this rank
Scored using Systems profile. This benchmark is the cluster's best systems contribution. Novelty (80) comes from the three-setting paired protocol that converts 'can agents handle physical constraints?' into controlled variables, plus nine genuinely new suites. Rigor (75) is strong — agent-isolated verifiers with adversarial anti-cheat screening, McNemar-tested harness effects, chance-corrected failure-stage baselines, and released tasks and trajectories — docked for single-attempt headline numbers and LLM-generated failure labels without human agreement statistics. Non-Obviousness (80) is earned by the resets-beat-oracle-state finding (28→53% vs 28→45%) and stage-concentration results that no competent practitioner would have guessed. Completeness (75) and Resilience (78) are high: the disclosure of family-bias risks, the soccer-task confound, and the Privileged-as-approximate-upper-bound caveat is direct and non-minimizing. Impact (82) reflects a substantial released artifact that plausibly becomes the reference benchmark for embodied agent evaluation. Problem & Motivation: Coding agents powered by LLMs suggest a third way to acquire robot skills — directly controlling robots, writing robot programs, or training policies — beyond manual programming and data-driven visuomotor policies. Recent isolated successes suggest a paradigm shift, but the capability boundary is unknown: which robotic tasks can general-purpose coding agents solve, under what physical-world constraints, and where do they fail? Existing benchmarks cannot answer this. Robotics benchmarks (LIBERO, RoboCasa, BEHAVIOR-1K, HumanoidBench, etc.) are built around a fixed observe-act interface for learned policies; coding-agent benchmarks (SWE-Bench, Terminal-Bench) impose no physical-world constraints like partial observability, no resets, or a running clock. The gap is a benchmark that both spans diverse embodiments/capabilities and measures how sensor-only access, irrevocability, and real-time pressure degrade agent performance. Key Idea: The core insight is that physical-world constraints can be isolated as controlled experimental variables rather than baked into the task design. By fixing a task's initial scene, success rule, and time limit while varying only three factors — access to exact simulator state, ability to reset, and whether the simulation clock waits — the Privileged/Standard/Realtime protocol turns 'how close to a real robot is the agent?' into a paired, measurable axis. Combined with the agent-native design (the agent chooses its control approach: direct action output, writing a controller program, or training a policy), this lets the benchmark measure a capability boundary rather than a single fixed pipeline. A second key move is stage-level failure annotation: decomposing tasks into ordered world-state stages (task graphs) so failures can be located, compared across agents and settings, and attributed to stage types (precise vs. coarse, material vs. mechanism, etc.). Methodology: The pipeline has three layers. (1) Task packaging: every task is a Harbor-format container with instruction.md, a frozen initial scene verified by hash, resource caps (30 min–4 h wall-clock, 10B+10B token budget, CPU/memory/GPU/disk caps), and a verifier in a separate no-network container; tasks must fail when the robot does nothing and pass with a reference solution (686 full, 78 partial, none visible to the agent). (2) Evaluation protocol: in Privileged, the agent shares a container with the simulator, submits a low-level trajectory that the verifier replays from a fresh process; in Standard, the simulator is an HTTP service exposing only proprioception, RGB-D observations, and action chunks, with success graded on the live episode; in Realtime, the same service never pauses, using a stated slowdown factor. (3) Analysis: 427 core tasks are decomposed into task graphs (2,411 stages, 5.6/task); GPT-6.1 Sol (with Claude Sonnet 5.5 for the remainder, then reviewed) labeled 6,779 attempts with progress maps, one failure stage, up to two failure phenomena, and root causes. Control approaches of 1,489 sampled attempts were labeled by an agent. Statistical machinery includes chance baselines for failure-stage concentration (position-frequency and stage-type-rate baselines), McNemar tests for harness comparisons, and 95% intervals on concentration figures. Critical design decisions: agent-controlled verification isolation (well justified, with explicit anti-cheat screening where an agent tries to pass without solving); LLM-written failure labels with frozen prompts and worked-example iteration (partially justified — human oversight on earlier versions, but final labels unverified at scale); core-set selection by author judgment plus a screening agent (GPT-6 Luna), with the family-bias risk acknowledged. Key Results: Eight agents were evaluated on the 456-task core set (901 tests), one attempt per test, results from a public leaderboard. GPT-6 Astra in Codex leads: 33.6% (153/456) Standard, 77.5% (303/391) Privileged, 31.5% (17/54) Realtime. Claude Opus 5.5 (25.0%/59.3%/7.4%) and Gemini 4 Argon (24.1%/42.7%/9.3%) follow; the best of the remaining five is Kimi 3.1 Pro at 10.1% Standard. The three strongest agents together solve 48% of Standard tests, but in 14 of 22 Standard suites with ≥5 tests, at least half of tests go unsolved by all three. Headline findings: (a) the Privileged→Standard drop is large and decomposable — resets raise GPT-6 Astra from 28% to 53%, exact state to 45%, both to 68% vs. 77% Privileged; (b) precise stage types (assemble, strike, adjust pose, catch, insert) fail 24–46 percentage points more often in Standard, vs. 1–20 for coarse types; at precise stages resets solve 36% of failures vs. 21% for state and 19% for a repeat-attempt proxy; (c) failures concentrate: 56–61% of failure pairs share a stage vs. 31–37% chance, and the most common failure stage matches across settings in 57% of tasks (9% chance); (d) weaker agents fail before making contact at 9.1–18.5% of contact stages vs. 2.7–3.7% for the strong three; (e) harness matters: GPT-6 Astra solves 34% in Codex vs. 22% in Claude Code (p<0.001); (f) on a two-version soccer task, 17/20 GPU-equipped attempts trained RL policies and all 4 wins used trained policies, vs. 0/20 wins with CPUs only — though the two versions confound GPU, library, training copies, and instruction. Baselines are the current frontier of commercial coding agents (November 2026 list prices; mean Standard attempt $27.1 for GPT-6 Astra, ~4× Claude Opus 5.5/Gemini 4 Argon). Tested at 'standard' benchmark scale for agents but unusually broad for robotics; no stress-scale claims. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (primary) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. Genuinely novel: the three-setting paired protocol that measures the cost of state access, resets, and real-time pressure as isolated variables; the agent-native design leaving the control approach to the agent; 9 new suites (RoboARC, DexHandExam, RoboPaint, RoboDynamicExam, Embodied Olympics, iSpatialGym, Embodied Safety Exam, RoboEngineer) covering deformables, dynamics, safety, and sim-to-sim engineering; and the quantified findings on resets-vs-state and failure-stage concentration. Standard combinations: containerized harness execution (directly from Harbor/Terminal-Bench), 26 of 35 suites adapted from existing benchmarks, and stage-taxonomy failure analysis, which is a competent application of established error-analysis practice at new granularity. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and load-bearing: the controlled runs adding state/reset features to the Standard interface, the no-success-signal run as a repeat-attempt proxy, and the four-way model-harness crossover with paired exact McNemar tests. Chance baselines are constructed for the failure-stage concentration claims, and several confounds are probed (same-stage-reached matching, first-episode-only counts, exclusion accounting for 500 of 5,272 failures with per-agent breakdowns). Code, task definitions, and 6,779 labeled attempt trajectories are released (github.com/mll-lab-nu/embodied-first-exam; huggingface.co/datasets/MLL-Lab/embodied-exam-data). Concerns: (a) one attempt per test with no confidence intervals on headline rates — the authors flag this themselves; differences between weaker agents (11–46 tests solved) are within noise of a single test (2–9 pp swings); (b) the failure labels and control-approach labels are LLM-generated, and the primary labeler (GPT-6.1 Sol) shares a family with the top model (GPT-6 Astra), a circularity risk the authors disclose but do not quantify with human agreement statistics on the final labels; (c) the core set was screened by GPT-6 Luna (same family), acknowledged as potentially biasing against that family; (d) evaluation is simulation-only, with a single two-agent buzz-wire real-robot demonstration; (e) 'Privileged as upper bound' is explicitly approximate (4 tasks solved Standard-only by GPT-6 Astra, 18 by Gemini 4 Argon). The anti-Goodhart engineering (verifier isolation, fail-when-inert checks, pre-registration integrity screening) is notably strong. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a built benchmark/infrastructure, evaluated through a public leaderboard), with a strong empirical-analysis component. Practical: Yes — tasks run in Docker containers on commodity hardware (4–16 cores, 4–39 GiB RAM, GPU only where a suite needs one), runnable via a single 'harbor run' command. Efficient: Attempt costs are non-trivial at agent scale ($27.1 mean list price per GPT-6 Astra Standard attempt; weaker Flash-class models spend more and solve less), and full-leaderboard reproduction implies thousands of container-hours, but per-task evaluation is bounded by design. Effective: The evidence shows the framework measures what it claims (paired settings, isolated verifier), but it measures a simulation proxy; the real-robot transfer of the interface is demonstrated on one task with two agents, not evaluated systematically. Scalable: The 700 non-core tasks and the framework's modular suite format imply headroom, but Realtime coverage (54 dynamic tasks only) is compute-limited today, and multi-seed evaluation would multiply cost roughly linearly. The work delivers a substantial software artifact (benchmark, harness integrations, verifier tooling, trajectory dataset, leaderboard) rather than stopping at paper form. Strengths: - The paired-setting protocol is a real conceptual contribution: it converts the vague question 'can coding agents handle physical constraints?' into controlled comparisons, and the resets-vs-state ablation (28→53% vs. 28→45%, both 68% vs. 77%) is a genuinely informative, non-obvious empirical result — resets beat oracle state at precision stages. - Verification integrity is engineered, not asserted: agent-isolated verifiers, hash-checked frozen scenes, fail-when-inert and pass-with-reference requirements, adversarial pre-registration screening, and removal of expert policies/demonstrations from adapted benchmarks. - Stage-level failure analysis with chance-corrected baselines yields actionable structure (failures concentrate at the first stage; material and body stages fail at 66% and 45% once reached; weaker agents fail pre-contact) rather than aggregate scores alone. - Breadth with discipline: 47 robots across nine embodiment types and 35 suites, with the adapted suites' scenes, success rules (sometimes tightened), and physics kept intact, making the benchmark a superset rather than a replacement. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state plainly: each agent makes a single attempt per test (so run-to-run variation is unmeasured; future work will add repeats and confidence intervals); stage-level and control-approach labels come from agents (with disclosed family-bias risk for GPT-6.1 Sol labeling GPT-6 Astra); all results are in simulation; Realtime coverage is limited to 54 dynamic tasks due to compute. They also acknowledge the core-set screening bias from GPT-6 Luna, the soccer-task confound (GPU, library, training copies, and instruction changed together), that stage-category failure rates do not show the category causes failure (category–suite–robot confounding), and that Antigravity CLI's session-ending behavior on content-filter blocks may partly explain Gemini 4 Argon's gap. This is direct, non-minimizing limitation disclosure — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No human agreement study on the final LLM-written failure labels: earlier prompt versions were human-reviewed, but nothing quantifies label accuracy for the released 6,779-attempt dataset, and root causes are at the coarse 'Control' level in 47% of failures — the taxonomy's cognitive categories may be under-validated. - Headline cross-agent claims (e.g., the three-strongest ordering, the 64 tests Opus 5.5/Argon solve that Astra fails) rest on single attempts without the paired statistics the harness comparison receives; several agent rankings could not survive one reseed. - The 'Privileged as upper bound' framing invites misuse: since it holds only over task sets and replays open-loop, per-task comparisons across settings in downstream citations will likely ignore the caveat. - No baseline from a specialized embodied-agent system (e.g., a coding agent with a curated skill library or a task-specific scaffold), so the numbers bound unmodified general agents only; the paper's choice, but the capability-boundary conclusion is about one operating point. - Success rules for the 9 new suites were written by the authors, and Embodied Safety Exam's grading from physical simulator state is novel enough that no external validation of its verifier exists beyond the internal fail-when-inert check. - Realtime results (n=54, several agents at 0–1 tests solved) are too thin to support setting-level conclusions beyond 'harder'; the 63%-unsolved figure has wide uncertainty. - Cost analysis uses list prices of November 2026 and tokens logged by harnesses; billed/reproducibility costs may differ substantially. Bottom Line: For anyone building or evaluating coding agents — especially with an eye toward embodied deployment — this is now the reference benchmark for physical-world agent evaluation and its resets-vs-state and failure-localization findings are worth the read on their own; for visuomotor-policy researchers there is likely no alternative covering this ground, though the single-attempt leaderboard numbers should be treated as provisional until multi-seed results land.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Open Vision Banana (OVB), a fully open, reproducible recipe that fine-tunes open-weight FLUX.2-Klein 4B/9B image generators into unified multi-task perception models (semantic/referring/reasoning/instance segmentation, depth, surface normals) via RGB-encoded prediction targets, and releases the data pipeline, training code, and all checkpoints. - Why it's important: The proprietary Vision Banana system showed generators can become generalist perceivers, but its model, data, and code are closed, leaving the community unable to determine which components drive the result; this work closes that reproducibility gap with public data and models. - How it does it: Perception tasks are cast as conditional image editing — annotations are rendered as RGB targets with randomized class–color legends, trained with the base generator's rectified-flow objective (with a validity mask for undefined geometry pixels), and decoded by deterministic task-specific readouts. - The good: The zero-shot 9B model surpasses Vision Banana's reported Cityscapes performance (73.9 vs. 69.9 mIoU), and training-free legend ensembling adds up to +8.7 mIoU on Cityscapes and +15.0 mIoU on COCO-Object by majority-voting over passes with different color legends. - The missing: Legend ensembling's headline numbers require 20–90 diffusion passes per image, and the paper reports no end-to-end latency/compute comparison against single-pass specialists; instance segmentation also trails Vision Banana substantially (37.4 vs. 47.5 cgF1). - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building unified generative perception systems or studying test-time scaling — the design-choice ablations (color memorization, palette, replay fractions, adaptation scope) are genuinely informative, but readers seeking only a stronger off-the-shelf segmenter should use SAM 3 or specialist models.

Problem & Motivation: Vision Banana [23] demonstrated that a proprietary image generator (Nano Banana Pro) can be instruction-tuned into a generalist visual perception model that renders task outputs as RGB images, but its base model, data, code, and implementation details are all private. Practitioners and researchers therefore cannot verify which design choices (color encodings, prompts, data mixtures, adaptation scope) account for the results, nor whether the paradigm transfers to publicly available generators. The paper addresses this gap: can an open-weight generator, trained exclusively on public data, match a closed generalist, and what design choices matter most? Key Idea: The core insight is that perception via a generator is dominated by low-level output conventions — the model learns to delineate regions early but reliably binding them to prompted colors much later (oracle relabeling reaches 85.9 mIoU at 12.5K training steps when the standard readout gives 51.1). This motivates two moves: (1) randomized, well-separated color legends during training so the model follows arbitrary prompt-specified mappings instead of memorizing fixed ones (fixed-color training collapses to 7.1 mIoU when colors change at inference), and (2) legend ensembling — run multiple passes with different random class–color legends at fixed generation seed and fuse per-pixel majority votes — a training-free test-time-scaling method that corrects color–class binding errors. Methodology: The pipeline is: (1) encode each task's annotation as an RGB target (segmentation via per-sample random legends from a 64-color farthest-point-sampled CIELAB palette; depth as per-image-normalized inverse depth in grayscale; normals via a fixed camera-space (x,y,z)→RGB affine map); (2) fine-tune the full FLUX.2-Klein transformer (VAE and text encoder frozen) with the rectified-flow objective, L_FM = E[Σ_j m_j ‖v̂_j − (ϵ−z_y)_j‖² / (C·Σ_j m_j)], where the validity mask m_j excludes undefined geometry regions (~8% of non-zero-shot geometry target pixels); (3) decode generated RGB back into predictions with deterministic readouts (nearest-palette-color snapping, connected components, GrabCut refinement for instances). Training uses 2.1M pairs (zero-shot) / 3.8M (non-zero-shot) from public datasets, 100K steps at global batch 192 on ~512² aspect-ratio buckets, AdamW, FSDP, bf16 — about 73 h on 16 GH200 GPUs for 4B and 79 h on 32 for 9B. Mixtures include ~15% text-to-image replay and ~25% editing/identity-reconstruction data to preserve generation. Controlled design-choice studies (37.5K-step 9B runs) cover class–color mappings, palette size, generation/editing shares, adaptation scope, validity masks, training duration, and LoRA vs. full fine-tuning. Critical decisions: random legends + mixed subset/full-set/negative-class prompts (well justified by the S1 collapse experiment); 64-color palette (justified by sweep over 32–200 colors); full-transformer adaptation (justified — last-k blocks fail badly, e.g., 4.5 Cityscapes mIoU with last-4). Key Results: Zero-shot OVB 9B: Cityscapes 73.9 mIoU with legend ensembling (65.4 single-pass) vs. Vision Banana 69.9 and zero-shot specialist SAM 3 at 65.2; COCO-Object 53.0 mIoU (90-pass, 38.7 single-pass) vs. best specialist CorrCLIP 49.4. Referring segmentation (RefCOCOg val): 57.4 cIoU zero-shot, 69.2 non-zero-shot — behind Vision Banana's 73.8. Reasoning segmentation (ReasonSeg val): 67.9 gIoU zero-shot with Gemma4 query rewriting (74.6 non-zero-shot) vs. Vision Banana's 79.3 (both using stronger LLM reasoners). Instance segmentation (SA-Co/Gold): 37.4 cgF1 zero-shot vs. Vision Banana 47.5 and SAM 3 54.1. Depth: NYUv2 δ1 97.4% (zero-shot 9B), 99.0% (non-zero-shot), rivaling Marigold V2 (98.0%); KITTI degrades under non-zero-shot training (95.3→83.2 δ1 for 9B). Normals: 13.51° mean error on NYUv2 (non-zero-shot 9B) vs. Marigold V2's 16.6°. Generation retention: ImgEdit-Bench Basic roughly retained (9B 3.89 vs. base 3.89), but GenAI-Bench VQAScore drops for all models (−0.027 to −0.050). Frozen features improve: OVB 9B beats DINOv3 7B on TokenCut CorLoc (56.3 vs. 54.8) and SPair-71k semantic correspondence (61.9 vs. 56.1). Baselines are current (2025–2026 systems: SAM 3, SenseNova-Vision, Marigold V2, Lotus-2), though Vision Banana depth numbers are acknowledged as not directly comparable (metric vs. aligned depth). Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (legend ensembling as training-free test-time scaling for generator-based segmentation), NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the color-binding vs. region-delimitation dissociation and the design-choice interaction analysis), and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (the open recipe, pipeline, and checkpoints). The core paradigm — RGB-encoded perception targets on a diffusion/flow generator — is standard prior art (Painter, DICEPTION, Vision Banana); the genuinely novel elements are the test-time scaling method, the demonstrated color-memorization failure mode, and the systematic open ablation of choices a closed system left unspecified. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are extensive and targeted: adaptation scope, palette, class–color mapping, replay fractions, training duration, validity masks, LoRA ranks (64–1024), each with matched compute and cross-task retention guardrails. The oracle-relabeling diagnostic (Table 7) cleanly separates color-binding from region errors — an unusually convincing causal analysis. Reproducibility is a headline strength: data construction pipeline, training/evaluation code, and final/intermediate/ablation checkpoints are all released (openvisionbanana.github.io). Weaknesses: most perception evaluations are single-run with no error bars or significance tests (generation benchmarks use 3 seeds); headline ensembling numbers report the peak of the consensus curve against pass 1, which is a favorable choice; the fixed generation seed and fixed legend draws across models aid controlled comparison but mean single-seed protocol; instance-segmentation readout depends on a Qwen3-VL presence gate plus non-trivial post-processing tuned on the evaluation benchmark's conventions. The non-zero-shot models train on training splits of some evaluation benchmarks, which is standard but inflates comparisons against zero-shot baselines in the same table. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a built, released model family evaluated across benchmarks; also strong EMPIRICAL content). - Practical: Runs on GH200 GPUs; LoRA variants (rank 64–128, 66 GiB/GPU) fit far smaller clusters, though 4B/9B diffusion inference per pass is heavier than a discriminative segmentation head. - Efficient: Training is moderate (~73–79 h on 16–32 GH200s), but the best accuracy requires 20–90 inference passes per image, multiplying generation cost accordingly; single-pass performance is reported transparently. - Effective: Evidence shows the models solve segmentation and geometry tasks at or near generalist SOTA on public data, but the flagship comparisons to Vision Banana inherit its unverifiable self-reported numbers, and depth comparisons mix alignment protocols. - Scalable: Only 4B→9B scaling is tested; behavior at 10× scale or on higher-resolution dense prediction is claimed by extrapolation only, and the 512-token text window already forces prompt splitting for 80-class COCO. Delivers a substantial software artifact: data pipeline, training/eval code, and all checkpoints. Strengths: - Genuinely novel, well-analyzed test-time scaling method: legend ensembling is simple, training-free, and the paper explains why it works (color-binding errors, +34.4 IoU on 'train' class, 6% low-agreement pixels holding 58% of errors). - The oracle-relabeling diagnostic establishing that region delineation is learned long before color binding is a real empirical finding with design implications beyond this paper. - Full reproducibility of a previously closed paradigm, including intermediate and ablation checkpoints — rare and valuable for the field. - Honest multi-task trade-off accounting: the paper reports generation-quality drops (GenAI-Bench −0.027 to −0.050 VQAScore), KITTI depth regressions under non-zero-shot training, and where LoRA falls short (−5 mIoU Cityscapes vs. full fine-tuning at matched samples). Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state the main limitation directly: open base generators perceive more weakly than proprietary ones (frozen Nano Banana Pro reaches 70.2 gIoU on raw ReasonSeg queries vs. 24.1 for the open base), which caps OVB's referring/reasoning/instance performance relative to Vision Banana. They acknowledge Vision Banana's depth scores are not directly comparable (metric vs. aligned), that non-zero-shot improvements confound benchmark data with other mixture changes, that the geometry depth/normal allocation (10/20) was fixed before a reduced-budget comparison favored 20/10, and that the UGE editing suite shows inconsistent retention (9B non-zero-shot drops 4.03→3.68). They confront limitations directly rather than minimizing them — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Headline legend-ensembling gains quote the peak of the consensus curve against pass 1 (the fixed-preset numbers, e.g., 73.9 on Cityscapes at 20 passes, are more moderate); a skeptic would want the preset consensus as the primary number with peak as secondary. - No end-to-end compute/latency accounting for the 20–90-pass ensembles against single-pass baselines — the accuracy gain is not placed in a cost-normalized comparison. - The instance-segmentation readout (color snapping, gap filling, GrabCut, presence gate) is a long engineering chain whose components are not individually ablated; some pipeline constants were presumably tuned against SA-Co/Gold conventions. - No statistical uncertainty on the close comparisons (e.g., 73.9 vs. 69.9 mIoU against Vision Banana rests partly on a proprietary self-reported number under a slightly different setup). - Geometry ablations are done at reduced budget (37.5K steps, batch 8) and the authors concede the full-scale best allocation is unestablished; ScanNet normals actually degrade with non-zero-shot training, which is not deeply investigated. - Evaluation resolution is capped near 512² training buckets, and behavior on very high-resolution dense prediction or video is untested. Bottom Line: A practitioner building generative or unified perception systems gains real, actionable knowledge here — the color-randomization insight, design-choice interactions, and legend ensembling justify reading — even though anyone needing only a top segmenter today would still pick SAM 3 or a specialist over these checkpoints.

#14 — Highly Innovative (77)

Evolving Infra: Agent-Adaptive LLM Serving at Scale (10 ▲ )

Hao Kang, Weili Xu, Ziyang Li, Zheng Du, Hanchen Li, Tian Xia, Song Bian, Tushar Krishna, Huizi Mao, Ion Stoica, Song Han · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 12 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Evolving Infra, an agent-adaptive prefill-decode (PD) disaggregated serving system that decouples compute allocation from KV cache management so nodes switch phases in place (~6.2 s vs 754 s relaunches) and KV eviction/routing follow agent context management (forks, sub-agents, compaction) rather than access recency. - Why it's important: Agentic workloads (coding, math, computer-use) dominate LLM inference demand, and their shifting prefill/decode composition makes static PD splits lose up to 24% throughput while LRU eviction drops KV that paused agents still need — directly inflating latency and cost in production clusters. - How it does it: A symmetric engine serves both phases without relaunch, host memory of all nodes forms a shared KV pool readable in either phase, a cluster-wide directory counts active agent branches referencing each KV block, online-fitted iteration-time models (separating cached from uncached tokens) drive a statistically gated phase-split planner and TTFT-predicting router. - The good: End-to-end measurements on up to 256 NVIDIA GB300 GPUs across three distinct agent workloads (PutnamBench, Claude Code traces, OSWorld 2.0) show 1.10–2.73× Dynamo's throughput, 81–95% less lost KV reuse, and up to 4.12× lower mean E2E latency, with ablations isolating each component's contribution. - The missing: The primary comparison is against a single baseline (Dynamo v1.5.1); Arrow is a reimplementation and several strong alternatives (SGLang runtime role switch, semi-PD, MemServe, PPD) are argued away or not run, and most trace-replay runs are single-seed closed-loop replays. - Read it or not: Worth reading for systems researchers and infrastructure engineers building agent-serving stacks — the decoupling insight, motivation measurements (Figures 2–3), and the branch-count eviction design are directly reusable; skip it if you only care about model/algorithm work.
Why this rank

Problem & Motivation: Operators of LLM inference clusters serving agents face three compounding problems that conventional PD-disaggregated systems handle poorly. First, the best prefill/decode node split differs sharply across agent workloads (best static split ranges from 2P7D for decode-heavy math agents on PutnamBench to 6P3D for prefill-heavy computer-use agents on OSWorld) and shifts over time as workload composition changes — the best static split (5P4D) loses up to 24% of throughput versus the per-10-minute best split. Second, agent harnesses fork contexts, spawn sub-agents, and compact histories, so KV reuse depends on whether an active branch still references a block, not on access recency: after a 359 s sub-agent call, 98% of the next prompt matches cached KV, but only 14% after a 12 s compaction. Third, existing machinery makes adaptation costly: Dynamo's planner relaunches engines (681 s average switch, node offline), Arrow's in-place switches strand the node's KV (55.5% lost KV reuse over 34 switches), cache-aware routers overload the few nodes holding popular prefixes (P95 TTFT 27–34 s), and shared memory pools load fetched KV into GPU memory only at prefill start (P95 TTFT rises to 95 s). The beneficiaries are cloud/inference providers running agentic workloads at scale. Key Idea: Decouple node phase from KV storage: because every node runs a symmetric engine and all KV lives in a shared host-memory pool indexed by a cluster-wide directory that tracks branch reference counts driven by agent context-management events (fork, compaction, branch finish, KV transfer), a node can switch between prefill and decode in ~6 s without losing KV, freeing the router to balance predicted TTFT instead of trading cache locality against load, and letting eviction prioritize zero-reference-count blocks (replaced histories, finished sub-agents, duplicate transfer copies) before LRU. The second enabling idea is online-fitted linear iteration-time models that separate cached from uncached tokens (plus a query-key-pair attention term and a MoE expert-activation term φ(B) for decode), letting the planner size the split from the average work of a request — a workload property robust to sub-agent bursts — with a two-standard-error gating rule that suppresses spurious switches. Methodology: The system has an infrastructure layer and a policy layer. Infrastructure: (1) a symmetric SGLang-derived engine with one scheduling loop for both phases and a bidirectional RDMA KV-transfer protocol (reusing Mooncake transport), so a phase switch is a router routing-table change plus an in-place drain (0.7 s measured for one switch; 6.2 s average including drain); (2) a shared KV pool formed from all nodes' host memory (L2, deduplicated across tensor-parallel ranks, holding 4× GPU KV capacity), where prefill nodes pull KV from peer L2 over RDMA and complete the full GPU restore while the request queues (decode nodes only write); (3) a KV directory extending Dynamo's event-driven prefix tree with, per block per node, a count of active branches referencing it, maintained via harness-supplied branch IDs and per-branch versions (compaction increments the version, releasing counts on dropped blocks; same-phase transfers move counts, cross-phase transfers keep both; decode→prefill switches reset counts). Policy: prefill iteration time is modeled as T = c₀ + c₁·t_uc + c₂·A + c₃·t_rst (A = t_uc·t_c + t_uc(t_uc+1)/2 query-key pairs), decode as T = d₀ + d₁·φ(B) + d₂·B with φ(B) = 1 − (1−k/E)^(t_fwd·B); coefficients are fit online by nonnegative least squares during a collocated warmup (models converge to <7% mean error within a minute) and periodically re-measured terms are updated. The planner evaluates all N−1 candidate splits via a min-of-phase-throughputs objective (Equation 5) on the average request work over a 600 s window divided into 10 slices, switching only when a candidate's mean gain exceeds twice its standard error. The router sends each request to the prefill node with the smallest predicted TTFT (remaining batch time + queued service times + exposed fetch remainder + a copy-price for duplicate KV). Critical design decisions: (a) separating cached from uncached tokens in the prefill model — well justified, since counting full input length is exactly what makes Arrow over-provision prefill; (b) branch-reference-count eviction rather than agent pausing (ThunderAgent-style) — justified empirically: on GB300, KV capacity never binds (peak demand ≤86% of capacity), so pausing gains nothing (0.95×); (c) mean-work-based planning with statistical gating — justified by showing coarse signals flip between 2P7D and 8P1D in opposite error directions. Key Results: On 9 nodes (36 GB300 GPUs, TP4) serving GLM-5.2 (Putnam, Claude Code) and Kimi K2.6 (OSWorld), NVFP4 quantized, FP8 KV, MTP speculative decoding: throughput 1.10–2.73× Dynamo across nine stationary settings; lost KV reuse reduced 81–95% (e.g., CC/126 agents: 1.01% vs 7.78%); mean E2E latency reduced up to 4.12× (CC/126: 13.2 s vs 54.4 s); P95 TTFT reduced up to 13.92×. Under a shifting composition (Putnam → mixed → OSWorld over 3 hours), Evolving Infra tracks the per-10-minute best split online, achieving 2.14× Dynamo's throughput and 1.28× the best static split's. Phase switches average 6.2 s versus 754 s for Dynamo relaunches (>100×). Ablations: latency varies ≤1.8% across four initial splits (all converge to 4P5D on CC); enabling online adaptation at the best static split costs only 0.3% throughput; infrastructure + KV-aware routing/eviction alone reach 1.37× the best static split's throughput; async KV fetching alone gives 1.12× over upstream SGLang (prefill idle time 23.6% → 14.4%). Scale: gains hold on 256 GB300 GPUs (P95 TTFT stays 10–14 s while static PD degrades to 418 s); a Frontier simulation of 3,072 GPUs with 8 partitions and 30,720 agents shows 1.42× throughput over static splits via hierarchical per-partition planning. Open-loop replay: sustains 1.0 agents/min, 2× static 4P5D. The paper also reports offline profiling is expensive (10,752 GPU-hours for a 3-hour trace on 256 GPUs even with binary search). Baselines: Dynamo v1.5.1 (current, open-source, reasonable primary baseline); Arrow is a reimplementation (code unavailable); Llumnix tested only on H200 due to Arm incompatibility; SGLang's runtime role switch excluded because it rejects speculative decoding; ThunderAgent compared in a fixed-split ablation. Tested at standard-to-stress scale (36–256 real GPUs, simulated 3,072). Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL with a NEW FORMULATION element. Genuinely novel: the decoupling of PD phase from KV storage enabling cheap in-place phase switches while preserving cluster-wide KV, and the branch-reference-count directory that makes eviction follow agent context management (compaction, forks, transfers) rather than recency — existing agent-aware systems (Continuum, ThunderAgent, KVTether) assume contexts only grow and don't adapt the split. The iteration-time models are competent applications of roofline-style linear modeling, and the statistical switch gating is standard practice; the routing is a natural consequence of async fetching making cache locality obsolete. The overall design is a well-motivated synthesis of known components (HiCache-style tiering, Dynamo-style KV indexing, Mooncake transport, continuous batching) with the decoupling and branch-counting as the new core. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and genuinely informative: per-component throughput contributions (Figure 8b), initial-split sensitivity (Figure 8a), model convergence time (Figure 8c), async-fetch cost isolation (Table D.5), and a ThunderAgent comparison testing the paper's own causal claim about what causes KV loss (Table D.4). Motivation measurements are quantified carefully (lost KV reuse defined against an idealized unlimited-cache oracle). Weaknesses: no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests on the headline closed-loop runs (single 1-hour replays after 30-minute warmup); the open-loop runs admit each configuration ran once; the Arrow baseline is the authors' reimplementation on their own engines, which could understate Arrow; code is open-sourced (https://github.com/mit-han-lab/EvolvingInfra), which supports reproducibility, but the proprietary GLM-5.2 and Kimi K2.6 weights and trace availability partially gate reuse. The 3,072-GPU result is simulation (Frontier, extended by the authors to model their own fetch behavior — the simulator assumes fetches complete before prefill at no charge, an assumption favorable to their design). No benchmark-gaming concerns; evaluation spans three third-party workloads, not just the authors' own. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a built serving framework evaluated on real GPU clusters). - Practical: Runs on commercially available hardware (GB300/B200/H200 nodes with SGLang-derived engines and RDMA), though current flagship results use very high-end GB300 hardware; needs harness cooperation (branch IDs and finish notifications) that most agent frameworks would have to emit. - Efficient: The mechanism itself adds ~0.3% throughput overhead when adaptation is unnecessary, needs no extra GPUs (KV pool is host memory already present), and replaces up to 10,752 GPU-hours of offline profiling with ~1 minute of online fitting. - Effective: Evidence shows it solves the stated problem on real traces and benchmarks across three workload archetypes, with latency/throughput/KV-reuse improvements measured end-to-end, not proxied. - Scalable: Tested to 256 real GPUs with maintained gains and 3,072 GPUs in simulation; beyond that, the hierarchical partitioning is proposed but not deployed, and router/directory state at 10× scale is claimed manageable, not measured. Delivers a software artifact: open-source system code at the GitHub URL above; no dataset or trained model release noted. Strengths: - The core decoupling (symmetric engine + phase-agnostic shared KV pool) is a clean architectural insight that resolves a real, quantified trade-off — the paper measures exactly what it costs to switch phases under current systems (681 s Dynamo, 55.5% KV loss Arrow) and exactly what its design costs (0.7 s, 0.3% KV loss). - The branch-reference-count directory is a genuinely new mechanism: it translates harness-level context operations (compaction versions, fork IDs, transfer semantics) into per-block, per-node reference counts, fixing a failure mode (LRU evicting paused-agent KV, accounting for 34–46% of Dynamo's lost reuse on CC) that recency-based and priority-based schemes provably cannot address. - The motivation section is unusually rigorous: Figure 2's measurements (best split spanning 2P7D–6P3D; 24% static-split throughput loss; recency not predicting reuse) establish the problem before proposing anything, and Appendix D.4's ThunderAgent comparison tests the paper's own causal story against a competing explanation and wins. - Honest reporting of trade-offs: the planner trades P95 TTFT for throughput on Putnam (raising P95 TTFT above Dynamo at two of three concurrencies), and the open-loop run exposes a real failure case (a bad 2P7D switch at minute 75 causing target misses at 0.75 agents/min). Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge: the planner's throughput-first objective raises P95 TTFT above Dynamo on decode-heavy Putnam at 224 and 288 agents; the open-loop run misses latency targets at one arrival rate due to a suboptimal planner switch; SGLang's runtime role switch is excluded because it rejects speculative decoding (a comparison gap stated openly); Llumnix could not run on GB300 Arm CPUs and was tested only on H200; Arrow's code is unavailable so a reimplementation was used; the 3,072-GPU result is simulation with an idealized fetch model. They confront limitations relatively directly, particularly in appendices where failure cases and comparison exclusions are documented rather than buried. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Single-baseline dependence for headline numbers: most Figure 6 results compare only against Dynamo; the best-static-split comparison appears only at the lowest concurrency, and newer competitors (semi-PD, MemServe, PPD, KVTether) are discussed in related work but never run. - No repeated runs or variance estimates on the one-hour closed-loop replays; with throughput gaps of a few percent in some settings (e.g., 0.98–1.38× vs best static), run-to-run variance could matter, as the authors themselves note when explaining why offline binary search needs repeated runs. - The simulation extension of Frontier embeds the authors' own assumption that KV fetches complete before prefill at zero cost — the simulated 3,072-GPU result therefore inherits the design's key favorable assumption rather than testing it. - The system requires the harness to tag branch IDs, report branch finishes, and signal compaction; the paper does not measure the deployment friction or the effect of partial/misbehaving harness instrumentation (e.g., a harness that never reports finishes would pin counts and starve eviction of exactly the blocks the design targets). - KV-directory and router state scale (prefix-tree size, event throughput at 30k+ concurrent branches) is claimed feasible via partitioning but never stress-tested on real hardware beyond 256 GPUs. - Host-memory pool sizing (4× GPU capacity) is evaluated only on GB300 nodes with ~1 TB host memory; on nodes with smaller host-to-GPU memory ratios, the argument that capacity never binds — and hence that branch-count eviction beats pausing — may not hold, and the paper does not test this sensitivity. Bottom Line: A practitioner building or operating agentic LLM serving infrastructure gains concrete, reusable value here — the decoupled phase/KV architecture, the branch-reference-count eviction design, and the motivation measurements are all things current open-source stacks (Dynamo, SGLang/HiCache) genuinely lack — making this the strongest published treatment of agent-adaptive PD serving to date despite a thin baseline field and single-seed headline runs.
