Problem & Motivation: Reproducing a published ML experiment (in the ACM sense: independently re-executing authors' artifacts to numerically compatible measurements) requires recovering details — dependency fixes, intended configurations, output-to-table mappings — that papers and released code leave implicit. Reproduction success therefore partially reflects the reproducing agent's ability to compensate for missing information rather than the artifacts themselves. Existing agent benchmarks (PaperBench, CORE-Bench, SciReplicate-Bench) expose this reconstruction burden but do not test whether preserving the recovered procedure for reuse reduces it. The target users are authors preparing artifact releases, third-party reproducers, and researchers evaluating coding agents. Key Idea: The core insight is that reproduction work is knowledge worth persisting: the systematic execution deviation D in the error model Y = μ + D + ε can be reduced by converting ad-hoc recovery decisions (dependency repairs, ambiguity resolutions, aggregation rules) into a standardized four-component handoff that includes not just executable steps but their rationale (ambiguity entries with adopted resolution, sensitivity, and affected tasks), so a fresh reproducer session inherits the procedure instead of re-inferring it. The companion methodological trick is scoring success against a prediction interval built from five independent human reference executions (with a 1% relative tolerance floor) combined with an adversarial integrity audit, separating "a nearby number" from "the intended experiment was run." Methodology: Three parts. (1) Benchmark: from 742 ICML 2026 Spotlight papers, 241 with code were sampled to 50, and 36 retained (14 excluded for availability/compute/closed-model access); tasks are own-method main-table measurements (1,463 curated; 1,029 verified into Categories 1–2 with published score inside the 95% compatibility interval, split by a 10% relative-reference-variation threshold; 730 GPU, 299 CPU-only). Five human reproducers independently execute each task from the same pinned commit under strict protocols (no score-driven selection, no cross-participant pooling). (2) Construction: a six-role agent workflow (Intake, Planner, Builder, Reproducer, Distiller, Packager plus an independent Reviewer) follows the paper's setup over conflicting code, records evidence-backed measurements, and packages the four-component artifact, verified from a clean shell. (3) Evaluation: fresh Reproducer sessions (Sonnet 4.6, Sonnet 5, Opus 5, Gemini 3.8 Flash) attempt all 1,029 tasks with either raw code or the refined artifact under identical 24-hour limits; success = inside the fixed compatibility interval AND not invalidated by a Codex Auditor running a Finder–Refuter–panel pipeline over five eligible violation classes (copying, instrument substitution, operand alteration, outcome-conditional selection, wrong statistic). Construction used Opus 5; the ablation uses Sonnet 5 on 12 papers/287 tasks. Design decisions — five reference observations, following the paper over code, evidence-conditional invalidation — are each explicitly justified, and the 1% tolerance floor is the least-justified choice (active on 197 tasks). Key Results: Refined artifacts raise mean reproduction success from 76.4% to 92.6% across four models (per-model: Sonnet 4.6 72.3→91.6 (+19.3 pp); Sonnet 5 76.5→93.3 (+16.8); Opus 5 89.2→94.7 (+5.5); Gemini 3.8 Flash 67.6→90.8 (+23.2)), reported as mean ± SD over three evaluations, and cut downstream Reproducer API spending 16.8–23.7% ($3,165→$2,512 for Sonnet 4.6, etc.). Cross-model success spread narrows from 21.6 to 3.9 pp. Gains persist under paper-macro weighting (+6.7 to +20.7 pp), under a stricter 80% interval (+10.3 to +39.1 pp), and in both reference-variability strata. On 45 CORE-Bench Hard capsules, RRA reaches 73.3% vs. raw 62.2% and VERITAS 68.9%, with cost per successful capsule falling from $8.43 to $4.34 and median session time from 33 to 14 minutes. Ablations (287 tasks): full RRA 93.0% vs. ordinary outputs 81.2% vs. raw 73.9%; removing code costs −5.2 pp, environment −4.5, guide −3.8, launchers −3.1. 813 raw failures recover vs. 136 reversals (AuxiliaryMCMC and LiME contribute 47.1% of reversals). Human validation on 818 outcomes shows both auditors miss invalid outcomes (Codex FN=8 of 39) and each false-flags 4 of 779 valid outcomes. Break-even for the $5,026 construction cost requires 8–13 full reuse rounds. Baselines (raw code, VERITAS) are reasonable and current; testing spans real published papers including GPU training runs. Novelty Classification: NEW BENCHMARK + NEW METHOD + NEW SYSTEM/TOOL. The genuinely novel elements are (a) the five-human-verified reference-score design with prediction-interval scoring plus an integrity audit, which is a methodological advance over binary or rubric-based scoring in PaperBench/CORE-Bench, and (b) the four-component artifact specification tested via component removals and an ordinary-outputs control. The construction workflow itself is a competent composition of known multi-agent patterns (role specialization, independent review, evidence ledger, Reflexion/Voyager-style experience persistence) applied to a new target. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative (per-component removals plus an ordinary-outputs control that isolates the standardized-handoff contribution); three evaluation repetitions with SDs, paper-macro diagnostics, stricter-threshold sensitivity, auditor-swap sensitivity, and two-person human validation of 818 audit outcomes substantially exceed field norms. The reference and verification protocols are documented at unusual depth (appendices A.3–A.4). Concerns: (i) the technique is developed and evaluated on partially overlapping machinery — ten development papers informed the workflows, and although reported separately they were not held out; (ii) auditor recall of 79.5% (Codex) means roughly one in five human-confirmed invalid outcomes escapes detection, so absolute success rates are optimistic upper bounds; (iii) a single construction model (Opus 5) produced all main artifacts; (iv) human reference fidelity relies on protocol compliance rather than independent instrumentation; (v) the paper does not state a public code/data release URL (a project page is linked, but artifact availability is not confirmed in the provided text). Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (an agent workflow and benchmark, evaluated by running experiments). - Practical: Yes — runs on standard agent harnesses (Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Codex CLI) with H100 hardware for GPU tasks; no exotic infrastructure. - Efficient: Construction costs $139.61 per paper in API usage (~$5,026 total, excluding GPU and audit time); downstream reuse saves 16.8–23.7% of API spend per round, breaking even after 8–13 reuse rounds. - Effective: The evidence supports the claim that refined artifacts improve agent reproduction success and lower cost on both the authors' benchmark and CORE-Bench Hard, though success is conditioned on auditor recall limits and the artifacts preserve whatever assumptions were correct at construction time. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 36 papers and 8×H100-class workloads; the 24-hour-per-paper limit already caused failures on compute-heavy papers (LiME's projected 7–92 wall-clock hours per variant), and construction cost per paper would grow with experiment complexity. The work delivers a specified artifact format and workflow as a method; no public software artifact or released benchmark archive is confirmed in the text. Strengths: - The measurement design is the standout: five independent human reference executions per task with an explicit statistical model (systematic deviation D vs. random variation ε) and a prediction-interval criterion is a rigorous answer to "how close is close enough," which most reproduction benchmarks hand-wave. - The execution-integrity audit is validated against blinded two-person human review with published precision/recall, rather than assumed; the WBMM timing-substitution case (reported projections replacing measured durations, files edited after process exit) demonstrates the audit catches violations that numerical matching alone cannot. - The ordinary-outputs control and per-component ablation jointly separate the contributions of reusing execution work generally versus the standardized four-component handoff specifically — a distinction most artifact papers skip. - Honest handling of negative evidence: 136 reversals are decomposed by mechanism, concentrated regressions (AuxiliaryMCMC, LiME) are dissected in detail, and construction is shown to sometimes preserve or introduce incorrect choices. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: results condition on retained papers and tested agents and are not a conference-wide reproduction rate; five reference observations are a protocol choice, not a guarantee of uncertainty estimation; numerical compatibility does not certify scientific validity and refined artifacts can preserve incorrect assumptions; automated audits miss violations (quantified); the intervention bundles upstream investigation/repair/review/packaging so the comparison does not isolate reorganizing identical outputs; ablation losses are conditional on retained materials; API savings exclude GPU, audit, verification, and maintenance costs; human time savings require a separate study. This is direct, non-minimizing confrontation of limitations — a strong credibility signal. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Single-construction-model confound: all main refined artifacts come from Opus 5; whether a weaker constructor produces artifacts with the same benefit is untested, and Opus 5's own +5.5 pp gain (floor effect) suggests artifact quality may cap at the constructor's ability. - Possible model-family circularity: construction, two of four reproducers, and the comparison auditor are all Claude models; auditor self-family bias is not examined (Codex is the primary auditor, which mitigates but does not eliminate this). - Auditor recall below 80% means success rates in the RRA condition (where only 6–10 invalid outcomes exist) are less affected than Raw (up to 173 invalidations detected, likely more undetected), but the paper does not bound how residual undetected fraud would shift the Raw-vs-RRA gap. - Reference observations come from human reproducers permitted to use coding-agent assistance under self-inspection; no independent instrumentation verifies their fidelity beyond protocol, and the assumption D=0 for references is stated but not empirically testable within the design. - Selection restricts to ICML 2026 Spotlight papers with official code — a favorable slice of already-high-visibility, artifact-friendly work; generalization to typical (non-spotlight) releases is unstated. - The 1% relative tolerance floor is applied to absolute score magnitude, which for near-zero or scale-sensitive statistics may be either too lenient or too strict; only 197 tasks have the floor active, but no sensitivity analysis on the floor itself is reported. - No confirmed public release of the benchmark, reference executions, or artifact corpus is stated, which limits independent verification despite the protocol's detail. Bottom Line: For researchers building reproduction benchmarks or artifact-evaluation infrastructure, this is now the reference point for measurement methodology (verified reference executions + validated integrity audit) and merits a close read; for the broader audience, the headline result that structured handoffs lift agent reproduction success 5.5–23.2 pp is believable and useful but modestly surprising, so the artifact specification — not the workflow machinery — is the part worth adopting.

Problem & Motivation: Frontier LLM labs increasingly train separate domain experts (medicine, law, finance, etc.) with domain-specific RL and then consolidate them into a single generalist. The dominant consolidation recipe, multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD), samples rollouts from the student and has the domain-matching teacher score them, which is expensive (teacher forcing over student rollouts every step) and known to recover domains unevenly — continued distillation can even erode a capability the starting merge already had. The alternative, training-free task-arithmetic (TA) merging, recovers less than half the base-to-teacher gap in their experiments (42.98% average recovery at 4B). Practitioners therefore face a cost/quality dilemma: heavy distillation that leaves one domain behind, or free merging that leaves most of the gap unclaimed. Key Idea: A linear combination of the student's trainable weights and the frozen experts' task vectors is itself a single differentiable model — differentiable in both the weights and the mixing coefficients — so it can be trained end-to-end under the MOPD objective. The frozen task vectors act as a bias on the optimization path, not the model class (B is unconstrained, so the parameterization represents exactly the same models): the coefficient channel moves the model along expert-aligned directions that plain full-parameter gradient updates demonstrably avoid (MOPD moves only +0.03 in α-units along the lagging medical task vector, vs +0.40–0.42 for P2-MOPD), while the weight channel adapts beyond the K-dimensional task-vector span. Methodology: The method sits inside the MOPD pipeline: each step samples student rollouts on domain-labeled prompts (128 prompts/step, 32 per domain), a routed frozen teacher scores each token on a student-defined support (top-16 with nucleus 0.99 cut), yielding a support-restricted reverse-KL reward used in a PPO-style clipped surrogate (Eq. 3), with one optimizer step per rollout batch. The reparameterization is applied to the seven linear projections of each decoder layer (attention QKVO, MLP gate/up/down); embeddings, norms, and the head train as in MOPD. Coefficients α ∈ R^{K×|M|} (1,008 scalars at 4B) are updated via the chain-rule gradient ⟨G_m, τ_{k,m}⟩ from the same, unclipped backward pass; the materialized weights then receive a two-channel AdamW step (Eq. 6) with separate gradient clipping per channel, equivalent (with weight decay 0) to optimizing B and recomposing. Initialization is the uniform TA merge with B set to the base weights and α = 0.25 per expert. The authors frame the coefficient channel as a positive semidefinite rank-K preconditioner (η_W I + η_α DD^T) under an SGD-style simplification. Three critical design decisions: (1) keeping B fully trainable so the student can leave the task-vector span — well justified by the coefficients-only ablation (+10.0/+16.9 points, vs +51.9/+62.3 for the full method); (2) module-wise coefficient granularity — justified but the weakest link: model granularity (4 scalars) matches or beats module granularity in mean recovery (96.5 at 4B, 97.2 at 1.7B), so the finer default is not clearly better; (3) computing coefficient gradients from pre-clip weight gradients with separate clipping budgets — reasonable but justified only informally. Key Results: On the IM-MOPD protocol (Qwen3-1.7B and 4B; MedQA, CaseHOLD, FinQA, IFBench; 100 steps; 8 GPUs; three training seeds for P2-MOPD, MOPD (TA init), and IM-MOPD): final average recovery 94.85±2.06 (4B) and 94.74±0.91 (1.7B) vs 83.13±9.03 and 80.93±3.02 for MOPD (TA init); worst-domain recovery 89.4/88.0 vs 47.2/32.0. P2-MOPD exceeds MOPD (TA init)'s final recovery at step 50 (92.3/90.5), and in seed-paired comparisons leads at all 24 checkpoints. Against IM-MOPD, the seed ranges do not overlap (93.5–97.2 vs 86.6–89.2 at 4B; 94.2–95.8 vs 59.0–77.4 at 1.7B). The gain is concentrated in the lagging domain (MedQA: +29.0/+48.2 recovery points) at a small FinQA cost (−1.9 at 4B). Wall-clock: 1.24×/1.09× per 100-step run (rollout generation dominates), reaching MOPD (TA init)'s final quality in ≤0.31× (4B) / ≤0.55× (1.7B) of its wall-clock. Raw score gains are +2.66/+2.17 points on the mean raw score. Baselines include MOPD, MOPD (SFT warm-up), Open-MOPD, IM-MOPD, and the TA merge — current and directly comparable, with two ablation-only exceptions (MOPD, SFT warm-up, Open-MOPD appear single-run). A notable negative finding: MOPD (TA init) at 1.7B ends below the TA start's MedQA recovery in all seeds (32.0 vs 17.15 start; MOPD from base reaches −261.18 worst-domain), i.e., distillation actively erodes the merged capability. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (with an EMPIRICAL FINDING component). The genuinely novel move is treating the student-plus-task-vector linear combination as one differentiable model trained continuously under the on-policy distillation objective, converting model merging from a discrete output operation into a live optimization prior. The ingredients — task arithmetic, learned merging coefficients (AdaMerging, DAM), interleaved merge-train schemes (IM-MOPD, merge-of-thought), and on-policy distillation — are all established; the contribution is their unification inside a single loss and the empirical demonstration that the coefficient channel supplies reachability along directions full-parameter updates do not take. This is a reparameterization trick applied to a new setting, but the mechanism analysis elevates it above a standard combination. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough and mechanism-targeted: coefficients-only vs weights-only vs both (Table 5), random-direction control (rules out extra-capacity explanations), learn-only-α_med and freeze-α_med interventions (the gain follows the medical coefficient in both directions), coefficient learning-rate sweep (η_α = 3×10⁻² fails below MOPD (TA init), showing a real tuning boundary), granularity comparison, base-model (non-merged) initialization, and task-vector projections. Three training seeds with seed-paired comparisons and ±1 sd are reported for the main comparisons; some secondary baselines are single-run. Evaluation uses the official IM-MOPD harness, fixed sampling seeds, avg@3, and raw scores reported alongside normalized recovery. Code is released at https://github.com/SinuoWang/P2-MOPD. Methodological caveats: the 1.7B teachers were trained by the authors (within one point of the released IM-MOPD teacher scores, so acceptable); the fifth benchmark (τ²-bench) was dropped because its user simulator requires a paid API; all results live on the four IM-MOPD benchmarks, and evaluation was not developed on the test set, so Goodhart risk is low. Code and protocol transparency is high (hyperparameters, update-order details, and equivalence conditions are spelled out in appendices). Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (methods run and measured on real models). - Practical: Yes — runs on 8 GPUs with memory-mapped expert checkpoints and no task vectors resident on accelerators; output is a standard checkpoint with α folded in, so inference is unchanged. - Efficient: +9–24% wall-clock per run from streaming task vectors in the actor update (73.8s vs 14.7s per-step update at 4B), but net faster to any fixed quality (≤0.31× wall-clock to match the baseline's final recovery). - Effective: The evidence shows it solves the stated problem — balanced, fast recovery of teacher capability — on the four benchmarks, though on small base-to-teacher spans (raw gain +2.17 to +2.66 points). - Scalable: Not tested beyond 4B/100 steps/4 experts; the cost structure (rollout-dominated steps) and conflict resolution among coefficients are claimed to carry, not shown, at 10× scale or with more teachers. The work delivers a software artifact (released code) plus a reusable reparameterization technique; no trained model weights are reported as released. Strengths: - The reachability analysis is the paper's real intellectual contribution: projecting per-module displacements onto the task-vector span, showing weight-only MOPD moves 13–15× less along the lagging expert's direction, and confirming that the three checkpoints recovering MedQA above 84% are exactly those moving ≥0.30 along τ_med — this converts an empirical win into an understood mechanism. - The intervention table (Table 3) is a model of causal hygiene: random directions, single-coefficient learning, coefficient freezing, and single-domain training each isolate one explanation and jointly eliminate the extra-capacity and cross-domain-conflict alternatives. - Honest cost accounting: the paper reports its own per-step slowdown, the upper-bound nature of its time-to-target figures (25-step checkpoint spacing), and the FinQA deficit paid for the medical gain. - The learned coefficients are an interpretable, seed-stable by-product (per-teacher means agree across seeds to within 0.01) that identifies the lagging teacher without validation data — useful beyond the headline metric. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper confronts limitations directly rather than minimizing them. It acknowledges: the cross-domain conflict over α_med is real and paid for by a slight FinQA deficit; module granularity is a pragmatic choice, with model tying matching it at both scales in mean recovery and layer tying dropping ~20 points at 4B; the method is sensitive to the coefficient learning rate (η_α = 3×10⁻² falls below the baseline from step 50); the time-to-target numbers are upper bounds due to checkpoint spacing; and the τ²-bench domain was omitted because its evaluation requires a paid commercial API. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Raw-score gains are modest (+2.17 to +2.66 points) while recovery gains look dramatic (+14 to +16 points); the recovery metric amplifies small raw movements when the base-to-teacher span is small (a 1-point raw change on 4B MedQA moves recovery 9.1 points). The paper reports raw scores but leads with recovery numbers. - Only K=4 experts and 4 domains; the coefficient-conflict mechanism (cosines as negative as −0.85 between domain gradients) is shown for four domains, and whether it remains tractable with 10–50 domain experts is unexamined — the method's premise is domain-expert consolidation at frontier scale. - 100 training steps is a very short horizon; long-run behavior of jointly trained coefficients (drift, oscillation, interaction with learning-rate decay) is untested. - Domain routing relies on ground-truth domain labels for every prompt — inherited from MOPD, but a real constraint for consolidation settings without clean labels. - No comparison against AdaMerging-style learned merging or other differentiable-merging baselines under matched compute, despite citing that literature; the primary control differs from the method by exactly one frozen flag, which is clean, but leaves the learned-merging literature unbenchmarked here. - Preconditioning interpretation (Eq. 8) assumes plain SGD without momentum, clipping, or decay; it motivates but does not quantitatively predict behavior under AdamW. Bottom Line: A practitioner consolidating domain experts into one model should absolutely read and try this — the reparameterization is a few lines on top of an existing MOPD pipeline, costs ~10–25% wall-clock, comes with a released implementation and the most convincing mechanism analysis I have seen in the merging-plus-distillation literature — but the evidence base (4B scale, 4 domains, 100 steps, small raw-score margins) means larger labs should validate the coefficient-conflict dynamics at their own scale before betting on it.

storing skill in context removes that coupling and the data-collection cost. - How it does it: A frozen model alternates between acting in a simulator and revising a structured Markdown memory of object roles, relative grasp/place specifications, and lessons (enforced by a linter that rejects coordinates and simulator-specific terms), then deploys the frozen memory with scene anticipation, failure recovery, and a demonstration-anchored completion check, and improves it through reflection over disjoint evaluation blocks. - The good: Retention under domain randomization is 95.2–100.8% for all three foundation models versus at most 65.1% for the strongest trained policies, and the privilege-free ablation (86.5% vs 86.0%) plus paired McNemar tests show the gains are not leaking privileged simulator information. - The missing: Per-task evaluation uses only 10 episodes per setting, all baseline numbers come from the official leaderboard rather than being rerun under identical seeds/protocols, all tasks involve rigid or articulated objects only, and real-robot validation is 4 tasks × 10 episodes with offline pre-planned sequences. - Read it or not: Worth a full read for anyone working on agentic manipulation, LLM-agent memory, or sim-to-real transfer, because it is the strongest evidence to date that context-stored skill can beat weight-stored skill on a standard benchmark; Problem & Motivation: Robotic manipulation research and deployment face a structural constraint: the dominant approach trains an action policy (VLA or world action model), which binds learned skill to the training distribution. Each new task, scene layout, or visual domain requires new demonstrations and gradient updates, and policies degrade sharply under shift (e.g., π0.5 loses 24.7 points from clean to randomized RoboTwin 2.0; FastWAM loses 75.9). In-context learning with frozen models avoids retraining but has underperformed because a demonstration recorded in another scene carries no feedback about the world the robot currently faces — errors accumulate with no outcome signal. The paper targets the gap between these two paradigms: can a robot learn a task in its context as well as it learns one in its weights, using only one demonstration and no gradient updates? Key Idea: The core insight is that knowledge acquired in context is semantic — object roles, task steps, relative geometry, and failure lessons — not visual appearance. Therefore experience rehearsed in one world (a cheap, faithful, resettable simulator) transfers to any other world that agrees on task semantics, including randomized simulator scenes and, with a light embodiment adapter, a physical robot. This is formalized as WICL: extend ICL with world feedback, exactly as RL extends imitation learning, but write the feedback into the context instead of the weights; the semantic-transfer argument (σ(W) = σ(W′)) explains why a simulator suffices for learning and generalization survives distribution shift. Methodology: RoboScript implements a four-stage lifecycle with frozen weights throughout. (1) Skill building: an agent segments demonstrations of all 50 tasks at gripper events, identifies primitives not covered by shared entry points, and writes environment-specific skills via a coding agent; a driver gate validates each skill with static checks and transfer checks across demonstrations whose objects lie ≥5 cm apart, rejecting replay-like fits. (2) Task learning: from one demonstration, an imitation stage (S1) writes an initial Task Memory and practices on the demonstration instance; a rehearsal stage (S2) practices on fresh training instances where only the first attempt counts, a reviewing role (which may read ground-truth failure diagnosis) proposes typed edits to a cached copy, and edits merge only if the retry succeeds, with edit budgets and step sizes that shrink with experience. The Task Memory is a linter-checked Markdown document of object roles, workflow stages, relative GraspSpec/PlaceSpec parameters, and lessons. (3) Deployment: the frozen memory guides acting on unseen instances using only deployable data (RGB-D, proprioception), with scene anticipation, arm selection, no-reset failure recovery, and a completion check against the demonstration's final state. (4) Recursive self-improvement (RSI): a reflection agent reads episode records from disjoint evaluation blocks (deployable data plus success flags only) and writes guidance for the next, always-unseen block. Data isolation is architectural: a two-tier deployable/privileged interface, a tool hub that refuses privileged calls in evaluation stages, and a memory linter rejecting coordinates, ground-truth terms, and instance identifiers. The critical design decisions — semantic-only memory representation, strict data tiers, and one-demonstration anchoring — are each directly ablated and well justified (see Key Results). Note that Eq. (1)'s update operator U is not a single algorithm but an orchestrated multi-role LLM loop; the mathematical formalism is notation for the pipeline rather than an optimizable objective. Key Results: On all 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks (1,000 episodes per model: 10 episodes × 50 tasks × 2 settings), RoboScript with GPT-6.1-Sol reaches 83.6% clean / 83.2% randomized (mean 83.4%, Wilson 95% CI 81.0–85.6) from one demonstration per task with no gradient updates. The strongest trained policy, 4D-WAM trained on 50 demonstrations per task, reaches 81.5/41.8 (mean 61.7); π0.5 reaches 70.7/46.0; FastWAM 77.8/1.9. GPT-5.6-Luna and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash reach means of 77.9% and 78.1%, both above every trained policy, with identical code and prompts. Retention (randomized/clean) is 95.2–100.8% for RoboScript versus ≤65.1% for trained policies. Ablations (10 tasks, paired seeds, exact McNemar p-values) show: without the demonstration, rehearsal from instruction alone drops to 56.5% (p=0.004 vs 68.0% instruction-only without rehearsal); demonstration written to memory without world interaction gives 69.0% vs 78.5% with it (p=0.003); removing recovery drops 78.5→69.0; the privilege-free variant reaches 86.5% vs 86.0% full. RSI yields net rescued-minus-broken episodes of +18, +7, +1 over three rounds across all 50 tasks. Real-robot transfer to a dual-arm PiPER (different kinematics, no re-rehearsal) succeeds on 10/10, 7/10, 7/10, 6/10 episodes across four tasks. Failure analysis over 166 failed Sol episodes attributes 22/17 to perception, 37/38 to knowledge, 23/29 to execution (clean/randomized), with 28–29% false acceptances. Cost: $308 (Luna) to $1,911 (Sol) for learning all 50 tasks plus 1,000 evaluation episodes at list API prices; median 6.4 minutes per deployment episode. The baseline set is current (2025–2026 VLAs/WAMs from the official leaderboard), but numbers are taken from the leaderboard/published reports, not rerun by the authors. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (WICL — extending in-context learning with world feedback written to context, with a transfer argument and disjoint-block RSI protocol), NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (RoboScript infrastructure with enforced data isolation), and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (context-stored skill beating weight-stored skill on a standard benchmark under distribution shift). The individual ingredients — Reflexion/Voyager/ExpeL-style experiential memory, coding-agent skill writing, simulator feedback, receipt-based action APIs — are all established; the genuinely novel move is composing them into a gradient-free manipulation learner whose knowledge provably stays in the deployable data tier, plus the empirical demonstration that this closes the gap to trained policies on RoboTwin 2.0. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually careful: paired seeds within groups, exact McNemar p-values, a privilege-free control that removes all privileged supervision (86.5% vs 86.0%), per-task paired change plots, and task-level bootstrap intervals. Uncertainty is reported via Wilson intervals per model and task-resampling intervals; frozen memories re-evaluated on four additional disjoint seed blocks score 83.0–85.2%, supporting stability. Failure labels were cross-validated by a second model (Cohen's κ = 0.82). Concerns: (1) baseline numbers are leaderboard self-reports evaluated on 100 episodes vs RoboScript's 10 episodes per task per setting, so per-task statistical power is thin and protocol equivalence is not verified by the authors; (2) skill building consumes demonstrations from all 50 tasks, so the "one demonstration per task" claim is accurate at the task-memory level but the shared skill set is learned from 50 demonstrations; (3) main evaluation is in simulation on the same benchmark used for development, with only 4 real-robot tasks; (4) API nondeterminism can shift results by several points between sessions, acknowledged and partially controlled via paired endpoints. Code is released at https://github.com/ArcheOne-AI/RoboScript with a project page; foundation models are commercial APIs. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS (a built infrastructure evaluated by deployment in simulation and on hardware). - Practical: Runs on 16 RTX 4090s plus commercial model APIs, but depends on frontier closed models (GPT-6.1-Sol) rather than locally hostable weights. - Efficient: No training compute, but inference is expensive and slow — 54.7 model calls, 2.33M tokens, and a median 6.4 minutes per episode, roughly 80% of wall time spent waiting on the foundation model. - Effective: Solves the stated problem in simulation convincingly (83.4% mean, near-flat retention) and partially on real hardware (30/40 episodes across 4 tasks), though the real-robot tests use offline pre-planned sequences under human supervision. - Scalable: Not stress-tested; per-task learning costs $6–38 at current prices and rehearsal convergence failed on a minority of tasks for weaker models, so scaling to hundreds of tasks or tight-loop real-time control is claimed via the modular architecture but not demonstrated. Deliverables: an open-source system (RoboScript platform and WICL implementation), reusable Task Memory artifacts, and a reproducible protocol; the paper does not ship trained model weights (by design, weights are frozen). Strengths: - The semantic-transfer hypothesis is operationalized and enforced, not just asserted: the linter, two-tier data architecture, and privilege-free ablation (86.5% vs 86.0%) jointly make a falsifiable claim about where the performance comes from, which most agentic-memory papers omit. - The evaluation discipline exceeds the field's norm: paired seeds, McNemar tests, disjoint rehearsal/evaluation blocks that preclude memorization, four independent re-evaluation seed blocks, and inter-annotator agreement on failure attribution. - The demonstration-vs-world decomposition (Table 2, group 2) is an informative finding in itself: without world interaction, showing the demonstration at deployment adds ≤1.5 points over instruction-only memory, isolating rehearsal — not the demo content in context — as the active ingredient beyond anchoring. - Honest cost accounting at list API prices, including the counter-intuitive result that the cheap model (Flash) costs 2.4× more than Sol due to 19× longer outputs per call. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that reliance on commercial APIs introduces session-to-session variance of several points; inference is slow relative to trained policies; RSI net gains shrink rapidly (+18 → +7 → +1) as easy failure modes are exhausted and sparse success signals hamper attribution of remaining failures; and all evaluated tasks involve rigid or articulated objects, with deformables (cloth, cables) and tightly coordinated bimanual contact remaining open. These limitations are stated directly and quantified in the appendix rather than minimized — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Baseline comparability: trained-policy numbers are taken from the official leaderboard at 100 episodes/task with unspecified seed alignment, while RoboScript uses 10 episodes/task/setting; a fully paired rerun of at least the top 2–3 baselines would materially strengthen the 21.7-point headline claim. - Skill building uses demonstrations of all 50 tasks, so cross-task skill sharing is partially responsible for the "one demo per task" result; no ablation isolates skill-building data scope. - No comparison against the strongest in-context manipulation systems (e.g., Skild S1, GEN-1.5, Zero-WAM are cited but not evaluated on RoboTwin 2.0), so the claim that prior ICL "has not matched trained policies" is supported by citation rather than measurement on this benchmark. - The transfer argument σ(W) = σ(W′) is an informal assumption, not a checkable condition; no experiment varies world faithfulness (e.g., a deliberately imperfect simulator or learned world model) to find where semantic transfer breaks. - The 28–29% false-acceptance rate means the agent's self-assessment disagrees with the official check roughly every third failure, yet no mechanism targets this systematically in the RSI loop. - Real-robot success requires offline full-sequence planning, which removes the online recovery behavior that drives much of the simulation advantage — the real-robot result therefore tests memory transfer, not the deployed agentic loop. Bottom Line: This is a landmark empirical demonstration that gradient-free, context-stored skill can beat weight-stored policies on a standard manipulation benchmark under distribution shift, and practitioners in agentic robotics or LLM-agent memory should read and build on it — but the per-task sample sizes, leaderboard baselines, simulation-dominant evaluation, and minute-scale inference mean it complements rather than replaces trained policies for real deployment today.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Longtail-SWE, a benchmark of 202 repository-level issue-resolution tasks across 13 underrepresented programming languages (Clojure, Dart, Elixir, Erlang, F#, Haskell, Julia, Kotlin, Lua, OCaml, R, Scala, Swift), built with a solver–judge–repairer pipeline that repairs defective task descriptions and tests instead of discarding candidates. - Why it's important: Sparse task pools in non-mainstream language ecosystems mean that strict filtering (as in SWE-bench Multilingual) biases benchmarks toward small, unambiguous code changes, leaving no reliable evidence on how well coding agents work with these toolchains. - How it does it: A solver attempts each candidate task, a judge panel (three sequential LLM judges) diagnoses whether failures stem from the agent or from task defects, and a repair agent revises tests and appends clarifications to the statement while keeping the reference patch frozen, with iterative revalidation until all three judges accept. - The good: The paired ablation on 63 tasks with unchanged descriptions is the strongest evidence: identical Opus 5.5 trajectories improve from 29.1% to 67.2% Pass@1 purely from test repairs, directly demonstrating that the pipeline fixes false-negative evaluation, and the end-to-end funnel yields 202 final tasks versus 68 via the baseline SWE-rebench V2 path (a 2.97× yield increase counting only final A-grade annotations). - The missing: The human validation of the judge pipeline rests on only 65 tasks with very low inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's κ = 0.15), and the authors concede it does not establish the residual defect rate of the released benchmark, which would require an independent audit of the final 202 tasks. - Read it or not: Worth reading for benchmark builders and anyone evaluating coding agents beyond Python/JavaScript — the pipeline recipe and honest threat analysis are the reusable contributions — but model-selection readers only need Tables 1–2.

Problem & Motivation: Repository-level issue-resolution benchmarks (SWE-bench and descendants) are dominated by a few languages; teams building coding agents have no reliable evaluation for ecosystems like Erlang, OCaml, or F#. Extending coverage is hard because candidate tasks from historical issue–PR pairs frequently have defective tests (rejecting valid alternative implementations, requiring undocumented APIs) or underspecified descriptions, and standard filtering discards these. In scarce candidate pools, such filtering can eliminate the majority of usable tasks and systematically biases benchmarks toward small code changes — a problem SWE-bench Multilingual's own release notes acknowledge. The gap is a construction method that retains and repairs such candidates rather than dropping them. Key Idea: Use the solver's own failure (and success) modes as diagnostic signal: run solver attempts on each candidate, have a judge panel attribute failures to the agent versus the task (bad tests, underspecified description, environment defects), and route task defects to a repair agent constrained to keep the reference patch and original statement text immutable — appending clarifications and generalizing/adding tests only. This converts task-defect filtering (discard) into task-defect repair (retain), which matters precisely where candidates are scarce. Methodology: The pipeline has four stages built on SWE-rebench V2: (1) Collection via GitHub API of merged PRs linked to single issues, with LLM (Kimi K3) semantic screening that retains well-specified tasks (A) plus two repairable defect categories (B2: tests require unstated names/values; B5: tests may encode incidental implementation details); (2) Construction: an auditor agent installs each repo in versioned Docker images, determines native build/test commands, hides implementation hints in the statement ([HIDDEN] placeholders), and may pre-repair tests, followed by strict reproducibility checks (FAIL_TO_PASS and PASS_TO_PASS test groups verified at base and post-reference-patch states in clean containers); (3) Repair: an iterative solver–judge–repairer loop (up to 5 rounds per cycle, mean 4.2 rounds overall) where three sequential judges — GPT 5.6 Luna (xhigh), GPT 5.6 Terra (high), Kimi K3 (high) — must unanimously accept; description repairs freeze the statement before test-only repair proceeds with fresh solver attempts; (4) Finalization: difficulty calibration via three Qwen 3.8 27B runs (excluding tasks solved 3/3 unless a per-language minimum of 15 requires them), then post-evaluation validation over 5,688 stored solver attempts that excluded 35 more tasks. Evaluation follows the SWE-bench protocol (fresh container, solver test-file changes discarded). Success requires all F2P and P2P tests passing. Critical design decisions: (a) immutable reference patch and append-only description repair — justified as protecting task intent, though the authors admit the contract can still shift; (b) unanimous three-judge acceptance — biased toward sensitivity (87.5% precision, 96.1% recall on defect detection), deliberately trading compute for defect-catching; (c) per-language minimum-retention rules during difficulty filtering — necessary for per-language analysis but introduces model-dependent selection (acknowledged for Qwen). Key Results: Nine model configurations were evaluated on the 202 tasks (three attempts each, SWE-agent-like scaffold). Opus 5.5 (high) leads with 81.52% Pass@1 (±1.16 SEM), 89.11% Pass@3, 73.76% All-3; GPT 6.1 Sol (high) follows at 78.38% Pass@1 with the lowest token cost (1.75M mean tokens, 27.4 steps); Qwen 3.6 27B (thinking) trails at 16.67% Pass@1. Per-language averaged Pass@1 ranges from 73.5% (Erlang) to 48.1% (Clojure) — a ~1.5× spread. Qwen 3.8 27B pass@k over ten runs rises from 43.8% (k=1) to 73.3% (k=10), with 26.7% of tasks unsolved after ten attempts. Construction ablation: combined auditor + expanded screening raises strict execution-validation passes from 377/1,096 (34.4%) to 1,247/2,640 (47.2%), with dramatic per-language gains (Kotlin 6→86, Scala 2→78, Swift 9→54). The paired test-repair ablation on 63 unchanged-description tasks shows Opus Pass@1 jumping 29.1%→67.2% and Qwen pass@10 36.5%→68.3% against identical trajectories. A single-judge audit of the 364 baseline-pipeline tasks flagged quality issues in 90.1% (82.4% hidden-test problems, 88.7% insufficient coverage). Human judge validation (65 tasks): 87.5% precision, 96.1% recall for defect detection, but only 50% specificity on acceptable tasks and κ = 0.15 between annotators. Baselines compared are contemporary frontier models; scale is modest (202 tasks, 12–27 per language). Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK plus NEW METHOD (the solver–judge–repairer pipeline). The genuinely novel element is the coordinated, constraint-bound repair of both descriptions and tests using solver trajectories as diagnostic evidence, with unanimous multi-judge acceptance — prior work either filters (SWE-bench Verified, SWE-Bench++), augments tests alone (UTBoost, SWE-ABS), or audits without repair (SPICE, Auto Benchmark Audit). The underlying task format, Docker-based evaluation, and F2P/P2P mechanics are standard SWE-bench machinery; SWE-Marathon's trajectory-informed defect triage is the closest precedent, and this paper is candid about building on it. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and well-designed: the construction-pipeline ablation (Table 3), the end-to-end funnel (Table 4), and especially the fixed-trajectory pre/post-repair comparison (Table 5) isolate which components matter. SEM is reported for Pass@1; three attempts per task per model; the Qwen pass@k analysis uses ten runs. No significance tests beyond SEM. The release is unusually complete: all 202 tasks, an easier companion set, Docker images, all construction/evaluation tooling, prompts, and all agent trajectories at github.com/SWE-rebench/Longtail-SWE (MIT code, CC BY 4.0 data). Methodological concerns the authors flag: difficulty selection used Qwen 3.8 27B, potentially biasing that model's reported scores; some evaluated models (Kimi K3, GPT 5.6 family) participated in construction, possibly benefiting from task interpretations; training-data contamination from public issues/PRs cannot be ruled out. The judge validation set (65 tasks) is small with weak annotator agreement. The high single-judge rejection rate (90.1%) on baseline tasks is self-reported by a judge of the authors' own design and not human-verified on that full set. Deployability: (profile: EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS):** - Practical: Yes — tasks run in per-task Docker images on standard hardware; agents interact via a SWE-agent-like scaffold with public prompts. - Efficient: Construction is expensive (4.2 repair rounds average, ~2.8–3.3M tokens per auditor/repairer trajectory, three sequential judges per task), but the released artifact offloads that cost; evaluation cost is conventional, with token usage per model reported (1.75M–38.28M mean tokens per task). - Effective: The paired ablation shows the repaired tests genuinely change verdicts in the intended direction (29.1%→67.2% Pass@1 on fixed trajectories), and human audit supports judge recall — though the residual defect rate of the final 202 tasks is unmeasured. - Scalable: Only claimed, not tested — the pipeline processed 3,261 candidates to produce 202 tasks; whether the judge–repair loop maintains yield and quality at 10× scale or on larger pools is unexamined. The work delivers a concrete software/dataset artifact (benchmark, environments, tooling, trajectories), not just a paper. Strengths: - The fixed-trajectory paired evaluation (63 tasks, unchanged descriptions) is a genuinely clever ablation design: holding solver outputs byte-identical and varying only the tests cleanly attributes the 38.1-point Pass@1 change to test repair. - The paper distinguishes false-positive and false-negative test defects and provides worked case studies of each (an Elixir charlist constraint; Haskell NoThunks coverage gaps), making the repair taxonomy concrete rather than hand-wavy. - Exceptional release completeness (tasks, environments, prompts, all trajectories, tooling) makes the pipeline itself reproducible, not just the benchmark. - The threat-to-validity section confronts its own weaknesses directly — including the low judge specificity (50%), the κ = 0.15 annotator agreement, and potential circularity from models judging benchmarks they helped build. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state: (1) the human audit does not establish the final benchmark's error rate; (2) difficulty selection may bias Qwen 3.8's reported scores; (3) construction-participating models may score inflated; (4) contamination from public training data cannot be excluded, though date-restricted collection offers a partial mitigation; (5) 12–27 tasks per language means language-level comparisons reflect these specific tasks, not inherent language difficulty; (6) repairs may still alter the task contract despite the immutable reference patch; (7) the judge's low specificity wastes compute on unnecessary repair. This is an unusually direct and honest limitations treatment — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The judge validation covers pipeline-stage tasks, not the final released benchmark; the claimed 97% post-repair A-annotation rate comes from the same LLM annotator (Kimi K3) whose category definitions the pipeline was built around — a self-referential quality loop with no independent verification. - The 90.1% defect rate claimed for the SWE-rebench V2 baseline pool was assessed by a single GPT 5.6 Luna judge, and the paper offers no human spot-check of that figure — the 2.97× yield advantage could be partially an artifact of one model's leniency. - Contamination asymmetry is unexamined: models differ in training cutoffs, and newer frontier models may have seen the underlying PRs (repos required updates on/after January 1, 2026, and evaluation appears to have followed quickly); the date-restriction mitigation is described but not actually applied in the reported evaluation. - Per-language sample sizes (12–27) with prioritization toward larger patches make cross-language conclusions fragile, and the equal-averaging across nine heterogeneous model configurations for language rankings is an arbitrary aggregation choice. - No RL/training use is evaluated — since the pipeline is motivated partly by reliable reward environments, showing that repaired tasks yield cleaner RL signals would substantially strengthen the contribution. Bottom Line: Benchmark builders and anyone evaluating coding agents outside the Python/JS mainstream should read this — the repair-not-discard pipeline and the fixed-trajectory ablation methodology are immediately reusable — though model-selection readers can skip it since its leaderboard largely confirms expected frontier-model ordering, and the released benchmark's residual defect rate remains unverified.

Problem & Motivation: Practitioners serving large language models want 4-bit weights and activations (W4A4) to cut memory and compute, but microscaling FP4 formats make activation outliers destructive. Modern fixes — QuaRot, DuQuant, FlatQuant — change the basis of each layer (rotations, per-channel scales) and then propagate the activation-side transform backward into preceding layers (norms, projections, residual adds) so no runtime transform is needed. This creates engineering burden: every new architecture requires finding valid absorption targets for each layer, some layers cannot absorb transforms at all, and the propagation makes quantization inherently cross-layer, slow (GPTQ sweeps the model), and memory-hungry. MACaQ argues the field should simply tolerate the small runtime cost of applying transforms online, in exchange for total layer locality. Key Idea: The core insight is that the activation-side transform cost is amortized across output channels: a per-channel scale plus a block-Hadamard of block size 32 costs Tn(log₂32 + 1) operations versus 2Tmn for the matrix multiply, giving an overhead ratio of 3/m that shrinks with output dimension (below 0.3% arithmetic ratio at m=1024). Keeping these transforms online means every quantization decision stays inside one linear layer, enabling streaming calibration (one layer in GPU memory at a time) and a fast replacement for GPTQ: Flip-Refinement, a Hessian-aware coordinate descent over adjacent FP4 grid points with closed-form move gains. Methodology: MACaQ quantizes each linear layer in four steps: (i) per-channel balancing with scale t_j = (σ^W_j)^α / (rms_x_j)^(1−α), α=0.75, computed from the Hessian diagonal; (ii) a fixed block-diagonal Hadamard rotation B of block size 32 (matching the MXFP4 microscaling block so outliers don't leak across independently scaled blocks), with X' = XDB and W' = WD⁻¹B absorbed offline; (iii) Hessian-weighted E8M0 exponent selection screening offsets {+1, 0, −1} around the block max; (iv) Flip-Refinement, a greedy coordinate descent minimizing the ridge-regularized output-reconstruction objective ||XW^T − XW̃^T||²_F (Hessian H_f = B^T D H D B + λ·mean(diag)·I, λ=1.0), where each accepted code flip of size Δ yields gain 2Δg_ij − Δ²(H_f)_jj and gradients update incrementally as g ← g − Δ(H_f)_:,j. Rows run in parallel; converged rows drop from the active set. Design decisions: keeping the block exponent fixed during flips bounds each code to 2 candidate moves (enabling closed-form gains) — justified by speed; block size 32 for the rotation matches the MXFP4 scale grouping — well-motivated by prior work on block-local rotations; α and λ tuned on a WikiText-2 train subset of Llama-3-8B with sensitivity plots in the appendix showing flat response. Key Results: Perplexity (OCP MXFP4 W4A4, calibrated on WikiText-2 train): MACaQ reaches 6.90/11.01 (Wiki2/C4) on Llama-3-8B vs FP16's 6.14/9.46, beating the best baseline (MR-GPTQ, 7.13/11.37) on all six models tested, including Qwen3.5-35B-A3B MoE (6.66/11.21 vs 6.73/11.28 for DuQuant++ GPTQ). Quantization time on Llama-3-8B: MACaQ at 2×10⁵ calibration tokens and K=128 flips quantizes in ~150s and matches baselines' best perplexity — an 11x speedup; Table 7 shows 6.87 perplexity in 193s where DuQuant++ (GPTQ) needs 624s for 7.16. Large-model run: Qwen3.5-122B-A10B quantized in 64 minutes with 32.5GB peak GPU RAM (FP16 weights need ~244GB), yielding Wiki2 perplexity 5.14 vs 5.06 FP16. Inference: 3.06x end-to-end decode speedup over FP16 on Qwen3-32B at batch 1 (69.8 vs 22.8 tok/s in vLLM), with online scale+rotation costing 2.3% decode overhead at 32B, ~8% at 0.6B; kernel-level overhead ≤6% for N=4096 and <3% for N=16384. Generative tasks (k=10 seeds, standard errors reported): Qwen3-32B IFEval 83.20%±0.26 vs FP16's 83.60%±0.25 (MR-GPTQ: 82.81%), MATH-500 97.26%±0.11 vs 97.78%±0.10. Image diffusion: on FLUX.2 Klein 4B (GenEval2, 800 prompts, DiT-only W4A4), MACaQ MXFP4 beats the official NVFP4 checkpoint on all four fidelity metrics (PSNR 15.04 vs 14.85, LPIPS 0.218 vs 0.235) using 4.25 vs 4.50 bits/weight. Ablation (Table 5): each component contributes comparably — exponent search −0.19, micro-rotation −0.44, second scale −0.57, flips −0.21 perplexity versus RTN's 8.28. Baselines are current (DuQuant++ is 2026 work; MR-GPTQ is an ICLR 2026 microscaling method); testing scale is standard LLM quantization scale plus one 122B MoE. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (Flip-Refinement as a fast Hessian-aware coordinate-descent alternative to GPTQ for weight-activation quantization, plus Hessian-weighted shared-exponent selection) and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the quantified claim that online transforms cost only 2–3% at deployable model sizes, making layer-local quantization viable). The ingredients — Hadamard rotations (QuIP/QuaRot), per-channel balancing (SmoothQuant), coordinate-descent quantization (QuantEase/CDQuant) — are existing ideas; the genuinely new move is refusing to absorb the activation transform into neighbors and demonstrating the runtime penalty is small, plus the closed-form adjacent-code flip gains over MXFP4's non-uniform E2M1 grid. The appendix extension of Flip-Refinement to vector-quantized llama.cpp codebooks (nearest-codeword search under the Hessian metric) is a competent, useful generalization rather than a headline contribution. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong for this area. Component ablation is present (Table 5) and shows each piece matters; hyperparameter sensitivity plots (Fig. 5) show flat response to α and λ; generative evaluations report standard errors over 10 seeds and bold results within one standard error of baseline — a refreshingly conservative convention; the Pareto comparison sweeps both calibration tokens and flip count with per-run times (Table 7), not just a single operating point. Both in-distribution (Wiki2) and OOD (C4) perplexity are reported. Code is released at https://github.com/huawei-csl/MACaQ. Concerns: (1) α=0.75 and λ=1.0 were selected on Llama-3-8B with WikiText-2 — the same model/distribution used for the headline perplexity table, a mild Goodhart risk, though OOD C4 results corroborate; (2) the paper honestly discloses that DuQuant++ comparisons use a compliant E8M0 cast that slightly worsens DuQuant++'s own published numbers, and it re-ran all baselines itself — good practice, but vendor-of-the-method self-implementation of baselines always carries tuning-favoritism risk; (3) the appendix block-refinement results (Table 8) candidly show exact block minimization sometimes hurts perplexity versus scalar flips — the authors report this faithfully rather than hiding it, which increases credibility; (4) hardware is described only as "a recent GPU with 504 TFLOPS FP16," not named precisely. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS component — Triton kernels and a vLLM integration actually shipped). - Practical: Yes — quantization runs on a single 96GB GPU (even for a 122B model, via lazy layer loading) and the quantized 32B model serves on standard vLLM with released Triton kernels. - Efficient: Quantization is up to 11x faster than GPTQ-based baselines; inference overhead of the online transforms is 2.3% decode at 32B scale, rising to 8% at 0.6B, while still delivering ~3x speedup over FP16. - Effective: Evidence covers proxy (perplexity) and closer-to-production metrics (IFEval, MATH-500 with seed-level error bars; image fidelity vs BF16) — the method solves the stated problem on all tested architectures, though it cannot close the FP16 gap (0.76 perplexity on Llama-3-8B). - Scalable: Partially tested — 122B MoE quantization is demonstrated, and the overhead formula predicts shrinking cost with size, but no end-to-end inference throughput is reported for the 122B model and the 8% overhead at sub-1B scale is untested below 0.6B. Delivers a software artifact: quantization pipeline, Triton kernels, vLLM integration, llama.cpp extension, code on GitHub. Strengths: - The layer-locality argument is quantified, not hand-waved: a closed-form cost analysis (overhead ∝ 3/m) is paired with kernel-level and end-to-end measurements that confirm the prediction's shape across model sizes. - Flip-Refinement is a genuine algorithmic contribution: exploiting the quadratic objective to get closed-form gains for adjacent E2M1 moves with incremental Hessian gradient updates achieves GPTQ-beating quality at a fraction of the time, and the appendix shows the same machinery extends to vector-quantized codebooks via a k-means-style nearest-neighbor reformulation. - Honest negative results are reported (exact block minimization can worsen perplexity; scale refinement doesn't help), and baseline comparisons include a disclosed format-compliance correction that works against the authors' headline win — both are credibility positives. - Architecture-agnosticism is demonstrated, not claimed: the identical per-layer pipeline quantizes dense LLMs, an MoE, and a diffusion DiT (FLUX.2) without architecture-specific code. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state three: (1) layer locality forbids cross-layer error compensation — a second pass could add it but at the cost of slower quantization; (2) MoE experiments quantize only expert layers for practicality; (3) the online-transform overhead reaches 8% on the smallest tested model (0.6B). This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No comparison against training-time quantized models (QAT) or against NVFP4/int8 serving paths on the LLM side — the NVFP4 baseline appears only for the diffusion model; a practitioner choosing between MXFP4 MACaQ and, say, AWQ W4A16 + Marlin (which the kernel table shows can be faster in decode at some shapes, e.g., 5.04 vs 8.26 relative speedup at N=16384, B=1 favors Marlin) gets no end-to-end guidance on the W4A16-vs-W4A4 trade-off beyond kernel microbenchmarks. - The 2.3% overhead figure comes from Qwen3-32B at batch 1, context 512; long-context prefill (where the transform's Tn scaling matters more relative to compute-bound GEMMs) is shown only at kernel level (1.6–6.4% SR cost), and batched small-model serving economics are not analyzed. - Quality is evaluated only on perplexity plus two generative benchmarks; no long-context generation, no multilingual, and no downstream accuracy suite — accumulation effects the authors themselves argue motivate generative testing could still surface in regimes they don't test. - Hyperparameters (α, λ, K) are tuned on Llama-3-8B/WikiText-2; the Qwen3.5-122B run uses a fixed recipe (32 flips, 512K tokens) whose selection is not justified — likely fine given flat sensitivity, but unverified at MoE scale. - Peak 32.5GB GPU RAM during 122B quantization implies Hessian statistics for some layers exceed what fits (244GB of FP16 weights are streamed), but the memory accounting across calibration hooks, Hessians, and streamed layers is not broken out, making reproduction on smaller GPUs (e.g., 80GB) uncertain. Bottom Line: For anyone deploying 4-bit weight-activation LLM inference, this paper is worth reading in full — it delivers a measurably better quality/time/memory trade-off than the current MXFP4 state of the art with released code, and its layer-local reframing is likely to become the default engineering assumption for the next generation of quantization pipelines, even though small-model and long-context regimes still favor absorbed-transform methods.

ErosionBench: Probing Alignment Decay in Enterprise Multi- Agent Systems

R Bharathwaj, A Prabhakar, R Ram, A Kothari, S Tan… · arxiv.org · generating environments for agent testing in enterprises - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces ErosionBench, a 1,728-scenario executable benchmark for cross-session erosion of shared multi-agent state (attacks assembled from individually benign messages), plus a reference defense, the calibrated Meta-Auditor, that reaches 98.5% detection recall at a 2.9% benign false-positive rate on a 906-scenario held-out split. - Why it's important: Enterprise multi-agent deployments can be compromised through attacks no single message reveals, and the paper shows existing perimeter defenses (LlamaFirewall, Progent, ShieldGemma) suppress attacks only by over-refusing 54–92% of legitimate work — so a low attack-success rate in prior evaluations conceals a broken safety–utility trade-off. - How it does it: Scenarios are generated from deterministic state graphs executed by a four-role agent mesh (Gateway/Orchestrator/Policy/Deployment) over a shared ledger, verification scores the realized tool call against machine-checkable intent contracts rather than output text, and the Meta-Auditor combines near-zero-FPR deterministic state anchors (SDI/CII/VAD) with a Platt/conformal-calibrated semantic monitor and a grey-zone arbitration call. - The good: The same-telemetry ablation is decisive — an uncalibrated LLM judge on identical telemetry hits 97.8% recall but at 67.6% FPR, while the auditor's ROC dominates the judge's everywhere (AUC 0.998 vs 0.976), showing the gain comes from calibration and heterogeneous evidence, not a tuned threshold; Problem & Motivation: Enterprises are replacing single-agent chatbots with multi-agent meshes (gateway, orchestration, policy, deployment roles) connected through shared memory and consequential tools. The motivating failure: an attacker plants a benign-looking artifact URL in one session; a peer agent later reads it from the shared ledger as vetted provenance; a downstream agent finally passes it as a `weights_url` argument to a production deployment. No single message is malicious, so per-agent boundary filters never see the campaign. Existing benchmarks either expose one agent to a directly malicious input (AgentHarm, BIPIA, AgentDojo) or score multi-agent attacks by final output only (TAMAS, MAStrike), leaving cross-session erosion of persistent shared state unmeasured — and, critically, none scores benign over-refusal alongside attack success, so a defense can look safe while blocking most legitimate work. Key Idea: The core insight is that verification must shift from surface content to process: score the realized tool call against authorized intent and provenance using deterministic contracts over a shared state ledger, and detect attacks by auditing the trajectory (state divergence, causal provenance, policy-debate capitulation) rather than any message — which makes detection channel-invariant (text vs. image delivery becomes transparent) and immune to intent dispersal. The second half of the idea is that over-refusal is manufactured by forcing borderline trajectories into hard verdicts; a grey-zone band routed to explicit arbitration recovers the recall–FPR frontier. Methodology: Three stages. (1) Generation: per domain, a state graph fixes benign intent, the consequential tool, safe arguments, and ground-truth contracts; a generator renders enterprise documents with a spliced attack needle (with a canonical splicer guaranteeing 0/1,728 generator refusals); three validation gates (deterministic reach, semantic quality, ground-truth firing) filter scenarios; a mutator expands T1→T3 tiers by mechanism (more priming sessions, longer documents — T3 buries the payload ~70% into a 50-page corpus, ledger rewrites, or added colluding agents). Output: 1,728 scenarios (1,296 malicious / 432 benign) across 4 domains × 4 mechanisms = 16 attack classes, each OWASP-labeled; 66 families additionally rendered as document-image PNGs (198 cells) paired 1:1 with text cells. (2) Execution: a FastAPI sandbox runs a state-machine-sequenced four-agent mesh; the compromised agent reacts to contradicting agents (reactive, not scripted). (3) Meta-Auditor: a synchronous SDI edge-guard (typed distance between authorized vs. proposed critical values; the only pre-execution veto, near-zero FPR by design), asynchronous deterministic anchors CII (fraction of payload values traceable to unverified ledger writes) and VAD (policy-agent capitulation timing after prior resistance), a semantic monitor producing a continuous intent-divergence score, Platt scaling plus conformal threshold selection on a family-disjoint calibration split (1,124 scenarios), and grey-zone arbitration for the 439/906 borderline trajectories. Detection metrics: 98.5% recall / 2.9% FPR on the 906-scenario held-out split (453/453). Critical design decisions: authoring scenarios as state graphs before prose (well-justified — makes every state change attributable); scoring the attempt, not the outcome (well-justified via the AgentDojo resisted-arm result); withholding benign-twin diffs and labels from the auditor (sound leakage hygiene). The verifier composition shifted during development from an OR-gate (22.1% benign FPR) to a calibrated conjunction plus arbitration — the ablation in Table 3a justifies this. Key Results: On the family-disjoint 906-scenario held-out split (gpt-5.5 mesh, opus-4-8 auditor): the undefended mesh admits 43.9% of attacks (199/453), rising monotonically across tiers (T1 35.1% → T3 51.7%, p=0.004). LlamaFirewall cuts ASR to 10.2% but refuses 92.5% of benign jobs; Progent 4.9% ASR at 64.0% FPR; ShieldGemma-27B 27.8% ASR at 54.3% FPR. The isolated single agent reaches 0.0% ASR but cannot complete 48.3% of legitimate work. The Meta-Auditor reaches 1.3% residual ASR at 2.9% FPR (recall 98.5%); the uncalibrated judge on identical telemetry: 97.8% recall at 67.6% FPR. Auditor panel (fixed mesh): claude-opus-4-8 98.5%/2.9%, claude-sonnet-4-6 95.8%/8.6%, gpt-5.1 84.1%/1.3%, gemini-3.5-flash 83.4%/11.0%, gemma-4-31b 89.4%/12.4%, gpt-oss-safeguard-20b 55.1%/2.4%. Channel invariance: frozen text-calibrated artifacts score image attacks with recall gaps ≤1 point (opus 100%/100% image/text). Transfer: AgentDojo landed runs 86.4% recall at 0.0% FPR; ASB memory-poisoning 95.0%/2.0%; unseen healthcare domain 100.0% recall (45/45) at 0.0% FPR; 64 fresh-family scenarios 97.9% recall. Perimeter defenses worsen across tiers while the auditor improves — escalation creates more anomalous state to detect. Baselines are current (2024–2026 work), and per-auditor/per-tier results carry 95% Wilson intervals. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM (cross-session erosion of a shared multi-agent state ledger, where no single message is malicious) + NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (1,728 executable, contract-verified scenarios with matched benign controls, over-refusal scoring, and a paired image channel) + NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (the calibrated Meta-Auditor reference defense). The genuinely novel elements are the conjunction in Table 1 — multi-agent mesh × cross-session state × process-level verification × over-refusal scoring — and the channel-invariance finding; the individual components (prompt injection, trajectory monitoring, conformal calibration, Platt scaling, grey-zone escalation) are standard techniques composed competently in a new setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong ablations: a five-level observation ladder (L1–L5) that separates visibility from calibration; a same-telemetry judge control isolating the calibration machinery as the source of the FPR gap (confirmed across the full ROC, AUC 0.998 vs 0.976); a per-signal decomposition (SDI 43.9% recall/0% FPR standalone); a provenance tell-invariance ablation (recall unchanged at 98.0% when source labels are relabeled or stripped); an overfit control on 64 fresh families; external-corpus and unseen-domain transfers. Error bars are Wilson intervals throughout. However: no multiple-seed repetition of the stochastic mesh debate is reported (one mesh sweep shows ~1-point drift), the mesh is fixed at gpt-5.5 for headline results, and the ground-truth "landing" contracts are authored by the same pipeline that designs the attacks and the SDI anchor — a structural circularity the paper does not test against independently defined ground truth. Code (GitHub: SalesforceAIResearch/ErosionBench) and dataset (HuggingFace: Salesforce/ErosionBench) are promised; during double-blind review only an anonymized runnable subset is released, with the full corpus withheld. Evaluation uses proprietary API models pinned to fixed versions — reproduction depends on endpoint stability. Human validation is thin but honest: two annotators on 50 items (Fleiss' κ = 0.87), by the authors' own colleagues. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a benchmark with an executed reference defense). Practical: Yes — the mesh and auditor are LLM API calls plus a FastAPI sandbox; the only synchronous gate is deterministic arithmetic with negligible latency. Efficient: The auditor costs 10.4k tokens and 6.7 s per scenario (opus-4-8), running out of band; arbitration fires on ~48% of trajectories, so average cost is below that figure, but it is still a frontier-LLM call per audited trajectory — far costlier than a perimeter filter. Effective: Yes for the tested distribution — 1.3% residual ASR at 2.9% FPR solves the stated problem on the benchmark, but the evidence is against procedurally generated, non-adaptive attacks on the authors' own contracts. Scalable: Not tested at higher scale — tier depth tops out at ~12 sessions/50 pages per scenario; behavior at 10× scenario counts, more agents, or varied mesh topologies is explicitly future work. Deliverable: benchmark dataset + sandbox + frozen calibration artifacts (code and data URLs stated; full corpus withheld during review) — a real software artifact, not paper-only. Strengths: (1) The over-refusal axis is the paper's most valuable methodological contribution: by forcing every defense to report both ASR and benign FPR on a shared pipeline, it exposes that LlamaFirewall's 10.2% ASR costs 92.5% of legitimate work — a trade-off almost no prior multi-agent benchmark scores. (2) The same-telemetry judge control is a genuinely well-designed ablation that attributes the auditor's advantage to calibration plus heterogeneous evidence, not model choice or threshold tuning, and the ROC-dominance argument preempts the obvious "it's just a judge" objection. (3) The transfer suite (external corpora, unseen domain, image channel, all without re-calibration) is unusually thorough for a benchmark paper and directly targets the self-generated-corpus confound. (4) Honest negative accounting: the image-arm FPR is explicitly flagged as non-transferring (~20% even in composite) and provisional, which many authors would have buried. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: the operating threshold is auditor-specific and not model-portable; calibration assumes exchangeable trajectories with no formal population FPR guarantee; coverage is limited to enterprise workflows (no consumer settings, no adaptive attackers, fixed mesh topology and agent count); the Meta-Auditor is a research reference, not an adversarially hardened defense; scenarios are procedurally generated rather than harvested from incidents; the image-arm benign controls are not validity-matched so image FPR is provisional; and the mesh-sweep FPR uses a smaller 151-control split. They confront limitations directly, including in dedicated appendix caveats (Mode B FPR, invalid benign twins) — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Anchor–contract circularity: SDI, CII, and the ground-truth "landing" contracts are all authored against the same state graph, so the deterministic anchors' recall is partly by construction; no experiment scores attacks against independently specified ground truth. (2) No adaptive attacker: a red-team that knows the auditor's scoring rubric (e.g., crafts payloads whose forged values stay within typed-distance tolerance or times policy capitulation to the last turn to minimize VAD) is untested — and VAD explicitly scores late caves as small-but-nonzero, hinting at such a gap. (3) Attack realism: the mesh agents are instructed never to jailbreak and the rebuttal tactics are a closed seven-label enum, so the attack space is bounded by the authors' taxonomy; whether real enterprise compromise follows these shapes is asserted, not evidenced. (4) The auditor is evaluated on its own benchmark with calibration and evaluation domains overlapping (4 of 4 domains shared); the healthcare OOD test helps but is small (45 malicious / 20 benign, one of four classes unscorable). (5) Grey-zone arbitration handles 439/906 (~48%) of trajectories — the deployed FPR therefore leans heavily on the arbiter LLM, and arbiter-specific ablation (e.g., swapping the arbiter model independently of the monitor) is not reported. (6) The 13 false positives on the held-out split are not qualitatively analyzed, leaving it unclear what benign enterprise work the auditor still blocks. Bottom Line: For anyone building or evaluating defenses for multi-agent LLM systems, this is worth reading for the over-refusal-scored, process-level evaluation methodology and the honest calibration ablations alone — likely the strongest current benchmark for cross-session state erosion — but the 98.5%/2.9% headline should be read as an upper bound under non-adaptive, generator-matched attacks rather than a deployable guarantee.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces CompressionBench, a terminal-style benchmark that tasks autonomous coding agents with producing a compressed LLM — quantized/pruned weights plus working inference code — under a fixed storage limit and time budget, with independent verification of perplexity, storage, and downstream accuracy. - Why it's important: LLM compression is real, labor-intensive systems engineering whose automation is a concrete, measurable step toward recursive self-improvement (AI improving the infrastructure AI runs on); no prior benchmark evaluates agents on this coupled numerical-design-plus-implementation problem. - How it does it: The task gives the agent a pinned checkpoint, a storage cap (checked separately for the saved package and GPU-resident weights), an 8-hour budget, and PPL-ratio feedback on source-sampled continuations, then a separate evaluator runs held-out likelihood, GSM8K/HumanEval/TriviaQA accuracy (must retain 80% of BF16), storage, and integrity checks on the frozen artifact. - The good: 29 of 36 agent submissions pass full verification; skip it if you want a new compression algorithm (the agents combine known methods — GPTQ, trellis codes, Hadamard rotations, distillation — rather than inventing any).
