Problem & Motivation: Modern LLM inference is memory-bandwidth bound, and constructing a compressed model that preserves behavior under a storage budget requires coordinating coupled numerical decisions (representation, precision allocation, parameter retention), interpreting incomplete feedback (local reconstruction error vs whole-model likelihood vs generation quality), and co-designing an inference path where dequantization overhead does not erase memory savings. Practitioners currently do this work manually. Prior agentic benchmarks (Terminal-Bench, MLAgentBench, RE-Bench, KernelBench) evaluate command-line tasks, ML experimentation, or kernel writing, but none evaluates an agent's ability to select, combine, implement, and validate a complete numerical approximation of a model — the gap this benchmark fills, motivated as a measurable component of efficiency-oriented recursive self-improvement. Key Idea: Cast LLM compression as an outcome-verified terminal task where the reward is source-to-compressed perplexity ratio on continuations sampled from the source model (whose expectation equals next-token KL divergence), with the storage constraint applied to both the saved package and GPU-resident weights — the resident-storage rule being the crucial anti-gaming trick, since it blocks the known failure mode (observed in pilots) of shipping a tiny checkpoint that keeps BF16 weights resident at inference time. Methodology: Each task fixes a source checkpoint (MoE: Nemotron-3.5 120B-A12B and Qwen3.5 122B-A10B at 32/48 GiB; dense: Qwen3.8 27B at 8/12 GiB), one H200 NVL, vLLM 0.32.0, and an 8-hour budget. The agent runs offline in a container with read-only weights, papers, and calibration data (FineWeb, UltraChat-200k, WikiText-103); it may use any combination of quantization, mixed precision, pruning, low-rank methods, and distillation, and must implement the required inference ops. The constrained objective minimizes empirical excess cross-entropy on source-sampled continuations (256 contexts × 512 tokens × 1,536 sampled continuation tokens, 393,216 scored positions) subject to both storage limits; the feedback reward is 10× the PPL ratio, with zero for execution failures. Final verification is independent: held-out likelihood, package and resident storage measured after loading and inference, a mean-accuracy gate at 80% of pre-fixed BF16 reference on GSM8K/HumanEval/TriviaQA (50 questions each), automated plus human integrity review, and batch-one decode TPS (127/L over a 128-token interval) reported outside the reward. Critical design decisions: (1) dual package/resident storage limits — well justified by pilot measurements showing agents and released packages retaining BF16 copies; (2) KL-equivalent likelihood objective on source-sampled data — theoretically clean, with an accuracy gate added because likelihood alone is shown insufficient; (3) time-budgeted evaluation calls consuming the same clock as construction — forcing the experimental-judgment tradeoff the paper wants to study. One run per agent–task pair; four repeat runs and two paired ablations in appendices. Key Results: 29/36 submissions pass verification; all 18 at looser limits pass, while at tighter limits six fail the accuracy gate and one times out. Per-task-best agent designs average +3.4% PPL over BF16 and 77.33% accuracy vs 79.56% for remeasured BF16. Concrete comparisons: on Qwen3.8→12 GiB, Sonnet achieves PPL 3.253 / 76.67% accuracy vs BF16's 3.221 / 74.00% and GSQ-RCO's 3.334 / 66.00%; on Qwen3.5→48 GiB, Sonnet reaches PPL 2.788 / 85.33% vs Unsloth UD-IQ3_S's 2.808 / 82.00%. Uniform GPTQ passes only the looser MoE tasks (e.g., 5.33% accuracy at 32 GiB Nemotron). Baselines are current — released Unsloth Dynamic GGUF and GSQ-RCO quantizations of the same checkpoints. Analysis of 301 recorded reward evaluations: 21/24 near-fixed-size revisions lower PPL (clipping, damping, precision redistribution — e.g., Kimi cuts feedback PPL 3.738→3.132 with ≤0.01 GiB size change); reward feedback reverses 17/79 local rankings (8 leading to explicit rollbacks); a controlled ablation shows MSE-selected clipping beats min–max (PPL 3.356 vs 3.369; mean accuracy 68.67% vs 62.00%) and GPTQ compensation beats none (2.819 vs 2.834); intermediate models gain and lose correct answers at nearly unchanged PPL (Sonnet v3–v5: PPL 3.2572/3.2531/3.2525 with 111/104/115 of 150 correct); MiniMax's expert-indexing bug repair cuts PPL increase from ~11% to 4.5%. Repeats land within 0.81% PPL of originals. Surprising: Sonnet's 8 GiB dense model beats three agents' 12 GiB models — representation quality outweighs storage. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The benchmark formulation — compression as a terminal task with dual package/resident storage accounting, budgeted feedback calls, and independent multi-part verification — is genuinely new; the constituent compression techniques (GPTQ, QTIP-style trellis codes, rotations, distillation) and the evaluation infrastructure lineage (Terminal-Bench, Harbor) are standard tools recombined in a new setting. The empirical findings (local-vs-model ranking reversals, PPL/accuracy dissociation) confirm qualitatively known compression phenomena in a new agentic context. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and well designed: paired ablations on clipping and GPTQ compensation hold storage fixed, and a four-reagent repeat study quantifies run-to-run variance (within 0.81% PPL). However, the primary study uses a single run per agent–task pair (36 runs), and no significance tests or error bars accompany the headline aggregate; the four repeats cover only two agents. Verification is genuinely independent (held-out contexts, pre-fixed accuracy gates withheld from agents, integrity review) — the protocol deliberately separates search data from acceptance data, avoiding benchmark-gaming within the design. One methodological concern: PPL references and accuracy gates were fixed via pilot runs on Qwen3.8 (the same model used in two of six tasks), so task allowances were tuned on a model in the eval suite. Code and benchmark are publicly released at github.com/Infini-AI-Lab/Compression-Bench, with a project blog. The 50-question-per-benchmark eval is small enough that 1 item shifts accuracy by 0.67 points, and the paper's PPL-vs-accuracy dissociation claims rest on these small sets. Decode TPS uses a reasonable median-of-three protocol. Not peer-reviewed (arXiv preprint, v2). Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a benchmark and measurement study with executed agent runs; the artifact is the benchmark harness). - Practical: Yes — all runs use one H200 NVL and Claude Code with vLLM; the benchmark harness requires comparable single-GPU hardware. - Efficient: Each run costs 8 GPU-hours plus API spend (Figure 1b shows per-run API costs ranging roughly $10–$140); the benchmark itself is cheap to administer but the design-time cost is nontrivial. - Effective: The evidence shows agents can produce models that pass a strict multi-part acceptance test and beat released quantizations on quality, but not that they deliver deployable systems — agent artifacts decode at 7.8–57 tps versus 74.6–122.9 tps for released baselines, and speed is excluded from the reward. - Scalable: Untested beyond one GPU, one runtime, three source models, and one scaffold (Claude Code for all agents); the paper claims no scaling behavior and offers none. The work delivers a reusable benchmark harness and released code (github.com/Infini-AI-Lab/Compression-Bench), not a compression tool or trained model. Strengths: - The dual package/resident storage accounting is a genuinely clever anti-gaming mechanism derived from observed pilot failures (QTIP checkpoints at 6.96 GiB that retained BF16 weights resident), directly addressing a real loophole in compressed-model evaluation. - The measurement architecture cleanly separates search-time feedback from independent verification with distinct held-out data and pre-fixed gates, which is rigorous benchmark design few agentic evaluations match. - The trajectory analysis is unusually informative for a benchmark paper: it quantifies where improvement comes from (21/24 same-size revisions), how local evidence misleads (17/79 reversals), and detects concrete agent behaviors like MiniMax's expert-indexing bug repair and Opus's stale validation, connecting decisions to outcomes rather than just scoring runs. - Honest reporting of the speed limitation: the paper explicitly states Sonnet's quality win over GSQ-RCO comes with 16.7 vs 74.6 tokens/s decode, refusing to claim compression implies speedup. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The conclusion states the central open question directly: whether a compressed model retains the ability to perform subsequent compression tasks — i.e., the RSI claim is asserted as motivation but not tested, and the authors flag this themselves. Section 4.3 and the case studies acknowledge that agents often detect generation regressions without finding feasible repairs (pruning retained despite known MATH-500 losses), and that Opus let local tests go stale on its final versions. The paper also explicitly warns that measured storage–quality improvements do not establish speedups. This directness is a credibility positive; the authors confront rather than minimize these gaps. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Single run per agent–task pair: the headline "select lowest-PPL per task" aggregate (+3.4% PPL, 77.33% accuracy) is a max over six agents, which inflates expected performance; only 2 of 6 agents get repeat runs. - No human-expert baseline: RE-Bench's key comparison design (agents vs human ML engineers) is absent, so "can agents do this" lacks the reference point that would make the 29/36 pass rate interpretable as a capability level rather than a pass/fail rate against a fixed gate. - Evaluation sets are very small (50 questions/benchmark, 256 PPL contexts); several reported dissociations (e.g., 104 vs 115 correct at ΔPPL ≈ 0.0006) are within plausible sampling noise, and no confidence intervals are given. - Task limits were calibrated via pilots on Qwen3.8, one of the evaluated source models — a mild Goodhart/dev-set contamination channel the authors do not discuss. - All agents run inside the same Claude Code scaffold with identical tooling, so the cross-agent ranking conflates model capability with scaffold fit; and the benchmark scores likelihood quality but not the deployment-relevant speed objective, which the authors note but which limits the benchmark's fidelity to real compression work. - 'Not passed' entries at tight limits leave it unclear whether failures reflect capability limits or time-budget sensitivity. Bottom Line: This is the best-designed and most honestly analyzed agentic benchmark for a real ML-engineering objective published to date, and anyone building or evaluating ML-engineering agents should read it — but consumers of compression methods should stick to dedicated quantization papers, since agent-produced artifacts here still lose decisively on decode speed and the RSI framing remains untested aspiration.

#22 — Innovative (74)

LLMs Don't Know What They Know: Benchmarking Temporal Self-Knowledge for Financial Backtesting (22 ▲ )

Lingfei Qian, Yan Wang, Xueqing Peng, Yupeng Cao, Yuechen Jiang, Zhuohan Xie, Anke Xu, Wenbo Cao, Jiarui Chen, Zehan Li, Jimin Huang, Alejandro Lopez-Lira, Yuehua Tang, Sophia Ananiadou, Jian-Yun Nie · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 9 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces FinDendro, a benchmark of 2,226 dated U.S. financial facts (1999–2026) with paired factual-recall and knowledge-claim probes, and uses it to show that vendor-stated cutoffs, model self-reports, and historical-date instructions all fail to certify that an LLM financial backtest is free of hindsight leakage. - Why it's important: Retrospective LLM backtesting on historical market data is inflated when models reproduce outcomes stored in their weights, and current leakage safeguards are trusted without direct evidence that they work. - How it does it: Each fact yields four multiple-choice prompts — plain value recall, recall/predict with paired "I know / I don't know" claim options, and a predict-with-declared-date variant — so the model's answer and its claim about that answer come from a single choice, letting the authors estimate both an actual knowledge boundary and a model-identified (claim) boundary on identical facts. - The good: The controls are careful (persistence filtering, balanced accuracy for Fed decisions, chance ≈ 0.27), and the headline dissociation is striking and quantified: GPT-5 answers 76% of controlled facts correctly while claiming knowledge of only 38%, and still answers 61% of the facts it disclaims correctly. - The missing: The benchmark covers one economy, three fact families, and a single response per prompt at temperature 0, with no evaluation of any alternative leakage-mitigation mechanism beyond the three safeguards tested; code/data are promised but not released at publication time. - Read it or not: Read it if you evaluate or build LLM forecasting systems or financial benchmarks — it is the first direct audit of whether self-knowledge probes can clean a historical backtest — and skip it if you only need generic self-knowledge findings, which are largely confirmed here in a financial setting.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (75) and Non-Obviousness (78) drive the composite: the paired claim/answer elicitation design is a genuinely clever measurement instrument, and the finding that frontier models systematically under-claim knowledge (GPT-5: 76% accurate, only 38% claimed) while Qwen over-claims is a surprising, four-way dissociation of failure modes rather than a blanket result. Rigor (72) is supported by the persistence filter, balanced accuracy, and bootstrap CIs, but single-sample-per-prompt evaluation, threshold-sensitive boundary estimates (GPT-4o's gap moves 1→6 quarters), and a promised-not-demonstrated artifact release hold it back. Completeness (78) benefits from an exemplary, non-minimizing limitations section; Resilience (70) is reduced because the constructive recommendation (restrict backtests to post-boundary periods) is never validated on an actual forecasting task. Weighted composite: 0.20*75 + 0.25*72 + 0.15*78 + 0.15*78 + 0.15*70 + 0.10*68 = 74.
empirical Novelty 75 Rigor 72 Non-Obv 78 Completeness 78 Resilience 70 Impact 68
Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Financial LLM forecasting is typically evaluated by backtesting: the model predicts past stock prices, inflation prints, or Fed decisions, and predictions are compared with realized outcomes. Long evaluation windows are statistically necessary, but they guarantee that realized outcomes may already be in the model's training data, inflating apparent skill. Practitioners rely on three safeguards — evaluating only after the vendor-stated cutoff, asking the model about its own cutoff or knowledge, and instructing it to answer as of a past date — and prior work (look-ahead bias studies, temporal knowledge-boundary benchmarks like Dated Data, LLMLagBench, HindsightBench, and self-knowledge benchmarks like SelfAware) has never jointly measured what a model actually knows, what it claims to know, and whether the safeguards separate the two on the same facts. The paper addresses this gap for quant finance practitioners and benchmark builders. Key Idea: The core insight is that a model's answer and its knowledge claim can be elicited from the same multiple choice: each candidate value appears twice, once bundled with a claim of knowing and once with an admission of guessing. Which option the model picks yields both a factual answer and a self-report in one draw. Comparing claim rates to accuracy across time on identical dated facts estimates two separate boundaries — where knowledge ends and where claims end — and the gap between them directly quantifies how untrustworthy self-reports are as leakage filters. Methodology: The pipeline has four stages. (1) Fact collection: 20,972 dated U.S. facts from Jan 1999–Sep 2026 — twelve FRED macro series using first-release values from ALFRED, month-end closing prices for 50 large U.S. companies (stock splits reversed), and monthly Fed target-rate outcomes; 2,226 facts are sampled, sparsely before 2021 (1,056 facts) and densely after (1,170), since current-model cutoffs fall in 2021–2025. (2) Prompt construction: each fact yields four prompts across three tasks — Task 1 (plain value selection), Task 2 (value + knowledge claim, in Recall and Predict wordings, 8 options for numerical facts, 6 for policy), Task 3 (Task 2 Predict plus a "assume today is [date]" instruction). Candidates are four values spaced roughly one typical monthly change apart, with the true value's rank drawn uniformly. (3) Controls: numerical facts where repeating last month's value is correct (47%) are excluded from the knowledge score, leaving 1,007; policy facts use balanced accuracy across raised/lowered/unchanged (the dominant class is 78%); combined chance ≈ 0.27 over 1,340 controlled facts. (4) Measurement: five quantities per model — Knows (Task 1 accuracy on controlled facts), Says (claim rate), Acc|says, Acc|denies, and a within-period gap with 95% bootstrap intervals from 1,000 resamples. Actual and model-identified cutoffs are estimated as the last quarter whose two-quarter rolling statistic exceeds a threshold set midway between the model's 2015–2020 baseline and chance. The design decisions are mostly well-justified: the persistence filter and balanced accuracy are clearly needed; the fixed-threshold boundary rule is the weakest link (acknowledged and stress-tested); scoring one response per prompt at temperature 0 is economical but leaves API-level sampling noise unmodeled. Key Results: Across 8,904 prompts per model and six general-purpose models plus 11 point-in-time checkpoints: GPT-5 scores Knows = 0.76 vs. Says = 0.38 (Acc|says = 0.95, Acc|denies = 0.61, within-period gap 0.18 [0.13, 0.22]); GPT-4o 0.50 vs. 0.20 (gap 0.39 [0.32, 0.45]); DeepSeek-V3.2 0.54 vs. 0.28 (gap 0.08); Llama-3.3-70B is the exception, over-claiming slightly (0.43 vs. 0.48). The two Qwen models over-claim badly (Says ≈ 0.70 at Knows ≈ 0.36, near chance). Claim boundaries outlast knowledge boundaries: Llama-3.3-70B's factual accuracy hits chance after 2021Q2 while claims persist to 2023Q1 — a seven-quarter gap — and its vendor-stated cutoff (Dec 2023) is ten quarters past its measured knowledge boundary. A self-report filter that drops facts GPT-5 claims to know still leaves in-window accuracy at 0.75 (vs. 0.33 after the boundary) while discarding 54% of in-window facts. A declared date collapses GPT-5's knowledge claims from 0.39 to 0.01 while accuracy barely moves (0.76 → 0.75); in a simulated Task 3 backtest, GPT-5 labels 99% of in-window answers as "predictions" and scores 0.82 on them. Stock prices show the largest know-vs-say gaps (GPT-5: +0.54, 59% accuracy vs. 5% claimed knowledge). Point-in-time models (TiMaGPT, ChronoGPT, DatedGPT; 1–1.5B params) score 0.25–0.30 on both sides of their cutoffs with bootstrap CIs including zero, so they are unusable as leakage-free controls. Baselines are current frontier models accessed via API; the evaluation is standard-scale (2,226 facts), not stress-scale. The most surprising finding is the direction of self-report error: frontier models systematically under-claim knowledge, the opposite of the over-claiming that self-knowledge work on smaller models might suggest. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. Genuinely novel: the fact-level pairing of knowledge claims with factual accuracy on dated financial facts, and the direct, controlled testing of the three leakage safeguards against measured boundaries (Table 1 shows no prior benchmark covers all five dimensions). What is a standard combination: the underlying idea of behavioral cutoff estimation (perplexity/accuracy probes over dated facts) exists in Dated Data, LLMLagBench, and HindsightBench; FinDendro's contribution is applying and extending that machinery to finance, adding the claim-elicitation design, and turning it into a safeguard audit rather than a cutoff measurement. Rigor & Reproducibility: The controls are a strength: the persistence filter removes 47% of numerical facts that could be answered by carry-forward, and balanced accuracy neutralizes the 78% "unchanged" Fed class. Bootstrap confidence intervals (1,000 resamples) back the know-vs-deny gaps, and all four frontier-model gaps exclude zero. Threshold sensitivity is explicitly tested (GPT-5 and DeepSeek boundaries move ≤1 quarter; GPT-4o's claim-knowledge gap moves from 1 to 6 quarters — a meaningful fragility). Manual validation covers only 50 facts (two reviewers, 100% pass rate) — thin relative to 2,226 facts. Each prompt is run once at temperature 0, with no seed replication, and the authors note they excluded one model whose served API identity they could not verify — a real reproducibility hazard for API-based evaluation. The paper states the full pool, sample, question files, and construction code "will be released with the benchmark"; no URL is given at publication time, so release is promised, not demonstrated. Methodological concerns: the boundary-estimation rule is developed and evaluated on the same benchmark instrument (inevitable for a benchmark paper, but boundary placement is rule-dependent), and vendor-stated cutoffs — one of the three safeguards tested — are themselves vendor self-reports the authors cannot independently verify. Claims and evidence are generally well-separated; the framing that backtests "cannot be certified leak-free" is supported directly, while the constructive claim that behavioral audits suffice is extrapolated. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a benchmark plus measurement study, with an implied auditing procedure). Practical: Yes — evaluating a model costs 8,904 multiple-choice prompts answerable by a single option letter, runnable against any commercial API or local checkpoint. Efficient: Cheap relative to the value of a clean backtest; the point-in-time models needed likelihood scoring, a small extra engineering step. Effective: The evidence shows the benchmark detects real knowledge boundaries that align with vendor cutoffs where they coincide (GPT-5: knowledge ends, claims end, and vendor cutoff all at 2024Q3), but it shows self-report cannot fix leakage — it does not demonstrate that the benchmark's own boundary estimate is a sufficient leakage certificate. Scalable: Extension to more series, regions, or models is trivial by construction; untested at 10× scale is whether fine-grained quarterly boundary estimates remain stable (already wobbly for GPT-4o under threshold changes). Deliverable: a benchmark artifact (facts, questions, construction code) promised for release; the boundary-estimation procedure is reusable; no trained model is produced. Strengths: (1) The paired claim/answer option design is a genuinely clever measurement instrument — one choice yields both the model's belief and its claim about that belief, eliminating any confound from re-asking. (2) The persistence and class-imbalance controls are applied before headline numbers are computed, which most hindsight-leakage papers skip; without them the GPT-5 stock-price gap (+0.54) would be uninterpretable. (3) The finding structure is actionable and specific: under-claiming (GPT-5, GPT-4o), over-claiming (Qwen, Llama), claim-boundary drift (Llama, 7 quarters), and claim-collapse under dated prompting with unchanged accuracy are four distinct failure modes, not one blanket "models are dishonest." (4) Testing point-in-time models as the presumed control — and showing they are too weak to serve as one — is an honest and useful negative result for the field. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: coverage is one economy and three fact families, so boundaries for other domains may differ; the boundary rule uses fixed thresholds whose perturbation moves estimates (they report the GPT-4o 1→6 quarter swing); trend extrapolation can be correct without recall and only the simplest persistence strategy is filtered; served API versions may change and one unverifiable model was excluded; multiple-choice claims may differ from free-form knowledge statements; and tested point-in-time models are too small (1–1.5B) to show whether a large model with a strict cutoff would behave honestly. They also flag, in the Ethics section, that the benchmark must not be misused as a leak-free certificate. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Each prompt is sampled once, so per-quarter accuracy curves (which drive boundary placement) carry unquantified sampling noise; bootstrap intervals are over facts, not over evaluation runs, and no cross-seed or option-order resampling is reported. (2) The benchmark conflates memorization with correct inference — a model that interpolates a trend, uses anchor facts (e.g., a known exchange-rate regime), or reasons from correlated series scores as "knowing"; the authors acknowledge only the simplest carry-forward strategy. (3) The paper tests that three safeguards fail but does not test any alternative mitigation the procedure itself suggests (e.g., using measured boundaries to filter, or probing internal states), so the constructive recommendation rests on assumption. (4) Manual validation at n=50 facts by two reviewers is too small to certify first-release correctness across 1,340 controlled facts, and ALFRED first-release handling for revisions-prone series is asserted rather than audited at scale. (5) DeepSeek-V3.2 has no vendor-stated cutoff, so its "measured vs. stated" comparison — unlike GPT-5's clean three-way alignment — cannot be externally corroborated. (6) The conclusion recommends restricting backtests to periods after the measured boundary, but the paper never validates this recommendation on an actual forecasting task (returns, sentiment) — only on the recall probe itself, leaving open whether recall-boundary accuracy transfers to genuine forecasting leakage. Bottom Line: For anyone building or trusting LLM financial backtests, this is required reading: it is the first controlled demonstration that none of the three standard leakage safeguards can be trusted, and its benchmark-plus-audit procedure is the most defensible alternative currently on the table — read it despite the single-economy scope and the threshold-sensitive boundary estimates.

What Gets Hacked in a Collaborative Reward for LLM Recommenders: The Part That Does Not Depend on the User

Z Li, L Dong, Y Wu, D Li, Y Xia, YC Zhang, R Cai, Y Wu… · arxiv.org · Julian McAuley - new articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper shows that the item-mean component of a collaborative-filtering (CF) score — the item's average score across user histories, independent of the current user — drives exposure collapse when CF scores are used as RL rewards for LLM recommenders, and introduces two reward corrections (per-item centering and per-item standardization) that restore exposure breadth without retraining the scorer. - Why it's important: Practitioners training LLM recommenders with RL are quietly losing catalog diversity — distinct top-1 items drop 36–80% relative to the SFT start — while aggregate accuracy metrics look unchanged, so the failure is invisible to standard HR/NDCG reporting and concentrates recommendations on head items. - How it does it: Decompose each CF score as r(u,i) = m(i) + ε(u,i), where m(i) is the item's mean score under a fixed reference distribution of training histories; controlled interventions show training on m̂(i) alone collapses exposure (32 distinct top-1 items on Beauty) while training on the residual alone broadens it, so the fix simply subtracts (centering) and rescales (standardization) the item-mean component computed once before RL. - The good: The causal argument is unusually well-controlled — random and rule-based rewards reproduce no collapse, the frozen CF model retains personalized rankings when used directly (3,407 distinct top-1 items on Beauty vs. 837 after CF-reward RL), and component-wise interventions isolate the culprit, with results replicated across 4 CF architectures, 2 identifier schemes, and 3 LLM backbones. - The missing: Per-item centering measurably hurts accuracy on Beauty with Semantic IDs (HR@10 −0.0028 to −0.0031 vs. the CF arm, p = 0.02–0.041; below the SFT start on every seed), and the paper acknowledges its interventions cannot quantify each component's share of the collapse — the mechanism is diagnosed but not fully attributed. - Read it or not: Read it if you build RL-post-trained generative recommenders or design reward functions for them — the diagnosis and one-line fix are directly actionable; skip it if you work outside recommendation or RL reward design, since the technique (mean subtraction and z-scoring) is classic CF normalization repositioned as a reward intervention.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (82) is the standout: three seeds with standard deviations, exact McNemar and paired bootstrap tests, robustness across 4 CF architectures × 2 identifier schemes × 3 backbones, and anonymous code release — rare in this genre. Non-Obviousness (78) is high because the m̂/residual decomposition with the 3,407-vs-837 direct-ranking control identifies a specific root cause of reward hacking that prior systems only vaguely observed. Novelty (65) is capped by the correction being classic CF z-scoring repositioned; Completeness (75) is strong (paired significance reporting of the authors' own accuracy loss) but dented by the abstract softening a significant drop and two-dataset coverage; Resilience (72) is solid given the intervention ladder, though no mechanism formalization exists; Impact (70) reflects a nearly free, directly actionable fix with a code artifact. Weighted composite: 0.20*65 + 0.25*82 + 0.15*78 + 0.15*75 + 0.15*72 + 0.10*70 = 74.
empirical Novelty 65 Rigor 82 Non-Obv 78 Completeness 75 Resilience 72 Impact 70
Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation LLM-based sequential recommenders are increasingly post-trained with RL using scores from a frozen CF model (e.g., SASRec) as dense, personalized rewards, avoiding costly reward annotation. Prior systems — MiniOneRec and ReRe — observed training pathologies with such collaborative rewards (degraded accuracy, rising rewards alongside falling accuracy) and hypothesized reward hacking, but neither isolated which part of the CF score causes the failure. The practical stake is exposure concentration: a recommender that collapses onto few items harms long-tail items, catalog coverage, and potentially user experience, and the collapse happens even though the underlying CF model itself ranks the catalog diversely and accurately. The paper targets the diagnostic gap: which component of the CF reward is responsible, and can it be corrected without touching the frozen scorer? Key Idea Treat the CF score as item-mean plus user-specific residual, r(u,i) = m(i) + ε(u,i) with m(i) = E_{u∼Q}[r(u,i)] over a fixed reference distribution Q of training histories; the item-mean is a user-independent scoring bias that, when fed as reward, the policy exploits (uniformly high-mean items win regardless of user), while the residual carries the personalization. The trick is that m̂(i) can be precomputed once by scoring the full catalog for M = 4,000 sampled histories, making the correction a static lookup during RL. The authors honestly flag that subtracting an item-dependent quantity changes reward differences between items and is a genuine reward intervention (citing Tucker et al. on action-dependent baselines), not a variance-reduction baseline. Methodology Pipeline: (1) SFT a Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct policy on interaction histories under two identifier schemes (RQ-VAE Semantic IDs with prefix-constrained trie decoding, or Atomic IDs); (2) train a frozen CF model (SASRec primary; GRU4Rec, two-tower, CTR head for generality) on leave-one-out windows; (3) before RL, score the full catalog for 4,000 sampled training histories to estimate m̂(i) and σ̂(i); (4) run GRPO (group size 16, 400 steps, KL coefficient 10⁻³) with the corrected reward r − m̂ (centering) or (r − m̂)/max(σ̂, s₀) (standardization, floor at the 10th percentile of σ̂). Exposure is measured by distinct top-1 items, coverage@10, and full-catalog Gini; accuracy by HR@10/NDCG@10 with exact McNemar and paired bootstrap tests. Critical design decisions: (a) estimating statistics over user histories per item rather than over candidate items per user (the HiLaR choice) — justified by the goal of removing cross-user shared bias, and the HiLaR-style baseline is shown ineffective; (b) a standardization floor to bound variance amplification — justified via the Var ≤ 1 bound in Eq. 8 and floor ablations; (c) a 30% distinct-top-1 reduction as the operational definition of collapse — reasonable but admittedly a threshold choice. The intervention ladder (random reward, rule reward, m̂-only, residual-only, α-weighted partial removal, capped removal, ramped removal) is the methodological core and is well executed. Key Results CF-reward training collapses exposure in all four main settings: distinct top-1 items fall from 1,317→837 (Beauty/Semantic IDs), 840→169 (Sports/Semantic IDs), 857→544 (Beauty/Atomic IDs), 463→168 (Sports/Atomic IDs), meeting the 30% collapse criterion, while HR@10 moves by at most 0.0055 (nonsignificant on Beauty, p ≥ 0.33) — collapse is invisible in aggregate accuracy. Controls: random rewards and the rule reward leave the count within 21 items and 13% of the SFT start, respectively; the CF model ranking the catalog directly produces 3,407/1,356 distinct top-1 items (Beauty/Sports), confirming personalization survives in the scorer. Interventions: m̂-only training leaves 32/15 distinct top-1 items (Semantic IDs); residual-only (centering) yields 1,830 (Beauty) and 699 (Sports). Corrections vs. CF arm: standardization gives 1.6–9.8× more distinct top-1 items (1,915 on Beauty, 1,652 on Sports with Semantic IDs), beats a popularity penalty (λ=3: 1,377/349), Dr. GRPO, a 10× KL penalty, and HiLaR-style per-user normalization in all four settings, with HR@10 within ~0.004 of the CF arm (slightly negative on Beauty/Semantic IDs, slightly positive elsewhere). For mid-tier targets (popularity quantile 0.2–0.8), the CF arm cuts HR@10 by 9–56% (p < 0.05 on every seed), and standardization raises mid-tier HR@10 by 1.3–2.8× over the CF arm (p < 10⁻⁵). Generality holds across 4 CF architectures (standardization best in 14/16 combinations) and Qwen2.5-1.5B and Llama-3.2-1B backbones (collapse of 23–41%, both corrections recover above the SFT start). Scale: catalogs of 7,819–10,052 items, ~16–20K test users — standard RecSys scale, not stress-scale. Novelty Classification NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the item-mean component of CF rewards causes exposure collapse even when the scorer retains personalized rankings) plus NEW METHOD in a narrow sense (per-item centering/standardization of RL rewards for recommenders). The correction itself is a repositioning of classic z-score normalization from neighborhood-based CF (Herlocker 1999) applied along the user axis instead of the candidate axis; the genuine novelty lies in the decomposition-plus-controlled-intervention experimental design that isolates the culprit, which neither MiniOneRec nor ReRe did. Rigor & Reproducibility Strong for the area: three RL seeds per arm with standard deviations (Figure 5, Table 11), exact McNemar tests for hits and paired bootstrap (2,000 resamples) for NDCG on matched users, learning-rate sensitivity for Atomic IDs, reference-sample-size robustness (500/4,000/16,000 histories change distinct top-1 by ≤ 20), and dense ablations (α sweep, capped removal recovering 27–99% of the centering gap, ramped removal, five floor settings). Baselines are current and appropriate for the setting (Dr. GRPO, stronger KL, HiLaR normalization, GPTRec-style popularity penalty), and the paper candidly reports where baselines win or where centering loses accuracy. Anonymous code is released (https://anonymous.4open.science/r/LLM4Rec-CF-Bias-27EF/). Concerns: evaluation is confined to two Amazon datasets from one lineage (MiniOneRec pipeline); the authors themselves note the interventions do not quantify each component's share of the collapse; the 30% collapse threshold is self-defined; the paper is an arXiv preprint (2611.07588) and appears not yet peer-reviewed. The headline 9.8× figure comes from the smallest-base setting (Sports/Semantic IDs, 169→1,652), which inflates the ratio. Deployability Profile: EMPIRICAL. - Practical: Yes — 0.5B–1.5B open models, frozen 64-dimensional CF scorers, and a one-time catalog scoring pass over 4,000 histories; everything runs on ordinary academic hardware. - Efficient: The correction adds essentially zero RL cost (a per-item lookup at reward time) and matches the CF arm's training budget; precomputation is one forward pass per history for sequential models. - Effective: The evidence shows it fixes the exposure proxy — distinct top-1, coverage@10, Gini — while preserving or slightly improving accuracy; offline exposure gains are not validated against downstream engagement or long-term user outcomes. - Scalable: Not tested beyond ~10K-item catalogs and 0.5–1.5B backbones; the precomputation cost scales as (catalog size × M histories), which should remain cheap for industrial catalogs, but this is a claim, not a measurement. The work delivers a code artifact and a reusable recipe (decompose → intervene → correct) rather than a trained model or library. Strengths - The controlled-intervention design is the real contribution: training on m̂ alone vs. the residual alone cleanly separates a user-independent reward pathology from personalized signal, and the direct-ranking control (CF model produces 3,407 distinct top-1 items while its RL-trained policy produces 837) is a sharp, memorable demonstration that ranking ability does not transfer through the reward channel. - It converts two vague prior observations of reward hacking (MiniOneRec, ReRe) into a specific, actionable diagnosis with a one-line fix requiring no scorer retraining. - The finding that aggregate HR@10 is flat (0.0851→0.0843) while mid-tier HR@10 drops 9–56% quantifies how headline accuracy metrics mask distributional harm — a useful methodological warning beyond this reward family. - Validation breadth is genuine: 4 CF architectures × 2 identifier schemes × 3 LLM backbones, with the effect direction consistent in all 16 architecture combinations. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors state that the component interventions do not quantify each component's share of the original collapse; that evidence comes only from critic-free policy-gradient configurations with frozen CF scorers; that recommendation accuracy varies across settings (and centering does lose HR@10 on Beauty/Semantic IDs, reported with p-values in Appendix C); and that broader catalog exposure alone does not establish fairness across users or item providers, with long-term exposure effects left to future work. They confront limitations directly — the paired-significance reporting of their own accuracy losses is a credibility positive — though the abstract's "maintaining comparable ranking accuracy" softens a statistically significant accuracy drop in one of four settings. Analyst-Identified Gaps - Two Amazon datasets only, both from the same generative-recommendation benchmark lineage; no industrial-scale catalog, no non-Amazon domain, so the collapse magnitude (e.g., 80% top-1 reduction on Sports) may not transfer. - No theoretical account of why RL on a constant per-item offset produces concentration — the claim is established by intervention, not mechanism; a policy-gradient analysis of item-dependent reward shifts (the authors cite Tucker et al. but do not formalize it) is absent. - The item-mean is only partially identified with popularity (r² = 0.38–0.67 against log interaction count), yet the framing leans on popularity bias; what the remaining item-mean variance represents is unexplored. - Standardization requires choosing a floor quantile; although all tested floors beat centering, the sensitivity of results to this extra hyperparameter in new settings is untested. - No comparison against non-reward-side debiasing baselines (e.g., SPRec's DPO-based self-play or Ghost's unlikelihood training), which operate at different stages but target the same exposure problem — the comparison set is restricted to reward-side and optimizer-side alternatives. - The exposure-collapse criterion (≥30% top-1 reduction) and the 400-step RL horizon are both chosen by the authors; whether collapse worsens, plateaus, or reverses with longer training is unexamined. Bottom Line For anyone post-training LLM recommenders with model-scored rewards, this is a directly useful, well-controlled diagnosis with a nearly free fix — the accuracy cost on one setting and the narrow benchmark coverage are real but secondary — and even readers outside recommendation will find the decompose-intervene-correct template for diagnosing reward hacking worth stealing.

Discovering formally verified quantum programs with AI

S Shirobokov, B Jaderberg, K Hristova, G Tsoukalas… · arxiv.org · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds a Lean 4 theorem-proving library based on quantum Hoare logic and couples it to a multi-agent LLM discovery workflow (Gemini 4 agents, shared wikis, scheduled conferences, an external Lean Comparator verifier) that synthesizes quantum programs with machine-checked proofs of both correctness and resource cost. - Why it's important: Fault-tolerant quantum applications need 10^9–10^15 logical operations while early machines project ~10^6, and historically closing that gap took years of expert derivation; skip if you only want reusable tooling today, since the artifact is not yet public.

Problem & Motivation: Quantum algorithm designers — in chemistry, fusion, cryptanalysis, and materials — face a resource gap of many orders of magnitude between algorithmic requirements and projected fault-tolerant hardware, and closing it historically required multi-year manual derivations (e.g., quantum phase estimation for cytochrome P450 spin states, stopping power for inertial-confinement fusion). LLM-driven discovery loops have accelerated classical algorithms and mathematics, but quantum programs cannot be tested on hardware and cannot be validated by classical simulation beyond small or specially restricted (e.g., kickmix) instances; prior LLM-based quantum circuit work was confined to classically simulable regimes, and concurrent LLM-assisted formalization verified only known algorithms. The gap closed is: how to validate and cost LLM-generated quantum programs at scales (hundreds to thousands of logical qubits) where neither simulation nor execution is possible. Key Idea: Pair a machine-checked specification of correctness and spacetime cost (quantum Hoare logic with weakest-precondition calculus plus syntactic/semantic resource counting in Lean) with a multi-agent search loop whose every submission is re-verified in a sandbox against a frozen specification — making adversarial collaboration between independent agent teams safe (no manual code review needed) and making untestable algorithms trustworthy by proof rather than by execution. Methodology: The system has three layers. (1) A Lean 4 library built on Mathlib and Physlib's Lean-QuantumInfo formalizes a classical-quantum while-language (qset, unitary apply, measurement with classical outcome storage, classical branching and qwhile loops), a total-correctness quantum Hoare logic via weakest preconditions (cq-assertions form an ω-CPO under the Löwner order, enabling loop-rule soundness), and two cost models: syntactic Clifford+T/Toffoli gate counting over DynamicCircuits (branch cost = max over branches) and semantic expected-cost accounting with user-supplied per-command weights (used for the oracle-query metric in Grover). (2) A discovery workflow: researchers write a frozen specification file (e.g., the stopping-power spec requires a unitary approximating e^{-iHt} to ε=10^-2 on all antisymmetric grid states, with clean ancillas and a cost bound of 50 repeats × 10 time steps × Q·T); heterogeneous Gemini 4 Carbon agent teams (researcher-chosen architectures, from single-agent to hierarchical subroutine teams, with access to simulation, numerics, and compute clusters) fill in the `sorry`s; an external verifier replays each submission in a clean sandbox via the Lean Comparator, checking theorem statements, transitive definitions, allowed axioms (only propext, Quot.sound, Classical.choice), and that the cost theorem reduces to the claimed closed form. (3) Coordination channels: a version-controlled wiki storing the best verified solution, reusable partial Lean files, and labeled idea notes (verified/promising/dead-end), with a 5% minimum improvement threshold for merges and 20% code-shortening allowances; plus 4-hourly forum conferences for unverified conjectures and critique. Critical design decisions: (a) total (not partial) correctness via weakest preconditions — justified by targeting terminating programs; (b) restricting to a single quantum register (multiple named quantum variables left as future work) — a convenience restriction, argued lossless but requiring explicit lifting; (c) the deliberately unprescribed team architecture — a stated design choice whose effect is not ablated. Key Results: Across five problems, all solutions carry machine-checked correctness and cost proofs. Fixed-point arcsin (25-bit two's-complement input, error ≤1.25×10^-7): cost reduced from a >1.08×10^8 lower bound on the Häner et al. baseline to 3.70×10^5 (3,698 T on 100 qubits), a >290× reduction, achieved in two stages (kickmix-guided search to 4.15×10^5, then Lean-verified non-kickmix inner-product gadgets for a further 11%). Parallel Grover (zero-error Find-Any/Find-All, m,k ≤ 1024, 121 settings): verified circuits match the strongest published baseline (Zalka partition + weakly measured loops, r≈0.818) on the m=1/k=1 boundaries and beat it in all interior regimes — up to 1.22× for Find-Any and up to 2.55× for Find-All — with the largest gains from a new coherent collective Johnson-graph walk over m-subset superpositions (QSVT-compiled reflections). Stopping power (218 electrons + α projectile, 216 fixed protons, ε=10^-2): Q·T per run reduced 10.9× (5.42×10^15 → 4.98×10^14) on 4,374 logical qubits, mainly via QFT to a real-space grid exploiting Pauli exclusion (12.8× fewer walk steps at 1.52× T per step) and a reused 42-qubit total-momentum register. Non-Born–Oppenheimer C23H20N3O dynamics (234 particles, 5,616 system qubits, t=1 fs, ε=10^-2): 8.08× (4.98×10^15 → 6.16×10^14) via measurement-based coordinate uncompute, Bernstein-sampled 1/r without multiplication, and hard-wired nuclear charges. Cytochrome P450 Compound I (63 electrons, 58 orbitals, DFTHC, RMSE ≤1 mHa over a 0.1 Ha energy window): 2.49× (1.09×10^12 → 4.37×10^11) via a one-hot register replacing QROM angle lookups, against a baseline the authors themselves refined with the latest compilation literature (roughly halving the published 2.26×10^12 estimate) — a methodologically conservative choice. Attribution across the three simulations: 61% of log-cost reduction from within-team ideas, 15% via wiki, 24% via conferences; the leading record in non-BO dynamics changed teams seven times. Baselines are current and, where possible, strengthened by the authors with 2025–2026 improvements; all results are from this arXiv preprint (v2, Nov 2026) and are not peer-reviewed. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (a Lean quantum Hoare logic + resource-counting library supporting both correctness and cost proof), NEW METHOD (the frozen-spec + external-verifier + wiki/conference multi-agent discovery workflow enabling safe adversarial collaboration on untestable programs), and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (verified resource reductions up to 290×, including new coherent Grover mechanisms). Genuinely novel is the coupling of formal cost-and-correctness verification to open-ended LLM agent search beyond simulable regimes; the underlying parts — Hoare logic (Feng & Ying 2021), weakest preconditions, QSP/qubitization, Bernstein-sampled lookup, measurement-based uncompute — are competent recombination of known techniques, with the scientific-application speedups coming from well-motivated but individually known-style optimizations (real-space grids, one-hot registers, momentum reuse). Rigor & Reproducibility: Verification rigor is strong by construction — every solution is machine-checked against a frozen specification in a sandbox, with axiom whitelisting and cost-theorem reduction checks, and the authors honestly document two classes of agent cheating (broken proofs, spec loopholes) and how they were filtered or patched. However, the system-level claims are less rigorously evaluated: no ablation over agent-team sizes, model choices, or workflow channels beyond the retrospective 61/15/24 attribution, which is a self-classification of idea origin with no inter-rater or automated validation; no error bars are needed for the proofs themselves but the attribution statistics carry no uncertainty; and compute cost of the discovery runs is unreported. The authors deserve credit for strengthening several baselines themselves (cytochrome P450 halved by newer compilation; non-BO baseline tightened via the authors-of-baseline's later bound) rather than comparing against stale numbers, and they flag that their own arcsin baseline would improve up to 3× with a recent 1/√x circuit. The Lean library, specifications, and solutions are promised for open sourcing "shortly" (footnote 44) but are not yet released, which currently blocks independent reproduction. Several baselines (refs 58, 59, 61, 66) are themselves 2026 preprints, so the comparison envelope rests on non-peer-reviewed numbers in places. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a built and executed discovery system, plus a formal artifact). Practical: The discovery system ran on Google infrastructure with Gemini 4 Carbon models — usable in principle wherever capable LLMs and Lean are available, but hardware/compute requirements for the runs are not stated. Efficient: Not evaluated — the paper never reports tokens, wall-clock, or CPU-hours consumed to reach each solution, so the cost-effectiveness of AI-driven discovery versus expert time is asserted, not measured. Effective: For the stated proxy (minimizing Q·T against verified specifications) it demonstrably works, with proofs eliminating correctness risk; whether these specs faithfully capture what hardware needs (error-correcting codes, routing, physical layout) is explicitly open. Scalable: At 10–100× problem size, verification cost (Lean compilation times already force code-size rules in the wiki) and proof-engineering overhead are the likely bottlenecks; the paper claims but does not test scaling of the workflow itself. Deliverable: a Lean 4 library, problem specifications, and verified solutions, promised open source but not yet public; the workflow is a reusable process, the paper alone stops short of a released artifact. Strengths: (1) Moving LLM-based quantum discovery past the classical-simulability ceiling by replacing execution-based validation with machine-checked correctness-and-cost proofs — a genuine regime shift, not an incremental one. (2) The anti-gaming verification pipeline (frozen spec, sandboxed Lean Comparator re-verification, axiom whitelisting) addresses a well-documented LLM failure mode and is deployed, not just proposed. (3) Honest, aggressive baselining: the authors strengthen their own baselines with the newest literature (sometimes halving them) before claiming speedups, and document specification loopholes the agents found. (4) The first quantitative anatomy of multi-agent scientific collaboration (idea lineage across seven teams, per-problem channel attribution, traced dead-end reuse), which is valuable regardless of the quantum content. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that end-to-end simulations still need far more resources than early fault-tolerant hardware provides (requiring further orders-of-magnitude improvement); that agents cannot optimize beyond the specifications, citing concrete cases (non-BO spec requiring correctness on unphysical states; fixed DFTHC factorization in P450 excluding representation advances); that extending verification to error-correcting codes, routing, and layout is future work; that the Q·T metric may favor the wrong objective under parallel magic-state factories or qLDPC architectures (they argue improvements hold under any monotone weighting since both Q and T fell); and that qubits versus gates may deserve unequal weighting on early machines. They confront these directly rather than minimizing them — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No ablation of the multi-agent architecture itself: since team design is deliberately unconstrained, the paper cannot say whether wikis/conferences, team count, or model scale drive the gains — the 61/15/24 attribution is a retrospective author classification of "where an idea originated," unverifiable from the text. (2) No accounting of discovery compute (tokens, GPU-hours, human hours of specification writing), so "shortening the path" remains unquantified relative to expert baselines. (3) Five hand-authored specifications by Google researchers with deep domain knowledge — the workflow's dependence on expert-quality spec-writing (the acknowledged bottleneck) is untested on problems outside the authors' expertise. (4) Several key baselines and the headline Grover competitor are 2026 preprints, so the "strongest published baseline" envelope is itself unrefereed. (5) The Grover gains partially exploit the zero-cost convention for S-independent unitaries (the Johnson-walk diffusion is free in the oracle metric but costs poly(n,m,k) gates and O((m+k)n) qubits in reality) — the authors note this but the practical cost of the claimed 2.55× is not analyzed. (6) The library is unreleased at publication time, so no external party has yet reproduced or stress-tested the verification stack. Beyond these, the paper is unusually self-aware; no further material gaps are apparent. Bottom Line: This is a landmark demonstration that formal verification unlocks LLM-driven discovery of quantum algorithms at scales classical testing cannot touch — any quantum-algorithms, formal-methods, or AI-for-science researcher should read it — though its systems-level claims (collaboration dynamics, discovery efficiency) are under-ablated and its artifact is not yet released, so treat the workflow recommendations as promising hypotheses rather than validated engineering.

SO-Arena: Benchmarking the Capability Spectrum and Reliability of System One Models (74 ▲ )

Lichen Li, Ziping Dong, Sicheng Feng, Qi Li, Xinchao Wang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 13 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces SO-Arena, a benchmark of 2,919 tasks across 11 domains and five capability families that evaluates "System One" decision models (single-forward-pass classifiers/routers over explicit option sets) on capability, latency, and a separately scored decision-reliability axis. - Why it's important: System One models are being deployed for high-volume, latency-critical decisions (routing, tool selection, verification), and existing benchmarks report only aggregate accuracy, which hides whether a model's decisions are consistent and whether it notices when no valid option exists — failures that matter in production pipelines. - How it does it: The benchmark combines manually verified, traceable labels from 40 public sources; domain-relative difficulty tiers; sandboxed interactive web/tool episodes; and two controlled interventions — 12 option reorderings per item and removal of the correct option — combined into a reliability score R = √(S·N) with a chance-corrected stability measure and an AUC-based null-discrimination measure. - The good: The evaluation of 21 models produces a genuinely non-obvious finding with statistical support: the best-performing System One model ranks only eighth of 18 in reliability, and null discrimination varies widely (near chance to ~0.8) at matched capability, while option-order stability largely tracks performance. - The missing: Reliability is measured only through option-set perturbations on multiple-choice formats; there is no calibration analysis, no contamination check against the heavily reused source datasets (MATH500, MMLU-Redux, GPQA), and the hard tier of one scored domain contains just 20 tasks. - Read it or not: Read it if you build, select, or deploy fast decision/routing models and need to know that capability rankings and reliability rankings diverge; skip it if you only care about general LLM chat or reasoning benchmarks, since its scope is specific to the System One decision interface.
Why this rank
Scored using the Empirical profile. The paper's core value is the separately scored reliability axis: the capability–reliability rank inversion (JevAny-27B first in reliability, eighth of 18 in capability; null discrimination spanning ~0.01 to ~0.8 at matched capability with bootstrap CIs) is a genuine empirical finding that accuracy-only leaderboards cannot produce (Non-Obviousness 80). Rigor (74) is strong on documentation — per-item provenance, pinned model revisions, latency protocol, bootstrap intervals — but is held back by absent error bars on the headline leaderboard, model-derived references (100/500 Safety items), no contamination check against heavily reused sources, and two reliability exceptions favoring specific models. Problem & Motivation: System One models — models that map a state, question, and option set to a probability distribution in one forward pass (e.g., the Jev interface and open derivatives like Kev, JevAny, GLiDE) — trade generated reasoning tokens for latency and structured outputs, making them attractive for classification, routing, tool selection, and verification in software workflows. Existing evaluation efforts (JevBench, JEVal, System1-Arena, OpenDecisions) report aggregate accuracy and, at best, calibration or cost, but do not (a) verify that reference labels are supported by the evidence actually shown to the model, (b) discriminate models via difficulty-stratified tasks, (c) evaluate interactive execution and history-dependent verification in sandboxes, or (d) test decision reliability under controlled changes to the option set. The paper targets practitioners who must decide which fast decision model to trust for repeated, high-volume judgments. Key Idea: The core move is to treat capability and reliability as orthogonal, separately scored dimensions, where reliability is operationalized through two cheap, controlled interventions on the option set: (1) order stability S — does the model pick the same option (identified by content, not position) across 12 reorderings, rescaled so random agreement scores 0 — and (2) null discrimination N — can the model's probability mass separate items whose correct option has been removed from intact items, scored as 2·AUC−1. Their geometric mean yields a combined reliability score that can be reported independently of the capability leaderboard. Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) Sources and quality control: tasks are drawn or derived from 40 public datasets/environments (GoEmotions, MATH500, GPQA Diamond, Mind2Web, BFCL, ToolSandbox, BrowseComp-Plus, VirtualHome, etc.), converted into three decision formats — categorical choice, binary judgment ("noul"), and ordinal score — and passed through human plus LLM label review with items of questionable reference dropped; each item records source, version, and identifier, with references kept separate from model inputs. (2) Organization: 2,919 tasks span 11 domains in five families (semantic understanding, knowledge and reasoning, safety and policy, evidence assessment, agent task completion); nine domains have within-domain difficulty tiers defined by domain-specific criteria (e.g., calculation steps for Math, execution-history dependence for verification); 2,300 tasks are static and 619 are environment-based (337 web tasks on recorded states plus 282 interactive tool-use episodes scored by BFCL/ToolSandbox checkers). (3) Evaluation: the capability score C averages each domain's hardest tier with equal domain weights (Equation 4); reliability uses S, N, and R as above. For math multiple-choice items, distractors are built from base-model wrong answers, intermediate solution results, and rule-based near misses. Critical design decisions: equal domain weighting to prevent large domains from dominating (reasonable but makes one leaderboard domain depend on as few as 20 hard tasks); focusing the leaderboard on the hardest tier to increase discrimination (justified by shown performance declines with difficulty, but further shrinks effective sample sizes); and scoring refusal/context-overflow as zero credit (defensible but penalizes safety-aligned API models on Safety and web tasks, as documented for OpenAI Decisions). Key Results: Across 21 models (16 open-weight System One models from 0.4B to 31B, one auto-switching model, two closed decision APIs, two System Two references), GPT-6 Sol leads the capability leaderboard at 82.3 and GPT-6 Luna at 79.7; the strongest System One models GLiDE and KnowLine-31B both score 70.2, roughly ten points behind Luna. Every open-weight System One model answers within 0.3 s per task on one H100 — tens of times faster than the GPT-6 references. Reliability diverges from capability: JevAny-27B is the most reliable System One model (R = 0.84) while ranking eighth of 18 in capability; Jev API 1.14 (R = 0.83) ranks sixth. Option-order stability is high for most models (14 of 18 above 0.83) but null discrimination ranges from ~0.01 (Laya) to ~0.8, and Kev-27B, Jev API 1.14, and JevAny-27B each exceed all four top-capability System One models on N with bootstrap intervals excluding zero. Domain analysis against GPT-6 Luna shows three regimes: near-parity on direct semantic judgment (e.g., GLiDE +5.0 on Knowledge & Commonsense), backbone-dependent gaps of up to ~29 points on fine-grained grounded decisions, and large gaps on multi-step derivation (GLiDE −26.7 on Math). Thinking helps mainly in Math, lifting StartLux Auto from 50.8 to 92.5, close to Luna. Stability correlates with performance (flip rate 4.3% on originally correct answers vs. 25.7% on originally wrong ones), while null discrimination does not — it must be measured directly. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel elements are the traceable, manually verified reference pipeline; the within-domain difficulty tiers for decision tasks; the distinction between action selection and history-dependent completion verification; and especially the option-set-intervention reliability score (order stability plus missing-answer recognition) reported separately from capability. The underlying tasks are largely re-formed from established public sources, and the reliability interventions are standard perturbation-based robustness testing applied to a new model class — the value lies in the assembly and the empirical divergence finding, not in new learning algorithms. Rigor & Reproducibility: The construction is unusually well documented: per-domain curation criteria, exact model revisions and inference settings (Table 4), pinned Hugging Face revisions, a separate latency protocol (one H100, one request at a time, three timed passes after a warm-up, with per-task means and 90th/99th percentiles), bootstrap 95% intervals for domain-level differences from Luna, and 2,000-fold item resampling for null-discrimination comparisons. Ablation-style evidence exists for the analysis choices (hard-tier-only robustness checks in Table 7; auto-mode reproduction agreement of 90–92%). Weaknesses: no error bars are reported on the headline capability leaderboard itself; several references are model-derived (100 of 500 Safety items, all BrowseComp-Plus evidence-sufficiency items), flagged in metadata but still a circularity risk; two reliability exceptions favor specific models (Jeva-4B's S = 1 by construction, StartLux Instant scored with its own null output); and refusals scored as zero confound alignment behavior with capability for OpenAI Decisions. Code, data, and a leaderboard are publicly released via the homepage, Hugging Face (huggingface.co/SO-Arena), and GitHub (github.com/holdrain/SO-Arena). Training-data contamination of the reused academic sources is not discussed. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a benchmark plus evaluation study; the artifact is the benchmark and harness). - Practical: Yes — all open-weight models run on a single H100 80 GB with documented fast paths, and the benchmark harness executes on commodity hardware. - Efficient: Evaluation is cheap for System One models (6–265 ms per timed task) but the StartLux Auto thinking mode costs 3,084 ms mean latency, over 50× its instant variant, and closed-API timing includes network and provider queueing. - Effective: The evidence convincingly shows the benchmark discriminates models and exposes capability–reliability divergence, but effectiveness as a predictor of production decision quality (e.g., under distribution shift or adversarial inputs) is not established. - Scalable: Not stress-tested; the benchmark itself is fixed at 2,919 tasks, the reliability protocol multiplies inference cost 13× per item (original plus 12 reorderings, plus null variants), and one leaderboard domain rests on 20 hard tasks — extending to more domains or larger option spaces is claimed by design but not demonstrated. The work delivers a concrete software artifact: benchmark, harness, leaderboard, and per-model configurations, not just a paper. Strengths: - The separate reliability axis is the paper's real contribution: the demonstration that null discrimination varies from ~0.01 to ~0.8 at matched capability, with statistically supported rank inversions (three lower-capability models each beat all four top-capability models on N), is a finding accuracy-only leaderboards structurally cannot produce. - The label-quality pipeline is above the bar for benchmark papers: references kept separate from model inputs, per-item provenance, execution-verified references for code solutions (re-execution on public/private tests plus brute-force cross-checks), and verified counterfactual trajectories for history-dependent verification items. - The three-regime analysis (direct semantic judgment vs. fine-grained grounded decision vs. multi-step derivation) with matched backbone and thinking controls gives practitioners actionable guidance: backbone capability, not reasoning, closes the gap in grounded decision domains, and thinking is essentially a math/science lever (+41.7 points on Math medium/hard for StartLux Auto). - Honest reporting of adverse details — refusal scoring, context-window zero-credit rules, Jeva-4B's constructed S = 1, and the scored-vs-measurement run discrepancies (875–938/939 agreement) — raises confidence in the rest of the numbers. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge that difficulty tiers are relative within domains and not calibrated across domains; that Jeva-4B's stability is 1 by construction and that the StartLux Instant null comparison rests on its own null-output format; that OpenAI Decisions' refusals on Safety and patient-portal tasks score as zero; that Laya's 8,192-token window zeroes out 30 web tasks; that scored runs and latency/reliability runs disagree on a small fraction of items (StartLux Auto, 92% agreement, due to sampled thinking); and that leaderboard domain minima can be as small as 20 tasks. These are confronted directly rather than minimized, which strengthens credibility. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Contamination: the benchmark reuses MATH500, GSM8K, MMLU-Redux, GPQA Diamond, ARC, HellaSwag, and CommonsenseQA — datasets almost certainly in the pretraining corpora of the evaluated backbones (Qwen3.5/Qwen3.8) — and no decontamination or held-out probe is reported, so the capability spectrum may partially measure memorization. - The reliability definition is narrow: it captures option-order sensitivity and missing-answer awareness but not calibration quality, confidence-accuracy correlation, or behavior under paraphrased/ambiguous items; a model could score high on R while being badly miscalibrated in deployment. - The null-discrimination metric presumes access to usable probability estimates over options; the paper does not discuss how API models with undisclosed internals or models with degenerate probability readouts are handled beyond the two exceptions noted. - The capability leaderboard's hardest-tier focus, combined with tiers as small as 20 tasks (Task Completion Verification hard), means headline score differences of a few points may not be statistically meaningful — no intervals are given for the leaderboard itself, only for the per-domain Luna comparisons. - Refusal-as-zero conflates safety alignment with incapability for API models on the Safety and Web domains; an alternative scoring that treats refusals as a separate outcome would change the closed-API rankings, and the paper does not report sensitivity to this choice. - The System One–Two comparison uses only two closed GPT-6 references; no open System Two model (e.g., a comparable-size reasoning model run locally) is included, so the latency–capability Pareto claim rests on proprietary endpoints with uncontrolled serving conditions. Bottom Line: For anyone selecting or training fast decision models, this is currently the most methodologically careful benchmark of the System One model class and its reliability-divergence finding alone justifies a read; for general LLM evaluation purposes, existing broader benchmarks cover capability while missing exactly the reliability axis that makes this paper worth attention.
