Problem & Motivation: Recent frameworks for agent harness evolution — iteratively rewriting an agent's prompts, skills, tools, orchestration, or source code while keeping model weights frozen — report aggregate benchmark gains and present this as progress toward recursive self-improvement. The paper argues a higher average score is not a more useful agent: averages hide newly lost tasks, deployment cost is rarely reported, and gains measured on evolution tasks may not transfer. The gap addressed is the absence of paired, task-level, cost-aware, and transfer-aware evaluation in this subfield; the intended audience is researchers building evolution methods (AHE, HyperAgents, A-Evolve, GEPA, Darwin Gödel Machine-style systems) and practitioners deciding whether to deploy evolved agents. Key Idea: Treat harness evolution as a redistribution process, not a monotone improvement process, and audit each evolutionary operator with decision-specific evidence rather than a shared aggregate score. The reusable trick is a set of four controlled diagnostics: (1) paired Seed-vs-Champion 9×9 success-transition matrices over repeated passes (coverage as a "flow" of gains and losses), (2) common-process Parent expansion where each Champion spawns three Candidates under one fixed analyzer/mutator to measure whether current score predicts future improvement, (3) Component isolation (Seed + A, Seed + B, Champion) with generic-reminder controls to measure change specificity and non-additive interactions, and (4) frozen-pool admission replays scoring gate rules by best-Candidate retention normalized by retained-set size. This is a genuine methodological insight, not just a benchmark. Methodology: The study uses a common operator framework instantiated by four recipes — AHE (newest-Parent selection, debugger-report analysis, observability-grounded mutation), HyperAgents (score-weighted selection with child-count penalty, editable operators), A-Evolve (highest-score selection, behavior-only trajectory judge, strict-improvement gate), and GEPA (per-task Pareto selection, reflection with Train-batch validation filter) — each run on two harnesses (MiniSWE 2.4.5, source-editable; Codex 0.143.0, outer-layer-only) with GPT-5.4, on τ3-Banking (97 general tasks) and Terminal-Bench 2 (89 coding tasks), each split Train/Validation/Test with 20 generations per lineage. Metrics are Reliability (Avg@k), empirical Coverage (Pass@k), task turnover (gained/lost tasks), and recorded-USD evolution/deployment costs (Equations 2–3). RQ1 uses eight-pass frozen evaluations with pass-half stability checks and a 22-case trace audit of behavioral categories; RQ2 evaluates held-out Test splits and external transfer to τ2-bench (278 tasks, 22,240 evaluations) and DeepSWE v1.1 (113 tasks × 8 passes per configuration); RQ3 runs the four controlled diagnostics. Critical design decisions: (a) separating select/analyze/mutate/gate for mechanism analysis — justified by the operators being the only decision points determining gain generation and retention; (b) the size-normalized retention metric for gate — defensible but nonstandard, and the paper is appropriately careful about its interpretation; (c) freezing Component boundaries before evaluation — a good practice that guards against post-hoc selection. AGE then installs four operator revisions into A-Evolve: regression-aware tie-breaking in select, a behavior-grounded trajectory judge in analyze (0–10 scores, Observed/Inferred verdicts, explicit char budgets), dependency-closed mutation with diff inspection and surface checks, and score-first cost-aware admission (equal-score candidates admitted only on verified cost reduction). Key Results: Phenomenology: reliability improves in 11/16 lineages and coverage in 10/16, but all 16 Champions both gain and lose coverage (gains 1–15 tasks, losses 2–10); e.g., MiniSWE/A-Evolve on τ3-Banking nets only +1 coverage (7 gained, 6 lost) and one general-task case gains +5.2 Avg despite losing ten covered tasks. Eight of eleven reliability-improving Champions cost more per trial (e.g., τ3-Banking Codex AHE: $1.108 vs $0.983/trial), though AHE/MiniSWE on τ3-Banking reaches 56.7% Pass@4 versus Seed's 54.6% Pass@8 at lower total deployment cost. Generalization: Test reliability improves in 10/16; transfer coverage falls for 7/8 Champions on τ2-bench but rises for 7/8 on DeepSWE (e.g., Codex AHE +8.0 Pass@8 on DeepSWE), with reliability sometimes moving opposite to coverage. Mechanisms: original select rules beat the 25% random best-Parent baseline only on coding tasks (59.5%, 55.7%) and fall below random on general tasks (17.5%, 8.8%); 15/16 specific Components beat generic reminders; two HyperAgents general-task cases show significantly negative interaction (−6.3 and −6.6 points, 95% task-paired intervals excluding zero); constrained admission retains the reporting-panel best in only 6 of 15 pools versus 15 under original rules. AGE: beats A-Evolve on reliability and coverage in all four settings — τ3-Banking: 34.0/66.0 (MiniSWE) and 38.1/67.0 (Codex) Avg@8/Pass@8 versus Seeds at 27.4/54.6 and 30.3/56.7; Terminal-Bench 2: 71.8/89.9 and 73.5/92.1 versus Seeds at 65.9/86.5 and 69.9/89.9 — while losing fewer Seed-covered tasks in three of four settings and at comparable deployment/evolution cost to other methods. Baselines (AHE, HyperAgents, A-Evolve, GEPA) are current and central to this subfield; the expert review (8 experts, direction agreement 6/8, endorsement 6.75/8) is supportive but small. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING plus NEW METHOD (secondary). The genuinely novel contributions are the operator-level diagnostic protocol (Parent expansion, component isolation with reminder controls, admission replays) and the redistribution/turnover findings, which collectively reframe how harness-evolution progress should be measured. AGE itself is a competent combination of established ideas — regression-aware tie-breaking, trace-grounded diagnosis, dependency checking, cost tie-breaks — applied to settings the diagnostics identified, and its value is as validation of the analysis rather than as a standalone method. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablation-style evidence is unusually strong for this area: component isolations, generic-reminder controls, interaction estimates with 95% task-paired intervals, frozen-pool replays with predeclared checkpoints, pass-half stability checks, and complete audit ledgers (7,760 + 7,120 paired executions; 22,240 transfer evaluations). No multiple search seeds or significance tests on the headline AGE comparison are reported — AGE runs use a single seed (0) per setting — and several aggregate conclusions rest on small task counts (Terminal-Bench deltas of 1–2 tasks, i.e., 1/89 ≈ 1.1 points per task). Code is released at https://github.com/simple-agent-lab/RSIHub. Concerns: AGE's operator revisions are derived from diagnostics run on the same two benchmarks used for its evaluation (a Goodhart's Law risk the paper does not test via a third held-out benchmark); the four compared methods' lineage artifacts come from the authors' own RSIHub re-implementations, so absolute numbers may not match original papers; and the expert review is 8 raters with no inter-rater reliability reported. The paper is an arXiv preprint (2611.07624, dated Nov 5, 2026), not yet peer-reviewed. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS artifact — the RSIHub framework). - Practical: Yes — everything runs on commercial API access (GPT-5.4) with standard harnesses (MiniSWE, Codex CLI); no special hardware. - Efficient: Evolution costs $723–$2,373 per lineage in recorded calls and deployment costs $0.64–$1.11 per trial; AGE sits mid-pack on evolution cost (e.g., $1,070.6 vs AHE's $1,235.0 on τ3-Banking/MiniSWE), but evolved agents frequently carry a per-trial cost premium, which the paper quantifies rather than hides. - Effective: The evidence shows improved reliability/coverage on the tested benchmarks and mixed transfer; whether this constitutes the claimed "practical improvement" depends on accepting the paper's own preservation-aware framing, which is well-argued but self-defined. - Scalable: Only claimed, not tested — 20 generations, ≤100-task benchmarks, one model (GPT-5.4); behavior at 10× tasks, multiple models, or longer horizons is unknown, and the pass-half instability on τ3-Banking suggests variance grows with noise. The work delivers a software artifact (RSIHub framework, code released) plus reusable diagnostic protocols; AGE weights are code/config artifacts, not model weights. Strengths: - The coverage-as-flow analysis (all 16 Champions both gain and lose tasks, with paired 9×9 transition matrices over 8 passes) is a decisive, well-powered empirical result that directly contradicts how progress is currently reported in this subfield. - The operator-decomposition methodology (select/analyze/mutate/gate replays with shared downstream processes) is a genuinely reusable experimental template that other groups can apply to any evolution framework, not just the four studied. - Reporting deployment cost in recorded USD alongside reliability, and showing that higher per-trial cost can coexist with cheaper coverage attainment (cost-to-coverage curves), is the kind of honest accounting Kapoor et al. called for and most evolution papers omit. - The constructive loop is unusually tight: each AGE operator revision is tied to specific diagnostic evidence (Tables 4–8), and the paper distinguishes what the analysis supports from what the end-to-end comparison shows. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that neither benchmark gains nor expert endorsement establish deployment safety; that evolution can introduce regressions and unintended tool use (Ethics Statement); that transfer "selectively preserves gains" and must be assessed per outcome and per target; that strict admission can discard useful alternatives; and that pass-half comparisons show aggregate trends on τ3-Banking are sensitive to execution variability. They confront the cost premium and regression phenomenon directly rather than minimizing them — a credibility positive. They do not, however, explicitly flag the single-seed AGE runs or the same-benchmark provenance of their revisions. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Single search seed (0) per AGE setting with no variance estimate; the claim that AGE "improves in all four settings" is consistent with favorable noise given margins of 1–6 reliability points on 20–27-task validation panels. - The diagnostics-to-revision pipeline is trained and evaluated on the same two benchmarks; a third, fully held-out benchmark would be needed to rule out that AGE's gains are partly fit to the diagnostic distribution. - Only one frontier model (GPT-5.4) is tested; all operator-revision conclusions could be model-specific, and the harness–paradigm interactions the paper itself documents make cross-model generality non-trivial. - Several headline deltas rest on single-digit task counts (e.g., GEPA/Codex on Terminal-Bench 2: −3.4 Pass equals 3 tasks), and no significance tests accompany the Table 10 comparison. - The 22-case behavioral audit and the 8-case component matrix are selective samples; selection criteria are stated and frozen, but the generalization of the behavioral taxonomy (state preservation, grounding, completion) beyond these cases is not quantified. - The expert review lacks inter-rater agreement statistics and any control condition (e.g., reviewing a randomly generated revision), so the 6–6.75/8 endorsement numbers are hard to benchmark. Bottom Line: This is the most careful measurement-focused study of agent harness evolution published to date, and anyone building self-improving agents should adopt its paired gain/loss, cost, and transfer reporting — but treat AGE as a plausible validation of the analysis rather than a proven general recipe, given the single-seed, same-benchmark evaluation.

ROCm InferaSim: Cut LLM Serving Trial Costs and Deploy the Best Configuration

A Raina, Y Fu, Z Jiejing, P Razaghi, S Patel, R Gupta… · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds ROCm InferaSim, a framework that predicts LLM serving performance (TPOT, TTFT, throughput, tails) across serving engines, parallelism layouts, precisions, and disaggregation choices from a handful of short "anchor" measurements plus analytical transfer laws, replacing per-configuration GPU trials. - Why it's important: Exhaustively measuring all candidate serving configurations for their search space would cost ~25,000 GPU-hours; operators currently tune by hand with a few expensive trials, so a sub-second predictor changes serving configuration from a hardware search into a CPU search. - How it does it: The core trick is partitioning serving choices into anchor-defining ones (precision, backend, engine — which change the kernels) and transferable ones (batch, TP/EP/PP width, replicas — which only change per-GPU work), measuring each kernel set once on at most one node, then analytically scaling the GPU-divisible work while keeping the fixed per-step cost (kernel launches, sync, sampling) constant. - The good: The evaluation is unusually thorough: 8.1% median TPOT error across 172 measured fixed-length configurations on three engines, 5.5% throughput error on 159 disaggregated deployments with no disaggregated anchor, and 93.4% correct ordering of decisive throughput pairs — with a direct head-to-head where ported Vidur gets 40% TPOT error on the same rows versus 7.2%. - The missing: Every measurement is on AMD MI355X hardware only, and the paper's own limitation section concedes NVIDIA validation is entirely future work; several error numbers degrade (TTFT 13.6–23%, one SGLang MoE agentic row at 2.01× ITL error factor). - Read it or not: Read it if you build or operate LLM serving infrastructure or work on performance modeling/simulation of inference systems — it is the most complete serving performance-predictor evaluation published to date — skip it if you only care about NVIDIA-based deployments today.

Problem & Motivation: Operators deploying LLMs face a combinatorial configuration problem: choosing a serving engine (vLLM, SGLang, ATOM), parallelism layout (TP/EP/PP/attention-DP), numeric precisions, scheduler settings, speculative decoding, KV-cache tiering, and prefill-decode disaggregation. The best configuration depends on model, hardware, workload, and objective (TTFT, interactivity, or throughput), and each hardware trial holds GPUs for a median 3.4 minutes plus engine startup — measuring the paper's 226 fixed-length configurations cost 204 GPU-hours, and full search coverage would take ~25,000 GPU-hours. Existing solutions fall short in two documented ways: operator-level simulators (Vidur, APEX, LLMServingSim, AIConfigurator) must re-profile per model/engine/kernel-library change, support no MoE models (Vidur), and ship no AMD GPU data; pure analytical roofline models ignore the fixed per-step cost of kernel launches and scheduling, which dominates scaling — naively halving a measured 4-GPU DeepSeek-V4-Pro step time to predict 8-GPU performance yields 44% median error. Key Idea: Classify every serving choice by whether it changes the kernel set. Anchor-defining choices (checkpoint, precisions, attention/MoE backend, graph capture, speculative method, engine, GPU) require one measured "anchor" — a sweep of complete engine step times on at most one node. Transferable choices (batch size, context length, TP/EP/PP widths, replicas, load, host-memory KV) are predicted by analytical laws that hold the fixed per-step cost f (taken from the anchor's batch-1 step) constant and scale only the GPU-divisible remainder, e.g., s_w'(b) = f + (s_w(b) − f)·ρ_w→w'(b). This reduces the TP4→TP8 transfer error on DeepSeek-V4-Pro from 44.1% (naive halving) to 0.9%. Targets larger than a node are handled by a reduce–measure–restore loop adapted from the authors' own training-performance-prediction work (ref. [43]), with disaggregated pools, host-tier KV, and queueing newly modeled for inference. Methodology: The pipeline has seven stages (Fig. 3): (1) a serving spec compiles model/hardware/recipe/workload into an op graph; (2) a harvester produces an anchor — a decode sweep over captured batch sizes, a five-point prefill sweep fitted as T(n) = F + c₁n + c₂n², an optional packed-prefill probe, and a provenance signature (engine version, prompt length, real-weights flag, prefix-caching-off flag); (3) kernel models (Origami GEMM prediction plus own attention/communication/pipeline models) power measurement-free simulate mode; (4) a step cost model predicts any step given batch, context, and layout; (5) an analytical predictor outputs means, memory, and capacity; (6) a discrete-event simulator (DES) advances a virtual clock through arrivals, admission, scheduling (token budget, chunked prefill, captured-batch padding), paged/leaf-LRU prefix caching, host-KV tiering, and replica routing, with cache hit rate as an output rather than an input; (7) a tuning agent (deterministic seed sweep + DSPy/ReAct LLM loop over 36 levers and 24 objectives, with legality checks on HBM and SLOs, the LLM never pricing anything) and a four-tier mix planner search predictions. Critical design decisions: (a) keeping the fixed per-step cost across TP widths — strongly justified by ablation (0.9% vs 44.1%/18.5% for alternatives); (b) modeling MoE expert imbalance from recorded router logs evaluated at both anchor and target EP — justified, since a single value would cancel and make wider EP look free, and measured busiest-rank factors run 1.4–2.1× vs 1.2× for a uniform router; (c) reading decode step time at the graph-capture padded size rather than interpolating — well argued, since interpolation would understate step cost. Key Results: All on AMD Instinct MI355X nodes (8×288 GB HBM3E each). Anchored mode on 172 fixed-length configurations (8 models, 3 engines, TP2–8, 1–256 clients) from 11 anchors (9.1 GPU-hours to collect): 8.1% median TPOT error, 8.8% throughput, 13.6% TTFT; 93% of configs within 20% on TPOT. On 95 held-out AgentX agentic runs: error factors 1.08 (throughput), 1.14 (ITL), 1.23 (TTFT). On 159 disaggregated InferenceX deployments with no disaggregated anchor: 5.5% throughput, 5.3% interactivity, 16.9% TTFT. Ranking: 93.4% of decisive throughput pairs ordered correctly (anchored), 89.0% in measurement-free simulate mode; predicted Pareto frontiers retain 83% of measured-frontier configurations (170/206) with 0% median throughput loss. Pipelines: 11.6% median TPOT error on 24 two-node pipelines projected from single-node anchors; per-stage hop cost measured at 920–1130 µs. Speculative MTP runs predicted at 8.9% throughput error. Baseline comparison: ported Vidur achieves 34–40% error on 30 SGLang Llama-3.1-8B rows vs 7.2–14% for InferaSim; against AIConfigurator and APEX the comparison is via reported numbers only (Table 12). Search cost: 192 seed searches scoring 56,328 candidates in 3–8 CPU-hours; the mix planner's 5-candidate short list contains a within-12%-of-best deployment in 22 of 23 feasible slots. Note the scale caveat: some per-model rows are tiny (DeepSeek-V4-Pro fixed-length n=2), and much of the held-out evaluation corpus (262 InferenceX runs) is a third-party benchmark rather than independently adversarial data. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (anchor-and-transfer performance prediction for serving, with the fixed-cost-preserving transfer law) plus NEW SYSTEM/TOOL. The genuinely novel elements are the anchor/transferable-choice taxonomy with the fixed-floor scaling law, the inference-specific reduce–measure–restore extensions (disaggregated pools, host-KV tiers, queueing), and the end-to-end integration with an LLM-driven tuning agent where predictions replace trials. The components are a competent combination of known ideas — analytical roofline modeling, discrete-event simulation, training-projection methods from the authors' prior work, and LLM-agent search loops — applied to a setting (MoE-heavy, disaggregated, agentic serving on AMD hardware) where prior tools demonstrably fail. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually strong: Table 18 checks individual modeling decisions against measured runs (e.g., transfer law 0.9% vs 18.5%/44.1% alternatives; PP model 2.3–9.2% vs 14.9–26.1% serial model), Appendix E validates harvest integrity checks (real weights vs random: 1.337× decode error; prefix caching on/off: 68 ms vs 782 ms fits), and run-to-run noise (1–4% on p99) is reported to contextualize tail errors. No confidence intervals or significance tests on the headline medians, and per-model sample sizes vary from 2 to 67. Code/scripts and anchor artifacts are promised with the camera-ready version but are not yet released; engine containers are public. Methodological concerns: (a) anchors match targets by signature fields, not kernel traces, so an unverified kernel-set identity is an assumption; (b) the tool was developed and evaluated on overlapping corpora (the paper is transparent about which runs are anchors vs held out, and Goodhart risk is mitigated by held-out splits, but the scheduler models are engine-specific and tuned on the same engines they score); (c) 262 of the scored fixed-length runs come from InferenceX, whose measurement setup the authors do not fully control; (d) the vendor affiliation (AMD) with all evaluation on AMD's own newest GPU warrants independent replication, which the promised release should enable. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a built prediction/tuning tool, evaluated against measured deployments). - Practical: Runs on one CPU core per prediction (0.17–0.48 s including a DES run); anchors need brief access to a single node of the target GPU type. - Efficient: 9.1 GPU-hours of anchors replace 204 GPU-hours for 226 configurations and ~25,000 GPU-hours for full search coverage — a ~2,700× measurement reduction on the search. - Effective: Evidence supports the stated purpose (ranking and near-best selection: 93.4% pair accuracy, 83% frontier retention) better than absolute precision (TTFT up to 23% error, one agentic cell at 2.01× ITL factor). - Scalable: The method's premise is that larger deployments need no more measurement (a 24-GPU disaggregated target costs the same to predict as one GPU); validated to 24 GPUs (two nodes) and 2,048 clients, but 10–100× clusters (hundreds of GPUs, hierarchical routing, cross-datacenter prefill) are untested and the flat topologies modeled (single mesh tier, one NIC pair profile) may not hold. The work delivers a software artifact (predictor, harvester, DES, tuning agent) plus a reusable anchor artifact format; public release is committed but not yet available. Strengths: - The central insight — separating kernel-set-defining choices from work-scaling choices and preserving the fixed per-step cost under parallelism transfer — is simple, well-argued, and quantitatively decisive (0.9% vs 44.1% on the motivating case). - Evaluation breadth is exceptional for a systems paper: three engines, 13 models, fixed-length, agentic (AgentX trace), disaggregated, multi-node pipeline, speculative decoding, and host-KV offload workloads, with 529 measured configurations scored against predictions. - Diagnosis-before-modeling discipline: several findings are independently interesting measurements, e.g., pipeline TPOT grows 920–1130 µs per stage because SGLang disables CPU-GPU overlap under PP; random-token benchmarks overstate MoE expert imbalance (hottest expert 46× fair share in prefill vs ~1.4× on real code); crossing nodes costs almost nothing per hop inside a step. - Honest coverage accounting: the paper consistently separates what anchors cover (scored for accuracy) from what is merely ranked, and marks extrapolated targets. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The Limitations section (§7) is brief and direct: all measurements are on MI355X; the method is hardware-agnostic in principle but NVIDIA evaluation is explicitly future work. Elsewhere the authors acknowledge that anchors are not verified against kernel traces, that anchors measured outside their range are flagged rather than corrected, that SGLang EP routing needed a fitted parameter (half the I_d surplus), that TTFT carries higher error (16.9–23% on splits and agentic traffic), and that simulate mode is ranking-only. This directness is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Single-vendor, single-architecture validation: every transfer constant (per-hop overhead, custom all-reduce α/B, host-time fit) is MI355X- and often engine-specific; generality of the anchor framework to NVIDIA, where kernel-launch costs, graph capture semantics, and NCCL behavior differ, is asserted but not shown. - Signature-based anchor matching without kernel-trace verification is a silent-failure mode the authors note but do not quantify — how often would a naive user's anchor silently mismatch? - Engine-specific scheduler models in the DES are the stated reason per-step costs "mostly cancel" in simulate mode, yet simulate mode's absolute errors are never scored — only ranking — so its cost model's absolute fidelity is unknown. - No error bars or significance tests on headline medians, and minimum cell sizes as low as n=2 (DeepSeek-V4-Pro fixed-length) undermine per-model claims. - The deployment-mix and planner results restrict candidates to anchor-covered runs, which is the favorable regime; planner performance in the harder simulate-only regime is tested only on a separate simulate-mode tier study, not on hardware. - No comparison against AIConfigurator on the authors' own hardware (it is NVIDIA-only, hence excluded, but a reimplementation or a shared-hardware baseline would strengthen the case beyond the single Vidur head-to-head). Bottom Line: For anyone operating or building LLM serving systems — especially on AMD hardware or facing multi-node/disaggregated configuration decisions — this is the strongest published serving-performance predictor and clearly worth reading; NVIDIA-centric practitioners should treat it as a rigorous, well-evidenced template whose numbers do not yet transfer to their stack.

Delyan Boychev, Ivo Petrov, Dimitar I. Dimitrov · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 9 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces an exact, FlashAttention-style tiled algorithm and Triton kernel that fuses additive relative-position attention terms (covering Shaw, Transformer-XL, DeBERTa, and T5 mechanisms) into fused attention computation, eliminating the dense N×N bias matrix that all existing backends materialize. - Why it's important: Learnable relative-position encoders (used in Parakeet, Canary, SeamlessM4T, DeBERTa, ProtTrans, genomics models) generalize to long contexts better than RoPE/ALiBi but are currently so slow and memory-hungry beyond short sequences that practitioners replace them and retrain from scratch; skip it if you work exclusively with RoPE-based autoregressive LLMs.

Problem & Motivation: Additive relative-position attention augments attention logits with learnable terms depending on the query–key offset (Shaw et al., Transformer-XL, DeBERTa disentangled attention, T5 bucket biases). These mechanisms remain the backbone of conformer-based speech models (Parakeet, Canary, SeamlessM4T v2, Phi-4-multimodal), DeBERTa text pipelines, and biological sequence models, and empirically extrapolate to longer contexts better than RoPE/ALiBi. Unlike RoPE's per-token rotations, their pairwise offset-dependent terms require per-pair lookups or gathers into a dense N×N bias matrix, reintroducing exactly the quadratic HBM bandwidth bottleneck that FlashAttention eliminated. Programmable backends like FlexAttention express score modifications as pointwise callbacks that cannot see tile structure, causing redundant lookups and atomic-contention gradient accumulation. Practitioners currently abandon these encodings (Flashzoi, Flash-Swin) or accept dense-bias costs. Key Idea: Treat relative-position terms as low-rank, offset-structured tensors whose block structure across the attention matrix can be exploited at tile granularity rather than as opaque per-pair lookups: (1) each contiguous query group of size G reaches only N+G−1 relation rows, so projections can be restricted to reachable ranges; (2) tiles outside the diagonal band |δ| < Δ map all pairs to one saturated relation row, so one entry per query/key plus the bias can be broadcast across the tile instead of performing |I|·|J| lookups; (3) in backward, each offset δ = i−j has a single writer per query, so gradient accumulation by offset (rather than by relation row) removes all O(N²) atomic additions and yields deterministic gradients. Methodology: The paper first gives a unified canonical score equation S_ij = τ(q_i·k_j + q_i·a^Q_φ(i,j) + k_j·a^K_φ(i,j) + b_φ(i,j)) + M_ij subsuming four mechanisms via relation tables (A^Q, A^K ∈ R^{R×d}, b ∈ R^R) and an offset map φ. The forward pass (Alg. 1) is a FlashAttention-style tiled loop with online softmax, extended by: group-wise preprojection Z^Q = Q_g(A^Q_{Ω_g})^T restricted to reachable rows Ω_g (halving projection work and storage for identity maps at N ≫ G, G=128 aligned to tile size); host-side precomputation of per-tile saturation ranges so each tile either broadcasts one relation entry or does per-score lookups only in the diagonal band; and bucketed maps expanded to 2Δ+1 clipped rows so they reuse the saturation logic. The backward pass (Alg. 2) uses the two-pass query-parallel/key-parallel schedule: the query pass accumulates τ·dS_ij by offset into dZ̃^Q with on-chip boundary sums for |δ| ≥ Δ, followed by bucket folding and matrix-product reductions (dA^Q = (dZ^Q)^T Q, etc.), with symmetric key pass for dK, dV, dZ̃^K. The backward is proven exact via lemmas (App. B) covering online softmax, tile locality, saturated tiles, reachable ranges, bucket expansion, and atomic-free accumulation. Key design decisions: G aligned to tile size (1.6% column overhead at 8K — justified by measurement), bucket expansion replacing index lookups with clipping (justified via Lemma B.4), and saving vs. recomputing Z^Q/Z^K as a user-selectable compute–memory tradeoff (justified in ablations: 0.42–0.50× memory for 1.1× slowdown). Implemented in Triton with compile-time specialization on relation terms, map type, Δ, masking, packing, dropout, and precision; Hugging Face and NeMo adapters require no weight changes. Key Results: At 8K tokens on an H200 (FP16, 12 heads, d=64, 16K-token budget): forward speedups of 1.8–6.4× and backward speedups of 2.0–21× over the fastest production baseline per mechanism (e.g., Shaw forward 279 vs 211 TFLOP/s for FA4+decomposition, backward 166 vs 7.9 TFLOP/s for FlexAttention+decomposition); peak memory reductions of 2.9–128× forward and 1.4–54× backward. Against generalist engines augmented with the authors' own relation decomposition, the full method still wins 1.1–2.2× forward and 1.7–228× backward (the 228× is T5 backward, where FlexAttention's atomic accumulation collapses to 0.76 TFLOP/s). Gains shrink for TXL (1.4–2.4×) because identity maps keep projections quadratic for everyone — an honest, mechanistically explained result. Every production DeBERTa backward baseline fails the authors' FP32 correctness check from 4K tokens; the proposed method passes everywhere. End-to-end: Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v3 transcription of full TED-LIUM 3 talks reaches 1103 vs 613 RTFx (1.8×) and 11 vs 27 GiB with matched WER (2.89 vs 3.01); Canary-1B-v2 fine-tuning speeds up steps 1.09–1.36× and trains on 15–18-minute windows where the SDPA path runs out of memory; DeBERTa-v3-base on BIGPATENT trains 2.19–2.39× faster at 2K–4K tokens with accuracy matched within 0.3 points and flat 7.1 GiB memory. Ablations (Table 7) show atomic-free gradients carry most of the backward gain (2.9–4.4× latency without them) and projections most of the forward gain (2.0–2.9×). Baselines are current and strong (FlexAttention, FlashAttention-4, FlashInfer, FlashDeBERTa, NeMo) and are additionally tested with the authors' decomposition, an unusually fair setup. Caveat: the method loses to production systems on T5 backward at 128–256 tokens (0.75–0.82×) due to setup overhead, which the authors state. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD plus ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The genuinely novel elements are the unified offset-structure formulation spanning four mechanisms and the three tile-level tricks — reachable projection ranges, saturation-broadcast reuse, and offset-owned atomic-free gradient accumulation — that programmable backends cannot express. The underlying scaffolding (online softmax, two-pass backward, tiled recomputation) is standard FlashAttention machinery competently extended; the paper is explicit about building on the Triton two-pass schedule. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and isolate every component (Tables 7 and 10), including HBM-traffic measurements via Nsight Compute. Correctness is validated per-tensor against an independent FP32 eager reference with explicit tolerances (5% relative / 0.03 absolute, or ℓ2 within eight rounding units), and this check usefully disqualifies competing backends rather than being waived. Timing methodology is detailed (L2 flushing, 50 ms warmup, medians of ≥10 runs, random system order, recorded clocks/temperature), and results cover three GPU architectures. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported for the timing benchmarks (standard for kernel work, but the end-to-end fine-tuning results are single runs and the WER gap at 9-minute windows — 3.73 vs 4.34 — is attributed post-hoc to repetition loops in one or two recordings). Code is promised to be open-sourced with benchmark scripts and result files but is not yet released ("We will open-source...", App. H); no URL is given. No Goodhart risk: the method is evaluated on standard models (Parakeet, Canary, DeBERTa-v3) and public datasets (TED-LIUM 3, BIGPATENT), not an authors' benchmark. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a built Triton kernel library evaluated by benchmarking and deployment in production model pipelines). - Practical: Runs on commodity NVIDIA GPUs (H200/H100-class, RTX PRO 6000, RTX A6000) via Triton/PyTorch with Hugging Face and NeMo adapters requiring no weight changes. - Efficient: Strictly cheaper than every baseline it replaces at ≥1K tokens (e.g., 24 MiB vs 3.0K MiB forward for T5 at 8K), though it loses at very short sequences on some mechanisms and is 1.1× slower if projections are recomputed to save memory. - Effective: Evidence covers exactness (FP32-reference checks), matched downstream quality (WER within 0.09–0.28 points on transcription, accuracy within 0.3 points on classification), and large throughput/memory gains — the strongest deployability case in the paper. - Scalable: Tested to 8K tokens and ~25-minute audio; TXL-style identity maps remain quadratic in projection cost at 10×–100× scale, and no attention-level test exceeds 8K, so beyond-8K behavior is claimed by monotonicity arguments rather than measured. The work delivers a software artifact (Triton kernel library with model adapters), pending the promised open-source release; reusable techniques include the offset-owned gradient accumulation schedule and the bucket-expansion reduction. Strengths: - The core insight — that relative-offset maps have tile-level structure (reachable ranges, saturation regions, per-offset gradient ownership) that pointwise programmable callbacks cannot exploit — is a real algorithmic contribution, not just kernel tuning, and each piece is separately justified by ablation and proof. - The unified formulation of Shaw/TXL/DeBERTa/T5 under one canonical score equation is itself useful: one kernel family serves four model families, and the backward-pass proofs (App. B) establish exactness and determinism rather than leaving them implicit. - The evaluation holds the method to a high bar: baselines are given the authors' own relation decomposition, a correctness gate disqualifies numerically failing competitors, and gains are explained mechanistically (e.g., why TXL gains least, why T5 backward collapses under atomics). - Honest reporting of unfavorable results: production systems win at short lengths on T5, the Canary transducer overhead erases speedup in fine-tuning, and the limitation of identity maps is stated quantitatively. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly (a credibility positive). They state: (1) identity maps keep projection work and space quadratic in N, with the linear-memory alternative costing 2.0–2.9× forward slowdown; (2) maps whose relation rows do not span contiguous offsets fall back to slower, non-deterministic FP32 atomic accumulation; (3) the implementation favors generality over hardware specialization — no warp specialization or asynchronous bulk transfers (as they note FA3/FA4 use), left as future work. In the end-to-end sections they also candidly report where the method gives no speedup (Canary fine-tuning step overhead, Parakeet short segments). Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No code is available at review time; every number depends on a promised release, and Triton kernels of this complexity (per-length-bucket autotuned, compile-time specialized) often degrade in real integrations. - Attention-level tests use a single head dimension (d=64); conformer and DeBERTa deployments use other widths, and tile-size tuning tables are only covered for compute capabilities 8.0/8.6/9.0. - End-to-end quality evidence is limited to fine-tuning and inference on pre-trained checkpoints; no from-scratch training or pretraining shows the exactness tolerance (5% relative) does not drift training dynamics, and the Canary WER degradation at 9-minute windows (3.73 → 4.34) is explained by decode-loop diagnosis rather than controlled for. - The T5 backward "228×" figure in Table 2, while technically labeled, risks overstatement in citation since the decomposition-augmented FlexAttention baseline is pathological at that configuration; the honest production-baseline number is 13×. - Sequence-length scaling beyond 8K is extrapolated from monotonicity of memory growth, not measured; the FLOP-accounting convention (crediting projection FLOPs uniformly) is defined by the authors and differs from FlashAttention-2's convention, though the paper discloses this. Bottom Line: For anyone scaling TXL/DeBERTa/T5-style or conformer speech models past ~1K tokens, this is the strongest available kernel solution with unusually well-executed evidence backing it, and the offset-structure tricks will likely be absorbed into FlashAttention-class libraries regardless — its main weaknesses (unreleased code, 8K-token ceiling, fine-tuning-only quality evidence) are exactly what the promised open-source release and follow-up work should resolve.

Junhao Shen, Qing Zong, Yue Guo, Zhanqiu Zhang, Yiwen Guo, Hong Cheng · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 11 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces MMDM, a benchmark of 5,448 questions across 16 task categories for evaluating System-1 decision models (models that emit a probability distribution over query-specified options in a single forward pass), together with an evaluation of 28 such models. - Why it's important: Decision models are increasingly embedded in agent and routing pipelines, but existing benchmarks reuse contaminated public test sets and do not jointly test long contexts, large option spaces, interdependent options, multi-select, and soft probabilistic targets — so reported scores may not reflect deployed decision quality. - How it does it: It combines source-grounded rewrites (preserving answers and evidence while reformulating states, queries, and distractors), semantic recompositions, and executable-mechanism constructions (truth tables, SQLite replay, exact combinatorial enumeration) with a unified state–query–options interface and three answer semantics: hard single-select, hard multi-select, and soft-label distributions. - The good: The construction pipeline is unusually rigorous — 744,723 candidate instances filtered through semantic checks, an option-only probe for shortcuts, five-model majority screening, and independent human review of 928 borderline cases with 97.3% initial inter-annotator agreement — and the evaluation surfaces clean capability dissociations (e.g., 78.75% world-knowledge accuracy vs. 47.95% constraint planning for Perplexity Decider-V1.2; best multi-select accuracy of only 36.81% across all 28 models). - The missing: There is no autoregressive-LLM baseline under the same state–query–options interface, so the reported failures cannot be attributed specifically to the decision-model paradigm rather than to general LLM limits on these task types. - Read it or not: Read it if you build, select, or deploy decision-scoring models or agent tool-routing components — the category-level breakdowns, calibration curves, and scaling analyses are directly actionable; skip it if you only care about general LLM evaluation, where MMLU-Pro/LongBench-style suites cover adjacent ground.

Problem & Motivation: System-1 decision models output structured option probabilities in one forward pass for tasks like intent routing, tool selection, and rubric scoring, and are increasingly used inside agent software pipelines. Existing evaluations (JEVal, DecisionBench, JevBench, DecideBench, ReflexBench, Jev Evaluation) mostly reuse widely circulated public benchmarks, so test-set contamination can inflate scores; and none jointly cover complete multi-select recovery, soft (non-one-hot) distributional targets, large option spaces, and long contexts. Practitioners selecting a decision model for a workload therefore lack a contamination-resistant, capability-fine-grained measurement tool. Key Idea: Evaluate decision quality through a single state–query–options interface with three answer semantics — a unique correct option, a complete equally-valid set, or a reference probability distribution — over freshly authored or semantically recomposed instances whose answers are grounded in retained source evidence or computed by an executable mechanism, so that correctness is checkable while surface content is new. A secondary idea is the SB-F (Separation–Balance F-score), a product of separation of correct options from the strongest distractor and balanced mass across the correct set, designed to diagnose multi-select failures that exact accuracy conceals. Methodology: The benchmark formalizes an instance as (state s, query q, options O), with the model fθ mapping to a point on the (K−1)-simplex; references are one-hot (single-select), uniform over a valid set G (multi-select), or aggregated outcome probabilities (soft-label). Metrics are strict ordering accuracies (any tie or failed request counts as incorrect), SB-F, Soft Brier error, Score nMAE (expected-score error normalized by rubric range), and ECE for calibration. Data construction uses three routes: (1) source-grounded rewrites of 62 public datasets (QuALITY, LongBench v2, BIRD, ComplexFuncBench, ToolTalk, HelpSteer2, etc.) preserving answers/evidence; (2) recompositions grounded in source databases/agent histories; (3) 2,568 newly constructed questions from executable mechanisms — truth-table enumeration for interdependent reports, schedule feasibility enumeration for constraint planning, version-sensitive workflow simulation cross-checked independently, SQLite replay for transactional state, and exact combinatorial enumeration for sampled-rubric score distributions. Quality control masks state+query (option-only probe) to remove shortcut instances, screens with five frontier models (auto-accept at 4–5 votes, 928 borderline cases to two independent human reviewers plus adjudication). The evaluation protocol preserves query and all options, deterministically truncates the middle of over-long states, recursively groups option sets exceeding a model's option cap, hides reference cardinality from models, and counts capacity failures as incorrect. 28 models plus a uniform-random reference are evaluated. Key Results: On 4,112 hard single-select questions, WeMM-JEV 27B leads at 76.00%, KnowLine 31B at 75.07%, Perplexity Decider-V1.2 at 74.42%; closed models Jev 1.14.0 (67.17%) and Microsoft Decision-1 (61.36%) trail open 27B models. The best hard multi-select accuracy is only 36.81% (WeMM-JEV) and no model exceeds SB-F 0.20. Capability dissociations are large: Perplexity V1.2 scores 78.75% on world knowledge but 53.95% on option logic and 47.95% on constraint planning; GPT-6 Luna Decisions beats Jev on intent routing but loses by large margins on workflow decision, state tracking, and tool selection. Accuracy and probability quality diverge: WeMM-JEV and KnowLine differ by <1 point in single-select accuracy, but KnowLine has roughly half the Soft Brier (0.1233 vs 0.2327) and under a third the Score nMAE (0.0624 vs 0.2203); Jev achieves the lowest Soft Brier (0.1101) while KnowLine achieves the lowest Score nMAE. Calibration analyses show overconfidence patterns differ by model and task (Jev: 0.969 mean confidence at 97.6% accuracy on retrieval routing but 50.0% accuracy at 0.968 confidence on emotion; category-weighted ECE roughly doubles for Jev from 0.054 to 0.106). Scaling profiles reverse rankings: at 8K–16K tokens Intern-Decision 4B beats OpenJev 4B 34.5% vs 15.5%, but on 129–1,024 options OpenJev wins 26.0% vs 8.3%. On 284 shared multi-select questions, models rank a valid option first 60–89% of the time but place the entire correct set above distractors far less often (e.g., Jev 181 valid tops but only 57 complete-set successes), with narrow probability margins in ~46% of complete-set successes (median across models). Matched-cohort comparisons report paired-bootstrap 95% CIs (e.g., Perplexity over Jev single-select: +7.93 points, CI [6.41, 9.44]). Scale: standard benchmark scale (5,448 items, 28 models), not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK with an element of NEW FORMULATION (unified single-select/multi-select/soft-label evaluation of a defined model class, plus the SB-F metric). The genuinely novel parts are the joint coverage of complete multi-select recovery and soft distributional targets under one interface with contamination-resistant instances, and the executable-mechanism construction families. The individual ingredients — rewriting to mitigate contamination, Brier/ECE metrics, LLM-assisted data validation, option-cap grouping — are standard techniques competently combined for this new setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are effectively present as diagnostics: matched-cohort analyses (fixed question sets across models), native-vs-grouped multi-select breakdowns, option-only shortcut probes, task-conditioned ECE, and separation/balance decomposition of SB-F. Statistical treatment is partial: paired bootstrap CIs (2,000 resamples, source-parent-grouped) are reported for the five-model matched cohort, but the full 28-model Table 2 has no error bars, no seed variation (single deterministic run), and no significance tests; option-order sensitivity is untested. The dataset is released on Hugging Face (huggingface.co/datasets/shenjunhao/mmdm), the toolkit on GitHub (github.com/mmdm-benchmark/mmdm), with a hosted leaderboard (mmdm-benchmark.github.io). Methodological concerns: (1) models run under heterogeneous context budgets and option caps with different native/grouped mixes, so cross-model comparisons partially confound model quality with deployment settings (partially mitigated by matched cohorts); (2) the evaluator's use of N=|G| as the multi-select cutoff and grouping parameter, while hidden from the model, shapes the metric definition; (3) a large share of instances derive from public benchmarks, so the contamination-resistance claim rests on the rewrite quality rather than a demonstrated contamination test (e.g., no perplexity-based or canary-based contamination check is reported); (4) the baseline field is current (2026-era decision models) but there is no non-decision-model baseline. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a released benchmark plus a large evaluation campaign; no new model is trained). - Practical: Yes — the toolkit runs against hosted APIs and locally deployable open checkpoints; the benchmark itself requires only inference calls, with the Qwen3.5-4B tokenizer as the common length measure. - Efficient: Evaluation cost is moderate but non-trivial: option sets up to 1,024 and inputs to ~65K tokens, with recursive grouping multiplying request counts for models with small caps (e.g., Quyet-1.0-Large needs 896 grouped calls out of 5,448). - Effective: The evidence shows the benchmark measures real capability axes — rankings flip across context length vs. option count, and accuracy diverges from calibration and distribution quality — supporting its stated purpose as a diagnostic testbed, though downstream workload correlation is not demonstrated. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 64K tokens and 1,024 options; behavior at 10× scale is unclaimed, and the grouping protocol's accuracy collapse (multi-select 0–7% on grouped catalogs) suggests current models will not extend gracefully. The work delivers a concrete software artifact: dataset, evaluation toolkit, and leaderboard — not just a paper. Strengths: - Executable answer verification is the standout: interdependent-report instances are checked against independent truth-table implementations, state histories against SQLite replay, and rubric distributions against exact combinatorial enumeration — giving label correctness guarantees most rewritten benchmarks lack. - The three-track answer semantics (single-select, complete multi-select, soft distribution) expose failure modes that aggregate accuracy hides, and the paper quantifies them precisely (e.g., valid-top-choice rates of 64–89% collapsing to 35–65% coverage of the full correct set; expected scores accurate within 0.05 nMAE while total-variation distribution error stays above 0.30). - Honest metric design and analysis: the SB-F separation/balance decomposition, category-weighted ECE, and the explicit demonstration that expected-score accuracy can be good while the underlying distribution is wrong are genuinely useful diagnostics for practitioners choosing between models. - Broad, current model coverage (28 models spanning closed APIs and open 0.6B–35B checkpoints) with matched-cohort and bootstrap-CI secondary analyses. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state three: (1) text-only, fixed state–query–options decisions — no multimodal or interactive trajectories; (2) multi-select questions concentrate in four categories and soft targets come mostly from rubric scoring, so subjective-judgment evaluation is narrow; (3) despite rewriting and recomposition, prior exposure to underlying public source material may still inflate scores. They confront these directly rather than minimizing them, which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No autoregressive-LLM baseline (e.g., the same options presented to a general-purpose model via logit readout or constrained decoding). Without it, the paper cannot establish whether the observed failures — multi-select collapse, constraint blindness — are specific to the decision-model paradigm or generic LLM weaknesses, which weakens the claim that these are "priorities for decision-model development." - No empirical contamination check: the paper argues rewrites mitigate memorization but runs no detection experiment (e.g., testing a model's source-benchmark accuracy vs. its MMDM accuracy), leaving the central motivation partially unvalidated. - The multi-select protocol's recursive grouping retains up to |G| options per group using the reference cardinality N as an evaluator-side parameter; although cardinality is hidden from model inputs, the evaluation-defined tie-breaking and grouping path makes the multi-select metric partially protocol-dependent rather than purely model-dependent. - Option-order robustness is untested; single-select accuracy could be sensitive to option permutation, and the deterministic pipeline reports one ordering. - The SB-F metric is author-defined with no analysis of its behavior under adversarial or degenerate predictions beyond the uniform reference (where it is trivially zero), so its interpretation as a "quality" measure is asserted rather than validated. - Capacity failures counted as incorrect conflate model capability with deployment configuration for capped models, and while matched cohorts mitigate this, headline Table 2 numbers mix these regimes. Bottom Line: For anyone building or selecting decision-scoring models for agent pipelines, MMDM is currently the most complete and honestly constructed testbed in this niche and worth adopting; for the broader LLM-evaluation community, it is a competent benchmark-paper execution whose findings would be considerably stronger with a general-LLM baseline and a demonstrated contamination test.

Flex-RSI: Benchmarking Recursive Self - Improvement of Frontier Agents

J Zhang, J Wang, Z Yu, Y Cai, W Chow, C Choy, Z Dou… · arxiv.org · recursive self-improvement - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Flex-RSI, a 24-task benchmark that measures whether a frozen frontier model, operating inside a modifiable agent harness (executor + improver), can recursively improve both its task solution and its own harness on vision and robotics tasks under a fixed budget, with final solutions scored on hidden test splits. - Why it's important: RSI benchmarks to date concentrate on ML research tasks or model training; this one targets the vision/robotics setting where agents are increasingly deployed, each attempt consumes real compute, and self-improvement claims have rarely been tested from identical starting artifacts at matched budgets. - How it does it: A two-component harness alternates rounds — an executor edits the solution (accepted only if it beats the incumbent on withheld validation data by a noise margin δ), then an improver edits the executor's prompts/tools/workflow and its own instructions — with every run starting from the same general-purpose harness and starter solution. - The good: The paired-run ablation (Table 8) isolates harness editing causally: enabling the improver raises test score in 6 of 7 otherwise identical run pairs, by 2.0 to 40.0 points, plus three clearly supported cross-task findings over 177 runs of 18 models. - The missing: Every model is run once per task ("where a run was repeated, the latest run is reported"), with no seeds, error bars, or significance tests; several headline model comparisons (e.g., Gemini 4 Argon's 89.0 over only 9 tasks vs. Opus's 91.6 over 20) are means over non-overlapping task subsets. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or evaluate agentic self-improvement systems or care about open-vs-closed weight gaps in harness evolution; skip it if you need weight-level RSI evidence — the authors state the benchmark does not cover that.
Why this rank
Scored using Systems profile. Novelty (75) — a new benchmark class where harness editing is a measured variable rather than a confound, though the underlying machinery recombines known self-modification ideas. Rigor (65) is the weak point: one run per model-task cell, no seeds or significance tests, and headline leaderboard comparisons over non-overlapping task subsets, partially offset by excellent contamination controls and the causally informative 7-pair frozen-harness ablation. Non-Obviousness (70) — the feedback-granularity gap (1.6 vs 16.9 median gain) and token-spend uncorrelation are actionable surprises. Completeness (75) is strong because the authors directly confront the harness-only scope; Resilience (68) is limited by statistically unsupported close model orderings; Impact (75) reflects a released benchmark, harness, and leaderboard. Weighted composite: 0.15*75 + 0.15*65 + 0.10*70 + 0.15*75 + 0.15*68 + 0.30*75 = 72.

Problem & Motivation: Teams deploying frontier models as agents face a practical question: given only a new task, can the agent use task feedback to improve the way it works (its harness — prompts, tools, memory, control loop) under a fixed budget, not merely its answer? Existing agent benchmarks (MLE-bench, RE-Bench, PaperBench) keep the harness fixed and score only the produced solution; existing RSI evaluations (RSI-Exam, OpenRSI Index) stay within ML research or large-scale model training. Nobody has measured solution-and-harness improvement together on general vision and robotics tasks — a setting where the agent must build working pipelines/policies, spend real GPU-hours, and deliver a better solution within hours to days. Key Idea: Formalize the harness as H = (E, I) — an executor that operates on the task solution and an improver that operates on the harness, including itself — so that Eq. (3), I(E, I; τ), makes the recursion explicit while a strict validation-gated acceptance rule (Eq. 2, retain a candidate only if S(s̃; D_val) > S(s; D_val) + δ) keeps solution changes honest. Because every run starts from the same task-agnostic harness and starter solution with fixed evaluator, splits, and budget accounting, differences between runs are attributable to the models themselves, and the protocol cleanly separates three questions: solution improvement, harness-attributable improvement, and harness transfer across models. Methodology: The benchmark comprises 24 tasks in six areas — Action (RoboDojo, RoboCasa365, H*Bench Active Search, RoboLab, LIBERO-MAX, LIBERO-PRO, Embodied-SWE), Reasoning (EgoExoMem, QuantiPhy, ABO mass estimation, ARC-AGI-1/2/3, VSI-Bench), Creation (Image Editing, Multi-turn Editing, Video Generation, Text-to-Image), Reconstruction (3D Tracking, Scene from Photo, Scene from Video), Perception (Visual Search, Video Quality), and one Infrastructure task (accelerating the MiniMax H3 VAE decoder). Each task supplies a starter solution, development data (with labels, agent-accessible), hidden validation and test splits, and a budget limiting wall-clock time, GPU hours, model usage, validation evaluations, and rounds. In each round: (1) the executor edits the accepted solution using D_dev, (2) the candidate is kept only if its validation score exceeds the incumbent's by margin δ (initialized to twice the starter's validation-score standard deviation), (3) the improver reviews all trajectory records τ_{1:t} and rewrites both harness components. Evaluation reports the test score of the final solution and its gain over the starter; models are compared via rank-based scores (share of other models beaten per task, averaged into area and overall scores). Agent code runs in a sandbox with no access to validation/test data. Two controlled analyses extend the main runs: 7 frozen-vs-self-improving harness pairs (settings identical except the improver runs or not) and 4 harness-transfer runs where a weaker model starts from a stronger model's final harness. Key Results: Across 177 runs of 18 models (11 closed-source, 7 open-weight) on the 20 tasks evaluated with ≥6 models: (1) Self-improvement raised validation score in 150/177 runs (85%), median +10.4 points; closed-source models improved in 94% of 85 runs (median +14.9) vs. 76% of 92 runs (median +8.5) for open-weight. (2) Gains concentrate where the agent builds the solution: on 3D Tracking, RoboLab, and Active Search, median validation rose from 19.4, 8.3, 23.0 to 62.2, 45.8, 52.7, while ARC-AGI-1/2 (median starters 91.9/82.5) gained a median of 0 points; on build-tasks, models that start 0.9 points apart end 38.8 points apart. (3) Feedback granularity matters: on tasks where the evaluator records only success/failure (RoboCasa, LIBERO-MAX, LIBERO-PRO, ARC-AGI-3), the median open-weight gain falls to 1.6 points vs. 16.9 for closed-source — on RoboCasa specifically, 5.6 vs. 51.2. (4) Open-weight models fall furthest behind where outputs must pass strict physical/exactness checks: Physics score 0.0 for all four open-weight models on Scene from Video vs. 70.7 for Claude Opus 5.5; ARC-AGI-3 best open-weight score 0.9 vs. 44.2. (5) Leaderboard: Claude Opus 5.5 91.6, Gemini 4 Argon 89.0, GPT-6.1 Sol 77.0; best open-weight, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, 49.1. (6) Paired runs: enabling harness editing raised test score in 6/7 pairs (+2.0 to +40.0); a stronger model's harness transferred gains to a weaker model on only 2 of 4 tasks and never closed the gap. (7) Cost: median 49.7M tokens per run, and token spend is uncorrelated with score (rank correlation −0.05). Baselines are current frontier models (Claude Opus/Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6.x, Gemini 4/3.8, Grok 4.6, plus Qwen3.8, GLM-5.3, DeepSeek-V4.1, Gemma-4, MiniMax-M3); scale is standard-to-stress (simulated robot suites, 47–600-item test splits), not toy. Surprising finding: spending more tokens buys nothing, and ARC-AGI-3 starts at 3.8 and barely improves (4.1) despite huge headroom. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel elements are (a) a shared-protocol evaluation where harness editing is a measured variable rather than a fixed scaffold or a confound, and (b) the causal paired-run evidence that harness editing contributes to gains. The executor/improver decomposition, validation-gated acceptance, and self-modifying-agent machinery are standard combinations of known ideas (Reflexion-style memory, Darwin Gödel Machine / STOP-style self-modification, RE-Bench-style hidden-test evaluation) recombined for the vision/robotics domain; the four cross-task findings (build-vs-answer, feedback granularity, strict-check difficulty, cost-uncorrelation) are competent empirical syntheses rather than new mechanisms. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and load-bearing: the frozen-vs-improving harness pairs (Table 8) and harness-transfer runs (Table 9) directly test the benchmark's central claims rather than assuming them; a noise margin δ guards against noise-driven acceptance. However, each model is run once per task (latest run reported for repeats), and no seeds, error bars, or significance tests are reported for the main leaderboard — the single paired-run comparison with n=7 is suggestive, not statistical. Task cards (Appendix A) are unusually detailed about split construction, seed control, sandbox restrictions, and anti-contamination checks (e.g., excluding initial states used in other splits). Code, tasks, and a maintained leaderboard are at https://flex-rsi.github.io; closed-source models are accessed via vendor APIs (self-reported generations, though scored by the benchmark's own fixed evaluators). Concerns: (a) rank-based scoring over partially non-overlapping task sets makes cross-model comparison fragile (Argon's 89.0 covers 9 tasks, Opus's 91.6 covers 20); (b) four Creation/Reconstruction tasks use a frozen VLM judge (GLM-4.5V), which the paper partially mitigates with programmatic checks and SIFT/RANSAC deformation penalties; (c) adaptive reuse of a single validation split across rounds invites adaptive-overfitting — a risk the related-work section itself cites (Yao et al., 2026b) but the paper does not quantify; (d) four tasks were evaluated with only two models and are relegated to Table 12. The shared citation convention (many 2026 arXiv preprints) suggests much of the surrounding evidence base is not yet peer-reviewed; this report itself is a preprint. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS — a built benchmark and harness infrastructure, evaluated by deploying 18 models through it. Practical: Runs on commercially available hardware; open-weight models are served on the authors' own GPUs, closed models via public APIs, and tasks constrain solutions to at most ~4×80GB GPUs. Efficient: Median 49.7M tokens per run (middle 80%: 8.6–93.4M) — measurable and comparable, though GPU-hours per run vary by task. Effective: The evidence shows the protocol measures what it claims (gains are validation-gated and test-scored on hidden splits), but "improvement" is harness-level only; no weight-level self-improvement is tested. Scalable: Not tested — the paper does not examine whether findings hold at larger budgets, more rounds, or on out-of-distribution tasks, though it cites prior work suggesting harness-evolution gains can shrink OOD. Deliverable: a benchmark artifact (tasks, starter solutions, evaluators, protocol, leaderboard) plus a general-purpose starting harness; no trained model weights are released because none are trained. Strengths: - Causal decomposition of the improvement signal: the frozen-vs-improving paired runs (6/7 pairs favor harness editing, up to +40.0 on Open Drawer for DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash) answer a question most self-improvement papers leave as a confound — whether harness edits, not just more solution iterations, drive gains. - Experiments designed as measurements, not showcases: identical starting harness/starter solution, noise-margined validation gating, sandboxed held-out data, and explicit budget accounting make cross-model differences genuinely attributable to the agent. - The feedback-granularity finding (open-weight models gain a median of 1.6 points under binary success/failure evaluators vs. 16.9 for closed-source) is a non-obvious, actionable insight for anyone designing evaluators for self-improving agents. - Task cards document contamination control (no initial physical state in two splits, no panorama sharing between splits, hash-ordered splits) at a level of care rare in benchmark papers. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The conclusion states directly that the measured improvement is harness-level: model weights never change, most tasks involve no training, and Flex-RSI "does not measure a model that modifies its own parameters" — extending to weight-level RSI is left to future work. The paper also implicitly limits scope via reporting rules: only 20 of 24 tasks enter the main leaderboard (four had two models), and single runs per task are disclosed. The authors confront these limitations directly rather than minimizing them, which strengthens confidence in the stated findings. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No repeated runs or variance estimates for the main results; with n=1 per model-task cell, the leaderboard ordering of models separated by a few points (e.g., three models within 0.1 on Video Quality) is not statistically supported. - The headline leaderboard compares models over different task subsets; a per-task paired win-rate restricted to commonly-run tasks would be more defensible than mean-of-area ranks over 9 vs. 20 tasks. - Adaptive validation reuse across rounds is acknowledged as a risk in the related-work survey but never measured for Flex-RSI's own runs (e.g., final-validation vs. test degradation per round). - VLM-judged tasks (Image Editing, Multi-turn Editing, Text-to-Image, parts of Creation scoring) introduce judge dependence; the paper does not report judge-model agreement with human ratings or judge-ablation results. - The ARC-AGI-3 result (3.8 → 4.1) shows the protocol can produce near-zero improvement, but the paper offers only speculative explanations ("the agent likely has to build a working solution") rather than diagnosing the failure mode. - Findings 1–3 rest on grouping 20 tasks into small cells (e.g., 4 binary-feedback tasks, 7 single-answer tasks); no formal cross-task statistical test backs the generalizations. Bottom Line: For researchers building or evaluating self-improving agents, this is currently the most carefully controlled harness-vs-solution decomposition available outside ML-research domains and is worth reading in full; for everyone else, the four findings can be extracted from Section 5 without reproducing anything.

RESHPart: Feedback-Reshaped Spectral Embedding for Hypergraph Partitioning

R Liang, Z Feng, B Khailany · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces FRESHPart, a spectral hypergraph partitioning framework that iteratively reshapes spectral embeddings via hyperedge reweighting driven by embedding geometry and prior partitioning outcomes, and shows it achieves the best reported cut quality on the Titan23 VLSI benchmark suite. - Why it's important: Hypergraph partitioning directly governs wirelength and congestion in VLSI physical design, where even a few percent cut reduction translates into real chip quality, and the dominant multilevel paradigm has been hard to beat with spectral methods. - How it does it: The core trick is treating the Laplacian as an adjustable 'lens' rather than a fixed operator: spherical K-means identifies ray-like structure in the embedding, hyperedges are reweighted by how many rays they span (Geometry Feedback) and by how often they appear on cut boundaries of diverse high-quality candidate partitions (Search Feedback), then the bipartite Laplacian is re-solved to produce a better-aligned embedding. - The good: Average cut reduction over hMETIS of 25.21% at ε=20% and 13.09% at ε=2% on all 22 Titan23 benchmarks, exceeding the strongest prior numbers (22.53% and 12.16% from SHyPar), with every benchmark finishing under 120 s on a single V100, plus ablations showing feedback reshaping beats simply spending 3× more search budget on the base embedding. - The missing: There is no code release, no error bars or multi-seed variance on Titan23, and the diagnostic analysis that motivates the method is performed on the same benchmark suite used for the headline evaluation, so the ray-concentration story is partly validated on its own tuning set. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on EDA partitioning or spectral methods for graphs/hypergraphs; skip it if you need multi-way (K>2) partitioning or a reproducible artifact today, since the method is bipartition-only and no implementation is released.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Non-Obviousness (78) is the paper's strength — identifying ray-like spectral geometry as the explainable cause of projection-based partitioning gains, then deliberately reshaping it via hyperedge reweighting, follows the phenomenology-to-mechanism pattern of strong empirical work. Rigor (74) is solid thanks to the equal-budget ablation that rules out 'just more compute', out-of-suite ISPD98 transfer, and current baselines, but loses points for no variance reporting on randomized components and diagnostics run on the headline benchmark. Novelty (75) is high for a new empirical finding plus method, while Completeness (68) and Impact (60) are held back by the absence of any code release, many hand-tuned constants, and bipartition-only scope; Resilience (68) is moderate given the correlational nature of the geometry explanation. Weighted composite: 0.20*75 + 0.25*74 + 0.15*78 + 0.15*68 + 0.15*68 + 0.10*60 = 72.
