Problem & Motivation: Practitioners using adaptive curricula (PLR, ACCEL, SFL) train RL agents on environment distributions that evolve with student capability. Prior UED work optimizes the curriculum-construction rule and implicitly assumes a fixed, healthy student update; meanwhile, deep RL outside UED has documented parameter growth, dormant neurons, feature-rank collapse, and critic instability. The gap this paper addresses: no one has systematically asked whether the student remains trainable under the distributions adaptive curricula produce, even though adaptive UED creates an extra feedback loop in which learner degradation changes which environments are encountered next. A motivating comparison shows PLR beats domain randomization on sampled return while simultaneously exhibiting larger gradient norms, more aligned representations, and weaker value–outcome rank correlation — performance metrics alone hide optimization strain. Key Idea: The key idea is the coupling argument plus controlled learner-only intervention: in adaptive UED, the curriculum rule C(p_k, H_{k+1}) consumes student-generated signals, so a degraded student changes its own future training distribution — meaning a fixed curriculum rule can realize different curricula when paired with different learners. Operationally, the insight is that you can test whether observed optimization pathologies matter by stabilizing only the learner (weight clipping constrains ‖φ‖∞ on the critic; HL-Gauss bounds the prediction-head gradient to [−1, 1] via categorical cross-entropy over a Gaussian-smoothed histogram target) and observing both performance and how the unchanged PLR rule's realized curriculum shifts (lower PVL scores, shorter episodes, comparable structural complexity of replayed levels). Methodology: The pipeline has three phases. (1) Diagnosis: PPO agents are trained under PLR in Kinetix at Small/Medium/Large complexity for 2B environment steps (5 seeds, IQM aggregation, 95% stratified bootstrap CIs), tracking weight magnitude, gradient norm, value prediction mean/std, Spearman correlation between value predictions and empirical returns, effective rank (99% variance threshold on singular values), and representation cosine similarity; PLR's Positive Value Loss (PVL) replay priority is compared against measured learnability L = p(1−p). (2) Intervention screen: eight established interventions (weight clipping at 4 clipping-scale factors, weight decay, spectral norm on actor/critic/both, ReGen, HL-Gauss at 4 bin counts) are screened on Small, then a factorial ablation of WC × HL is run across all three complexity levels. (3) Scaling and transfer: the selected WC+HL configuration is evaluated across DR/SFL/ACCEL, a 5B-step horizon on Small, parallelism from 128 to 4096 environments, the full 3×3 zero-shot cross-complexity grid (sampled return and human-designed holdout solve rate), and the Kinetix lifelong protocol (S→M→S sequential shifts with optimizer and replay buffer retained). The critic loss is the explicit objective L_V(φ) = E_t[(V_φ(s_t) − V̂_t)²], replaced under HL-Gauss by histogram cross-entropy with scalar recovery as the expectation over predicted bins. Critical design decisions: diagnosing on PLR specifically because its replay priorities are transparently student-dependent (well justified); choosing WC+HL as a practical configuration rather than claiming optimality (honestly framed, especially since HL adds little over WC alone in Large); and holding curriculum rule, architecture, and interaction budget fixed across comparisons (well justified for isolating learner effects). Key Results: The paper reports results as training curves rather than single headline numbers, so exact deltas must be read from figures. Quantifiable anchors from the text and figures: baseline PLR return and value–return Spearman correlation (≈0.88 falling toward 0.75 in Large) deteriorate over 2B steps, with weight magnitude growing past ~1.2×10² and effective rank declining sharply in Large; WC+HL maintains stronger and flatter Spearman correlation (≈0.9+) and stable effective rank, with the largest return improvement over baseline in the Large configuration, where WC alone also substantially outperforms HL alone. Extending to 5B steps, baseline return declines after the 2B mark while WC+HL continues improving — the gap widens with horizon. Increasing rollout parallelism from 128 to 2048 environments improves baseline performance with saturation at 4096, but WC+HL improves over baseline at every parallelism level, including 128. Stabilization improves zero-shot return/solve rate across all nine train(S/M/L)×eval(S/M/L) combinations, with the largest gains for agents trained on Medium and Large, and improves retention on the Medium holdout set through the S→M→S sequential shift, where the baseline loses much of its Medium-stage gain upon returning to Small. Baselines compared (PLR, DR, SFL, ACCEL) are current and standard for this benchmark; the paper explicitly does not claim WC+HL is globally optimal. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (learner-side optimization pathologies recurring across UED mechanisms and coupling to future training distributions) plus a partial NEW FORMULATION (learner trainability as an explicit design and evaluation principle for UED). The interventions themselves are standard: weight clipping and HL-Gauss are imported from Elsayed et al. (2024) and Farebrother et al. (2024), and the diagnostic metrics are standard plasticity/representation probes. The genuinely novel element is connecting the deep RL stability literature to UED's curriculum–student feedback loop and showing that a stabilized student changes the curriculum realized by an unchanged rule — the priority–learnability mismatch under PLR is a new empirical observation, framed as a learner-side cousin of the regret-stagnation phenomenon of Beukman et al. (2026). Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: an 8-intervention screen, hyperparameter sweeps for both selected interventions (clipping factors 1/2/4/8; HL bins 21/51/101/201, showing robustness to bin count), and a factorial WC×HL decomposition across all three complexity levels. Uncertainty is handled with 5 seeds per configuration, IQM aggregation, and 95% stratified bootstrap CIs; no parametric significance tests are reported. Code, data, or model weights are not stated as released in the provided text. Methodological concerns: (1) hyperparameters and interventions were selected on the same benchmark (and partly the same Small configuration) used for headline evaluation — a mild Goodhart risk, though the transfer and cross-mechanism experiments mitigate it; (2) the causal chain is explicitly left correlational — the authors repeatedly and correctly note that pathologies may be symptoms rather than causes, and that the intervention results 'do not establish parameter growth as the direct cause'; (3) evaluation is confined to Kinetix, which is the authors' and collaborators' ecosystem (the Kinetix authors are co-authors of the closely related Beukman et al. work), so independent-benchmark validation is absent; (4) the paper is a preprint and has not, per the provided text, undergone peer review. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS-adjacent artifact in the stabilization recipe, but no released tool is stated). - Practical: Yes — the interventions are two small changes (an ∞-norm clip after each critic update and a binned cross-entropy critic head) that run on standard PPO infrastructure with no architectural or hardware requirements. - Efficient: Essentially free relative to the baseline — same architecture, same 2B interaction budget, no extra environment interaction or curriculum computation; only negligible per-update overhead. - Effective: The evidence shows improved solve rate, return, value ordering, and representation health on Kinetix training, transfer, and shift tasks — a genuine behavioral outcome, not just a proxy, though all within one simulator family. - Scalable: Tested to 5B steps and 4096 parallel environments (saturating there); behavior at 10× beyond that, or on other domains, is claimed only by analogy, not measured. The work delivers a reproducible training recipe (WC with scaling factor 2 + HL-Gauss with 51 bins, hyperparameters fully tabulated) rather than a software artifact; no library, CLI, or checkpoint release is mentioned. Strengths: - The reframing of UED evaluation — report whether the student remains trainable, and distinguish the curriculum rule from the curriculum realized — is a genuinely useful conceptual contribution that follows directly from the coupling analysis, not a slogan. - The diagnosis-to-intervention loop is unusually disciplined: every pathology identified in Sec. 3 (parameter growth, value-ordering decay, rank collapse) is checked again after the intervention (Fig. 6), so the stabilization is shown to do what it was chosen to do. - The factorial ablation honestly surfaces an inconvenient result — HL adds little over WC alone in Large — and the authors adopt WC+HL as a practical default without overselling synergy. - The breadth of the robustness sweep (4 curriculum mechanisms, 3 complexity levels, 5B-step horizon, 128–4096 parallelism, 3×3 transfer grid, sequential shifts) substantially raises confidence that the effect is not an artifact of one configuration. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that evidence is limited to Kinetix and PPO; that hyperparameter sensitivity, probe choices, and intervention interactions constrain causal attribution; that they do not claim weight clipping and HL-Gauss are uniquely effective; and that continual learning under curriculum-induced non-stationarity remains an open, difficult extension. They also repeatedly flag within the body that their associations 'do not establish causality' and that the retention experiment 'does not distinguish among' forgetting, interference, and plasticity-loss mechanisms. This is direct, non-minimizing confrontation of limitations — a strong credibility signal. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the acknowledged limitations, a critical reviewer would flag: (1) no head-to-head comparison with the most directly related remedy — Beukman et al. (2026)'s million-environment parallelism — only a parallelism ablation showing saturation at 4096, so the relative cost-effectiveness of stabilization versus rollout scaling on equal compute is not established; (2) the diagnosis section's central observation (PLR beats DR while showing worse trainability diagnostics) is left mechanistically unexplained, and the paper does not test whether DR-trained learners with the same intervention show proportionally smaller gains, which would discriminate between 'stabilization helps degraded learners' and 'stabilization helps everyone'; (3) all curriculum mechanisms are evaluated with the same PPO learner, so it is unknown whether curriculum choice and stabilization interact (e.g., whether learnability-based SFL inherently selects more trainable students); (4) no released code is mentioned despite heavy hyperparameter tabulation, limiting independent reproduction; (5) the value–return Spearman correlation is computed against the agent's own empirical returns, which are policy-dependent, so the 'degraded ordering' metric could partially track distribution change rather than critic failure — the authors note target distributions differ across settings but do not fully resolve this confound for the within-run comparison. Bottom Line: For anyone training agents under adaptive curricula or studying plasticity in deep RL, this paper is worth reading in full — it converts a vague worry about learner degradation into measured diagnostics, a free two-line fix, and a concrete evaluation practice, and no prior work covers the curriculum–trainability coupling with comparable breadth; its main casualty is confidence in fixed-horizon UED benchmark numbers obtained with unstabilized PPO students.

Interpretable Cyber -Physical Attack Detection in Smart Grids: A Leakage-Controlled Multi-Testbed Evaluation of Fusion, Robustness, and Observability Limits

MR Hoquea, S Sharif, RS Kandezy, Y Banad · arxiv.org · cyber model training - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a leakage-controlled, multi-testbed evaluation framework built around an interpretable time-windowed fusion Random Forest for smart-grid attack detection, showing that shuffled evaluation inflates macro-F1 by 0.05–0.12 across five model families and that detectability is bounded by which observation layer (headers, physics residual, or state manifold) a detector reads. - Why it's important: Smart-grid ML detectors are typically validated on clean, temporally shuffled data, producing security claims that an adaptive adversary (the premise of the domain) can silently invalidate; the paper quantifies this optimism on real IEC-104 traffic and IEEE 14/118-Bus physics testbeds. - How it does it: It runs one interpretable detector through four increasingly stringent evaluation protocols (shuffled → chronological), grades attacks from feature-space worst cases to physics-feasible stealthy FDI (a = Hc, evolution-strategy evasion), and complements residual-based bad-data detection with a rate-invariant PCA off-manifold consistency test fitted on estimated states. - The good: The IEEE 118-Bus end-to-end validation is unusually honest: the manifold test detects 1.00 of trials down to 0.05°/step but only 0.48 at 0.02°/step (vs. 0.14 temporal), and the authors report this degradation against their own analytical prediction rather than hiding it. - The missing: Cyber and physics are never evaluated on one aligned system — fusion is shown on a topology-free real dataset, physics attacks on simulated testbeds with a simulated cyber layer, and real traffic only cyber-only — so the central fusion claim is established piecewise, not end-to-end. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or benchmark grid/CPS attack detectors — it is a rare negative-results-rich evaluation study that names exactly which attacks each observable can and cannot see; skip it if you want a new detection architecture, because the paper explicitly disclaims one.

Problem & Motivation Cyber-physical smart-grid intrusion detection has an evaluation problem. The strongest fusion detectors (e.g., the topology-aware GNN of Sweeten et al. on the same paired dataset) are opaque deep models, and nearly all detectors in the literature are validated on clean, temporally shuffled data — a protocol that leaks adjacent correlated windows across train/test splits and ignores drift. In a security domain whose premise is an intelligent adversary, robustness against deliberate manipulation is rarely measured at all. Practitioners (grid operators, security researchers) therefore cannot tell whether published detector performance would survive (i) honest temporal evaluation, (ii) an adaptive or physics-feasible attacker, or (iii) an attack whose effect lives in a layer the detector never observes. The paper closes these three gaps: it quantifies protocol-induced optimism, separates feasible from infeasible adversarial stress, and formalizes an observability taxonomy mapping each attack class to the minimum observation layer required to detect it. Key Idea The core insight is an information-theoretic boundary claim: a detector can only recover what is present in the layer it reads. A value manipulated inside a SCADA payload is absent from network headers, so no function of header features can recover it — an argument the paper supports both on real IEC-104 traffic and in a physics-controlled testbed with ground truth. A second, related insight under the physics testbed is that temporal (forecasting/CUSUM) and spatial (off-manifold residual) consistency detectors fail on orthogonal attack regimes — slow ramps versus manifold-aligned injections — so a rate-invariant manifold test, fitted on the estimated states an operator actually observes and with dimension chosen by benign-only cross-validation, closes the slow-ramp evasion that defeats forecasting-aided detection, at a common 5% false-alarm target. Methodology The study orchestrates three data sources: dataset 1 (SmartGrid-CyberPhysical-Attack-Dataset, paired cyber/physical captures, six classes), testbed 2 (IEEE 14-Bus in pandapower, DC and full AC WLS state estimation, extended to IEEE 118-Bus), and dataset 3 (real IEC-104/61850 HMI traffic). Dataset 1 windows (Δ=0.5 s, inner-join on time bins) yield 1,529 fused windows with 34 features (22 physical means/stds, 12 cyber packet statistics); the detector is a 300-tree Random Forest with balanced class weights, interpreted via SHAP, plus a selective-prediction abstention policy. Four protocols are compared (shuffled 5-fold CV, time-blocked CV, rolling-origin with 8 origins, chronological 75/25 hold-out) across five model families (RF, histogram gradient boosting, per-window MLP, TDNN, logistic). Adversarial evaluation grades four feature-space attackers (random search, PGD transfer via a 2-layer MLP surrogate, adaptive, adaptive-joint) at ε=0.10, with adversarial training and randomized smoothing (σsm=0.10) as defenses; on IEEE 14-Bus, physics-feasible attacks constrain perturbations to a = Hc and a (1,λ) evolution strategy optimizes the state offset c against the forest. The observability taxonomy trains one detector under three views (cyber-only, physics residual-only, fusion) over three attack classes (structural, naive value, stealthy FDI) at a calibrated 5% FPR. The AC study solves a 72-measurement/27-state WLS estimator by Gauss–Newton over time-varying loads, compares a Holt/CUSUM temporal test against a PCA off-manifold CUSUM (K=6 on 14-Bus, K=8 on 118-Bus, selected by benign-only cross-validation), all thresholds calibrated on independent benign streams. Critical design decisions: fitting the manifold on estimated (not true) states is well-justified as deployment-realistic; benign-only K selection is justified against a badly miscalibrated cumulative-variance rule (K=165/235 on 118-Bus); the single uniform metering-noise level is acknowledged as a simplification but not justified further. Key Results Headline numbers: on dataset 1, fusion macro-F1 falls from 0.96±0.01 (shuffled) to 0.93±0.06 (time-blocked), 0.88±0.06 (rolling-origin, range 0.77–0.97), and 0.80 (single 75/25 hold-out, n=381); the protocol gap (0.05–0.12) exceeds the spread among the four non-linear families under honest evaluation (0.03), and the TDNN is both most inflated by shuffling (0.99) and most penalized (0.12 drop). Feature-space attacks degrade clean macro-F1 (0.96) to 0.67 (adaptive) and 0.34 (adaptive-joint); adversarial training recovers to 0.82/0.55, randomized smoothing to 0.80 under the adaptive attack but at a 9.1% benign false-positive rate. On IEEE 14-Bus, an ES physics-feasible evasion drives FDI recall to 0.26 under limited observability (clean macro-F1 0.89), partially recovered to 0.53 by feasible-space adversarial training. On real IEC-104 traffic (7,107 windows, 637 attack), structural attacks are caught at recall 0.87–0.98 while semantic value manipulation collapses to 0.11–0.35 at 2.4% FPR, with non-overlapping Wilson intervals. The taxonomy shows cyber-view recall 1.00 on structural, physics-view 0.99 on naive value, fusion 1.00 on both, and stealthy FDI at 0.06 (chance) for every view. On the AC testbed, snapshot bad-data detection is blind (KS p=1.00, AUC 0.51, 4° bias achieved with zero flags); the temporal test detects steps at onset (AUC 1.00) but falls to 0.60 at 0.05°/step and 0.10 at 0.02°/step, while the manifold test holds P(detect)=1.00 across all ramp rates on 14-Bus. On IEEE 118-Bus (235 states, 700 measurements), the ordering reproduces but degrades: manifold/fused hold 1.00 down to 0.05°/step, then 0.48/0.40 at 0.02°/step vs. 0.14 temporal — a ~3.4× advantage, but materially weaker than the analytical prediction and honestly reported as such. Baselines are current where they exist (the same dataset's GNN authors' future work is directly taken up), though the topology-aware GNN itself is not reimplemented. Novelty Classification NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING plus a modest NEW FORMULATION: the genuinely novel elements are (1) the leakage-controlled multi-family protocol comparison quantifying that evaluation choice dominates model choice, (2) the observability taxonomy localizing each attack class to its minimum observation layer with a formal information argument, and (3) the controlled temporal-vs-spatial detector comparison on one AC testbed at a common false-alarm target. The primitives — stealthy FDI (Liu–Ning–Reiter), forecasting-aided and subspace detection, randomized smoothing, SHAP, selective prediction — are all standard, and the authors explicitly and credibly disclaim new-detector novelty, framing the contribution as unification and quantification. Rigor & Reproducibility Rigor is above average for this subfield. Ablations are present and informative: physical-only (0.77) vs. cyber-only (0.85) vs. fusion (0.96) under shuffled CV; a K-sensitivity sweep showing the plateau K∈[4,20]; a topology-free GCN control (0.83/0.70) explicitly framed as a sanity check, not a baseline comparison; a graded-knowledge attacker sweep. Interval estimates are used where sample sizes demand them (15-split CI [0.947, 0.954] on the feasible-FDI detector; Wilson CIs on IEC-104 recalls; rule-of-three bounds on zero-miss results); false-alarm rates are measured on held-out benign streams and reported alongside every detection figure. All code, generated benchmarks, and figure-reproduction scripts are released (github.com/INQUIRELAB/smartgrid-cyberphysical-fusion, PolyForm Noncommercial / CC BY-NC 4.0), with named scripts per experiment. Methodological concerns: (1) dataset 1's class-capture confound is flagged by the authors themselves (class label confounded with recording session; SHAP top features are packet count and summed IP length), making dataset-1 numbers an upper bound; (2) the DC-model stealthy constructions in Sections 5.2–5.3 are only provably stealthy against the DC estimator they target, and the paper carefully distinguishes this from AC-stealthiness; (3) the detector is developed and evaluated on the same testbeds it characterizes (no held-out external grid), though the two IEEE systems and real traffic partially mitigate this. This is a preprint (arXiv:2611.10950), apparently not yet peer-reviewed. Deployability Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS-adjacent artifact — released code and generated benchmarks — but evaluated as experiments, not deployed infrastructure). Practical: Yes — a 300-tree Random Forest trains in 0.8 s and infers at 0.30 ms/window, and the physics testbeds run in pandapower on commodity hardware. Efficient: Costs are trivial relative to deep/graph alternatives, though randomized smoothing's 9.1% benign false-positive rate and the IEC-104 operating point of ~6 false alarms per 8-hour shift would need substantial tuning before operator-facing use. Effective: Effective against the proxy tasks it tests (temporal splits, feature-space and DC-feasible attacks, real IEC-104 behavioral attacks); the paper is explicit that these are scoped proxies and that the fully aligned real-traffic/real-topology case is untested. Scalable: Tested up to IEEE 118-Bus with the estimator solved at every timestep, and the result degrades there (manifold 1.00 → 0.48 at the slowest ramp), so scaling behavior is measured rather than merely claimed — favorably, the paper treats this degradation as its most useful finding. The work delivers a software artifact (released code, two generated benchmarks, reproduction scripts), not a hardened tool or trained production model. Strengths - Disciplined leakage-controlled evaluation: running five model families through an identical four-protocol ladder and showing the TDNN (the model most exploiting temporal structure) is simultaneously the most flattered by shuffling (0.99) and most penalized honestly (0.12 drop) is a sharp, transferable methodological finding for all time-series CPS detection work. - The observability taxonomy converts a vague "fusion helps" claim into a testable partition with an impossibility argument (a payload value absent from headers is unrecoverable by any header-based function), supported both on real traffic and a ground-truth-controlled testbed. - Unusual negative-results candor: the authors report that their analytical bias-budget prediction fails on IEEE 118-Bus (predicting near-certain detection at 0.02°/step; simulation gives 0.48), that fusion can fall below the single best view at tiny steps (0.42 vs. 0.50 at 0.10°), and that their dataset's FDI class has a trivially strong marginal signature (~11 benign σ in current variance) that flatters macro-F1. - The distinction between feature-space worst cases (upper bounds, infeasible as grid manipulations) and physics-feasible attacks is consistently maintained, preventing a common overclaim in grid adversarial-ML papers. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors confront limitations directly and at length (a credibility positive). They state: cyber and physics are never fused on one realistic system; the fusion claim is established piecewise across three disjoint testbeds; dataset 1's class-capture confound makes its numbers an upper bound; the cyber layer on IEEE testbeds is simulated; the manifold is a linear PCA fit on a synthetic load model with a single uniform metering-noise level; no PMU data (SCADA-only estimator); the 118-Bus bias-budget explanation for the 0.48 detection rate is offered as a hypothesis, not an established cause; no quantitative cross-protocol (IEC-61850/MMS) evaluation was run; and the fusion model itself is standard. The scope statement in Section 1 is made once and consistently honored — every claim is explicitly scoped to its supporting testbed. Analyst-Identified Gaps - No comparison against the actual topology-aware fusion GNN of Sweeten et al. under the temporal protocol — the paper's central comparative claim ("shuffling inflates more than models differ") is established among weaker families; whether a strong topology-aware model also suffers the same protocol inflation is asserted by analogy, not measured. The authors note this as future work but do not flag how much it limits Claim 1's generality. - The IEEE 14-Bus cyber features in the taxonomy are simulated, so the "independent confirmation" of the real-traffic boundary is weaker than it reads; the paper flags this in a parenthetical but the taxonomy's clean partition (1.00/0.99/0.06) depends on attack constructions the authors themselves designed. - The benign load model is synthetic with a single noise level; real load traces could shift the manifold dimension and the 0.36° detection gate, and the paper's claim that the test "should retain its behavior" is untested extrapolation. - The abstention/escalation policy is evaluated on dataset 1, where physical features are already inside the fused model, so escalation routes to a human, not a new observation layer — the operationally interesting case (cyber-only escalation to physics) is only sketched (0.75→0.79) and not developed. - The gradient-masking explanation for PGD ≈ random search on forests is cited from prior work but not verified experimentally (e.g., no non-adaptive vs. adaptive transfer-gap analysis). - Defense evaluation stops at empirical robustness of smoothing/adversarial training on one ε; no certified-radius figures are computed despite citing certified defenses as a priority. Bottom Line A practitioner benchmarking grid or CPS attack detectors should read this paper: it does not offer a better detector, but it is one of the few honest evaluation studies in the area, and its quantified protocol-inflation results, observability taxonomy, and measured 118-Bus degradation boundary will change how credible detection claims in this subfield should be read — more so than most of the deep fusion papers it implicitly critiques.

TL;DR:** - What it does: This paper builds FAME-QP, an open-source GPU solver for dense convex QPs in linear MPC that combines constraint-dependent pre-inverted operators, fused single- and two-kernel ADMM iterations replayed via CUDA graphs, automated execution-mode selection, penalty-bank probing, and lazy operator updates for changing problem matrices. - Why it's important: Real-time MPC for legged robots and Koopman/world-model-based controllers needs QP solves within millisecond control periods, and existing GPU solvers either carry oversized dense operators (ReLU-QP), lack online matrix updates, or are orders of magnitude slower; keeping the whole solve on-GPU also avoids CPU–GPU transfer latency in GPU-native robot pipelines. - How it does it: It exploits diagonal (box-bound) constraint rows to shrink the pre-inverted ADMM operator by up to 4×, fuses an entire ADMM iteration into one or two kernels replayed through CUDA graphs, and caches a bank of five penalty operators so penalty adaptation is a pointer switch rather than a refactorization. - The good: The ablation study cleanly isolates each mechanism — fusion plus graph replay cut per-iteration time from 140 µs to 4.37 µs at n=128, constraint-structure extraction yields 1.67–4.00× storage and 1.07–3.03× iteration-time reductions, and penalty probing cuts complete-solve time 1.4–3.3× — with gains shown to multiply rather than overlap. - The missing: All evaluation is on dense QPs with at most n=1400 (random QPs) and n=2000 (LMPC) on a single laptop GPU (RTX 3080 Laptop, 48 SMs), so no evidence exists at the 10×–100× problem scales where the paper's GPU-native motivation (large world-model MPC) actually lives, and sparse/horizon-structured QPs are explicitly deferred to future work. - Read it or not: Read it if you implement GPU-based real-time control or GPU QP solvers — the operator-shrink and CUDA-graph execution recipes are directly reusable — skip it if you care about large-scale or sparse QP solving beyond the condensed LMPC setting.

Problem & Motivation: Linear MPC must solve a convex QP every sampling period, and increasingly the surrounding pipeline (parallel simulation, learned latent dynamics, Koopman lifting, inference) already lives on the GPU, so a CPU-native QP solver adds transfer latency. Existing GPU options leave gaps: ReLU-QP stores a dense pre-inverted operator of size (n+2m)² and cannot update matrices between solves; cuOSQP runs float32 and is slow (326 ms at n=1400 vs. 1.95 ms for FAME-QP in float32); interior-point GPU solvers (qpax, CuPIQP) are hard to warm-start and far slower in this benchmark (CuPIQP: 449 ms mean step at n=2000). The target users are robotics/control researchers and practitioners who need millisecond-latency dense QP solves, including problems where the Hessian and constraint matrix change at every step. Key Idea: The core insight is that the pre-inverted ADMM operator K⁻¹ (the expensive, cached asset in ReLU-QP-style schemes) can be made much smaller by separating constraint rows that act diagonally on individual decision variables (box/input bounds, G=D) from genuinely dense rows: the diagonal block is absorbed into an elementwise update and never stored or multiplied, shrinking the operator from ~(n+2m)² to n(n+2mc) (factored) or (n+mc)² (stacked) entries, where mc is the dense-row count. Everything else — fusing the iteration into one kernel, choosing stacked vs. factored by a calibrated bandwidth/launch-overhead model plus measured graph timings, snapping an adaptive penalty to a cached five-entry operator bank, and lazily re-inverting only the selected bank entry when matrices change — is competent systems engineering built around this structural reduction. Methodology: FAME-QP solves (1) via OSQP's ADMM splitting with relaxation α and diagonal penalty ρ = ρ·diag(b), eliminating the dualized primal multiplier and pre-computing M = K⁻¹ so each iteration is a matrix–vector product plus elementwise projection/clipping, terminated by OSQP-style primal/dual residual tests. Pipeline: (i) setup — modified Ruiz equilibration (10 passes), constraint-structure detection (box / split / general), penalty-bank construction (five entries, factors of 10 around ρ₀=0.1), CUDA-graph capture of jchk=10 iterations plus the termination test, then a probing phase that runs ≤400-iteration trials per bank entry to select the starting ρ (and γ for split constraints), re-centering the bank at most twice; (ii) solve — scale incoming q, l, h with cached scaling matrices, warm-start z and λ (optionally horizon-shifted), replay the graph once per pass, host-read five scalar residuals, adapt ρ by OSQP's residual-balancing rule snapped to the bank, rebuild r after switches. Execution modes: single-kernel (stacked operator W = [M, MG⊤; GM, GMG⊤], one fused kernel per iteration, alternating buffers) vs. two-kernel (factored F = [M, MC⊤] then C, saving mc² entries at the cost of one extra launch). Mode selection uses a calibrated per-device iteration-time model t_iter ≈ n_ker·τ + t_stream(b_op) to prune, then measured graph timings decide (two-kernel kept only if >10% faster). Matrix updates (changes in P or G) trigger rescaling and either full or lazy bank re-inversion. Precision is user-fixed or auto-selected via a power-iteration condition-number estimate κ(K) with the rule u₃₂κ(K) ≤ 0.01ε → float32. Key design decisions: (a) constraint-structure exploitation — well justified, backed by ablation; (b) fixed five-entry penalty grid — justified by ablation showing widening the bank alone changes iterations ≤5%; (c) model-prune-then-measure selection — justified, since the model alone misplaces the stacked/factored crossover by ~2×. The stated objective is ADMM convergence to OSQP's KKT-based residual test (9); no new convergence theory is offered. Key Results: All experiments run on an NVIDIA RTX 3080 Laptop GPU (48 SMs, 16 GB) with an i7-11850H; CPU baselines are OSQP, PIQP, ProxQP, Clarabel, DAQP; GPU baselines are cuOSQP, ReLU-QP, qpax, CuPIQP, CUDA MPC (authors' own reimplementation, source unavailable), and πMPC. Dense random QPs (n=20–1400, five seeds, accuracy matched at ℓ∞ error ≤10⁻³ against Clarabel at 10⁻¹⁰, setup excluded): FAME-QP float64 beats every GPU baseline at every size and every CPU baseline for n≥220; speedups 1.2–25.9× over DAQP and 1.5–4.3× over ReLU-QP over n=220–1400; at n=1400, 1.95 ms (float32) vs. 5.01 ms (float64) vs. 326 ms (cuOSQP). Closed-loop random LMPC (n=400–2000, 50 steps, mean step time): 0.658–4.23 ms for FAME-QP, 3.2–7.3× faster than ReLU-QP and 3.2–13.8× faster than πMPC, with smaller standard deviations; closed-loop costs agree within 0.06%, though FAME-QP's worst bound violation is 2.0×10⁻³ vs. ~10⁻⁴ (πMPC) and <10⁻⁶ (CuPIQP, CUDA MPC) — FAME-QP is fastest but least accurate of the GPU methods on constraint satisfaction. Unitree G1 humanoid push recovery in MuJoCo (n=29N, 2 ms period): mean QP time 0.650–1.04 ms across N=10–20, 2.3–3.1× faster than ReLU-QP and always under the 2 ms budget (ReLU-QP exceeds it for N≥15); CoM RMS 18.7–20.5 mm, comparable to ReLU-QP. Skydio X2 quadrotor KQ-LMPC tracking with per-step changing P and G (n=280, 50 Hz): mean QP time 12.5±3.2 ms vs. 59.2±4.8 ms for CuPIQP (4.7×), 99th-percentile latency 17.6 ms vs. 72.1 ms, tracking RMSE 2.7 mm vs. 3.4 mm. Ablations quantify each component separately (fusion+replay: 140→4.37 µs/iteration at n=128; structure extraction: 1.07–3.03×; probing: 1.4–3.3× with setup cost recovered after ~36–122 solves; lazy updates roughly halve update and median step times with identical solutions). Tested scale is standard, not stress-scale; results are single-GPU, single-hardware, simulation-only. This is a preprint (arXiv:2611.13766), not stated as peer-reviewed. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL with ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION components. The genuinely novel element is the combination, not any single ingredient: ADMM with pre-inverted operators and penalty banks is inherited from ReLU-QP, CUDA-graph replay from CuPIQP/CUDA MPC, Ruiz scaling and the residual test from OSQP. What is new is the constraint-dependent diagonal/dense operator decomposition (up to 4× smaller operators), the calibrated stacked-vs-factored execution-mode selection, and lazy bank refresh enabling online matrix changes that ReLU-QP cannot handle — a competent synthesis of known ideas applied to dense MPC QPs, with the structure exploitation being the most defensible claim to novelty. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are strong: fusion/graph replay, constraint structure, operator-form selection, penalty probing, and lazy updates are each isolated with matched data and settings, and the authors decompose combined gains multiplicatively rather than claiming one factor. Accuracy matching across solvers is handled carefully (tolerance sweep against a Clarabel reference), a good practice many solver papers skip. Weaknesses: no confidence intervals or significance tests; five seeds per random-QP size but no error bars in Fig. 1 beyond min–max bands; CUDA MPC is the authors' reimplementation; stopping criteria are admittedly non-equivalent across solvers (mitigated by a secondary accuracy comparison); benchmarks exclude setup time, which is fair for amortized MPC but favorable to FAME-QP given its probing cost; all results on one consumer laptop GPU in simulation. Code is open-sourced at https://github.com/santoshrajkumar/fame-qp. No benchmark is authored by the paper itself (random QPs reuse ReLU-QP's generator), avoiding self-benchmark Goodharting, but the solver was presumably developed and tuned against these same benchmarks. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a built solver, evaluated on benchmarks and simulated deployments). Practical: Yes — runs on a consumer RTX 3080 Laptop GPU with CUDA; no exotic hardware. Efficient: Low cost per solve (0.658 ms at n=400 in float64; 4.37 µs/iteration at n=128 fused+graph-replayed); setup with probing costs extra and is amortized after ~36–122 solves, which fits MPC but not one-shot use. Effective: Yes for the stated problem — dense LMPC QPs solved under millisecond periods with matched accuracy and working closed-loop control in MuJoCo — though FAME-QP's constraint-violation accuracy (2.0×10⁻³) is the worst among GPU baselines at the compared tolerance. Scalable: Claimed motivation includes large world-model MPC, but the largest tested dense QP is n=2000 on 16 GB VRAM; nothing above n=1400 for cold solves, no multi-GPU or batched-QP evaluation, and the dense operators scale quadratically, so 10× scale is untested and the paper itself defers sparse/horizon-structured formulations to future work. Delivers a real software artifact (open-source solver); no trained model or dataset. Strengths: - The constraint-structure decomposition is a real, measurable idea: it cuts operator storage 1.67–4.00× and iteration time 1.07–3.03× with provably identical iterates (solutions match within 10⁻¹²), directly attacking the dominant memory-bandwidth bottleneck of pre-inverted-operator ADMM. - Execution engineering is unusually careful: the iteration-time model is explicitly calibrated per device, shown to misplace the crossover by ~2× (hence measured-timing tie-breaking), and the automatic selector picks the faster form at 30/36 sweep points, never exceeding 9.5% overhead over the better fixed form. - Support for per-step changing QP matrices (lazy bank refresh) with demonstrated 4.7× speedup over CuPIQP on a changing-matrix Koopman LMPC closes a genuine capability gap versus ReLU-QP. - Honest component attribution: the authors show the speedup over ReLU-QP comes mainly from per-iteration cost, not fewer iterations (similar iteration counts at 10⁻³ accuracy), which resists the temptation to conflate mechanisms. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state in the conclusion that FAME-QP targets dense QPs and that sparse and horizon-structured formulations are future work; they acknowledge single-precision residual stagnation near 10⁻⁶ (returning solved_inaccurate at 100× tolerances); they acknowledge the model-based crossover is inaccurate (~2×) and therefore back it with measured timings; they note setup cost of probing is recovered only after ~36–122 solves; and they flag non-equivalent stopping tests across baselines. They confront limitations directly, which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No evaluation of batched/independent QPs (e.g., ensemble or scenario MPC), which is the natural strength of pre-inverted-operator ADMM on GPU and the main use case of closest baseline CuPIQP's "batched" design; the paper competes only on single-problem latency. - All GPU-vs-GPU comparisons occur at a fixed accuracy-matching criterion derived from one reference solver (Clarabel); constraint-violation data in Table I shows FAME-QP is fastest but least accurate among GPU methods, and no high-accuracy (≤10⁻⁶) regime is benchmarked, where ADMM is known to weaken versus interior-point methods. - Single hardware configuration: no data on other GPUs (e.g., server-class A100/H100 with different bandwidth/SM ratios), so the calibrated mode selection and reported speedups may not transfer; τ and bandwidth calibrations are per-device, but this is never tested cross-device. - The humanoid controller's prediction model is a linearization about one bent-knee stance; no evidence on how far the disturbance regime extends before the linearization or LQR pre-stabilization fails, and no comparison against any CPU solver (e.g., HPIPM, the standard MPC baseline) in the closed-loop experiments. - Probing evaluation uses a held-out setup instance but the bank/probing policy was developed on the same random-QP family it is evaluated on; no out-of-distribution QP family tests the policy's generality. - πMPC's very large standard deviations (e.g., 9.06±12.39 ms) suggest outlier-heavy behavior that is reported but not explained or investigated. Bottom Line: For anyone building GPU-native real-time MPC, this is worth reading and using: it is a well-engineered, open-source solver with credible component-wise evidence and the best reported single-solve latencies on dense MPC QPs at n up to ~2000, but it does not supersede sparse-structured solvers (HPIPM) at larger scales, high-accuracy regimes, or batched-QP workloads.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces SparseRead, a model-agnostic reading control layer for LLM agents that governs what external content (webpages, PDFs, tables, code repositories) enters the model context, reducing total token consumption by 15.7–92.9% (median 61.4%) and wall time by 23.0–89.0% (median 53.7%) while preserving or improving task quality in 29 of 30 tested settings. - Why it's important: External observations account for 60–80% of tokens in agent trajectories, and unmodified agents can spend up to 17.3× more tokens than necessary without quality gains — a direct cost and latency problem for anyone deploying web-facing or repository-scale agents. - How it does it: The core move is turning artifact access into explicit admission control: the agent states a structured Read Intent, pluggable Reader backends return source-anchored evidence with coverage tracking, and a Budgeted Read Gate enforces a per-episode exposure budget capped at 2× the faithful full-view length, with a guaranteed full-view fallback. - The good: The evaluation is broad and honest — 6 models (including Claude Opus 5), 5 scenarios spanning long-doc QA to materials-science script generation, 3 agent frameworks, 5 baselines including ACON and observation masking, plus component ablations and a small formal exposure bound with proof. - The missing: No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported for the headline results, the task-score metric is never precisely defined in the paper, and no public code release for SparseRead itself is stated. - Read it or not: Worth reading for agent-infrastructure and context-engineering practitioners building long-horizon agents on paid LLM APIs; less useful for readers seeking algorithmic novelty in retrieval or compression, since the backends are deliberately off-the-shelf.

Problem & Motivation: LLM agents that read webpages, documents, repositories, and tool responses receive content at object granularity even when each decision needs only a small evidence slice. The authors call this "over-reading": they measure that annotated supporting evidence covers a median of 3.17% of source tokens per LooGLE question and ~5.8% of answerable Qasper questions, yet native agents expose entire artifacts. Because admitted content persists in later model calls, one broad read compounds across the trajectory (formalized as replay-weighted exposure Σ|e_i|R_i). Prior work addresses fragments of this — KV-cache compression and long-context architectures reduce compute but do not decide what the model should see; ACON and observation masking compress or drop content after acquisition; iterative/agentic RAG locates passages but offers no artifact-level contract for evolving intents, coverage tracking, bounded exposure, and fallback. The gap is a general admission-control mechanism sitting between the agent and heterogeneous external resources. Key Idea: Treat reading as a stateful, budgeted evidence-acquisition loop rather than an unconditional data transfer: (1) a Read Intent Protocol makes the agent's per-access information need and per-slot source coverage explicit state; (2) Adaptive Reader Backends decouple where evidence is located (BM25, hybrid retrieval, column queries, key-path lookup, exact computation) from what is exposed (anchored snippets, lossless compact views, operation results); (3) a Budgeted Read Gate admits sparse evidence only while cumulative raw exposure E ≤ L (the length of the cheapest faithful full view), falling back to the full view otherwise — yielding a proven worst-case exposure of 2L per episode, adapted from ski-rental online budgeting. The sharp distinction between processing scope (what the Reader computes over, e.g., an entire table) and model exposure (what enters context, e.g., one computed sum) is the conceptual lever. Methodology: SparseRead separates a control plane (intent validation, Reader selection, evidence record, gate) from an evidence plane (registered Readers for text/PDF, structured data, collections, script libraries). The shared contract is Read Intent → EvidencePack (source-anchored evidence, scope processed, exposed size, per-slot coverage, SHA-256 artifact fingerprint for version invalidation). The agent drives five stable actions {scout, focus, collect, refine, verify}; the protocol never declares sufficiency — stopping remains the agent's decision. Reader selection solves r = argmin Ĉ(r|g) subject to p̂_valid(r|g) ≥ τ = 0.6, where reliability is the lower end of a 95% Wilson interval over manually authored calibration requests (not evaluation tasks), grouped by artifact type, size band (≤8K, 8–32K, >32K chars), and intent type; costs are estimated in characters including follow-up reads. The Gate enforces E ≤ L by checking serialized payload size before* delivery — the paper shows post-delivery checking overshoots to 2.10–2.33× the full view while pre-delivery checking keeps all runs within 1.62–1.93×. Proposition 4.1 proves the 2L bound (Appendix A); the proof is straightforward but complete and the constant 2 is shown tight. Critical design decisions: (a) intent enforcement lives in the core runtime, not model compliance — well justified, since guarantees hold even if the model misbehaves; (b) calibration is decoupled from evaluation data — well justified and explicitly documented; (c) character-based rather than token-based budgeting — pragmatic but means the bound is not directly a billed-token bound, a limitation the authors themselves concede. Key Results: Across 30 settings (6 models × 5 scenarios on NanoBot), SparseRead reduces tokens 15.7–92.9% and wall time 23.0–89.0%, preserving or improving score in 29/30 (one regression: GLM-5.1 on AI for Science, −0.10). Long-context reading saves 76.5–92.9% of tokens; Web deep search gains 5–14 score points while saving 31.0–43.0% of tokens; Opus 5 saves 41.0–89.0% of tokens, showing benefits persist for frontier models. Against baselines (Naive, RAG Static, RAG Agent, ACON, observation masking) across 15 settings, SparseRead preserves or improves score in every setting and achieves both lowest tokens and lowest time in all five multi-file-diagnosis settings with score gains of 17.8–34.5 points. ACON loses score in 5 settings and increases both costs in 6; RAG Static scores below Naive in 9 of 15. Cross-framework (NanoBot, OpenCode, OpenClaw; 18 settings) median token reductions are 65.0%, 65.2%, and 30.6%, with three score decreases of 0.013–0.031. Ablations: combined intents cut repeated reads from 4.8 to 1.5/task and evidence failures from 25% to 5%; hybrid retrieval hits 65.3% evidence coverage at 1,490 median characters vs. BM25's 60.1% at 1,497. The paper reports 100% coverage of scenario-relevant tasks in each source benchmark (LooGLE, PinchBench, QwenClawBench, SpreadsheetBench Verified, FRAMES, BrowseComp-Plus, MDGYM) rather than cherry-picked samples. Baselines are current (2025–2026 work including ACON from ICML) and configurations are documented in detail. No error bars or statistical tests are reported; some ablations use three repeats, main results do not state repetition. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (a deployable reading control layer integrated into three agent frameworks) plus NEW FORMULATION (artifact admission control with explicit intent/coverage state and a per-episode exposure budget with a worst-case bound). The individual ingredients — BM25/hybrid retrieval, tool-output pruning, observation masking, online budgeting — are existing; the genuinely novel part is the unified Read Intent → EvidencePack contract, the scope-vs-exposure distinction, and the pre-delivery budgeted gate with a 2L fallback guarantee. ReadAgent, IRCoT, and Adaptive-RAG are related but lack the coverage tracking and admission guarantee. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations cover all three components (intent handling, Reader location methods, gate budget checking), and the ablations are appropriately self-critical — e.g., the authors state the location-method experiment "does not isolate the incremental benefit of the configuration selector." Calibration is explicitly separated from evaluation data with a pre-fixed τ = 0.6. No error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported for main results; a couple of ablation cohorts use three repeats. No public code, data, or artifact release for SparseRead is mentioned in the paper. Methodological strengths: pre-declared 100% task coverage of benchmark subsets, detailed baseline configurations (Appendix D), end-to-end cost accounting including RAG reranking and ACON compressor calls. Concerns: the task-score metric is used everywhere but never formally defined in the main text or visible appendices; the exposure-bound experiment uses separate cohorts of five tasks, which is thin; several cited works are arXiv preprints (2025–2026), so some baseline comparisons inherit preprint-level maturity. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a built runtime evaluated through three deployed agent frameworks with real models). - Practical: Yes — it runs as a shared runtime with thin adapters around existing harnesses (NanoBot, OpenCode, OpenClaw) and commercial/open-weight models, with no model retraining or separate compression model. - Efficient: Strictly cost-reducing in all 18 cross-framework settings (median token reduction 30.6–65.2%); the Gate's 2L bound caps the downside of selective reading, and native-fit bypass avoids the protocol tax on small artifacts (Appendix C shows forced sparse reading would add 49–310% tokens on unsuited tasks). - Effective: Evidence supports the stated problem on high-sparsity tasks (evidence density 3–6% of source), but the score metric is undefined, and effectiveness on tasks needing holistic document understanding is only probed via 8 boundary tasks, not stress-tested. - Scalable: Only claimed, not tested beyond artifact size bands above 32K characters and multi-file workspaces; the 2L guarantee is per-episode, not per-session, so sessions with many episodes have no aggregate bound — the paper says this but provides no 10×–100× experiment. Delivers a software artifact (runtime, Readers, adapters) in paper form; no public repository is stated. Strengths: - The scope-vs-exposure distinction is a genuinely useful conceptual contribution: it lets a Reader scan an entire table but expose only the computed result, unifying retrieval, compact views, and exact source operations under one contract. - The evaluation design is unusually careful for a systems paper: 100% pre-declared task coverage of benchmark subsets, calibration requests disjoint from evaluation tasks, and end-to-end cost accounting for all baselines. - The Budgeted Read Gate converts an empirical heuristic into a system with a worst-case guarantee (2L), and the ablation showing pre-delivery vs. post-delivery budget checking (1.93× vs. 2.33× overshoot) demonstrates the mechanism matters in practice. - Honest boundary probing: Appendix C explicitly documents where forced sparse reading fails (up to +309% tokens) and shows the Gate avoids it, rather than hiding the regime where the method does not apply. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state: the 2L bound does not cover replay-weighted context, billed tokens, latency, or multi-episode sessions; preview and protocol metadata are excluded from the bound; the location-method ablation does not isolate the adaptive selector's benefit; forced sparse reading is harmful on low-sparsity tasks (motivating native-fit bypass); one model–scenario regression (GLM-5.1 on AI for Science, −0.10); fallback retires prior sparse observations, sacrificing prefix-cache reuse from that point. This is direct and credible engagement with limitations — a strong positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The task-score metric driving all quality claims is never defined in the provided text, making headline claims like "+0.598 score delta for Kimi-K2.5 on NanoBot" impossible to interpret or audit. - No variance reporting: with single-run (or unstated-repetition) agent trajectories, score deltas of ±0.01–0.03 in the cross-framework table may be noise; only three qualitative regression cases are acknowledged. - Baselines omit the closest related systems the paper itself discusses — ReadAgent, SWE-Pruner, and Squeez are cited as compatible backends but never run as competitors, so the claim that the unified contract beats dedicated pruning is untested head-to-head. - Read-intent generation adds model-issued tokens per access; the paper counts total tokens but never itemizes the protocol's own overhead (prompt engineering, SKILL.md guidance, intent serialization), so the true net cost of the control plane is unquantified. - The reliability threshold τ = 0.6 and the Wilson-interval calibration are validated only by outcomes; no sensitivity analysis of τ is provided. - All three harnesses are of the same lineage/authorship ecosystem; no evaluation on widely used third-party harnesses (e.g., SWE-agent-style or WebArena harnesses), limiting external validity of the portability claim. Bottom Line: A practitioner building or operating long-horizon agents against paid APIs gains concrete, well-evidenced cost and latency reductions (median 61% tokens saved) from a design worth imitating, and the paper's honest boundary analysis makes it more useful than most context-compression work — but the undefined score metric, missing statistical rigor, absent code release, and untested head-to-head comparison with dedicated pruning systems keep it short of a definitive result.

Confucius4-R2T2: A Stable-Prefix Streaming ASR Model for Real Real-Time Transcription (28 ▲ )

Daniel Huang, Qi He, Shaoxiong Duan, Yingjie Li, Qiao Cheng, Yitao Duan · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 9 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Confucius4-R2T2, a streaming ASR model built by post-training Qwen3-ASR-1.7B with a new Longest Stable Prefix (LSP) supervision scheme so that its emitted text is provably never revised, while reaching a total macro WER/CER of 5.76 at 160 ms chunks (U=1) — within a claimed ~0.6 points of the base model's full-context decoding and better than three evaluated commercial APIs. - Why it's important: Streaming transcripts are increasingly consumed by machines (translators, voice agents) that act on each token immediately, so a revised token means wasted downstream computation or a wrong action; prior streaming ASR reduces but does not eliminate revision. - How it does it: The key move is supervising the decoder on the Longest Stable Prefix — the longest of the full-context model's own earlier partial outputs that is entirely a prefix of its full-context output — plus an explicit Wait token for deferral, trained via SFT then GRPO reinforcement learning with the audio encoder and projector frozen. - The good: The strongest evidence is the matched comparison: the unadapted base model at 160 ms chunks is unusable due to severe hallucination, while R2T2 at the same chunk size achieves 5.76 total macro error (6.40 with U=0), with gains transferring to 10 languages never seen in post-training (18 test sets, average 9.60 vs. the base's 30.75 at the same setting). - The missing: The paper reports no runtime RTF/throughput measurements (lag is a retrospective audio-timeline metric), no ablation of the eight RL reward components (explicitly deferred), no SFT-only ablation, and no significance tests or multiple seeds. - Read it or not: Worth reading for speech/streaming-systems researchers and anyone building latency-sensitive voice pipelines who needs machine-consumable, immutable partial transcripts; skip it if you only care about offline ASR accuracy, where the base model already suffices.
Why this rank

Novelty (72) is anchored by the NEW FORMULATION classification: the model-admissible Longest Stable Prefix target with proved monotonicity/admissibility/maximality properties turns a folk concept into a precise object, and stability is achieved behaviorally with zero architectural change. Rigor (68) is limited by missing SFT-vs-RL and reward-component ablations, no seeds or error bars, and retrospective-only latency measurement — offset by the formal appendix, current baselines including commercial APIs, and open weights/code. Resilience (65) drops on the unmeasured sub-1-RTF assumption and self-distillation ceiling; Impact (75) reflects the released 1.7B model and code, a real deployable artifact for voice pipelines. Problem & Motivation: Streaming ASR output is increasingly fed to downstream machines — live translators, voice agents deciding when to respond or call tools — that act on each emitted token. When a recognizer later revises an early token ("flicker"/"revision"/"hypothesis instability"), the consumer must discard or redo work, or an agent takes a wrong side effect. Prior mitigations are inference-time commitment heuristics (Local Agreement, hold-n, mask-k) or indirect stability training; both lower revision rates without guaranteeing that earlier output is never modified. The gap: a streaming model with stability as a hard guarantee, while keeping accuracy near full-context models and latency under ~500 ms. The authors are a NetEase Youdao team; the target domain is production Chinese/English transcription consumed incrementally. Key Idea: Reformulate the streaming supervision target. Instead of training on truncated audio → truncated transcript, train on audio prefix → Longest Stable Prefix: the longest output the full-context model itself produced at some earlier time that is entirely a prefix of its full-utterance output ¯y, or Wait if no such output exists at the current cut point. Because the label is (proved) monotone under the prefix order, consistent with ¯y, and maximal among model-admissible (actually-produced) prefixes, stability emerges from learning when to commit rather than from architectural causalization or commit rules; the Wait token separates the timing decision from the content decision inside the existing vocabulary. Methodology: Three phases. (1) LSP annotation: the frozen Qwen3-ASR-1.7B decodes each utterance progressively at 80 ms intervals; the longest earlier output that is a full prefix of ¯y is tracked, agreement intervals are merged, and each training cut gets either the stable prefix or the prefix plus a Wait token (Eq. 7); 10% of examples keep the full utterance to preserve offline ability. (2) Two-stage post-training of only the language decoder (encoder, 300M-param AuT with 1–8 s dynamic attention windows, and projector frozen): cross-entropy SFT for one epoch (AdamW, lr 1e-5, batch 64) on ~1,500 hours / 600k utterances of proprietary Chinese–English audio with noise (SNR 10–35 dB), reverberation, and language-tag-flip augmentation; then GRPO RL with an eight-component reward (CER 0.30, precision 0.15, length 0.15, repetition 0.125, language consistency 0.15, tail 0.05, word accuracy 0.05, cut marker 0.025) squashed through tanh(3R_raw). (3) Inference without model changes: encoder KV-cache reuse of completed 8 s windows, Wait-terminated decoding (a Wait prediction ends the update at pre-fill), bounded context (W=1 retained window, ~16 s audio), and pre-fill verification of a U-token revisable suffix — the verification step of speculative decoding with the previous suffix as draft. A "streamability" AUC metric (0.493 for Qwen3-ASR-1.7B, the highest of models tested on 1,860 Buckeye utterances) selects the backbone. Critical design decisions: freezing the bidirectional encoder (justified by cited evidence that LoRA causalization hurts above ~300 ms chunks, at the cost of re-encoding the active window each update); anchoring labels to the model's own output ¯y rather than ground truth (deliberate, to keep stability separate from accuracy, but it inherits the base model's errors); all-or-nothing credit instead of the partial-credit final-anchored label of Hoang et al. 2026 (justified by a model-admissibility argument and worked examples, at the acknowledged price of later emission). Key Results: On 13 English/Chinese test sets (AMI, GigaSpeech-clean, LibriSpeech clean/other, VoxPopuli, Earnings22, TED-LIUM, RealSI; WenetSpeech net/meeting, SPEECHIO 06/07, CN-RealSI), R2T2 at 160 ms with U=1 achieves the lowest total macro error among ranked configurations at 5.76, vs. 6.40 for U=0 (withholding one token cuts macro error ~10% at a cost of a few tenths of a second mean lag), surpassing AssemblyAI (8.97) and two commercial APIs (14.21 and 19.35), and approaching the base model's full-context decode with a claimed ~0.6-point gap; the unadapted base at 160 ms hallucinates severely (macro 21.01, reduced by "nearly three quarters"). On VoxPopuli R2T2 slightly beats the full-context reference (3.17 vs. 3.14 — essentially tied). At 80 ms/U=0 mean retrospective lag stays below 0.5 s in both languages. Cross-lingual transfer to 10 untrained languages (18 test sets): R2T2 averages 9.60 (U=1) / 8.40 (U=0) vs. 30.75 for the base at the same 160 ms setting and 5.99 for base full-context. Baselines are current (2025–2026 open-source and commercial systems, including Voxtral Realtime and Nemotron 3.5). Tested at standard benchmark scale, not stress-scale; no seeds, error bars, or significance tests are reported. Note this is an arXiv preprint with self-run evaluation of proprietary training data — vendor-adjacent numbers warrant moderate confidence, though the model and code are released for verification. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (the model-admissible final-anchored LSP target, with proved monotonicity, admissibility, and maximality properties, differentiated from McGraw & Gruenstein's all-future criterion and Hoang et al.'s final-anchored label) plus NEW METHOD (LSP learning: converting a full-context ASR model to a guaranteed stable-prefix streaming model with no architectural change and a frozen encoder). The inference techniques (cache reuse, bounded context, speculative-decoding-style suffix verification) are competent engineering combinations of known ideas applied to this setting; the streamability AUC metric is a useful but incremental diagnostic. Rigor & Reproducibility: The formal appendix is unusually rigorous: five propositions and a maximality theorem with proofs, plus counterexamples separating the three stable-prefix definitions in the literature. Ablations are partial: chunk-size (80 ms–2 s) and U sweeps are reported, but the eight RL reward components are not ablated ("Component-specific effects require controlled ablations" — acknowledged), there is no SFT-only-vs-RL ablation, and no W= sweep for bounded context. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests. Model weights and code are released (huggingface.co/netease-youdao/Confucius4-R2T2; github.com/netease-youdao/Confucius4-R2T2), aiding reproduction, but training data is proprietary and cannot be regenerated. Methodological concerns: training and evaluation share the authors' curation (RealSI transcription done by the authors); the base model may have seen evaluation data in pre-training (acknowledged); commercial APIs evaluated via approximate API-based lag estimates with undisclosed server-side buffering; lag scoring excludes high-error utterances. The self-distillation target inherits the base model's full-context errors, and no stronger-teacher comparison exists. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a trained model plus serving techniques, evaluated on benchmarks; no production deployment is reported). - Practical: Yes — a 1.7B-parameter model with open weights runs on commodity GPUs, with configurable chunk sizes from 80 ms to 2 s requiring no retraining. - Efficient: Per-update cost is bounded (active 8 s window re-encoded, retained text re-prefilled) via cache reuse and Wait-terminated decoding, but each update still re-encodes ~8 s of audio, strictly heavier than a causal-interleaved design (which the authors compare against only theoretically); no RTF or throughput is actually measured, so the sub-1-RTF claim is an assumption, not a result. - Effective: Benchmarks show it solves the stated problem on standard test sets (accuracy within ~0.6 points of full-context, lowest ranked macro error, sub-0.5 s lag at 80 ms/U=0), though lag is a retrospective proxy and excludes execution, queueing, and transport time. - Scalable: Bounded 16 s context means per-update cost is constant in stream length by construction, but only benchmark-length audio is tested; no long-hours continuous-streaming measurement, and only the 1.7B scale is evaluated. The work delivers a real software artifact: open model weights and code (HF + GitHub), not just a paper. Strengths: - The formal treatment of the supervision target is the paper's real intellectual contribution: Theorem 1 (LSP is the longest self-consistent, model-admissible target) and the counterexamples separating it from the all-future and final-anchored definitions turn a folk concept into a precise, comparable object. - Stability is obtained behaviorally with zero architectural change — no causalization, no extra heads — preserving the bidirectional encoder's accuracy and keeping one checkpoint for both streaming and full-context modes; the result (usable 160 ms streaming from a model that hallucinates at that chunk size unadapted) validates the design. - Empirically strong and honest evaluation: current baselines including three commercial APIs, a latency-priority/quality-priority trade-off (U) exposed at inference without retraining, and cross-language transfer on 18 unseen-language test sets. - Open-source release of weights and code makes the central claims checkable despite proprietary training data. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly, which strengthens credibility: the all-or-nothing LSP credit is conservative and biases toward later emission; streamability as a gauge for general streamization (e.g., simultaneous translation) and the question of whether a stronger teacher would help are explicitly open; a fixed U-token budget is not a fixed millisecond delay under BPE tokenization; retrospective lag excludes runtime/queueing/transport and API buffering is undisclosed; fluicker frequency itself is not measured; the base model may have seen evaluation data in pre-training; the causal-interleaved comparison is theoretical and unimplemented; deployment performance and broader generalization "remain priorities for further evaluation." Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No end-to-end runtime measurement: the sub-1-RTF requirement that makes the caching design correct is asserted, never benchmarked (GPU type, throughput, and per-update wall-clock are absent). - No ablation separating SFT from RL, or of individual reward components, so the reader cannot tell which training signal carries the hallucination suppression. - Self-distillation from ¯y caps the student at the base model's full-context judgments; the ~0.6-point gap claim rests partly on post-training data effects, and no comparison against a stronger external teacher or a forced-aligner-based labeling baseline is run. - Lag scoring excludes utterances with high recognition error, which selectively removes the hardest (and likely slowest-to-stabilize) cases from the latency numbers. - Evaluation is Chinese/English-centric with post-training languages matched to the proprietary data; the 10-language transfer gains are relative to a broken 160 ms baseline, not to a properly adapted multilingual system. - Only one backbone scale (1.7B) and one W (bounded-context) setting are tested; the claim that bounded context suffices for long streams is supported by citation, not by experiment. Bottom Line: For practitioners building streaming speech interfaces where downstream consumers act on emitted text, this is the strongest publicly available stable-prefix ASR artifact and a clearly argued method worth adopting or building on; for general ASR accuracy alone, the unmodified Qwen3-ASR-1.7B in full-context mode covers the same ground with less machinery.

Load Balancing with Item Fragmentation and More Bins than Items: Linear-Time and Exact

B Bals, T Flouri, K Kobert, SP Pissis, L Stougie · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper proves that the NP-hard Load Balancing with Item Fragmentation (LBIF) problem admits an exact O(N)-time algorithm when the number of bins B is at least the number of items N, and shows an optimal assignment always exists in which every bin receives at most two fragments. - Why it's important: LBIF underlies the workload-distribution logic of widely deployed phylogenetics codes (RAxML-NG, ExaBayes), and the prior (OPT+1)-approximation runs in O(N log N + B), which is not strongly polynomial in N when B is huge — the common many-cores/machines regime. - How it does it: The core move is a two-phase constructive argument: (i) an O(N) arithmetic test (based on each item needing f_i = (−s_i) mod ℓ forced fragments of size ℓ−1, plus block-divisibility conditions) decides whether OPT = 1, and (ii) if not, a greedy phase that fills bins while preserving the invariant |S| ≤ |C| always yields a valid assignment with combinatorial load exactly 2 — hence optimal. - The good: The structural theorem (OPT ≤ 2 always achievable for B ≥ N) plus the complete four-condition characterization of when OPT = 1 (Corollary 3.3) turn an NP-hard problem into a linear-time exact solution in this regime, with full proofs of both invariants and correctness. - The missing: There is no implementation, no integration into the phylogenetic software that already uses the predecessor algorithm, and no empirical measurement of the practical effect of removing the O(B) term or of switching from (OPT+1)-approximate to exact solutions. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on scheduling/divisible-load theory or maintain load-balancing code in phylogenetic/HPC tools; skip it if you want systems benchmarks or the site-repeats variant, which is only mentioned, not solved.
Why this rank

Non-Obviousness (75) and Novelty (70) lead: proving that an NP-hard production-relevant problem (LBIF, embedded in RAxML-NG/ExaBayes) always admits an optimal solution with at most two fragments per bin in the B ≥ N regime — collapsing it to an exact O(N) algorithm — is a surprising structural result, with the checkable four-condition OPT=1 characterization and the first strongly polynomial (OPT+1)-approximation as concrete payoffs. Rigor (75) reflects complete, self-contained invariant-based proofs with explicit assumptions, minus some credit for the compressed sufficiency argument in the OPT=1 test that merits independent verification and the absence of any implementation. Completeness (65) is held back by the untested HPC-adoption claim and unexamined open directions, while Resilience (75) is high because the claims are proven and tightly scoped; Impact (50) for a theory paper is middling — the pseudocode is implementable in a day and the corollary closes a real asymptotic weakness, but no artifact ships and the site-repeats variant is untouched.
