Problem & Motivation: The paper addresses LBIF, introduced by Kobert et al. (WABI 2014): given N items of positive integer sizes summing to W and B bins, assign all item mass (fragmenting items across bins) so each bin load is ⌊W/B⌋ or ⌈W/B⌉, minimizing the maximum number of distinct item fragments in any bin (the combinatorial load). The motivating domain is parallel phylogenetic inference: partitions (items) of alignment sites (sizes) must be spread over processors (bins) that need near-equal site counts but pay per-partition overhead. Kobert et al. proved LBIF NP-hard and gave an O(N log N + B)-time (OPT+1)-approximation used in RAxML-NG and ExaBayes. Two gaps motivate this work: the running time is not polynomial in N alone when B ≫ N, and the approximation is not exact even when exactness is achievable. The B ≥ N regime arises whenever cores outnumber divisible jobs — e.g., per-chain likelihood balancing in Metropolis-coupled MCMC and re-balancing after processor faults. Key Idea: When bins are at least as numerous as items, an optimal solution always uses at most two fragments per bin, and the OPT = 1 case is decidable by a purely arithmetic necessary-and-sufficient condition: every item size s_i must admit a decomposition into k_i fragments of size ℓ and h_i = ℓ·m_i + f_i fragments of size ℓ−1, where f_i = (−s_i) mod ℓ is the minimal number of (ℓ−1)-fragments making the remainder divisible by ℓ. Running the OPT = 1 test first and the greedy ≤ 2 algorithm second yields exactness in O(N). Methodology: The framework is combinatorial algorithm design with invariants (no optimization or data-structure machinery; all operations are O(1) arithmetic and multiset updates). Phase 1 (Algorithm 3) tests OPT = 1 in three steps: (1) for each item compute f_i = (−s_i) mod ℓ, fail if s_i < f_i(ℓ−1); assign f_i fragments of size ℓ−1 to distinct (ℓ−1)-bins; fail if F = Σf_i > B − t (where t = W − B(ℓ−1) is the number of ℓ-bins) or if (B − t − F) mod ℓ ≠ 0; (2) bulk-fill the remaining r = B − t − F (ℓ−1)-bins in blocks of ℓ fragments of size ℓ−1 (full blocks preserve divisibility by ℓ), failing if items are exhausted; (3) slice every residual item, now divisible by ℓ, into ℓ-fragments for the t ℓ-bins. Phase 2 runs when the test fails: Algorithm 1 iterates over large items (size ≥ ℓ) while |S| < |C|, filling as many whole (ℓ−1)-bins and ℓ-bins as possible with each, capped by |C| − |S| to preserve the invariant |S| ≤ |C|; Algorithm 2 then, while both a small and a large item remain, fills each bin with one small item plus a residual fragment of one large item, and finishes with exact matching once S = C. Two invariants — total remaining item size equals total remaining bin load, and |S| ≤ |C| — carry through both algorithms (Lemmas 2.1, 2.2, 2.5, with Observations 2.3 and 2.4 guaranteeing availability of large items and exact matching). Critical design decisions: (a) restricting Phase 2 to at most two fragments per bin, justified by the structural result itself; (b) the |C| − |S| cap in Algorithm 1, well justified as the exact mechanism preserving Invariant 2; (c) the block-of-ℓ decomposition in the OPT = 1 test, justified via coprimality of ℓ and ℓ−1 (Observation 3.1). The trivial case ⌈W/B⌉ = 1 is handled separately. Key Results: All results are proven, not measured. Theorem 1.3: an exact algorithm for LBIF with B ≥ N runs in O(N) time and O(N) space (output as quadruple records with omitted interchangeable bin indices). Lemma 2.8: the two-phase greedy always achieves combinatorial load ≤ 2. Lemma 3.2 / Corollary 3.3: OPT = 1 holds if and only if four arithmetic conditions on the multiset {s_i}, ℓ, and B hold — itemwise size lower bounds, Σf_i ≤ Bℓ − W, a block-count inequality Σ⌊(s_i − f_i(ℓ−1))/(ℓ(ℓ−1))⌋·ℓ ≥ Bℓ − W − Σf_i, and the mod-ℓ condition (Bℓ − W − Σf_i) mod ℓ = 0. Corollary 1.4: combining the exact algorithm (B ≥ N) with Kobert et al.'s (B < N) yields an O(N log N)-time (OPT+1)-approximation for all B — the first strongly polynomial approximation for LBIF. No baselines, benchmarks, or error bars exist by design; the sole quantitative comparison is asymptotic running time against Kobert et al.'s O(N log N + B). Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION is not claimed (the problem is Kobert et al.'s); the contribution is a NEW METHOD — an exact O(N)-time algorithm for the B ≥ N regime — plus a NEW EMPIRICAL-FINDING-equivalent structural theorem (OPT ≤ 2 always suffices for B ≥ N) and the corollary strongly-polynomial approximation. The techniques themselves (greedy filling with invariants, divisibility arguments, Nagy-style residue counting) are elementary; the novelty lies in proving that this hardness problem collapses to linear time in the many-bins regime, which was not obvious given NP-hardness. Rigor & Reproducibility: Proofs are complete and self-contained: both invariants are established per algorithm, termination and validity are proven (Lemmas 2.6–2.8), and the OPT = 1 test is proven correct in both directions (Lemma 3.2), yielding a genuine characterization rather than a heuristic. Running-time bounds are tight by direct iteration counting (≤ 2N iterations total). There are no ablations, seeds, or significance tests because there are no experiments. No code or artifact is released; the paper argues the algorithms are simple enough for adoption in RAxML-NG and ExaBayes but does not report an implementation. No methodological red flags apply (no benchmark tuning, no evaluation data), though the paper's correctness rests entirely on the reviewer-checked proofs — the proofs as printed are short and I found no gaps, but the f_i-based arguments (e.g., minimality of f_i and the block-greedy sufficiency in Step 2) deserve independent verification, as the ⇐ direction of Lemma 3.2 relies on a somewhat compressed sufficiency argument for the block-filling step. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: THEORETICAL (constructive algorithms with proofs; no primary experimental claim). - Sound: Assumptions (integer sizes, B ≥ N, ⌈W/B⌉ > 1 handled separately) are explicit, and the proofs cover both correctness directions; the only soft spot is the compactness of the sufficiency argument in Step 2 of Algorithm 3. - General: The result holds for all B ≥ N instances of the exact problem definition; outside this regime nothing new is proven beyond the Corollary 1.4 combination, and the site-repeats (data-dependent load) variant is explicitly out of scope. - Tight: Not applicable in the bound sense; the O(N) running time is arguably optimal since input reading takes Ω(N), and the OPT ≤ 2 guarantee is tight in the sense that OPT = 1 instances are exactly characterized rather than assumed. - Implementable: Fully constructive — the three algorithms are given in pseudocode using only arithmetic and multiset updates, so a practitioner could implement them in a day; no reference implementation ships, and no follow-up operationalization is reported. The work delivers algorithms on paper only: no library, CLI, dataset, or trained model is released. Strengths: - A clean, surprising structural theorem: for B ≥ N the NP-hard problem always has an optimum with at most two fragments per bin, which the authors correctly identify as the hinge that makes linear-time exactness possible. - The OPT = 1 characterization (Corollary 3.3) is a genuine, checkable set of four arithmetic conditions — more useful than an existence statement, since it doubles as an implementable test. - The combined Corollary 1.4 closes a real asymptotic weakness of an algorithm embedded in production phylogenetics software: it removes the dependence on B, making the (OPT+1)-approximation strongly polynomial for the first time. - Execution quality: the invariant-based analysis is disciplined, and each design decision (the |C| − |S| cap, block extraction) is tied to a specific lemma rather than asserted. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors implicitly scope the result to B ≥ N and to the fixed-load formulation; they note the site-repeats variant (where workload depends on data, not just site counts) is a different problem not addressed here, and that related splittable-scheduling and fragmented-bin-packing literatures do not apply because the objective fixes every bin's load. They do not include a dedicated limitations section; the concluding remarks pitch the result as a theory contribution and teaching material rather than claiming deployment. This is honest scoping rather than minimization, though the practical-adoption claim (drop-in for RAxML-NG/ExaBayes) is made without implementation evidence. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No implementation or microbenchmark accompanies the O(N) claim; for realistic N (number of partitions is typically small — tens to thousands), the O(B) term in the old algorithm may be dominated by other overheads, so the practical benefit over Kobert et al. is asserted, not demonstrated. - The output representation omits explicit bin indices for batch records (j = ⊥); expanding these records into per-bin assignments costs O(B), which slightly qualifies the O(N)-space/output claim — the authors state this honestly, but the end-to-end cost of materializing an assignment is O(B) regardless. - The paper does not discuss whether the exact solution's combinatorial load of 2 (versus the previous OPT+1) translates into measurable runtime or memory improvements in phylogenetic likelihood computation; the motivating HPC benefit remains untested. - Numerical magnitude of item sizes s_i and W is unaddressed: the arithmetic is O(1) per operation only in the word-RAM sense; sizes can be as large as W, and modular/floor operations on multi-word integers could matter — not discussed. - No lower-bound argument for why O(N) cannot be beaten in some other model, and no exploration of whether the OPT ≤ 2 structure extends to B < N or to the site-repeats variant — natural open directions left unexamined. Bottom Line: A short, cleanly proved theory result that a scheduling-theory reader will appreciate for turning a production-relevant NP-hard problem into a linear-time exact algorithm in the many-bins regime, but practitioners should treat the HPC payoff as unverified until someone actually ships the implementation — and the proof-writing is elementary enough that the paper doubles as good coursework, exactly as the authors suggest.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a two-phase LLM-driven pipeline that extracts a machine-readable execution recipe (run command, setup steps, required data/checkpoints, produced metric) from a repository's documentation, rebuilds the environment, runs the experiment, and compares the obtained metric to the paper's claimed value — plus a taxonomy of why automatic result-level reproduction fails. - Why it's important: Reproducibility studies in ML overwhelmingly measure proxies (artifact existence, environment builds); nobody has measured at corpus scale whether code actually regenerates the published number, and knowing which failure blocks reproduction tells authors and venues what to fix cheaply. - How it does it: It treats the "how to run it" procedure as extracted metadata — formalized as rdip:ExecutionRecipe, a prov:Plan-style extension to the RDIP provenance profile — so the same automated extraction applies to any unseen paper, with a streaming execution phase that discards artifacts after comparison. - The good: The positive-control ablation is genuinely diagnostic: on three known-reproducible artifacts, autonomous extraction reproduces 0/3 but the identical execution-and-comparison machinery with hand-written gold recipes reproduces 2/3, cleanly isolating recipe extraction (not execution) as the bottleneck. - The missing: The headline 0-of-17 result rests on a single open-weight 24B extractor, a 17-repository attempted set, and a 3-artifact control set; no multi-model comparison of recipe extraction is run, so the claim that extraction (not the specific model) is the bottleneck is only indirectly supported. - Read it or not: Worth reading for reproducibility researchers and artifact-evaluation infrastructure builders — it converts a vague community complaint into a measured, machine-classified failure distribution — but skippable for practitioners who mainly need the actionable artifact-documentation checklist.

Problem & Motivation: ML researchers, reviewers, and artifact-evaluation committees currently cannot tell whether a published repository reproduces its paper's headline number without manual, one-at-a-time replication effort (as at ReScience C). Prior work stops one step short: checklists and badging verify reporting, and the companion SRAF study reconstructs environments for 96 repositories and finds only ~26 build — but a repository that installs cleanly is not shown to reproduce its numbers. The paper closes the gap between "does it build" and "does it produce the claimed metric," and does so without hand-writing run commands per repository, which would neither scale nor generalize. Key Idea: Treat the reproduction procedure itself as extracted metadata rather than human-supplied input: an LLM reads the repository documentation and emits a structured rdip:ExecutionRecipe (runCommand, ordered setupStep, requiresDataset, requiresCheckpoint, producesMetric, entryPoint, recipeConfidence), which is lifted into the study's RDIP provenance graph so the run procedure becomes queryable, SHACL-validatable, and comparable against the claimed EvaluationResult. A second key methodological move is the positive-control design: three known-reproducible artifacts run under both extracted and gold recipes, separating "the engine can't do anything" from "the artifacts don't reproduce." Methodology: The pipeline has two phases competing for one 48 GB GPU. Phase 1: Mistral-Small-24B (served locally, open-weight, reproducible) reads repository documentation and emits a JSON recipe; a conservative prompt prefers evaluation-over-training commands, converts URLs to explicit download steps, selects the paper-matching configuration in multi-method toolboxes, and lowers recipeConfidence rather than inventing placeholder values; a deterministic mapper converts JSON to RDIP triples (recipe as prov:Plan, reproductions as a second prov:Activity following the same plan). Phase 2: per repository, clone, isolated virtual environment, run setup+command as a single shell script (so working-directory/env changes persist), parse the metric from the log, compare to the extracted claim within 5% relative or 0.01 absolute tolerance (a uniform, auditable band chosen deliberately over per-metric thresholds), record the outcome, and delete all artifacts (streaming, resumable — no disk accumulation). Failure classification is automatic from run logs into machine-detectable reasons. Three critical design decisions: (1) recipe-as-metadata for generality — well justified by the positive-control argument; (2) uniform tolerance — defensible, explicitly argued against metric-tuned thresholds; (3) single open-weight extractor — flagged by the authors themselves as a threat, with indirect (entity-F1) evidence from SRAF that extraction difficulty is model-family-invariant. Key Results: On the 96-repository corpus: 26 build, 17 are attempted (9 pre-skipped as not reproducible by construction or mismatched repos), 13 yield an extracted recipe, and 0 of 17 reproduce their headline number automatically. Recipe quality is the crux: 13 run commands were extracted but only 6 were concrete (7 contained unresolved placeholders, 4 repositories had no command at all); checkpoints were identified for only 2 of 17. Failure taxonomy (26 buildable repos): 18 documentation/artifact gaps (7 placeholder commands, 4 no command, 3 paper-repo mismatch, 1 dead checkpoint link, 1 gated dataset, 1 model too large for one GPU at 176B, 1 no numeric result), 4 not-reproducible-by-construction metrics, 4 harness-side failures. The self-reported recipeConfidence was a usable filter: all 6 concrete recipes rated high; all 9 low-confidence ones were non-runnable, with only 2 placeholders over-rated. Positive controls: gold recipes reproduce 2/3 (CIFAR-10 obtained 94.25 vs. claimed 94.37; SST-2 93.23 vs. 92.70); the third fails on environment rot (a deprecated pytorch_lightning API). Autonomous recipes reproduce 0/3, failing exactly in the documentation-gap modes the taxonomy names. Baseline context: prior SRAF results are the only comparison point — no independent system is compared against, but no comparable system exists for this task. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (result-level automatic reproduction with recipe-as-extracted-metadata), NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the 0/17 funnel and the artifact-gap-dominated failure distribution), and a modest NEW FORMULATION (rdip:ExecutionRecipe as a prov:Plan extension to an existing provenance profile). The genuinely novel part is framing execution procedure as extraction target and pairing the null result with a positive-control ablation that localizes the bottleneck. The components — LLM extraction, virtualenv execution, log parsing, provenance graphs — are individually standard; the combination and the measurement target are not. This is a workshop poster, and the evaluation scale reflects that. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strengths: the extraction-vs-execution ablation is exactly the control a skeptical reviewer would demand and is absent from most null-result papers; failure classification is machine-generated from logs rather than human-assigned; the harness-side failure family is explicitly quarantined as a threat to validity, and two studies were reclassified after a harness fix; code, prompts, gold recipes, control set, per-study logs, and the corpus are all released (https://github.com/open-rdip/rdip-sraf-repro, Zenodo doi:10.5281/zenodo.19919042); claimed numbers come from the same imperfect extraction pipeline, and the authors state this precisely and correctly note it cannot explain the 0/17 result since no comparison was ever reached. Weaknesses: no error bars or seeds (partly moot with a deterministic funnel), no multi-model extraction comparison (single Mistral-Small-24B; the cross-model evidence cited is entity-F1 from the companion SRAF paper, not recipe extraction), tiny sample sizes (17 attempted, 3 controls), and no external baseline system — though none exists. The result is a preprint/poster at IJCKG 2026 workshops, not peer-reviewed archival publication at the level of a main-conference paper. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a measurement study with a built, run pipeline). Practical: Yes — single 48 GB GPU, local open-weight model, no proprietary services; controls ran on one GPU. Efficient: Reasonable — streaming architecture caps disk usage, extraction is one pass with a 24B model, though the two-phase GPU handoff serializes work. Effective: As a measurement instrument, yes — the gold-recipe controls (2/3 reproduced) prove the execution machinery works; as an autonomous reproducer, deliberately and informatively no (0/17). Scalable: Claimed via streaming design but not tested — the corpus is 96 repositories; behavior at 10×–100× (more heterogeneous artifacts, longer runs, training-from-scratch papers) is untested. Delivers a software artifact: open-source extractor, pipeline, and failure classifier, plus an archived corpus and per-study provenance graphs. Strengths: (1) The positive-control ablation is the paper's intellectual centerpiece — it converts an otherwise unfalsifiable null result into a localized, falsifiable claim about where the bottleneck sits, and the 2/3 gold-recipe success (94.25/94.37, 93.23/92.70) credibly validates the execution half. (2) The failure taxonomy is machine-generated from logs, so it scales and is auditable, and its mass in the documentation/artifact family yields a constructive, actionable conclusion (most failures are cheap author-side fixes, not compute limits). (3) The PROV-O grounding of the recipe (prov:Plan with qualifiedAssociation/hadPlan, ordered setupStep values as plans to encode load-bearing ordering) is clean ontology engineering that lets original and reproduction share one provenance record. (4) Unusually careful threat analysis — the authors explicitly prove claim-extraction error cannot explain their headline result and separate harness failures from artifact failures. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly rather than minimizing them: (i) claimed values are extracted, so reproduction verdicts are against extracted claims — though they show no corpus comparison ever occurred; (ii) some failures were harness-side and are quarantined as a validity threat; (iii) the attempted set (17) and control set (3) are small and results are not population estimates; (iv) single-extractor dependence, with indirect cross-model evidence from SRAF (entity-F1 of 0.230–0.273 across three models) offered as suggestive but explicitly labeled non-conclusive. They also note environment rot as a time-dependent confound and pre-skipping of non-reproducible-by-construction metrics. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The central claim — "extraction is the bottleneck" — rests on one 24B model; a frontier hosted model or a tool-using agent (which the authors themselves cite, e.g., SWE-agent) might extract runnable recipes where Mistral-Small fails, so 0/3 autonomous could be a model-capacity result, not a task-difficulty result; the SRAF entity-F1 evidence is a different task. (2) The gold recipes were hand-written by the same authors who designed the extractor and prompts — experimenter familiarity could make gold recipes succeed where an independent reproducer's recipes would not. (3) The three positive controls are trivially reproducible artifacts (small CIFAR-10 classifiers, a BERT SST-2 model) with auto-downloading data; the execution half is validated only on the easy end of the difficulty spectrum, so "the execution machinery is sound" may not transfer to larger, multi-stage experiments. (4) No inspection of whether the paper's headline metric always corresponds to what a repository's evaluation command reports (metric selection mismatch could silently inflate the placeholder/no-command counts). (5) The 5%/0.01 uniform tolerance is asserted as auditable but never validated against a reproduction where the obtained value sits near the boundary. Bottom Line: A rigorous, unusually honest measurement study that converts the reproducibility community's vaguest complaint into a concrete, machine-classified failure map and correctly identifies LLM-based recipe extraction as the open research problem — small in scale and single-model, but the best available instrument of its kind and essential reading for anyone building artifact-evaluation or automated-reproduction infrastructure.

Energy-Efficient Reinforcement Learning for Large Language Models

R Sharma, N Vegesna, Y Zhang · arxiv.org · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR:** - What it does: This paper introduces EE-RL, an online GPU frequency controller that selects separate clock frequencies for the generation and training phases of LLM RL post-training (GRPO) while the workload runs, and reports 4.1–16.9% whole-allocation GPU energy savings per valid training token at under 2% throughput cost. - Why it's important: RL post-training is a large and growing energy cost — the paper cites Olmo 3 32B reasoning post-training using 17× more datacenter energy than its instruction-tuned sibling — so clock-level savings without extending GPU allocation time translate directly into electricity cost and infrastructure headroom. - How it does it: The controller runs short candidate-frequency trials against a regression-predicted governor reference at matched token workload (normalizing for response-length drift), keeps the most energy-efficient setting retaining ≥98% of governor throughput, and re-checks the choice as workloads change — with distinct search protocols for synchronous, drained-asynchronous, and in-flight-asynchronous execution. - The good: The evaluation is unusually honest and complete for a systems-energy paper: matched seeds, all-in energy accounting (including waiting GPUs and search overheads), 360 headroom comparisons across two GPUs and four execution modes, plus a workload-normalized sensitivity analysis in Appendix E. - The missing: Controller evaluation uses a single matched seed per configuration, so the learning-quality claim (validation-accuracy deltas of −0.14 to +0.90 pp) and the run-level throughput bound rest on one run each, which the authors admit cannot establish equivalence. - Read it or not: Worth reading for systems engineers running large-scale RL post-training on H100/GB200-class fleets — this is the first careful treatment of phase-aware DVFS in the coupled generation/training setting — but ML researchers focused on algorithmic contributions can skip it.

Problem & Motivation: RL post-training of LLMs alternates between autoregressive rollout generation (largely memory-bandwidth-bound) and batched policy training (more compute-bound), plus log-probability scoring and weight refit. The default GPU governor runs all phases near peak clock (1980 MHz on H100, 2062 MHz on GB200), so memory-bound work and inter-pool waiting burn power without throughput gain. Operators of RL training infrastructure pay for this energy across every allocated GPU, active or idle, and offline frequency tuning is impractical because the optimal setting shifts with model, batch size, allocation, and response-length distribution. The paper closes the gap that prior RL systems work (HybridFlow, AReaL, ReaL) optimizes placement and scheduling but not frequency, while prior energy-aware serving/training work (Zeus, Perseus, DynamoLLM) does not handle the coupled, variable-workload stages of RL post-training. Key Idea: Compare any candidate frequency setting against a counterfactual prediction of the governor on the same token workload — using a regression on log-transformed token counts (generated tokens, valid training tokens, longest response) fitted only on governor observations — so that response-length drift is not confounded with the frequency effect, and measure energy over the entire GPU allocation (including waiting pools) per valid training token rather than per update. This equal-work, whole-allocation accounting is what makes short online trials statistically meaningful in a workload that changes every update. Methodology: The pipeline is: (1) a characterization phase sweeps fixed generation/training frequency pairs across workloads, allocations, and execution modes (colocated synchronous, disaggregated synchronous, asynchronous with drained or in-flight weight updates) to quantify headroom; (2) an online controller calibrates for 15–45 governor updates, fits the per-phase governor-time predictor (log-time ~ log(1+token counts)), then interleaves 3–12-update candidate trials with governor observations; (3) a candidate passes if it retains ≥98% of predicted throughput and lowers energy per valid training token, is confirmed on fresh observations, and is locked with a 20-update/10-update monitoring window (sync/drained) or continued 1:2 governor-to-candidate blocks (in-flight). The objective is minimizing e = E/N = P/q subject to a throughput-loss budget. Critical design decisions: (a) using valid training tokens rather than updates as the unit of work — well justified, since response lengths vary; (b) fitting the reference only on governor data so candidates cannot contaminate their own baseline — well justified; (c) mode-specific search (sequential pool search for async, waiting-pool idle dropping at 345 MHz) — justified by arrival-order analysis, though the combined active-plus-idle savings are not decomposed. In-flight trials are treated as blocked experiments because responses can span a clock change, with block length set from calibration noise against a 2% standard-error target. Key Results: Fixed-frequency sweeps (208 H100 and 85 GB200 comparisons, 4 matched seeds each, updates 5–25) show colocated synchronous savings of 5.08–11.53% with <2% throughput loss; disaggregated synchronous savings up to 28.23% (Qwen, 8/32 H100, 1500/1200 MHz) at −0.36% throughput; asynchronous drained/in-flight savings up to 21.85%/21.69% with <2% throughput change. The online controller, including all search and adaptation costs, saves 7.00–16.94% energy per valid token across eight configurations on H100 (Qwen3-30B-A3B and Mistral-NeMo 12B), all under 2% full-interval throughput loss; the largest is 16.94% for disaggregated synchronous Qwen (22.44% after locking). Baselines are the native governor on matched seed/workload/topology — a fair but self-referential baseline (no external DVFS controller is compared). Surprising findings: in all four asynchronous runs the controller ends up slowing only training, never generation; and after-lock savings exceed full-interval savings (e.g., 22.4% vs 16.9%), because trial overheads are amortized. Appendix E's work-normalization shifts savings by <2 points but reveals two Mistral runs' throughput "gains" were workload artifacts, and drained Qwen's true loss is 2.19%, slightly over the 2% budget. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (an online per-phase frequency controller for RL post-training) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (quantified phase-dependent headroom on H100/GB200, and the finding that training is the useful control target under overlap). The genuinely novel elements are the equal-work governor-prediction comparison under variable token workloads and whole-allocation energy accounting in the RL setting; the underlying mechanisms (DVFS, P∝V²f, roofline reasoning, blocked online experiments) are standard combinations of known ideas applied to a new, harder setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: Headroom sweeps use 4 matched seeds per row with a defined geometric-mean ratio estimator (Appendix A); controller results use one matched seed per configuration, supplemented by a pooled-governor work-normalized sensitivity analysis — the authors flag this limitation themselves. The token-work predictor is ablated: it cuts median throughput-prediction error from 1.57%→0.59% (Qwen/32 H100) and 5.28%→0.31% (Nemotron/64 H100), and adding longest-response reduces RMS time error from 0.085→0.044 on Mistral. No code release is mentioned. No component ablation of the controller (prediction vs. search vs. confirmation vs. feedback) exists — the authors admit this. GB200 measurements carry a stated run-to-run-variation caveat. Training-reward deltas are correctly framed as diagnostics, not accuracy evidence. No Goodhart-style contamination of the reference is possible (governor-only fits), which is methodologically clean, but the learned-quality equivalence claim rests on n=1 seeds and pre-lock trial-level acceptance does not bound run-level throughput (one config exceeds the 2% budget after normalization). Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS — a controller evaluated on real H100 and GB200 clusters at 16–64 GPUs and 30B–49B models. - Practical: Yes — runs on commercially available H100/GB200 hardware using NVML energy counters, no instrumentation beyond frequency control. - Efficient: Controller overhead is quantified (search costs reduce savings from ~20–22% post-lock to 6.5–16.9% full-interval; in-flight calibration costs 45 updates), and in-flight runs spend roughly a third of after-lock time on governor blocks. - Effective: Evidence shows real whole-allocation energy reduction at bounded throughput cost on the tested GRPO workloads; learning-quality equivalence is only proxied (single-seed validation deltas, training-reward diagnostics). - Scalable: Not tested beyond 64 GPUs or 25–560 update horizons; the authors argue longer production runs would amortize search better, but persistent in-flight governor blocks cap recoverable savings — this is a claim, not a measurement. The work delivers a described controller, not a released artifact: no library, code, or tool is stated as publicly available. Strengths: - The equal-work comparison methodology (governor-fitted token-count regression with longest-response feature, validated with a 9-run forward-prediction study) solves the real confound in online energy control — workload drift of 2–3% is the same magnitude as the effect being measured — and this is empirically verified rather than assumed. - Comprehensive, honest energy accounting: waiting GPUs, idle dropping, clock-transition costs, and search overheads are all included, and the paper explicitly reports that naive post-lock numbers would overstate savings (22.4% vs 16.9%). - The empirical finding that asynchronous RL makes training the sole useful control target (generation slack absorbs slowdown) is a non-obvious, actionable insight for anyone tuning these systems. - Execution-mode-aware controller design (rendezvous-based drained search vs. blocked in-flight experiments) shows genuine engagement with the scheduling semantics rather than a one-size-fits-all knob. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors directly acknowledge: GRPO-only evaluation (PPO's value model would add stages); one matched seed per controller configuration with no component ablations; single-seed learning-quality comparisons that cannot establish accuracy equivalence; workload/allocation dependence requiring fresh search on new deployments; confounded active-vs-idle savings in drained mode; and the trial-level vs run-level throughput-budget gap, with a proposed accumulated-budget controller as future work. This is unusually forthright limitation disclosure — a strong credibility signal. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the acknowledged points: (1) no comparison against any alternative energy-saving baseline (e.g., a static power cap via nvidia-smi, Zeus-style tuning, or a trivially scheduled low-clock policy), so the controller's adaptivity premium over a well-chosen static pair is only implied by the workload-dependence argument, not measured; (2) learning quality is evaluated only on final validation accuracy over ≤560 updates — whether persistent asynchronous timing changes (policy age 2, clock-induced arrival shifts) affect late-stage convergence on longer horizons is unexamined; (3) GB200 results are marred by acknowledged run-to-run variation but still headline the abstract's 28.2% figure, which comes from a single H100 disaggregated row; (4) CPU/network/cooling energy is excluded, so whole-datacenter savings at the claimed 10–30% GPU savings are smaller in proportion; (5) the 2% throughput allowance is arbitrary — no Pareto sweep of allowance vs savings is reported; (6) evaluation covers only 25–560 updates on ≤49B models, whereas the motivating Olmo-3 scale and production horizons of thousands of updates are extrapolated. Bottom Line: For teams operating RL post-training clusters on H100/GB200 hardware, this is the best-documented treatment of phase-aware GPU frequency control available and its whole-allocation, equal-work accounting methodology is worth adopting wholesale; for anyone else, the core insight (memory-bound RL phases have large DVFS headroom, and training is the target under async overlap) can be absorbed from the summary alone while awaiting a released implementation and multi-seed validation.

Jiajun Chen, Shicheng Fang, Jiahao Lu, Yuxin Wang, Xipeng Qiu · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 12 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces GTAGym, a web-server environment that reconstructs 150 tasks from GTA V main-story missions (GTAVBench, with an instruction-in-screenshot GTAVBench-AGI branch), verifies outcomes automatically from engine states, and generates parameterized task batches with reward signals for reinforcement learning. - Why it's important: AAA open-world games are an attractive sim-to-real testbed for vision-language agents, but task outcomes there have historically required human annotation, which blocks both scalable evaluation and RL training on such tasks. - How it does it: Missions are manually decomposed into subtasks with executable success/failure predicates over a Babylon.js reconstruction of GTA V (built on GTA_SZ), and template-based sampling of parameters (route length, turn count, actor speed, pursuer count) yields procedurally varied training instances with sparse rewards. - The good: The evaluation is credible and diagnostic — six frontier models plus a 3-participant human baseline (best model 70.9% vs human 89.8%), with a manual first-error taxonomy across 900 trajectories showing Calibration and Regulation failures dominate at 63.2%, and a timing ablation showing accuracy drops 22.3 points when inference pauses are removed. - The missing: The RL result is thin — a single model trained on only 50 generated on-foot tasks (the easiest category), evaluated against benchmark tasks the authors generated themselves, with the native GTA V transfer (15%→23%) measured on just 100 tasks with human video review and no significance testing. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or benchmark interactive VLM/game agents and need verifiable AAA-style tasks or a picture of where current models fail at closed-loop control; skip it if you want a strong RL method — the training contribution is a small, standard GRPO+LoRA run.

Problem & Motivation: Researchers building vision-language agents for commercial 3D games face a verification problem: whether an agent completed a mission-derived task is hard to check automatically, unlike sandbox games (Minecraft) where engine state yields programmatic rewards. Prior work splits into three camps — verifiable sandbox tasks (MineDojo, GameWorld), agents acting in commercial games with human/VLM judging (Cradle, Lumine, SIMA, GameVerse), and offline gameplay benchmarks (GameHorizon-Bench, VideoGameBench) — and no prior environment combines real-AAA mission objectives, automatic state-based scoring, web-based parallel execution, and RL instance generation. The intended users are agent researchers who currently must pay humans or a VLM judge to score game trajectories, and RL practitioners who lack reward sources outside Minecraft-style sandboxes. Key Idea: The core move is reconstruction-for-verification: rather than instrumenting the actual GTA V engine, the authors manually decompose 75 main-story missions into subtask specifications (goal, interaction order, completion constraints, NPC behaviors) and re-implement them in an open Babylon.js city where every subtask gets an executable success/failure predicate over engine state — bringing MineDojo-style programmatic task verification to AAA-mission-derived gameplay, and reusing the same template as both an evaluation instance and a parameter-sampled RL generator. Methodology: The pipeline has four stages. (1) Task extraction: humans decompose 75 GTA V missions into subtasks from walkthrough videos, producing 103 online 3D tasks across nine categories (road/on-foot/aquatic/vertical/aerial/indoor navigation; following/interception/evasion) plus 47 image-based shooting/sniping tasks (150 total). (2) Scenario reconstruction: the 3D environment is built in Babylon.js on the GTA_SZ asset base; navigation paths are traced from source minimaps and matched to city geometry by turn count; dynamic-interaction tasks use scripted NPC controllers (pursuer scanning sectors of 12 m radius/90° angle, collision-induced slowdown). (3) Evaluation: a closed-loop screenshot→JSON keyboard/mouse action loop (keys with hold durations ≤1 s, relative mouse displacement) served over the web with parallel execution; the GTAVBench-AGI branch hides the instruction in the first screenshot and delegates context management to the Codex harness with automatic history compression. Scoring is binary from engine-state predicates, micro-averaged over 150 tasks. (4) RL generation: templates expose sampling parameters θ (start/destination positions, heading, route length, turn count, movement mode, actor speed, pursuer count) drawn within user bounds subject to feasibility checks, Eq. (1); episodes give sparse terminal rewards. The RL experiment trains Qwen3.8-27B with GRPO and rank-32 LoRA on Q/V projections (lr 1e-6, 8 rollouts × 4 tasks per update, eight H200 GPUs) using reward R = S + 0.3(1−S)·P − 0.1·1{N>100}, where P is clipped A*-computed traversable-distance reduction. Design decisions worth noting: reconstruction in Babylon.js rather than the real engine (justified by open access and state access, but never validated for visual fidelity against the real game); a 1 s default action cap with inference-time pausing (ablated in Section 5.4); and distance-progress shaping applied only to failed rollouts (reasonable, not ablated). Key Results: On GTAVBench-AGI with the Codex harness, GPT-6-Astra reaches 70.9%±4.4 overall versus 89.8%±1.4 for three human players; GPT-6.1-Sol gets 66.9%, and the non-OpenAI models cluster at 33–42% (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash 38.2%, GLM-5.3-Flash 41.8%, Kimi-K3 33.1%, Qwen3.8-27B 34.2%). The AGI protocol (screenshot-only instructions + Codex harness) improves all six models by 0.9–10.0 points over the JSON protocol. Aerial navigation is 0% for all models (human 45.8%); interception ≤41% and evasion ≤25% for every model. Manual error analysis over 900 trajectories (565 with a categorized first error) attributes 63.2% of first errors to Calibration or Regulation rather than Perception or Planning; GPT models recover from first errors within ten decisions at 65.7%/49.3% versus 21.6–25.6% for others. The timing ablation (GPT-6.1-Sol, 103 3D tasks) shows 66.3% at a 0.5 s action cap vs 62.1% at 1 s vs 60.5% at 2 s, and a fall to 39.8% when the simulation runs during inference — direct evidence that inference latency, not just capability, gates dynamic tasks. RL: on-foot accuracy rises 54.2%→72.9% (mean over three seeds), overall 34.2%→38.9%, OOD categories 31.8%→34.8% (vertical 46.7%→73.3%, aquatic 57.6%→69.7%), but road driving stays at 3.3%, aerial/interception at 0%, and shooting drops 73.6%→68.1%; on 100 native GTA V tasks, success rises 15%→23%. Baselines are current frontier models, though the comparison set is skewed toward two OpenAI models. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL with a NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING component (latency/pause sensitivity of dynamic-control tasks). The genuinely novel element is engine-state-verified task instances reconstructed from commercial AAA missions, coupled with a parameterized generator that turns the same templates into RL reward sources — the Table 1 feature matrix is fair in showing no single prior system has this combination. The algorithms (GRPO+LoRA, template-based procedural generation à la Procgen, screenshot-action GUI-agent protocols à la OSWorld) are all standard; the contribution is competent integration into a new setting, not a new method. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: action-duration caps, unpaused evaluation, reasoning-effort comparison, and harness (JSON vs Codex) trade-offs, plus a detailed manual failure-mode taxonomy with published annotation criteria (Appendix C). Each model configuration is run with three seeds, and Table 2 reports population standard deviations; the RL result reports means over three seeds. Code (github.com/ljbro/GTAGym) and the benchmark (huggingface.co/datasets/OpenMOSS-Team/GTAVBench) are public. Methodological concerns: the human baseline is only three participants, one attempt each; category sizes are small (vertical n=5, indoor n=8, following n=6), so per-cell numbers carry wide uncertainty despite the reported σ; the first-error taxonomy and recovery annotations are manual and by the authors, with no inter-annotator agreement reported; and the native GTA V transfer success is judged by human video review without a second annotator. The RL training instances are generated by the authors' own generator to match benchmark distributions — a self-referential setup, though spatial separation from benchmark routes is enforced and no benchmark tasks are trained on. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a built environment, evaluated by deployment, with an embedded EMPIRICAL evaluation study). Practical: Runs as a web service with a shared screenshot-action interface; RL training needed eight H200s, but evaluation runs against API models on ordinary hardware. Efficient: The unpaused result (accuracy 39.8%, 448 s of game time on 103 tasks) shows the inference-action cycle is the cost bottleneck; input-token costs balloon from 4.32M to 11.20M per task when the action cap halves. Effective: The engine-state verifiers demonstrably work (humans score 89.8% with correct task completion semantics), but the evidence that generated RL environments build general game skills extends only to on-foot navigation and modest OOD gains. Scalable: Only 50 training instances and one task template were used for RL; scaling generation to the full 9-category template set is claimed by design but untested. Deliverable: a real software artifact — open-source environment, 150-task benchmark dataset, prompts, and an RL recipe — not just a paper. Strengths: (1) The engine-state evaluator for mission-derived AAA tasks is a real solve for a genuine bottleneck — it removes human/VLM outcome judging, which prior commercial-game benchmarks (GameVerse, Lumine) require. (2) The latency ablation is a substantive, non-obvious empirical finding: removing inference-time pausing costs 22.3 points and zeroes out all dynamic-interaction categories, cleanly separating "can't control" from "too slow to control." (3) The manual error taxonomy across 900 trajectories (Calibration+Regulation = 63.2% of first errors; recovery rates per model) is more diagnostic than typical leaderboard reporting and localizes the failure to closed-loop control rather than perception. (4) Honest negative results are reported: 0% aerial navigation for every model, RL gains that are category-uneven, and a shooting regression after RL. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors directly confront persistent model weaknesses (aerial control, evasion, interception), show that models cannot choose appropriate action durations even when allowed longer holds (66.6% of actions exceed 1 s at a 2 s cap), and document context-compression pathologies (Kimi-K3 dropping goals, GLM carrying reversed minimap markers). They note the turnaround-based protocol with paused simulation diverges from real-time play and quantify exactly how. There is no dedicated limitations section, but the analysis sections confront failures head-on rather than minimizing them — a credibility positive. The dependence on the GTA_SZ reconstruction is acknowledged in the acknowledgements but its fidelity implications are not discussed. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The 3D environment is a Babylon.js reconstruction, not GTA V — no evidence is offered that its visuals, physics, or control dynamics resemble the commercial game, yet the native-GTA-V transfer result (15%→23%) implicitly assumes the reconstruction is a useful proxy; the 8-point gap between benchmark and native performance is consistent with a sim-to-real gap the paper never analyzes. (2) The RL experiment trains on the easiest category only, on 50 instances from the authors' own generator, with a single model and no comparison to simpler alternatives (e.g., supervised fine-tuning on successful trajectories, or prompting improvements), so the claim that the generator "supports RL" rests on one small run. (3) Manual error annotation without inter-annotator agreement or blind labeling risks bias toward the paper's taxonomy. (4) No significance testing anywhere — with n=5 vertical tasks and three participants, several per-cell comparisons (e.g., GLM's ±28.3 on vertical) are statistically fragile. (5) The evaluated model list, while current, includes two OpenAI models and names vendor-reported model versions from API documentation; capability differences (e.g., Astra's interception 41% vs others' 0%) are not cross-checked on any second benchmark. (6) Task realism is unvalidated: reconstructed routes are matched by turn count on available geometry, and simplified mechanics (fixed scanning sectors, collision slowdown) may make evasion/interception systematically different from the source missions. Bottom Line: Practitioners building interactive game or GUI agents gain a genuinely useful, open artifact — verifiable AAA-derived tasks plus a parallel web harness — and a sharp picture of closed-loop control as the frontier models' bottleneck, but the RL component is a proof-of-concept sketch, and anyone needing fidelity to the real GTA V engine or a stronger training recipe should treat this as infrastructure to build on rather than a result to adopt.

MotionGraphicsBench: Evaluating Motion Graphics Generation with Programmatic Verification (8 ▲ )

Jiaju Ma, Ashvini Kumar Jindal, Chuhua Wang, Sumithra Bhakthavatsalam · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 10 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces MotionGraphicsBench, a 100-instance benchmark of expert-curated SVG motion-editing tasks, each paired with a prompt-specific deterministic Python verification program that grades whether a generated animation satisfies every requested spatial, appearance, and temporal requirement. - Why it's important: Evaluating LLM-generated motion graphics is currently done either by comparing against a single reference animation (which penalizes valid alternatives) or by VLM judges (which are stochastic and uninterpretable); Problem & Motivation LLMs can now animate a static vector graphic from a natural-language request, but nobody can reliably grade the result. A single motion request combines several spatio-temporal conditions ('rotate both blades opposite directions around the center screw, pause, then return'), and because humans describe animation through relative spatial and temporal relationships rather than exact keyframes (the paper cites Talmy; Tversky & Lee), many different animations validly satisfy one prompt. Existing evaluation has two failure modes: reference-similarity metrics (as in LottieGPT/OmniLottie-style benchmarks) penalize valid deviations from one target trajectory, and VLM judges are stochastic and uninspectable at the level of individual prompt requirements. The people with this problem are researchers and practitioners building text-to-animation and agentic design tools (the paper comes out of Figma, a design-tool vendor, with Stanford). The gap closed is the absence of a deterministic, per-requirement, human-validated evaluator for motion edits grounded in real-world designs rather than synthetic templates — the closest prior system, MoVer, maps prompts to first-order spatio-temporal predicates but was evaluated only on 5,600 template-generated synthetic prompts. Key Idea Treat evaluation as per-instance program synthesis, not metric design: because each motion-edit prompt imposes different requirements, pair every benchmark instance with its own small deterministic verification program, and build that program automatically by a writer agent that must classify a set of human-labeled 'approved' and 'rejected' example animations correctly, while an independent synthesizer agent that cannot see the candidate program generates adversarial positive/negative test animations to expose checks that are too permissive or too strict. This decouples 'did the animation satisfy the requested relationships' from 'does it match one reference trajectory,' and the check-level reports make failures attributable to specific prompt clauses rather than a single opaque score. Methodology The pipeline has three stages. (1) Instance construction: 100 source animations are selected from LottieAnimation-660K by a complexity score C = P(T) + 0.25·P(O) + P(K) over animated property types, objects, and keyframes, with 1,000 median-complexity candidates manually reviewed; a geometry-completion step recovers hidden layer geometry so the input static SVG contains every element the requested edit needs; an LLM (GPT-5.6 Sol) drafts the motion edit prompt from the SVG and source Lottie, and a human reviewer approves/edits/revises it. (2) Verification-program construction: a writer agent implements each prompt's requirements as Python checks over an animation matrix (per-frame SVG geometry, transforms, visibility, styles keyed by document path, rendered via Chromium from the open-source MoVer rendering engine); a test-case synthesizer creates up to 20 deterministic transformed test animations per instance, adapting the positive/negative mix to label imbalance, with a one-round challenge protocol; every candidate program must pass all positive examples (source Lottie + human approvals) and fail all negatives, and frozen programs are then evaluated on a disjoint held-out set. (3) Model evaluation: 47 configurations from 32 LLMs across 12 providers generate GSAP JavaScript animations for all 100 instances (one attempt per instance for most configurations, 32 attempts for a 15-model cohort, 51,200 total attempts); pass@1 is the unweighted mean of per-instance success fractions, and pass@k uses the standard unbiased estimator. Success requires every check to pass with no execution error. Critical design decisions: (a) formulating the task as editing an existing complete SVG (isolating motion from graphic generation) — well justified as a designer workflow and for isolating the measured capability; (b) synthesizer blindness to the candidate program — well justified as preventing test-case gaming, though synthesized labels are model claims, not human judgments; (c) freezing programs before evaluation — sound, but the human-labeled construction data (25 of 29 generation configurations) overlaps the models later scored, which the authors acknowledge only for the Table 5 correlation, calling it descriptive. Key Results On the 180-animation held-out set (90 approvals, 90 rejections, from Gemini 3.1 Pro, Gemma4, GPT-5.5, and Sonnet 5), the verification programs achieve 93.3% raw agreement, 90.0% approval recall, and 96.7% rejection recall, versus 83.3%/82.2%/84.4% for a GPT-6 Astra VLM judge receiving up to 64 timestamped frames. An audit of all 12 disagreements attributes 9 to over-strict timing/coordination/geometry checks and 3 to missed relative motion between sub-elements. On a descriptive 1,578-animation comparison across 16 configurations, program scores track human approval with Spearman 0.971 (mean program success 28.8% vs. human 24.6%). Across all 47 configurations, pass@1 spans 6.0% (Qwen 3.6 27B thinking) to 67.7% (GPT-6 Astra max), mean 30.3%; the 16 proprietary models average 38.8% versus 21.8% for the 16 open-weight models. For the 15-model, 32-attempt cohort, pass@32 spans 38.0% to 95.0% (mean 36.7% → 73.7%), with higher-performing configurations plateauing earlier (top-5 gain 2.6 points on the last budget doubling vs. 6.7 for bottom-5; Spearman −0.86 between pass@1 and final gain). The task is hard for everyone: no configuration exceeds 67.7% pass@1, and the median instance-level pass@1 is 20.6%. Among 29,632 failed attempts, 93.6% pass at least one check and 31.6% fail exactly one — most failures are near misses. Dominant failure modes: reference-pose mismatch (41.5% failure rate, 94.3% coverage), motion-trajectory mismatch (38.8%), event-coordination mismatch (32.4%). A notable diagnostic: in 125 of 1,500 configuration–instance pools (8.3%), every individual check passes in some candidate but no single animation passes all checks. Baselines: the only automated-evaluation baseline is one VLM judge; no reference-similarity metric baseline is run. Tested at standard benchmark scale (100 instances), not stress scale. Novelty Classification NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK and NEW METHOD (per-instance verifier synthesis pipeline). The genuinely novel elements are: (a) deriving benchmark prompts from real professional Lottie animations rather than templates, with human review; (b) per-instance, human-readable deterministic verification programs rather than shared metrics or VLM judges; and (c) the writer/synthesizer construction loop validated against held-out human consensus labels. The underlying ingredients — MoVer-style animation matrices, counterexample-guided synthesis, LLM-generated test cases (CodeT, TestGenEval, HardTestGen), and human-validated judges — are existing; the contribution is a competent, well-validated combination applied to a new domain rather than a new algorithmic primitive. Rigor & Reproducibility Ablations in the classic sense are limited, but the validation design is careful: programs are frozen before evaluation on a disjoint held-out set, every one of the 12 disagreements is individually audited and tabulated, construction and evaluation annotations are separated, and the full 47-configuration inventory with token limits, temperatures, and effort labels is published. Error bars, multiple seeds, and significance tests are not reported (pass@k curves use 32 attempts per instance, which partially addresses variance). Two annotators independently judge each animation with consensus on disagreement, but inter-annotator agreement cannot be reconstructed from the exports and is not reported — the authors admit this. Code/data: the benchmark is released at https://huggingface.co/datasets/figma-ai/motion-graphics-bench; the renderer reuses the open-source MoVer repository; verification programs appear inspectable but no explicit code-release URL for the pipeline is stated. Methodological concerns: (1) verification programs were constructed from human-labeled outputs of 25 generation configurations, several of which are also among the evaluated models — a mild Goodhart/circularity risk for those models' scores, acknowledged only for the Table 5 correlation; (2) the held-out alignment set covers only 4 generation configurations, so alignment on other models' output distributions is unverified; (3) the VLM baseline is a single model chosen by the authors; no multi-judge or reference-metric comparison; (4) synthesized test-case labels are model claims, though only used during construction. This is an arXiv preprint (arXiv:2611.10592, Nov 2026), not stated as peer-reviewed. Deployability Profile: EMPIRICAL (a benchmark plus an evaluation methodology, validated by experiment). - Practical: Yes — verification runs Python checks over frames rendered by a headless browser (Chromium) from the open-source MoVer renderer; no special hardware beyond what any LLM evaluation harness needs. - Efficient: Far cheaper than the VLM baseline, which must ingest up to 64 images per judgment; the deterministic programs run once per animation and produce interpretable reports, though building them required 1,585 human-labeled animations up front. - Effective: The evidence shows the programs solve the stated problem (matching human pass/reject decisions) at 93.3% on held-out data, but 9 of 12 errors are false rejections from over-strict thresholds, so the verifier is biased toward rejecting borderline-valid animations. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 100 instances; scaling requires the multi-agent construction plus human labeling per instance, and the paper does not measure per-instance construction cost or whether program quality holds on complex deformation, large scenes, or interactive behavior — it explicitly claims it does not cover these. The work delivers a concrete software artifact: a public HuggingFace dataset with inputs, prompts, and frozen verification programs, plus reusable construction prompts and libraries described in appendices; the full construction pipeline code is not explicitly linked. Strengths - The verifier-alignment validation is the real contribution: 93.3% held-out agreement with a 10-point margin over a strong VLM judge, plus a 0.971 Spearman correlation on model rankings and a complete case-by-case audit of every disagreement — most benchmark papers never validate their own metric this way. - Grounding in real professional Lottie designs (selected from a 660K corpus by a scored complexity ranking with manual review) avoids the synthetic-template artifact that limits MoVer and Self-Consistency, and the geometry-completion step (recovering hidden layer paths so the SVG contains every element the edit needs) is a thoughtful, non-obvious construction detail. - The check-level reports enable failure analysis that a scalar metric cannot: per-mode failure rates over 16 categories with explicit coverage accounting, near-tied-model behavioral profiles (e.g., GPT-6 Astra vs. Fable 5.1 differ in reference-pose vs. coordination errors at comparable pass@1), and the 8.3% of pools where checks are satisfied by different candidates but never by one animation. - The pass@1-to-pass@32 plateau analysis (top models saturate earlier; Spearman −0.86 between pass@1 and gain) is a useful, quantified empirical finding for anyone sampling-based-generating animations. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors state: (1) detailed single-shot motion edit prompts do not capture multi-turn refinement from shorter, underspecified requests; (2) experiments use only GSAP generation, and other mechanisms (CSS, SMIL, other JS libraries) may yield different scores, even though verification is format-independent; (3) 100 instances do not cover complex deformation, large scenes, or highly interactive animation. They also candidly disclose in the appendix that initial annotator agreement rates cannot be reconstructed and label the Table 5 score comparison as descriptive due to construction overlap. This is direct, non-minimizing disclosure — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps - Training/evaluation circularity beyond what is acknowledged: several configurations used to build the verification programs (e.g., GPT-5.6 Sol max, Opus 5 max, Kimi K3 max, Qwen 3.8) are also in the 47-configuration and 15-model pass@32 evaluation populations. The separate generation batch mitigates animation-level leakage, but the programs' thresholds were calibrated on those same models' failure styles, potentially inflating their measured scores relative to unrepresented models. - The held-out alignment evaluation uses only 4 generation configurations (90/90 labels, 12 disagreements); alignment claims for the other 43 configurations rest on the contaminated descriptive correlation, not on independent human validation. - Only one VLM judge baseline (GPT-6 Astra); no comparison against alternative judges, judge ensembles, or the reference-similarity metrics the paper criticizes, so the 10-point margin's generality across judge choices is unknown. - No inter-annotator agreement statistic (only post-discussion consensus labels are retained), so the 93.3% ceiling's meaning is unclear — if human–human agreement is ~90%, the program's headroom over humans is small; if 99%, there is substantial room. - Frame-based verification samples at the source frame rate; fast or sub-frame events could be missed or misjudged, and no analysis of sampling-density sensitivity is provided. - The benchmark evaluates only general-purpose LLMs writing GSAP; no dedicated animation-generation system (LottieGPT, OmniLottie, Vector Prism, VAnim, etc.) is scored on it, so the benchmark's headline difficulty numbers cannot be situated against domain-specific systems. Bottom Line For anyone evaluating LLM-based motion or agentic-design generation, this is currently the most credible measurement instrument available in its niche — the validated per-instance verifier approach is worth adopting on its own — but its 100-instance scale, single-judge baseline comparison, and construction/evaluation model overlap mean its leaderboard numbers should be treated as indicative rather than definitive.

Cleared the Bar, or Lowered It? An Assurance Lattice for Verifying AI-Generated Software Against Intent

S Al-Nawah · salahmyn.me · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a formal theory of software assurance for AI-generated code, in which "done-ness" is a three-coordinate lattice state (structural, semantic, observational) over a code-to-intent graph, paired with a governance theory that separates coverage gaps (detectable in a state) from requirement weakenings (detectable only as a change), and specifies fail-closed transaction rules that make bar-lowering a recorded, human-signed event. - Why it's important: LLM coding agents demonstrably game cheap proxy checks (deleting tests, editing CI, special-casing tests), and the most dangerous exploit — weakening the requirement until the defect is out of scope — leaves every current signal green, so teams certifying agent output at scale have no mechanism that distinguishes "cleared the bar" from "lowered the bar." - How it does it: The core move is splitting checking into three independently computed axes on a deterministic code-to-intent graph, proving the four intuitive truth-levels form a canonical path through a sublattice with a meet-preserving valuation, and using transitivity of entailment (Proposition 4) to show no check over the current criterion-invariant pair can detect a weakening — so weakening must be governed on the change axis with hash-pinned intent text and human-only semantic sign-off. - The good: The paper is unusually honest about its own epistemics — every design element is labeled exercised/implemented/specified/conjectured, the demonstration's construct-validity limits are stated plainly, and the theory yields five falsifiable predictions with named refutation conditions. - The missing: The empirical evidence is a single-author, single-repository seeded demonstration (four drift instances, a four-mutant mutation score, a 41-statement lexical-router corpus) with drifts constructed by the author of the rules that catch them — no adversarial evaluation, no external repositories, and no comparison against any automated baseline detector. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on agent governance, AI-code assurance, or requirements-traceability tooling and want a rigorous, well-pedigreed conceptual frame with explicit testable commitments; skip it if you need evaluated systems or empirical detection rates, which the paper explicitly defers to future work.
