Problem & Motivation: LLM agents on ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld make sequences of tool-call decisions where terminal outcome rewards tell PPO nothing about which intermediate actions mattered. Step-level rewards solve this but typically require step annotations (Lightman et al.), extra Monte Carlo rollouts (VinePPO), or a separately trained evaluator (AgentPRM, SWEET-RL, TARL). The authors target practitioners training agentic RL policies who want denser credit signals at near-zero marginal cost, using signals already computed inside the policy — attention maps — as a relevance prior over past steps. Key Idea: The core trick is treating the policy's own attention graph as a free backward-credit estimator: starting from the terminal step, multiply attention edge weights backward through the step graph (with 0.85 per-hop decay and a negative recency-correction term, η = −0.25, that deliberately down-weights recent steps), fuse per-layer allocations by geometric mean so only cross-layer-consistent dependencies survive, then gate the magnitude by a confidence score (terminal covered mass, allocation entropy, layer TV-agreement) and set the sign from whether the trajectory outcome beats a running EMA baseline. The authors are careful to frame attention as a heuristic relevance signal, not causal attribution. Methodology: ATTNSR intervenes only at the reward interface of token-level PPO. (1) During actor replay for old log-probabilities, detached post-RoPE Q/K tensors are captured, blockwise-aggregated into per-layer step graphs G(l) = 0.5·G_AA + 0.5·G_AO over assistant-assistant and assistant-observation attention, with the historical submatrix not renormalized (preserving mass relative to the rest of the context). (2) Relevance propagates backward via a(l)_k = ρ·Σ_{j>k} a(l)_j·G(l)[j,k] (Eq. 3), then is standardized in log space, recency-corrected, and softmaxed per layer; layers fuse to p_i,k by geometric mean. (3) A confidence C_i ∈ [0,1] (covered mass clipped at 0.20, inverse normalized entropy clipped at 0.15, layer-consistency via total variation) multiplies a signed budget B_i = β·C_i·(R_i − R̄_t) with β = 0.25 and a batch-shared EMA baseline (0.99 decay), giving s_i,k = B_i·p_i,k at assistant-step endpoint tokens. (4) These rewards enter GAE and value targets unchanged in the PPO losses; actor attention is detached and no loss backpropagates through reward construction. Critical design decisions: non-renormalized sub-graph attention (justified as preserving context mass, but not ablated); the negative recency bias (justified intuition, no ablation of η); and the length-independent budget bound |Σs_i,k| ≤ β (explicitly noted as breaking return-preservation / policy invariance — an acknowledged deviation from RUDDER-style redistribution). Hyperparameters are fully tabulated (layers 8–18 step 2, ρ = 0.85, κ = 4, T = 1). Key Results: With Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct + rank-64 LoRA on 8×H200, four data epochs: ALFWorld success 91.24% → 97.08% (PPO → ATTNSR), beating adapted TARL (96.72%), FlowTracer (95.62%), and AgentPRM (91.97%) at matched training budgets, though the margin over TARL is a single task (266 vs 265 of 274); unseen-task success rises more than seen (89.55% → 97.76%). ScienceWorld score improves at all four checkpoints (44.53% → 46.35% at epoch 4) with mean environment steps down 29.9% (30.68 → 21.51). WebShop is mixed: success +0.80 pp but score −1.04 pp, with intervals spanning zero. GRPO reference and baselines are reasonably current (2025–2026 works, authors' own adaptations), though GRPO uses a different optimization budget and is explicitly flagged as non-comparable. The linear step-reward control recovers under one-fifth of the gain (+1.10 vs +5.84 pp). Cross-backbone checks show +3.28 pp (Qwen3-4B) and +7.66 pp (Qwen2.5-3B, 79.56% → 87.23%); a 3B GRPO token-advantage variant goes from 34 to 55 of 274 tasks, but with 34.7% format-error rates. Trajectory analysis shows ALFWorld's aggregate step reduction comes from fewer prolonged failures (24 at ~104 steps), not shorter successful trajectories, which the paper reports honestly. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (with a NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING component). The genuinely novel element is extracting step-credit from the policy's own attention during the existing replay pass — no rollouts, no reward model, no attribution backward pass — with confidence gating and outcome centering. It is closest to FlowTracer (attention-induced information-flow credit, Dong et al. 2026), and the surrounding machinery (PPO, GAE, EMA baselines, geometric fusion) is standard; the contribution is the specific allocation-and-gating scheme and the empirical demonstration that it beats positional shaping, not a new RL formulation. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are above average for this area: a positional-reward control isolating attention allocation, two backbone replications, a GRPO variant, an asynchronous-config variant, per-checkpoint results, and category-level breakdowns. Statistical testing is careful and unusually honest — exact McNemar on matched tasks with 10,000-resample paired bootstrap, with the authors reporting that only ALFWorld survives Bonferroni and that WebShop intervals include zero. However: one training run per method with no seed variance anywhere (stated repeatedly); wall-clock and peak-memory overhead of attention extraction unmeasured; the GRPO comparison conflates budgets; ALFWorld is near ceiling (91.24% PPO baseline), leaving little headroom and making the headline 5.84 pp gain rest on 16 net tasks; and the TARL/AgentPRM/FlowTracer comparisons are authors' own adaptations with no paired significance testing. Code is promised at https://github.com/fairyshine/AttnSR (anonymized repository with reward-extraction implementation, launch configs, and per-episode artifacts). No Goodhart-style benchmark reuse is apparent — evaluation uses fixed held-out splits with no best-checkpoint selection. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (and partially SYSTEMS, since a code artifact is released). Practical: Yes — runs on 8×H200 with LoRA and open 3–7B models, all standard infrastructure (VeRL, Megatron, vLLM). Efficient: Conceptually near-free (reuses the replay forward pass; quadratic query–key arithmetic retained but blockwise), yet the paper does not measure the actual wall-clock or memory overhead, so the efficiency claim is unverified. Effective: Evidence supports the stated problem on long-horizon tasks (ALFWorld significant, ScienceWorld suggestive with 29.9% fewer interactions), but not on short-horizon tasks (WebShop null), so effectiveness is conditional on trajectory length. Scalable: Untested beyond 7B/32k-context; the authors themselves flag longer contexts and horizons as future work, and attention-quality degradation in longer contexts is an unexamined risk. Deliverable: a code artifact (reward extraction and allocation implementation, launch configurations) plus a reusable reward-shaping recipe; not a standalone library or trained model release beyond the recipe. Strengths: - The positional-reward control is the paper's strongest asset: it directly tests whether any budget-respecting dense reward explains the gain, and shows it does not (92.34% vs 97.08%), which most step-reward papers omit. - The reward interface design is clean and modular — intermediate rewards placed at step endpoints flow through existing GAE/value machinery with no change to PPO losses, making adoption trivial in standard RLHF stacks. - Statistical reporting is unusually candid for this subfield: Bonferroni-adjusted significance, matched-task pairing, and explicit admission that ScienceWorld and WebShop effects do not survive correction. - The trajectory analysis distinguishes "fewer prolonged failures" from "shorter solutions" on ALFWorld rather than over-claiming efficiency, and the appendix diagnostics (parse events, natural termination, repetition rates) are thorough. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state: attention is relevance, not causal contribution (Jain & Wallace); policy invariance is not guaranteed since shaping changes the return (β-bounded but nonzero); WebShop shows no detectable gain and short-horizon benefit is an open hypothesis; all results are single-run with no seed variance; wall-clock/memory overheads are unmeasured; the "greater benefit on complex, long-horizon tasks" is a hypothesis, not established; the GRPO and asynchronous variants change multiple factors and permit no component attribution; and the 3B source-tree differences beyond attention code confound the cross-backbone check. This is a credibility positive — the limitations section and appendix consistently under-sell rather than over-sell. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No ablation over the choice of attention layers (8–18), the hop decay ρ, the recency weight η, or the AA/AO 0.5/0.5 mixture — the method has ~10 hyperparameters and only the allocation-vs-positional axis is ablated, so sensitivity is unknown. - The ALFWorld baseline sits at 91.24%, so the headline result hinges on 16 of 274 tasks; a harder split or a weaker baseline model with more headroom would be more informative, and near-ceiling results invite variance-driven flukes even with the paired test (single run, single greedy decode per task). - No comparison against the cheapest natural alternative: sampling-based step attribution or a simple gradient-saliency baseline (ACPO is cited but not compared), and no test of whether a random or uniform attention allocation within the confidence-gated budget matches performance — the control only covers temporal position. - Attention quality under 32k-token packed sequences with tensor/context parallelism is asserted to work but never validated (e.g., by checking whether backtracked relevance correlates with human-judged step importance), leaving the core hypothesis unverified mechanistically. - Greedy single-rollout evaluation means stochastic policy variance is unmeasured; multiple decodes per task would cost little and materially strengthen the discordant-task counts. Bottom Line: This is one of the more honest and mechanically clean entries in the LLM-agent credit-assignment literature — the zero-extra-rollout attention-reward trick is genuinely useful and well-controlled on ALFWorld — but with single runs, near-ceiling headline tasks, and a null result on the shortest-horizon benchmark, a practitioner should treat it as a promising, cheap heuristic to try alongside their PPO runs rather than a validated replacement for process reward models; reading the method and ablation sections is worthwhile, the strong claims are not yet load-bearing.

Adapting the Process of Adaptation: Darwinian, Lamarckian, and Agent-Directed Evolution in AI

AW Lo, C Zhao · arxiv.org · recursive self-improvement - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds a theoretical framework, based on the Brennan–Lo evolutionary growth model, that proves a strict ranking of adaptation speeds — Darwinian < Lamarckian < agent-directed evolution — and shows formally that faster self-directed search accelerates convergence to a misspecified objective just as it accelerates convergence to the correct one. - Why it's important: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) systems that generate, evaluate, and retain their own modifications are now being built (FunSearch, AlphaEvolve, Darwin Gödel Machine), and the paper addresses whether this speedup can be made safe when evaluation criteria are imperfect — a central AI-alignment concern. - How it does it: The core move is to measure maladaptation as "growth regret," proved exactly equal to a KL divergence between environmental and behavioral distributions, so adaptation speed becomes the exponential decay rate of a KL term that each evolutionary mechanism reduces through a distinct channel (selection, inherited learning, and agent-chosen search). - The good: The theorems are clean and complete: κ_D = 2Δ, κ_L = −2 log(1−λ), κ_A = κ_L + 2G_N(ρ), with the search gain G_N(1) = 1 + 1/2 + ··· + 1/N growing as log N, and Theorem 5 shows a misspecified target leaves the agent's measured adaptation rate untouched while capping true regret at R_{p_new}(p̃) > 0. - The missing: The framework's key reduced-form assumptions — that learning and search always move behavior toward the true optimum, that variants are scored by distance to that optimum, and that parameters λ, ρ, and the target are fixed across generations — are stipulated rather than derived or validated against any real AI system, so the mapping to RSI is by analogy only. - Read it or not: Worth reading for AI-safety theorists and economists working on evolutionary models of capability growth who want a compact set of provable stylized facts; practitioners building RSI systems will find no operational guidance, and ML researchers wanting empirical evidence should look elsewhere.

Problem & Motivation: The paper addresses a gap in how the AI-safety and economics communities think about recursive self-improvement: current RSI systems (the Darwin Gödel Machine, AIDE2, multi-agent RSI) can modify and evaluate their own code, but there is no formal theory comparing how fast adaptation proceeds when it is driven by natural selection alone, by selection plus inherited learning, or by an agent that also controls its own search effort. The motivating stake is that self-directed adaptation may accelerate capability gains beyond the pace at which humans can evaluate them, and the authors want to know whether faster adaptation necessarily means better outcomes. The questions are: how much faster can learning and self-directed search adapt than natural selection, what determines optimal search effort, and can speed amplify convergence to unintended behavior? Key Idea: Growth regret — the expected log-growth a population forfeits by behaving as f instead of the environment-optimal p — is exactly the KL divergence D_KL(Bern(p) || Bern(f)), and each evolutionary mechanism eliminates this regret through a distinguishable channel whose long-run exponential decay rate can be computed in closed form. This single identity converts an AI-safety question (how fast do different self-improvement regimes adapt, and toward what?) into a tractable stochastic first-passage/asymptotics problem on a two-lineage branching-style population model. Methodology: The framework is a discrete-generation, asexually reproducing population model in the Brennan–Lo tradition, with two lineages (an "adapted" lineage holding the post-shift optimum p_new and a "maladapted" lineage starting at p_old) sharing an environmental state X_t ∈ {α, β} with probability p of α; natural selection updates lineage shares multiplicatively via realized reproductive success. Three mechanisms are layered on this common substrate: Mechanism D (fixed behaviors, selection only); Mechanism L (a partial-adjustment learning rule f_{t+1} = f_t + λ(p_new − f_t) with λ ∈ (0,1) inherited by offspring); Mechanism A (each generation the agent generates N variants x_{t,j} = f_{t−1} + ρU_{t,j}(p_new − f_{t−1}) with U uniform on (0,1) and ρ a "reach" parameter, an external evaluator keeps the closest variant, and learning then applies). Adaptation speed is measured by adaptation time (generations to shrink regret to a fraction ε of its initial value) and adaptation rate (the a.s. exponential decay rate of regret). The safety extension, Mechanism Ã, redirects search, evaluation, and learning toward a misspecified target p̃ ≠ p_new while selection still operates on true reproductive success. Critical design decisions: (1) the reduced-form assumption that all variants move toward the target (stated as such, but it presupposes a uniformly correct improvement direction — weakly justified); (2) an external evaluator that perfectly identifies the variant closest to the target (idealized; the paper acknowledges the agent need not know p_new, but perfect evaluation is strong); (3) fixed λ, ρ, and N across generations — explicitly flagged in the conclusion as excluding the RSI feedback loop where improved capability improves future improvement. Key Results: The headline theoretical results are: Theorem 1 gives κ_D = 2Δ where Δ = R_{p_new}(p_old), with an unbounded "seed penalty" — expected Darwinian adaptation time grows as log(1/q_0)/Δ as the adapted lineage's initial share q_0 → 0, and adaptation is impossible at q_0 = 0. Theorem 2 gives κ_L = −2 log(1−λ) with uniformly bounded expected adaptation time in q_0 (no seed penalty). Theorem 3 gives κ_A = κ_L + 2G_N(ρ); Proposition 4 shows G_N(1) = 1 + 1/2 + ··· + 1/N ~ log N (so the rate gain grows as 2 log N in the easiest case) while for ρ < 1 the gain saturates at −log(1−ρ). Proposition 5 shows the cost-minimizing variant count N is nondecreasing in ρ and nonincreasing in λ and per-variant cost c, and can be zero for hard problems (e.g., N = 0 at ρ = 0.005). Theorem 4 establishes the strict ranking κ_D < κ_L < κ_A when λ > 1 − e^{−Δ}, with matching expected-time ranking for stringent thresholds. Numerically (200,000 Monte Carlo paths; p_old = 0.40 → p_new = 0.60, q_0 = 10⁻⁴, λ = 0.10, N = 1, ρ = 0.5, giving Δ = 0.0811, κ_D = 0.162, κ_L = 0.211, κ_A = 0.824), reaching 1% of initial regret takes ~145 generations (Darwinian), 22 (Lamarckian), and 6.2 (agent-directed, N=1), falling to 3.9 at N = 10; at the 0.1% threshold: 160 / 33 / 9.0 generations. Theorem 5 is the safety payoff: under a misspecified target, the agent's regret relative to the evaluator's target decays at the full κ_L + 2G_N(ρ), its true regret converges to the strictly positive R_{p_new}(p̃), more variants only accelerate convergence to the wrong behavior, and the population recovers only via natural selection at rate 2R_{p_new}(p̃) — slow when p̃ is near p_new. All baselines are the paper's own nested mechanisms (L is A with N = 0; D is the selection-only benchmark); there is no comparison to external adaptation models. Scale is a two-lineage toy model, not a stress test. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (analytical): the genuinely novel elements are (a) the exact growth-regret-as-KL-divergence identity used as a common metric for comparing evolutionary adaptation mechanisms, and (b) Theorem 5's result that search effort monotonically accelerates convergence to a misspecified target at an unchanged measured rate. The machinery itself — Kelly-criterion/KL growth arguments, partial-adjustment learning, best-of-N search, and Moran/Fisher-type selection dynamics — is a competent combination of known ideas from evolutionary biology, information theory, and inference-time-compute scaling (Brown et al. 2024; Snell et al. 2024), applied in a new setting; the agent-directed "choosing how many variants" decision is the closest to new but is a straightforward cost-benefit analysis on top of Theorem 3. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper is rigorous by the standards of economic theory: five lemmas with full proofs (optional stopping for first-passage bounds, strong-law arguments, an integral representation of G_N via Tonelli, a ratio-of-power-series monotonicity lemma), all delivered in an appendix. Ablation-style structure is present — the three mechanisms are nested, so each theorem isolates its added channel, and the numerical section varies λ, N, ρ, and q_0 systematically across figures. The Monte Carlo study uses 200,000 simulated histories and reports 5th–95th percentile bands, which is a form of uncertainty quantification, though no formal significance tests and no seed variance for the analytical claims (which are a.s. statements, so this is minor). No code or data release is mentioned. Methodological concerns: the entire evaluation is on the authors' own constructed model with no external validation against any real adaptation process; the numerical section illustrates rather than tests the theorems; and the paper cites several 2026 references (OpenAI's Navier–Stokes claim, AIDE2, multi-agent RSI) that are cited as motivation but whose claims are taken at face value. This is a preprint (arXiv:2611.07048) and has not, as far as the document indicates, been peer reviewed. The AI-use disclosure (Appendix A) states that AI systems checked derivations and drafted text, with author review — reasonable but worth noting for proof-verification purposes. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: THEORETICAL (with illustrative Monte Carlo simulation, but no primary experimental claim about real systems). - Sound: Assumptions are explicit and proofs appear complete; the weakest assumption — that every generated variant's improvement direction is correct toward the target with random magnitude — is acknowledged as reduced-form but is doing heavy lifting. - General: Results hold for i.i.d. two-state environments with permanent shifts, two lineages, fixed parameters, and behavior interior to (0,1); these are restrictive relative to real non-stationary, high-dimensional adaptation, though the two-lineage case reportedly extends to more. - Tight: The characterization results are exact (a.s. limits, not bounds); the first-passage bounds in Lemma C.2 are loose but only used for scaling limits, which are tight in the stated limits. - Implementable: The results are qualitative stylized facts, not algorithms; the optimal-variant-count rule N*(ρ, λ, c) could inform search-budget heuristics, but the paper does not operationalize this, and no follow-up work is cited. The work delivers no software artifact, dataset, or trained model — it stops at paper form (plus figures from simulations not stated to be released). Strengths: - The growth-regret/KL identity (Proposition 2) is a genuinely useful measurement contribution: it gives a single, interpretable, information-theoretic yardstick that makes Darwinian, Lamarckian, and agent-directed adaptation commensurable, and it connects cleanly to the Kelly-criterion and fitness-value-of-information literatures. - The seed-penalty result (Darwinian expected time diverging as log(1/q_0)/Δ and adaptation being impossible at q_0 = 0, versus uniformly bounded time under learning) is a crisp, non-obvious insight that cleanly explains why inheritance of acquired traits matters even when selection is available. - The misspecified-target theorem (Theorem 5) is the paper's most valuable safety result: the decomposition into an unchanged measured adaptation rate, a strictly positive residual true regret, and a slow natural-selection correction rate quantifies the "faster but wronger" phenomenon that reward-model-overoptimization work (Gao et al. 2023) has observed empirically. - The nested construction of the three mechanisms (L ⊂ A, D as benchmark) makes every comparison interpretable as the marginal effect of one added channel — a well-executed experimental-design choice in a purely theoretical paper. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that the model keeps learning effectiveness, variant reach, search effort, and the evaluation criterion fixed across generations, thereby excluding the RSI feedback loop in which improved capability enhances the improvement process itself — they flag this as the key direction for future research. They also acknowledge (footnote 1) that mutation is excluded, so Darwinian adaptation at q_0 = 0 is impossible by construction; they label the learning and search rules as reduced-form assumptions that specify direction and speed rather than mechanism; and they note the numerical parameters are illustrative. They confront limitations directly rather than minimize them — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The correctness of the improvement direction is assumed: every variant moves toward the target by construction, so the framework cannot represent genuinely wrong or harmful candidate modifications — precisely the failure mode (e.g., the Darwin Gödel Machine deleting logging markers) the authors invoke in Section 8.2. The model's adaptation is toward-target by fiat; real misalignment often involves search finding off-target solutions. - The evaluator is assumed perfect relative to its (possibly wrong) target and to have noiseless access to variant quality; the interaction between noisy evaluation and search effort — where reward-model overoptimization actually arises — is not modeled, so Theorem 5's clean separation between measured and true regret is partly an artifact of deterministic evaluation. - The two-state environment with a single permanent shift is minimal; no results cover recurring shifts, correlated environments, or continuous state spaces, so claims about "adaptation" in realistic settings rest on the simplest possible case. - The mapping to AI systems is by analogy table (Appendix A.2) without any empirical calibration: no attempt to estimate λ, ρ, or Δ for any real RSI system, so the quantitative gap between 145 and 6.2 generations, while illustrative, carries no evidence about actual AI timelines. - The two-objective (speed-maximizing vs. cost-minimizing) agent in Section 6.3 omits a risk-averse or safety-constrained objective — the very case most relevant to the paper's own safety argument — so the optimal-search analysis and the safety analysis are not integrated. - Natural selection is cast as the corrector of misspecified evaluation (Theorem 5(iii)), but for AI systems there is no clear analogue of realized reproductive fitness operating independently of the evaluator; the paper's most reassuring result may not transfer to its motivating domain. Bottom Line: A theoretically polished and internally consistent paper that gives AI-safety researchers a compact, provable vocabulary (growth regret, seed penalty, the speed-direction separation of Theorem 5) for discussing recursive self-improvement, but practitioners seeking validated predictions about real RSI systems will find the reduced-form assumptions and uncalibrated toy environment leave the empirical question wide open — read it for the framing and Theorem 5, not for guidance on building or governing systems.

J Yin, V Grover, K Zhou · arxiv.org · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds WARPLINE, a framework that automatically instruments GPU kernel binaries (SASS) with low-overhead semantic-event probes, aligns the resulting trace with hardware-counter time series and recovered program logic on a unified timeline, and feeds this evidence to LLM coding agents in a closed-loop kernel optimization harness. - Why it's important: LLM agents optimizing tensor-core GPU kernels currently tune blind — hardware profilers show utilization but not per-warp timing, and source/IR-level tracers perturb the kernel through recompilation, so agents spend optimization budget on the wrong bottleneck. - How it does it: The core trick is automatic binary analysis (static abstract evaluation plus a grounded dynamic run) that identifies warp groups, work loops, and barrier topology, then grafts probes directly into the final SASS with coordinated record compaction, instruction scheduling, register selection, and per-warp buffer sizing — no recompilation, no source annotations. - The good: The fidelity evidence is compelling: across 35 kernels, WARPLINE achieves 1.2% median tracing overhead and 99.9% median instruction preservation, versus 1.6–13.2% overhead and 4.6–32.7% preservation for Proton, IKET, FlashInfer, and Neutrino, and it is the only tool that traces closed-source cuBLAS/cuDNN kernels. - The missing: There is no ablation isolating which of the four probe optimizations (O1–O4) matter, no code release URL is stated, and the agentic study (10 problems, one agent model, one GPU, one harness) cannot separate the tracer's contribution from the skill package and evaluator bundled with it. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on GPU performance tooling, binary instrumentation, or LLM-driven kernel optimization; skip it if you want generalizable agentic-optimization methodology, since the evaluation is narrow (10 benchmark problems, B200 only, no public artifact).

Problem & Motivation: Teams and agents optimizing tensor-core GPU kernels (GEMM, attention, convolution with TMA, warp specialization, software pipelining, mbarrier synchronization) need to know where time goes inside a kernel. Hardware profilers (Nsight Compute) report aggregate utilization and stall counts but not which warp stalled when; intra-kernel tracers (Proton, IKET, FlashInfer's profiler, Neutrino) insert probes at source, IR, or PTX level, which participate in compilation and perturb register allocation, scheduling, and even performance (some instrumented builds run >10% faster than the uninstrumented kernel). Source-level probes also break when an agent rewrites the kernel, and none of these tools can instrument closed-source library kernels. The optimization loop therefore requires either an expert to place probes each round or the agent operates on incomplete, possibly distorted evidence. Key Idea: Treat the compiled SASS binary as the universal, stable instrumentation point: recover the kernel's program logic (warp roles, work loops, barrier topology) through static abstract evaluation grounded by one dynamic run, plan semantic events (spans and instants: waits, TMA/MMA issues, commits, warp lifetimes), then graft probe instructions into the binary while coordinating their clock reads, buffer stores, register allocation, and issue-slot placement with the kernel's own stall schedule — so the trace describes essentially the original program, at any edit level (source, IR, or PTX), including closed-source binaries. Methodology: Three stages. (1) AutoTracer: the Program Cartographer statically abstractly evaluates SASS under the launch configuration to find warp groups, work loops, and barrier topology; a dynamic instrumented run captures values static analysis cannot prove (shared-memory dispatch indices, mbarrier slots/parities, execution counts), reused only when static checks prove dependence solely on kernel and launch config. The Probe Plan maps SASS PCs to two event levels (Lifetime: warp start/end; Pipeline: loops, data movement, tensor-core ops, synchronization). The Probe Graftor inserts probes preserving original instruction order, with four optimizations: O1 record compaction (segments share slot-advance and clock reads; e.g., 5 records in 13 instructions incl. 2 stores instead of 25 incl. 5), O2 instruction selection/scheduling (16-byte wide stores placed where stall samples show low memory pressure, minimal-stall placement, stores on least-used scoreboards), O3 register selection (unused registers first, then occupancy-safe raises, then liveness-proven dead registers, with uniform registers for addresses), O4 per-warp trace-buffer sizing from dynamic counts. (2) Evidence Integrator: collects 19 Nsight Compute PM sampling time series, assigns warp-group roles, pairs waits with the arrivals/copies/commits completing their phase per barrier slot, aligns hardware series to the trace via an affine fit on warp lifetimes, and produces a kernel summary with blame-shifting analysis plus a query API. (3) Agentic Optimizer: a skill package guides a coding agent (Claude Sonnet 5.5) to read evidence, form hypotheses, and edit source/IR/PTX; an evaluator checks correctness on multiple inputs and times candidates via CUPTI with ABBA ordering, L2 flushes, medians, and a half-band acceptance threshold (candidate must improve beyond half the parent's latency range). Key design decisions: binary-level instrumentation to preserve execution (well justified by the fidelity data showing baselines distort kernels), the static-plus-grounded-dynamic hybrid (explicitly justified, with soundness guards), and the half-band noise-aware acceptance rule (sensible; not ablated). Key Results: On NVIDIA B200 (sm_100a, 148 SMs) across 35 open-source kernels in Triton, CuTe DSL, and CUDA C++, plus 3 closed-source kernels: AutoTracer median overhead 1.2% (range −2.1% to 5.4%) vs. Proton 4.8%, IKET 1.6%, FlashInfer 13.2%, Neutrino 10.3%; instruction preservation median 99.9% (99.4–100%) vs. Proton 9.9%, IKET 32.7%, FlashInfer 5.4%, Neutrino 4.6%. Record counts are comparable to manually placed baseline probes (0.4–2.0×; AutoTracer records more in 41/70 comparisons), ruling out under-recording as the source of low overhead. Closed-source kernels: 0.21% (cuBLAS nvJet GEMM), 3.07% (cuDNN SDPA), 0.32% (cuDNN conv) overhead at 99.85–99.99% preservation; baselines cannot trace these. Offline analysis+instrumentation: 13–77 s per kernel (median 30 s). On 10 SOL-ExecBench Triton problems (6 rounds × 60 min, same agent model and evaluator): 7.69× geometric-mean speedup and 18.1% SOL efficiency vs. 6.94×/16.3% for a bare agent and 6.13×/14.5% for NVIDIA's KDA; 6 wins/4 ties/0 losses vs. Bare; lower cost (30.7 min and 44 model requests/round vs. 33.5/54 for Bare and 59.9/108 for KDA). Three expert-written production Triton kernels improved 1.22× (causal attention), 1.34× (MXFP8 GEMM), 1.58× (SDXL convolution). Two case studies on SDXL convolution show the unified timeline enabling diagnoses no single tool supports: bunched epilogue stores (154.6→151.6 µs) and compiler-inserted cluster-barrier fence rounds visible only in SASS, removed via a PTX edit (146.4→144.2 µs). Baselines are current (Proton CGO 2026, Neutrino OSDI 2025, IKET shipped with CuTe DSL 4.6.1), though each was used only on its supported language. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL and NEW METHOD (automatic semantic-event identification at SASS level with behavior-preserving binary probe grafting, plus the unified trace+hardware+logic evidence interface); secondarily NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (quantified evidence that source/IR/PTX tracers perturb the measured program — some builds >10% faster with <27% preservation). Prior SASS-level frameworks (SASSI, NVBit, Xtrace) exist; the genuinely new part is automating event discovery from the binary (so agents get evidence with zero human instrumentation) and integrating it with hardware counters and barrier-topology-derived dependency analysis for agent consumption. The agentic optimizer itself is a competent combination of known ideas (skills + evaluator loop). Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong on the tracing side: full distributions (ranges and medians) for overhead and preservation, execution-weighted preservation metric, a record-count comparison explicitly ruling out the under-instrumentation confound, noise bands from repeated uninstrumented runs, and a carefully defined timing protocol (ABBA ordering, L2 flushes, medians, half-band acceptance). Missing: no per-optimization ablation of O1–O4; no multiple-seed repeats or significance tests for the agentic study (10 problems, geometric means, ties defined as within 3%); the agent comparison bundles tracer + skills + evaluator into one intervention, so the marginal value of each is unmeasured; baseline probes were manually placed by the authors, which may understate baseline quality. No code, data, or artifact URL is mentioned anywhere in the paper — a major reproducibility gap for a tool paper. Evaluation is confined to sm_100a/B200; the authors state porting beyond it is future work. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a built tracing/analysis/harness pipeline evaluated by running it, with empirical tracer measurements). Practical: Yes for B200/sm_100a owners — it needs only the kernel binary and Nsight Compute, but is currently Blackwell-specific. Efficient: 1.2% median runtime overhead and ~30 s one-time analysis cost per kernel version, far below the 60-minute optimization rounds; clearly cheaper than expert manual instrumentation. Effective: Evidence shows it solves the stated problem for agents on the tested benchmarks (faster kernels, fewer requests), but only on 10 problems with one agent model; effect on production kernels (1.22–1.58×) is the strongest deployment-relevant evidence. Scalable: Not tested beyond 35+3 kernels on one GPU; the paper only claims, rather than demonstrates, per-version automation as kernels evolve (though the 30 s regeneration cost supports the claim). The work is currently paper-form; no library, CLI, dataset, or trained model release is stated. Strengths: - The fidelity metric and results are the paper's best asset: 99.9% median execution-weighted instruction preservation at 1.2% median overhead directly substantiates the central claim that the trace describes the original program, with the side finding that competing tracers' instrumented builds sometimes run >10% faster than the kernels they claim to measure — a diagnostic that matters beyond this paper. - Automating semantic-event identification from SASS (warp groups, barrier topology, wait↔commit pairing) is a real technical advance over NVBit-style frameworks that require the user to say what to trace, and it uniquely enables closed-source kernel analysis. - The case studies are unusually well-chosen: the compiler-inserted cluster-barrier rounds exist only in SASS, invisible to source-level tracers and unattributable in hardware profiles, demonstrating capability no evaluated alternative offers. - The optimization evaluation controls cost and model (same agent, same evaluator, same budget), and reports agent activity (summary reads, trace queries, NCU runs), giving some visibility into whether the evidence is actually used. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The only explicit limitation is architectural portability: "Extending AutoTracer beyond sm 100a is future work." The authors also candidly acknowledge static analysis's inherent limits (shared memory and inter-warp communication are not fully modeled statically), which they mitigate with guarded dynamic observation. They do not otherwise confront limitations such as evaluation breadth, artifact release, or the confounded agentic comparison — a minimization relative to the paper's strong claims about the full optimization loop. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No ablation of O1–O4 (record compaction, scheduling, register selection, buffer sizing): the 1.2% median overhead is a system number; a reviewer cannot tell which optimizations are load-bearing or how overhead behaves on pathologically long kernels (buffer wrap-around, O4 estimates demand from one dynamic run — non-stationary kernels could drop events). - The agentic headline (7.69× vs. 6.94×/6.13×) conflates three interventions (tracer, evidence interface, skills+evaluator); a bare-agent-plus-evaluator arm is the obvious missing control, and 10 problems with a single agent model and single seed per configuration is thin for a 1.11×/1.25× claimed margin. - No public artifact: a systems paper whose whole value is an automated pipeline offers no way to verify, reuse, or extend it, and binary instrumentation of proprietary SASS encodings is fragile across driver/toolkit updates (they test exactly one driver/toolkit version). - Baseline tracer probes were manually placed by the authors at Pipeline-level events "wherever supported" — a stronger evaluation would use each tool's native best-practice instrumentation. - Hardware-series alignment relies on an affine fit to warp-lifetime traces across separate runs; no quantification of alignment error is given, yet downstream case-study conclusions depend on it. - The affine timing model, NCUs lock-step CTA observations, and SOL-efficiency denominators all assume the traced run is representative; nothing is said about kernels with high run-to-run variance beyond noting Mamba2's fluctuation. Bottom Line: For anyone building GPU performance tooling or agentic kernel-optimization loops, this is worth reading for its quantified demonstration that binary-level, automatically planned instrumentation is both feasible and dramatically higher-fidelity than current practice — but it is a single-architecture, unartifacted preprint whose agentic gains rest on a 10-problem, confounded comparison, so treat the optimization-loop claims as promising rather than established.

EMPIRE: EXPLICIT METHOD FOR DATASET PARTI

TU INTEGER · openreview.net · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces EMPIRE, an integer linear programming formulation that partitions NER datasets into splits while jointly controlling entity leakage, context leakage, split sizes, and per-class entity balance through a single trade-off parameter α. - Why it's important: Reported NER F1 on native splits is inflated by entity memorization (prior work shows F1 correlates log-linearly with train-set entity frequency), so benchmark numbers in domains like biomedicine overstate generalization by a large margin. - How it does it: Sentences are clustered (K-means over α-weighted concatenations of entity-occurrence and entity-masked embedding vectors), and cluster-to-split assignments are chosen by a Gurobi-solved ILP that maximizes frequency-weighted entity disjointness minus size-weighted cross-split cluster similarity, subject to split-ratio and class-proportion constraints discovered by a feasibility pre-check. - The good: The class-balance analysis is the strongest result — removing the constraint strands 20–32 entity classes across splits and depresses F1 by 0.11–0.14 for reasons unrelated to generalization, a confound that plausibly contaminates prior leakage-reduction evaluations including MinCut. - The missing: Downstream evaluation relies on a BiLSTM-CRF (a 2015-era architecture) on all 24 datasets and Llama-2-7B on only 5 datasets with a single seed and no significance testing, leaving untested whether the F1-inflation finding holds for the modern encoder-based models that actually top NER leaderboards. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or evaluate NER benchmarks, especially in entity-recycling domains like biomedicine or law, where the ILP and the class-balance analysis offer a concrete, reusable splitting tool; skip it if you only need the qualitative finding that entity leakage inflates F1, which Babl et al. (2025) and Golde et al. (2025) already established.

Rigor (70) benefits from 24 datasets, Holm-corrected Wilcoxon tests, and unusually honest solver reporting (MIP gaps up to 247%), but is capped by single-seed training, a 2015-era primary evaluation model, and a partial Goodhart risk (leakage measured in the embedding space used to build splits). Resilience (68) is limited by the untested assumption that leakage-reduced splits actually improve evaluation fidelity. Problem & Motivation: NER practitioners and benchmark maintainers need train/test splits that measure generalization rather than memorization. Standard random or temporal splits permit two leakage forms: entity leakage (the same (entity, tag) target appears in both train and test, so models recognize it from memory) and context leakage (test sentences share templates with train sentences, e.g., "admitted to [X] for observation"). This matters most in domains with small entity universes — roughly 20,000 human protein-coding genes recur across biomedical studies — where reported F1 correlates strongly with entity overlap. Prior work quantifies the problem (Elangovan et al. 2021; Fu et al. 2020; Golde et al. 2025) but offers limited solutions: MinCut (Babl et al. 2025) separates entities but ignores context similarity and class proportions and can relax split sizes; DataSAIL (Joeres et al. 2025) assumes one label per sample, which fails for NER sentences carrying multiple entities. No existing method jointly controls entity leakage, context leakage, and per-split class distributions. Key Idea: Cast the entire dataset-splitting decision as one integer linear program over cluster-assignment variables, where a single normalized objective α·(disjointness) − (1−α)·(information leakage) selects which leakage to remove, while hard constraints pin split sizes (ε=0) and each entity class's share of every split (tolerance δ). The enabling move is clustering: grouping sentences into K=50 super-nodes shrinks the O(n²) pairwise similarity structure to O(K²), making the NP-hard problem tractable, and the K-means feature space itself is α-weighted so clustering and objective agree on what "similar" means. Methodology: Three stages. (1) Input & clustering: entities are stemmed (NLTK Snowball) into targets; sentences are embedded with entity-masked all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (every mention replaced by a placeholder token so embeddings encode context, not identity); K-means clusters them into K=50 groups (α=1 skips clustering and assigns individual sentences); count matrices A (target × cluster) and Acls (class × cluster) are built. (2) ILP: binary variables X (cluster→split), Y (target present in split), S (target in exactly one split), Z (cluster pair separated); constraints enforce exact cluster assignment, big-M target-presence projection, split-size lower bounds, per-class proportion bounds (1−δt), and exactly-one-split isolation; the objective maximizes α·ΣfᵢSᵢ/D_max − (1−α)·IL/I_max, both terms normalized to [0,1]. A feasibility pre-check (a secondary ILP minimizing ε + Σδt) finds the tightest achievable tolerances. Solved with Gurobi 13.0.2, 2–4 hour time limits, 32 GB RAM. (3) Evaluation: four split metrics (entity disjointness, leave-one-out entity coverage ratio, Hellinger distance, information leakage as mean cross-split cosine similarity) plus downstream test F1 for a BiLSTM-CRF (all 24 datasets) and fully fine-tuned Llama-2-7B (5 datasets, UniversalNER-style instruction format). Critical design decisions: (a) the α-weighted cluster feature space — justified but the confound between α and clustering granularity (α=1 uses no clustering) is only partly addressed; (b) one-way big-M projection to halve constraint count — sound, since spurious Y only blocks the objective; (c) entity masking before embedding — well-motivated so the similarity metric measures context, not entity identity. Key Results: Across 24 NER datasets (700–40,000 instances, 1–25 classes, 9 domains): EMPIRE (α=1, δ) raises entity disjointness by +10.1 pp over native splits and cuts ECR by 29.9 pp (p<0.001, Wilcoxon signed-rank, Holm-corrected), essentially matching MinCut (+10.7 pp) while improving Hellinger distance (−0.024) where MinCut degrades it (+0.099); MinCut partially achieves its disjointness by relaxing split sizes (e.g., AnatEM train 49.6%→51.1%). With α=0, EMPIRE lowers information leakage by 0.020 (δ) / 0.062 (δ=1) versus 0.013 for the authors' TopSim greedy baseline. Downstream: removing entity leakage drops BiLSTM-CRF test F1 by 0.087 (EMPIRE α=1, δ*) and 0.191 (MinCut) on average, lower on 19/24 and most datasets; removing context leakage alone does not (α=0: −0.009, not significant) — evidence that much of native-split F1 reflects entities seen in training. Llama-2-7B on 5 datasets tracks the BiLSTM-CRF (Pearson r=0.85 over 30 pairs; α=1: −0.115; α=0: +0.014), though without significance tests. The paper honestly reports solver limits: 6–18 of 24 solves hit the time limit depending on configuration, with MIP gaps up to 247% (FabNER) and 186% (TASTEset), and full disjointness at ε=0 is provably infeasible on 12 of 24 datasets because the largest shared-entity connected group exceeds the largest split. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (the ILP formulation jointly controlling entity leakage, context leakage, split sizes, and class balance is genuinely new — the paper's claim to be first here is credible) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the asymmetric effect: entity-leakage removal lowers F1, context-leakage removal does not; and the class-stranding confound under unconstrained splitting). The ingredients are standard — K-means clustering, big-M ILP linking, cosine-similarity objectives from DataSAIL, disjointness scoring from prior leakage work — so the contribution is a well-executed formulation combining known ideas for a setting (multi-label sentences needing class balance) where existing tools fail, not a new algorithmic primitive. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: cluster count K (50→200 leaves split quality within run-to-run noise but raises median MIP gap 5.0%→11.3% and time-limited solves 12→23 of 24), embedding model (Qwen3-0.6B and Jasper-600M vs MiniLM, with the subtlety that scoring splits in each encoder's own space inflates leakage up to 0.51), and the class-balance floor δ (costs α=1 at most 3.2 pp disjointness but up to 15.3 pp for α=0 on some datasets). Statistics: two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, Holm-corrected, with ±1 SD across datasets — but tests treat datasets as the unit, and model training uses a single fixed seed (42) with no seed variance for the F1 numbers. Code is uploaded as supplementary material with a detailed reproducibility statement; all 24 datasets are public. Methodological concerns: (1) the α=1 vs α<1 comparison confounds the objective weight with clustering granularity (K=0 vs K=50), which the authors note but do not resolve; (2) the information-leakage metric is computed in the same MiniLM space used to build the splits, a partial Goodhart risk, partially mitigated by the multi-encoder ablation; (3) TopSim is the authors' own baseline rather than an established method; (4) many solves terminate with large MIP gaps, so reported split quality reflects feasible incumbents, not optima, on hard datasets like FabNER and bc5cdr. This is an anonymous ICLR 2027 submission, not peer-reviewed results. Deployability: EMPIRICAL profile. Practical: Runs on 8 CPU cores and 32 GB RAM for the ILP (no GPU needed for splitting), but requires the commercial Gurobi solver, which the authors acknowledge limits accessibility since open-source alternatives (SCIP, CBC) are considerably slower. Efficient: Solves take up to 2–4 hours per dataset-configuration; entity-only mode (α=1, K=0) is substantially cheaper than the O(K²) similarity mode; K-means clustering is what makes it feasible at all. Effective: The evidence shows the splits do reduce leakage metrics and that entity leakage inflates F1 — but the method's implicit purpose (producing more trustworthy generalization estimates) is supported only indirectly, via lower F1 on leakage-reduced splits, with no external validation that those F1 values are closer to true out-of-distribution performance. Scalable: Untested beyond 40,000 instances; the paper's own ablation shows degradation (23/24 time-limited solves at K=200) and the authors admit that adding samples requires full re-optimization, so scaling to web-scale corpora is claimed (clustering "allows... millions of samples" in Appendix A.3) but never demonstrated. Delivers a software artifact: complete code including the ILP implementation, feasibility pre-check, baselines, and training pipelines, though no public repository URL is stated in the text. Strengths: - The joint formulation is real: the exactly-one-disjoint constraint (Eq. 5), the one-way big-M projection that halves constraint count, and the normalization that makes α a true interpolation weight are careful ILP engineering, and the feasibility pre-check that finds tightest achievable (ε, δ) before the main solve is a practical touch most splitting papers lack. - The class-balance confound finding is a genuine contribution to the leakage literature: showing that δ=1 splits strand 20–32 entity classes, leave 2–8 datasets with under 200 gold test spans, and depress F1 by 0.11–0.14 through class starvation rather than harder generalization — with a decomposition (Figure 3b) that fully accounts for the recovery gap by training-support band. - Honest solver reporting: per-dataset MIP gaps, time-limit counts, and the clean feasibility characterization (full disjointness at ε=0 requires the largest shared-entity connected group to fit in the largest split — verified on all 24 datasets) set a high evidential standard. - Breadth of the evaluation: 24 public datasets across 9 domains with two model families whose F1 deltas correlate at r=0.85. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The limitations section is direct and covers: NP-hard ILP sensitivity to dataset size and K, with solver timeouts; dependence on commercial Gurobi, limiting accessibility; the cluster-level surrogate mismatch for α<1 (optimizing centroid similarity rather than sample-level leakage); and static partitions requiring expensive re-optimization when data changes. The authors also candidly note in the results that α=1's disjointness shortfall on hard datasets "lies mostly in the data" and that α=0.5 interpolates rather than dominates. This is a credibility positive: limitations are confronted, not minimized. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The downstream evaluation omits the models that define current NER state of practice: a fine-tuned encoder (DeBERTa-v3, which the paper itself cites) or a modern LLM. BiLSTM-CRF is a 2015 architecture and Llama-2-7B is a 2023 base model tested on only 5 of 24 datasets with no significance testing; the headline claim that entity leakage inflates F1 is therefore established for dated models only. - Single seed (42) for all model training and a single embedding space for the leakage metric; the Wilcoxon tests capture across-dataset variance, not training variance, so per-dataset F1 deltas of 0.01–0.03 could be noise. - The α=1 vs α<1 configurations differ in clustering granularity (K=0 vs K=50), so the comparison between "entity mode" and "context mode" conflates objective with representation; a K=50, entity-disjointness-only variant would decouple these. - No demonstration that the leakage-reduced splits actually improve evaluation fidelity — e.g., correlating split-level leakage with a known ground-truth generalization gap, or testing on a domain-transfer task — so "lower but more trustworthy F1" remains an assumption. - Solver non-optimality (gaps up to 247%) means EMPIRE's reported quality on the hardest datasets understates what the formulation could achieve but also means the method's practical ceiling on large, entity-dense corpora is unproven; there is no comparison against simpler heuristics (e.g., connected-component-aware greedy assignment) that might achieve similar disjointness without an ILP solver. Bottom Line: A practitioner building or auditing NER benchmarks — particularly in biomedicine, law, or finance where entities recur — gains a concrete, well-engineered splitting tool and an important warning about class-balance confounds, and this beats MinCut for that purpose; readers wanting evidence about modern model evaluation will find the qualitative claim confirmed but the model coverage dated.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces PCBRouteAgent, a multimodal LLM agent that separates PCB routing into a Global Routing Planner (producing structured routing guides: MST-based connection topology, routing order, corridors, via-transition regions) and a Detailed Routing Executor (realizing traces via KiCad's native push-and-shove router with bounded local recovery), coupled by a feedback-driven replanning loop. - Why it's important: Reliable automatic PCB routing on real boards still requires manual intervention, and existing LLM agents evaluated in the PCBWorld environment complete fewer connections than rule-based autorouters on complex boards, at high API cost. - How it does it: The core trick is a structured, patchable "routing guide" as the interface between LLM-level planning and native geometric execution: the executor attempts bounded local fixes first, and only unresolved failures return as structured evidence (failed attempts, blocked positions, via-site candidates, history) that the LLM converts into validated local guide patches while preserving already-accepted routes. - The good: The strongest evidence is the same-backbone comparison: with Claude Haiku 5.5, PCBRouteAgent raises clean-pass rates from 0.633/0.343/0.00/0.00 to 1.00/0.929/0.80/0.10 across the four PCBWorld-Bench splits while using ~131× fewer model calls, 8.8× fewer tokens, and 4.3× lower API cost than the PCBWorld interactive agent. - Read it or not: Worth reading if you work on LLM agents for EDA/physical design or agentic plan–execute–repair architectures, since the structured-feedback replanning pattern and honest efficiency analysis are reusable; skip it if you want a fundamentally new routing algorithm, since the geometric core is KiCad's existing PNS router.

Problem & Motivation: PCB routing — connecting all pads of each electrical net with copper traces and vias while satisfying clearance, width, via, and signal-specific design rules — remains labor-intensive on complex boards despite decades of rule-based autorouters. Recent learning-based and LLM-agent approaches struggle with a coupled decision problem: a locally feasible route can block later connections, and a repeatedly failing connection may need a topology or layer change rather than another local attempt. The PCBWorld benchmark showed that LLM agents with access to native KiCad routing operations still lag rule-based routers on real boards. The gap this work targets is board-level coordination: deciding connection priorities, space allocation, and layer usage across an evolving board, rather than treating each net as an isolated path-finding problem. Key Idea: Treat the interface between LLM planning and native geometric execution as a structured, incrementally-patchable routing guide (connection topology, ordering, soft corridors, via-transition regions), and make failure information structured and actionable — the executor does bounded local recovery first, then returns evidence packets (last reached position, blockers, candidate via sites, prior failed shapes) that the multimodal LLM converts into validated local guide patches preserving accepted routes. This keeps the LLM out of per-waypoint geometric decisions while giving it exactly the evidence needed for board-level revisions. Methodology: The system is a plan–execute–repair loop (Algorithm 1). (1) Board representation: from the KiCad board, netlist, and rules, build multimodal inputs — four images (layout, front/back copper state, connectivity demand) plus a structured text sidecar with pad coordinates, layers, clusters, and rules. (2) Guide initialization: per net, build a weighted graph over disconnected connectivity clusters (edge weight = minimum Euclidean pad distance with a layer-incompatibility penalty) and take a minimum spanning tree (Prim-style) as the connection topology; order nets by total spanning-tree length (shortest first); per connection edge, define axis-aligned bounding-box corridors expanded by δ = 1.5 mm, split at the midpoint into two layer-specific corridors with a via-transition region when endpoints are on different layers. (3) Guided execution: the executor compiles edges into tasks, selects source/target anchors, generates candidate waypoints in corridor overlaps, and invokes KiCad's native push-and-shove router; layer transitions are attempted only within designated via regions; completion is verified by electrical connectivity, not by a successful tool call. (4) Bounded local recovery: PNS walkaround/shove, alternative waypoints, one grid-based A* detour, stage backtracks, and alternative anchors, capped by retry/execution budgets. (5) Feedback-driven replanning: unresolved failures produce structured feedback packets; the multimodal LLM generates a GlobalGuidePatch (ΔGt = Mθ(I, S, Gt, Dt, Kt; Psys, Preplan)), validated for consistency (cluster/corridor/layer references, stage overlaps, via-region coverage) with one bounded correction round, then merged. Budgets: 12 replans per board, ≤4 per connection, 5 batch rounds. Critical design decisions: (a) MST initialization — justified as avoiding combinatorial topology search, but the Euclidean-distance weight ignores congestion; (b) soft corridors rather than exact geometry — well-justified to preserve local flexibility; (c) LLM-only layer changes and vias (the executor never places a via outside a planned region) — a deliberate restriction that enables replanning but is not ablated against executor-initiated vias. Key Results: On PCBWorld-Bench (247 boards: D2 = 128 synthetic two-layer, D3-A = 99 small real-world, D3-B = 10 medium, D3-C = 10 large with >100 pads), evaluated with the official KiCad-based evaluator, PCBRouteAgent with Claude Opus 5.5 achieves clean-pass rates of 100% (D2), 94.9% (D3-A), 100% (D3-B), and 40% (D3-C), versus best baselines of 100% (KiCadRoutingTools/Freerouting on D2), 81% (PCBWorld PPO w/o finish on D3-A), 64% (Freerouting on D3-B), and 30% (Freerouting on D3-C). It also beats the published PCBWorld GPT-5.4 agent (42% D3-A, 0% D3-B). On D3-C it reaches 0.949 mean routability and cuts average DRVs from Freerouting's 32.0 to 6.3 (−80.3%), though 6 of 10 boards remain incomplete. Ablation (Table 5, same executor): removing LLM replanning drops clean-pass to 0.961/0.535/0.00/0.00, isolating 41.4 and 100 percentage-point gains on D3-A and D3-B. Same-model efficiency comparison (Haiku 5.5, both frameworks local): across 247 boards, 131× fewer model calls (22,529→172), 8.8× fewer tokens (105.7M→12.0M), 4.3× lower API cost ($20.72→$4.77), 14× less cumulative runtime (36.4→2.6 h). Costs of completion: D3-B wirelength is 10.9% higher than Freerouting; D3-A wirelength rises from 150.8 to 165.5 mm and vias from 0.22 to 0.79 with LLM replanning. Baselines are current within the PCBWorld setting (published Table 22 @1 values plus local reproductions), though only 10 boards each in D3-B/D3-C make those splits statistically fragile. Case studies show early routes blocking later signals (70/83 on one D3-C board) and a USB D+/D− differential pair routed independently (34.03/36.49 mm vs. matched 30.25 mm in the reference). Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL with elements of NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely new part is the structured-guide-plus-patch-replanning architecture for engine-grounded PCB routing and the quantified demonstration that the same LLM backbone performs far better and cheaper inside this framework than in PCBWorld's per-action loop. The components are individually standard: global/detailed routing decomposition (TritonRoute/OpenROAD), MST topology, bounding-box corridors, A* detours, ReAct/Reflexion-style feedback agents — the contribution is their specific integration and the structured failure-evidence protocol, not a new routing algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations exist and are targeted: the w/o-LLM variant (same executor and scripted recovery) cleanly isolates the LLM replanning contribution on all four splits, and the same-backbone Haiku comparison isolates the framework effect. However: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests; one scored board per instance (single rollout); the D3-B result explicitly includes retries of unscored model-response failures and up to five guarded angle-repair passes (accepted only if connectivity/DRC/wirelength do not worsen), so it is not a strict @1 estimate — the authors flag this honestly; the PCBWorld–Opus comparison was skipped on cost grounds, so the strongest backbone is never run in the baseline framework; no comparison to a dedicated rule-based replanner with the same executor. The method is developed and evaluated on the same PCBWorld-Bench environment (though the benchmark pre-exists this paper and D3 boards are real designs, mitigating Goodhart concerns). Code and prompts are publicly released at https://github.com/chip-ai-agent/PCBRouteAgent with a project page at https://chip-ai-agent.github.io/research/pcbrouteagent. This is a preprint (arXiv), not peer-reviewed; the PCBWorld baseline itself is a KDD 2026 workshop paper. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a built agent system with benchmark evaluation, plus released code — leaning SYSTEMS). - Practical: Runs on standard hardware against KiCad plus commercial LLM APIs; the artifacts are .kicad_pcb files, so adoption friction is low. - Efficient: Per-board API cost is $0.0002–$0.39 depending on split (Haiku), and it is 4.3× cheaper and 14× faster cumulatively than the PCBWorld agent; per-board wall time of 516 s on D3-C is the weakest point. - Effective: Evidence shows it solves the stated connectivity-plus-DRC problem on boards up to ~100 pads, but not beyond — 40% clean-pass on D3-C — and the USB case study shows it does not yet solve signal-integrity-aware routing. - Scalable: Not tested: D3-C tops out at 10 boards with >100 pads; behavior on 4-layer boards, >1,000 pads, or differential/signal-class constraints is only claimed via future work. The work delivers a released software artifact (agent code, prompt templates, algorithm) but no trained model weights; it stops short of a production router. Strengths: - The structured failure-evidence protocol (failed attempts, last reached position, blocker candidates, via-site suggestions, history of previously failed shapes the planner must not repeat) is a concrete, transferable pattern for plan–execute–repair agents well beyond PCB routing. - The same-backbone, same-evaluator efficiency comparison (Tables 6–8, including tokens per completed edge and cost per clean-pass board) is unusually honest for an agentic system paper and strengthens the framework claim more than headline clean-pass numbers alone. - The w/o-LLM ablation is correctly designed: it keeps the executor and scripted recovery fixed, so the LLM's contribution (up to 100 percentage points of clean-pass on D3-B) is attributable rather than confounded. - The failure analysis is candid and specific: it reports a board where its own output passes connectivity checks but routes a USB differential pair as independent 34.03 mm/36.49 mm traces, and dissects exactly why an early power route blocked later signals. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state: (1) large-board completion remains the main failure mode (6/10 D3-C boards incomplete); (2) early routing decisions can block later connections absent look-ahead in ordering and repair; (3) completed connectivity does not imply electrical validity — differential-pair relationships are not represented in the task specification or checker, so signal-specific constraints require explicit modeling; (4) improved completion costs wirelength (10.9% over Freerouting on D3-B) and vias; (5) the D3-B result includes retries and angle repair, so it is not a strict @1 estimate; (6) the ablation does not compare against a dedicated rule-based replanner or a general-purpose agent with the same execution tools. This is a direct, non-minimizing treatment of limitations — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No evaluation of the PCBWorld interactive agent with Claude Opus 5.5 — skipped for API cost — so the framework-vs-backbone attribution rests on Haiku comparisons only, and headline Opus numbers cannot be decomposed into model quality vs. framework quality. - The "guarded angle-repair" post-processing (up to five passes accepting only non-worsening changes) is a system component evaluated only via its end-to-end effect; its standalone contribution is never measured, and it is applied to Opus outputs but its interaction with the reported @1 convention is murky on D3-B. - All real-world splits are two-layer boards; no multi-layer evaluation despite layer-transition planning being a core component, and D3-B/D3-C contain only 10 boards each — split-level differences (e.g., 100% vs. 40%) could be dominated by a handful of boards. - The MST initialization uses pure Euclidean distance plus a layer penalty, ignoring congestion and obstacle density; no alternative weighting (e.g., DRC-aware or congestion-aware) is tried, so the initialization's quality is unexamined. - The LLM's board understanding is never tested in isolation (no probing of whether the multimodal input is actually used vs. the structured text); the planner's dependence on vision is asserted, not ablated. - Wirelength/via "costs of completion" comparisons partially conflate method quality with whether baselines leave nets unrouted — acknowledged by the authors, but no completion-normalized physical-cost metric is proposed. - No evaluation against Freerouting with a proper tuning pass or against commercial autorouters, so the practical gap to industrial tools is unquantified. Bottom Line: A practitioner building LLM agents for EDA or physical design gains concrete, reusable value here — the structured-guide/patch-replanning pattern and the cost-per-success accounting are the best-documented versions of this architecture I have seen for tool-grounded agents — but anyone seeking a better PCB router should note the geometric core is KiCad's own PNS engine and large-board performance (40% clean-pass) still trails what a tuned classical flow would need; read it for the agent architecture, not for routing algorithms.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces PISA, a prompt-adaptive cost-aware single-model LLM router based on soft cluster memberships and per-model logistic capability predictors, and PISA-E, an extension that jointly selects ensemble composition and cardinality at inference time using a training-free strict-majority (Poisson-binomial) success surrogate. - Why it's important: Web services serving heterogeneous LLM requests must balance response quality against per-query inference cost, and existing ensembles fix their size and composition regardless of the prompt or the operator's cost preference, wasting money on easy queries and under-performing on hard ones. - How it does it: The trick is to reuse per-model capability estimates (softmax memberships over X-means centroids fed into per-model logistic heads) inside a Poisson-binomial strict-majority probability as a tractable surrogate for ensemble success, so subsets of varying size can be scored and greedily selected without any ensemble-specific training, with a single scalar α trading quality against cost adjustable at inference time. - The good: The evaluation is broad and careful — four routing benchmarks (LLMRouterBench Track-2, RouterBench, FusionBench, SPROUT;
