Problem & Motivation: Operators of LLM-backed web services (search, recommendation, agents) face heterogeneous prompts and heterogeneous pricing across a model pool: always calling the expensive model wastes money, always calling the cheap one sacrifices quality, and different requests justify different spending. Single-model routing addresses this but cannot exploit complementary model strengths; ensembling exploits them but typically fixes ensemble size and composition at training/configuration time, offers a single operating point, and often optimizes cost only implicitly. The gap the authors target is a router where both which models to call and how many to call are decided per prompt, under an explicit cost–quality preference that can change at inference time without retraining. This is a real problem for cost-sensitive deployments, and the paper correctly identifies that prior work (LLM-TOPLA, DFPE with fixed teams; SelectLLM with fixed cardinality; ThriftLLM restricted to classification) covers only parts of it. Key Idea: The core insight is that a training-free surrogate for ensemble success — the probability that a strict majority of selected models answer correctly, computed by a Poisson-binomial dynamic program over per-model capability estimates under a conditional-independence assumption — is good enough to compare candidate ensembles of different cardinalities, and that under this surrogate even-cardinality ensembles are provably dominated by odd-cardinality subsets (removing one model lowers the majority threshold and the cost while never lowering the surrogate). This reduces the combinatorial subset-selection problem to scoring ⌈k_max/2⌉ greedy prefixes of a per-prompt utility ranking. The secondary idea, self-weighted BERTScore resolution (weighting both candidate and reference responses by estimated capability), extends MBR decoding cheaply. Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) Capability estimation: prompts are embedded with Qwen3-Embedding-8B, ℓ2-normalized embeddings are partitioned by X-means (which also picks K), soft memberships u(x) are computed via softmax over −β·cosine distances, and one L2-regularized logistic head per model maps u(x) to a capability estimate p̂_m(x) (regularization via 5-fold CV over 10 log-spaced λ values); correctness labels threshold benchmark scores at 0.5. (2) Subset selection: models are ranked by the linear utility J = α·p̂ + (1−α)·(1−C̄), where ensemble cost is normalized by the sum of the k_max largest average model costs; odd-cardinality prefixes up to k_max=11 are scored by the Poisson-binomial strict-majority probability and the argmax-utility subset is queried in parallel. (3) Response resolution: the final answer is the ensemble response maximizing self-weighted BERTScore similarity (Eq. 16). The framework is a constrained linear-scalarization selection problem, not a learned end-to-end system. Critical design decisions: (a) the conditional-independence assumption in the Poisson-binomial surrogate — examined via a Gaussian-copula alternative (Appendix B) that helps some resolvers but not the default; (b) cost modeled as training-set average per model (prompt-independent), a simplification that is stated but weakly justified; (c) greedy prefix search instead of exhaustive subset optimization — validated in Appendix E against exhaustive search on two benchmarks with comparable trade-off curves. The odd-cardinality dominance argument is correct for the surrogate, though it ignores any benefit extra responses might confer at the resolver stage. Key Results: On single-model routing, PISA achieves the highest macro-average hypervolume among the evaluated routers in both settings: 37.41 (ID) and 22.85 (OOD) versus 35.78 and 21.33 for EmbedLLM-MF, the strongest competitor, ranking first in six of eight benchmark–setting combinations. For ensembling, at α=1 PISA-E reaches 75.27% (ID) and 63.24% (OOD) macro-average task performance, exceeding the best deployable baselines (SelectLLM, DFPE) by 2.09 and 2.87 points; at intermediate operating points it matches or beats the best competitor's performance at ~36% (ID, 73.78% at 84×10⁻⁴ vs 73.18% at 132×10⁻⁴ USD/query) and ~25% (OOD, 60.85% at 292×10⁻⁴ vs DFPE 60.37% at 387×10⁻⁴) lower cost. Sweeping α from 1.0 to 0.3 cuts average cost 21.5× (ID) and ~106× (OOD) for 4.5–12.7 point performance drops. Adaptive cardinality beats the best fixed-k variant by 0.28 (ID) and 1.80 (OOD) HV points, and prompt-dependent ranking beats a fixed-global-ranking ablation by 4.96 (ID) and 0.91 (OOD) HV points. Notably, fixed k=1 beats PISA-E on RouterBench in both settings, and even at α=1 PISA-E routes 21.56% of ID queries to a single model. Baselines are current and recognizable (EmbedLLM, Avengers-Pro, SelectLLM, LLM-TOPLA, DFPE, LLM-Blender PairRanker, MBR), though several ensemble baselines are evaluated at a single operating point rather than a frontier. The oracle gap remains large (91.78% ID macro performance), showing substantial headroom. Tests are at standard benchmark scale, not stress scale. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW METHOD with an empirical finding. The genuinely novel elements are the ensemble-routing formulation with jointly adaptive composition and cardinality under an inference-time-adjustable cost–quality preference, the Poisson-binomial strict-majority surrogate with the odd-cardinality dominance argument, and the empirical demonstration that cardinality should be prompt-dependent. The components themselves are standard: soft k-means memberships, per-model logistic regression, majority-vote probability calculus, MBR/BERTScore decoding — the contribution is their composition into a training-free selection framework, not any individual technique. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough: Poisson-binomial vs Gaussian-copula surrogate, five resolver variants, adaptive vs six fixed cardinalities, prompt-dependent vs fixed-global ranking, greedy vs exhaustive subset search, k_max sensitivity (1–11), and hypervolume reference-point sensitivity for both PISA and PISA-E. Five seeds (11, 22, 33, 44, 55) with reported sample standard deviations; no significance tests. Code or model release: not stated. Methodological concerns: (1) all evaluation replays pre-recorded benchmark responses, so reported costs exclude the router's own overhead (embedding a prompt with an 8B model, X-means distances, BERTScore over up to 11 responses), which is material for a paper whose headline claim is cost reduction; (2) HV reference points are author-chosen, though the sensitivity analysis mitigates this; (3) hyperparameters are selected on validation task performance at α=1 while results are reported across α, a mild Goodhart risk; (4) baselines for ensembling are often single-operating-point methods compared against a tunable frontier, which flatters the frontier in cost terms though the authors report direct like-for-like comparisons too. No training/evaluation contamination is apparent — OOD evaluation uses genuinely held-out task groups (≈20–26% of prompts). Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (methods trained and evaluated offline on benchmark data; no live deployment). - Practical: Yes — the router is embeddings plus logistic regression plus a small dynamic program, runnable on a single CPU/GPU alongside any model pool. - Efficient: The selection stage is near-free, but the reported cost savings exclude embedding, resolver, and orchestration overhead, and the quality-first operating point on Track-2 costs 774×10⁻⁴ USD/query (over 5× the best baseline at α=0.75 macro level), so efficiency depends heavily on α. - Effective: The evidence shows it improves macro-average cost–performance on four offline benchmarks with strong ablations, but effectiveness in a live system with real latency and overhead is a proxy-based inference, not a measurement. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 40-model pools and ~44k prompts; the Poisson-binomial DP and greedy prefixes scale trivially with M, but capability-predictor retraining per new model and the accuracy of average-cost assumptions at larger pools are unexamined claims. The work delivers a method described in an algorithm (Algorithm 1); no library, CLI, or trained artifact is mentioned as released — it stops at paper form. Strengths: - The strict-majority surrogate with the odd-cardinality dominance argument is a clean, correct, and genuinely useful reduction: it makes training-free, cardinality-adaptive ensemble selection tractable and is the paper's real intellectual contribution. - The ablation suite actually isolates each claimed mechanism (surrogate type, resolver, adaptive cardinality, prompt-dependent ranking), and the authors report where components fail — e.g., fixed k=1 beating PISA-E on RouterBench and the copula estimator not helping the default configuration. - Inference-time α adjustment over a single fitted router (21.5×–106× cost sweep without retraining) is a practically meaningful property that fixed-ensemble baselines structurally cannot offer. - Honest treatment of evaluation fragility: reference-point sensitivity analyses for both HV comparisons are provided rather than left to reviewers. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge that the greedy prefix search does not guarantee the optimal subset (mitigated empirically in Appendix E), that the strict-majority surrogate is only a proxy since the resolver outcome also depends on inter-response relationships, that the copula alternative shows the independence assumption matters for some resolvers, that fixed cardinalities remain competitive on some benchmarks (RouterBench), and that HV depends on reference-point choice (addressed with sensitivity analyses). They confront these limitations directly rather than minimizing them, which strengthens credibility. They do not explicitly discuss the offline-replay evaluation setup or the exclusion of routing/resolver overhead from reported costs. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The cost model uses a single training-set average per model, ignoring prompt-dependent cost variation (e.g., output length on reasoning-heavy prompts); this is stated as a design choice but never ablated, and it directly feeds the cost term being optimized. - All results come from replaying pre-recorded benchmark responses, so conditional-independence properties, latency, parallel-query overhead, and BERTScore compute cost are never observed in a live loop; the headline "36% cost reduction" is against benchmark-recorded invocation costs only. - No statistical significance testing; several headline margins (e.g., 0.60 and 0.48 percentage points at matched-cost operating points, and the 0.28 ID HV margin over fixed k=1) are within roughly one standard deviation for some benchmarks. - Ensemble baselines (PairRanker, MBR, DFPE, LLM-TOPLA) use fixed top-k teams from global training performance while PISA-E adapts per prompt, so part of the gap over them conflates adaptive selection with the ensembling mechanism itself — though the fixed-global ablation (Table 7) partially controls for this. - Resolver behavior under even-cardinality ensembles is never tested: the odd-cardinality optimality proof holds only for the surrogate, not for the self-weighted BERTScore resolver, where an extra response could plausibly help. - No code or artifact release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility of a system paper with many tuned hyperparameters (β, K, k_max, per-benchmark configurations). Bottom Line: For anyone building cost-aware multi-LLM serving, this is worth reading for the strict-majority surrogate and the demonstrated value of prompt-adaptive ensemble cardinality — the most complete treatment of adaptive ensemble size in the routing literature — but the offline-replay evaluation and unreported system overhead mean the cost-savings claims need live-system replication before production trust.

Global Surveillance Under the Lens: Reconstructing Passive Dolev-Yao Intruders

P Modesti · arxiv.org · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds an automated toolchain, extending the AnBx protocol compiler, that reconstructs and validates passive Dolev–Yao intruder executions from PCAP captures of Java-serialised TCP traffic against a formal protocol specification. - Why it's important: State actors passively record encrypted traffic for 'harvest now, decrypt later' analysis, and no existing verification or forensics tool can check whether a concrete captured trace is consistent with a protocol specification's symbolic security model. - How it does it: The AnBx compiler's compile-time Dolev–Yao analysis is materialised as executable receive-side checks, which a generated passive intruder role evaluates against Java-serialised objects extracted from the PCAP, with interleaved sessions disambiguated by enumerating candidate channel assignments and scoring them with a lexicographic tuple (clean sessions, −failed checks, total checks). - The good: The evaluation over 121 protocols shows 97.8% object recovery and 94.2% successful reconstruction at one session, 89.3% at two and three concurrent sessions, and targeted experiments demonstrate that the checks discriminate role-mapping mismatches and detect 65 of 100 injected mutations. - The missing: All captures are self-generated under a man-in-the-middle Docker topology the authors control, with the protocol suite drawn from the authors' own compiler distribution, so no independently captured operational traffic and no external baseline comparison is evaluated. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on formal-methods tooling for security protocols or network forensics bridging symbolic models and concrete traffic; skip it if you need passive analysis of non-Java, non-pre-modelled protocols, which is explicitly out of scope.

Problem & Motivation: The Dolev–Yao model's dominant form is the active intruder, supported by tools like OFMC, ProVerif, and Tamarin, but real bulk surveillance (framed via the Snowden disclosures and the economics of harvest-now-decrypt-later from Blanco-Romero et al.) is passive: the adversary records traffic and analyses it later. The paper identifies a concrete tooling gap: verification tools synthesise symbolic attacks but cannot validate a concrete network trace against a specification, while forensics tools like Wireshark or Zeek display bytes without protocol semantics. The beneficiaries are analysts assessing what captured protocol executions expose to a passive observer, and protocol designers wanting to gauge resilience to retrospective analysis. The surveillance framing is explicitly defensive — the goal is to make recoverable information explicit, not to build an intelligence-collection system. Key Idea: The core trick is to reuse the protocol compiler rather than write a new analyser: the AnBx compiler already performs Dolev–Yao deduction at specification-compile time, and this analysis can be materialised as executable receive-side checks (well-formedness, equality, inversion, seen) in a generated intruder role, which is then fed reconstructed objects extracted from the PCAP. Session ambiguity in interleaved captures is resolved by enumerating all (N!)^(K−1) candidate channel-to-session assignments and letting the specification-derived checks themselves score which reconstruction is consistent. This turns a symbolic verification artifact into a forensic validator — deduction performed in advance, evaluated on concrete observations. Methodology: The pipeline has five stages. (1)–(2) Dockerised protocol execution under a passive man-in-the-middle star topology produces a PCAP. (3) TShark extracts raw application-layer payloads per directional TCP stream (using the `data` field rather than `tcp.payload` to avoid dissector interference); complete streams are saved and object extraction is deferred to a generated `ObjCheck` class that reads each stream in one pass with `ObjectInputStream`, preserving the Java serialisation reference table to resolve `TC_REFERENCE` handles and handle `TC_ENDBLOCKDATA` markers. (4) `sessionbuild.py` pairs directional streams into bidirectional connections, groups connections into connected components by shared endpoint IPs, and enumerates candidate arrangements ((N!)^(K−1), capped at 120) when a component holds M > K connections. (5) Two passes: Pass A runs ObjCheck per candidate and snapshots per-step `.ser` files; Pass B compiles and runs the passive intruder role per candidate per session, parses `CHECK #`/`check FAILED!` markers, and scores candidates by the lexicographic tuple (n_clean_sessions, −total_failed_checks, total_checks). Critical design decisions: deferring object extraction to full-stream deserialisation rather than byte-level splitting (well-justified — object boundaries are undetectable by magic-number scanning); rejecting timestamps as a correctness criterion in favour of specification-guided scoring (justified empirically — 17.6%–25.5% of K=2 protocols required a non-identity arrangement); and treating the intruder as just another agent role so check generation applies uniformly (a clean architectural move, though it inherits the compiler's typing discipline, which is stricter than the type-free Dolev–Yao term model). The paper is careful to define the checks as consistency conditions, not a proof of security. Key Results: On 121 protocols (Needham–Schroeder, Woo-Lam, Carlsen, Andrew Secure RPC, TMN, ISO, Diffie-Hellman variants, SET and iKP families), single-session (N=1): 97.8% object recovery (451/461) and 94.2% successful reconstruction (114/121) with the standard JDK provider; 97.0% and 92.6% with Bouncy Castle. DY check accuracy is 99.8% under both providers (2 failed checks each). Multi-session on the 112 parallel-capable protocols: 89.3% successful reconstruction at both N=2 and N=3, with ~97.2% object recovery. The per-object rate is stable across N while the per-protocol rate drops, because any single session missing an object fails the protocol. Provider-specific failures cluster: all three BC-only failures involve Diffie-Hellman serialisation. The candidate-selection loop is shown to be necessary, not decorative: 9/51 K=2 protocols at N=2 and 13/51 at N=3 select a non-identity arrangement. Three iKP-family protocols at N=2 recover every object yet fail cross-session freshness checks because no candidate pairs matching sessions — an honest reporting of a residual failure. Runtime: ~54.2s (JDK) / ~61.5s (BC) per single-session run, with 75%+ consumed by Docker orchestration; actual protocol execution is 1.4% of total. Mutation detection (Section 4.6.3): 65/100 injected mutations flagged across 20 protocols — 34/40 deletions, 28/40 duplications, but only 3/20 cross-session swaps, which the authors correctly attribute to the Dolev–Yao limit that a keyless adversary cannot distinguish same-shaped ciphertexts. Baselines are effectively nonexistent: there is no competing tool to compare against, which the related-work table (Table 8) argues is because no prior tool combines PCAP input, executable output, and formal validation. Scale is standard (121 protocols, ≤3 sessions), not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL and NEW FORMULATION, with an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION component. The genuinely novel element is the operational instantiation of a passive Dolev–Yao intruder as compiler-generated receive-side checks evaluated over PCAP-reconstructed objects — no prior tool combines PCAP input, executable output, and specification-based validation (the closest precursor, Garcia & Modesti's attack-trace reconstruction, handles only abstract OFMC traces with an active intruder and single sessions). The extraction machinery (TShark + Java deserialisation) and the lexicographic scoring are competent engineering of standard techniques; the candidate-enumeration approach to session disambiguation is straightforward combinatorics made useful by specification-guided scoring. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablation-style evidence is present and unusually honest: the hand-written-implementation experiments isolate wire-format dependence from compiler/AnBxJ dependence (3 programs, all recovered exactly); the role-mismatch experiment is a well-designed 2×2 matrix showing failures attributable solely to identity-equality checks; the mutation study separates check-failure from check-count-deficit signals and excludes protocols with dirty baselines. Timing is reported with means, medians, and standard deviations per stage, and the authors correctly attribute the JDK-vs-BC runtime gap to run-to-run Docker variability rather than claiming a real performance difference. No multiple seeds or significance tests for the accuracy figures, though the deterministic pipeline makes this less critical. Code is released: the AnBx compiler at https://paolo.science/anbx/ and the pipeline at https://github.com/paolo-mo/passive-dolev-yao-intruder. Methodological concerns: (1) the entire evaluation is on self-generated captures using protocols shipped with the authors' own compiler distribution — a self-referential setup where the checking tool and the checked implementations come from the same toolchain (Goodhart risk, though the hand-written experiments partially mitigate extraction-side circularity); (2) no external baseline comparison is possible or attempted; (3) the paper is an arXiv preprint (2611.07170), not stated as peer-reviewed. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL/SYSTEMS — a built toolchain evaluated by running it. Practical: Yes — it runs on a 2014-era laptop (Intel i7-4700HQ, 16 GB RAM, Windows 11) with commodity software (TShark, Docker, OpenJDK, Ant, Python). Efficient: Reconstruction-specific cost is 11.7–14.2s per protocol excluding Docker; Docker capture dominates (41–46s) but is an artifact of the lab setup, not inherent to reconstruction. Effective: It demonstrably solves the stated proxy — consistent reconstruction of controlled captures — but the mutation study shows only 65% of tampered traces are flagged, so as a validator it is partial by design, and effectiveness on real operational traffic is untested. Scalable: Not beyond N=3; the candidate space grows factorially as (N!)^(K−1) with a hard cap of 120 arrangements (feasible to N≤5 at K=2), and content-based pruning for larger N is deferred to future work. The work delivers a concrete software artifact (compiler extension, Python orchestration scripts, generated Java intruder code) with a public repository — not paper-form only. Strengths: - The central reframing — compiler-derived symbolic checks as offline forensic validators over reconstructed traffic — is a genuinely new bridge between formal verification and network forensics, and the paper is precise that the checks are consistency conditions, not security proofs. - The evaluation design goes beyond headline numbers: the hand-written implementation experiments (including a pure-JDK program with no AnBxJ on the classpath, and a hybrid RSA+AES program exercising interface-typed and byte[] wire paths) cleanly establish that extraction depends only on the wire format. - Unusually candid negative reporting: the iKP cross-session freshness failures at N≥2, the BC-specific Diffie-Hellman serialisation failures, the unexplained 0x67 byte in NSL, and the 3/20 cross-session swap detection rate are all reported and correctly explained via the Dolev–Yao information limit rather than spun as tool failures. - The candidate-scoring mechanism is validated as load-bearing (Table 4 quantifies exactly when the time heuristic fails), not presented as an afterthought. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state directly: no decryption without keys and unsuitability for forward-secret protocols like TLS 1.3; the requirement for an AnBx specification and channel-to-step map (validation is impossible for undocumented protocols); no support for stateful behaviour like session resumption or key rotation; dependence on deployment metadata (`.properties`) matching the PCAP; the factorial candidate-space cap with an unexercised heuristic fallback; the heuristic lexicographic scoring with fragile textual-marker parsing; the Java-only wire format and deserialisation-vulnerability risk of running on untrusted PCAPs; and — most importantly — that all captures are self-generated, so the evaluation establishes feasibility, not performance on independently captured operational traffic, with the absence of any public corpus noted. This is a direct, non-minimising limitations section, which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the acknowledged limitations, a reviewer would flag: (1) the entire protocol suite comes from the AnBx/OFMC distribution and the authors' own prior work (SET/iKP families are compiled through the same toolchain), so the 121-protocol figure overstates breadth of independent validation — the tool has never seen a protocol implementation it did not help generate, except the three toy hand-written programs; (2) the passive intruder in the capture configuration is realised by network topology (Docker star), meaning the PCAPs are produced under exactly the conditions the reconstruction assumes — a fully orchestrated loop with no noise, packet loss, reordering, or middleware (proxies, NAT traversal, TLS-underlying transport) that real captures would contain; (3) no comparison of reconstruction effort or output quality against even a partial baseline (e.g., Zeek custom dissector or manual Wireshark analysis) to substantiate the practical-impact claim; (4) the mutation study covers only 20 of 121 protocols and three mutation classes, and the 65% flag rate — with cross-session swaps nearly undetectable — means the tool's validator role is thin, which the paper explains but does not treat as a spur to strengthen the checks; (5) the Docker capture stage is a lab artifact, yet its cost is baked into the headline runtimes without a capture-method-neutral timing breakdown (partially given via the PCAP-measured protocol execution time). None of these undermines the feasibility claim; they do bound the generalisation claim. Bottom Line: This is a solid, honestly reported proof-of-concept that uniquely connects formal protocol specifications to concrete captured traffic for the passive-adversary case, and practitioners in formal-methods-based security analysis will gain from reading it — but itsJava-only, self-captured, own-toolchain evaluation means it is a laboratory demonstration of feasibility, not yet a usable forensic instrument for real-world surveillance analysis.

LowRAM: Low-Rank Keys and Amortised Values for Composable KV Cache Compression at Test-Time (10 ▲ )

Teresa Delgado, Hugo Hazard, Martin Benfeghoul, Jun Wang, Zafeirios Fountas · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 9 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces LowRAM, a post-training KV cache compression pipeline that fits a per-head test-time predictor mapping keys to values (storing exact residuals only for the worst-predicted tokens) and compresses keys via cross-layer low-rank factorisation, composing with quantisation and eviction to reach 26.9× compression at 94.5% of baseline performance on long-context benchmarks. - Why it's important: The KV cache dominates memory and caps batch size and throughput in long-context LLM serving, and most open-weight models still use full caches, so cheap, composable post-training compression directly increases serving capacity without retraining. - How it does it: The core move is asymmetry: exploit the previously unused within-head redundancy where values are predictable from keys (a per-head two-layer MLP fitted during prefill, with error-ranked residual storage), while compressing keys separately with xKV's cross-layer shared SVD basis, since keys predict poorly but are low-rank. - The good: The ablations are convincing and quantitative — removing the residual store drops recovered LongBench performance from 99.0% to 64.9%, replacing the MLP with a linear predictor drops it to 57.5%, and sharing the predictor across heads costs 19.5 points — showing exactly which components carry the method, and the throughput crossover (5× peak decode throughput at 262K context, batch 28) is measured, not claimed. - The missing: Evaluation is confined to LongBench and RULER (both long-context proxy suites), with no general-capability benchmarks (e.g., MMLU, GSM8K) to detect off-distribution degradation, and no comparison against the strongest predictive-compression baseline (AQUA-KV) on equal terms; long-generation settings are untested. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building LLM inference systems or working on KV compression — the asymmetric key/value design and the source-target analysis (reconstruction error correlates weakly with downstream performance) are genuinely useful insights — but skip if you only care about methods validated beyond synthetic/long-context QA workloads.

Problem & Motivation: Autoregressive decoding requires caching keys and values for every prior token; this cache grows linearly with context length and batch size and becomes the dominant memory cost, capping throughput in long-context serving. Architectural fixes (GQA, multi-head latent attention, linear attention, state-space models) require pretraining, so most deployed open-weight models (Llama, Mistral, Qwen) carry full KV caches. Existing post-training compression exploits three redundancy axes — token eviction, quantisation, and low-rank factorisation across tokens/layers/features — leaving the redundancy between keys and values unexplored, even though both are projections of the same hidden state. The paper targets operators serving long-context inference on frozen pretrained models who need aggressive compression without finetuning. Key Idea: Within each attention head, the value vector is largely a learnable function of its own key, so the value cache can be replaced by a small per-head map (fit once per context at test time) plus exact residuals for only the hardest-to-predict tokens; keys, which resist prediction, are instead compressed by their low-rank cross-layer structure. The linear branch of the predictor is initialised from the Slim Attention prior (pseudoinverse of the key projection times the value projection), giving an offline-computable near-inverse of the GQA key/value projections as a starting point. Methodology: The pipeline has four stages. (1) Source-target analysis: per-layer predictors are trained under a matched 3× budget to reconstruct each layer's keys or values from alternative sources (previous/current-layer keys/values/concatenations), evaluated on both reconstruction MSE and recovered LongBench performance; current-layer keys→values wins on downstream performance. (2) Key compression: following RoPE inversion (rotations re-applied at attention time), xKV factorises layer-grouped key caches as K_l ≈ A·B_l with a shared basis A; a randomised Cholesky-QR replaces exact SVD for a 4× factorisation speedup. (3) Value amortisation: a per-head two-layer MLP with residual branch f(k) = W2·ReLU(W1·k + b1) + b2 + k·W_lin is fitted layer-by-layer during prefill to minimise MSE to the cached values; per-token reconstruction errors are ranked and exact residuals stored for the top-p fraction. (4) Efficiency mechanisms: a FOMAML meta-learned initialisation (offline, one pass over FineWeb-Edu, <5 min per model) reduces per-context adaptation to 2 gradient updates; landmark-guided selective reconstruction (ShadowKV-style chunk retrieval with a persistent buffer) reconstructs only the top-k chunks per decode step. The compression ratio is defined by explicit byte-level accounting (harmonic mean of key/value ratios, with eviction and selective-reconstruction overheads included). Critical design decisions: per-head rather than per-layer predictors (well-justified by a 19.5-point ablation), error-ranked rather than random residual placement (random selection collapses to <40% NIAH accuracy vs. 98% for MSE-ranked), and basing design choices on downstream recovery rather than reconstruction error (justified by the weak error-performance correlation shown in Figure 3). Key Results: Tested on Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and Qwen3.5-4B across RULER (4K–64K) and LongBench (>10K subset for extreme compression). At 4× compression, LowRAM recovers 96.0–99.6% of baseline on LongBench and RULER except Llama on RULER (93.9%); value amortisation alone keeps keys exact and stays at 98.2% (RULER) / 99.3% (LongBench) at 4×. The full stack (LowRAM + eviction + TurboQuant at 4-bit keys / 2-bit value residuals) reaches 26.9× compression at 94.5% of baseline on Mistral LongBench >10K, versus 10.0× for eviction alone (91.6%) and 7.5× for quantisation alone (92.3%) at the 90%-recovery threshold. Efficiency: meta-initialisation cuts TTFT overhead from 26.3× (150 updates) to 1.3× baseline; LowRAM-SR sustains batch size 28 where the baseline OOMs and reaches ~5× peak decode throughput at 262K context. Baselines (H2O-style eviction with an attention-predictor, TurboQuant, xKV) are current, though some are author-adapted; Qwen3.5-4B ratios are reported relative to only its full-attention layers' cache. A notable negative-space finding: quantisation composes synergistically (raising Llama RULER recovery at 4× from 93.9% to 99.4% because cheaper residuals buy more of them), but eviction composes poorly at short contexts because the fixed predictor cost is not amortised. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (value cache amortisation — a test-time learned key→value map with error-ranked residual storage — plus the asymmetric pipeline) and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (within-head key-to-value predictability as an exploitable redundancy axis, and the observation that reconstruction MSE does not track downstream performance). The key-compression half (xKV), RoPE inversion, Slim Attention linear prior, ShadowKV-style selective retrieval, TurboQuant, and FOMAML are all existing components; the contribution is the source-target analysis and the principled asymmetric composition, which is more than a mechanical combination but builds heavily on prior parts. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough: component removal (Table 7), residual-selection strategy comparison with attention-output MSE and n=200 NIAH accuracy (Figure 5), a full sweep of adaptation budget vs. Slim initialisation (Table 8), joint vs. per-head W_lin (Table 9), and complete compression-ratio sweeps (Tables 10–11). No error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported; single-seed runs are implied throughout. Reproduction settings are detailed in appendices, but no public code, data, or model release is mentioned. Methodological concerns: evaluation rests entirely on LongBench and RULER, so unknown is whether compression degrades capabilities outside long-context QA/retrieval; the headline baseline comparison in Figure 1 uses an adapted eviction method (AttentionPredictor) and a modified TurboQuant (QJL omitted, with the authors' own justification); Qwen3.5-4B compression ratios are relative to a subset of layers, which flatters direct comparison; and the 90%-recovery threshold for Table 4 is a self-chosen operating point. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS component — kernels, TTFT/throughput measurements). - Practical: Yes — all components (per-head MLPs, randomised Cholesky-QR, chunk retrieval) run on standard GPU hardware; meta-training is a one-off <5-minute single-GPU job per model. - Efficient: Favourable at long context — 4× memory reduction, 1.3× TTFT overhead with meta-init, 5× peak decode throughput at 262K tokens — but with a fixed per-head-parameter cost that makes it a net loss below ~2–3K tokens, and full per-context fitting (150–300 updates) costs 26–55× TTFT if amortisation is not available. - Effective: Evidence supports the stated goal on long-context benchmarks (94.5% recovery at 26.9×), but effectiveness on general workloads, multi-turn conversation, and long generation is untested; decode-time new tokens are stored exactly, sidestepping one failure mode by scope limitation. - Scalable: Tested up to 262K context and batch 28 with memory-bound crossover behaviour measured; beyond that, only argued — landmark-pool retrieval cost grows with prefix length and is not stress-tested above 262K. The work delivers no released software artifact; it stops at paper form with detailed hyperparameters. Strengths: - The central empirical insight — values are strongly predictable from within-head keys while keys are not, and key errors are more harmful than value errors because they perturb attention logits before softmax — is established by a controlled source-target analysis rather than asserted, and it directly motivates the asymmetric design. - The finding that reconstruction MSE correlates weakly with downstream performance (Figure 3), and the resulting choice to select residuals by error while validating by downstream recovery, is a genuinely non-obvious methodological point for the predictive-compression literature. - The ablation depth is exemplary: the residual store (−34.1 pts), non-linear predictor (−41.5 pts), and per-head modelling (−19.5 pts) are each isolated, and the eviction-composition failure at short contexts is diagnosed precisely (fixed predictor cost not amortised) rather than hidden. - The synergy analysis with quantisation (2-bit residuals buy more residuals, netting higher recovery at higher compression) is a concrete, actionable result for stack design. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that long generations are not evaluated (would require periodically re-compressing generated suffixes rather than a single prefill-time fit), and that the split between context-general and context-specific key-to-value structure — inferred only indirectly from warm-start/Slim gains vs. adaptation gains — is unresolved. They also openly discuss that LowRAM degrades on short contexts (RULER 4K) and composes poorly with eviction there, and quantify the accuracy cost of meta-initialisation (1.4–4.4 points on RULER, 2.4 on LongBench >10K). This is direct, quantified confrontation with limitations — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No evaluation beyond LongBench/RULER: the community cannot tell whether 2-bit residuals and 4× key compression degrade reasoning, coding, or instruction-following capabilities that these benchmarks do not probe. - AQUA-KV, the closest prior predictive method (and the one whose probing configurations the source-target analysis revisits), is analyzed but never compared head-to-head as an end-to-end baseline at matched compression. - Test-time fitting of per-layer, per-head networks introduces a per-context data-dependent transformation with no reported variance across contexts or seeds; single-run recovered percentages could shift by points. - The meta-learned initialisation is trained on FineWeb-Edu — a distribution unlike many served workloads (code, dialogue, multilingual) — and the paper does not test whether meta-init quality degrades off this distribution. - Byte-level compression accounting (Appendix C) is self-defined; the selective-reconstruction and landmark overheads are included, which is good, but cross-paper comparability of the 26.9× figure is not established. - Selective reconstruction caps attention at 2464 tokens per decode step regardless of true attention spread; tasks requiring genuinely global attention over long prefixes are not isolated. Bottom Line: A practitioner working on LLM inference or KV compression should read this: the key→value amortisation idea is a real, previously unexploited redundancy axis with strong ablated evidence and measured throughput gains, but the method is validated only on long-context QA benchmarks, ships no code, and its short-context and general-capability behavior remain open questions.

SplatAnything: Gaussian Spacing Normalization for Feed-forward 3DGS across Arbitrary Scenes (61 ▲ )

Hao Yu, Zhenwei Wang, Yongzhen Hu, Yuning Gong, Junta Wu, Xiaowei Zhou, Hujun Bao, Tengfei Wang, Chunchao Guo, Sida Peng · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 9 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces SplatAnything, a feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting framework whose core contribution is Gaussian Spacing Normalization (GSNorm) — replacing radial-distance scene normalization with normalization by the median Gaussian center spacing — plus a 7-dataset cross-domain benchmark with controlled viewpoint extrapolation and input sparsity. - Why it's important: Feed-forward 3DGS models fail to generalize across scene scales, camera baselines, and focal lengths because supervision targets for Gaussian scales become ambiguous; a one-line normalization fix that removes this ambiguity transfers across the whole model family built on geometry foundation models. - How it does it: GSNorm rescales geometry, depth, and camera translations so that the scene-level median of per-pixel Gaussian spacing (approximately depth divided by the geometric mean of focal lengths) equals 1, canonicalizing the spacing statistic that actually determines required Gaussian scale. - The good: A controlled ablation (Table 3) shows GSNorm beats both RDNorm and post-hoc scale calibration under identical architecture and training across 1–64 input views (e.g., DISTS 0.198 vs 0.223 at 4 views), directly supporting the claimed mechanism rather than a generic performance win. - The missing: The benchmark, protocol, co-visibility thresholds, and alignment procedure were all designed by the authors, and evaluation is perceptual-metric only (LPIPS/DISTS in the main tables), with no error bars, seeds, or significance tests; monocular results also lag SHARP on 4 of 7 datasets. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building feed-forward 3DGS or geometry-foundation-model pipelines, since the normalization-space insight is cheap to adopt and empirically validated; skimmable if you only need benchmark numbers on datasets you don't use.

Rigor (70) is lifted by the scale-calibration ablation that cleanly falsifies the post-hoc-correction alternative, then dragged down by a self-designed evaluation protocol, no error bars or seeds, and no confirmed code/weights release. Non-Obviousness (75) is the paper's strongest dimension: identifying that spacing, not distance, is the statistic the supervision target must be commensurate with is a real, derivation-backed insight. Problem & Motivation: Feed-forward 3DGS methods reconstruct a 3D Gaussian scene in seconds by predicting per-pixel Gaussian attributes on top of a geometry foundation model, and are used for fast 3D reconstruction and content creation. These geometry backbones output geometry in a radial-distance-normalized (RDNorm) space — the mean radial distance of 3D points to the reference camera is scaled to a canonical value. The paper's core observation is that RDNorm does not canonicalize the spacing between neighboring Gaussian centers, which depends on depth and focal length even after RDNorm. Since adequate surface coverage requires Gaussian scale to match local Gaussian spacing, the effective supervision target for predicted Gaussian scales shifts by up to 4.5× across scene categories (Fig. 4: relative median spacing of 0.30 to 1.36 after RDNorm). The same local image content therefore maps to different Gaussian-scale targets in different scenes, producing holes (under-sized Gaussians) in small object-centric scenes and over-smoothing (over-sized Gaussians) in large outdoor scenes, and capping cross-scene generalization for a single model. Key Idea: The core trick: define the scene-level normalization factor from a representative statistic of Gaussian spacing instead of a radial statistic. Under per-pixel prediction and a locally constant-depth approximation, horizontal and vertical Gaussian spacing are d ≈ D/f, so the paper uses the geometric mean d ≈ D/√(fx·fy) and sets the normalization factor to the median of this quantity over all valid pixels and views (Eq. 10). Because the median is equivariant to positive scaling, this exactly canonicalizes the scene-level median Gaussian spacing to 1 by construction. The key insight is identifying which statistic to canonicalize — spacing, not distance — because spacing is what the Gaussian-scale target must be commensurate with. Methodology: Pipeline: (1) a frozen WorldMirror 2.0 geometry foundation model estimates per-view depth, intrinsics, and poses from N input images (4–64 at inference) in RDNorm space; (2) GSNorm rescales depth, geometry, and camera translations by sg = median(Dᵢ(u)/√(fx,ᵢ·fy,ᵢ)) into Gaussian-spacing-normalized space; (3) a Gaussian Backbone (initialized from and fine-tuned from the WorldMirror 2.0 backbone) plus a lightweight from-scratch GSHead predict per-pixel opacity, rotation, log-space scale (clamped at 0.3), and SH coefficients, with Gaussian centers fixed at the unprojected points; (4) a voxel-merge strategy (from AnySplat) reduces redundant primitives from overlapping views. Training uses MSE + LPIPS rendering losses (λ = 1 each) for 20,000 iterations on 64 NVIDIA H20 GPUs with 4–32 input views at dynamically varying 504–1024 resolution. Training data spans 14 datasets (8 synthetic, 6 real, ~21k scenes). Critical design decisions: canonicalizing via the median (robust; justified against mean sensitivity to outliers), fixing Gaussian centers to unprojected geometry (ablated — predicts center offsets degrades DISTS by ~0.004–0.008 across view counts), and a scene-level scale alignment between predicted and ground-truth camera trajectories during training. The paper also contributes a benchmark protocol: source views sampled from a compact contiguous trajectory arc, target views selected by occlusion-aware symmetric co-visibility Csym ∈ [0.20, 0.60), and a fixed-span strategy so that 1/4/8/16/32/64-view settings share spatial coverage and differ only in density. Key Results: On the authors' 7-dataset benchmark (ScanNet, NRGBD, DL3DV, Tanks & Temples, Mip-NeRF 360, ETH3D, DTU) averaged over 4–64 input views, SplatAnything achieves the best DISTS/LPIPS on all seven datasets in both pose-free and pose-conditioned settings — e.g., pose-conditioned DISTS of 0.185/0.186/0.215/0.251/0.219/0.133/0.184 on ScanNet/NRGBD/DL3DV/T&T/Mip360/ETH3D/DTU, versus the strongest baseline Mirror2-GS (Pose Cond.) at 0.195/0.231/0.239/0.304/0.272/0.201/0.315. Baselines are current (AnySplat, YoNoSplat, DA3-GS, Mirror2-GS, QuerySplat, DepthSplat, TokenGS, tttLRM, ReSplat; ICLR 2026-era and 2025–2026 arXiv methods). Gains are largest on DTU and T&T (object-centric/large-scale, where RDNorm variation is worst). Two notable counter-results: (1) on monocular input (Table 2), SHARP beats SplatAnything on ScanNet (0.223 vs 0.238 DISTS), NRGBD, DL3DV LPIPS, ETH3D, and DTU; (2) ReSplat achieves higher PSNR in several settings (e.g., 19.03 vs 18.39 at 4 views pose-conditioned), which the authors attribute to ReSplat's over-smoothed outputs degrading under extrapolation. Inference latency is 411 ms for 4 views and 11,037 ms for 64 views on one H20 — faster than DA3-GS/QuerySplat/TokenGS but ~1.7× slower than Mirror2-GS and AnySplat. The method was tested at standard academic scale, not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (normalization space for Gaussian prediction) + NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (cross-domain extrapolation protocol). GSNorm is genuinely a new and well-argued choice of canonicalization statistic, but it is a one-line change to an existing normalization scheme, and the rest of the system (frozen geometry backbone + per-pixel attribute head + voxel merging) is a competent assembly of established components; the benchmark's co-visibility-controlled extrapolation protocol is a useful methodological contribution but built from standard co-visibility concepts. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and targeted: normalization space (RDNorm vs RDNorm+scale-calibration vs CDNorm vs DNorm vs GSNorm, Table 12), post-hoc scale correction (shown insufficient), and four training design choices (backbone fine-tuning, fixed centers, data scaling, view-sampling strategy, Table 13). The scale-calibration ablation is the strongest piece of evidence — it shows that correcting Gaussian scales after prediction in RDNorm space does not recover GSNorm's performance, isolating the mechanism to the prediction space itself. Weaknesses: no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests anywhere; the primary metrics are perceptual (LPIPS/DISTS) chosen following SHARP, with PSNR relegated to an appendix discussion that argues against the metric where the method loses; the evaluation benchmark is designed by the authors and used to evaluate both their method and baselines, so protocol choices (co-visibility interval, trajectory-arc source sampling) may favor the proposed method; no code or model weights release is stated beyond an unresolvable "Project page" link. The method is trained on 14 datasets but evaluated on 7 disjoint ones — no training/eval contamination is apparent from the listed data. Deployability: (4-property check):** Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS artifact component). - Practical: Yes — runs on a single H20 GPU in BF16 at 411 ms (4 views) to 11 s (64 views), though H20 availability is region-constrained and no consumer-GPU numbers are given. - Efficient: Moderate — 1.7–1.8× slower per-scene than Mirror2-GS and AnySplat at equal view counts, but 3–28× faster than DA3-GS, QuerySplat, and TokenGS. - Effective: The evidence supports solving cross-scene/cross-scale generalization on perceptual metrics, but the effect is measured on the authors' own extrapolation protocol, and monocular results show it does not dominate in the hardest sparse regime. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 64 input views and ~1K resolution; 64-view latency of 11 s suggests superlinear cost growth, and behavior at 10× scene scale (city-scale captures) is claimed only implicitly via MatrixCity training data, not measured. The work delivers a trained model and benchmark protocol (project page referenced); no public code/weights URL is confirmed in the text. Strengths: - Identifies a precise, previously unnoticed failure mode (RDNorm leaves up to 4.5× variation in median Gaussian spacing across scene categories) and traces it to a concrete supervision-ambiguity mechanism, rather than treating cross-scene degradation as an opaque generalization gap. - The fix is a derivation, not a heuristic: the spacing statistic d ≈ D/√(fx·fy) follows directly from the pinhole model, and the median's scale-equivariance makes the canonicalization exact by construction. - The scale-calibration ablation cleanly falsifies the alternative explanation (that post-hoc scale correction would suffice), which is the kind of control most normalization papers omit. - The benchmark's fixed-span, co-visibility-controlled protocol decouples input density from scene coverage — a genuinely better-controlled design than standard interpolated-view evaluation, reusable by future work. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that SplatAnything depends on geometry priors from a foundation model and may degrade when reliable geometry cannot be recovered from extremely sparse or challenging inputs, and that it primarily reconstructs visible regions, leaving holes in unobserved areas (with generative priors named as future work). They also candidly discuss, in the appendix, that ReSplat beats them on PSNR and argue the metric favors over-smoothing — a transparent, if self-serving, treatment of an unfavorable number. The limitations section is brief but does not minimize; it correctly frames the method as bounded by its geometry backbone. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Evaluation on a self-designed benchmark: the co-visibility interval [0.20, 0.60), the fixed-span source sampling, and the similarity-transform alignment for pose-free methods are all author choices; no external or pre-existing protocol is used to corroborate the headline claims, so the magnitude of the gains on standard benchmarks (e.g., interpolated views, standard splits) is unknown. - Monocular underperformance is under-examined: the paper shows SplatAnything loses to SHARP on most datasets with a single view but attributes this only implicitly to the geometry prior bottleneck; no analysis of why GSNorm's advantage disappears in this regime. - The claimed robustness to "arbitrary camera configurations" is tested on perspective inputs up to ~100° FoV (via the panoramic appendix experiment) but with a single generated-panorama demonstration, not a systematic FoV sweep. - No geometric evaluation (depth accuracy, alignment error, hole fraction) is reported — only rendering metrics — so the claim that GSNorm improves the geometry of the predicted Gaussians is inferred from visual artifacts rather than measured. - Efficiency claims omit memory footprint and training cost is 64×H20 for 20k iterations, which is nontrivial and unexamined for reproducibility by smaller labs. Bottom Line: A practitioner building feed-forward 3DGS on geometry foundation models should read this — GSNorm is a near-zero-cost change with controlled-ablation support, and the benchmark protocol alone is worth adopting — even though the headline numbers rest on an author-designed evaluation and stronger monocular alternatives like SHARP exist for the single-view regime.

Adaptive Semantic-Causal Graph Integration for Robust Knowledge Graph RAG

T Ugai, T Morita · ceur-ws.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces CausalHippo, a RAG framework that adaptively fuses HippoRAG-style semantic graph retrieval with CausalRAG-style causal path verification via a three-layer controller (dynamic weighting, confidence-based switching, two-pass adaptation), and evaluates seven configurations on MuSiQue, Webis-CausalQA-22, and a new synthetic Causal-Reasoning-QA benchmark. - Why it's important: Similarity-driven RAG retrieves topically relevant but causally spurious evidence, which matters for applications where unsupported causal claims are costlier than abstention; existing semantic-graph and causal-retrieval methods are deployed as fixed, non-adaptive postures. - How it does it: A logistic gating function scores causal-evidence density (path count, node coverage, query ambiguity) to apportion retrieval weight between semantic and causal indices, with a confidence gate that falls back to semantic retrieval when causal evidence is sparse, and a post-retrieval pass that re-blends weights based on causal alignment of first-pass candidates. - The good: The honest statistical analysis (paired t-tests, 10,000 bootstrap replicates, Holm correction) and the label-aware finding that hybrid integration lifts causal abstention from HippoRAG's near-zero Unknown Recall (0.033) to 0.447 are the most credible contributions. - The missing: The adaptive controller does not statistically outperform a well-tuned static hybrid (CausalHippo-Fixed) on any metric, so the headline mechanism — adaptivity — is supported only against weaker baselines (CausalRAG, HippoRAG), and the strongest gains are measured on the authors' own synthetic benchmark. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building hybrid/causal RAG pipelines who need a careful, negative-results-included evaluation template and a new causal-discrimination benchmark; skippable for practitioners seeking a retrieval method proven superior to simpler static weighting.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (75) is the best in this cluster: paired t-tests with bootstrap and Holm correction, validated parity-tested reimplementations of both baselines, released code and per-question logs. Completeness (80) is exceptional — the paper reports head-on that its own adaptive controller does not significantly beat its static ablation — and Impact (65) is supported by the released Kotlin artifact and a new causal-discrimination benchmark. Novelty (58) is a specific composition of known gating techniques plus an LLM-generated dataset, and Resilience (70) is held back by hyperparameter circularity on the authors' own synthetic benchmark and the absence of any validated operating envelope for adaptivity. Weighted composite: 0.20*58 + 0.25*75 + 0.15*60 + 0.15*80 + 0.15*70 + 0.10*65 = 68.

Problem & Motivation: Graph-based RAG systems face a tension between two failure modes: semantic-graph retrieval (e.g., HippoRAG) over-retrieves causally irrelevant but topically adjacent passages, while causal-path retrieval (e.g., CausalRAG) loses bridge documents needed for multi-hop reasoning when explicit causal evidence is sparse. Practitioners building knowledge-intensive QA over knowledge graphs currently must pick a fixed retrieval posture, and the paper argues the optimal balance depends on query complexity and evidence density. The target applications are Semantic Web scenarios where distinguishing causation from correlation — and abstaining when evidence is insufficient — is paramount, such as AI-safety-relevant reasoning (the work is funded under a Japanese AI-safety R&D program). Key Idea: Treat semantic connectivity and causal directionality as complementary retrieval signals whose relative influence should be gated by measured evidence density rather than fixed a priori. The core mechanism is a sigmoid gate over a hand-crafted logit — α·min(N_paths/τ,1) + β·coverage − γ·ambiguity − δ — that allocates the non-lexical retrieval budget between causal and semantic weights, backed by an absolute-evidence confidence switch (fallback to semantic when causal evidence is thin) and a post-retrieval re-blend based on how well semantic candidates align with the causal subgraph (node and path match scores). Methodology: The pipeline has an offline indexing stage (HippoRAG semantic graph, LLM-OpenIE-extracted directed CausalGraph, BM25 lexical index, all embedded with text-embedding-3-small) and an online four-phase retriever: (1) causal path discovery via seed-node cosine similarity and directed expansion up to H=2 hops with θ_sim=0.8; (2) dynamic weighting via the logistic gate (α=2.0, β=2.0, γ=1.5, τ=3.0, δ=0.5) with fixed W_bm25; (3) confidence-based switch normalizing node/path counts against saturation thresholds (τ_nodes=6.0, τ_paths=3.0) and rescaling the causal weight; (4) two-pass adaptation interpolating the causal weight toward a target derived from causal-alignment scores of top-N first-pass candidates (w_node=0.7, w_path=0.3, λ=0.7). Everything is implemented in Kotlin with faithful re-implementations of HippoRAG and CausalRAG validated by parity testing against Python outputs; generation and extraction use 'gpt-5.4-mini' at T=0 via OpenAI API. Hyperparameters come from 20-sample pilots per dataset. Critical design decisions: hand-set logistic coefficients (justified only by pilot data and a post-hoc 3×3 sensitivity grid, not learned); the coverage-over-path-count finding from sensitivity analysis; and K=5 retrieval cutoff as a 'conservative compromise' (asserted, not ablated). Key Results: Across three 300-sample benchmark subsets with K=5 and seven configurations: on Webis-CausalQA-22, CausalHippo achieves Faithfulness 0.940 and Groundedness 0.910 (best) but CausalRAG leads EM (0.360) and HippoRAG leads F1 (0.549); on MuSiQue, HippoRAG leads F1 (0.403) and Recall@5 (0.622) while CausalHippo leads MRR@5 (0.822) and nDCG@5 (0.600); on the authors' Causal-Reasoning-QA, CausalHippo leads aggregate F1 (0.459) and EM (0.367), and label-aware analysis shows HippoRAG collapses on non-causal abstention (Unknown Recall 0.033 vs. 0.447; F1(False) 0.073 vs. 0.447). Aggregate F1: CausalHippo 0.446, CausalHippo-Fixed 0.445, CausalRAG 0.440, HippoRAG 0.414. Statistically, the only significant gain over CausalRAG is Recall@5 (+0.040, 95% CI [0.0167, 0.0667], adjusted p=0.0088); no significant advantage over CausalHippo-Fixed. Failure analysis attributes 85.5% of MuSiQue errors (194/227) to incomplete retrieval chains. Baselines are current and reasonable (HippoRAG NeurIPS 2024, CausalRAG ACL 2025 Findings), tested at small scale (300 samples each). A notable honest finding: Ragas Faithfulness is shown to be a broken metric for concise causal answers (HippoRAG scores 1.0 for an ungrounded narrative while scoring 0.0 for the exact correct answer). Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (adaptive three-layer routing over semantic+causal+lexical indices) plus NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (Causal-Reasoning-QA, 10,000 GPT-4.5-generated long-context examples with causal/correlation/insufficient-evidence labels and a multi-agent review pipeline). The genuinely novel element is the joint adaptive integration of causal-path gating with graph-semantic retrieval; individually, the components are standard — logistic feature-based gating, confidence-based fallback, and post-retrieval re-ranking are known techniques (the paper itself credits DAT, Adaptive-RAG, and confidence-switching prior work), so the contribution is a specific composition plus an unusually candid empirical characterization of when it does and does not help. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative (four CausalHippo variants isolating Phases 3 and 4), the sensitivity analysis over the two main gating coefficients is a genuine strength, and significance testing with bootstrap + Holm correction exceeds typical workshop-paper practice. Error bars/CIs are reported for the key comparison; multiple seeds are not discussed (LLM generation at T=0 partially mitigates variance but API-level nondeterminism is unaddressed). Code and experimental materials are released at https://github.com/takanori-ugai/CausalHippo, with per-question metric logs for recomputation. Methodological concerns: (1) the sensitivity analysis and hyperparameter pilots touch the same Causal-Reasoning-QA data used for headline results, a Goodhart risk (though only 20-sample pilots and a coarse 3×3 grid); (2) the headline benchmark demonstrating causal discrimination is the authors' own LLM-generated dataset — although hyperparameters derived from it (β=4.0 optimal) actually differ from the deployed configuration (β=2.0), and the human-annotated Webis-CausalQA-22 corroborates some findings; (3) the deployed configuration is not the sensitivity-optimal one, which is never reconciled; (4) single LLM, single embedding model, single K. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a built system artifact). - Practical: Runs on standard infrastructure calling OpenAI APIs (gpt-5.4-mini, text-embedding-3-small) on the JVM; no exotic hardware required. - Efficient: Adaptive routing was reported no slower than the fixed variant, but the shared stack with sequential LLM calls for OpenIE and path extraction is acknowledged as a substantial latency source; no throughput or cost numbers are given. - Effective: Evidence shows it improves grounding and causal abstention over graph-only retrieval and retrieval depth over CausalRAG, but only a proxy for the full claim — answer-level causal reliability is measured on a small subset and a largely synthetic benchmark, and the adaptive core does not beat static hybrid weighting. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 300-sample subsets and 10k-example index corpora; scaling behavior of the OpenIE-based causal graph construction and multi-pass retrieval at 10–100× corpus size is claimed nowhere and unknown. The work delivers a software artifact (Kotlin codebase, released), a new benchmark dataset, and per-question logs; no trained model weights. Strengths: - Unusually honest evaluation for this venue: the paper explicitly reports that its own adaptive mechanism does not significantly beat its own static ablation, quantifies exactly where gains hold (Recall@5 vs. CausalRAG) and where they do not, and diagnoses a metric artifact (Ragas Faithfulness rewarding verbosity over correctness) that the community should know about. - The causal abstention result is substantive: Unknown Recall 0.447 vs. 0.033 and F1(False) 0.447 vs. 0.073 against HippoRAG demonstrates a real, category-level failure of semantic-only retrieval that hybridization fixes. - The sensitivity analysis yields a non-obvious, actionable finding — node coverage (β) is a more reliable gating signal than raw path count (α), with peak F1 at α=0, β=4.0 — which matters for anyone implementing evidence-density gating. - Engineering care: line-by-line Kotlin ports with parity testing against the original Python baselines, unified LLM/embedding stack, and released per-question logs enable genuine recomputation. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors directly state: dependence on OpenIE causal-extraction fidelity; an explicit coverage–precision trade-off where the Confidence-Based Switch can over-filter semantic bridge documents and high-noise distractors still induce over-assertion of causality; confinement to three benchmarks with 300-sample subsets (with an argued exclusion of GraphRAG-Bench); latency from the shared retrieval stack and sequential LLM calls; and that adaptive routing is not a universal win over a well-tuned static hybrid. This is a credibility positive — the paper confronts its non-dominance head-on rather than minimizing it. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The central adaptive controller (Phases 2–4) is never shown to significantly outperform the static hybrid on any metric; the paper frames this as 'selective' benefit but never identifies a query-level characteristic that predicts when adaptivity wins, leaving the mechanism without a validated operating envelope. - Hyperparameter provenance is circular-adjacent: pilots (20 samples/dataset) and the sensitivity grid both touch evaluation data, and the sensitivity-optimal setting (α=0, β=4.0) contradicts the deployed one (α=2.0, β=2.0) with no reconciliation or test of the optimal setting on the other two benchmarks. - Causal-Reasoning-QA is generated and reviewed by LLMs (GPT-4.5-preview), so 'ground truth' causal labels inherit generator biases; no human validation sample size or agreement statistic is reported for the 10,000 examples. - No comparison against simpler adaptive hybrids (e.g., Adaptive-RAG-style complexity routing without a causal graph), so the marginal value of the causal modality specifically — versus any query-adaptive mechanism — is not isolated. - Only one generator LLM and one embedding model are tested; conclusions about grounding and faithfulness may be model-family-specific. - Statistical testing is limited to the aggregate 300-sample subsets; per-category claims (e.g., confounding-variable failures at 11/12) rest on single-digit-to-low-double-digit counts with no uncertainty quantification. - MRR@5 of 0.822 on MuSiQue with Recall@5 of 0.586 is an unusual inversion relative to the baselines' profiles and is not explained. Bottom Line: A practitioner building causal or hybrid RAG gains real value here — a released Kotlin implementation, a usable causal-discrimination benchmark, a documented metric pitfall, and the finding that coverage-based gating beats path-count gating — but should treat the adaptive controller as an unproven refinement over simple static weighting rather than a demonstrated advance.

SUMONE: A Simple and Efficient Summarizer for Plug-and-Play Agent Memory

J Zhang, A Li, C Zhang, Y Wang · arxiv.org · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces SumOne, a 2B-parameter standalone summarizer trained via masked reconstruction to compress long agent interaction histories, cutting estimated inference cost by ~78% on DeepSearchQA and ~75% (wait: 22% of Full History cost, i.e., ~78% reduction) on DeepSearchQA and ~75%... — precisely: it reduces total per-query inference cost to 22% of Full History on DeepSearchQA (F1 0.48 vs. 0.52) and to 58% on SWE-bench Verified (0.59 vs. 0.63 resolved rate), while transferring across downstream models and harnesses without fine-tuning. - Why it's important: Long-horizon agents accumulate trajectories that hit context limits and inflate API cost; a task-agnostic, reusable compressor removes the need to retrain memory logic per task, agent, or harness. - How it does it: The core trick is using masked reconstruction as an RL reward: a summary is scored by how well a frozen 9B reconstructor, conditioned on the summary, can recover randomly masked blocks of the original trajectory (LLM-judged precision+recall minus a length penalty), optimized with GRPO. - The good: The Prompt-2B vs. SumOne ablation isolates the training objective and shows reconstruction-based RL is what matters (DeepSearchQA 0.29 → 0.48, LongMemEval-S 0.43 → 0.47), not merely using a small standalone model. - The missing: No error bars, seeds, or significance tests anywhere; the training set is only ~5K trajectories from two domains, and the reconstruction signal depends on an LLM judge whose noise/saturation is never quantified. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building agent context/memory systems or RL-from-reconstruction training loops; skip if you only need a quick production fix, where prompting or recency truncation baselines already cover much of the ground.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (76) is the driver — using frozen-model masked reconstruction as a GRPO reward for a separate compressor is a genuinely new formulation that decouples memory training from task outcomes — and the reward-swap ablation (0.41→0.48 F1 under fixed budget) credibly isolates it. Non-Obviousness (74) follows from the same insight. Rigor (65) is pulled down by the complete absence of error bars or significance tests, an uncharacterized LLM judge defining both the reward and the evaluation of preserved information, and weights that are promised but not released. Resilience (65) suffers because several headline-adjacent margins (e.g., 0.59 vs 0.57 vs 0.56 on SWE-bench) are within plausible noise, and the MI framing is decoration. Impact (60) is real cost savings but no public artifact yet. Weighted composite: 0.20*76 + 0.25*65 + 0.15*74 + 0.15*68 + 0.15*65 + 0.10*60 = 68.5 ≈ 68.
