Problem & Motivation: Long-running LLM agents (search, coding) accumulate append-only histories that raise inference cost and eventually exceed context windows. Existing context-management approaches either use simple heuristics (truncation, prompt-time self-summarization, as in Codex/Claude Code compaction), tie memory management to a specific task workflow or agent training loop (HiAgent, FoldGRPO, learned context folding), or expose a general memory interface that the agent must additionally interact with (A-MEM). Learned standalone summarizers typically require downstream task outcomes as supervision, coupling them to a specific solver. The gap: a memory compressor that is task-agnostic in training, lightweight at deployment, and information-dense in output — usable by any agent without retraining. The intended users are builders of multi-step tool-using agents who face context limits and per-token API cost. Key Idea: Train the summarizer against an information-preservation proxy rather than task outcomes: a summary S is good if a frozen reconstructor D can recover randomly masked blocks of the expired history H from (C, Mask(H), S) — i.e., S reduces the conditional entropy H(H_Ω | S, H_Ω̄, C) (the paper gives the mutual-information interpretation I(S; H_Ω | H_Ω̄, C) but never estimates it; reconstruction quality is the surrogate). That reconstruction score, plus a length penalty, becomes the GRPO reward. This is a clean transplant of masked-reconstruction self-supervision (BERT/MAE/BART-style) into the reward slot of an RL loop for a separate compressor model. Methodology: Four stages. (1) Summarization: a Qwen3.5-2B summarizer π_θ generates a structured summary S of the expired history H given retained context C (system prompt, task, prior memory, recent turns). (2) Masked reconstruction: H is split into ~512-token blocks at natural boundaries; 50% are masked; a frozen Qwen3.5-9B reconstructor regenerates the missing blocks conditioned on C, the visible history, and S. (3) Reward and RL: an LLM judge (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash) scores each reconstructed block on precision and recall; Q(S) = mean over blocks of (r_i + p_i), and the reward R(S) = Q(S) − λ|S|/L_max with λ = 0.1; GRPO (group-normalized advantages, G = 8 samples per prompt) updates only the summarizer. (4) Deployment: the reconstruction pipeline is discarded; only the 2B summarizer runs at compaction time. Training used ~5K compaction instances (16K/32K context lengths) from OpenSeeker-v1-Data (web search) and SWE-smith (software engineering), 600 GRPO steps on 8×H20 GPUs. Critical design decisions: (a) the reconstruction-as-reward move — well justified by the Prompt-2B vs. Recon-RL ablation; (b) mask ratio 50% — empirically ablated (25% gives too weak a signal since the summary is redundant; 75% over-taxes the reconstructor); (c) length penalty λ — ablated, with 0.1 optimal and 0.5 clearly harmful (DeepSearchQA 0.37). The judge-based scoring is less justified: judge noise is not characterized. Key Results: Main settings use Qwen3.5-35B-A3B with OpenCode as the downstream agent, 32K compaction threshold. DeepSearchQA: SumOne 0.48 F1 vs. Full History 0.52, Self-Summary 0.44, Prompt-2B 0.29, CoMem 0.32; total cost $0.038/query vs. $0.170 (Full History) and $0.044 (Self-Summary); input tokens 2.83M → 591K. SWE-bench Verified: 0.59 resolved vs. 0.63 Full History, 0.56 Self-Summary, 0.57 CoMem; cost $0.071 vs. $0.286; input 4.1M → 1.09M tokens. LongMemEval-S (isolated memory): SumOne 0.47 overall, beating Prompt-2B (0.43) and CoMem (0.31), below Full History (0.77), with the most balanced per-category profile. Transfer: the same checkpoint generalizes across four downstream models (e.g., on SWE-bench with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash: 0.74 vs. 0.78 Full History at ~48% of cost; with GLM-5.3: 0.66 vs. 0.74) and four harnesses (OpenCode 0.48 vs. 0.52; OpenHands 0.46 vs. 0.49; Codex 0.47 vs. 0.55; DS Harness 0.42 vs. 0.50). With task-specific RL downstream, SumOne reaches 0.68 on SWE-bench, above Self-Summary's 0.65 at lower cost. Notably, Recency Truncation (0.16 F1 on DeepSearchQA) is far worse, showing summaries carry real information. Baselines are current and reasonably chosen (CoMem is the key learned-compression competitor); scale is standard-benchmark scale, not stress-scale. No error bars or significance tests are reported anywhere, and some margins (e.g., Codex harness: SumOne 0.47 vs. Self-Summary 0.47; DS Harness 0.42 vs. 0.41) are within plausible noise. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD with an element of NEW FORMULATION. Genuinely novel: using frozen-model masked reconstruction as the GRPO reward for a separate summarizer, decoupling memory training from both task outcomes and the downstream agent. The components — masked reconstruction (BERT/MAE/BART), GRPO (DeepSeekMath), structured summarization prompts, standalone compressor architecture (CoMem) — are all established; the combination and, specifically, the reward design are the contribution. MemTrain (cited) is the closest prior, but it trains the agent's own memory; SumOne trains an external module. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are a genuine strength: reward-signal ablation (Prompt-2B / Summ.-Judge-RL / Recon-RL on identical initialization and budget), mask-ratio sweep (25/50/75%), and length-penalty sweep (λ ∈ {0.01, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5}), each with downstream and LongMemEval numbers. Missing: no seeds, confidence intervals, or significance testing; no ablation of the reconstructor scale (9B) or judge model; single judged-by-DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash scoring introduces an unquantified reward-noise channel. No code or weights released yet — the reproducibility statement promises release only "upon acceptance." Cost numbers are self-computed from list prices with stated assumptions (no cache discounts), which is transparent but not independently verified. No Goodhart-style contamination issue is apparent since reconstruction training is on the same distribution but not the evaluation instances themselves; however, SWE-smith trajectories and SWE-bench Verified overlap in domain, so the "task-agnostic" claim is tested mostly in-domain. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (trained system with benchmark evaluation; a 2B summarizer artifact). - Practical: Yes — the deployed component is a 2B model runnable on a single modest GPU (training needed 8×H20, but inference does not). - Efficient: Very — summarization costs $0.001/query and replaces 2.83M/4.1M input tokens with ~591K/1.09M; the expensive reconstructor and judge exist only in training. - Effective: Mostly — it recovers 92–94% of Full History task performance at 22–58% of cost and beats all compression baselines on the main benchmarks, though it consistently loses to Full History and its LongMemEval overall score (0.47 vs. 0.77) shows substantial absolute information loss. - Scalable: Unverified beyond 32K compaction thresholds and two domains; whether one 2B compressor handles much longer horizons or unfamiliar domains (the authors' own stated limitation) is extrapolation, not evidence. Deliverable: a trained 2B model checkpoint and method, promised for release but not yet public — currently a paper plus reproducible recipe. Strengths: - The reward-design insight is real and well-isolated: swapping only the reward signal (judge-only vs. reconstruction) under fixed budget changes DeepSearchQA F1 from 0.41 to 0.48, directly evidencing that reconstruction ground supervision — not RL machinery — drives the gain. - The plug-and-play claim is backed by actual transfer experiments across four downstream LLMs and four harnesses with one checkpoint, rather than asserted. - Honest cost accounting: summarization cost is reported separately, and the deployment pipeline genuinely excludes training-time components, so the 70–78% cost reduction claim is deployment-faithful. - Compatibility with downstream RL (Table 2: 0.68 on SWE-bench with task-specific RL) demonstrates the module composes with, rather than conflicts with, standard agent training. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state two: (1) training data is concentrated in web-search and software-engineering trajectories, so broader domains may have different memory requirements; (2) the training signal depends on a frozen reconstructor and an LLM judge whose capabilities may cap the learned summarizer. Both are stated plainly in the conclusion, and the judge/reconstructor dependency is flagged again in the method discussion — a credibility positive. They do not minimize; they simply do not test either limitation. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No variance reporting at all; several headline-adjacent comparisons (SumOne vs. Self-Summary on Codex and DS Harness; 0.59 vs. 0.57 vs. 0.56 on SWE-bench) could vanish under seed noise. - The LLM judge both scores training rewards and implicitly defines what "preserved information" means; if the judge favors fluent paraphrase or specific content types, the summarizer optimizes judge preferences, and no human or alternative-judge validation of the reward is provided. - Only ~5K training instances — the paper does not test whether the objective scales with data, which matters for the "general memory module" ambition. - The masked-reconstruction objective rewards recovering verbatim-style content; there is no evaluation of whether it preserves information not expressible in the masked blocks (e.g., cross-block synthesis), and LongMemEval multi-session scores (0.41 vs. Prompt-2B's 0.51) hint it may not. - The mutual-information framing (Eq. 4) motivates the method but is never measured or even approximated — it is decoration, not analysis. - Cost comparisons use list prices for API models where caching discounts would materially change the Full-History baseline, potentially overstating SumOne's cost advantage in production. Bottom Line: For anyone building or researching agent memory systems, this is a worthwhile read — the reconstruction-as-reward formulation is a genuinely reusable idea with a credible ablation behind it — but practitioners wanting a drop-in solution today should note that weights are unreleased and the compression baselines (Self-Summary, CoMem) already narrow the gap, so the contribution's value rests on the objective, not on an unbeatable system.

Decouple to Reuse: Fine-Grained Knowledge Augmentation for Time Series Foundation Models

Y Wu, Q Liu, Y Guo, W Su, J Li, P Xu, X Chen, Y Yue… · arxiv.org · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces TimeFKA, a two-stage framework that decomposes pre-training time series into trend and seasonal components, consolidates each into shared residual-quantization codebooks, and uses task-adaptive retrieval and gated fusion from these codebooks to augment frozen Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) for downstream forecasting. - Why it's important: Zero-shot TSFM forecasts degrade under domain shift in Web deployments (demand prediction, resource provisioning), and existing retrieval augmentation injects whole retrieved windows that mix reusable patterns with context-specific noise. - How it does it: The core trick is decoupling knowledge reuse to the decomposition level — instead of retrieving similar whole windows, it learns separate trend and seasonal residual codebooks so a query can combine the trend from one context with the seasonality from another, then fuses retrieved pattern tokens into the frozen backbone representation via a lightweight gated adapter. - The good: Averages over five runs and four horizons across eight datasets and four TSFM backbones show consistent MSE reductions in all 29 backbone-dataset settings (10.7% for ChronosBolt-base, 26.0% for TTM 2), with a controlled random-codebook ablation isolating that the learned codebooks — not just adapter training — drive the gains. - The missing: Baseline comparison (Table 2) is run on only one of the four backbones (ChronosBolt-base), parametric-adaptation baselines (e.g., UniTS, LoRA variants) are motivated in the introduction but never empirically compared, and gains shrink to 0.6–1.9% on Traffic for the strongest backbones. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building retrieval- or memory-augmented adaptation for TSFMs, since the decomposition-level retrieval idea and cross-backbone codebook transfer results are genuinely instructive; practitioners just needing better forecasts on standard benchmarks can skim it.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Completeness (68) and Resilience (62) are the dimensions that pull the composite down: the motivating parametric-adaptation baselines (LoRA-style, UniTS) are never actually run despite framing the contribution against them, evaluation is confined to the same saturated LTSF benchmarks the method was developed on, and the cross-backbone codebook transfer result — the standout claim — is left mechanistically unexplained. Novelty (72) is solid for a decomposition-level retrieval composition, and Rigor (68) benefits from the random-codebook control and five-run standard deviations, but baseline point estimates lack variance, significance tests are absent, and gains shrink to ~1-2% on the strongest backbones. Problem & Motivation: Operators of Web services (e-commerce demand, cloud resource provisioning, transportation) need forecasting models that generalize across heterogeneous deployment domains. TSFMs pre-trained on diverse temporal corpora offer a path, but service-specific demand levels, usage cycles, and workload dynamics differ from pre-training patterns, limiting zero-shot accuracy. Existing fixes split into parametric adaptation (per-domain fine-tuned parameters, costly to maintain across domains) and knowledge augmentation (e.g., TS-RAG retrieves whole historical windows from the pre-training corpus). The authors identify a specific gap in the latter: whole-window similarity conflates reusable trend/seasonal regularities with context-specific variations — they demonstrate with a motivating example that a retrieved window's distribution differs substantially from the query, while the trend from one context plus the seasonal component from another yields lower matching error (MSE 0.823 vs 1.076 in their Figure 1 example). Key Idea: The central insight is that useful temporal knowledge is compositional: the trend pattern matching a query may live in one pre-training window and the matching seasonal pattern in another, so pre-training knowledge should be organized as independently retrievable decomposition-level patterns (trend and seasonal residual codebooks) rather than as source windows, with a small task-specific adapter learning how to combine and fuse these patterns into the frozen TSFM representation. Methodology: TimeFKA is a two-stage pipeline built on channel-independent univariate processing with classical trend/seasonal decomposition. Stage I (Shared Knowledge Consolidation): samples contexts from the Chronos pre-training corpus (futures excluded), decomposes each into trend and seasonal components, encodes each with the frozen TSFM patch encoder, and trains L=2 levels of residual-quantization codebooks (K=256 vectors per level, per component) via row-wise nearest-neighbor hard quantization. The loss is a reconstruction MSE plus a weighted (λ_align=0.25) codebook-alignment term, with stop-gradients on the residual-update branch so only codebooks and reconstruction heads train. Stage II (Task-Adaptive Augmentation): for a downstream input, the frozen encoder embeds the raw series and its two components; multi-scale retrieval blocks query the frozen codebooks at both residual levels; retrieved tokens (2L per patch position) receive trainable component-, level-, and position-identity embeddings, are aggregated by a linear layer (HyperAgg), and are injected into the original frozen representation through a sigmoid-gated residual fusion (GateFuse: R' = R + G⊙Δ). The adapter trains per downstream task with the TSFM's native loss (e.g., multi-quantile pinball for Chronos-Bolt) while backbone and codebooks stay frozen. Critical design decisions: (1) decomposition-based decoupling — justified by the motivating analysis and the w/o-Decomposition ablation; (2) hard quantization with stop-gradients on residuals (standard RQ practice, reasonable but means retrieval is non-differentiable); (3) frozen codebooks during Stage II — claimed to preserve reusability, and supported by the cross-backbone transfer experiment, though it also means knowledge cannot update, which the authors concede. Key Results: Tested at standard academic scale: eight multivariate benchmarks (ETTh1/2, ETTm1/2, Electricity, Exchange-rate, Traffic, Weather), context length 512, horizons {96, 192, 336, 720}, five runs per setting, on a single A100-40GB. Against zero-shot, TimeFKA reduces average MSE by 10.7% (ChronosBolt-base), 10.4% (TimesFM 2.5), 15.4% (Moirai 2), and 26.0% (TTM 2); the largest single gain is TTM 2 on Electricity (MSE 0.4892→0.1638, ↓66.5%). Against five knowledge-augmentation baselines (RAFT, SARAF, TS-RAG, TS-Memory, MEMTS) on ChronosBolt-base, TimeFKA is best or tied-best on seven of eight datasets; e.g., on Traffic it cuts MSE 13.6% versus zero-shot while RAFT achieves 1.9% and TS-RAG 1.9%. Inference costs 4.844 ms on ETTm1 (+3.3% over zero-shot), 1.25× faster than RAFT and 1.48× faster than TS-RAG. Codebooks learned with ChronosBolt-base transfer to the other three backbones (16.81–51.91% MSE reduction over zero-shot on ETTm1) and down to ChronosBolt-Tiny (9M). Cross-dataset adapter transfer beats MEMTS by 2.69–13.45% MSE. Baselines are recent (2024–2026) and appropriate for the knowledge-augmentation family. Notably absent from head-to-head tables: any parametric-adaptation baseline, and any supervised fine-tuning lower bound. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD with a supporting NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel element is decomposition-level (trend/seasonal) retrieval from residual-quantized pattern banks replacing window-level retrieval, plus the demonstrated cross-backbone reusability of the learned codebooks. The constituents are standard: classical seasonal-trend decomposition, residual vector quantization, identity-embedding aggregation, and gated residual fusion — the contribution is their specific composition for TSFM augmentation, not any new primitive. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: random frozen codebooks underperform the learned ones (and often zero-shot), removing decomposition hurts, removing identity embeddings causes the largest degradation, and replacing gated fusion with direct addition hurts. Hyperparameter sensitivity (K, L, λ_align) is reported in Appendix B. TimeFKA results carry ± standard deviations over five runs; baselines in Table 2 appear as point estimates (no variance reported for them, and no significance tests). Code is available at an anonymous repository (github.com/yuppielqx/TSFM-Component-Token-Adapter). Concerns: (1) the ablation and mechanism studies are confined largely to ETTh2/ETTm1, leaving breadth thin; (2) some baselines OOM on Electricity/Traffic (MEMTS), so comparison coverage is uneven; (3) Electricity, Weather, and Traffic are omitted for TimesFM 2.5 because they appear in its pre-training corpus — handled transparently, but it removes three of eight datasets from one backbone column; (4) evaluation uses only the standard LTSF benchmark suite, which is known to saturate and to reward methods tuned on it; the codebook and adapter are developed and evaluated on the same benchmarks. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS-flavored efficiency study). - Practical: Yes — all experiments run on one NVIDIA A100-SXM4-40GB using public HuggingFace TSFM checkpoints. - Efficient: Inference adds only 3.3% latency over zero-shot (4.844 ms on ETTm1) and is faster than all retrieval-based baselines, because retrieval operates on compact codebooks (2×256 vectors) rather than a window index. - Effective: Evidence supports improved point-forecast accuracy over zero-shot and over five augmentation baselines, but effectiveness on the strongest backbones is small on some datasets (Traffic: 0.6–1.9% for Moirai 2/TTM 2), and the claimed Web-service motivation is tested only on academic benchmarks, not production workloads. - Scalable: Untested beyond a 1M-parameter to ~200M-parameter backbone range and single-GPU setup; scaling to much larger TSFMs or corpora is claimed only implicitly through the compactness argument, not measured. The work delivers code (anonymous repo) and a reusable artifact in the form of transferable trend/seasonal codebooks, but no trained universal model or packaged library beyond the repo. Strengths: - The motivating observation is concrete and quantified: combining trend and seasonal patterns from different retrieved contexts yields lower window-matching error than whole-window retrieval (Figure 1), which directly grounds the design rather than post-hoc rationalizing it. - The cross-backbone and cross-model-size codebook transfer experiments (Figures 3–4) elevate the work beyond a single-backbone adapter paper — pattern banks learned with ChronosBolt-base benefit TimesFM 2.5, Moirai 2, and TTM 2 without retraining Stage I, which is the strongest evidence that the codebooks capture backbone-agnostic temporal regularities. - The random-codebook control (Figure 5) is a well-chosen experiment that cleanly separates the contribution of learned pattern banks from that of adapter capacity — a control many adapter papers omit. - Honest, granular reporting: per-horizon results with standard deviations, transparent exclusion of TimesFM 2.5 results on datasets in its own pre-training corpus, and explicit OOM marking for MEMTS. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that the fixed trend–seasonal decomposition imposes a predefined organization of temporal knowledge, and that the frozen pattern banks cannot incorporate new knowledge during downstream adaptation; they propose data-driven pattern organization and continual codebook updates as future work. This is stated directly in the conclusion without minimizing, which is a credibility positive. They also caution in the case study that a single-window illustration "may not isolate the contribution of individual codes." Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No parametric-adaptation baseline is actually run despite the introduction framing TimeFKA against fine-tuning/prompt approaches; the comparison table includes only knowledge-augmentation methods, so the claim of a favorable adaptation-cost trade-off versus e.g., LoRA on a frozen backbone is unevaluated. - Supervised full fine-tuning of the backbone is also absent, so readers cannot tell how much headroom remains above any adaptation method on these saturated benchmarks. - The cross-backbone transfer result (codebooks learned with one encoder queried by another) is surprising and under-explained: patch embedding spaces of Chronos-Bolt (T5-based), TimesFM, Moirai, and TTM differ, and no analysis shows why nearest-neighbor quantization indices or embeddings remain compatible across encoders. - Gains on Exchange-rate for ChronosBolt-base are partly driven by the erratic H=720 split, and MSE/MAE variability across horizons (e.g., Moirai 2 ETTh2 H=720 with ±0.2349) suggests some results rest on high-variance averages. - The claimed Web-services domain shift motivation is never tested on an actual service workload; all eight datasets are standard public LTSF benchmarks, several of which overlap Chronos's pre-training corpus more broadly than the three explicitly excluded for TimesFM 2.5. - The paper is an arXiv preprint (2611.05993) with an anonymous repository, so results have not yet undergone peer review. Bottom Line: A practitioner adapting TSFMs to new domains gains a concrete, well-ablated, cheap-to-serve alternative to window-level retrieval augmentation — with the decomposition-level codebook transfer result as the standout insight — but should verify the marginal single-digit gains on strong backbones in their own setting before adopting it over simpler LoRA-style adaptation.

Signals from the Future: Future-aware Semi-Autoregressive Decoding for Diffusion Language Models

Y Park, J Kang, K Lee, H Kim, J Choi, SH Na · aclanthology.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces FUSA, a training-free decoding algorithm for full-attention masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) that reuses the future-block logits normally discarded during blockwise semi-autoregressive decoding, converting them into soft future tokens to guide which active-block tokens get committed. - Why it's important: MDLM inference speed is bottlenecked by how many tokens can be safely unmasked per denoising step; a decoding signal that commits more correct tokens per forward call directly cuts latency for billion-parameter diffusion LMs without retraining. - How it does it: FUSA alternates each denoising step between presenting the next block as [MASK] embeddings and as soft embeddings built from the model's own cached next-block distributions (top-p filtered, mixed with mask embeddings at α=0.65), and commits active-block tokens that either exceed a 0.95 confidence threshold or whose predictive distributions stay within a Jensen–Shannon divergence threshold ε across the two views — all within one model forward per step. - The good: The speedup is real and measured: 2.10–3.94× wall-clock over Top-1 decoding on LLaDA-8B-Instruct with score gains (e.g., MBPP pass@1 42.80 vs. 37.74 for Top-1, +5.06), plus controls (temporal-only, threshold-only, shuffled/random/argmax future ablations) that isolate the soft-future stability signal as the source of the gain. - The missing: Main benchmark scores are reported from a single deterministic run with no significance testing, and several headline margins are small (GSM8K +1.29 over confidence decoding, HumanEval ties on LLaDA-1.5), so which gains are robust is unclear. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building inference-time decoders for full-attention diffusion LMs (LLaDA/Dream lineage), since the free-lunch reuse of future logits is a concrete, transferable trick; skippable if you have already moved to block-causal architectures (LLaDA2.x, Block Diffusion) where the signal is unavailable by construction.
Why this rank

The composite is pulled down by Resilience (62) — single deterministic benchmark runs with no error bars leave small margins (GSM8K +1.29, HumanEval ties on LLaDA-1.5) vulnerable to scrutiny, and the deployment-relevant comparison against block-causal diffusion systems is explicitly absent — and by Completeness (68) for the same exclusions. Impact (70) is supported by released code and measured wall-clock speedups of 2.10-3.94x. Weighted composite: 0.20*65 + 0.25*72 + 0.15*70 + 0.15*68 + 0.15*62 + 0.10*70 = 68.

Problem & Motivation: Full-attention MDLMs (e.g., LLaDA-8B) decode via blockwise semi-autoregressive sampling: tokens are denoised in parallel within the active block while future positions are forwarded as [MASK]. Those forward passes already compute predictive distributions for future positions, but standard decoders discard them and reset future positions to mask. Practitioners deploying MDLMs pay for this computation and get nothing back, and confidence-based commitment — the dominant acceleration heuristic — is myopic: a locally confident token can still be revised once more context is denoised. The paper asks whether the model's own next-block predictions, available for free, can serve as evidence for deciding which active-block tokens are safe to commit. Key Idea: Test each active-block hypothesis under two views of the immediately following block — masked vs. soft (probability-weighted embedding mixture built from the model's cached next-block logits) — and commit tokens whose predictions are stable across the two views. The underlying empirical observation is a stability contrast: hypotheses later revised during decoding show larger distributional shifts under soft-future context than hypotheses eventually retained (e.g., in the arithmetic probe, wrong Top-1 hypotheses lose probability mass under the soft-future probe while correct ones gain). Because full-attention MDLMs attend to future mask positions anyway, this probe costs zero additional forward calls. Methodology: FUSA plugs into standard blockwise MDLM decoding. Each denoising step performs one forward pass. In a mask-future step, the next block B_{b(t)+1} is [MASK] embeddings and its logits are cached; in the following soft-future step, those logits are converted to soft embeddings g_j = α·E_mask + (1−α)·Σ_{v∈TopP} p̃(v)E_v (top-p=0.85 filtering) and injected as temporary inputs, never committed to the state. Commitment uses an enlarged set: tokens with confidence ≥ τ_high=0.95 are committed immediately (fast path); remaining positions are unmasked when confidence ≥ τ_floor AND D_JS(p_{t−1}, p_t) ≤ ε between consecutive-step distributions; a fallback commits the highest-confidence argmax if nothing qualifies, guaranteeing progress. Critical design decisions: (1) mixing soft tokens with mask embeddings at α=0.65 to avoid distribution drift — well justified by the α-ablation showing both extremes collapse (α=0 gives 6.75% on GSM8K); (2) JS divergence as a symmetric, bounded similarity between two non-reference distributions — reasonable, though heuristic; (3) perturbing only the immediately next block (K=1) — ablated against K=2 and K=∞, with a plausible but explicitly non-formal mechanism offered for why local probes win. The method requires architectural prerequisites (future positions in the forward pass, active block attending to them, re-injectable embeddings) that hold only for full-attention MDLMs. Key Results: On LLaDA-8B-Instruct (single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000), FUSA achieves the best score among eight decoding baselines (Uniform, Entropy, Top-1, Top-2, Confidence, EB-Sampler, KLASS, LRD) on all four benchmarks: GSM8K 75.89 (81.18 steps), MATH500 34.40 (102.69 steps), HumanEval pass@1 37.20 (85.37 steps), MBPP pass@1 42.80 (62.90 steps), versus Top-1 at 73.92/33.00/35.98/37.74 with 256 steps each. Wall-clock speedups vs. Top-1: 2.79× (GSM8K), 2.10× (MATH500), 2.82× (HumanEval), 3.94× (MBPP); peak memory increases only 252 MiB. Baselines are current and reasonably strong (EB-Sampler and KLASS from NeurIPS 2025, LRD a 2025 soft-refinement method), though LRD pays ~264 steps everywhere. Transfer to LLaDA-1.5 with unchanged hyperparameters stays competitive (best-or-near-best scores) but with thinner margins, and Top-1 beats FUSA on LLaDA-1.5 HumanEval (38.41 vs. 35.98) at 3× the step cost. On CoDA-1.7B-Instruct, FUSA gets 4.94× (HumanEval) and 3.25× (MBPP) speedups with +0.78 MBPP pass@1. KV-cached inference via adapted DualCache reaches 96.35 TPS (2.35× over uncached FUSA) at 77.56% GSM8K accuracy (−0.83). Long-form WritingBench (100 prompts, 1,024 max tokens): 1.62× speedup at comparable critic score (4.718 vs. 4.678). Diagnostic support: cross-task trajectory analysis (400 samples) shows Revised-vs-Retained JS gaps of +.081 to +.136 with bootstrap CIs excluding zero on all four benchmarks. A surprising negative result: broader future perturbation (K=∞) hurts, indicating the signal is local. Note the absolute capability levels are modest (MATH500 ~34%). Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (FUSA decoder) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the soft-future stability contrast between revised and retained hypotheses). The genuinely new move is repurposing already-computed future-block logits as a two-view stability probe with zero extra forward cost — an idea not present in confidence-based (Fast-dLLM), temporal-stability (KLASS), or soft-latent-refinement (LRD) decoders. The ingredients (confidence thresholds, top-p filtering, JS divergence, blockwise decoding) are standard; the novelty lies in their composition and in the diagnostic evidence, not in any new mathematical framework. Related soft-token work (residual context, soft-masked diffusion) is adjacent but used for other purposes. Rigor & Reproducibility: Above average for a decoding paper. Ablations isolate the mechanism: temporal-only control (soft-future adds +5.06 MBPP over temporal stability alone), threshold-only alternation control (alternation without the JS/floor rule fails, e.g., MBPP 37.35 vs. 42.80), future-representation controls (shuffled/random/argmax), α and (τ_floor, ε) sensitivity grids, and K-window ablation. Diagnostic claims carry 95% paired bootstrap CIs (10,000 resamples, seed fixed). Hyperparameters are selected on dev subsets from training splits, then transferred unchanged to LLaDA-1.5 and CoDA — a good guard against per-benchmark overfitting. Code is released (github.com/yangryeol/FUSA). Weaknesses: main benchmark scores are single deterministic runs with no error bars or significance tests — on HumanEval (164 problems) and MATH500 (500 problems), 0.4–1.3-point margins are within plausible sampling noise; only the Uniform baseline is seed-averaged. The WritingBench evaluation uses the benchmark's own fine-tuned critic rather than human judgment (acknowledged). Evaluation is confined to the LLaDA/CoDA model family on standard small benchmarks; the paper does not develop on and evaluate on the same data, and the ablation grid on GSM8K/MBPP test sets is reported transparently with dev-set selection stated. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (an inference-time decoder, actually run and profiled). Practical: Runs on a single RTX PRO 6000 (24GB-class workstation GPU; 16.6 GB peak) with released code, so yes. Efficient: Zero extra forward calls, +252 MiB memory, O(BV)+O(Fd) cache — overhead is small and the 2.10–3.94× speedups are measured wall-clock, not step-count extrapolation. Effective: Evidence covers the stated problem (faster decoding at equal-or-better quality) on four benchmarks, two additional models, KV-cached inference, and long-form generation — though quality evidence rests on benchmark graders and one critic model, and gains shrink on LLaDA-1.5. Scalable: Untested beyond 8B models and 1,024-token generations; KV-cache compatibility is shown at 5-shot GSM8K only, and behavior at much longer contexts or larger models is claimed only implicitly. The work delivers a software artifact (released decoder code) plus a reusable diagnostic probe. Strengths: - The core insight is genuinely free-lunch: future-block logits are already computed under full attention, and turning them into a two-view stability probe adds no forward calls — a clean exploitation of an architectural property specific to full-attention MDLMs. - The ablation suite is unusually decisive for a decoding paper: the temporal-only, threshold-only, and shuffled/random/argmax controls collectively rule out the three most likely alternative explanations (temporal convergence, view alternation per se, soft noise), and the α-ablation (6.75% at α=0 vs. 75.89% at α=0.65 on GSM8K) pins the mechanism. - Hyperparameters selected on dev splits transfer unchanged across LLaDA-1.5 and CoDA-1.7B, providing genuine out-of-setting evidence rather than per-benchmark tuning. - Honest framing of the diagnostics as stability (retention) rather than correctness, with the arithmetic probe explicitly labeled a counterfactual intervention rather than a benchmark. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that FUSA applies only to full-attention MDLMs and not to strict block-causal architectures (Block Diffusion, LLaDA2.x); that they do not compare against separately trained block-diffusion systems; that the long-form evaluation uses 100 English WritingBench prompts with a critic model, not human evaluation; that several hyperparameters may need re-searching for new models/tasks; and that wider future-perturbation windows are not always beneficial. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No error bars or significance tests on the main benchmark comparisons; given test sizes (164–1,319 examples), several margins (GSM8K +1.29 over Confidence, HumanEval +1.22 over Top-1, MATH500 +0.80 over three baselines) may not survive resampling, and the deterministic single-seed protocol cannot detect variance. - The paper benchmarks only against training-free decoders on full-attention MDLMs; the practically strongest competing deployment path — fine-tuned block-causal systems like LLaDA2.0/2.1, Fast-dLLM v2, or SDAR — is explicitly excluded, so the deployment-relevant comparison (FUSA-on-LLaDA vs. a block-diffusion model) is absent. - The stability diagnostic measures whether a hypothesis is eventually retained, not whether it is correct; the causal chain from stability to task accuracy is supported only indirectly, and one could argue FUSA sometimes commits stable-but-wrong tokens (e.g., LLaDA-1.5 HumanEval where Top-1 wins). - KV-cache evaluation covers one benchmark (GSM8K, 5-shot); the interaction of soft-future injection with cached attention states — where future-block KV entries are stale by construction — deserves broader testing. - The OpenWebText unconditional-generation experiment (MAUVE 0.143→0.405 vs. same-checkpoint MDLM) is confined to a small open checkpoint and the ReMDM codebase; it does not speak to the 8B instruct models used elsewhere. Bottom Line: A practitioner deploying full-attention diffusion LMs should read and likely adopt FUSA — the speedups are measured, the ablations are credible, and the trick costs essentially nothing — but researchers betting on diffusion-LM serving at scale should weigh it against the (uncompared) block-causal alternative, and the quality-gain claims on small benchmarks deserve independent replication.

WaveGen: Truly End-to-End Waveform Generation via Internal Spectral Trajectory Learning (14 ▲ )

Sang-Hoon Lee, Ha-Yeong Choi · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 11 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces WaveGen, a single-stage diffusion/flow-matching (CFM) model that generates raw 24 kHz waveforms directly from text with no vocoder, neural codec, VAE, duration predictor, pretrained LLM, or SSL embeddings, and shows it reaches zero-shot TTS quality competitive with multi-stage systems (WER 1.47, SIM 0.75 on Seed-en with a 0.6B-parameter model trained on open-source Emilia data). - Why it's important: Modern TTS pipelines are brittle stacks of separately trained codecs, vocoders, and alignment modules whose errors compound and cap final quality; a truly end-to-end alternative would simplify training, remove upper bounds imposed by intermediate representations, and eliminate GAN-based vocoder training. - How it does it: The core trick is "Spectral Forcing" — the model jointly learns a low-resolution (64-bin Mel) internal spectral trajectory alongside the waveform trajectory inside one DiT, providing a structural inductive bias for text–speech alignment, combined with decoupled x-prediction/v-loss and a multi-scale energy-normalized spectral v-loss. - The good: The ablation evidence is unusually thorough: without Spectral Forcing the model catastrophically fails (WER 123.67 vs 4.96), and the E2E model beats an equal-NFE two-stage baseline (WER 2.91 vs 4.39, SIM 0.53 vs 0.46 on LibriTTS-scale training), directly supporting the central end-to-end claim. - The missing: Large-scale training stops at only 4 epochs (1.1M steps) on MP3-compressed Emilia audio, which the authors admit caps high-frequency fidelity, and the flagship 0.6B result actually switches to a different loss (multi-scale spectral x-loss) than the v-loss the paper advocates — an inconsistency that muddies the headline configuration. - Read it or not: Worth reading for TTS/speech-generation researchers and anyone tracking whether raw-waveform diffusion can replace cascaded pipelines; practitioners seeking deployable production TTS today can skip it, since current multi-stage systems (Qwen3-TTS, CosyVoice3) remain more proven.

Scored using Empirical profile (with a strong released artifact). Problem & Motivation: Zero-shot TTS has converged on multi-stage pipelines: codec language models (VALL-E, Qwen3-TTS, MOSS-TTS), Mel-spectrogram CFM models with neural vocoders (VoiceBox, E2/F5-TTS, ZipVoice), and latent diffusion models (VoxCPM, VibeVoice). Each stage adds training complexity and imposes a quality ceiling — codec models are bounded by codec capacity, Mel models by the vocoder, latent models by the pre-trained latent space. Earlier end-to-end text-to-waveform systems (FastSpeech 2s, EATS, VITS) suffered from unstable alignment, adversarial-training fragility, and poor zero-shot capability, and the one recent waveform diffusion attempt (E3-TTS) still depends on pretrained BERT text embeddings. The open question is whether a single model can directly map text to raw waveform at 24 kHz — a space of ~24,000 samples/sec requiring both linguistic alignment and waveform-energy modeling — and remain stable, scalable, and competitive. Key Idea: Spectral Forcing: instead of cascading text→spectrogram→waveform, co-generate a low-resolution internal Mel-spectrogram trajectory as an auxiliary target within the same conditional flow-matching model, so it acts as a frequency-rich internal guide for text–speech alignment rather than an external intermediate representation. This is paired with two supporting insights: (1) decoupled prediction and loss spaces — predict the clean signal (x-prediction, following JiT) but compute the objective in velocity space, which preserves waveform energy where v-prediction fails; and (2) a multi-scale energy-normalized spectral v-loss (extending Flow2GAN's single-scale spectral loss to 6 STFT resolutions) that balances frequency bands without letting high-energy regions dominate. The 24 kHz waveform is reshaped into a 100 Hz (or 50 Hz) resolution space to make diffusion tractable. Methodology: The system is a DiT with AdaLN-SOLA operating in CFM's rectified-flow interpolation (x_t = (1−t)x_0 + t·x_1). Pipeline: (1) reshape the noisy waveform into a low-resolution sequence and compute its noisy 64-bin Mel; (2) concatenate both noisy representations with average-pooled text embeddings (or filler-token conditioning in the 0.6B variant) and apply masked-infilling for prompt-based zero-shot generation; (3) pass through 14 shared DiT blocks (the alignment backbone) followed by two shallow disentangled DiT heads, one predicting the clean waveform and one predicting the clean Mel (Spectral Forcing targets); (4) convert x-predictions to velocities via v = (x_pred − x_t)/(1−t) and apply the masked velocity loss L_v in both domains; (5) add the multi-scale spectral v-loss (Eq. 5), computed on the waveform-domain velocity difference with ground-truth energy normalization, at six spectral scales (nbin 512→16). Total objective: L_wave + 0.1·L_spec + 0.1·L_ms-v-spec. Critical design decisions: Mel (not linear) spectrogram as the forced target because linear diverges (NaN in Table 4); 64 Mel bins as an information bottleneck strong enough to force alignment but weak enough not to turn the model into a denoiser; and 14-shared/2-disentangled head split, since fully shared blocks underperform (WER 7.83) and too many disentangled blocks degrade alignment. Inference uses Euler ODE with 32 NFE and CFG 2, plus a prompt-anchoring scheme that fixes the prompt region to a GT-interpolated state during sampling to correct a train–inference mismatch of masked infilling. Key Results: On the Seed-en zero-shot benchmark, the 0.6B WaveGen (trained on ~100k hours of open-source multilingual Emilia, 11 epochs, 8 GPUs) achieves WER 1.47 and SIM 0.75, beating or matching F5-TTS (1.83/0.67), ZipVoice (1.70/0.69), CosyVoice3-RL (1.68/0.69), Qwen3-TTS-0.6B (1.50/0.70), and approaching Qwen3-TTS-1.7B (1.50/0.71), with GT at 2.14/0.73; on Seed-zh it gets CER 1.75, SIM 0.80. Subjective MTurk evaluation (20 raters, 100 samples/model) gives WaveGen-B nMOS 4.000 and sMOS 3.988, comparable to F5-TTS, CosyVoice3, and Qwen3-TTS. Scaling is shown from 113M→407M on both LibriTTS (0.5k h) and Emilia (120k h): e.g., Emilia WER drops 4.27→2.37 with the larger model. Ablations (LibriTTS, WaveGen-S) quantify each component: no Spectral Forcing → WER 123.67; v-prediction instead of x-prediction → DNSMOS collapse (2.65 vs 3.45); removing the multi-scale spectral loss → WER 5.57 vs 4.96 final; disentangled heads essential. E2E beats a two-stage baseline with equal total NFE (WER 2.91 vs 4.39) and RTF of 0.24 on an A100 (E2E, 113M... actually 407M) vs 0.16 for two-stage. Baselines are current and strong (2024–2026 systems with official checkpoints). NFE analysis shows ≥8 steps needed and saturation near 32–50. Notably, the model does all this without GAN training, adversarial losses, or any self-supervised features. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (Spectral Forcing as internal auxiliary-trajectory co-generation) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (first convincing demonstration that pure CFM text-to-waveform can match multi-stage zero-shot TTS at scale without GANs, SSL features, or intermediate representations). The ingredients are individually known — DiT, masked infilling, x-prediction (JiT), energy-normalized spectral losses (Flow2GAN), pre-net bottlenecks (Tacotron), average-pooling alignment (ZipVoice) — but the specific combination of joint waveform/spectral trajectory learning with decoupled prediction/loss spaces is a genuine synthesis, and the strict no-external-module formulation is a meaningful problem framing. Concurrent waveform-diffusion TTS work (WavTTS, BareWave, acknowledged in the paper) overlaps the NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING claim, which the authors handle transparently. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablation coverage is a standout: separate tables isolate Spectral Forcing (Table 4, including Mel-bin count), disentangled heads (Table 6), prediction/loss space (Table 7), the multi-scale loss (Table 8), NFE (Tables 11, 17), CFG scale (Table 16), training-step curves (Table 14), and spectral dropout (Figure 4) — each component demonstrably matters. Code and checkpoints are released (github.com/sh-lee-prml/WaveGen), training data is public (LibriTTS, Emilia), and full hyperparameters are provided. Concerns: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests on WER/SIM numbers; WER/SIM are computed by the authors themselves via Whisper/WavLM on a single benchmark family (Seed-en/Seed-TTS-eval), so Goodhart risk on the ASR metric exists; the subjective MOS has only 20 raters per condition with wide intervals; and the headline 0.6B model deviates from the ablated configuration (it uses ConvNeXt text encoder, filler-token conditioning, logit-normal t-scheduling, a different reshape, and — per Table 13/Appendix F — a multi-scale spectral x-loss rather than the v-loss the paper argues for), so the flagship result is not a pure test of the proposed loss. This is a preprint (arXiv 2611.12527, NeurIPS 2026 formatting); treat numbers as self-reported until independently replicated. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (trained models with quantitative and subjective evaluation; also delivers a SYSTEMS-style artifact). - Practical: Yes — a 407M model reaches RTF 0.24 on a single A100 without inference optimization, and training used 4–8 consumer-cluster GPUs. - Efficient: E2E is more expensive per-NFE than vocoding a Mel, but cheaper in total pipeline terms (no separate vocoder training, single stage); the two-stage baseline at equal total NFE was slower per quality unit and worse. - Effective: The evidence supports the stated problem on open-data benchmarks (WER 1.47/SIM 0.75 vs strong baselines), though high-frequency content above 8 kHz is degraded by MP3 training data — a proxy gap versus true studio-quality waveform generation. - Scalable: Claimed and partially shown (113M→407M, 0.5k→120k hours, 4→11 epochs all improve monotonically, Table 14/15), but training stops well before convergence (4 epochs, authors' own admission), so 10× behavior is extrapolated, not tested. The work delivers a concrete software artifact: released code and trained checkpoints at multiple scales, plus demo audio. Strengths: - Spectral Forcing is a genuinely interesting mechanism: turning the classic cascaded spectrogram target into an internal co-generated trajectory is a clean way to get alignment inductive bias without sacrificing the end-to-end formulation, and the Mel-bin ablation (Table 4) sharply characterizes it as an information bottleneck (256 bins → denoising failure at WER 126.5; 32 bins → fastest convergence). - The decoupled x-prediction/v-loss finding for raw waveform, with spectral evidence (Figure 2) showing v-prediction destroys energy estimation, is a transferable insight for high-resolution signal diffusion beyond TTS. - Demonstrating competitive zero-shot TTS without GAN training, without SSL features, and without a vocoder — on entirely open data and code — is a strong existence proof that challenges the field's multi-stage consensus, with unusually honest accounting of concurrent work (WavTTS, BareWave). - The E2E-vs-two-stage controlled comparison (same DiT, same masked infilling, equal NFE, Table 5) is the right experiment for the paper's thesis and directly shows cascade error propagation. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: (1) large-scale training was limited to 4 epochs by compute, with clear evidence (Tables 14–15) that more training would help; (2) MP3-compressed Emilia audio caps recoverable high-frequency detail above 8 kHz, so E2E models on such data generate weaker high-frequency content than LibriTTS-trained models; (3) Spectral Forcing dependency grows with dataset scale and can delay text–speech alignment, motivating the Tacotron-style bottleneck pre-net; (4) REPA guidance improves results (WER 4.96→3.54) but was deliberately excluded from headline models; (5) 48 kHz extension left to future work; (6) they concede WavTTS offers complementary waveform-diffusion optimization analyses. They confront limitations directly rather than minimizing them — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The flagship 680M configuration is not the ablated method: it swaps average-pooling for filler tokens, uses a different reshape/t-schedule, and (per Table 13) replaces the multi-scale spectral v-loss with a Mel x-loss that the paper itself says causes buzzing — yet Appendix F recommends the v-loss version. The exact mechanism behind the headline 1.47 WER is therefore not cleanly attributable to the proposed loss. - Evaluation is confined to Seed-en/Seed-TTS-eval with self-run Whisper/WavLM metrics; no LibriSpeech-Test, no human MOS for the 0.6B model (MOS covers only WaveGen-B), no cross-benchmark validation, and no confidence intervals or seeds anywhere. - The no-SSL stance is partly cosmetic: the total objective embeds Mel-spectrogram computation at six scales, text-dropout CFG tuning, and the bottleneck pre-net — hand-engineered signal-processing structure doing much of the work that SSL embeddings would do, so the "no external modules" claim is narrower than it sounds. - RTF comparisons (0.24 vs 0.16) use the 407M E2E model against a 226M two-stage pipeline; parameter-matched latency accounting is absent, and no streaming/low-latency variant is evaluated despite the field's demand for it. - Inference requires 32–50 NFE (8 minimum for usable quality), versus vocoder single-pass or distillable codec LMs; no distillation result is provided despite a promised "accelerated version." - Robustness to noisy/in-the-wild prompt audio, long-form synthesis, and non-Emilia speaker accents is untested; DNSMOS (3.60–3.72) sits below what HiFi-GAN-class vocoders typically achieve, hinting at a residual perceptual gap the objective metrics don't capture. Bottom Line: A practitioner in speech generation should read this: it is the most credible demonstration to date that single-model, GAN-free, open-data text-to-waveform diffusion can rival multi-stage TTS, and its x-prediction/v-loss and internal-trajectory findings will shape the next generation of waveform models — but the loss-space inconsistency in the flagship model and pre-convergence training mean it does not yet dethrone deployed multi-stage systems like Qwen3-TTS or CosyVoice3.

MM-DyGraph: A Dataset, Benchmark, and Model for Multimodal Dynamic Graphs

Z Wu, P Wang, L Chen, T Wan, Y Meng, X Wang… · arxiv.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces MM-DyGraph, the first benchmark for multimodal dynamic graph learning (four real-world datasets with text and images on nodes and edges, three tasks), plus TST-MF, a target-aware spatiotemporal fusion model built on the finding that naive modality concatenation helps some prediction targets and hurts others. - Why it's important: Real dynamic graphs (e-commerce, social, finance) carry text and image content, but existing dynamic-graph benchmarks (TGB, DTGB) are structure-only or text-only, so the community has had no way to measure whether or how visual signals help under temporal evolution. - How it does it: TST-MF runs two-stage cross-attention: a target embedding queries fused history and structural-neighborhood context, and that context embedding in turn queries modality-specific features, so fusion is conditioned on the prediction target and its spatiotemporal context rather than a static fusion rule. - The good: The core negative finding is convincingly demonstrated across 8 dynamic-graph backbones, 3 feature configurations, and 5 datasets with 3 seeds each — e.g., on GDELT edge classification, naive concatenation underperforms even a random-feature baseline, and instance-level analysis shows multimodality helps some instances while degrading others. - The missing: TST-MF itself is not a clean winner — on Google Map City link prediction it scores 89.08 AP transductive and 65.49 inductive versus 95.54/83.05 for DyGFormer with plain concatenation (and 96.41 for gated fusion), a large regression the main text does not confront. - Read it or not: Worth reading if you build dynamic-graph models or multimodal fusion methods and need a realistic testbed and evidence that uniform fusion fails; skippable if you only want a new SOTA model, since the proposed model's wins are inconsistent across datasets and tasks.
Why this rank

Rigor (72) is solid: 3 seeds, 12 models, public code/data, pruning and imputation sensitivity checks — but the headline model TST-MF loses badly on GMCT link prediction and the structural-alignment hypothesis is post-hoc with no intervention. Problem & Motivation: Dynamic graphs in production systems (recommendation, advertising, payment fraud, social platforms) carry multimodal content — product images and titles, review photos, transaction descriptions — but existing benchmarks study dynamic graphs with structure-only or text-only attributes (TGB, TGB 2.0, DTGB), and multimodal graph learning methods target static graphs. This leaves practitioners without (a) data to train/evaluate multimodal dynamic-graph models, and (b) any measurement of whether adding modalities actually helps downstream tasks. The paper closes this gap with a benchmark and a diagnostic study. Key Idea: The core insight is an empirical one: modality utility in dynamic graphs is target-dependent — the same modality can be informative for some prediction targets and act as a confounder for others, governed by the structural alignment between where the visual signal lives (node vs. edge) and the prediction target granularity (node retrieval vs. link prediction). The technical move built on this is target-conditioned hierarchical cross-attention: instead of fusing modalities with a fixed rule, use the target embedding as the query for spatiotemporal context retrieval, then use the retrieved context as the query for modality selection. Methodology: The benchmark construction pipeline: (1) acquire four sources (GDELT sociopolitical events, Google Map City POI reviews, Amazon Office/Industrial e-commerce, Yelp) and attach images scraped or downloaded from metadata; (2) dataset-specific pruning to increase multimodal density (e.g., removing Amazon users with no image-containing reviews); (3) VLM-based quality filtering using Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, which scores image-text relevance 0–10 with a reasoning trace, discarding scores below 6; (4) temporal bucketing (Δt = 15 min for GDELT/GMCT, 24 h for Amazon/Yelp). Three tasks: link prediction (AP, AUC-ROC; transductive and inductive; 70/15/15 chronological split following DTGB), edge classification (precision/recall/F1), and node retrieval (Hits@1/3/10 against 100 sampled negatives, plus a harder historical-negative variant). Embeddings use CLIP ViT-B/16 (512-d per modality, chunk-and-average for long text, duplicated text embedding for unimodal dimensional parity). TST-MF: a Spatial-Temporal Context Extractor (sequential Transformer over interaction history + structural neighbor aggregator) feeds a Hierarchical Target-Guided Modality Fusion module — context cross-attention with the target embedding as query, then modality cross-attention with the context embedding as query over modality-specific features, then an MLP head (12.0M parameters, DyGFormer-scale). Design decisions: two-stage (vs. single-stage) fusion is ablated; target guidance is ablated; spatial and historical branches are each ablated; missing-modality handling is compared across four imputation strategies (zero, mean, learned, duplication). The target-aware and hierarchical choices are justified by ablation; the hypothesis that structural alignment governs modality utility is argued from observational analysis rather than a controlled intervention. Key Results: Across 8 backbones (TGAT, CAWN, TCL, GraphMixer, FreeDyG, TPNet, SALoM, DyGFormer — recent methods including 2024–2025 NeurIPS/ICLR entries) × 5 datasets × 3 feature configurations: (RQ1/RQ2) Random features sometimes suffice — DyGFormer with random embeddings reaches 94.47 AP on GMCT link prediction transductive, and adding modalities yields mixed or negative effects (TCL on GDELT link prediction, DyGFormer on Amazon-Office). (RQ3) Gains concentrate where modality location aligns with the task: node retrieval on Amazon (node images) gains up to +40.7% relative over structure-only, while link prediction gains are negligible (+0.3% to +3.0%); inductive settings amplify harm from misaligned modalities. TST-MF reaches best or second-best on most dataset/task pairs — e.g., GDELT link prediction 93.98 AP transductive / 85.44 inductive vs. DyGFormer 92.46/83.05; Amazon-Office inductive 78.16 AP vs. 68.64 for concatenation; GDELT edge classification 53.56 precision vs. 47.54; GDELT node retrieval 81.62 Hits@10 transductive. However, on GMCT link prediction TST-MF (89.08 tr. / 65.49 in.) trails both DyGFormer-concatenation (95.54/83.05) and gated fusion (96.41/82.46). Node retrieval with random negatives saturates (100.00 Hits@10 on GMCT/Amazon for several models); the authors' supplementary historical-negative protocol is discriminative (GDELT transductive drops to 20–36 Hits@10). Tested scale is standard for the field (pruned sets up to 815K nodes / 1.36M edges; the full Yelp set at 2.1M nodes / 6.99M edges was not evaluable on a single A100). Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (first benchmark with images on nodes and edges of dynamic graphs, plus three tasks and a historical-negative retrieval protocol) and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (target-level inconsistency of naive multimodal fusion, with the structural-alignment observation). TST-MF is a NEW METHOD but a competent composition of existing pieces — target-as-query cross-attention, temporal and neighborhood encoders, CLIP embeddings — with the two-stage target-then-context conditioning as the genuinely new twist. Much of the empirical infrastructure (chronological splits, transductive/inductive protocol, metrics) follows DTGB/TGB conventions. Rigor & Reproducibility: Reasonably strong: 3 seeds with mean ± std on every number, 12 models × 5 datasets × 3 tasks, hyperparameters and per-model parameter counts published, ablations over four design choices, four missing-modality imputation comparisons, evaluation on unpruned "full" versions of GDELT/GMCT to check pruning sensitivity, recurrence-aware splits, and instance-level modality-masking analysis with 95% confidence intervals (Table 27). Code (github.com/LeslieWu999/mm-dygraph) and data (huggingface.co/datasets/LeslieWu999/MM-DyGraph) are public. Concerns: the detailed ablation table is relegated to the appendix (text truncated in the PDF, so component contributions on edge classification are not verifiable from the main text); the VLM relevance filter (threshold 6) is validated only by four case studies plus vague "manual supervision," so filtering bias is unquantified; the structural-alignment hypothesis is post-hoc and not tested via intervention; several headline comparisons are against the authors' own model on their own benchmark (no external leaderboard yet), and TST-MF's losses on GMCT are not flagged in the narrative. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (benchmark + model, experiments actually run). Practical: Yes — runs on a single NVIDIA A100 (40/80 GB) with AMD EPYC CPU, standard stack. Efficient: Comparable to backbones (TST-MF 12.0M params vs. DyGFormer 6.2M, SALoM 276.2M); VLM filtering and CLIP encoding are one-time preprocessing costs, but Qwen3-VL-8B scoring of every image-text pair is nontrivial at collection scale. Effective: Evidence supports the diagnostic claim (naive fusion is unreliable) and shows TST-MF competitive on most pairs, but not universal — GMCT link prediction regresses badly relative to simpler fusion, so the method does not fully solve the problem it poses. Scalable: Untested beyond ~1.4M-edge pruned graphs; the full Yelp set was declared infeasible on single-GPU hardware, so 10× scale behavior is claimed only implicitly. Delivers a software artifact: public dataset on Hugging Face, code on GitHub; no trained model weights mentioned. Strengths: - Genuinely first-mover dataset contribution: images attached to both nodes and edges across four domains with distinct temporal regimes (event bursts, periodicity, stability, growth), plus release of both pruned and full versions — an unusually honest artifact design. - The negative result is the paper's most valuable intellectual output: random-feature baselines saturating link prediction, concatenation underperforming random features on GDELT edge classification, and instance-level heterogeneity directly contradict the default "more modalities = better" assumption. - Methodological transparency rare for benchmark papers: imputation-strategy sensitivity, pruning-sensitivity checks on full data, historical-negative retrieval to break metric saturation, and recurrence-aware splits. - The fusion-mechanism comparison (gated, modality-attention, MoE, TST-MF on a shared DyGFormer backbone) isolates the fusion contribution from the temporal backbone, which is the right experimental control. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge that random-negative node retrieval saturates (Hits@10 near 100%) and add the historical-negative protocol; that pruning changes graph size and modality availability (mitigated with full-data experiments); that missing-modality imputation choice could confound results (four strategies compared); and that naive fusion can degrade performance (this motivates the work). They confront these limitations fairly directly. They do not acknowledge TST-MF's regressions on GMCT or the post-hoc nature of the structural-alignment hypothesis. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - TST-MF's headline framing as the effective solution is undercut by its own tables: on GMCT link prediction it loses to plain concatenation by ~6.5 AP transductive and ~17.5 AP inductive, and on Amazon-Industrial edge classification it trails DyGFormer by ~9 precision. The paper never analyzes when target-aware fusion fails. - The structural-alignment "governing factor" is inferred from five confounded dataset-task pairs (dataset and alignment co-vary); a within-dataset manipulation (e.g., swapping node/edge image placement) is absent. - Both modalities go through a single CLIP encoder — image representations may simply be weak; no stronger vision encoder or multimodal LLM embedding is tested, so "images don't help" may partially reflect encoder capacity. - VLM filtering at threshold 6 with reasoning-before-score prompting risks systematically removing hard/ambiguous images, potentially inflating apparent multimodal signal; only 4 anecdotal case studies validate it. - Full Yelp (the largest dataset, 6.99M edges) was never evaluated, so the benchmark's scale claims rest on pruned versions of three datasets plus one full dataset. - Ablation detail (Table 28) is appendix-only and truncated in the provided text, so the "w/o target" vs. "w/o hierarchical" split cannot be verified from the main paper. Bottom Line: A practitioner working on temporal GNNs or multimodal graph learning should absolutely use the benchmark and absorb the negative findings about naive fusion, but should treat TST-MF as a strong reference point rather than a settled solution, since its own results show target-aware fusion is not yet robust across datasets.

MetaPI: Constructing Prompt Injection Benchmarks from LLM Agent Benchmark

P Wang, C Xiang, W Qu, Y Li, J Zhang, GE Suh, Y Tian · arxiv.org · automated generated environments for agent testing - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces METAPI, a toolkit that automatically converts existing LLM-agent utility benchmarks (AppWorld, VitaBench, Terminal-Bench) into end-to-end indirect prompt injection (IPI) evaluation suites by generating injection points, authority-aware attack objectives, and adaptively optimized payloads inside the original environments. - Why it's important: Dedicated IPI benchmarks lag far behind fast-moving utility benchmarks (e.g., AgentDojo has 97 tasks vs. hundreds of tasks and rapidly iterating versions in utility suites), so security evaluation systematically understates real-world exposure of agents with high-privilege tools. - How it does it: A four-module pipeline — Benchmark Connector, Strategy Generator, Payload Optimizer, Outcome Validator — records benign agent trajectories, classifies actions/reads by necessity and data ownership, applies an owner-authority rule to decide which objectives count as genuine IPI, then runs PAIR-style black-box payload optimization capped at 12 rounds and re-validates attacks in the real environment. - The good: Across 183 generated attacks and 8 defenses spanning prompting, detection, model-level, and system categories, no defense achieves both strong utility and strong security — e.g., CaMeL hits 0.0% ASR but drops clean utility to 33.7% (vs. 82.5% undefended) on AppWorld, while defenses reporting near-zero ASR on AgentDojo show 20–45% ASR here. - The missing: All headline experiments use proxy-mode payload delivery (string substitution in the observation) rather than env-mode modification of the underlying environment state, the attack corpus is only 183 attacks over 107 tasks with single-run results and no seeds or error bars, and CaMeL's zero-ASR is partly attributable to acknowledged payload-delivery/integration limitations rather than proven resistance. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building or evaluating LLM-agent prompt-injection defenses — it delivers both a reusable evaluation methodology and a sobering negative result — but attack researchers seeking novel optimization techniques will find the payload search is a standard PAIR loop.
Why this rank
Scored using Systems profile. Novelty (78) is the top driver — the owner-authority threat model and meta-benchmarking architecture are a genuine new formulation, not just a new attack. Rigor (65) is dragged down by single-run results with no error bars, proxy-mode-only delivery, and the confounded CaMeL result, though third-party benchmarks and independently published defenses mitigate Goodhart risk. Completeness (72) is buoyed by unusually honest limitation disclosure (the CaMeL disaggregation), while Resilience (68) absorbs the LLM-judged ownership rule and the partially automatic claim. Impact (62) reflects a toolkit that is promised but not yet released, which materially limits its current practical value. Weighted composite: 0.15*78 + 0.15*65 + 0.10*72 + 0.15*72 + 0.15*68 + 0.30*62 = 68.
