Problem & Motivation: LLM-based Verilog generation is judged by cycle-accurate functional correctness, but training signals derived from simulation are misaligned with token-level learning in two ways. First, a module-level pass/fail discards partial correctness: a candidate that implements one output correctly and another incorrectly is treated identically to a wholly wrong module. Second, even signal-level scores (as in QiMeng-SALV) leave an attribution gap: static syntax-to-output connectivity (e.g., `assign mid = a & b; assign out = mid | c;`) does not establish that a statement is functionally responsible for an output's behavior under the observed test vectors, since other assignments or branches can override or compensate. The problem affects anyone training Verilog-specific LLMs (ChipNeMo-style teams, RTL research groups) where preference pairs built from coarse outcomes inject noisy supervision. Prior work (RTLCoder, VeriPrefer, QiMeng-SALV) closes part of this gap at signal level; CSCA targets the remaining statement-level attribution gap. Key Idea: Treat functional responsibility of an RTL statement as an empirical intervention effect: perturb the output-driving assignment (force to 0/1, hold, invert, or delete), re-run the identical testbench, and use the induced change in the target signal's mismatch count — clipped to [0,1] and averaged over successful interventions — as the statement's counterfactual credit. Fuse this with the signal's behavioral agreement score (1 − mismatch fraction) via a mixing coefficient α to get a continuous per-statement weight, then restrict the DPO log-ratio to exactly the tokens inside those credited statement spans. This is executable, test-distribution-dependent causal evidence — explicitly not formal causality — but more discriminating than co-occurrence or signal-level scores alone. Methodology: Two-stage pipeline. (1) Full-parameter SFT of Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct on 135K preprocessed CodeV-derived Verilog modules (2 epochs, LR 1e-5, batch 64, seq len 2048). (2) The SFT policy samples K=5 candidates per prompt; each candidate and the reference run on the same clocked testbench, yielding per-signal mismatch counts e_i(s) and behavioral scores r_beh(s) = 1 − e_i(s)/N. For each output-driving assignment located in a candidate, five local intervention variants are compiled and executed; counterfactual credit r_cf = mean over valid interventions q of clip((e_q(s) − e_i(s))/N, 0, 1). Combined credit w = clip(α·r_beh + (1−α)·r_cf, 0, 1), α=0.7; statements without a valid intervention fall back to behavioral score. Candidates are ranked by mean statement credit to form DPO chosen/rejected pairs, and a weighted DPO objective (Eq. 11–12) restricts the token-level log-ratio to credited spans via token weights (β for preference sharpness, LoRA adapters, ~7K steps, LR 5e-6). Three critical design decisions: (a) interventions restricted to combinational output-driving assignments (justified by reliability data — Delete fails 22.44/1000 due to compile errors, Invert 2.99/1000 due to timeouts); (b) positive-only counterfactual credit — interventions that reduce mismatches get zero credit rather than negative weight (conservative, avoids punishing fix-capable spans, but unstated alternative); (c) offline DPO with static preference pairs (chosen for reproducibility, acknowledged as underutilizing fresh candidates). Key Results: On VerilogEval 2.0 (156 problems per subtask) and RTLLM v2.0 (50 instances), with Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct backbone: greedy Pass@1 of 56.4% (Code Completion), 49.3% (Spec-to-RTL), 50.0% (RTLLM); at T=0.8, Pass@1/Pass@5 of 55.1%/66.0%, 47.4%/62.2%, 47.2%/60.0%. This beats the strongest Verilog-specific baseline QiMeng-SALV (54.5%/49.1%/46.0% greedy Pass@1) by relative 3.5%/6.7%/8.7%, and beats GPT-5.4-mini on most metrics while remaining behind Gemini-3.1-pro (75.0% greedy Pass@1 on completion) and the 671B DeepSeek-V3 on some metrics. Baselines are current and include the 2025 NeurIPS signal-level QiMeng-SALV — appropriately strong. Relative to the Qwen2.5-Coder base, gains are 72.5%/114.3%/38.9% greedy Pass@1. Ablations show complementarity (behavioral-only 42.8% vs counterfactual-only 43.2% vs full 47.4% Pass@1 on Spec-to-RTL); α sensitivity peaks at α=0.7 across all three benchmarks. Of 893,225 intervention samples, 53.2% produced no behavior change, 36.1% positive gain, 10.7% negative gain; mean nonzero gain +0.157. Cost: SFT 162.4 GPU-hours (8 GPUs, 20.3h); CSCA-DPO adds only 14.2 GPU-hours on 4 GPUs (LoRA, 0.264% of parameters). No statistical significance tests or multi-seed variance are reported. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION + NEW METHOD, with a supporting NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel element is the counterfactual-intervention statement credit mapped to token-weighted DPO — prior work stopped at signal-level rewards (QiMeng-SALV) or module-level preference pairs (VeriPrefer). The components are individually standard: mutation-style program perturbation, simulation scoring, DPO, LoRA; the contribution is the principled fusion and token-level localization, applied to a new setting. The paper honestly positions its interventions as test-adequacy-adjacent rather than formal causality. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong on ablations: component ablation (Table 2), α-sweep (Fig. 4), temperature sweep 0.0–1.0 (Table 3), per-intervention failure rates (Fig. 3), intervention-gain distribution over 893K samples (Fig. 5), training/inference cost accounting, and a qualitative case study. Missing: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests — several reported margins over QiMeng-SALV (e.g., 56.4% vs 54.5%) are within plausible sampling noise for 156 problems. Code and pipeline are released at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/CSCA-3B8C (anonymous repo, suggesting under-review status). Methodological concerns: the training testbenches derive from the reference implementations in the CodeV corpus and evaluation uses benchmark-provided testbenches — credit is explicitly test-distribution-dependent, so the framework optimizes behavior under the same verification distribution it is evaluated on (Goodhart risk the authors partially acknowledge); the abstract's comparison to "GPT-5.4-mini" involves self-run evaluation of a closed API model, not vendor-reported numbers, but the model naming in this preprint cannot be verified independently. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a training method run end-to-end with measured results). - Practical: Yes — runs on Icarus Verilog (open-source simulator) and 4–8 commodity GPUs; the counterfactual pipeline needs only compile-and-simulate infrastructure. - Efficient: Favorable — the CSCA stage adds 14.2 GPU-hours (~8.8% on top of SFT) via LoRA; inference costs are unchanged from ordinary sampling. - Effective: Evidence supports improvement over the same-backbone SFT and over signal-level baselines on standard benchmarks, but effectiveness is measured against testbench-defined proxies of functional correctness, not formal equivalence — which is inherent to the approach. - Scalable: Untested beyond 7B parameters and 135K training modules; the intervention corpus (893K simulations) shows the pipeline operates at that scale, but 10× larger models/corpora, sequential-heavy designs (where interventions are excluded), and richer inter-module dependencies are untested. Delivers a released artifact: data-construction scripts, training configs, and evaluation commands in an anonymous repository; no trained model weights are stated as released. Strengths: - The core insight — replacing static association with executable intervention evidence for statement-level credit — is a genuine conceptual advance over signal-level rewards, cleanly motivated by the compensatory-logic example in §3.2. - Unusually honest framing: the paper repeatedly states that credits are test-distribution-dependent empirical evidence, not formal causality, and the threats-to-validity section names specific failure modes (shared assignments, macros, generated blocks, sequential state). - The reliability analysis of the five interventions (Delete: 22.44 failures/1000 from compile errors; Invert: 2.99/1000 from timeouts) both justifies the design restrictions and gives practitioners actionable engineering data. - Controlled comparison discipline: identical backbone, SFT init, rollout budget, prompts, and harness across all CSCA variants and ablations isolates the credit-assignment mechanism. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: (1) counterfactual evidence is finite-trace empirical behavior, not formal equivalence; (2) attribution is error-prone for shared assignments, macros, generated blocks, and complex sequential state, mitigated by restricting to combinational output-driving assignments and skipping unsupported constructs; (3) single base model and single training corpus limit external validity; (4) offline DPO with static preference pairs underutilizes novel candidates. They confront limitations directly rather than minimizing — a credibility positive — though mitigation for (1) is largely "we follow standardized testbenches" rather than a technical fix. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No statistical rigor: single runs, no seeds, no confidence intervals — with margins over QiMeng-SALV as small as ~2 points on 156-problem benchmarks, several headline claims may not be significant. - The choice of α=0.7 is reported as optimal, but the optimal α could be benchmark-specific tuning; no held-out validation split for α selection is described. - Only direct-output-driving assignments receive credit; intermediate wires (e.g., `mid`) and control-flow logic driving conditional correctness get no intervention treatment, so the "attribution gap" is closed only for a subset of statements — the paper does not quantify what fraction of generated code is covered by eligible statements. - Sequential logic — central to real RTL — is explicitly excluded from interventions, yet the case study's headline fix (synchronous reset, modulo-1000 wrap) is sequential; how CSCA helps sequential designs generally is unaddressed. - Cross-backbone transfer is claimed as a property ("orthogonal to the backbone") but never tested on a second model. - The closed-model baselines (GPT-5.4-mini, Gemini-3.1-pro) are evaluated by the authors under unspecified prompting/few-shot conditions, a known source of variance in cross-model comparisons. Bottom Line: A researcher building verification-in-the-loop or preference-based training for code-generation models should read this: the counterfactual-statement-credit idea is genuinely new and the ablation evidence for it is convincing, but the narrow evaluation (single backbone, testbench-dependent credit, no significance testing) means the reported edges over QiMeng-SALV should be treated as promising rather than settled.

Interpretable and lightweight multimodal Transformer assessment of English education ecosystem health

M Lv, Y Wang, D Han · nature.com · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds a multimodal Transformer (text + audio + video) that predicts a five-dimensional, rater-annotated "Ecosystem Health Index" for English classroom sessions, explains its predictions via gradient-weighted attention attribution, and compresses it 8.2× (23.8M → 2.9M parameters) for edge deployment. - Why it's important: Classroom assessment today relies on questionnaires or single-indicator statistics that ignore coupled text/audio/video dynamics, and schools need cheap, auditable, on-device tools that will not leak recordings of minors. - How it does it: Modality-specific encoders feed bidirectional cross-modal attention and gated aggregation to regress an entropy-weighted five-dimension composite score, with distillation-then-head-pruning for compression and Grad-CAM-style gradient×attention maps for explanation. - The good: The evaluation is unusually honest for this literature — five seeds, bootstrap intervals, Holm-corrected paired Wilcoxon tests against nine baselines, five leave-group-out transfer protocols (+13.5% to +34.1% RMSE), faithfulness comparison against four attribution alternatives, and real device-level latency/energy measurements on Jetson Nano and Raspberry Pi 4B. - The missing: The target variable is a human rater judgment collected by the authors on their own 6,142-session Chinese higher-education corpus (MEED-6K), so all headline numbers are within-distribution fits to a construct whose external validity rests on two correlations (0.62 with student ratings, 0.58 with supervisory scores) and no independent replication. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on multimodal learning analytics or deploying auditable assessment models in schools; skip it if you want a new ML technique — the authors themselves state no component is architecturally new.

Problem & Motivation: Administrators and researchers want to assess the "health" of English-language classrooms — the coupled dynamics of teaching content, delivery, and learner behavior — from routine recordings rather than surveys. Existing approaches fail in three ways: factor-analysis/SEM methods assume linear relationships among pre-specified latent constructs; learning-analytics ML uses single-modality tabular features (e.g., LMS clickstreams); and prior multimodal fusion relies on early/late concatenation of hand-crafted features that cannot model fine-grained cross-modal interactions. Deployment additionally requires running on edge hardware in resource-limited schools, keeping recordings of minors on-site, and producing judgments traceable to observable behavior that a teaching committee can defend. The paper targets the specific gap of no prior Transformer-based system jointly processing text, acoustics, and video for ecosystem-level English-education assessment. Key Idea: There is no single new technical trick; the authors say so explicitly ("We do not claim that any single component below is new to machine learning"). The load-bearing idea is construct-first engineering: define the regression target as an auditable five-dimension composite (teaching input quality, cognitive engagement, interaction intensity, affective state, resource adaptability) with behavioral anchors, a three-rater protocol, entropy-based adaptive weighting, and an automatic cross-check used only for auditing so the network cannot game its own inputs — then wrap standard cross-modal attention, gated fusion, gradient×attention attribution, and KD+pruning around that construct. Methodology: Four-module pipeline: (1) modality-specific encoding — byte-pair-encoded text through a pre-trained language model (2 Transformer blocks, d=256), MFCC+F0+energy acoustic features at 10 ms hop (Conv1D + 1 Transformer block), and 17 facial action units plus upper-body pose keypoints (temporal conv + 1 Transformer block); (2) linear projection to a shared 256-d space, linear interpolation of audio/video onto the text time grid, then bidirectional cross-modal attention over all six directed modality pairs (8 heads) with residual addition; (3) sigmoid gated aggregation of the three fused streams, feed-forward layer, and a 5-output regression head combined via entropy weights (weights inverse to dimension-score entropy, recomputed on training data per fold); (4) EHI output. Training minimizes MSE plus L2 regularization (λ grid-searched), AdamW, lr 3e-4 (stated via grid search), cosine annealing over 80 epochs, early stopping on 10-epoch patience. Interpretability adapts Grad-CAM to multi-head cross-modal attention (ReLU-thresholded gradient×attention, aggregated per modality and per time step, 90th-percentile salient-interval selection). Compression: distillation with soft-label + feature-alignment loss (λ=0.5) into a half-width student, then sensitivity-based structured head pruning (elbow at <5% cumulative importance, ~30% of heads removed, 10-epoch fine-tune). Critical design decisions — linear temporal alignment, entropy weighting, and the audit-only automatic cross-check — are each tested against alternatives (Tables 2 and 7), which is well-justified, though learned temporal offsets actually beat interpolation by 0.0007 RMSE and were not adopted. Key Results: On MEED-6K (6,142 sessions, 20 institutions, 326 instructors, 4,870 students; 4,300/921/921 split), the full model achieves RMSE 0.0431±0.0009, MAE 0.0319±0.0008, R² 0.923±0.004 over five seeds, beating nine baselines: SVR (0.0834), gradient-boosted trees (0.0726), text-only BERT (0.0612), audio LSTM (0.0689), video TimeSformer (0.0654), early-fusion MLP (0.0581), tensor fusion (0.0536), MAG-BERT (0.0512), and MulT (0.0498) — the strongest baseline, beaten by a 13.5% relative RMSE reduction with p=0.004 (Holm-corrected) and a bootstrap difference interval of [0.0051, 0.0083]. Baselines are current and reasonably strong for this domain. Under stricter protocols error rises +13.5% (leave-one-instructor-out, RMSE 0.0489), +18.8% (leave-one-institution-out, 0.0512), +20.9% (course-type), +24.6% (cross-province, 0.0537), +34.1% (university→vocational, 0.0578). Attribution: GWAA scores comprehensiveness 0.312 / sufficiency 0.041 / AOPC 0.267, beating integrated gradients (0.274/0.050/0.231), attention rollout, raw attention, and LIME, at 0.34 s vs LIME's 14.7 s. Modality attribution shifts from text-dominant (47.3%) in healthy sessions to video-dominant (39.1%) in low-health sessions. Compression: distillation alone gives 4.7× at 8.4% RMSE degradation; +30% pruning gives 8.2× (2.9M params, 0.21G FLOPs) with 88.2% RMSE-based retention (RMSE 0.0482). Device results: 94 ms/session on Jetson Nano (FP16), 71 ms INT8; 473 ms on Raspberry Pi 4B (vs 4,310 ms for the teacher); energy 0.51 J vs 22.41 J on Pi. Subgroup RMSE gaps favor universities over vocational colleges by 0.0044 and higher- over lower-proficiency cohorts by 0.0041. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (MEED-6K, a 6,142-session multimodal English-classroom corpus with a published rubric and rater protocol — though not publicly redistributable) and a competent EDUCATION-SPECIFIC INTEGRATION of established ideas (MulT-style cross-modal attention, Grad-CAM adaptation, gated multimodal units, TinyBERT-style distillation, Voita-style head pruning). The GWAA attribution adaptation to cross-modal attention is a modest methodological increment over Chefer et al.'s relevance methods. Nothing else is genuinely novel, and the paper does not pretend otherwise. Rigor & Reproducibility: Rigor is above the bar for this venue and field: five seeds with standard deviations, 1,000-sample bootstrap intervals, paired Wilcoxon tests with Holm correction across nine comparisons, ablations of alignment strategy and output head, five transfer protocols, faithfulness metrics for attribution, subgroup error analysis, and explicit leakage controls (entropy weights and normalization computed only on train/validation; automatic cross-checks excluded from targets). Methodological concerns: the primary result is on a stratified random split where the same instructors and institutions appear on both sides — the authors flag this themselves and report the stricter protocols, but the headline numbers remain the flattering ones; the target is rater judgment (ICC 0.87 composite), so the ceiling and biases of the construct bound what the model can learn; the faithfulness evaluation is on the authors' own data and metric, with no human-subject validation (only informal consultation with five instructors); code and derived data ship as "Related files" with the article rather than a public repository, and raw recordings are restricted, so full external reproduction is not possible. No publication bias concern apparent; the generalization table is self-undermining in a credible way. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS component in the compression/deployment study). - Practical: Yes — the compressed model runs on commodity edge hardware (Jetson Nano, Raspberry Pi 4B) with no cloud dependency, which is the stated point. - Efficient: 2.9M parameters, 0.21G FLOPs, 71–94 ms on Nano, 1.94 J per inference on Pi — roughly an order of magnitude cheaper than the teacher and far cheaper than MAG-BERT-class models (115M params). - Effective: Within-distribution evidence supports the regression task (R² 0.923 vs rater judgment), but effectiveness for the real goal — actionable formative assessment — is shown only through one anecdotal case study and faithfulness proxies, not a user study or intervention trial. - Scalable: Not tested beyond the 20-institution corpus; the authors' own transfer table (+18.8% to +34.1% error across institutions, provinces, and institution types) shows degradation at even modest distribution shift, so any 10× or cross-context scaling claim would be unsupported. The deliverable is a paper plus code/derived data in supplementary files; no standalone library, pretrained weights release, or deployed product is described. Strengths: - The auditable target construct is the real contribution: behavioral anchors, three-rater protocol with adjudication (4.1% of judgments), ICC 0.87, a confirmatory five-factor check (CFI 0.94, RMSEA 0.052), convergent validity against two external criteria, and a demonstrated-comparison of four weighting schemes (entropy vs equal vs Delphi-expert vs learned, all within 4% RMSE). Most educational-AI papers assume their label; this one specifies it. - Honest generalization accounting: reporting +13.5% to +34.1% error under leave-group-out protocols and labeling the headline split as within-distribution is unusual and raises the evidentiary standard for this subfield. - End-to-end deployment accounting (platform × precision × batch latency, RAM, power, energy) on actual edge hardware, rather than FLOPs alone. - Ablations that could have undermined the design are actually run — learned temporal offsets beat the adopted linear interpolation, and DTW clearly hurts — reported transparently. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly and at length: (1) the corpus is Chinese higher education only, with up to a third more error under institutional-type shift, so the model is a within-population instrument; (2) the dataset excludes extreme outlier sessions, so behavior on disrupted classes is unknown; (3) the target is a human judgment inheriting rater blind spots; (4) the model captures co-variation, not causal direction, between delivery and learner behavior, and single-session scope misses slower dependencies; (5) entropy weighting treats covarying dimensions as independent; (6) faithfulness metrics are imperfect proxies and no formal educator user study was run (only informal consultation with five instructors). They also impose an explicit use boundary (formative reflection only, no punitive evaluation, no student-level inference). This candor is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The headline comparison (Table 6) is on the leakage-prone stratified split; the fairest comparison table would report all baselines under leave-one-institution-out too, since the model's margin over MulT (0.0067 RMSE) could shrink or reverse under transfer — only the full model's transfer numbers are given. - The "text dominates healthy / video dominates degraded" finding is a correlational pattern from the model's own attributions on the authors' data; no ground-truth behavioral coding verifies that the attribution maps correspond to pedagogically real events beyond one case study. - Construct validity rests on correlations of 0.62 (student ratings) and 0.58 (supervisory scores) — moderate at best, and both external criteria have their own known biases; the index's claim to measure "ecosystem health" rather than rater-consistent impressions of it is not stress-tested against learning outcomes (e.g., student achievement gains), which would be the decisive validation. - A general-purpose multimodal foundation model baseline (motivated at length in the introduction as the obvious alternative) is discussed but never evaluated, despite the privacy/latency arguments being testable with local inference. - The GWAA method is evaluated only on the model it explains, on the authors' own dataset, with proxy metrics; no comparison to Chefer et al.'s relevance propagation, the closest published method, is reported. - Fairness analysis covers institution type, proficiency, and class size but not gender or other protected attributes of instructors or students, which the responsible-use framing would seem to demand. Bottom Line: A practitioner in learning analytics or educational AI assessment gains a genuinely useful template — how to build an auditable label, test generalization honestly, and deploy on school hardware — from a paper whose individual ML components are standard, and anyone seeking a validated, transferable measure of teaching quality will need to look elsewhere or re-validate locally from scratch.

A Survey of the Training Process of LLM-Based Agents

TL;DR - What it does: This paper presents a process-centric survey of LLM-based agent training that organizes ~400+ works around a unified training pipeline — environment setup, data and trajectory construction, learning-signal design, and optimization objectives/schemes — rather than by application domain or algorithm. - Why it's important: Agent training is expensive and error-prone because choices at each pipeline stage (environment, data, signals, losses) interact in ways capability- or domain-organized surveys obscure; practitioners currently lack a structured map of these coupled design decisions. - How it does it: The survey formalizes a canonical agent training loop (Algorithm 1: environment setup → query collection → trajectory sampling → signal generation → model update) and dissects each stage, e.g., classifying query synthesis into direct/iterative/exploratory and learning signals along source, granularity, and form axes. - The good: The process-centric taxonomy is genuinely useful — the paper distills cross-stage trade-off tables (Appendix D) covering grounding, cost, verifiability, and noise risk per environment type, which no cited survey provides. - The missing: It is a pure survey with zero experiments; the authors admit comparative evaluation of training strategies would give "more meaningful and actionable guidance" but leave this resource-intensive work undone, so all claims are qualitative syntheses of self-reported results from heterogeneous, non-comparable papers. - Read it or not: Read it if you are building or training LLM agents and want a structured index of environment/data/signal design options with trade-offs; skip it if you need empirical guidance on which combination of choices actually wins — no head-to-head evidence exists here.

Problem & Motivation: The work targets the problem that general-purpose LLMs, even after standard pre-training and post-training, perform unreliably as environment-interactive agents because agent tasks demand multi-turn decision-making over unfamiliar observation/action spaces (browser operations, search queries, code edits) not covered by static input-output training. Researchers and engineers building trained (weight-updated) agents face a sprawling, fast-growing literature — the authors' trend plot shows agent-training publications growing from near zero in 2023 to roughly 2,000+ quarterly arXiv papers by 2026 — organized previously by capability (memory, planning, tool use), domain (web, GUI, multimodal), or algorithm (RL), none of which reveals how pipeline-stage choices interact. The gap closed is a process-level organization: what environment representation, data construction, and signal design jointly imply for a trainable agent policy. Key Idea: The core organizing insight is that agent training is structurally different from ordinary LLM post-training in three ways — environment interaction, trajectory (rather than single-pair) dependence, and long-horizon credit assignment — and that the same loss functions become agent-specific only when coupled with environment design, trajectory construction, and feedback granularity. Concretely, the paper renders this as Algorithm 1, a training loop whose stages (setup environment, collect query, sample trajectory, get signal, train) each become a distinct design axis. This is a framing/organization idea, not a technical algorithmic invention. Methodology: This is a survey, not an experimental method; the "method" is the taxonomy and corpus construction. The paper collection pipeline (Appendix A) combines broad arXiv keyword search, LLM-assisted screening (QWEN3-8B judging title/abstract for relevance, with the full screening prompt published), manual author verification, and snowballing from related surveys and representative papers; inclusion requires (1) LLM-based agent, (2) external environment interaction, (3) training-related methodology with policy parameter updates. The body proceeds through: §3 environment design (observation augmentation/simplification, history truncation/summarization, action formats like function calling and code actions); §4 data (query synthesis via direct prompting, context-aware, iterative extension, and exploratory reverse construction; trajectories via conversion, teacher/self/tree-search sampling, and special constructions like AgentTrek's tutorial replay); §5 training (signal source: expert/environment/model-based; granularity: trajectory- vs. step-level, mapping to the ORM/PRM debate; form: scalar reward, natural-language critique, preferences; losses: SFT/DPO/RL with observation masking and multi-turn modifications; schemes: offline vs. online, SFT-then-RL staging, curricula). Critical design decisions — e.g., centering only on main-policy parameter updates while deferring prompting, memory, and world models to §6 — are explicit and justified, though the depth per paper is deliberately shallow (acknowledged page-limit constraint). Key Results: Not applicable in the experimental sense — the paper reports no metrics of its own. Its quantitative content is bibliometric: a quarterly trend chart (Figure 2) showing LLM-agent arXiv papers growing to ~2,500/quarter and agent-training papers to a substantial subset by 2026. Synthesized findings are qualitative: e.g., loss masking on environment-observation tokens improves training (citing Jin et al. 2025); step-level signals are denser but noisier and algorithm-dependent (Wang and Ammanabrolu 2025); environment types differ systematically in verifiability and interaction cost (Table 1: QA/search partially verifiable at low/medium cost vs. GUI/embodied sparse and high cost). All cited performance numbers belong to the underlying papers and are not re-verified or compared here. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (of the survey space) — the genuinely novel element is the process-centric, pipeline-stage organization of agent-training literature with cross-stage trade-off tables, which differs from the cited capability/domain/algorithm-organized surveys (Xi et al. 2025; Zhang et al. 2026a; Du et al. 2026). The individual topic treatments (RLVR, DPO, SFT-then-RL, curriculum, PRMs, tree-search rollouts) are standard combinations of known ideas arranged under a new lens; no new method, dataset, or empirical finding is contributed. Rigor & Reproducibility: As a survey, rigor rests on corpus transparency, which is partially met: the collection methodology, inclusion/exclusion criteria, and the exact LLM screening prompt are published, and the authors state LLM screening was only auxiliary with all included papers manually verified. Limitations of rigor: no ablations or error analysis apply (no experiments); per-paper descriptions are intentionally brief, so a reader cannot reconstruct the evidence behind many stated trade-offs; the trade-off tables (Tables 1–3) are qualitative judgments without cited measurements supporting each cell; the trend estimate uses a broad "agent" keyword with LLM filtering, which risks noisy counts. No code, corpus release, or repository URL is mentioned for the survey itself — the paper collection is not released as a reusable dataset, only as citations. No Goodhart or self-reporting concern applies directly to the survey, but it inherits and relays self-reported numbers from primary papers without cross-checking. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: THEORETICAL/SYSTEMS hybrid does not apply cleanly — this is a SURVEY (position/synthesis with substantive content, no primary empirical claim), so the check is adapted: Sound: The taxonomy is internally consistent and the corpus procedure is documented, but the comparative claims (e.g., which signal granularity wins) are asserted from heterogeneous primary papers rather than tested. General: The pipeline framing plausibly covers most main-policy training work by construction (inclusion criteria filter for exactly these stages), but coverage excludes prompting-only agents, architectures, evaluation, and applications by design. Tight: Not applicable; the closest analog is whether the trade-off tables are actionable — they identify axes (verifiability, sparsity, cost, noise) but give no quantitative thresholds. Implementable: Yes in intent — Appendix D tables and the guidance text are designed as practitioner decision aids, and Algorithm 1 sketches a concrete training loop; no software artifact (library, CLI, dataset dump) ships with the paper, so it stops at paper form. Strengths: (1) The process-centric framing itself — structuring the field around environment/data/signal/scheme rather than re-treading the capability- or domain-based taxonomies of the ~10 cited competing surveys — is a real conceptual contribution that makes stage-interaction effects (e.g., data synthesis co-producing verifiable signals, §4.1↔§5.1.1) visible. (2) The signal taxonomy along three independent axes (source × granularity × form) with an explicit ORM/PRM mapping is the sharpest analytical structure in the paper and organizes a genuinely fragmented literature. (3) Appendix D's environment-level comparison table (observation/action space, verifiability, interaction cost for QA/search, tool, SWE, web, GUI, embodied) is a compact decision aid not found in the cited alternatives. (4) Transparent, reproducible corpus methodology including the release of the LLM screening prompt and honest disclosure of AI usage (linguistic polishing plus screening only). Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state three: (1) scope excludes architectures, evaluation, and specific applications, justified by coverage elsewhere; (2) per-paper descriptions are necessarily brief due to page limits, positioning the survey as a "high-level index"; (3) it is a "pure survey without any experiments or empirical results," with comparative experiments across training strategies acknowledged as "more meaningful and actionable guidance" but left to future work. This is direct, non-defensive confrontation of limitations — a credibility positive — and the third admission is the most substantive one, conceding that the survey's prescriptive value is untested. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The trade-off tables present qualitative judgments (e.g., "self-reward: low verifiability, high noise risk") without citing any measurement or aggregated evidence behind individual cells, so their practical reliability is unknown. (2) There is no quantitative cross-method comparison anywhere — even a meta-table of reported success rates on WebArena/SWE-bench/OSWorld under different training recipes would have been feasible and materially more useful than prose. (3) The survey corpus is not released as a machine-readable dataset (bibliography, tags, classifications), limiting reproducibility and reuse despite the careful collection procedure. (4) The tension between rapid literature growth and shallow per-paper treatment means the survey may lag the frontier it charts — several 2026 ICLR/ACL citations suggest currency, but the depth trade-off means few papers get more than one sentence. (5) The "agent training vs. LLM training" distinction (§2) is asserted, not demonstrated — no evidence is given that treating these differences explicitly changes training outcomes relative to naive post-training application. Beyond these, no fabricated weaknesses; the paper is honest about what it is. Bottom Line: A practitioner designing an agent training pipeline will genuinely benefit from the pipeline-organized map and trade-off tables — it is the best entry index into this literature — but anyone seeking evidence-based guidance on which design combination to pick must go to the primary (or future comparative) work, as this survey deliberately stops at structured description.

Problem & Motivation: Developers in regulated sectors (specifically Indonesian government, banking, and enterprise teams) cannot upload source code to cloud AI services, ruling out hosted code analysis. Local-first tools solve the privacy problem but are stuck with 16–24 GB-class models that are weaker than hosted frontier models, and the standard remedy — training on the code the tool sees — would destroy the privacy guarantee. Who has this problem: any organization whose compliance regime forbids code egress. The gap this addresses is twofold: (1) no measured baseline exists for such local-first analyzers under pinned, reproducible conditions, and (2) no established, privacy-preserving governance mechanism exists for iteratively improving the local model without ever exposing user code or shipping unreviewed model changes. Key Idea: The core insight is authority separation plus honest measurement: scanner evidence is authoritative and model text is advisory-only, so the model can be improved (even badly, even poisoned) without ever affecting what vulnerabilities are reported. Layered on this is a measurement insight the paper earns empirically — that grounding metrics must be abstention-adjusted, because the dominant grounding failure mode is the model citing invented identifiers, and a prompt change can 'improve' grounding simply by citing nothing. The governance framing (cheapest-first intervention ladder, preregistered gates, separated roles) is competent assembly of known ideas (LoRA/QLoRA, model cards, registered reports, constraint-aware SOC evaluation) rather than a new technical trick. Methodology: The pipeline has four stages: (1) file inventory with a skip policy (secrets, binaries, >1 MB files, symlinks); (2) two deterministic scanners — Semgrep with local rules for five CWEs (89, 78, 22, 79, 798) and tantular-callgraph, a pure-Python interprocedural scanner that traces source-to-sink paths and reports explicit uncertainty; (3) normalization, redaction, and bounded AST-aware evidence extraction; (4) optional advisory explanation via a loopback Ollama endpoint, validated against a fixed output schema plus a lexical overclaim guard (tested on 57 adversarial paraphrases, 7 documented gaps) and a 27-shape secret-redaction suite (4 gaps). Evaluation uses 33 synthetic cases with 78 annotated outcomes in a ground-truth manifest, deterministic proxy checks (evidence grounding, impact separation, remediation soundness), Wilson 95% intervals, and exact McNemar tests for paired comparison, run on an Apple M4 Pro with 24 GB under pinned sampling. Critical design decisions: (a) authority separation — well-justified, it bounds the blast radius of any model failure; (b) deterministic lexical proxy metrics instead of human ratings — acknowledged as a construct-validity weakness; (c) preregistration with frozen thresholds and fail-closed provenance — well-justified by the two validity hazards they themselves documented. Key Results: On the synthetic corpus, Semgrep + callgraph achieves precision 0.843 / recall 0.915 versus Semgrep alone at 0.818 / 0.766; callgraph alone is 0.938 / 0.638. The callgraph adds 7 detections Semgrep misses with zero added false positives. Explanation grounding is the bottleneck: the Tantular model reaches 0.57 grounded (Wilson [.48,.66]) versus 0.95 for qwen3:8b on identical prompts (27 vs 0 discordant pairs, p < 0.001, n = 120 per model), while qwen3:8b is worse on remediation soundness (3 vs 20 losses, p = 0.0005) — no model dominates. The concise prompt profile nominally raised grounding from 0.56 to 0.72 (p = 0.087, not significant) but was rejected for losing 12 remediation samples; forensic re-scoring shows 8 of its 80 samples cited nothing, and abstention-adjusted grounding drops to 0.65. Baselines are current for the local-model setting but the comparison is confounded by model family and quantization, which the authors state. Scale is small (toy-to-standard: 33 synthetic Python cases, 40 findings × 3 seeds, one machine) and the paper explicitly labels its rates as regression floors, not real-world estimates. There are no results for the self-improvement loop — none are claimed. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING + partial NEW FORMULATION. Genuinely novel: the two empirical findings — (F3) that grounding failures are exclusively invented identifiers and abstention inflates the conventional metric, and (F4) that Ollama's automatic compatibility migration can silently swap model weights mid-evaluation — are non-obvious, independently useful, and directly generalizable to any local-LLM evaluation. The authority-separated architecture is a sensible but standard safety design. The governed loop and preregistered protocol are a disciplined recombination of existing ideas (LoRA/QLoRA, registered reports, SLSA provenance, model cards, Kapoor & Narayanan leakage controls, the authors' own SOC constraint-aware evaluation) applied to a new setting; the weight-space-edit rung leans on a non-peer-reviewed blog source. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations exist for the scanner layer (per-scanner and per-CWE breakdowns in Table I). Paired statistics with Wilson, McNemar, and planned Clopper–Pearson/Bonferroni and Benjamini–Hochberg corrections are specified. Reproducibility is the paper's most unusual strength: the authors audit their own artifacts and report that their published 57% figure cannot be reproduced (per-sample outputs not retained, commit captured after the run with dirty flag discarded), while separately releasing source, corpus, reports, and forensic re-scoring at github.com/ghifiardi/tantular-cyber. Concerns a reviewer should still flag: the entire quantitative basis is a 33-case synthetic corpus built by the same team that built the analyzer (construct and external validity); the model comparison confounds family with quantization (Q8_0 vs Q4_K_M); no human ratings exist yet; the grounding check is purely lexical; and preregistering a protocol for work the same team will execute and report, without an external reviewer for the freeze itself, limits the incentive-alignment benefit preregistration usually provides. No error-bar reporting issue — intervals are given where applicable. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a built, released tool evaluated on its own benchmark, with a proposed-but-unrun improvement process). - Practical: Yes — runs on a consumer Apple M4 Pro with 24 GB via Ollama, no cloud dependency beyond loopback. - Efficient: Median explanation latency 25.9 s (Tantular model) vs 12.9 s (qwen3:8b) per finding, both feasible for interactive use; the smaller-context intervention produced no speed-up. - Effective: Detection evidence is credible within its synthetic scope; explanation effectiveness is only partially demonstrated — grounding at 0.57 means the advisory layer fails its own primary quality check nearly half the time, and usefulness is unmeasured. - Scalable: Not tested — 33 Python cases, 5 CWEs, one machine, one Ollama version; no evidence anything transfers to real repositories or other languages, and the paper says so. The work delivers a software artifact (Apache-2.0 tool, benchmark corpus, evaluation reports, forensic re-scoring) and a reusable evaluation-protocol template; the self-improvement loop and remediation extension stop at design form. Strengths: - The forensic honesty is exceptional and rare: reporting that your own published figure (57%) is non-reproducible, that a prompt intervention's apparent gain was an abstention artifact, and that your serving infrastructure changed weights under test mid-run — and then converting each into a fail-closed control — is exactly the evaluation hygiene the field preaches and rarely practices. - Finding F3 (grounding failures are invented identifiers; abstention must be reported beside the grounding rate) is a small but immediately actionable methodological correction for anyone building evidence-grounded explanation systems. - Authority separation is a well-executed design decision that makes the whole governance story coherent: because the model cannot suppress or create findings, the risk of each improvement cycle is bounded, and detection can be gated independently of model quality. - The preregistered protocol is specific to the point of being checkable — frozen thresholds, per-response provenance digests, cluster-aware paired analysis, mandatory ablation and transfer to a second differently constructed set, and a no-optional-stopping rule. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors are thorough and direct: all rates come from 33 synthetic Python cases on one machine and do not transfer to real repositories; explanation checks are lexical proxies that cannot judge correctness or usefulness; the overclaim guard can be passed by novel phrasing; the model comparison confounds family with quantization; two arms are exploratory due to the migration hazard; some latency samples overlapped concurrent workloads; the seven real-world pointer locations are descriptive with unverified upstream labels; the 57% figure is non-reproducible and is reported rather than replaced; cycle 1 changes no weights so no 'learning' claim is possible. This confrontation with limitations is a strong credibility positive — the threats-to-validity section reads like a self-review rather than a defense. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The benchmark corpus is constructed by the same team as the analyzer, with ground truth they wrote themselves — the 0.843/0.915 detection numbers could partly reflect shared assumptions between scanner and benchmark author, and no independent benchmark (e.g., a curated real-vulnerability set like PrimeVul or Big-Vul subsets) is used even as a spot check. - The preregistration is self-administered: the same team freezes, executes, and grades cycle 1, and the 'independent evaluator' is a role, not an external party — the paper does not address who audits the auditor. - The weight-space-edit rung (rung 4) is motivated by a citation to a personal blog post ('Sparks of weight-space programming'), not peer-reviewed work, yet it occupies a full rung of the ladder with a detailed replication protocol attached. - All 33 cases are Python; the five CWEs are covered but the paper is silent on how the grounding failures observed (invented identifiers) might interact with languages or frameworks where identifier extraction is harder. - The overclaim guard has 7 documented gaps out of 57 paraphrases and is purely lexical, but the protocol gates safety on 'guard interventions do not increase' — a proxy gating a proxy, with human review only on a sample. - No comparison to any existing local-first or LLM-assisted security tool (e.g., IRIS-style LLM+static-analysis hybrids) even at the architecture level, so the detection baseline is internal rather than external. Bottom Line: A practitioner building locally served LLM evaluation pipelines gains concrete, hard-won operational lessons here (per-response weight digests, abstention-adjusted grounding, self-audited provenance) that are worth the read, but anyone seeking evidence that the governed self-improvement loop actually improves a security analyzer will have to wait for the follow-up paper the authors promise to write.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Agent Detector, an open-source Windows endpoint sensor that detects unsanctioned LLM agents by correlating the identity of remote LLM services with process behaviour, configuration, installation records and execution history, backed by a 9-class agent taxonomy, a 39-tool/184-endpoint catalog, and a controlled evaluation bench. - Why it's important: Enterprise security teams currently see roughly a third of their real AI footprint, and LLM agents let employees create shadow IT artifacts at near-zero cost that act autonomously with user privileges — a governance gap with no adequate existing instrument. - How it does it: The core move is anchoring behaviour to identity: a process is flagged as a probable agent only when it talks to an identified LLM endpoint (via DNS-cache inversion or provider-dedicated IP ranges) AND has a shell among its descendants, complemented by configuration, inventory and forensic-history evidence. - The good: The controlled bench directly measures the central claim — two behavioural rules flagged every constructed behavioural twin (precision 0.69/0.71) while Agent Detector achieved precision 1.00, recall 1.00 on 12 synthetic agents and 0 false positives on 9 benign workloads, and the paper candidly explains why even these flattering numbers overstate the result. - The missing: The evaluation runs on a single workstation with synthetic agents that poll real APIs with invalid keys, no real agents, no field deployment, and the detector was iteratively fixed against the same bench (versions 0.3.0→0.3.2), so the headline precision/recall numbers measure the bench's designers, not a fleet. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or buy endpoint security, govern AI tooling in an enterprise, or study agent governance; skip it if you want statistically grounded detector benchmarks or academic novelty in ML itself — the bench is explicitly too small to rank detectors.

Problem & Motivation: Shadow IT — software used inside an organization without IT approval — is an old, underestimated governance problem, and generative AI accelerated it: survey data cited include 78% of AI users bringing their own AI tools to work (Microsoft/LinkedIn 2024, n=31,000) and 44% of employees admitting policy-violating AI use (2025, n=48,000). The paper argues the agent wave changes the growth rate, not just the scale: agents make tool creation nearly free, act with user privileges, and leave second-order artifacts (scripts, MCP servers, automations) that are themselves unsanctioned, sometimes agentic. Existing detection instruments each miss part of the problem: network proxies/CASB see connections but not processes or laptops off-network; software inventories see only installed products; local runtimes generate no external traffic; and encrypted-traffic-analysis research answers probabilistically without attributing to a user. The specific gap: product-less agents (a 30-line Python script) have no installer, no signature, no history of their own, and are the primary target population. Key Idea: The behavioural-twin argument plus identity-anchored correlation. Formalized: describe a program's footprint as (β, ι) — behavioural features vs. identity strings; for any detector f depending only on β and any twin pair with β(a)=β(b), ι(a)≠ι(b), f(a)=f(b), so a behaviour-only detector must either miss the agent or flag the benign twin (e.g., the same polling script pointing at PyPI instead of an LLM API). The corollary design principle: behaviour is only evaluated for processes already identified as talking to a model service, which converts the detection problem from classifying behaviour to attributing identity — obtainable on the endpoint from the Windows DNS client cache and provider-dedicated address ranges. Methodology: The paper has four components. (1) A deterministic compounding model of shadow IT: X_{t+1} = (1−δ+σφ)X_t + ρA_t, where σφ>δ (agentic artifact reproduction rate exceeds retirement rate) implies exponential growth — explicitly illustrative, not fitted to data. (2) A taxonomy: 9 agent classes (command-line coding agents, desktop agents, AI-native IDEs, IDE assistants, local runtimes, agentic browsers, frameworks/SDKs, home-made agents, agent infrastructure) crossed with 6 footprint layers (software identity, runtime structure, network, installation, configuration, history), showing C8/C9 classes have evidence only at run time. (3) Agent Detector: a Go binary (~3.9 MiB, ~5,500 LOC, std-lib only) run hourly as a SYSTEM scheduled task via Microsoft Intune; six parallel collectors (processes, TCP table, DNS cache via undocumented DnsGetCacheDataTable, BAM/Prefetch traces, inventory/config, environment variables) feed candidate inspection and a correlator that emits per-(tool, user) findings with level/confidence/approval attributes and six generic rules (llm-api, probable-agent, relay-candidate, local-llm, mcp-server, browser-automation). Privacy by design: no content read, secrets masked, API keys recorded by name only. A detect-and-inform loop shows an acknowledgement-required notice per user session instead of blocking. (4) A controlled bench of 12 synthetic agents (Python/Node/PowerShell), 3 AI components, 9 benign workloads including 3 constructed twins, run 5× in standard-user and administrator configurations against a signature baseline (D0) and two behavioural rules (D1, D2), plus DNS-expiry and intermittent-agent timing experiments. Key design decisions: anchoring on identity rather than scoring behaviour (justified by the twin argument and measured in RQ6); inform-not-block (argued, not measured); periodic scanning rather than continuous telemetry (a cost trade-off whose recall cost is measured at ~1/3 detection for intermittent agents). Key Results: On the bench (12 agents, 9 benign, majority outcome over 5 runs, standard user): Agent Detector precision 1.00 [0.74, 1.00], recall 1.00 [0.74, 1.00], F1 1.00; D1 (interpreter + port 443 + shell) precision 0.69, recall 0.75, F1 0.72; D2 precision 0.71, recall 0.83, F1 0.77; D0 (signature-only) recall 0.00. D1/D2 flagged all 3 behavioural twins and npm install; Agent Detector flagged 0/9 benign. Two of Agent Detector's detections held in only 3/5 runs (OpenAI agent, intermittent agent). The timing experiments are the most informative quantitative results: attribution of a CDN-hosted provider's connection through the DNS cache ended when the cache entry expired — no attribution after 295 s across 12 agents; OpenAI's entries (TTL ≤60 s) yielded attribution for only 55 s, 10 s, and 0 s in three repetitions; a randomly-timed scan saw the intermittent agent at 0.38 rate (95% CI [0.23, 0.54]). Scan cost: 154 ms median, 22.3 MB peak working set, <10 s CPU/day at hourly cadence; 168 ms elevated. In-situ cross-check on the author's real workstation: 9/9 expected tools at expected levels, with one instructive catalog-drift finding (a shared Copilot config folder producing a spurious residue). Undeclared relays, ephemeral agents (5 s), and WSL 2 agents were missed by all periodic detectors. The paper explicitly notes the confidence intervals overlap across detectors and the bench cannot rank them. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM (endpoint detection of unsanctioned LLM agents as a distinct governance question) + NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (Agent Detector and its open catalog) + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the quantified DNS-cache attribution window and the twin-based demonstration that structural behavioural rules fail). The genuinely novel elements are the problem framing, the behavioural-twin formalization, and the end-to-end inform-not-block design coupled to an acknowledgement record; the individual techniques — DNS-cache inversion, Prefetch/BAM forensics, process-tree correlation, catalog matching — are standard Windows forensic practice combined competently for a new target. The compounding model is textbook linear-difference recursion applied to make a qualitative point, not a new formal result. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablation-like coverage is strong in one sense: every finding's supporting evidence layer is itemized (Table 9), and each detector's per-episode outcomes are reported with exact Clopper–Pearson intervals. The paper is unusually honest about internal validity: it discloses that versions 0.3.0–0.3.2 were fixed in response to bench episodes (B09, CDN-hosted agents), so those episodes are no longer held-out tests; that the bench samples asymmetrically (baselines ~1 Hz vs. Agent Detector 3×/24 s, favouring baselines); and that the favourable-case design flatters Agent Detector. Error bars are given but the authors correctly state they overlap for all detectors, making the bench exploratory, not confirmatory. Code, catalog, bench, and scripts generating every table are open source (github.com/jeremy1392/IntuneAgentDetector, v0.3.2, catalog 2026.11.09); run provenance (commit, SHA-256, catalog version) is recorded and scoring refuses mismatched runs. Methodological concerns a reviewer must flag: single machine, single user, one consumer Windows edition; synthetic agents poll with invalid keys rather than streaming real completions, so the footprint token-streaming characteristics of real agents are untested; twins were constructed by the authors; no external or field validation; the non-trivial dependence on undocumented APIs (DnsGetCacheDataTable returned an empty table on the tested build; resolver cache keys inferred experimentally) makes results build-specific — the authors say this themselves. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a built tool evaluated by controlled deployment on one machine). Practical: Yes — a 3.9 MiB static Go binary running on stock Windows 11 with Intune, no special hardware. Efficient: 154 ms median scan, 22.3 MB peak, <10 s CPU/day per laptop at hourly cadence, negligible versus EDR agents. Effective: Evidence covers the stated problem (visibility with informed acknowledgement) only on a synthetic bench; real-world effectiveness, prevalence, and false-positive rates on actual fleets are unmeasured and explicitly deferred to a proposed silent field study. Scalable: Per-endpoint cost is bounded and low by construction; the untested scaling risks are catalog maintenance across a fast-moving ecosystem (documented drift incidents) and the fleet-level SIEM/notice load — neither measured. Delivers a real software artifact: open-source detector, YAML catalog, evaluation bench, Intune packaging scripts, plus a reusable analytical artifact (the taxonomy and twin argument). Strengths: - The behavioural-twin argument is a genuine, simple, and correct impossibility-style observation that reframes the design space: it explains in advance why a plausible detection strategy (structural behaviour rules) must fail, and the bench then measures exactly that failure rather than merely asserting it. - The evaluation's honesty is itself a contribution: the paper distinguishes claims from measurements throughout, reports the versions fixed against its own bench, quantifies the decay of its own best-case (DNS TTL 60–300 s; 0.38 intermittent detection), and refuses to interpret overlapping confidence intervals as a ranking. - The taxonomy/catalog pairing is operationally useful beyond the paper: 9 classes × 6 layers with per-class visibility, and a dated, open, 184-entry endpoint catalog including aggregators, gateways and relays that other practitioners can maintain independently. - The detect-and-inform loop is a thoughtful governance contribution — coupling detection to a recorded, versioned user acknowledgement — with a serious GDPR/French-labour-law analysis (works-council consultation, data minimization limits of hourly activity timelines) that most security tools omit entirely. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly and at length (Sections 11.9, 12.4): one workstation, one Windows edition, one user; synthetic agents that poll with invalid keys and keep signals continuously present; the bench being too small to rank detectors; dependence on undocumented Windows APIs that may change per release (with a concrete failure already observed); DNS-cache attribution windows of 1–5 minutes for CDN-hosted providers; missed ephemeral agents, WSL 2/VM/container agents, cloud agents, and undeclared relays; catalog drift with two documented real incidents; privilege-dependent coverage; deliberate evasion by a local administrator being out of scope; the llm-api counting generosity in the detection threshold (construct validity); and the absence of any field data on prevalence or population false-positive rates. The DNS-cache machine-wide inversion creating a potential false-positive mode on shared CDNs is also acknowledged as unestablished for a population. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No real agents were run: the synthetic agents reproduce the exact footprint the detector looks for (circularity risk — the detector observes what the bench was built to emit), and real agents' intermittent connection-holding and shell-spawning patterns, which the paper admits are decisive for a periodic scanner, are represented by a single synthetic episode. - The baselines are strawman-adjacent by the authors' own framing: D1/D2 are two structural rules, while the acknowledged stronger behavioural baselines (token-streaming timing/volume features, Sysmon/EDR continuous telemetry correlating DNS resolution with process creation) are described as future work rather than tested, so the multi-signal-vs-behavioural comparison is one-sided. - The in-situ cross-check reads the same kinds of sources as the detector, so it validates logic, not ground truth — a point the authors concede but which means there is zero independent validation anywhere in the paper. - The acceleration model's key parameter σ (rate at which agentic artifacts reproduce autonomously) is admitted to be unmeasured anywhere; the exponential-growth claim therefore rests on mechanisms, not evidence, and the paper's own caveats concede the third mechanism is "plausible but unmeasured." - No precision estimate exists for the machine-wide DNS-cache inversion on realistic CDN-heavy traffic; the benign set was small and CDN-overlap-poor, so the 1.00 precision may not survive contact with ordinary browsing and developer traffic. - The inform-not-block design is argued, never measured: notice fatigue, user behaviour after acknowledgement, and whether informed acknowledgement changes shadow-AI usage are all untested, despite being the mechanism that turns the tool into "governance." Bottom Line: A practitioner running Windows fleets should read this: it is the first serious, open, honestly-evaluated treatment of a problem every enterprise now has, its catalog and taxonomy are immediately reusable, and its twin argument will save anyone from building the wrong detector — but treat the precision/recall numbers as a demonstration on the authors' own bench, not as evidence of fleet performance, and wait for the field study the authors themselves call for.

Problem & Motivation: LLM agents increasingly distill trajectories of past tasks into reusable "lessons" (rules, workflows, reasoning strategies) that are injected into future tasks without parameter updates. Because a trajectory carries only a binary success/failure label, any distiller must guess which actions caused the outcome; wrong guesses become lessons that mislead the agent later. The paper targets memory-induced degradation: agents failing tasks they would solve without memory. Prior memory work (AWM, ExpeL, ReasoningBank) supplies lessons stripped of their source trajectories, giving the agent no way to check them — even though the evidence to catch a bad lesson usually remains in the original run. The problem affects anyone deploying self-improving agents where reliability on already-solved tasks matters as much as learning new ones. Key Idea: Keep every lesson linked to its source evidence (a diagnostic "compilation" and the raw trajectory), and let the agent itself descend those links at test time — using ordinary read/bash tools — whenever the lesson is incomplete, contested, or failure-derived. This converts reliable memory reuse from a storage-time admission problem into an execution-time verification problem: the agent checks whether a lesson is supported and applicable before following it. Methodology: Memory construction is one compiler pass over a fixed corpus Dtrain = {(x_i, r_i, s_i)} of no-memory runs. For each run, a compiler LLM produces (a) a compilation — a structured diagnosis of key decisions (successes) or plausible failure causes (failures), explicitly flagged as unverified interpretation — and (b) at most three insights, each a separate markdown document stating what to do, when it applies, and its source run id. All layers are linked and frozen read-only; insights are never merged, filtered, or updated, so conflicts are allowed and resolution is deferred to test time. At test time, the agent (a ReAct-style Pi terminal agent) receives all insights plus three most-similar past runs in its first message, and is prompted to descend to compilations/raw runs when an insight lacks actionable detail, conflicts with another, or comes from a failed run, and after any action failure. The paper also contributes an evaluation methodology: it decomposes memory effects into Gain (Pr(M=1|B=0)) and Regression (Pr(M=0|B=1)) against a majority-of-3 no-memory baseline, with a rerun-no-memory floor to separate true regression from run-to-run noise. Critical design decisions: (1) freezing memory and deferring conflict resolution to the agent (justified by the observation that distillers lack causal labels); (2) inlining all insights rather than retrieving (justified for small corpora, acknowledged as a scale limitation); (3) prompt-encapsulated descent triggers rather than a learned retrieval policy (simple, but entangled with the specific prompt). Key Results: Across 8 suites on 5 benchmarks (ALFWorld seen/unseen, ScienceWorld, PlanCraft seen/unseen, AppWorld normal/challenge, τ3-bench retail), with deepseek-v4-flash as backbone: WikiTrace averages 90.2 vs 79.5 No Memory (+10.7), 87.0 for Insights Only (+3.2), and 81.6–81.7 for AWM/ReasoningBank (ExpeL 80.3). WikiTrace is the only memory method that matches or exceeds No Memory on every suite. Regression is 4.5% vs 6.5% (Insights Only), 7.5–9.7% (rerun band and prior methods), and it is the only method whose Regression CI lies entirely below the rerun band; Gain exceeds the rerun baseline by 35 points vs 7–14 for prior memory methods. Diagnosis: 52% of degradation cases trace to a followed memory item (20% wrong items), LLM-judged over 355 cases. Descent occurs on 44% of hard tasks vs 22% of easy ones; runs where evidence changes the plan (43% of descents) lead Insights Only by 8.3 points. Cost: 1.17× per-task test-time cost vs Insights Only; the advantage persists when baseline build budgets are inflated (AWM ×9, others ×3). Results replicate on GLM-5.3-flash (92.7 avg, +1.8 over Insights Only). Baselines are current (AWM, ReasoningBank, ExpeL) adapted to a shared frozen-memory protocol; the Insights Only ablation is the strongest control in the paper. Tested at standard benchmark scale, not stress-scale (≤134 test tasks per suite, ≤54 training runs). Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (evidence-linked procedural memory with test-time descent to source trajectories) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the Gain/Regression decomposition and a taxonomy attributing ~52% of degradation to followed memory items). The genuinely novel move is preserving the lesson→source-run link and making reassessment the agent's job during execution; the components are standard — hierarchical memory organization, file-based corpus access via terminal tools (following DCI), and compiler templates borrowed from ReasoningBank/SkillOpt — so the contribution is a new combination and framing rather than a new algorithmic primitive. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and well-designed: the Insights Only control isolates source-evidence access; descent-vs-stay analysis quantifies when evidence helps; trigger/target/effect labeling (with three-judge majority and inter-judge agreement, Cohen's κ = 0.77/0.63, Fleiss' κ = 0.49 for effect) explains the mechanism; memory-subset experiments (successful-only, failed-only, both) and cost-matched baseline builds probe alternative explanations; a second backbone tests generalization. Three trials per suite with standard deviations, and 10,000-resample paired bootstrap CIs for Gain/Regression, are reported. Code is released at https://github.com/yukyeongleee/wikitrace. Concerns: all cause-of-degradation and descent analyses rest on LLM judges (gpt-5.6-sol, GLM-5.3, Claude Opus 5.5) reading agent reasoning — the authors concede these describe what the reasoning states, not what caused the outcome; the Descent/Stay comparison is confounded by self-selection of when to descend (partially acknowledged); the paper is a preprint. Baseline method implementations are official but modified to the frozen-memory protocol, which disadvantages ReasoningBank's continual updates — a protocol choice that favors the proposed setting. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a memory system plus agent harness evaluated across benchmarks). - Practical: Yes — it runs as read-only markdown files mounted in a sandbox accessed via read/bash by a standard ReAct terminal agent, requiring only API LLMs. - Efficient: Modest overhead — 1.17× per-task test-time cost relative to inlining the same insights, memory reads cost no environment steps, and one compiler call per training trajectory for construction. - Effective: Strong evidence on the stated problem — best on all 8 suites, +3.2 over the matched insight-only control, and the only method with Regression below the no-memory rerun floor — but effectiveness depends on the descent prompt and small memory; no test of whether an off-the-shelf agent benefits without the tailored prompt engineering. - Scalable: Not tested — all insights are inlined into the first message, and the authors state that a memory too large to inline needs retrieval, which this work leaves open; behavior at 10–100× memory size is unknown. The work delivers a released code artifact plus a reusable evaluation methodology (Gain/Regression with rerun floors); no trained models or datasets. Strengths: - The Insights Only ablation is a genuinely strong control: identical insights, identical agent, difference restricted to source links and the descent prompt — which makes the +3.2-point and 6.5%→4.5% Regression claims directly attributable to the proposed mechanism. - The Gain/Regression decomposition with a rerun-no-memory floor is a methodological contribution: it exposes degradation that average accuracy hides and correctly discounts regression caused by run-to-run noise. - The mechanistic analysis (when/why/how the agent descends, with quantified trigger and effect categories) goes beyond aggregate scores and supports the causal story with ablation-grade evidence. - Honest framing of what compilations are — unverified interpretations, not verified causes — which is exactly the epistemic weakness the system is designed to let agents compensate for. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that (1) compilations and insights from failed runs may be wrong — a source link enables checking but does not verify; (2) all insights are inlined, so the prompt grows with memory and large-memory retrieval is left open; (3) cause-of-degradation and descent labels come from an LLM judge and describe stated reasoning, not actual causation. These are stated directly in a Limitations section, which is a credibility positive; the authors do not oversell the verification aspect. They do not acknowledge the small training corpora (38–54 runs), the protocol changes that weaken continual-memory baselines, or the self-selection confound in Descent/Stay comparisons (though a caveat about descent being the agent's choice appears in Section 5.1). Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Scale: memory sizes here are tiny (≤ ~200 insights); both the inlining strategy and the descent policy were developed and evaluated in the same small-memory regime, so the central scaling claim is extrapolation, not evidence. - The descent prompt is heavily engineered (per-benchmark policy edits, memory rules, explicit descent triggers); the paper does not test sensitivity to this prompt, so some of the gain may be prompt-tuning rather than the evidence-linking idea per se. - τ3-bench evaluation discards the authors' original split in favor of a custom 38/76 split by customer, complicating comparison with published numbers. - The frozen-memory offline protocol strips ReasoningBank of its continual update mechanism; a continual-memory comparison (where WikiTrace insights would also be refreshed) is absent. - All judge models used for labeling are commercial LLMs at unspecified prompt versions — labels are not human-validated on even a small sample. - Only two backbones are tested, both at high/medium reasoning effort; interaction with weaker models that may descend inappropriately (costing tokens) or stronger models that need less memory is unexplored. Bottom Line: For anyone building experience-reusing LLM agents, this paper is worth reading for both its mechanism and its evaluation methodology — the Gain/Regression decomposition alone should become standard practice in this subfield — though the core idea is a well-executed framing of known components whose behavior beyond small, inlined memories remains unproven.

WorldFoundry: Towards Unified Infrastructure for World Intelligence (54 ▲ )

Juanxi Tian, Jiadong Hou, Baiang Li, Xin Lin, Zhengbo Jiao, Weijia Zhang, Yeying Jin, Truong Nguyen, Haitian Zheng, Zhifei Zhang, Jianfei Yang, Ming-Hsuan Yang, Felix Heide, Wei Xiong, Enze Xie, Wanhua Li · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 10 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces WorldFoundry, an open-source infrastructure that unifies discovery, execution, artifact management, and evidence-traceable evaluation of 270 generative models, 74 benchmarks, and 62 metrics across video, 3D/4D, interactive-world, and embodied-action systems, built on an operational definition of generative world models. - Why it's important: Generative video, 3D, and embodied systems use incompatible runtimes, formats, and evaluation protocols, so 'model support' conflates catalog inclusion with validated performance — reproducible comparison of whether systems actually behave as world models is currently near-impossible. - How it does it: The core mechanism is a contract-based lifecycle: declarative manifests resolve models/benchmarks into executable configurations, JSON-serializable GenerationRequest/Result/ArtifactRef contracts decouple execution from evaluation, and evidence scorecards grade each claim as diagnostic, benchmark-comparable, or exact reproduction. - The good: The evidence-layer design — separating execution readiness from evaluative claims with provenance-linked scorecards — is a genuine and transferable discipline for a field where benchmark numbers are routinely compared across non-equivalent conditions. - The missing: The empirical validation is almost entirely qualitative (screenshots of generations and one OpenVLA LIBERO-10 episode); the promised latency/memory overhead profiling and interface-consistency checks are described but no quantitative numbers are reported, and there is no head-to-head comparison against the closest prior infrastructure, OpenWorldLib. - Read it or not: Worth reading if you build, integrate, or benchmark generative world models and need a catalog plus a reproducibility/evidence framework; skip it if you want a formal contribution beyond the (essentially standard) latent-dynamics definition or quantitative infrastructure benchmarks.

Impact (78) leads — a genuinely released open-source artifact spanning 270 models and 74 benchmarks with provenance-linked evidence scorecards, a real contribution to a fragmented field. Novelty (68) and Non-Obviousness (70) rest on the evidence-taxonomy design separating execution readiness from evaluative claims, which attacks a real failure mode; the formal definition itself is a re-statement of standard latent-dynamics abstractions. Rigor (55) and Resilience (58) are pulled down by the core gap: semantic-preservation and consistency claims are asserted but never demonstrated quantitatively (no latency/overhead tables, no head-to-head with OpenWorldLib beyond a self-drawn feature table).
