Problem & Motivation: Researchers evaluating generative world models face infrastructural fragmentation: video generators, neural scene representations, interactive world models, and embodied policies ship with incompatible environments, input conventions, artifact formats, and evaluation protocols. This makes capabilities hard to compose, results hard to reproduce, and — critically — allows visually plausible generation to be mistaken for world modeling, since perception-centric benchmarks cannot distinguish systems that close the world-modeling loop (persistent state, intervention-conditioned dynamics, observational feedback) from those that do not. The authors argue the bottleneck is infrastructural, not only algorithmic, and that existing platforms (OpenWorldLib, Cosmos, Genie Envisioner, minWM) each cover only parts of the lifecycle. Key Idea: Two ideas carry the paper. (1) Conceptual: a generative world model is defined operationally as a learned, history- and control-conditioned latent dynamical system that maintains persistent state, evolves it under interventions, and assimilates observational feedback — 'closure of the loop, not visual plausibility' is the criterion separating generative world models from foundational generative models. (2) Systemic: evidence-aware infrastructure — durable artifact contracts and scorecards that explicitly distinguish catalog inclusion, runnable integration, bounded validation, and benchmark reproduction, so every evaluative claim is traceable to its supporting artifacts and execution conditions. Methodology: The paper first formalizes world modeling as z_t ~ q(z_t | h_t), z_{t+1} ~ p(z_{t+1} | z_t, c_t), ô_{t+1} ~ g(· | z_{t+1}) — state inference, forward simulation, and observation decoding — a functional (not architectural) abstraction rooted in latent-dynamics model-based RL (Ha & Schmidhuber, PlaNet, DreamerV3). It derives a five-capability progression (perceptual grounding; then the 'world-model spine' of persistent state modeling → dynamics-aware prediction → closed-loop interaction, with orthogonal controllable transformation) and a binary taxonomy (foundational generative vs. generative world models). WorldFoundry implements this via five components: (1) a Surface Layer (TUI, CLI, browser Workspace/Studio, Python API, MCP); (2) Unified Inference & Interaction where a manifest-driven resolver emits a GenerationRequest executed by a WorldModelRunner split into an Operator (task adaptation, native-argument translation) and a Pipeline (lifecycle, checkpointing, device placement, resident sessions for interactivity); (3) JSON-serializable Artifact and Representation Contracts (GenerationRequest/Result, ArtifactRef with hash and URI; run-level execution_plan.json, results.jsonl, run_manifest.json); (4) artifact-centered Evaluation & Evidence that scores persisted outputs independently of model runtimes and emits scorecard.json grading evidence as diagnostic, benchmark-comparable, or exact reproduction; (5) manifest-driven Model/Benchmark Zoos with independent tracking of source availability, runtime validation, and execution evidence. Critical design decisions: preserving model-native semantics rather than normalizing inputs (justified by the goal of comparability without homogenization); decoupling execution from evaluation via persisted artifacts (well-justified for rescoring and auditability); and treating the definition as functional rather than architectural (justified by the heterogeneity of the catalog, but it makes the taxonomy unenforceable by the infrastructure itself). Key Results: The current catalog comprises 270 model entries (64 video generation, 109 world models, 34 3D/4D, 53 embodied, 10 hosted APIs), 74 benchmarks (23 embodied AI, 33 video generation, 18 world model), and 62 canonical metrics; all 270 model entries are marked 'Runner verified' via end-to-end execution of documented reference workflows, and all 74 benchmarks 'Integrated & Verified' — with the caveat that verification scope is specific to the tested route, variant, and configuration. Validation was run on 128 NVIDIA A100/H100 (80 GB) GPUs. Empirical evidence is qualitative: representative generations from CogVideoX, Wan2.2, LTX-2.5, and MiniMax H3 (video); 30-second rollouts from SANA-WM, Matrix-Game-3, LingBot-World v1/v2, and Echo-WM (interactive); common-viewpoint renderings from VGGT, VGGT-Omega, DUSt3R, CUT3R (3D); and three closed-loop OpenVLA episodes on LIBERO-10, of which one single-object pick-and-place succeeded in 179 steps and two multi-stage tasks hit the 520-step limit. The stated purpose is to verify semantic preservation and interface consistency, not to rank models — no cross-family accuracy/F1/speedup tables are given. Latency and GPU-memory overhead profiling and integration-effort measurement are announced as part of the evaluation but no numbers appear in the text. The most substantive analytical insight is qualitative: scene recall (Matrix-Game 3.x, ReWorld) is distinct from persistence of action-caused state changes (an opened door staying open), and current benchmarks rarely measure the latter. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (WorldFoundry and its evidence-aware scorecard layer) plus a NEW FORMULATION at the conceptual level (the closure criterion and capability progression for classifying generative systems as world models). The formal definition in Eq. (1) is a re-statement of the standard latent-dynamics/POMDP world-model abstraction from model-based RL, not new mathematics; the infrastructure combines known engineering patterns (registries, declarative manifests, contract-based pipelines à la Diffusers/LeRobot/Cosmos) — the genuinely new element is the evidence taxonomy separating execution readiness from evaluative claims, applied to a broader modality span than OpenWorldLib, the closest prior system. Rigor & Reproducibility: There are no ablations in the scientific sense, no error bars, no seeds, and no significance tests — the 'validation' is existence-of-execution plus visual inspection, which is appropriate for a systems paper but weakly supports the claim of semantic preservation; no quantitative check that framework-mediated outputs match native implementations is actually reported (only asserted as a goal). Reproducibility is the paper's central design concern and is served well: code is released (github.com/OpenEnvision/WorldFoundry), project page at openenvision.org/WorldFoundry, with durable run manifests, per-sample ledgers, and reproducibility fingerprints. Methodological concerns: the comparison to OpenWorldLib and other platforms is a self-drawn feature table (Table 1) rather than a measured head-to-head; 'Runner verified' means execution of a reference workflow, not benchmark reproduction, though the paper is commendably explicit about this distinction; many cited works are 2026 preprints that cannot be independently verified here, and the paper itself is a non-peer-reviewed technical report (arXiv:2611.10771). Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a built tool evaluated by deployment and usage evidence). - Practical: Runs on commodity data-center hardware (A100/H100 80 GB) with configurable attention backends and quantization, though hosted-API entries require provider credentials and some benchmarks need licensed assets and judges. - Efficient: Inference-optimization mechanisms (FlashAttention 2/3, SageAttention, Triton kernels, NVFP4, multi-GPU parallelism) are exposed, but their effect is uncharacterized and no overhead numbers versus direct native execution are reported. - Effective: Evidence shows the system executes 270 heterogeneous models end-to-end and produces audit trails; the evidence that it preserves native semantics and that scorecards correctly gate benchmark claims is qualitative only. - Scalable: The catalog itself (270 models, 74 benchmarks) demonstrates breadth, but scaling behavior — integration cost per new model, overhead at 10× model count, non-A100/H100 hardware (B200/B300) — is explicitly untested and deferred to future work. The work delivers a concrete software artifact (open-source library, CLI/TUI/web surfaces, manifests, and registries), not just a paper. Strengths: - The evidence-aware evaluation layer is the strongest intellectual contribution: formally distinguishing catalog inclusion, runnable integration, diagnostic results, benchmark-comparable results, and exact reproduction directly attacks a real failure mode in this literature (scores compared across non-equivalent conditions). - The closure-based operational definition and capability progression give the field a usable vocabulary — the observation that scene recall is distinct from persistence of intervention effects is a sharp, testable diagnostic that current benchmarks conflate. - Genuine breadth of integration with per-entry readiness tracking (270 models across five families, 74 benchmarks, 62 metrics with declared input dependencies and direction conventions), which is a substantial curation and engineering effort. - The authors are unusually candid that visual plausibility is neither necessary nor sufficient evidence of world modeling, and structure the entire system around that claim. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that catalog inclusion, runnable integration, asset readiness, runtime validation, and benchmark eligibility remain distinct maturity states; that the framework is inference/interaction/evaluation only, with training infrastructure left to future work; that optimization effects have not been systematically characterized and validation is limited to A100/H100 (no B200/B300 access); that evaluation across other hardware is deferred; and that an optimization will be adopted only if outputs stay within a declared fidelity tolerance. They confront limitations directly, which is a credibility positive; the one place they minimize is the empirical-validation section, where promised quantitative profiling is not actually reported. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The central technical claim — that WorldFoundry preserves native semantics and yields results consistent with native implementations — is asserted as an evaluation goal but never demonstrated with numbers (no output-equivalence metrics, no interface-consistency measurements, no latency/memory tables). - No head-to-head against OpenWorldLib beyond a self-authored feature table; integration effort ('time to add a model'), the metric that would most justify the infrastructure, is mentioned but not quantified. - The operational definition is not operationalized by the system: nothing in the infrastructure tests whether a model maintains persistent state or assimilates feedback — the authors admit 'what current evaluations seldom measure is whether intervention effects persist,' yet ship no such probe, leaving the taxonomy as editorial rather than executable. - The empirical section mixes framework validation with literature summaries of model capabilities (e.g., Wan2.2, LingBot-Video, SuperMimic), blurring what was measured in-framework versus taken from prior reports. - Single-episode qualitative embodied results (one OpenVLA task suite) cannot support any claim about embodied evaluation at scale. Bottom Line: Practitioners integrating or benchmarking generative world models will genuinely benefit from WorldFoundry's catalog, contracts, and evidence discipline — this is the right infrastructure idea at the right time — but the paper's empirical support is thin (largely screenshots where numbers are promised) and its conceptual definition remains aspirational, so it should be read as a well-designed systems proposal whose payoff depends on the quantitative validation the authors have not yet delivered.

When Should Language Models Search? A Topology-Aware Analysis of Reasoning Strategies

D Bandyopadhyay, MDTA Khan, A Ekbal · aclanthology.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper shows that chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting and A*-style search solve substantially different subsets of reasoning instances, and introduces a Reasoning Topology Framework — 13 pre-generation structural features distilled into a branching coefficient — that predicts when search beats CoT (R² = 0.91 across clusters), enabling a feature-based router that outperforms trace-inspecting post-hoc routers. - Why it's important: A search costs ~24× the tokens of CoT (~12,452 vs. ~512 tokens/question on HotpotQA), so blindly applying search wastes compute and can actively reduce accuracy (91.1% of A failures on CoT-correct instances are overthinking); a cheap pre-generation router addresses both the correctness and cost penalty. - How it does it: A budgeted A* search over natural-language reasoning traces uses a rule-based depth-plus-coverage progress critic as an admissible heuristic (proven conservative under stated assumptions), and routing decisions are made from input-only structural features (lengths, connectives, hop estimates, answer-option counts) via XGBoost, never observing generated traces. - The good: The pre-generation topology router beats semantic-entropy, LLM-as-Critic, and LLM-as-Judge routers on all five benchmarks with LLaMA-3.1-8B (e.g., 91.10% on GSM8K vs. 87.28% for the best trace-based router; 77.35% on StrategyQA vs. 74.80% for A* alone), supported by McNemar tests (p < 0.005) and a Fluency-Correctness Asymmetry analysis explaining why trace inspection fails (38% of sampled disagreements have the wrong answer in the more fluent trace). - The missing: Router evaluation is within-dataset only (5-fold CV per benchmark) — the paper concedes no evidence of transfer to unseen benchmarks, and some hand-crafted features (input length, connective counts, answer format) may encode benchmark-identity signal, so the 'structure, not dataset' claim is partly confounded. - Read it or not: Read it if you build inference-time reasoning pipelines and must decide between CoT, self-consistency, and search under a compute budget; skip it if you need a deployable cross-domain router, since the paper itself stops short of demonstrating benchmark transfer.
Why this rank
Scored using the Empirical profile. Non-Obviousness (78) and Novelty (72) lead: the finding that cheap input-only structural features route better than trace-inspecting adjudicators, explained via the Fluency-Correctness Asymmetry, is genuinely counter-intuitive, and the R²=0.91 branching-coefficient relationship plus instance-level CoT/search complementarity is a new empirical contribution. Rigor (65) is comparatively strong — a scoped admissibility theorem with proof, McNemar tests, measured token costs, human validation of the heuristic, and released code — but dented by single-run stochastic evaluation, within-dataset-only CV that risks benchmark-identity leakage, and an R² fit on four cluster means. Completeness (70) benefits from rare honest negatives (LogicQA loss, 26.1% oracle-gap recovery), while Resilience (60) and Impact (55) are limited by the untested cross-benchmark transfer and a bare repo rather than a packaged tool. Weighted composite: 0.20*72 + 0.25*65 + 0.15*78 + 0.15*70 + 0.15*60 + 0.10*55 = 67.

Problem & Motivation: Practitioners deploying LLM reasoning at inference time face a fork: CoT generates one linear trace (cheap, but no backtracking — early mistakes propagate), while search-based methods explore branching partial traces (better on multi-hop problems, but expensive and sometimes harmful on simple questions — 'overthinking'). Prior work (Tree-of-Thoughts, MCTS-style reasoning, beam-search reasoning, LATS, rStar-Math) asks whether richer reasoning structures improve aggregate accuracy; none identifies which inputs benefit from search. The paper closes the gap of predicting, before any generation, whether branching will help or hurt, and of choosing a strategy per instance rather than per deployment. Key Idea: Route between CoT and A using problem structure computable from the input alone — a branching coefficient (BC = context sentences × estimated reasoning hops / question length) that predicts A advantage — rather than judging completed traces, because trace fluency systematically misleads post-hoc adjudicators (Fluency-Correctness Asymmetry). A* is deliberately used as a controlled diagnostic: it isolates frontier + path cost + heuristic without entangling evaluator design (ToT), rollouts (MCTS), or fixed-width pruning (beam search). Methodology: (1) CoT baseline: single autoregressive trace with greedy decoding. (2) Budgeted A over reasoning traces: a tree of partial-trace states; the LLM proposes N_c candidate next steps with self-reported confidences; goal nodes match answer-pattern templates; path cost g(n) sums unit step costs plus (1−confidence) penalties; the heuristic h(n) = ω_d·max(0, H_min − d_n) + ω_c·(1 − E(n)) combines a minimum-hop term with question-content coverage (quoted strings, proper names, numbers, non-stopword content terms matched against the partial trace). A theorem proves admissibility/consistency when ω_d + ω_c ≤ c_min under two assumptions (minimum-hop lower bound; non-goal continuation); human validation on 500 partial states shows the critic underestimates progress (0.43 vs. human 0.58, p < 0.001, max overestimation 0.14). Search ends at a node budget B with weighted voting over goal traces. (3) Topology features: 13 pre-generation features (lengths, connectives, negations, comparatives, hop count from dependency links, entities-per-sentence, distractor count, depth, answer-option count, and the derived BC). (4) Analysis and routing: k-means (k=4) clustering of features across pooled benchmarks; XGBoost topology router trained with stratified 5-fold CV (seed 42) per benchmark, compared against semantic entropy, LLM-as-Critic/Judge (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B), and a random-forest feature baseline. Critical design decisions: A as a controlled rather than best-in-class search (justified for isolating the effect of branching, though the authors admit the quantitative boundary is specific to their implementation); a deterministic rule-based critic instead of a learned verifier (validated conservativeness, keeping search lightweight); restricting the router to within-dataset CV (defensible but limits the headline claim, as the authors acknowledge). Key Results: On LLaMA-3.1-8B: A beats CoT on StrategyQA (74.80 vs. 64.52%) and HotpotQA (80.10 vs. 76.80%) but loses slightly on LogicQA (44.85 vs. 45.78%); oracles sit far above both (84.59%, 94.20%, 59.29% respectively), showing complementarity — on HotpotQA only 5.8% of instances are missed by both, and 31.5% are solved by exactly one strategy. Across models: on Qwen-0.5B, A lifts HotpotQA from 8.40 to 30.00 but not StrategyQA/LogicQA; on Qwen-2.5-14B, A wins HotpotQA (83.33 vs. 60.19) while self-consistency wins StrategyQA (80.06) and LogicQA (59.19). A advantage rises monotonically with branching coefficient across clusters (−0.4 pp in C1 to +11.4 pp in C4, R² = 0.91). The topology router reaches 77.35/49.01/82.41/91.10/81.52% (StrategyQA/LogicQA/HotpotQA/GSM8K/MATH), beating all trace-based routers, and recovers 26.1% of the StrategyQA oracle gap. Failure analysis: 91.1% of A failures on CoT-correct instances are overthinking, 8.9% premature commitment. Sensitivity on 300 HotpotQA questions: accuracy peaks at B=20 (78.7%), drops at B=30 (76.0%); K=1 (no real branching) still achieves 77.7%. A uses ~12,452 tokens/question (~24× CoT) at default settings, ~3,372 (~7×) at K=1. Baselines (CoT, self-consistency, ToT, semantic entropy) are current and appropriate; the paper honestly includes a benchmark (LogicQA) where A underperforms. NMF topic modelling independently corroborates: A wins 6 of 8 topics (66.2% of corpus), all multi-hop entity-chain topics. Code-generation spot-checks (HumanEval, MBPP, CodeContests) extend the no-uniform-dominance finding. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (instance-level CoT/search complementarity and its topological explanation via branching coefficient) plus NEW METHOD (a pre-generation topology router that beats trace-based post-hoc routing) — the A machinery itself is a standard, deliberately non-novel instantiation of A over LLM reasoning traces (closely related to ToT/RAP-style search), and the 13 features are hand-crafted proxies; the genuinely non-obvious contributions are (a) the R²=0.91 BC–advantage relationship and (b) the counter-intuitive result that input-only routing beats full-trace adjudication due to the Fluency-Correctness Asymmetry. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong on several fronts: admissibility theorem with explicit proof (Appendix I) and clearly scoped interpretation; human validation of the critic (500 states, paired t-test); 5-fold stratified CV with fixed seed for the router; McNemar significance tests (p < 0.005) for QA router gains; measured (not estimated) token costs; sensitivity sweeps over budget and branching factor on a fixed sample; human annotation with Cohen's κ 0.59–0.68; code released at https://github.com/newcodevelop/astar-cot-reasoning. Concerns: single-run results for stochastic A* branching (no multi-seed error bars on headline numbers); the topology router is developed and evaluated on the same five benchmarks it is analyzed on — within-dataset CV only, no held-out benchmark, so the R²=0.91 BC relationship and router advantage risk partly encoding benchmark identity (the authors flag this themselves); the fluency-correctness figure (38%) rests on sampled disagreement cases with limited sample sizes (100 per dataset, 2 annotators); the theorem covers only the depth-coverage heuristic, not the LogicQA-specific heuristic. All experiments run on 2×A100 80GB (~340 GPU-hours). Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a minor theoretical component). - Practical: Yes — all models served locally via Ollama/vLLM on 2×A100 80GB; no proprietary API dependency. - Efficient: The router itself is nearly free (XGBoost on 13 features, no LLM calls), but the routed-to A costs ~7–24× CoT tokens, so the router's value is precisely in avoiding A where it hurts. - Effective: Evidence supports the router within benchmark distributions (beats all baselines on 5 of 5 benchmarks tested for routing), but the paper demonstrates within-dataset generalization only — not cross-domain transfer — so the deployed claim is a proxy for the full 'adaptive reasoning by structure' vision. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 14B models and standard benchmarks (HotpotQA evaluated on a 500-question sample; 14B results on 243–651 overlapping paired examples per dataset); scaling behavior of the topology–advantage relationship to larger models or agentic/long-form workloads is claimed as future work, not shown. Deliverable: public code repository; the router is a small XGBoost model, easily reusable, but no packaged library or trained weights beyond the repo are stated. Strengths: - The pre-generation-beats-post-hoc routing result is a genuinely surprising, well-supported finding, backed by a mechanism (Fluency-Correctness Asymmetry: 38% of sampled disagreements have the wrong answer in the more fluent trace) plus human annotation showing disagreements are driven by coverage of the decisive reasoning path (correct method coverage 2.71–3.00 vs. 1.20–1.88), not style. - Honest inclusion of unfavorable evidence: A* loses on LogicQA, ToT collapses on GSM8K with LLaMA-3.1-8B (60.00 vs. 86.90 for SC), and the paper reports that its router recovers only 26.1% of the oracle gap — a rarity in this literature. - Methodological hygiene unusual for search-augmented reasoning papers: a scoped admissibility theorem with a working proof, human validation that the heuristic is conservative, measured token accounting, and hyperparameter sensitivity sweeps. - The framing of A* as a controlled diagnostic (isolating frontier/cost/heuristic from evaluator and rollout entanglements) makes the causal claim about 'branching itself' clearer than ToT/MCTS comparisons typically allow. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state: findings are conditioned on one budgeted A implementation (MCTS or beam search could shift the boundary); the 13 features are hand-designed proxies unlikely to capture full latent structure and are English-parser-dependent; A costs ~24× CoT tokens with token accounting from only a 300-question sample; long-form generation is untested; some features may retain benchmark-specific surface signal, so the router demonstrates within-dataset — not cross-benchmark — generalization; the router is binary (CoT vs. A*) and accuracy-oriented, excluding self-consistency and cost-aware multi-strategy routing. They confront limitations directly and at length, which strengthens credibility. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Single-run stochastic evaluation: A* branches with temperature 0.7, yet headline numbers have no multi-seed variance; only hyperparameter sensitivity is swept, not run-to-run variance. - The branching-coefficient claim (R² = 0.91) is fitted on 4 cluster means — four data points for a linear fit is statistically fragile, and cluster-level aggregation can inflate fit versus instance-level analysis; no instance-level regression or confidence interval on the slope is reported. - The random-forest baseline on hand-crafted features nearly matches the topology router on some benchmarks (e.g., 87.43 vs. 91.10 GSM8K, 80.12 vs. 81.52 MATH), so the specific 'topology' feature set's advantage over any input-only feature set is thinner than the narrative suggests. - No comparison against simpler compute-matched alternatives at equal token budgets (e.g., self-consistency with 24× samples, or budget-matched SC) — SC at 5 traces costs ~2,560 tokens and already beats A* on StrategyQA at 14B, so the cost-normalized frontier is not established. - The Fluency-Correctness Asymmetry is measured on sampled disagreement cases (n=100/dataset, 2 annotators) without confidence intervals, and fluency scoring methodology for the LLM-vs-human comparison is not detailed in the main text. - LLM-as-Critic uses DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B, a reasoning-specialized model, as a selector over traces generated by LLaMA-3.1-8B; whether a stronger or same-family critic changes the post-hoc routing conclusion is untested. - 14B router results on MATH (48.40%) are anomalously low versus 8B (81.52%) and are not explained, hinting at unmodeled model-capacity × topology interactions the authors themselves flag in the discussion. Bottom Line: A practitioner building inference-time reasoning systems gains real, actionable insight — route by cheap input structure, not by trace inspection, and reserve search for branch-heavy inputs — from this rigorously executed but within-benchmark-scoped study; it is the best-grounded treatment of the 'when does search help' question I have seen, and the honest negative results (LogicQA, 26.1% oracle-gap recovery, ToT collapse) make it worth reading despite the cross-benchmark transfer question remaining open.

#80 — Innovative (67)

MaxIM: Maximally Informative Incremental Summarization via Reinforcement Learning

J Jeong, G Tennenholtz, Y Chow, CW Hsu, C Boutilier · arxiv.org · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces MaxIM, an RL framework that trains an LLM summarizer to maintain a capacity-constrained incremental memory by using dense information-theoretic reward shaping—derived from a value-suboptimality bound—instead of sparse terminal task rewards. - Why it's important: Streaming AI agents must compress unbounded interaction histories into bounded working memory, but RL on sparse, delayed task rewards suffers severe credit assignment failures, and purely prediction-driven summarizers hallucinate ungrounded content that misleads the downstream agent. - How it does it: A pre-trained asymmetric critic (with access to privileged future targets during training only) computes step-wise pointwise-mutual-information rewards for two objectives—predictive sufficiency (summary's information about future task targets) and recursive consistency (summary's information about the local observed context)—which shape a PPO policy with mid-training cosine annealing of the shaping weight. - The good: On a post-cutoff arXiv reading benchmark with abstention-aware MCQ, MaxIM reaches 66.39% Abstain-MCQ accuracy at a 500-token budget versus 54.44% for task-only RL and 31.30% for prompted summarization, with a 48.55% vs. 32.23% gap on the early-section retention stress test; ablations cleanly isolate each component. - The missing: Both benchmarks are self-constructed with oracle-generated targets (synthetic MCQs; a re-generated WildChat user simulator with annotated latent states), so the headline gains are measured against tasks designed to match the method's own target structure, with no third-party benchmark or human evaluation. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on LLM memory agents, long-context compression, or reward shaping—it offers one of the more theoretically grounded treatments of the credit-assignment problem in memory management—skip it if you only want deployable memory systems, since no code or model release is stated and results are confined to two in-house setups.
Why this rank
Scored using the Empirical profile (with a theoretical component). Novelty (75) is the strongest dimension — a new formulation of bounded-memory summarization as a POMDP belief-state problem with dense PMI shaping derived from a value-suboptimality bound, plus a formalized hallucination failure mode — and Non-Obviousness (75) is high, particularly the counter-intuitive finding that task-only memory RL makes agents worse than no memory. Rigor (70) is anchored by SEM error bars, paired bootstrap tests, post-cutoff test papers, leakage-calibrated MCQs, and clean component ablations, but held back by self-constructed oracle-target benchmarks sharing a construction lineage with the shaping signals and no code/data release. Completeness (64) is good (direct limitations, cross-family judges, honest MemAgent win-rate nuance) while Resilience (60) drops because the closed synthetic loop and absent third-party benchmark leave generalization claims exposed; Impact (44) is low with no artifact released. Weighted composite: 0.20*75 + 0.25*70 + 0.15*75 + 0.15*64 + 0.15*60 + 0.10*44 = 67.

Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: AI agents in continuous streaming environments (long-horizon dialogue, goal-directed document reading, real-time personalization) cannot retain unbounded histories: long contexts degrade reasoning ("lost in the middle") and context windows are finite. The natural fix is a trainable summarizer that incrementally compresses the stream into a fixed K-token working memory consumed by a frozen action agent. Optimizing this summarizer with RL on downstream task utility fails in practice because task rewards arrive only at the end of long episodes, giving the policy no step-level signal about which features of the stream to retain. Conversely, supervising on surface-level reconstruction or myopic informativeness discards task-critical latent content or invites hallucination. The gap MaxIM closes is a principled, dense, step-wise training signal for bounded-memory summarization that does not require human preference labels. Key Idea: Treat the summary as a capacity-constrained belief state in a POMDP and prove (extending approximate information state theory) that the value suboptimality of acting from a compressed summary is bounded by sequential information loss I(Yt; Ht | zt). This converts memory design into MI maximization, operationalized by two complementary shaping rewards: predictive sufficiency, a variational lower bound (VPL) on −H(Yt | zt) computed as a PMI log-ratio log qϕ(Yt|zt) − log qϕ(Yt|znull) to cancel target difficulty; and recursive consistency, a forward-direction PMI I(zt; ˜Ht) = log qϕ(zt|˜Ht) − log qϕ(zt|˜Hnull) that penalizes tokens not supported by the local context, directly addressing a formalized hallucination failure mode (Lemma 1) where sufficiency alone can be gamed with fluent fabrication. The forward (rather than backward-reconstruction) direction of the consistency score is a non-obvious and well-argued design choice: fabricated sentences appended alongside true ones would not lower backward reconstruction likelihood but do receive zero/negative forward log-ratios. Methodology: The pipeline has three phases (Algorithm 1). (1) Synthetic data generation with privileged target access: for arXiv, 2,196 recent ar5iv papers split disjointly into critic/SFT (1,281), RL (533), validation (44), and post-cutoff test (338) sets, with 5 cross-section synthesis MCQs per paper (anti-leakage distractor calibration reducing no-summary accuracy from 67.5% to 27.6%); for WildChat, 7,968 English dialogues with causally annotated 10-key JSON user states, a trained user simulator, and regenerated trajectories (3,000 critic/SFT, 3,500 RL, 200 val, 500 test). Three summary quality tiers (high-quality, vague, hallucinated) train the critic. (2) A single unified Gemini 2.5 Flash critic qϕ is trained via cross-entropy on a six-way mixture covering conditional and null-baseline queries for both PMI rewards (Eq. 3). (3) KL-regularized PPO with GRPO-style group-relative (leave-one-out) advantages over G=8 rollouts, γ=0.9, backward-discounted return-to-go, centered sigmoid reward transformation with offline-calibrated slopes/midpoints, shaping weights (ws, wc) = (0.30, 0.11), and cosine annealing λs from 1 to 0 over RL steps 450–600 so late training optimizes pure task reward. Critical design decisions: PMI baseline subtraction for target-difficulty cancellation (justified by Proposition 6(i) and validated offline—within-paper spread increases 8.1×, downstream correlation rises from r=+0.050 to +0.324); forward-direction consistency scoring (well-argued); mid-decay annealing window (empirically supported: mid window 66.39% vs. 57.10% constant and ~61.2% for early/late windows). The theory assumes target mediation, memory causality, and compressed action selection (A1–A3), with an approximate-mediation extension (Proposition 3). Key Results: Tested at moderate scale (up to 25 chunks/turns per episode; ~64K RL trajectories per run). ArXiv, K=500 (N=338, ±SEM reported): MaxIM 66.39% Abstain-MCQ vs. Task-Only RL 54.44%, MemAgent RL 52.90%, Policy SFT 38.76%, Prompt-Only 31.30%, Best-of-N MI SFT 29.05%; abstention rate falls from 59–70% to 32.0%. Early-Section Stress Test (N=332): 48.55% vs. 32.23% (Task-Only) and 17.35% (Prompt-Only). Budget Pareto: MaxIM at K=100 (34.26%) beats Prompt-Only at K=500; MaxIM at K=500 (66.39%) beats Prompt-Only at K=2,000 (64.32%). Claim incorporation sustained at 26.8% in chunks 21–25 vs. 15.4–20.4% for baselines. WildChat (GPT-4.1 judge, N=500): MaxIM is the only method with positive Δ over the memory-free baseline on all axes on both cohorts (e.g., +0.30 Preference Retention on T≥10, N=158; p-values via 10,000-resample paired bootstrap); strikingly, Task-Only RL (Δ=−0.30 Satisfaction) and MemAgent RL (Δ=−0.28) are worse than no memory at all—a counter-intuitive and valuable finding showing imperfect beliefs actively mislead the agent. Contradiction rate 4.27% vs. 7.04–11.04% for baselines; grounded claims 40.3 vs. 21.0–23.1. Baselines are current and appropriate (MemAgent is ICLR 2026); ablations (Suff-Only drops −14.85 pp arXiv and raises WildChat contradictions +51.8%; MI-Only leaves a 16.09 pp gap) cleanly demonstrate synergy. Training overhead is modest: ≈1.25× (arXiv) / 1.17× (WildChat) FLOPs vs. sparse-reward RL, with zero test-time critic calls. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION + NEW METHOD + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. Genuinely novel: the derivation of dense PMI shaping rewards from a value-suboptimality/information-loss bound for capacity-constrained summarization, the formalized hallucination failure mode motivating forward recursive consistency, and the empirical demonstration that sparse-reward memory RL can underperform no memory on live utility. The components—PPO, GRPO-style advantages, asymmetric actor-critic, variational MI bounds (VPL, Barber & Agakov 2003), incremental summarization—are standard, but their combination into a calibrated, unified-critic shaping scheme for LLM memory is a substantive synthesis rather than a plug-together of prior memory systems (MemAgent/Mem-α use sparse rewards only). Rigor & Reproducibility: Strong for an industry lab paper. Ablations isolate each reward term (Table 3a) and the annealing window (Table 3b); error bars (SEM) and paired bootstrap significance tests with explicit p-values are reported; anti-leakage measures are unusually careful (post-cutoff test papers, disjoint splits by salted hash, MCQ distractor calibration with reported no-summary floors, 4-way forced-choice collapse analysis showing abstention is necessary); evaluation uses a cross-family judge (GPT-4.1) with Gemini cross-checks and randomized A/B ordering; offline critic validation (Table 8) quantifies why raw VPL fails. Concerns: no code, data, or model weights release is stated; the arXiv MCQ targets are generated by the same vendor's oracle model that also provides RL targets on WildChat, so evaluation and training objectives share a construction lineage (partial Goodhart risk, partially mitigated by the abstention protocol); judge-based WildChat utility metrics are LLM-as-judge, not human; theory assumptions (A1–A3, bounded rewards, target mediation) are stated but their empirical plausibility in open-ended settings is not stress-tested. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a theoretical component). Practical: Runs entirely on commercially available hosted LLMs (Gemini 2.5 Flash backbone/critic, TPU training) with black-box frozen agents—no gradient access to the downstream model is needed; at inference the method is a single summarizer call per turn, identical to baselines. Efficient: ≈1.17–1.25× training FLOPs vs. sparse-reward RL, <15% per-step wall-clock overhead during the shaping window, zero test-time critic cost, and O(T·K) generated tokens vs. O(T²·L_chunk) for full-context prompting. Effective: Evidence supports the stated problem on both benchmarks—higher task accuracy, better grounding, positive utility deltas over no-memory—but effectiveness is demonstrated only against the authors' own task constructions and an LLM judge, not in human-facing deployment. Scalable: Only claimed, not tested, beyond 25-turn horizons and K≤800 tokens; the Markovian one-step update means any missed information is irrecoverable at 10× horizons (the authors flag this), and no external retrieval fallback was evaluated. Delivers a paper only; no library, dataset release, or trained model artifact is mentioned. Strengths: - The theory-to-algorithm chain is unusually tight: Theorem 1 (value gap ≤ sequential information loss) → Proposition 1 (sufficiency objective) → Lemma 1 (hallucination failure mode) → Proposition 2 (consistency regularizer) → Proposition 6 (PMI estimator properties, baseline unbiasedness, critic shift), with each practical deviation (sigmoids, masked baselines, annealing) explicitly reconciled with the theory. - The counter-intuitive WildChat finding—that task-reward-only RL and MemAgent produce beliefs that make the assistant worse than having no memory at all (Δ=−0.28 to −0.30, p<0.05), while MI-shaped policies recover positive gains—is a genuinely informative result about intermediate-turn hallucination under sparse-reward RL. - Evaluation hygiene is above average: post-cutoff test papers, leakage-calibrated MCQs with reported chance floors, abstention-aware scoring that exposes the 87.7–94.0% forced-choice ceiling effect, cross-family judging, and a diagnostic (Table 10) that separates the training reward from live utility. - Cost accounting is concrete: relative FLOPs tables, cached baselines, teacher-forced critic scoring, and a demonstrated 3.4–4.9× token-compression gain over prompted summarization at matched accuracy. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors directly confront four issues (Appendix G.2): (1) the strict Markovian bottleneck makes early information loss irreversible, with hybrid retrieval-augmented memory named as future work; (2) critic training depends on an oracle target proxy Yt, and misspecification introduces an explicit mediation error floor (Proposition 3); (3) training-time compute overhead from critic passes during the shaping window; (4) LLM-as-judge self-preference bias, mitigated by cross-family judges but acknowledged to require human studies. They also flag privacy/surveillance risks of effective latent-intent tracking in the broader-impacts section. This is a direct, non-minimizing treatment of limitations—a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Both benchmarks are constructed by the authors with oracle targets matched to the method's shaping signals (synthesis MCQs; 10-key JSON states); a third-party long-context/memory benchmark (e.g., on real retrieval or agentic workloads) is absent, so generalization beyond oracle-defined targets is untested. (2) The user simulator that generates WildChat rollouts is itself trained on oracle annotations by the same model family used for critics, creating a closed synthetic loop whose fidelity to real user drift is unverified. (3) No comparison against non-RL memory alternatives that could compete on grounding, e.g., retrieval-based or hierarchical summarization hybrids, and no ablation of the 10-key JSON schema's role on WildChat. (4) Theorem 1's bound scales as √I/(1−γ)², which is likely loose in practice, and the paper never empirically estimates the bound's tightness against observed value gaps. (5) No release of code, data, prompts-as-artifacts, or model weights is stated, limiting reproducibility of a system with many calibrated hyperparameters (slopes, midpoints, weights, annealing windows). (6) All runs use a single backbone (Gemini 2.5 Flash); backbone sensitivity is unmeasured. (7) On arXiv, MemAgent beats MaxIM on pairwise Usefulness win rate (80.1% vs. 72.9% at t=20), a nuance that tempers the uniform-superiority narrative but is acknowledged only in passing. Bottom Line: A practitioner building RL-trained memory or context-compression systems should read this paper for its rigorous treatment of the credit-assignment and hallucination pathologies of sparse-reward memory RL and a credible dense-shaping recipe—but should treat the headline numbers as evidence on bespoke oracle-annotated tasks rather than proof of general-purpose superiority, and likely pair it with a retrieval-fallback architecture the authors themselves recommend.

EnzymeRSI: A dual-loop recursive self - improvement system for enzyme design

Y Hou, L Yang, Y Liu, W Tang, Y Yang, M Yang… · arxiv.org · recursive self-improvement - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces EnzymeRSI, a dual-loop recursive self-improvement system for enzyme design in which an outer loop evolves the agent harness (prompts, pipelines, skills, tool routing) without touching model weights, an inner loop develops prediction and selection algorithms on demand, and a specified cloud-laboratory path returns quality-controlled wet-lab measurements. - Why it's important: ML-guided directed evolution optimizes which candidates to assay while assuming the judging method is fixed; when the method itself is the bottleneck, wet-lab rounds are expensive, so a system that can evolve its own workflow and algorithms addresses the actual cost driver in protein engineering campaigns. - How it does it: The core move is partitioning the improvement space into two separately scored objects — harness assets and algorithm assets — each adopted only through pre-registered, paired, equal-budget comparisons with rollback, plus host-side gates that reject repeated predictions and affine-invariant submissions that would game Pearson-correlation scoring. - The good: The evaluation discipline is unusually honest and fine-grained: 196 outer-loop rounds with 142 paired comparisons across five ProteinGym assays, sealed test splits with sha256 manifests, frozen pre-experiment design records for wet lab, and reference-well-removal sensitivity analysis on noisy luminescence data. - The missing: No multi-round autonomous dry-to-wet campaign was actually run (explicitly deferred as a scope decision), the headline dry-lab gains are single-run and modest (mean dev-set Spearman gain +0.044; ThermoMPNN PCC 0.849 vs 0.840 for the unmodified base agent), and the multi-seed replication the authors' own protocol requires is left as future work. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building self-improving agents or evaluation contracts for autonomous science — the anti-gaming gates and tiered benchmark design generalize beyond enzymes — but skippable if you want a demonstrated autonomous wet-lab loop, which this paper specifies rather than delivers.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile (with a systems component, per the paper's own tagging). The score is dragged down by two dimensions: Practical Impact (45) — no code, gates, or artifacts are actually released despite the evaluation contract being the main contribution, and the headline autonomy claim (a closed dry-to-wet loop) is specified but never executed. Rigor (65) reflects serious test isolation undermined by missing multi-seed replication and vendor self-reported infrastructure. Problem & Motivation: Three active lines in protein engineering — active-learning-assisted directed evolution, protein-LM-driven in vitro evolution, and explicit epistasis modeling — all optimize which candidates to assay under a fixed judging method. When the bottleneck is a mismatched method or failing workflow rather than candidate selection, this route stalls, and each wasted wet-lab round is costly. Separately, existing harness self-improvement work (e.g., HarnessPro) benchmarks on coding tasks, where adopting a change costs a re-run; enzyme engineering requires adopting changes against real measurements that carry batch noise and QC status, and no evaluation basis exists for whether self-improvement was genuine, adopted, and reusable rather than a lucky second run. Key Idea: Treat research organization (the harness) and scientific algorithms as two separate, explicitly versioned objects of evolution, each subject to paired comparison at matched budget against a fixed control, with adoption rules fixed before comparison and a host-side anti-gaming layer (repeated-prediction pre-checks, affine-invariant-transform detection, sealed test sets with checksum manifests). The inner loop is triggered only when tool and workflow causes are excluded and a named method-capability gap exists — e.g., the RLuc case exposed design-rank vs measured-rank correlation of only 0.175, which the authors designate an inner-loop trigger rather than a harness problem. Methodology: A task is formalized as q = (parent sequence, objective/constraints, experimental context, visible data, multidimensional budget); the system maximizes task quality subject to budget, with outer-loop development, inner-loop training, and retries all charged to cost. Outer loop (Harness RSI): non-parametric version evolution over prompts, pipelines, skills, and subagents; each round produces one failure-mode hypothesis, one minimal change bundle with a falsification condition, and a paired comparison against the current version under identical model, permissions, data, and budget; outcomes are global adoption, scoped retention, or rollback. Inner loop (Algorithm RSI): asynchronous method development in an isolated sandbox over representations, losses, ensembling, and acquisition functions; MethodBundles must pass identity verification, shuffled-input inference checks, and registration by an independent evaluation layer. Wet-lab execution is delegated to ProtoPilot (protocol orchestration) and Operon-S1 (fast decisions: pre-screening, batch admission, QC) — both from the same company — with execution receipts stored separately from measurements. Critical design decisions: (1) separate scoring of protein/algorithm/system tiers rather than one weighted number — well justified by the OPSD first-place case, which came from the starting tool combination, not evolution; (2) trigger conditions distinguishing engineering faults, workflow failures, and method bottlenecks — reasonable but only partially exercised; (3) host-side gates against degenerate submissions (one reference framework's output was an exact affine transform of the official prediction and scored identically under Pearson correlation) — well justified by direct observation. Key Results: Outer loop, 5 ProteinGym assays (OTU7A stability, CD19 binding, OPSD expression, NPC1 viability, SCN5A fitness): 196 rounds, 142 paired comparisons, 12 adoptions (8.5%), mean dev-set Spearman gain +0.044. CD19 rose 0.314→0.335 over 39 rounds (first place; MIF reproduction matched official within 0.0004), the only first place produced by evolution; OPSD started at 0.680 (already above the leading official 0.656) and gained only 0.003 over 44 rounds. Inner loop: ThermoMPNN dev-set PCC 0.849 versus official starting point 0.804 and the best of ten reference frameworks (OpenRSI 0.834) — but the unmodified QwenCode base agent itself reached 0.840, so the system's margin over its own base is ~0.010. TadA-Bench: Spearman 0.307 vs 0.301 for the unmodified base, completing 20 formal evaluations in 1.13 h vs 2.24 h; the substantive move was replacing continuous regression with ordinal modelling over activity bins under train/test distribution misalignment. Wet lab (human experimental team; EnzymeRSI supplied nominations and rules): RLuc — of 32 non-pre-specified nominations, 10 reached ≥2× wild-type luminescence; all three inference-only candidates exceeded WT (2.30×, 1.98×, 2.43×), with only S287M robust to reference-well removal (WT-well CV 25.6–65.6%); design rank vs measured rank ρ = 0.175. A3A — a 50% cap on unmodified-C conversion selected Y130Q, raising 5mC conversion in the weaker CT context from 11.4% (WT) to 46.5% and reversing substrate preference in both contexts; the constraint frontier contains six distinct top choices across cap settings (Y130Q/K47T/Y132C at 50/60/10% caps). KOD-E — 189 single-substitution variants, 125 parent–descendant pairs; E485I+S451L reached 31.1× parent; two objective functions from the same parent (Q461A at 1.3×) selected divergent routes (E485I → 3.8× vs monotonic path via L457M), converging on the same triple mutant at 2.6×; a 7.4-parent-unit rank reversal at positions 676/680 (3.9 Å apart, contacting DNA) was explained by structure alone without activity labels. Baselines: ten RSI research frameworks (OpenRSI, ShinkaEvolve, RD-Agent, etc.) run under a shared contract — current for the RSI-agent comparison, but no protein-specialist ML baselines beyond the official ThermoMPNN and ProteinGym records. Tested at standard dry-lab benchmark scale and small wet-lab scale (40, 75, and 189 variants), not stress scale. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL plus NEW FORMULATION. Genuinely novel: the evaluation contract for self-improvement — tiered sealed benchmark resources, anti-gaming host-side gates (repeated-prediction and affine-invariant-transform pre-checks), separate scoring of harness vs algorithm contributions via a four-cell interaction term, and frozen pre-experiment wet-lab design records with QC-bearing evidence. The constituent techniques — LLM-agent prompt/pipeline evolution, protein language model features, ProteinGym, standard site-directed mutagenesis assays — are existing ideas combined in a new setting; the wet-lab autonomy component is specified but not demonstrated. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations: change bundles are individually disableable, and adopted changes are attributed (the CD19 gain traces to a single round-12 variant-input change). The statistical protocol specifies group-level paired gains, sign-flip tests, 10,000-sample paired bootstrap CIs over ≥3 independent evolution seeds — but the authors state that seed replication has not been performed; all headline comparisons rest on single runs without error bars. Test-set isolation is unusually serious: sealed parquet files with permission 000, sha256-frozen split manifests, network-disabled test scoring, and refusal of test environments without an audited --final flag. Code, data, or model weights release: not stated; the paper promises future release of host-side gates as a reusable evaluation contract. Methodological concerns: (1) outer-loop gains are measured on the development set the harness was permitted to use during evolution — the authors acknowledge this directly; (2) key infrastructure (ProtoPilot, Operon-S1, SEBio) is internal to the same organization, one item unpublished, so component claims are vendor self-reports; (3) the wet-lab experiments were executed by the human experimental team with EnzymeRSI supplying nominations and rules — decision support, not autonomous execution. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS component). Practical: Yes — runs on a single L40S with a locked QwenCode agent, and the cloud-lab path uses commercially available instruments; no exotic hardware is implied. Efficient: The TadA task completed 20 formal evaluations in 1.13 h (vs 2.24 h for the unmodified base agent); inner-loop training and all retries are charged against a multidimensional budget, but absolute compute costs of the 196-round outer loop are not stated. Effective: Partially — the evidence shows real but small dry-lab gains and credible single-round wet-lab decision support; it does not show the closed loop solving an end-to-end engineering campaign, which the authors concede. Scalable: Not tested beyond five assays and three enzyme systems; whether paired-comparison overhead (8.5% adoption rate over 142 comparisons) remains tolerable at larger task counts is unexamined. Deliverable form: the paper itself; no code, dataset, or trained model release is stated — the reusable artifacts (host-side gates, evaluation tiers) are promised, not shipped. Strengths: - The evaluation methodology is the real contribution: anti-gaming gates that caught an affine-transform cheating attempt and a 20×-reused CV split, tiered benchmarks whose permitted conclusions and forbidden inferences are stated explicitly per tier, and a four-cell interaction test separating harness from algorithm gains. This is transferable to any self-improving-agent research, not just enzymes. - Pre-frozen, prospective wet-lab validation with honest noise handling: the RLuc nomination record was frozen before measurement, and the reference-well sensitivity analysis (only S287M stays above 2× under all removals) is the kind of measurement-layer accounting rarely reported in ML-guided protein engineering. - The A3A constraint-frontier result — the optimal variant jumping discretely across three cap settings on the same 75 measured variants — is a clean, quantified demonstration that dual objectives cannot be folded into a static weighted score. - Unusually candid attribution: the paper states plainly that the OPSD first place came from the starting tool combination rather than evolution, and that the RLuc ranking failure remains open. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly, which strengthens credibility. They state three boundaries: (1) the +0.044 outer-loop gain is on the development set used during evolution, and only the CD19 first place was produced by the evolution itself; (2) the RLuc ranking gap is named as an inner-loop trigger but was never closed — the inner loop was exercised on stability and extrapolation tasks, not against this gap; (3) the cloud-lab commission/execution/receipt path is specified but has not carried a multi-round autonomous campaign, which they frame as a scope decision rather than an unresolved capability. They also note that RLuc was a prospective test while A3A and KOD-E recompiled rules on already-measured data — the latter two are analyses of how optima move, not prospective predictions. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The strongest head-to-head comparison is suppressed by framing: the unmodified QwenCode base agent reached ThermoMPNN PCC 0.840 and TadA 0.301, so EnzymeRSI's margins over its own substrate are ~0.010 and ~0.006 — within what single-run noise could plausibly produce, and the multi-seed test that would settle this is deferred. - The ten reference frameworks are RSI research agents, not protein-engineering specialists; no comparison against, e.g., a straightforward ESM2-finetuned baseline or an expert-designed active-learning pipeline at equal budget is reported for the outer-loop assays. - Component provenance: Operon-S1, ProtoPilot, and the cloud-lab execution system are same-organization artifacts (one unpublished), so the wet-lab pipeline's reliability claims rest on self-reported infrastructure with no independent evaluation. - The inner loop's headline tasks are external benchmarks (ThermoMPNN, TadA-Bench) while the motivating failure (RLuc ranking) is untested — the system's core claim (method bottlenecks get repaired on demand) is never demonstrated on the case that motivated it. - The four-cell interaction term for harness×algorithm cooperation is defined in the protocol but no measured interaction is reported. Bottom Line: A practitioner building self-improving or autonomous-science systems gains real, transferable value from the evaluation contract and anti-gaming mechanisms — likely the most rigorous treatment of self-improvement validity in the wet-lab-adjacent literature — but anyone seeking demonstrated autonomous enzyme engineering should treat this as a protocol paper whose headline autonomy claim remains unexecuted.

ProTEUS: A mutation-resolved world model for closed-loop protein evolution (13 ▲ )

Yikun Zhang, Minghao Guo, Guangxue Xu, Peter Yichen Chen, Wojciech Matusik, Wengong Jin, Jingjing Chai, Kaiyi Jiang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 11 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces ProTEUS, a protein-fitness world model pretrained on 182 deep mutational scanning assays that uses mutation-biased attention over joint sequence/MSA/structure representations to predict variant fitness, and demonstrates closed-loop experimental protein engineering yielding >10-fold activity improvements within ~100 tested variants on two enzymes. - Why it's important: Experimental screening can only sample a tiny fraction of the 20^L sequence space, and existing zero-shot PLM scores correlate only moderately with specific engineered activities; a model that efficiently aligns computation with wet-lab feedback reduces the cost and time of protein engineering campaigns. - How it does it: Variants are encoded in a joint 768-d latent space from ESM-2 3B, MSA Transformer, and ESM3 structure features aligned residue-by-residue, with a learned attention bias (β=10) added at substituted positions so the 12-layer transformer focuses on mutations in context; a two-step physics-constrained structure predictor using Gauss–Seidel projection supplies fast candidate-specific structural inputs. - The good: The mutation-bias ablation is convincing — removing it drops Spearman from 0.840 to 0.606, and the full three-modality model reaches 0.938 vs 0.807 sequence-only, directly supporting the architectural claim; Problem & Motivation: Protein engineering requires navigating rugged fitness landscapes where small sequence changes can produce large functional differences. Directed evolution and DMS can only sample a tiny fraction of the ~20^L possible variants, and epistasis complicates extrapolation to higher-order mutants. Existing computational approaches — sequence-based PLMs (ESM family), MSA-based models (Tranception, PoET), and multimodal models (SaProt, ESM-3) — show only moderate correlation with experimentally measured activity for proteins not well-represented in evolution, because natural sequence distributions reflect organismal fitness constraints rather than the specific activity being engineered. Active-learning methods like EVOLVEpro and MULTI-evolve align models to experimental objectives but suffer from low initial hit rates and poor generalization to untested higher-order mutants. The gap is a model with a rich variant representation that can both rank mutations zero-shot and efficiently absorb sparse experimental feedback to guide iterative engineering. Key Idea: The core insight is mutation-resolved attention: rather than pooling residue-level features into a single protein-level representation, ProTEUS adds a constant bias (β=10) to attention logits at substituted residue positions, forcing every attention head to attend explicitly to the (few) mutations while retaining full-sequence context. This is combined with pretraining on experimental DMS fitness measurements (not just evolutionary plausibility) to align the latent space with activity rather than natural selection. Methodology: ProTEUS has three coupled components. (1) MutationFormer: a 12-layer, 768-wide transformer with 12 heads that fuses per-residue features from frozen ESM-2 3B (sequence, 2560-d), MSA Transformer (768-d), and ESM3 (structure, 1536-d) via factorized adapters with a 64-d bottleneck, using a binary mutation mask and additive attention bias β=10 at substituted positions. Pretrained on 182 ProteinGym DMS assays (~2.5M variant measurements across 161 proteins) to predict assay-normalized fitness via MSE loss. (2) A physics-constrained all-atom structure predictor initialized from Boltz-1 weights, fine-tuned on ~180,000 PDB structures with two denoising steps and a differentiable Gauss–Seidel projection enforcing seven constraint families (chirality, E/Z, planarity, steric clash, etc.), trained through the projection via implicit differentiation. (3) A closed-loop nomination strategy: zero-shot ranks select the initial 30 single mutants; subsequent rounds combine zero-shot ranks, random-forest fitness predictions (fit on frozen ProTEUS representations), and ranks derived from all accumulated measurements to nominate higher-order mutants. Structural predictor benchmarks use CASP15, PoseBusters, and related suites; evolution benchmarks use held-out DMS assays and CombinGym multi-mutant datasets. Key Results: On pretraining test set (182 assays), ProTEUS achieves Spearman ρ = 0.933 and MSE = 0.115; the strongest evaluated baseline PoET-2 reaches 0.861. Scaling pretraining data 80-fold reduces MSE 56.3% (0.262 → 0.115), fitting a power law (~12.1% MSE reduction per doubling, R² = 0.989 in log space). Zero-shot on 19 held-out assays: highest macro-averaged Spearman among 15 methods tested (range ~0.10–0.30). Supervised fine-tuning: mean Spearman 0.549 vs 0.367 for ProteinNPT across 19 assays (p < 0.001, one-sided paired t-test). Higher-order K-vs-rest extrapolation: 0.448 vs 0.295 for MULTI-evolve across 40 dataset-K comparisons (80% win rate, one-sided Wilcoxon p < 0.05). Simulated 5-round evolution: normalized best fitness 0.741 vs 0.555 for EVOLVEpro on 10 single-mutant datasets. Structure predictor: median 9.4-fold speedup over 200-step Boltz-1; AlphaFold 3 runtimes 7.81–10.81× higher across atom-count bins; comparable complex LDDT (0.6406 for Boltz-1 reference, 0.6321 fine-tuned two-step predictor). Wet lab: levansucrase — Q34N 4.5× WT in round 0 (zero-shot), Q34N:G240W 8.94×, G23A:Q34N:G240W 14.03× WT in <100 tests; ALDH — L358I 2.02× zero-shot, S103V:A116K:H332N:L358I 6.85× WT (7.90× catalytic-rate-normalized) in 150 tests. Baselines are current and strong (PoET-2, ESM-3, ESM-C, Tranception, SaProt, ProteinNPT, EVOLVEpro, MULTI-evolve). Testing spans standard computational benchmarks and two real experimental campaigns at moderate scale. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (mutation-biased attention over multimodal joint embeddings pretrained on DMS fitness data) and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (integrated closed-loop world model with fast physics-constrained structure predictor). The mutation-attention bias is a simple but effective architectural modification; the structure predictor builds on Boltz-1 with an established projection technique (from the authors' prior ICLR 2026 work, ref 32); the closed-loop active learning framework combines known components (PLM embeddings + random forest + iterative nomination) in a new configuration with higher-resolution variant representations. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: mutation-bias strength (0/5/10/15/20 tested), input modality combinations (sequence/MSA/structure), and MSA sampling strategy are all individually varied. Statistical tests (one-sided paired Wilcoxon, paired t-tests) are reported with P values. Data-leakage analysis between pretraining and evaluation sets is thorough (MMseqs2 sequence identity <30% at ≥50% coverage, Foldseek TM-score <0.5). Code and models are available at https://github.com/yikunpku/ProTEUS. Limitations: zero-shot scores correlate poorly with wet-lab activity in round 0 (levansucrase ρ = −0.24, P = 0.21; ALDH ρ = −0.07, P = 0.70), yet the paper still claims these variants are "high-fitness" selections; the supplementary text admits embedding-based readouts showed no advantage over training-mean baselines for retrospective prediction in the final levansucrase round (MAE 2.007 vs 2.007). The work is funded by Foundry Biosciences with co-founders as authors and patents filed — this introduces a potential commercial bias in reporting. The structure predictor was developed and evaluated on the same benchmark suites (CASP15) in the authors' prior work, which risks overfitting to those benchmarks. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (computational benchmarks + two wet-lab experimental campaigns). - Practical: Structure predictor runs on NVIDIA A6000 and RTX-class GPUs; MutationFormer uses frozen public encoders (ESM-2 3B, MSA Transformer, ESM3); wet-lab pipeline uses standard E. coli expression and commercial assay kits. - Efficient: Two-step structure prediction is 9.4× faster than 200-step Boltz-1; the computational cost per variant for MutationFormer inference is not separately reported but likely dominated by frozen-encoder forward passes (ESM-2 3B is expensive at scale). - Effective: Wet-lab results demonstrate >10× (levansucrase) and ~7× (ALDH) activity improvements over WT, directly solving the stated problem for these two enzymes; zero-shot round-0 hit rates are modest (1 standout mutant per 30 tested) but nonzero. - Scalable: Not tested beyond two enzymes; the paper argues scaling via the DMS power-law fit and future autonomous labs, but generalization to a third, fourth, or fiftieth protein — especially membrane proteins or complexes — is untested. Delivers: open-source code and models (GitHub), trained checkpoints, and a documented experimental protocol; the structure predictor is a reusable standalone artifact. Strengths: - The mutation-bias ablation (0.840 → 0.606 Spearman without bias) is a clean, direct causal test of the core architectural hypothesis and is the paper's most convincing single result. - The data-scaling analysis on DMS measurements (power-law fit, exponent −0.187, R² = 0.989) is the first empirical evidence that protein functional activity data follows LLM-like scaling behavior, suggesting a new direction for the field. - Wet-lab validation on two enzymes with full variant lists (Tables S10–S11) and honest reporting of non-improved rounds (ALDH round 3: 4.69× vs prior 6.08×) adds credibility beyond purely computational claims. - Thorough leakage analysis between pretraining and evaluation sets (sequence and structural homology screening with explicit thresholds) exceeds the standard of care in comparable PLM benchmarking papers. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge: (1) zero-shot scores diverge from the specific engineered activity (ρ = −0.24 round 0 for levansucrase), framing this as motivation for the closed-loop approach; (2) the pretraining corpus (~2.5M measurements from ProteinGym) is small relative to text/vision datasets and noisy across assay conditions; (3) activity-based analyses in the supplementary text note that embedding readouts did not outperform training-mean baselines for retrospective prediction in the final levansucrase round; (4) statistical support for the local-activity-association claim in ALDH is marginal (P = 0.046 for 5-neighbor, P = 0.28 and 0.09 for 3- and 10-neighbor analyses, unadjusted for multiplicity). The discussion confronts limitations more directly than most applied ML papers. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Only two proteins are tested experimentally, both soluble bacterial enzymes with convenient colorimetric readouts; no membrane protein, antibody, or therapeutically relevant target is attempted. - The zero-shot round-0 batch is described as identifying "high-fitness variants," but the rank correlation with measured activity is negative or null in both campaigns; the apparent success (1 good hit in 30) could reflect a high variance-tolerance strategy rather than good ranking. - The random forest on frozen ProTEUS representations (used in the loop) is never ablated against a random forest on ESM-2 mean-pooled embeddings alone — so it is unclear whether the expensive multimodal representation adds value in the active-learning phase versus a simpler PLM baseline. - The "world model" terminology implies state-transition dynamics and action-conditioned prediction, but the system is a static fitness predictor with rank-based nomination; no temporal/dynamics modeling is present. - The levansucrase and ALDH assays measure activity in crude lysate or permeabilized cells without normalizing for expression in the primary screen; the ALDH catalytic-rate normalization is done post-hoc for only a subset, and the levansucrase multi-objective (activity × expression) optimization is conflated with a single activity readout. - No comparison to recent non-PLM active-learning baselines (e.g., Gaussian-process Bayesian optimization, which remains standard in protein engineering) is provided. Bottom Line: This is a solid, well-executed system paper with one genuinely useful architectural insight (mutation-biased attention) and strong computational benchmarks, but the "world model" framing overstates what is demonstrated — practitioners in protein engineering will benefit from the mutation-attention trick and the scaling evidence, yet should recognize that the experimental validation covers only two favorable enzymes and the zero-shot ranking itself performed poorly in both wet-lab campaigns.

Securing Web Agents with the Compile-Then-Execute Paradigm

A Chow, J Zhu, S Venuto, A Alharbi, B Alomair, R Popa… · arxiv.org · automated generated environments for agent testing - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Baya, a compile-then-execute web agent that compiles a user's request into a Python program against a manually constructed Trusted Website API before touching the live site, so untrusted web content can fill variables but never redefine control flow. - Why it's important: Reactive (ReAct) web agents expose their action selection to attacker-controlled page content, enabling indirect prompt-injection attacks that hijack a logged-in agent's authority; a structural defense that costs no utility would remove a major blocker to deploying web agents. - How it does it: The core move is time/process/privilege/information separation between compilation (a sandboxed coding agent that sees only typed API contracts and mock tests, never live pages) and execution (an isolated engine running the pre-compiled program), with replanning fed only restricted, API-generated error diagnostics. - The good: Across 84 WASP attack instances and three models, Baya achieves 0% intermediate and end-to-end attack success rate while also posting the highest aggregate utility (81.9% with Claude Sonnet-4.6) over API-enabled ReAct (59.0%) and browser-only ReAct (52.3%) on 581 WebArena Verified tasks. - The missing: The Trusted Website API for each website is hand-constructed and is itself in the trusted computing base; the paper offers no empirical path to automating this for arbitrary websites, which is the load-bearing assumption of the whole architecture. - Read it or not: Security researchers and agent-systems builders should read it — it is the strongest published demonstration that plan-then-execute can beat ReAct on utility, not just security, on a standard benchmark; practitioners only seeking a quick utility boost can skim Sections 5.3–5.6.
