Problem & Motivation: Web agents built on the ReAct paradigm interleave action selection with observations of webpages that inherently mix trusted interface elements with untrusted third-party content (reviews, forum posts, ads). Because the LLM decides its next action at the same moment it consumes untrusted text, indirect prompt injection can hijack the agent's control flow — a confused-deputy problem where the agent acts with the user's logged-in authority. Prior structural defenses (CaMeL, FIDES) proved compile-then-execute works for tool-calling agents with small, documented toolsets, but websites lack the required abstraction: REST APIs are heterogeneous, underspecified, and incomplete relative to UI functionality (Postmill's 16 REST endpoints cover only 33% of its tasks). The open problem is supplying the stable, semantically documented action space that ahead-of-time compilation demands, without sacrificing task utility. Key Idea: Fix the control flow as a compiled Python program before any live-site contact, and make the only channel from runtime back to the compiler a restricted error diagnostic (HTTP status, invalid-parameter names) that by construction cannot carry website-derived content. The enabling abstraction is the Trusted Website API: a typed contract per operation — signature Σ, preconditions P, postconditions/side effects Q, error domain E — implemented uniformly via either native REST endpoints or trusted Playwright wrappers for UI-only functionality, so the compiler plans over one consistent interface while untrusted data is confined to program variables and branch selection. Methodology: Baya has three components. (1) Offline, per-site Trusted API construction: humans normalize heterogeneous REST schemas, document implicit constraints (e.g., Magento's nested filterGroups semantics where same-index filters OR and different-index filters AND), and fill UI-only coverage gaps with Playwright-backed operations sharing identical signatures. (2) Compilation: a sandboxed coding harness (Claude Code/Antigravity/Codex depending on model) receives the task, an endpoint catalog, schema-search tools, and site-specific guidance; it emits a restricted Python program plus a mock-based unit-test file (testing success paths, error paths, and answer formatting). Programs may include narrowly scoped, data-only LLM calls for semantic judgment on pre-narrowed candidate sets. Compilation is enforced via filesystem allowlists, network sandboxing (zero allowed domains), and harness permissions. (3) Execution: an isolated engine runs the program against the live site; on failure, up to three replans occur using only the prior program and trusted-API-generated error text. The evaluation additionally adapts WebArena Verified's evaluators into an outcome-based common harness (converting url_match tasks to string_match, dropping NetworkEventEvaluator) so browser- and API-based agents are graded comparably. Critical design decisions: manual API construction (well-justified as a first step but never tested at scale); restricted error-diagnostic channel (well-argued — the paper notes request values may derive from website content, so it admits only explicitly trusted diagnostics); and bounded replanning (three attempts, justified by cost). A three-way task taxonomy (Safe / Safe with Influence / Replan-Needed) scopes the approach's applicability, citing prior work that 81% of WebArena tasks are Safe and none are Replan-Needed. Key Results: Utility on 581 valid WebArena Verified tasks (GitLab n=154, Shopping n=171, Shopping Admin n=150, Postmill n=106): with Claude Sonnet-4.6, Baya reaches 81.9% aggregate (92.9% GitLab, 71.3% Shopping, 81.3% Shopping Admin, 84.0% Postmill) vs. 59.0% for ReActweb+API and 52.3% for ReActweb; Baya ranks first or ties first in 9 of 12 model–environment combinations across three model families, and beats ReActweb+API on Postmill by ≥39.6 points under every model. Security on WASP (84 attack instances across 12 GitLab and 9 Postmill templates): 0% intermediate and end-to-end ASR for Baya in all configurations, vs. intermediate ASRs up to 52.8% (ReActweb+API, Postmill, Gemini) and end-to-end ASR of 5.6% (ReActweb+API, Postmill, DeepSeek). Against UCM (GitLab only), Baya matches its 0% ASR but wins utility 92.9% vs. 75.3%. Ablation vs. the authors' earlier JSON-plan interpreter (BayaJSON): code generation raises Claude macro-average utility from 66.9% to 82.4% (+28.0 points on Shopping Admin). Static analysis shows only 2.1% of 627 generated programs contain LLM-call paths (1.8% invoked at runtime); 16.7% use a deterministic fuzzy matcher. Cost: 1.37M tokens, $0.70, and 327 s per task for BayaCode — about 2.0× the cost and 3.8× the latency of ReActweb+API, but 30.3% faster and 82.6% cheaper than UCM. Baselines are reasonable (ReAct variants with and without API access, plus the UCM defense), though two other compile-style defenses (ceLLMate, CUA) could not be run at all. Note this is an arXiv preprint (arXiv:2611.06039); results are not peer-reviewed. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The compile-then-execute security paradigm itself is established (CaMeL, FIDES, and the authors' own position paper on compile-and-execute for web agents); the genuinely new contributions are (a) the Trusted Website API contract design that makes ahead-of-time compilation feasible over real websites — including the REST/Playwright dual-implementation pattern — and (b) the empirical demonstration that this restriction improves utility rather than trading it away, which contradicts the common assumption that security restrictiveness costs capability. The code-as-plan vs. JSON-plan ablation is a solid finding but builds on standard code-generation-agent practice. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: JSON vs. code representation (Table 5), runtime-LLM usage measurement via static and runtime analysis (Table 4), and the ReActweb vs. ReActweb+API split isolating API availability from the compile-then-execute architecture. Error bars, multiple seeds, and significance tests are not reported; with ~106–171 tasks per environment, several per-cell margins (e.g., GPT-5.6-Luna's 2.4-point aggregate edge) are likely within noise, and the paper does not claim otherwise. Code is released at https://github.com/apechow/Baya. Methodological concerns: (1) evaluation is confined to the four WebArena environments whose Trusted APIs the authors themselves hand-built — the security property is partly validated on infrastructure the authors curated, and the evaluation was developed on the same benchmark used for reporting; (2) the evaluation harness was modified (url_match→string_match conversion, 42 tasks dropped as bad/impossible, 31 cross-site tasks excluded, evaluator credit granted per execution mode), and although the appendix is transparent, this changes the benchmark relative to WebArena Verified as published; (3) Baya uses agentic coding harnesses (Claude Code, Antigravity, Codex) with different configurations per model, while ReAct baselines call provider APIs directly — harness effects are not disentangled; (4) latency figures come from serial execution on one stack, and cost figures are LiteLLM/OpenRouter estimates, not invoiced charges; (5) Claude Code internally calls claude-haiku-4.5 for helper operations, an uncontrolled variable. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a built system with benchmark evaluation; no deployment). - Practical: Yes — inference is via remote provider APIs; the host machine was a GPU-less n2-standard-8 VM with 8 vCPUs and 32 GB RAM. - Efficient: No — 1.37M tokens, $0.70, and 327 s per task is 2.0×/3.8× the cost/latency of API-enabled ReAct, though it beats UCM (4.0× slower, 82.6% cheaper) and the authors argue compilation cost amortizes via program caching (claimed, not measured). - Effective: The 0% ASR plus the highest aggregate utility on all three models shows it solves the control-flow-hijacking problem on the tested scope; the guarantee is architectural (by construction) but the empirical ASR of 0% is observational over 84 instances, not a proof against adaptive attacks. - Scalable: Untested beyond four preprocessed sites; the manual API-construction step, per-site API maintenance burden, and the Replan-Needed task class (excluded by design) all bound scaling, and the authors' proposed secure auto-onboarding is future work only. Deliverable: a released code artifact (GitHub repo), though the Trusted APIs are specific to WebArena sites; no trained models. Strengths: - The restricted-error-diagnostic replanning channel is a genuinely careful design: the authors recognize that request values can themselves derive from website content, so they admit only trusted-API-generated diagnostics rather than relying on superficial trust heuristics — this closes a subtle hole most plan-then-execute systems leave open. - The Trusted Website API contract (Σ, P, Q, E) is a reusable abstraction, and the worked challenges (Magento's OR/AND filter-group semantics, UI-only Postmill voting, exact-match REST search failing descriptive queries) provide the first concrete characterization of why raw REST APIs are insufficient for ahead-of-time web-agent planning. - The utility result is the strongest evidence yet that the security/utility tradeoff for structural defenses is not one-sided: Baya beats API-enabled ReAct by 11–23 points in aggregate while being architecturally more restricted, with the ReActweb+API baseline controlling for API access. - Transparent appendix: the evaluation-harness surgery (dropped tasks, evaluator conversions), sandbox policies, and cost-estimation methodology are all documented in detail rather than hidden. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that (1) per-task compilation incurs 2.0–4.4× cost and 3.8–5.5× latency overhead vs. ReAct, with amortization via caching argued but not measured; (2) manual Trusted API construction is a one-time trusted step that must be maintained as websites evolve, and automating it securely is open (they flag that a site-exploration onboarding agent could itself be poisoned by prompt injections — a direct and honest identification of the system's weakest link); (3) compile-then-execute excludes Replan-Needed tasks where untrusted runtime content determines actions; (4) the approach depends on choosing the right task abstraction level (too low-level is brittle, too high-level hides needed information); and (5) ReAct remains preferable for highly dynamic websites, exploration-heavy tasks, and multi-site workflows. This is direct, non-minimizing treatment of limitations — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No adaptive attacker: WASP templates are fixed injection formats; the prompt-injection literature the paper itself cites (Nasr et al., "The Attacker Moves Second") shows defenses evaluated against non-adaptive attacks routinely fall to adaptive ones. For a paper whose headline is 0% ASR, the absence of an adaptive-attack analysis is the largest gap, even though the by-design argument partially insulates it. - The 0% ASR claim conflates architectural prevention with empirical observation on 84 instances; outcome manipulation is declared out of scope, but the runtime data-only LLM calls (present in 1.8% of programs) remain an untested injection surface for degrading task outcomes. - Baseline coverage of the defense space is incomplete: ceLLMate and CUA are dismissed for integration reasons, so Baya is never empirically compared against another compile-style defense; only UCM (GitLab-only) is compared, and only with one quarantined-model configuration. - The dropped 42 "bad or impossible" tasks and 31 cross-site tasks, plus the per-execution-mode evaluator credit, mean Baya is evaluated on a task distribution its authors helped curate; no result on the unmodified WebArena Verified suite is reported. - Utility differences of 2.4 points (GPT-5.6-Luna aggregate) are within plausible sampling noise, yet the paper counts "highest aggregate utility with all three models" as a uniform win without statistical testing. - The claim that compilation cost "narrows or even reverses" under recurring workloads is asserted via citation to prior work, never measured. Bottom Line: A practitioner building or securing web agents should read this — it is the most convincing published case that compile-then-execute dominates ReAct on both security and utility when a complete trusted API exists, while the honest treatment of the manual-API-construction bottleneck tells you exactly what must be solved (secure automated site onboarding) before this paradigm leaves the benchmark.

Routed Continual Learning

Michael Philip, Mahesh Balakrishnan, David Geraghty, David Mao, Vidhya Venkat, Ilya Mironov · arxiv.org · 🥇Top AI Papers of the Week
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Routed Continual Learning (Routed CL), an architecture in which an LLM-based router, before each agentic run, jointly selects a memory system from a fixed five-system library and a stateful cluster of prior trajectories, and demonstrates that this improves normalized reward and cost over globally shared and routed-only ICL baselines on an interleaved benchmark stream. - Why it's important: Enterprise-scale agent fleets repeatedly encounter related problems but no single memory representation works everywhere, and a naively shared history becomes expensive and mixes irrelevant experience — the paper reports 65–72% API-cost savings versus Global ICL alongside higher reward, addressing a real deployment cost/performance pain point. - How it does it: A prompted (not trained) LLM router reads only the visible prompt, memory-system descriptions, and cluster summaries, and either reuses a cluster or creates one backed by one of five frozen memory systems (ICL, adapted ReasoningBank, and three PyMC/River-based statistical state systems); a Context Memory Adapter injects the selected cluster's state into the agent's context and updates that cluster from the trajectory. - The good: The evaluation is unusually careful — four frontier models, five matched rollouts, four staged conditions that isolate each capability, a frozen pre-registered evaluation contract, and a privileged ground-truth-assignment diagnostic showing the LLM router reproduces the expert mapping in 79% of cases (86% memory-system, 91% cluster agreement). - The missing: The five-system memory library was selected during exploratory development on the same CL-Bench tasks used for confirmation, so the headline result partly measures routing among systems hand-chosen for these tasks, and the paper tests no distribution of tasks unseen during that development; no code or weights release is stated. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone building persistent-memory or self-improving agent infrastructure — the staged-condition methodology and the finding that Global ICL collapses under task interleaving (+0.015 over stateless) are directly actionable — but skippable if you only want new memory representations, since all five are adapted from prior work.

Problem & Motivation: Agents deployed at scale encounter interleaved streams of related problems and could benefit from each other's experience, but it is unknown in advance which future problems a given experience will help with and no single memory representation works across settings. A global history preserves everything but is costly and mixes unrelated experience; one fixed compressed representation discards useful detail. The motivating example is the OpenAI cyber-capability evaluation where independently instantiated agents spontaneously built a shared message board that propagated exploit findings — the authors want such sharing to be deliberate and controlled rather than emergent. The problem targets teams running heterogeneous agent fleets (different models, different teams, no explicit cooperation) where prior experience should reduce token cost, improve reward, and prevent repeated mistakes. Key Idea: Treat continual learning as a joint routing decision over two axes — which memory system represents experience (learning mechanism) and which cluster of instances shares state (grouping) — decided online per instance by a prompted LLM with access only to the visible prompt, frozen system descriptions, and immutable cluster summaries, never task labels, raw trajectories, or rewards. The second enabling move is transparent deployment: the Context Memory Adapter intercepts the agent's prompt at standard framework hook points, injects a budget-bounded advisory derived from cluster state, and updates only the selected cluster, so agents need no modification or awareness of the memory layer. Methodology: The system has four components: (1) an LLM router making one structured-output call per instance (reuse(c) or create(m, δ)); (2) isolated stateful clusters with atomic read/update operations S_{c,t+1} = update_m(S_{c,t}, τ_t; θ_c); (3) a frozen library of five memory systems spanning three representation families — verbatim trajectories (ICL), distilled strategies (ReasoningBank, adapted with self-judged success labels and frozen local embeddings), and structured numerical state (Hierarchical Regression and Hierarchical Discrete-Event via PyMC, Persistent-Entity State via River's Bayesian regression); and (4) Context Memory Adapter, which derives cluster-specific schema bindings from a warm-up trajectory on first reuse, with deterministic validation and at most one repair attempt, and renders state as context advisories without ever acting in the environment or accessing rewards. Critical design decisions: (a) the router is prompted, never trained, and sees no labels — well justified as it prevents trivial label leakage; (b) the library was selected during exploratory development and frozen before confirmatory evaluation — reasonable protocol, but the selection happened on the same tasks later used for confirmation; (c) benchmark hardening (Sales Prediction container reset, Codebase Adaptation base-commit sanitization) closes leakage channels that historical CL-Bench runs may have exploited — well justified and honestly reported as breaking comparability with historical results. Key Results: On a 398-instance stream (301 CL-Bench instances across six tasks interleaved with 97 τ3-Bench banking instances), across four models and five matched rollouts: Routed CL achieves mean normalized reward of 0.213 (Gemini 3.7 Flash), 0.464 (GPT-5.6 Sol), 0.243 (Opus 4.7), 0.401 (Opus 5), versus Global ICL at 0.030–0.168 — a gain of 15–30% of the maximum attainable normalized reward. Estimated API cost drops 65–72% versus Global ICL (e.g., Opus 5: $316.61 vs $914.36 per rollout). Staged ablations: Global ICL adds only +0.015 mean stateless-reference gain over Stateless ICL under interleaving (versus +0.222 for Routed ICL, +0.280 for Routed CL), showing the original CL-Bench finding that naïve ICL is strongest does not survive heterogeneity. Routed ICL exceeds Global ICL by 0.117–0.241 reward points; adding memory-system selection (Routed CL vs Routed ICL) adds a further 0.002–0.076, with paired differences positive in 4/5 or 5/5 rollouts per model. Routing helps ICL but not ReasoningBank: Routed RB yields no consistent gain over Global RB and raises cost 8–29%, which the authors attribute to ReasoningBank's existing selective retrieval. The ground-truth diagnostic shows the router captures most of the achievable headroom on two models (+0.008 Opus 5, +0.014 GPT-5.6 Sol) but leaves 0.069–0.071 on the other two, concentrated on Code and Sales assignments. Baselines (Global ICL, Global/Routed ReasoningBank, Stateless ICL) are current and appropriate; scale is a standard single-benchmark scale, not a stress test. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (continual learning as joint memory-system + cluster routing) and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (the router + Context Memory Adapter architecture), plus a NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (Global ICL's collapse under heterogeneous interleaving, reversing the original CL-Bench conclusion). The individual memory systems are standard or adapted components — ICL, ReasoningBank from Ouyang et al., and statistical runtimes built on PyMC and River — so the genuine novelty is the routing layer over them and the clustered state partitioning, not the representations themselves; the closest prior (Eevee, ACE, Dynamic Cheatsheet) either routes prompts or maintains a single accumulated context rather than selecting among heterogeneous memory systems and partitions. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are effectively built into the staged-condition design (Stateless → Global ICL → Routed ICL → Routed CL isolates persistence, partitioning, and mechanism selection; Global RB vs Routed RB isolates routing on a fixed system). Variability is reported as mean with [min, max] ranges across five matched rollouts per model–condition, with the complete rollout (not the instance) as the unit of replication — appropriate given state coupling, but no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported, and five rollouts is thin for differences as small as 0.002 (Gemini). The evaluation contract was frozen before confirmatory runs, prompts and memory-system descriptions are reproduced verbatim in Appendix D, and cost accounting is fully specified. However, no public code, data, or artifact release is mentioned. Methodological concerns: (1) the memory-system library was selected during exploratory development on CL-Bench and then evaluated on CL-Bench — a Goodhart's Law exposure partially mitigated by freezing and by the ground-truth diagnostic, but not eliminated; (2) the ground-truth mapping itself was fixed during exploratory development, so it is a diagnostic rather than an upper bound, as the authors note; (3) costs are self-estimated from a frozen list-price schedule, not measured bills; (4) protocol hardening makes results non-comparable to historical CL-Bench numbers. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS component — a working middleware architecture, but evaluated via benchmark rollouts rather than production deployment). - Practical: Yes — everything runs on commercial LLM APIs with standard frameworks (the adapter attaches at hook points AutoGen-style frameworks already expose), plus open-source PyMC/River libraries. - Efficient: The routing itself adds one structured-output call per instance; net effect is cost-reducing — Routed CL costs 25–33% less than Routed ICL on three models and 65–72% less than Global ICL, though it costs 31–44% more than Global ReasoningBank on three models while gaining 0.189–0.358 reward. - Effective: The evidence shows improved reward and cost on the constructed interleaved benchmark, which is a good but still proxy stand-in for the claimed enterprise deployment scenario; no real multi-team production evaluation is reported. - Scalable: Untested — the paper explicitly does not evaluate simultaneous cluster updates, stale reads, or cross-model state reuse, and the pathological fragmentation behavior (GPT-5.6 Sol creating 23–27 τ3-Bench clusters, Opus 4.7 creating 86 in one rollout) suggests router behavior may degrade unpredictably as streams grow; the multi-cluster read/update extensions proposed as future work would raise further cost questions. The work delivers a described architecture and protocol but, per the available text, stops at paper form — no released library, CLI, dataset, or trained model is stated. Strengths: - The staged-condition experimental design is the paper's best asset: it cleanly attributes the headline gain to its three components (persistence contributes little under interleaving, clustering contributes most, mechanism selection contributes a smaller task-specific increment), rather than only reporting an end-to-end number. - The honest negative/nuanced findings raise credibility: routing helps ICL but not ReasoningBank (with a plausible explanation), the router leaves model-dependent headroom relative to ground-truth assignment, and the paper quantifies router agreement with expert assignment (86%/91%/79%) instead of only reporting end-task reward. - Benchmark hygiene is above average: the authors discovered and closed two leakage channels in the released CL-Bench runtime (persistent Sales workspace; Git database and pre-applied test patches in Codebase Adaptation) and explicitly flag that their numbers are therefore not comparable to historical runs. - The transparent-deployment constraint (prompt interception via existing framework hooks, no agent cooperation, no reward access, schema-bounded adapters with deterministic validation) is a genuinely deployable design rather than a benchmark-only construction. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that experiments are sequential (one instance at a time), that each rollout uses one model for all model-mediated roles, and that concurrent updates, stale reads, and cross-model cluster reuse are not evaluated, deferring distributed-deployment questions to future work (Conclusion). They acknowledge the memory-system library is "examples rather than a canonical taxonomy" and that the library and ground-truth mapping were fixed during exploratory development, testing selection within the library rather than synthesis of new families. They acknowledge benchmark modifications make results non-comparable to historical CL-Bench scores, and the Ethics Statement directly confronts the dual-use risk that pooled agent experience can create collective capabilities (citing the OpenAI incident) plus information-propagation hazards. These are confronted directly rather than minimized — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The core circularity the authors underplay: each of the three numerical memory systems maps almost one-to-one onto a specific benchmark task in the ground-truth mapping (HR→Sales, HDE→Cohort, PES→Spectrum), and the library was chosen during exploratory development on these same tasks. The "memory-system selection adds gains" conclusion therefore partly measures whether the router can recognize which bespoke system was built for which task — generalization to a genuinely new task distribution is untested. - Five rollouts with min/max ranges but no statistical testing cannot support the smallest headline claim: Gemini's +0.002 Routed CL-vs-Routed ICL difference is within noise, and even the 0.034–0.076 differences rest on five paired observations. - The fragmentation failure mode (23–86 clusters for τ3-Bench by two models) is reported descriptively but its reward impact is never attributed, and no mechanism (e.g., cluster merging, count regularization) is proposed — a real deployment hazard left unaddressed. - The single-cluster read/single-cluster update design means an instance relevant to multiple domains cannot draw on multiple memories; the authors mention multi-cluster access only as future work, but this is an architectural limit on the central claim of handling heterogeneous streams. - No comparison against simpler hybrid baselines, e.g., a heuristic classifier on prompt embeddings, or Dynamic Cheatsheet/ACE with partitioning — the routed-vs-global comparison is run only for ICL and ReasoningBank, so the full library's advantage over cheaper adaptive-context alternatives is not fully isolated. - No released code or harness, despite the paper's value hinging on a specific protocol (stream interleaving seeds, adapter validation, hardened environments) that others cannot currently reproduce. Bottom Line: A practitioner building agent memory infrastructure should read this for its rigorous staged attribution and the counterintuitive Global-ICL-collapse finding, but should treat the absolute numbers as benchmark-internal — the stronger alternative coverage on memory representations lives in the underlying ReasoningBank/ACE literature, and the routing idea here will need validation beyond a library co-designed with the evaluation tasks before it can be trusted generally.

Problem & Motivation: LLMs process every context token through the same attention mechanism with no token-level distinction between executable instructions, passive data, and auxiliary context. Practitioners building RAG pipelines and tool-using agents inherit three concrete failure modes: indirect prompt injection (adversarial instructions planted in retrieved documents or tool results), ambiguous binding when multiple instructions coexist ("execute the second task"), and unreliable execution control. Current instruction tuning teaches instruction-following implicitly via position and chat-template conventions, so a model has no principled way to decide which of several candidate instructions carries authority. The gap this closes is a training-time, token-level privilege-separation mechanism that survives contact with real agentic data flows. Key Idea: Make privilege a property of an explicit pointer binding rather than of position or role name: every span is wrapped in a typed block with a unique identifier using six reserved single tokens from a disjoint vocabulary region (so structure cannot be forged by subword composition of ordinary content), execution is permitted only through an exec block that references a specific instruction and data identifier, and training data is deliberately polluted with unreferenced competing instructions so that models keying on surface cues are penalized by the loss. The invariant learned: content reached through exec.instruction is authoritative; content reached through exec.input is material to read, never to execute. Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) Data construction: an automated serializer converts general instruction (3.25M single-turn + 59k multi-turn), RAG (27k + 8k), and tool-calling corpora (451k + 251k) into LLMON format — 4.4M examples, 4.6B tokens — plus distractor-augmented variants of Alpaca/Dolly (67k base examples expanded to 133k variants, sampled over d∈{1,2,3} distractor instructions and m∈{0,1,2,3} irrelevant data segments) and 130k prompt-injection examples where an adversarial instruction sits in an unreferenced data block. (2) Supervised fine-tuning: the six delimiters are installed as reserved tokens by remapping unused vocabulary slots (no embedding resize), then full fine-tuning of Granite-4.1-3B-Base and 8B-Base for 3 epochs at sequence length 4096 on 8×H100 with FSDP. (3) Reinforcement learning: five sequential GRPO stages (~169k prompts, multi-domain reasoning/RLHF/math) followed by a final DPO stage (β=0.1, lr 5×10⁻⁷) on ~1k on-policy preference pairs collected at agentic decision points where a tool result carries an injected instruction. Critical design decisions: reserved tokens in a disjoint vocabulary region (justified — prevents structural forgery); placing DPO last so general-capability RL cannot erode injection behavior (plausible but not ablated); 93.6% of tokens being ordinary capability data to preserve general performance (validated by the parity results). The framework is standard autoregressive language modeling with no architectural modification. Key Results: Tested at standard scale (3B and 8B base models, full fine-tuning) against author-trained Instruct chat-template baselines under matched corpora. On OPI (text-level injection), ASR drops from 100.0→0.1 (3B) and 96.3→0.02 (8B); on ASB observation-injection (agentic surface), 99.2→5.6 (3B) and 52.8→3.1 (8B). Capability parity holds: the six-category mean is unchanged at 3B (66.7→66.7) and drops 1.4 points at 8B (74.2→72.8), with math at 8B the largest regression (84.1→79.6); safety improves +8.8 (3B) and +6.2 (8B) points. Independent ARES red-teaming (~15k attack prompts, including a 20-turn Crescendo variant with DeepSeek-V3.2 attacker and GPT-OSS-120B judge) shows indirect-attack robustness rising from 2.8%→84.6% (3B) and 0.7%→79.8% (8B), but direct attacks reach only 32.7-37.1% and multi-turn 28.0-37.0%. The interpretability analysis is a notable non-result-driven finding: both models are indistinguishable through layer ~20, then sharply separate — LLMON sustains IFR of 55-89% across layers 25-38 (peaking at 89% at layer 28) while the Instruct model's largest single attention recipient on a distractor prompt is a distractor instruction (47.5%), and both models' IFR collapses at the final layer, implying the binding is a mid-to-late-stack computation. Baselines are current and reasonably strong (matched-corpora Instruct models, published 2024-2025 benchmarks), though defense baselines are absent (see Gaps). Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW METHOD with an NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING component. The genuinely novel elements are (a) carrying privilege via reserved single tokens plus identifier-based execution binding rather than in-band delimiters or role names, and (b) distractor-augmented supervision that trains referential binding under interference. Standard components applied competently: SFT→GRPO→DPO post-training pipeline, existing injection benchmarks, standard attention-weight analysis. The paper is a preprint (arXiv:2610.38120) building on a companion LLMON specification paper (Hind et al., 2026); the core idea relative to StruQ and SecAlign — which also train instruction-data boundaries — is the shift from role-based to pointer-based privilege, a real but incremental conceptual distinction that the paper does not empirically isolate. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are partial: the distractor augmentation is evaluated implicitly through the OPI/ASB/ARES results, but there is no ablation isolating the contribution of the RL/DPO stages versus SFT alone, nor of distractor augmentation versus clean LLMON data. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported; single-checkpoint results ("final-epoch") are given. The evaluation mixes the authors' own constructed distractor prompts (for the attention analysis) with two independent published benchmarks and an external red-teaming harness, which mitigates Goodhart concerns. The LLMON framework has a public repository (https://github.com/generative-computing/llmon), but no release of the 4.6B-token structured corpus or model checkpoints is stated. The Instruct baselines are author-trained rather than off-the-shelf, which is a strength for comparability but means no third-party verification. Methodological concern: the paper names StruQ, SecAlign, and spotlighting as closest related work but reports no numbers against them, so claims of advantage are argued, not measured. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (methods trained and evaluated on real benchmarks). - Practical: Yes — no architectural change, delimiters mapped to unused vocabulary slots, runs on 8×H100 for full fine-tuning of 3B/8B models; inference requires only a serializer/deserializer around standard serving. - Efficient: Modest overhead — delimiters add ~7-15% context length depending on complexity (authors acknowledge inference latency/throughput impact is unquantified); training cost is a full post-training pipeline, not a patch. - Effective: Strong evidence for the stated problem on indirect injection (three independent evaluations agree), but only a proxy for the broader goal of reliable execution control, and the learned invariant is explicitly not a guarantee (residual ASR 0.02-5.6%). - Scalable: Only 3B and 8B within one model family tested; the authors themselves flag that behavior at larger scales — where implicit instruction-following may already be stronger — is unvalidated, and the 7-15% token overhead compounds at long-document/agentic scale. The work delivers a methodology and training recipe; the LLMON notation tooling is open-source but the trained models and corpus are not stated as released. Strengths: (1) The reserved-token design choice is a real technical insight: placing structural delimiters in a disjoint vocabulary region makes the instruction-data boundary non-forgeable by content, addressing a specific weakness of in-band delimiter defenses. (2) Distractor augmentation is a well-conceived training objective — it converts the defense from "refuse suspicious text" (gameable) into "resolve a pointer" (structural), and the loss directly penalizes surface-cue heuristics. (3) The interpretability contribution (IFR/DAS/LEAK per-layer metrics) goes beyond benchmark numbers and yields a falsifiable mechanistic picture — the binding lives at layers 22-38, both models behave identically below layer 20, and IFR collapses at the final layer for both — which is the kind of analysis most defense papers omit. (4) Evaluation triangulation across two published benchmarks plus an external red-teaming harness with a different metric convention, replicated at two scales, is above the norm for security-training papers. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly and at length, which strengthens credibility: (i) single model family (Granite-4.1) at two scales, transfer to other architectures/corpora and larger scales unvalidated; (ii) 7-15% context-length overhead from delimiters with inference latency/throughput unquantified; (iii) the privilege invariant does not protect against direct or multi-turn attacks (robustness only 32-37% and 28-37%), and the defense is a learned behavior, not an enforced guarantee, so it should be one layer in a defense-in-depth stack; (iv) predominantly English training corpus with uncharacterized behavior on morphologically rich languages and very long documents; (v) the attention metrics establish correlation, not causation, and attention weights are an imperfect proxy for information flow. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No quantitative comparison against StruQ, SecAlign, or spotlighting despite these being identified as the closest training-time defenses — the reader cannot tell whether pointer-based privilege beats role-based structured queries by the margins the paper implies. (2) The RL/DPO stages are not ablated: it is unknown how much of the 0.02-5.6% residual ASR comes from the 130k injection-training examples and DPO pairs versus the LLMON structure itself, so the headline claim "explicit execution semantics can be taught through structure" is confounded with injection-specific preference data. (3) The attention metrics are analyzed only on the 3B pair and on author-constructed distractor prompts, not on the OPI/ASB attack distributions, so the mechanistic story is not tied to the attack results. (4) Robustness is measured against known attack taxonomies; adaptive attacks that deliberately mimic LLMON formatting (e.g., emitting reserved-token-like sequences or forging identifier references in content) are untested, and the disjoint-vocabulary argument is asserted rather than stress-tested. (5) The 1.4-point capability loss at 8B (concentrated in math, 84.1→79.6) deserves analysis given the paper's parity framing; no seeds/variance are reported to confirm it is not noise. Bottom Line: A practitioner building injection-resistant LLM agents gains a concrete, well-evidenced training recipe and a useful set of attention diagnostics from this paper, but the absence of head-to-head numbers against StruQ/SecAlign and an un-ablated RL stage mean it should be read as a strong existence proof that structural privilege can be trained in — not yet as the established best defense.

Chin-Yang Lin, Ryo Hachiuma, Jaesung Choe, Min-Hung Chen, Yu-Chiang Frank Wang, Yen-Yu Lin, Wei-Chen Chiu, Yu-Lun Liu, Cheng Sun · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 13 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Test-Time Baking (TTB), a modification of Test-Time-Training (TTT) layers that bakes cross-view attention outputs into a fixed-size fast-weight MLP, so a decoder-only view synthesis model renders novel views at constant per-token complexity instead of attending to a linearly growing KV-cache. - Why it's important: Decoder-only Large View Synthesis Models (LVSMs) achieve top quality but render at 1 FPS with 64 input views at 960p because per-token attention cost grows with context size, making dense-view, high-resolution rendering impractical for interactive use. - How it does it: The inner-loop objective of the TTT fast-weight MLP is retargeted from raw value tokens to the output of cross-view attention (so the MLP learns from attention rather than replacing it), plus a "context pair" that disentangles each context view into a camera-only rendering token (MLP input) and an RGB-carrying ground-truth token (mapping target) to fix a reconstruction-vs-rendering modality mismatch. - The good: The full ablation ladder (Table 4) shows each of the three components — context pairing, MSE inner-loop loss with T=3 steps, and cross-view-attention target — contributes measurably, and the stack reaches 30.20–31.33 PSNR on DL3DV with 64 views at a constant 23 FPS, versus DVSM's 31.11 PSNR at 1 FPS and LaCT's 28.30 PSNR at 10 FPS. - The missing: No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported, the headline ablations run at a reduced setting (patch 16, 720p, 8 GPUs) while main tables use patch 8 at 960p, and no code or model release is stated beyond a project page — plus the method is initialized from the DVSM checkpoint it benchmarks against. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on feed-forward novel view synthesis or amortized/linear attention architectures — the "bake attention outputs into fast weights instead of replacing attention" idea is transferable and well-evidenced here; skip it if you only care about sparse-view or generative view synthesis, where the gains are marginal or out of scope.

Scored using Empirical profile. Problem & Motivation: The paper addresses rendering-cost scaling in decoder-only LVSMs for novel-view synthesis. Decoder-only LVSM (Jin et al., ICLR'25) and DVSM prefill context views into a KV-cache; rendering each novel-view token attends to this cache, so per-token cost grows linearly with the number of context views and cached tokens. With 64 context views at 960p, DVSM renders at 1 FPS — unusable for interactive viewing. LaCT (ICLR'26) replaces cross-view attention with TTT layers to get constant-complexity rendering but drops quality substantially (28.30 vs 31.11 PSNR on DL3DV-64v); naive initialization from pretrained decoder-only weights does not close this gap. The practitioners affected are anyone deploying feed-forward view synthesis at high resolution or dense view counts. The gap TTB targets: constant-complexity rendering without LaCT's quality sacrifice. Key Idea: Repurpose the TTT fast-weight MLP's inner-loop optimization as an explicit distillation of cross-view attention: instead of learning to map keys to values (a linear-attention surrogate that replaces attention), the MLP is trained per-scene, at test time, to map camera-ray-only context tokens to the cross-view attention output of the corresponding RGB-carrying tokens. Attention is therefore retained at reconstruction time (where cost is paid once per scene) and amortized away at rendering time. A second insight is the reconstruction/rendering modality misalignment — the fast-weight MLP is written with image-bearing tokens but read with camera-only novel-view tokens — resolved by duplicating each context view into a camera-only "rendering" token (input) and an RGB "ground-truth" token (target), so the baked MLP never has to generalize across input modalities. The authors also frame the inner loop as few-step light-field optimization in latent space, which motivates a convergence-oriented MSE objective over LaCT's one-shot dot-product write. Methodology: The model builds on DVSM: L=12 decoder blocks, 768 latent channels, patch size 8, each block being Intra-view Attention → FFN → TTB layer → FFN, initialized from the DVSM checkpoint with zero-init on the TTB output projection. Inputs are Plücker ray maps patch-embedded; context tokens additionally patch-embed RGB. At each TTB layer, a fast-weight SwiGLU-MLP (4× expansion, shared QK projection, L2-unit-normalized) is optimized for T=3 inner steps with the Muon optimizer (5 Newton–Schulz iterations, weight-normalized) and a predicted per-token learning rate (base 0.01, softplus-parameterized), minimizing MSE between f_θ(W_k X_ctx-rend) and W_v(CrossAttn(X_ctx-gt) − X_ctx-rend) — i.e., residual learning. The baked MLP then updates three token streams (ctx-gt with feedback, ctx-rend, and later novel-view tokens). Rendering replaces cross-attention with a single MLP feed-forward per token: O(1) per token. Outer-loop training backpropagates the rendering loss (MSE + 0.2·perceptual) through all T inner steps exactly (no first-order approximation), with two layers of gradient checkpointing to fit 64-A100 training at 960p. A curriculum trains at 340p (100K iters) then finetunes at 480p/720p/960p (10K iters each) on DL3DV-10K. Critical design decisions: (1) retargeting the inner loop to attention output — well justified by ablation (+0.62 PSNR over context-paired TTT alone) and by a gradient-saliency analysis showing the baked MLP gains a wider effective view field; (2) context pairing — justified by t-SNE modality alignment plots and ablation (+0.66 PSNR); (3) a heuristic local-duplicate inference (k-means on camera poses, K=V/16 groups, B=16 views/group, hard routing) to overcome fixed MLP capacity — effective empirically but admittedly not learned. Key Results: On DL3DV (140 held-out scenes) at 960p with 64 input views: TTB reaches 30.20/0.897/0.131 PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS at 23 FPS and 65s prefill, versus DVSM at 31.11/0.920/0.104 at 1 FPS and 60s, and LaCT at 28.30/0.857/0.169 at 10 FPS. The local-duplicate variant reaches 31.33/0.919/0.108 — matching DVSM quality at 23× the FPS. At 16 views, TTB 27.00 vs DVSM 26.86 PSNR (TTB actually wins) at 23 vs 4 FPS. Zero-shot in-the-wild (MipNeRF360, Free, Hike) at 64 views, the duplicate variant outperforms DVSM on all three datasets (e.g., 25.05 vs 24.76 PSNR on MipNeRF360) at 23× FPS. Against LagerNVS (1B+ params, VGGT-based), TTB wins by 3–9 PSNR points with 3.1–9.5× faster rendering in the 512px setting. A scaling test to V=256 shows single-MLP TTB saturating at ~25.8 PSNR while the duplicate variant reaches 27.74 vs DVSM's 27.56, with FPS holding at ~68 vs DVSM's 12.6; the baked state is 324 MB fixed versus a KV-cache that OOMs an 80GB GPU around V=256. On 2-view Re10K at 512×512, TTB reproduces DVSM cross-attention quality (31.28 vs 31.17 PSNR). Baselines are current (CVPR'26/ICLR'26/arXiv'26) and the compared DVSM/LaCT numbers are the relevant frontier. End-to-end analysis (Table 15) shows TTB overtakes DVSM in total time after only 5–7 rendered views. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (repurposing TTT fast-weight inner loops to learn from attention outputs — a genuine reframing of TTT from attention-replacement to attention-amortization) plus a NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the reconstruction/rendering modality misalignment in fast-weight prefilling and its context-pair fix). The surrounding machinery — Muon inner loop, SwiGLU MLP, per-token learning rates, DL3DV training recipe, DVSM architecture — is a competent combination of existing components (LaCT, DVSM, Muon); the novelty lives in the retargeted inner-loop objective and the context-pair construction, not in the infrastructure. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are genuinely informative: a component ladder from TTT to full TTB (Table 4), inner-loop loss/step-count sweeps (Table 5), layer-design ablations for feedback and residual targets (Table 6), pretraining ablation showing the benefit of DVSM initialization scales with how much cross-view attention is preserved (Table 13), capacity scaling over K and MLP width (Table 12), and a V=256 scaling test (Table 11). However: (1) no error bars, seeds, or significance tests anywhere; (2) ablations run at a reduced configuration (8 GPUs, patch 16, 720p truncation) while headline tables use the full configuration — the interaction between setting and conclusions is acknowledged but not quantified; (3) the main model is trained on DL3DV and the primary evaluation is DL3DV, so in-domain evaluation dominates, though zero-shot MipNeRF360/Free/Hike and a separate Re10K finetune partially mitigate this; (4) the method is warm-started from the DVSM checkpoint of the same benchmark family, and one baseline (tttLRM) similarly warm-starts — fair, but a from-scratch comparison exists only at ablation scale; (5) parameter counts differ across compared methods (163M–379M–1052M), partially controlled via reported sizes but not via matched-compute comparisons; (6) no code or weights release is stated — only a project page (https://test-time-baking.github.io) with videos and an HTML viewer. Efficiency numbers are self-reported on the authors' hardware, as is standard. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a trained model and rendering pipeline evaluated on benchmarks, with an inference-time routing heuristic). - Practical: Yes — runs on A100-class GPUs (peak 18–23 GB inference memory at 960p, V=32), i.e., commercially available hardware; the compact fixed-size scene state (324 MB) is a genuine deployment advantage over KV-caches that OOM 80GB cards at V=256. - Efficient: Rendering is cheap (23 FPS at 960p vs DVSM's 1 FPS), but reconstruction is the new bottleneck — 18s at V=32 vs DVSM's 15s and LaCT's 3.7s — and training is expensive (64 A100s, 76 GB/it peak memory); the TTB−− linear-target variant trades ~0.8 PSNR for linear-time reconstruction. - Effective: The evidence shows it solves the stated problem (DVSM-level quality at constant rendering complexity) on in-domain and zero-shot benchmarks, though quality at V=64 requires the duplicate heuristic to fully match DVSM. - Scalable: Tested to V=256 with the duplicate variant (quality tracks DVSM, FPS constant at ~68), which is a real stress test, not just a claim; but the k-means routing is a train-time-untested heuristic, quality depends on a fixed per-group budget of B=16 found empirically, and behavior under highly non-uniform camera distributions is unexamined. The work delivers a trained model and inference procedure described in detail (pseudocode, hyperparameters, grouping algorithm) but no stated code/weights release; it stops at paper plus project page form. Strengths: - The central reframing — supervise the TTT fast-weight MLP on attention outputs rather than replacing attention — is a clean, generalizable idea, supported mechanistically by the gradient-saliency analysis (Fig. 4) showing the baked MLP acquires a wider effective view field, and structurally by the pretraining ablation (Table 13) showing preservation of cross-view attention is what makes DVSM weight reuse work. - The modality-misalignment diagnosis and context-pair fix are a genuine empirical finding about fast-weight prefilling in two-stream decoders; the t-SNE alignment evidence and the +0.66 PSNR ablation independently support it. - The efficiency analysis is unusually honest and thorough: end-to-end break-even at 5–7 views (Table 15), scene-state memory scaling with explicit OOM extrapolation for the baseline (Fig. 7), and a real V=256 stress test rather than an assumed scaling claim. - The ablation ladder is additive and complete — a reader can reconstruct exactly which design decision buys which PSNR, which is rare in this subfield. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state three: (1) fixed fast-weight MLP capacity causes quality saturation at large V, and the local-duplicate mitigation is a heuristic with learned routing left to future work; (2) inner-loop cross-view attention makes reconstruction quadratic in V, a drawback for single-shot/low-view-count use; (3) TTB is a reconstruction (interpolation) model, not generative — it cannot extrapolate to unobserved viewpoints. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section, a credibility positive. The supplementary further concedes that duplicate inference was designed post-hoc and not trained for. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No variance reporting: every PSNR delta the narrative rests on (e.g., 30.20 vs 31.11, or 27.00 vs 26.86 at 16 views) is within a range where seed variance could plausibly matter, and none is tested for significance. - The claim of being "on par with state-of-the-art" at 64 views holds only via the duplicate variant (31.33 vs 31.11); the plain single-MLP model is 0.9 PSNR behind DVSM, and the duplicate variant's hard, unsmoothed routing between independently reconstructed groups could show artifacts the aggregate PSNR metrics do not capture. - Ablation-setting versus main-setting discrepancy (patch 16/720p/8-GPU ablations, patch 8/960p main results) means the component contributions may not transfer quantitatively to the deployed configuration. - The 16-view in-domain win over DVSM (27.00 vs 26.86) sits inside the noise band, yet TTB−− (no cross-view attention at all) is heavily advocated as a practical variant without the same depth of evaluation as full TTB. - The light-field/latent-optimization framing is a motivating analogy, not a tested hypothesis — no experiment isolates the claimed convergence behavior of the inner loop beyond the T-vs-loss ablation. - Beyond view synthesis, the broader-impact claims (long-context LMs, world models, streaming 3D perception) are pure extrapolation with no supporting experiment. - No code/weights release is stated, which limits reproduction of the many interacting hyperparameters (Muon inner loop, per-token LR heads, zero-init, checkpointing scheme). Bottom Line: For anyone building feed-forward view synthesis systems or amortized-attention architectures, this is worth reading — the bake-attention-into-fast-weights idea is simple, well-ablated, and demonstrably closes a quality–speed gap that TTT-style replacement could not, though the absence of a code release, error bars, and significance testing means the tightest numbers deserve independent verification before adoption.

#87 — Innovative (66)

Autonomous Space Systems via Reinforcement Learning: Review, Challenges, and Future Directions

M Ramezani, MA Alandihallaj · preprints.org · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR:** - What it does: This paper presents a systematic review of reinforcement learning for spacecraft guidance, navigation, control, and mission autonomy across eleven application categories (253 retained works), with a uniform framework for extracting quantitative results, baselines, and validation fidelity, and concludes with a gap analysis, four proposed benchmark problems, and a staged flight-qualification pathway. - Why it's important: Space missions (pinpoint landing, cislunar operations, servicing, constellations) increasingly require onboard autonomous decision-making under uncertainty where classical optimal control and MPC are expensive, brittle, or cannot run onboard, and the field's published claims are riddled with incomparable metrics, weak baselines, and confusion between in-distribution robustness and true generalization — decisions worth hundreds of millions of dollars per mission ride on this evidence. - How it does it: The authors assemble the corpus via seed-plus-snowball search of 2018–2026 literature and impose a common comparison framework: seven metric families (terminal accuracy, optimality gap, robustness, training cost, inference cost, safety, statistical hygiene) and a two-axis, five-level validation-fidelity ladder separating dynamics fidelity from physical-testbed fidelity, applied row-by-row in per-category comparison tables. - The good: The cross-cutting synthesis (Section 14) tabulates all seventeen head-to-head RL-vs-classical comparisons with numbers on both sides and shows a consistent, metric-organized pattern — RL wins on distributional/off-nominal metrics (4 of 5) and loses on nominal optimality against converged references (0 of 5) — plus a quantified optimality-robustness trade (1–10% penalty in well-conditioned problems, two- to fivefold in chaotic dynamics) that no single primary paper states. - The missing: Only 31 of 253 retained works reach validation level L2 or above, and the review itself identifies that the corpus's most valuable validation cells (independent high-fidelity dynamics on a physical testbed; processor-in-the-loop with a real navigation filter) are essentially unoccupied, so the strongest conclusions about flight-worthiness rest on two flight demonstrations (InnoCube, Astrobee) and a thin intermediate evidence chain. - Read it or not: Essential reading for GNC engineers, mission autonomy researchers, and program managers deciding whether to fund or fly learned controllers; skippable for RL methodologists seeking new algorithms, since the review synthesizes rather than invents techniques.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. The two-axis validation-fidelity ladder and the metric-organized 17-comparison synthesis are genuine methodological contributions (Novelty 60, Non-Obviousness 65), and the no-imputation protocol plus candid publication-bias discussion give Completeness (75) unusual strength for a survey. The composite is pulled down by Rigor (68) — no inter-rater reliability for the 253-work classification and an undisclosed self-citation concentration — and by Practical Impact (55), since the benchmark problems and reporting standards are proposals, not released artifacts. Weighted composite: 0.20*60 + 0.25*68 + 0.15*65 + 0.15*75 + 0.15*68 + 0.10*55 = 66.

Problem & Motivation: Space-systems practitioners face a widening autonomy gap: landing-accuracy requirements have tightened from tens of kilometers to 10–100 m pinpoint landing; small-body missions spend months characterizing unknown gravity fields before close proximity operations; constellations of hundreds to thousands of satellites and on-orbit servicing both demand onboard decisions under communication delays of up to ~24 minutes one-way to Mars. Classical tools each carry structural limitations — trajectory optimization yields a single untracked trajectory with unbounded onboard run times, Lyapunov laws like the Q-law are sub-optimal and weight-sensitive, MPC is only as good as its predictive model, and robust adaptive control covers restricted uncertainty classes. RL shifts design effort to reward and simulator specification, moves computation offline, and yields fixed-cost closed-loop policies, but the field's evidence is fragmented: prior surveys (Izzo 2019, Tipaldi 2022, Habib 2022) tabulated frameworks without extracting quantitative results, recording baselines, or grading validation fidelity, so cross-paper comparison was impossible. Since 2022, hardware evidence has appeared (the InnoCube 3U in-orbit RL attitude demonstration in 2025, NASA Astrobee RL maneuvers on the ISS, air-bearing and cyber-physical testbeds), the algorithm palette widened (meta-RL, transformers, Mamba, multi-agent, LLM agents), safety became a subfield (run-time assurance, CBF filters, formal verification, AFRL STARS), and the study count crossed the threshold where cross-comparison yields conclusions no single paper states. Key Idea: The core contribution is not an algorithm but a measurement discipline: a two-axis validation-fidelity ladder (dynamics fidelity E0–E3 × physical fidelity P0–P3) and a seven-metric comparison framework applied uniformly to 253 works, which turns a scattered literature into a structured answer to the question 'when does learned control beat classical control, on which metrics, at what cost, and with what evidence quality?' A secondary, repeatedly-validated technical insight extracted from the corpus: confining learning to the parameters of a classical law (RL-parameterized Q-law weights, learned ZEM/ZEV gains, deep guidance over a conventional inner loop, MPC-shaped rewards) is the most successful design pattern, appearing independently in five categories and yielding stability inheritance at no extra cost. Methodology: The review follows a three-stage systematic protocol: (1) seed set from the reference list of the prior RL-specific survey (Tipaldi et al. 2022); (2) structured queries combining RL terms, platform terms, and application/method terms across principal journals, AIAA/AAS/IAC/IEEE conferences, and arXiv/NTRS, covering 2018–2026 with emphasis on 2022–2026, search closed July 2026; (3) forward and backward snowballing. Inclusion requires application of RL (or a directly-compared learning method) to a space control problem, at least one performance measure, and archival availability; duplicate conference/journal pairs are merged. Per-work extraction covers dynamics model, observation/action spaces, reward, algorithm, training budget, baselines, headline results with units, uncertainty models, Monte Carlo sample sizes, inference cost, and validation level, with an explicit no-imputation rule and a reported/not-recoverable distinction. The comparison framework defines seven metric families (M1 terminal accuracy, M2 optimality gap, M3 robustness via Monte Carlo, M4 training cost, M5 inference cost, M6 safety, M7 statistical hygiene). The five-level validation ladder (L0 idealized simulation to L4 flight) is explicitly softened into a two-axis E/P classification. Key design decisions: (a) refusing to impute or rescale numbers — well justified, since the frequent absence of comparable quantities is itself reported as a finding; (b) treating classical optimal control and MPC as baselines rather than subjects — appropriate to the framing; (c) classifying outcomes by metric type rather than application domain — an analytic choice that produces the review's most transferable conclusion, though the authors candidly note it is a hypothesis from ~12 studies, not a measured fact. Key Results: The review reports synthesis, not new experiments; headline extracted results include: (1) Of 253 retained works, 181 report a numerical result, 132 an explicit baseline, and only 31 reach validation level L2 or above; RPO (C8) is the strongest category with 11 of 38 at L2+, while low-thrust transfer, interplanetary, and surface mobility have zero at L2+. (2) The seventeen head-to-head comparisons with numbers on both sides split six RL wins, six classical wins, five splits, organized by metric type: RL wins 4 of 5 distributional/off-nominal comparisons, loses 5 of 5 nominal-optimality comparisons, wins both in-distribution combinatorial comparisons. (3) Quantified trade examples: attitude tracking — tuned quaternion-rate-feedback is ~8× better on mean error (0.0087° vs 0.073°) while RL is better in the tail on harder trajectories; attitude under 10–1000 kg mass variation — RL final error 4.53 ± 1.21° vs PID 6.77 ± 16.75° (14× lower dispersion); cislunar transfer — PPO uses 2.2–5.1× more propellant than GPOPS-II but converges under 10× navigation error in milliseconds; halo station-keeping — +2.9% Δv over 10.3 years, ~10% worse head-to-head but a single forward pass; G&CNETs — behavioral cloning converges in 48.9% of 16 perturbation cells vs 95.9% for RL; ADR planning — PPO visits 29.1 debris in-distribution vs MCTS 27.1, but collapses to 3.2 (8.1 with domain randomization) vs MCTS 15.0 when Δv budget is cut to a third. (4) Flight evidence: LeLaR on InnoCube met 1° pointing in 7/7 maneuvers vs 3/7 for the flight PD controller, with a 105 kB policy at 38 ms on a 40 MHz microcontroller; APIARY flew the first RL-controlled free-flyer maneuvers on the ISS. (5) Strongest scheduling result: a two-phase encoder-decoder + heuristic hybrid beats adaptive large-neighborhood search by >16% profit at 1200 tasks using <3% of its computation time. Baselines used are largely current and strong where the review demands them (converged indirect/collocation references, MPC, flight-heritage controllers), and the review explicitly flags categories where they are weak (Q-law/heuristic-only comparisons in low-thrust transfer; missing modern convex powered-descent baselines in EDL). Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (the metric-organized structure of RL-vs-classical outcomes and the quantified optimality-robustness trade across domains) plus NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK in proposal form (four proposed benchmark problems, a reporting standard, and the fidelity ladder as reusable methodology). What is genuinely novel is the systematic extraction of quantitative results with attached baselines and validation grades, and the cross-cutting finding that outcomes partition by metric type, not application domain; the underlying component techniques (systematic review, MDP formalism, PPO-dominated applications) are standard, and the review's own strongest technical claims are syntheses of primary results by other groups (Izzo, Gaudet/Furfaro, Zavoli/Federici, STARS). Rigor & Reproducibility: The review methodology is unusually well documented for a survey: explicit three-stage search with stated closure date (July 2026), inclusion criteria, per-work extraction schema, a no-imputation rule, and a reported/not-recoverable distinction. Ablation-equivalent evidence exists at the corpus level (the two-axis validation table showing which evidence cells the field never occupies; the formulation-vs-algorithm finding that four PPO configurations of the same docking problem span 0.1% to 99.3% success). The authors confront their own limitations directly: 17 comparisons from ~12 studies is a small, partly self-overlapping sample; classification of 'split' verdicts is a judgment call; coverage of Chinese-language literature is partial; publication bias means aggregate RL-wins statements should be read as upper bounds; and the metric-type partition is stated as a hypothesis, not a measured fact. Counts are self-declared as the authors' classification and 'indicative'. No code or dataset artifact accompanies the review itself (the proposed benchmark problems are future work); the review does point to existing reusable infrastructure (BSK-RL, OrbitZoo, STARS challenge problems, KSPDG). One methodological caution: several of the most heavily cited primary studies in the synthesis (Ramezani et al. [18, 21, 32, 90, 91, 115]) are from the first author's own group, an unflagged self-citation concentration. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a synthesis/survey with no primary experiments; assessed on the evidence it aggregates). - Practical: Yes — the reviewed policies are small MLPs (2–4 layers, 64–400 units); the flight-proven cases run in ~38 ms on a 40 MHz microcontroller and under 2 ms on rad-hard processors at 10 Hz loops. - Efficient: Inference cost is consistently low (sub-millisecond to tens of milliseconds); the cost burden sits in training (e.g., 5×10⁸ steps per sub-network for LeLaR, 10,000 parallel environments for Astrobee, GPU clusters) and in simulator throughput, which one study showed is the binding constraint rather than algorithm choice. - Effective: The evidence shows RL solves off-nominal and distributional robustness problems and mission-scheduling speed problems, but does not show nominal optimality (0 of 5 against converged references), and the review insists both sides be reported; out-of-distribution performance is negative in the clearest test. - Scalable: Not tested at 10–100× in most categories; the review documents that scaling claims are largely untested, with the debris-planning OOD collapse and the absence of hardware validation for multi-agent and robotic policies as the concrete limits. The work delivers no software artifact of its own; it stops at paper form, proposing (not releasing) benchmark problems, reporting standards, and a flight-qualification pathway. Strengths: - The two-axis validation-fidelity classification (dynamics fidelity × physical fidelity) is a genuine methodological contribution that exposes a structural blind spot: the corpus almost never occupies the cells (E2,P2) and (E2,P1) that would most strengthen flight claims, and the review correctly notes an air-bearing result and a high-fidelity Monte Carlo result measure different things and are not rankable on one axis. - Table 14.2 — every head-to-head comparison in the corpus with numbers on both sides, classified by metric type — is the kind of synthesis no prior survey attempted, and it yields a decision-relevant corollary: reporting only nominal optimality understates RL, reporting only robustness overstates it, and fewer than a dozen studies report both. - The review consistently records comparisons where learned control loses (QRF's 8× mean-error advantage, the 5.1× cislunar propellant penalty, the MCTS OOD win), which counters the field's publication bias rather than amplifying it. - The identification and cross-category validation of the 'confine learning to the parameters of a classical law' pattern (Q-law weights, ZEM/ZEV gains, deep guidance over inner loops, MPC-shaped rewards, learned sequencing + heuristic allocation) is a non-obvious, actionable architectural insight, and the review correctly ties it to the only clean stability argument in the corpus. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state: partial coverage of non-English (particularly Chinese-language) literature; results locked behind paywalls; strong publication bias making aggregate RL-wins claims upper bounds; category counts as indicative self-classifications; the small, overlapping, partly single-group sample behind the 17-comparison partition; the 'split' verdict being a judgment; the partition being a hypothesis not a measured fact; the absence of any formal stability certificate for a trained attitude policy on a nonlinear plant with actuator dynamics; the single-CubeSat empirical base for flight claims; no common powered-descent benchmark; no study with a realistic navigation filter; and no RL results for aerocapture (with the caveat that this is a limit of the search protocol, not a proof of absence). This is unusually direct limitation disclosure — a strong credibility signal; the one weakness they minimize is the concentration of cited evidence from their own group. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No statement of screening or data-extraction reliability (e.g., double review, inter-rater agreement), so the 'authors' classification' of 253 works into categories and fidelity levels is unverifiable. - The self-citation concentration (at least six heavily-weighted primary studies in Tables 3.1, 10.1, 11.1, 13.1 are Ramezani et al.) is never disclosed as a potential conflict in the synthesis, despite the review's own insistence on baseline transparency. - The review does not quantify inter-rater or cross-study comparability of its M1–M7 metrics; 'optimality gap' percentages are drawn from different objectives (quadratic cost, time, final mass, Δv) and the authors acknowledge these are not equivalent, but they still aggregate them into an ordered '1–10% vs two- to fivefold' summary. - The proposed benchmark problems, reporting standard, and flight-qualification pathway are asserted as contributions (contribution items 5–6) but the excerpted text does not evaluate them or provide the artifacts, so their practical value is unproven by the review itself. - Confidence in 2026-dated primary results (InnoCube details, Astrobee, Mamba-based proximity control) rests on preprint and recent-contract literature that has not had time for independent replication. Bottom Line: This is the most rigorous synthesis available of RL for spacecraft control and the first that a reviewer or flight-qualification board can actually trust to compare claims across categories — any practitioner deciding where learned control belongs in a GNC architecture should read it, and no existing survey covers the same ground with baseline-and-fidelity discipline; but it is a hypothesis-generating review whose most important products (benchmarks, reporting standards, qualification pathway) remain proposals rather than artifacts.

Adaptive reinforcement learning-driven personalized training plan generation and effect evaluation for college students' physical fitness tests

Q Zhou, J Gao · nature.com · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds an offline reinforcement learning system (improved PPO with adaptive state representation, four-component deficit-driven reward, and prioritized replay) that generates weekly personalized training plans for Chinese college students against the National Student Physical Health Standard, and evaluates it in a 16-week randomized field study. - Why it's important: Mandated uniform fitness curricula in China produce marginal gains for most students and overload risk for the least fit; instructors lack practical tools to individualize prescriptions for classes of 40+ students. - How it does it: The core move is treating historical student records as an offline decision problem: a validated student-response simulator supplies state transitions, actions outside the teaching policy's support are filtered by a density-ratio bound, and reward components are re-weighted by softmax over each objective's running deficit. - The good: The evaluation discipline is unusually strong for this literature — student-level cross-validation folds, a simulator-free fitted-Q cross-check (12.9% vs the simulator's 14.6% gain), ten seeds, prespecified mixed-model analysis of a 312-participant randomized trial (adjusted between-arm effect 4.71 points, 95% CI 3.92–5.50). - The missing: All offline results are mediated by a learned response model whose extrapolation error cannot be fully bounded, the field study was not prospectively registered, and 16 weeks cannot speak to retention or multi-site generalization. - Read it or not: Worth reading for applied RL researchers and educational-data-mining practitioners who want a template for honest offline-RL-plus-randomized-trial evaluation; RL algorithm specialists can skip it since the algorithmic machinery is standard.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (80) is the standout: a 312-participant randomized trial with prespecified mixed-model analysis, 10 seeds × 5 folds offline evaluation, a fitted-Q cross-check quantifying simulator optimism, and peer review — well above the norm for applied RL. Completeness (82) benefits from self-undermining disclosures (losing to SAC on 2/10 seeds, the safety mask driving the rationality gap). The composite is held back by Novelty (45) and Non-Obviousness (48): the paper candidly disclaims algorithmic invention, and the contribution is disciplined engineering plus evaluation template. Impact (70) reflects code/data accompanying the article and demonstrated real-world effect, though only at single-institution, 16-week scale. Weighted composite: 0.20*45 + 0.25*80 + 0.15*48 + 0.15*82 + 0.15*72 + 0.10*70 = 66.
