Problem & Motivation: Chinese college students' fitness has declined for roughly two decades, yet NSPHS-mandated training remains one-size-fits-all: students two standard deviations apart in VO2max follow identical jogging programs. Instructors acknowledge the mismatch but cannot individualize for large classes. Prior personalized-prescription work is either supervised (static, one-shot prediction with no closed-loop adaptation) or small-cohort RL with narrow action spaces; none targets the constrained setting of a mandated college fitness curriculum. The paper identifies three recurring failure modes when transplanting RL into this domain: fragile adaptability under academic-calendar nonstationarity, absent longitudinal effect tracking, and collapsing multiple conflicting objectives into a single reward. Key Idea: The central insight is an offline-RL formulation that respects the ethical constraint that no agent may experiment on students: a validated student-response model (GRU encoder with per-item linear readouts and student random effects) acts as the environment simulator, and returned reward for actions absent from the logged teaching policy is estimated only within support, enforced by a density-ratio filter (threshold 0.02) plus safety action masking. Supporting tricks are (i) a two-timescale adaptive state representation — encoder weights update fast, but the policy consumes only a slowly moving average refreshed every four weeks — and (ii) a softmax-over-deficits scalarizer that dynamically re-weights four reward components (fitness gain, safety, adherence, plan rationality) toward whichever objective lags. Methodology: Five-layer closed loop: input ingestion (NSPHS scores, demographics, four-week rolling training logs aligned to weekly cadence), adaptive feature extraction (population-referenced z-scores, 8-dimensional categorical embeddings, GRU hidden state appended to a 46-dim state vector), an improved PPO decision layer with a factored policy (categorical head for training content; squashed Gaussian for continuous intensity/duration/load; discrete frequency and recovery interval), plan rendering into weekly schedules, and dual-rate feedback (per-session and biweekly reward computation). The reward is r = adaptive weighted sum of four components, each operationally specified (Table 5): clipped composite-score change /10, logistic safety term on heart-rate ratio with ceiling 0.90·HRmax, adherence = completed-session fraction × enjoyment, and a five-rule rationality score sourced from ACSM/Gabbett/FITT-VP guidance. Two PPO modifications are defended explicitly: a bounded-staleness prioritized replay buffer (eviction at 4 policy updates, importance-sampling weights annealed β 0.4→1.0, likelihood ratio truncated at 1.2 à la V-trace) and cosine-annealed learning rate modulated by advantage variance. Training used 10 seeds × 5 folds, GAE λ=0.95, γ=0.97, minibatch 256, on two RTX A5000 GPUs at 8–11 GPU-hours per method. Design decisions (two-timescale separation, discrete frequency, bidirectional progression rate for deloading) are each given a justification; the discount-factor choice is supported by a sweep over {0.95, 0.97, 0.99}. Key Results: Offline cross-validation on 4,128 students / 12,684 test sessions (2021–2024 cohorts, grouped stratified 5-fold, no student spans folds): the full model achieves 14.6 ± 2.2% composite fitness improvement, 91.7 ± 2.3% plan rationality, 341 ± 29 episodes to convergence, and personalization JSD 0.42, versus vanilla PPO at 11.2%, SAC 12.6%, TD3 12.1%, DQN 9.7%, gradient-boosted trees 8.4%, rule-based 6.9%, conventional 5.8%. The margin over SAC is the narrowest (2.0 points, Cohen's d = 0.93), and the proposed model ranked first on only 8 of 10 seeds, slipping behind SAC on two — a candor that is rare in this literature. The 16-week randomized field study (n = 312, 156/arm, ITT mixed model): 13.8% experimental gain vs 7.1% control, group × time interaction 4.71 points (95% CI 3.92–5.50, p = 2.6×10⁻³¹); adherence 87.3% vs 71.6%; failing-band students gained 18.4 points with 73% crossing into passing; adverse events were mild and compatible with chance (2 vs 4 participants, risk difference 1.3 pp, CI −1.6 to 4.2). Response-model validation: calibration slope 0.92, R² 0.69, MAE 2.60 points on held-out weeks; fitted-Q evaluation returns 12.9% vs the simulator's 14.6%, an acknowledged 1.7-point model-induced optimism. Ablations attribute the largest single effect to the adaptive scalarizer (−2.3 pp when removed); the safety mask accounts for part of the rationality advantage (a candid finding the authors flag). Baselines are current and strong (SAC, TD3, tuned with identical budgets). Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, with a modest NEW FORMULATION element (support-constrained offline RL through a validated student-response simulator applied to a mandated fitness curriculum). The paper is candid that algorithmic novelty is limited: PPO, prioritized replay, V-trace-style corrections, two-timescale representation updates, and dynamic scalarization are each existing techniques; the contribution is their disciplined combination in a new domain at scale, plus a genuinely rigorous prospective trial that no prior NSPHS-aligned RL work offers. The authors explicitly disclaim a priority claim on applying RL to NSPHS curricula. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations cover all major components (adaptive reward, adaptive features, prioritized replay, safety mask, recurrent encoder, LR scheduling), and the safety-mask ablation yields a self-undermining but honest finding that masking — not reward design — carries much of the rationality gap. Statistical hygiene is above the norm for this venue: ten named seeds × five folds, bootstrap CIs, prespecified decision rules for assumption checks (Shapiro–Wilk, Levene), Tukey/Games–Howell/Holm-Dunn selection fixed in advance, per-seed variation reported, leave-one-cohort-out and alternative partitions in Table 13, and explicit refusal of post-hoc power calculations. Code, de-identified data, and analysis scripts are stated to be in "Related files" accompanying the article (no external repository URL given). Concerns: the entire offline evaluation is simulated through the authors' own response model (Goodhart risk partially mitigated by the fitted-Q cross-check and a 96.4% support-coverage figure); expert validation of plan rationality was done on only 300 plans by three raters; the trial was registered only retrospectively, which the authors disclose; single institution. The paper is peer-reviewed (Scientific Reports, article in press). Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS-adjacent deployment component). Practical: Runs on a two-GPU workstation (2× RTX A5000, 24 GB), which any university lab can afford. Efficient: 8–11 GPU-hours per method with O(T·(B+D)) update complexity; the weekly decision cadence makes inference cost trivial. Effective: The randomized trial shows real composite-score gains (4.71 adjusted points) and adherence improvement under realistic teaching conditions, though the authors correctly read it as robust association rather than a clean causal estimate given unblinded students/instructors. Scalable: Only claimed, not tested — multi-campus transfer, federated computation, and durability beyond 16 weeks are all flagged as future work; no evidence at 10× the 312-student deployment scale. The work delivers code and data artifacts with the article plus a validated response-simulator methodology; no packaged library or production system. Strengths: - The offline-RL protocol — validated response model with calibration statistics, prespecified MAE tolerance, density-ratio support filtering, and a simulator-free fitted-Q cross-check whose 1.7-point optimism gap is carried into the limitations rather than discounted — is a model of how offline RL should be evaluated in human-subject domains. - The randomized field study with CONSORT reporting, active adverse-event monitoring with physician adjudication, instructor rotation across arms, and an ITT mixed-model primary analysis exceeds the evidentiary standard of essentially all comparable educational-RL papers. - Operational transparency of the reward: every component, threshold, and its literature source (ACSM, Gabbett, FITT-VP) is tabulated so a reader can recompute the reward without the code. - Statistical candor: reporting that the model loses to SAC on 2 of 10 seeds, and that the safety mask rather than the scalarizer drives much of the rationality advantage, are self-undermining disclosures that increase trust in the rest of the numbers. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state plainly: single-institution cohort; simulator-mediated offline results whose systematic error in low-coverage action regions would be invisible to held-out checks; retrospective-only trial registration; 16-week horizon cannot establish durability; MAR assumption for dropout is untestable; equal tuning budget for SAC is not necessarily sufficient budget; excellent-band ceiling effects; no deliberate fairness optimization; the action space reduces pedagogy to a small numerical vector; privacy requirements of production deployment (they propose federated computation). This is direct confrontation rather than minimization — a strong credibility signal. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The response model is fitted on the same historical distribution from which policy support is drawn, so the density-ratio filter verifies nothing about the response model's accuracy in the sparse 3.6% of redirected action space — precisely where the learned policy might have the most headroom. - The control arm received the "standard departmental syllabus" with no attention-matching placebo beyond identical session duration and facilities; the 15.7-point adherence gap could partly reflect perceived personalization (the satisfaction quote "the workload felt right for me" is suggestive), which the authors mention (novelty/expectancy) but do not disentangle with a measurement. - No comparison against a simpler adaptive baseline such as an instructor-adjusted or online-supervised (weekly retrained) prescription scheme, which would isolate whether sequential RL — rather than mere personalization — drives the gain. - The 91.7% rationality metric is rule-conformance scored by the same five rules that partly shape the reward, creating a mild circularity; the 88.7% agreement with expert raters is reassuring but based on 300 sampled weeks. - No long-term injury or overtraining follow-up; a semester is too short to detect cumulative load-misferral, the very risk the safety mask is meant to control. Bottom Line: A practitioner in applied RL or educational data science gains a reusable template for rigorously deploying offline RL in a human-subject, nonstationary domain — the evaluation methodology is the real contribution and outweighs the standard algorithmic core — while an RL researcher seeking algorithmic innovation will find stronger material elsewhere.

LongBanana: An Expert-Verified Benchmark for Long-Context Multi-Reference Image Synthesis (28 ▲ )

Haoxiang Cao, Yuxuan Zhang, Penghui Du, Bo Li, Jiajiong Cao, Yingying Fan, Zimeng Wu, Yifu Luo, Mingzhe Zheng, Junwen Miao, Huaisong Zhang, Yang Yao, Yu Wang, Dongfu Jiang, Ping Nie, Wenhu Chen, Chaoqun Wang, Changqian Yu, Kelsey R. Allen · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 9 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces LONGBANANA, an expert-designed benchmark of 90 multi-reference image-synthesis cases (~32 reference images and ~20 constraints per case, 4,670 atomic checklist items) plus LONGBANANA-Eval, a graph-grounded agentic checklist scorer, and uses them to study agent-harness workflows for long-context image generation. - Why it's important: Current image-generation benchmarks cannot tell whether a system correctly used evidence scattered across dozens of references — a realistic image can pass holistic inspection while binding attributes to the wrong entity or leaking a hard negative — and this benchmark makes such provenance errors locally diagnosable rather than absorbed into one aesthetic score. - How it does it: Each task is modeled as an entity–relation graph whose nodes, edges, and whole-graph constraints are decomposed into atomic, visually verifiable checklist items scored by three rubric critics (Content Fidelity, Relational Binding, Global Constraint Satisfaction) that can call OCR, counting, layout, and identity-matching tools. - The good: The evaluator is validated against a large human-labeled pool (46,700 reviewed labels over 900 outputs) with strong inter-annotator statistics (89.4% exact agreement, 0.83 quadratic weighted κ on a 7,005-label double-labeled subset) and higher judge–human correlation than a single-pass VLM judge (Pearson 0.8707 vs 0.8413). - The missing: The preprint's own NeurIPS checklist answers "No" to open code/data release with executable reproduction instructions despite claiming a project page, and the benchmark is small (10 cases per subclass) with all three tested image backends being closed-source commercial models — no open-weight generator is evaluated. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or evaluate multi-reference image-generation or agentic generation systems and need a validated, fine-grained evaluation protocol; skip it if you work on single-reference editing or text-to-image quality metrics, where existing benchmarks cover the ground.

Non-Obviousness (68) reflects the insight that provenance errors must be localized rather than absorbed into holistic scores. Completeness (72) is a positive: harness-dependent RPR gains, the non-significant result, and taxonomy limits are all reported candidly. Problem & Motivation: Practitioners building image-generation agents (e.g., e-commerce ad assembly, storyboarding, product compositing) must synthesize one image whose content is distributed across many reference images, subject to distractor rejection, entity–attribute binding, counts, and layout constraints. Existing benchmarks target single-reference editing, personalization, or prompt following, and recent multi-reference benchmarks use fewer references and sparser cross-image constraints. Failures in this regime are provenance errors — right object, wrong reference; correct entities, violated relation — which holistic quality scores cannot detect or localize. The gap is a measurement target for dense evidence use: did the model select the right references, reject plausible distractors, bind attributes to the correct entities, and avoid unsupported content? Key Idea: Model each synthesis task as an entity–relation graph and convert every node (entity/attribute), edge (relation/binding), and whole-graph constraint into an atomic, ternary-scored checklist item, so that correctness is measured as constraint satisfaction at three localized levels rather than as a holistic image-quality judgment; scoring itself is then performed by an agentic judge that routes each item to a dimension-specific critic and calls deterministic verification tools where executable checks exist. Methodology: The pipeline has four benchmark-construction stages and two evaluation components. (1) Expert scenario authoring: trained aesthetics/annotation specialists write scenarios per taxonomy cell of a 3×3 taxonomy (Scene Composition: semantic coverage, relational graph consistency, layout; Visual Appearance: global conditioning, local binding, harmonization; Reference Reasoning: selection, temporal/state reasoning, counting). (2) Graph construction: an LLM structures each scenario into an entity–relation graph. (3) Prompt & reference synthesis: the graph guides generation of ~32 atomic reference images, optional backgrounds, and a target instruction; discriminative attributes are kept visible in references and omitted from text; at least 30 cases include ≥2 hard-negative references. (4) Checklist derivation and human curation: graph constraints become atomic items (observable condition, graph unit, references, criteria), reviewed by curators for feasibility and verifiability. LONGBANANA-Eval then parses each case, assembles item-specific evidence packets (with crops, and hard-negative identities for negative items), routes to three critics, and records evidence traces; item labels s∈{0,1,2} are averaged into dimension and overall scores. Human validation labels 46,700 judgments (900 outputs × 10 generation conditions) with primary annotation, second-pass review, expert adjudication, a 15% double-labeled subset, and a 5,604-label random audit (3.34% correction rate). Generation experiments compare FP-Direct (sliding 8-reference window), PD-Direct (a privileged, exactly-solved integer-program staging schedule over the construction graph — minimizing feedback-arc count, then relational stretch), three minimal agent harnesses (Hermes-Agent, OpenCode, OpenClaw; Claude Sonnet 4.6 shared), their RPR (ReAct–Plan–Exec–Reflect) variants, and three image backends under a fixed harness. Critical design decisions: graph-grounded checklists (well-justified — it is what enables error localization); PD-Direct's privileged graph access (justified as an intentional strong non-agentic baseline, but it changes the comparison); difficulty weights for P@70% frozen from human labels of one fixed reference pool (stated, though calibrated from the same conditions later compared). Key Results: Evaluator validation on the full 900-output audit pool: LONGBANANAEVAL reaches Pearson 0.8707 / Spearman 0.8602 / Kendall 0.6727 with expert overall scores versus 0.8413 / 0.8248 / 0.6437 for the single-pass VLM-as-judge (both Gemini 3 Flash); item-level exact ternary agreement improves from 50.99% to 66.81% (+15.82 pp) and opposite-end 0↔2 errors fall from 44.09% to 24.81% (−19.28 pp). Generation results (0–100 checklist-average): with Nano Banana 2 fixed, OpenClaw + RPR achieves the best overall average (78.4) and joint-best P@70% (47.8), beating PD-Direct (74.6, P@70% 35.6) and FP-Direct (68.4, P@70% 24.4); OpenClaw + RPR beats plain OpenClaw on 8 of 9 subclasses (+3.8 avg, +12.2 pp pass rate). RPR gains are harness-dependent: OpenClaw +2.3 pp (95% CI [+0.6, +4.2], p=0.0032), Hermes-Agent +1.7 pp (p=0.0239), OpenCode +0.5 pp (p=0.18, not significant); for OpenCode and Hermes, RPR raises average score but lowers P@70%. With harness fixed, Nano Banana 2 (78.4) dominates Seedream 4 (63.6) and GPT Image 1 (61.8) on all nine subclasses, with paired differences of +14.8 and +16.6 pp (p≈10⁻⁵). Tested at a small benchmark scale: 90 cases, 10 per subclass; ablations isolate ReAct, Plan–Exec, and Reflect components. Notable non-obvious findings: a graph-privileged non-agentic baseline remains competitive on appearance conditioning (98.8 GAC) and several subclasses against agentic systems; RPR hurts temporal/state reasoning for OpenClaw (over-revision drift). Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (first expert-verified benchmark for dense multi-reference, long-context image synthesis with hard negatives and unsupported-content rules) plus NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (LONGBANANA-Eval agentic checklist judge) and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (graph-privileged static scheduling vs adaptive agentic control). The genuinely novel elements are the graph-grounded checklist rubric with three-level error localization and the audited human-label validation protocol; the underlying ingredients — IFEval/TIFA-style atomic instruction decomposition, VLM-as-judge, ReAct/Plan–Execute/Reflect agent patterns — are standard techniques combined and applied to this new setting, and the RPR workflow itself is a conventional composition. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: the RPR component study isolates ReAct, Plan–Exec, and Reflect with weights recalibrated within the ablation table, and the paper honestly reports that no single harness dominates and that RPR can hurt (TSR drop). Statistical treatment is above-average for a benchmark paper: bootstrap 95% CIs and paired tests for generation comparisons, plus label-stability analyses (Kendall τ 0.95–1.00 across label revisions; ≤1.5 pp mean score drift). Inter-annotator agreement is reported (89.4% exact, κ=0.83), and judge validation is performed against fully covered human labels. Methodological concerns: (a) difficulty weights for P@70% are calibrated from human scores of the same ten generation conditions being compared — a within-sample calibration that could favor included systems; (b) the checklist is derived from the same graph used to construct the prompts and references, so benchmark and evaluation share one source of truth (mitigated by human curation, but it embeds the authors' structural assumptions into scoring); (c) the agentic judge shares its backbone (Gemini 3 Flash) with the VLM-judge baseline, so the comparison isolates the harness, not the backbone; (d) all three image backends are closed-source commercial models, and agent harnesses all use Claude Sonnet 4.6. Reproducibility: the abstract cites a project page (https://long-banana.com/) and a GitHub issue tracker, but the NeurIPS checklist explicitly answers "No" to open data/code access with executable reproduction instructions and "No" to full reproducibility disclosure — a significant flag for a paper whose central contribution is a released benchmark. No error-bar caveats on the human-label pool. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS/EMPIRICAL — a built benchmark plus an agentic evaluation pipeline, validated by deployment against human labels. Practical: Yes — everything runs on commercial API models (Gemini 3 Flash judging, Claude Sonnet 4.6 harnesses, three commercial image backends), with no specialized hardware required. Efficient: Not stated — no per-run compute, runtime, or API cost is reported (the checklist acknowledges this); the multi-stage agentic judge and multi-turn agent harnesses are inherently more expensive than single-pass judging and direct generation. Effective: The evidence supports the evaluator (0.87 Pearson with experts) and shows the benchmark detects structured failure modes; the best system reaches only 47.8% P@70%, confirming the task is far from solved rather than the benchmark validating any solution. Scalable: Only claimed — the benchmark is 90 cases and the IP-based staging is noted to solve in seconds for N≤32 entities, but scaling annotation cost (explicitly called expensive) and judge reliability beyond 90 cases is untested. Deliverable: intended as a public benchmark dataset plus evaluation tooling; as of this preprint, code/data are not publicly released with reproduction instructions. Strengths: - The graph-grounded checklist decomposition is a real methodological contribution: it converts an unmeasurable "did the model use the right evidence" question into ~4,670 atomic, ternary, evidence-linked judgments, enabling error localization that holistic VLM judges cannot provide. - The human-validation protocol is unusually thorough for an image-generation benchmark: 46,700 reviewed labels across all reported conditions, 15% double-labeling with reported κ, a random audit with a quantified 3.34% correction rate, and label-version stability analysis showing rankings are unchanged (Kendall τ ≥ 0.95). - The PD-Direct baseline is a genuinely strong and adversarially designed control — it receives privileged access to the construction graph and an exactly solved (integer-program) staging schedule — so the reported advantage of agentic workflows is evidence for adaptive control, not against a strawman. - Honest reporting of negative structure: RPR gains are shown to be harness-dependent (one non-significant), no harness dominates all subclasses, and the component ablation shows the three stages are complementary rather than individually monotonic. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state (Appendix E) that the 3×3 taxonomy covers only a subset of long-horizon synthesis (no video, 3D, or unrestricted multimodal planning), that the high-density design makes expert annotation expensive, and that LONGBANANAEVAL depends on specific backbone multimodal models and tool versions, which must accompany reported results. They confront these directly and concisely — a credibility positive — though the list omits the small per-subclass case count (10) and the closed-source-only backend pool. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Benchmark–evaluation circularity: checklist items are derived from the same entity–relation graph that generates the prompts and references; whatever the LLM-graph extraction and experts encode structurally defines both the task and its scoring, so the benchmark measures satisfaction of the authors' own constraint model. No independent task source (e.g., naturally occurring user requests) is tested. - The most important reproduction gap is self-acknowledged in the checklist but contradicts the abstract's release claim: no executable code/data link in this preprint, which for a Datasets & Evaluations submission materially limits immediate adoption. - Only closed-source backends (Nano Banana 2, GPT Image 1, Seedream 4) are evaluated, so the community's large open-weight generator ecosystem is unmeasured, and conclusions about "backend capability" are vendor-snapshot-specific and will age quickly. - With 10 cases per subclass, per-subclass score differences of a few points rest on very few tasks; bootstrap CIs are reported at the overall level, but subclass-level comparisons (the basis of several claims) lack per-cell uncertainty. - Human annotation cost and inter-annotator agreement are reported, but the annotators are the authors' own trained specialists from the construction pipeline; no independent-site replication of the label quality is provided. - The 8-reference backend budget for direct baselines is an implementation constraint; the paper does not test whether newer backends with larger multi-image context windows change the direct-vs-agent conclusion. Bottom Line: This is the most carefully validated evaluation instrument yet for dense multi-reference image synthesis and is worth adopting by anyone benchmarking agentic image-generation systems — provided the promised code/data release actually materializes — but its 90-case scale, closed-source-only backends, and graph-circular task design mean its headline numbers should be read as a first measurement of a new capability axis, not a settled leaderboard.

Trustworthy Recursive Self - Improvement with Statistical Guarantees

Z Gao, Z Qi, Y Cui · arxiv.org · recursive self-improvement - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces TRUST, an acceptance gate for recursive self-improvement (RSI) of LLM agents that adapts online multiple hypothesis testing with e-values to control the proportion of accepted updates that cause unacceptable performance loss. - Why it's important: RSI loops that accept updates via a greedy validation-score check mistake sampling noise and validation-reuse overfitting for real progress — the paper measures a 45.59% average false-acceptance rate for greedy gates — and each accepted bad update can permanently degrade the agent. - How it does it: Each round runs a sequential noninferiority test (H0: the candidate's population gain ≤ −ε) with a betting-style e-value whose boundary is corrected for validation-sample reuse, while an e-LORD/e-GAI-style allocator — steered by an LLM reading the candidate's history — spends a finite false-evolution-rate (FER) budget across rounds. - The good: Across 6 settings (3 benchmarks × 2 models, 30 rounds, 5 seeds), TRUST cuts mean FER0 from 45.59% (greedy) to 2.78% and mean maximum drawdown from 4.963 pp to 0.047 pp while achieving the highest mean final gain (24.84 pp) among non-degenerate gates. - The missing: The strongest statistical baselines (SGM-B/SGM-H) are degenerate — SGM-B accepts zero updates in all settings — so the gate comparison rests mainly on greedy and PACE, and the key Assumption 1 (that β upper-bounds reuse-induced optimism bias) is not estimable or empirically validated from data. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building self-evolving agent systems or working on anytime-valid inference, because it is the first serious attempt to port online FDR machinery to closed-loop agent acceptance decisions; skip if you only want a better proposer/harness — this paper deliberately does not touch candidate generation.

Problem & Motivation: Self-improving LLM agents modify their own harness (prompts, memory, routing, workflow) without retraining the underlying model. The literature focuses on proposing better candidates, but the acceptance decision is under-studied. A greedy gate that accepts any candidate beating the incumbent on a reused validation set suffers from two failure modes the paper grounds in adaptive data analysis (Dwork et al. 2015; Rogers et al. 2016): finite-sample noise and optimism bias from reusing validation data across rounds. Accepting an inferior update lowers current performance, and the loss persists through later rounds. Conversely, FWER-style statistical gates (the authors' prior SGM work) are so conservative they never accept anything, stalling improvement. The open problem: retain useful updates while bounding acceptance errors across rounds with a limited (200-example) validation pool. Key Idea: Reformulate sequential accept/reject decisions across RSI rounds as an online multiple testing problem under a new error criterion — the false evolution rate (FER), the expected fraction of accepted updates whose population score drop exceeds a tolerance ε — controlled by adapting e-LOND/e-GAI budget allocation, with three power-preserving tricks: (i) a noninferiority margin so small tolerated losses don't block acceptance, (ii) an exposure-weighted overlap correction (raising the null boundary by ζt,i·β for previously-seen validation items), and (iii) an LLM that reads historical context to spend more error budget on promising candidates. Crucially, the LLM only affects power (which testing levels get spent where), never the validity of the guarantee. Methodology: The paper defines a solver/proposer/gate loop over T rounds with filtrations tracking information flow. Each round: (1) the proposer generates a candidate harness edit given history; (2) an allocator sets testing level αt = min{αmax, ρt·Bt·(Rt−1+1)} where ρt = clip(wt·1/(T−t+1), ρmin, ρmax), Bt is remaining FER budget, and wt is an LLM-produced multiplier (G-Eval-style criteria over safety/contract/actionability/generalization/scope); (3) paired score differences Dt,i on up to n=40 draws from a 200-example pool feed a betting e-value Mt,m = Π(1 + ηt,i(Yt,i − u(β)t,i)/u(β)t,i) with corrected boundary u(β)t,i = pε + ζt,iβ and Yt,i = (1+Dt,i)/2; (4) accept at the first crossing of 1/αt (a stopping time). Theorems: (1) e-value conditional validity at arbitrary stopping times via nonnegative supermartingale arguments; (2) FERε(T) ≤ q under Assumption 1; (3) true evolution rate TER(T) ≥ 1 − rN,n − Te^{−κn} under n/N → 0 and bounded betting fractions; (4) a lower bound on final gain trading missed improvements (exponentially vanishing in n) against tolerated loss ε and αt-weighted excess loss. Critical design decisions: ε > 0 is necessary for Theorem 3 (at ε = 0 no positive betting fraction satisfies Assumption 2(c)) — well-argued; β is an assumed correction strength for reuse bias that the authors admit cannot yet be identified from data — under-justified; the LLM allocator is provably safe but its benefit rests on a single-seed case study and a 1.13 pp mean difference. Key Results: Tested on HotpotQA (Joint F1), DROP (token F1), APPS (test-case pass rate) with DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Qwen-3.8-Flash, 30 rounds, 5 seeds, 200 validation / 300 held-out test examples, in a closed-loop harness with 20 editable operators across reasoning/routing/memory/workflow. Headlines: mean final gain 24.84 pp (highest among non-degenerate gates); mean FER0 falls from 45.59% (Greedy) to 2.78%; mean MDD from 4.963 pp to 0.047 pp. Per-setting: e.g., HotpotQA/Qwen TRUST 27.72 pp gain vs Greedy 20.66 pp; DROP/DeepSeek Greedy 36.24 pp vs TRUST 31.47 pp (Greedy wins two settings on raw gain, but with FER0 of 35–41% and MDD up to 8.48 pp). Baselines: Greedy, PACE (single-round e-process, competitive but lower TER — e.g., 5.19–12.63% vs TRUST's 11.64–18.11% where compared), SGM-B and SGM-H (FWER gates that essentially never accept: SGM-B accepts zero updates everywhere, SGM-H accepts 3 updates total across all runs — these baselines are effectively vacuous). An overfitting stress test shows greedy validation gain of 24.44 pp collapsing to −2.15 pp test gain after 10 rounds of data reuse. Ablations show ε = 0.15 inflates FER0 to 57.68%, β = 0 gives FER0 23.33% vs 10% at β = 0.01, and removing LLM guidance costs 1.13 pp final score (43.78% vs 44.91% Joint F1). Note the reported TER for TRUST is still low (10–21%), meaning most improving candidates are rejected in practice. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM element (gate design for RSI with process-level guarantees, versus per-round or FWER alternatives) plus NEW FORMULATION (FER as an FDR analogue for self-improvement, connecting online e-value testing to closed-loop agent evolution) and NEW METHOD (the specific overlap-corrected, LLM-allocated e-value gate). The machinery is a competent adaptation of existing tools — e-LOND/e-GAI allocation, contextual online FDR (Chen & Kasiviswanathan 2020), betting e-values (Waudby-Smith & Ramdas 2024), noninferiority testing (Blackwelder 1982) — with the genuine novelty lying in the FER criterion, the exposure-weighted reuse correction, and the closed-loop theory connecting gate parameters to final gain. Rigor & Reproducibility: Proofs (appendices B–E) are detailed and appear correct: supermartingale validity at stopping times, budget nonnegativity, a Hoeffding-style conditional miss bound (Lemma 3), and a mixture extension. Experiments report mean ± standard error over 5 seeds, 30 rounds, 6 settings, with held-out test sets used only for reporting, ablations on q/ε/β, an LLM-allocator ablation, and mechanism case studies (including a detailed greedy failure trace). Concerns: (a) Assumption 1 — that β bounds the conditional mean of reused samples under the null — is untestable and unestimated; β is hand-set (0.01) with sensitivity showing sharp behavior; (b) the FER0 estimate for TRUST on HotpotQA/DeepSeek is 10.00% ± 10.00%, i.e., essentially one event across seeds, so empirical FER rates are extremely noisy; (c) two of four baselines are degenerate, weakening the 'beats state-of-the-art statistical gates' claim to a comparison with PACE alone; (d) small scale (200-example validation pool, 300-example test sets, three benchmarks); (e) no code, data, or model release is mentioned — Not stated. (f) Hyperparameters (q = 0.30, ε = 0.10, β = 0.01) were effectively tuned on the evaluation benchmarks, though on validation metrics only. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a theoretical component). Practical: Yes — it requires only an LLM API for solver/proposer/allocator and a small validation pool; no training or specialized hardware. Efficient: Cheap relative to alternatives — early stopping means fewer validation evaluations than a fixed-n greedy gate, plus one extra LLM call per round for allocation. Effective: Evidence shows it prevents degradation (MDD ≤ 0.27 pp, FER0 ≤ 10% empirically) while retaining meaningful gains, but TER of 10–21% shows it accepts few of the improving candidates, and the gain lower bound (Theorem 4) is asymptotic rather than a practical certificate. Scalable: Not tested beyond 30 rounds, 200 validation examples, and three benchmarks; Theorem 3 requires n/N → 0 with fixed T, which says nothing about long-horizon runs, and budget dynamics over hundreds of rounds are unexamined. The work delivers no software artifact — it stops at paper form (No code URL stated). Strengths: (1) The FER formulation is a genuinely apt translation of FDR thinking to agent self-modification — controlling the proportion of bad acceptances rather than any-bad-event probability is exactly the right relaxation for a setting where never accepting is useless. (2) The theory is honest about the closed loop: guarantees hold along the adaptive trajectory the gate itself induces, including at data-dependent stopping times, and the LLM is provably excluded from the validity argument. (3) The exposure-weighted overlap correction (raising the null boundary by ζt,iβ) is a simple, principled mechanism for reuse bias, with an ablation showing β = 0 yields 23.33% FER0 versus 10% with correction. (4) The empirical diagnostics go beyond headline scores — maximum drawdown, FER0, an overfitting stress test (validation +24.44 pp vs test −2.15 pp), and a traced greedy failure in APPS where a 'first_example_pass' stop rule raises validation F1 while dropping test pass rate from 75.07% to 67.00%. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: no method for identifying β from data or optimally tuning parameters; the theoretical guarantee can be conservative and only partly explains practice; the LLM allocator can misjudge candidates and pick poor multipliers; gate optimization for gain under safety constraints is left to future work. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Assumption 1 is the load-bearing wall: nothing verifies that β = 0.01 (or any value) upper-bounds the actual optimism bias of the proposer's reuse of validation feedback, so the FER ≤ q guarantee is conditional on an unquantified quantity; the framework offers no diagnostic for when the certificate is vacuous. (2) The statistical baselines are strawmen in practice — reporting SGM-B/SGM-H as comparisons when they accept ~zero updates inflates the apparent advantage; a tighter comparison would tune δ for SGM or use less conservative FWER spending. (3) Power is poor: TER of 11–21% means the gate discards most genuinely improving candidates, so 'balancing safety and gain' partly means 'accepting very little' — the gain advantage over PACE in DROP/DeepSeek is actually negative (31.47 vs 29.70 pp) and within ~1 SE elsewhere. (4) The LLM-allocator ablation (1.13 pp, one benchmark, with the mechanism supported by a single-seed case study) is thin relative to its prominence as contribution (a). (5) Benchmark hyperparameter selection (q, ε, β) appears tuned per the ablation grids on the same benchmarks used for the main table. (6) The guarantee concerns population-level FER at tolerance ε, but the headline empirical metric is FER0 (any non-improvement) — a stricter criterion than what the theory controls, creating a mismatch between what is proven and what is celebrated. Bottom Line: For anyone building self-evolving agents, this is the most rigorous treatment of the acceptance-gate problem to date and worth reading for its FER formulation and reuse-corrected e-value design — but treat the empirical superiority over statistical baselines as a comparison against one viable competitor (PACE), and treat the 'statistical guarantee' as conditional on an unverifiable bias assumption rather than a deployable certificate.

#91 — Innovative (65)

Towards Generalist Graph-Level Anomaly Detection

J Pan, Y Liu, Y Zheng, F Li, AWC Liew, S Pan · arxiv.org · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces GenGLAD, the first generalist graph-level anomaly detection (GLAD) framework — a single pre-trained model that detects anomalous graphs across unseen domains using only ~10 normal target graphs for adaptation. - Why it's important: Existing GLAD methods follow a one-model-per-dataset paradigm requiring large in-domain training data and per-dataset training cost, which is impractical for emerging domains (drug screening, fraud) where labeled/curated graphs are scarce; this work removes that per-domain training burden. - How it does it: The core move is memory-guided discriminative subgraph extraction trained with cross-domain motif injection (motifs from one domain injected into graphs of another to create labeled pseudo-anomalies), followed by test-time adaptation via a learned linear combination of four discrepancy scores between the extracted subgraph and prior/domain/class/instance contexts. - The good: GenGLAD ranks first on 9 of 10 transfer benchmarks in AUROC (e.g., 95.84% on AIDS vs. 90.59% for the best baseline SIGNET, 74.96% on DHFR vs. ~63.3%), while fine-tuning 2.1×–13.5× faster than baselines, and ablations (Table 3, full results in appendix) show each component contributes. - The missing: All evaluation is on small TUDataset benchmarks (188–2,000 test graphs) whose "anomalies" are minority classes, not genuine anomalies, and there is no comparison against adapting existing generalist node-level detectors (ARC, AnomalyGFM) or other transfer strategies to the graph-level setting — so the generalist claim is untested against the strongest plausible alternatives. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on graph anomaly detection or transferable anomaly detection generally — it formalizes a new problem setting with a competent first method; skip it if you need evidence on real anomaly distributions or at production scale, which the paper does not provide.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (80) is the strongest dimension — a genuine new problem formulation (generalist graph-level anomaly detection with few-shot cross-domain adaptation) backed by released code and thorough ablations, though the method itself is a competent composition of standard ingredients. Rigor (65) is held down by Goodhart concerns: the anomaly concept is defined by the paper's own pseudo-anomaly construction, benchmarks use minority-class labels as anomalies, and the key control (cross-domain vs. in-domain motif injection) is missing. Completeness (55) suffers from absent transfer-strategy baselines and a minimized limitations section; Resilience (60) is moderate because the generalist claim would strain under adversarial questioning about real anomaly distributions. Practical Impact (60) reflects the public code and fast adaptation but no released weights or real-world validation. Weighted composite: 0.20*80 + 0.25*65 + 0.15*65 + 0.15*55 + 0.15*60 + 0.10*60 = 65.

Problem & Motivation: Graph-level anomaly detection — flagging whole graphs (molecules, protein structures, ego-networks) that deviate from a majority population — is needed in toxic-chemical screening, fraudster-network detection, and multi-agent safeguarding. Practitioners in these domains face two pains: (1) anomaly annotations require domain expertise, so training is normally one-class and data-hungry, and (2) every new application scenario forces a new model, with high compute cost and sharp degradation when training data shrinks (Figure 1b shows baseline AUROC dropping with training-set size, some below 50%). Prior generalist anomaly detectors cover images, time series, tabular, and relational data, and node-level graph settings (ARC, AnomalyGFM), but none address the graph-level setting, where normal/abnormal patterns differ structurally across domains (dense fraud sub-structures vs. toxic molecular motifs) and homophily-based node-level assumptions do not transfer. The gap: no unified GLAD model that generalizes to unseen graph datasets with minimal in-domain supervision. Key Idea: Learn anomaly-discriminative subgraph extraction as the transferable capability, rather than transferring domain-specific patterns: train a GNN to select the substructure of any graph that best distinguishes normal from anomalous, using cross-domain motif injection to manufacture labeled pseudo-anomalies from normal-only data; at test time, score a graph by the discrepancy of its extracted subgraph against multi-level contexts (pre-trained prototype, domain prototype, few-shot normal class prototype, support-set similarity distribution) — so adaptation reduces to fitting a single linear weight vector over ~6–8 discrepancy scalars. This decouples "what is discriminative" (learned once, transferred) from "what is normal here" (estimated from 10 samples via discrepancies). Methodology: Two phases. Pre-training (memory-guided discriminative subgraph extraction): (i) unify unattributed graphs via structural attributes (32-d one-hot degree encoding ⊕ 32-d random-walk positional encoding, 64-d total); (ii) a GNN encoder produces node embeddings H, an importance module fθ scores nodes, and Gumbel-Softmax with temperature τ=0.5 converts scores to a binary node mask m, yielding subgraph G′; (iii) a bank of M=128 trainable memory tokens stores transferable patterns, with top-K (K=12) tokens retrieved by cosine similarity to a mean-pooled dataset context vector c, and node importance computed as max cosine similarity between node embeddings and retrieved tokens; (iv) pseudo-anomalies are built by attaching random-walk motifs sampled from other pre-training datasets (with node-level injection masks), and the model is trained on L_pre = L_graph + λ_n·L_node + λ_s·‖m‖₁, where L_graph is BCE on σ(1−cos(z_G′, t_c)) against the pseudo label and L_node penalizes including injected-motif nodes in the extracted subgraph. Adaptation (multi-dimensional discrepancy scoring): with the encoder and memory bank frozen, four discrepancy signals are computed per query — prior (−cos to pre-trained prototype), domain (cosine and Euclidean to context c), class-level (cosine and Euclidean to few-shot normal prototype q), and instance-level (1-D Wasserstein distance between query-to-support and support-to-support similarity distributions) — and a single learnable weight vector w (s = σ(w^⊤s)) is optimized with BCE for ~10 epochs, using only 10 normal graphs plus locally generated pseudo-anomalies (edge-shuffle structure perturbation and graph-bridging sample merging; cross-domain motifs are avoided at adaptation to prevent data leakage). Critical design decisions: unattributed structural-only inputs (justified by cross-domain feature incompatibility and citation of evidence that node features matter less in GLAD); cross-domain (rather than in-domain) motif injection for pseudo-anomalies (plausibly argued but never directly ablated against in-domain injection at pre-training); linear-only adaptation (justified by ablation showing mean/max/min pooling of the same scores collapses performance, sometimes below 50% AUROC). Key Results: Trained jointly on NCI1 + DD + COLLAB (10,288 graphs) and evaluated on 10 TUDataset benchmarks with n=10 normal shots, mean±std over 5 runs, fixed hyperparameters across all test datasets. GenGLAD achieves best AUROC on 9/10 datasets: AIDS 95.84±0.07 (best baseline SIGNET 90.59), DHFR 74.96 (best baseline ~63.34), COX2 62.92 (~52.73), BZR 63.89 (~58.91), MUTAG 90.75 (~89.55 CVTGAD), IMDB-B 74.11 (~67.84), REDDIT-B 73.63 (~73.85 MUSE, essentially tied); on ENZYMES it is second (54.37 vs. HC-GLAD 63.03 in few-shot-only). AUPRC tells the same story (best on 9/10, e.g., AIDS 98.79, DHFR 82.21). Baselines (GLocalKD, CVTGAD, SIGNET, MUSE, GLADPro, HC-GLAD, FANFOLD) are recent (2022–2026) unsupervised GLAD methods and are tested in two regimes; pre-training generally does not help them, and several fall below 50% AUROC or OOM in some regimes — evidence that the baselines are genuinely ill-suited to the transfer setting, though all are in-domain specialists rather than methods designed for transfer. Performance improves monotonically with more pre-training datasets (e.g., AIDS 87.56 with NCI1 only → 95.84 with all three). Ablations: removing L_node costs up to 16 AUROC points (IMDB-B 74.11→58.03); removing class discrepancy drops DHFR to 45.63; replacing the learned scoring module with mean/max/min pooling collapses AUROC to 6–62 on several datasets. Adaptation is fast: 0.42s total fine-tuning on AIDS (vs. 0.85–5s+ for baselines; fastest baseline GLADPro 2.1× slower, HC-GLAD 13.5×), on a single RTX 4090. Subgraph explanation quality (Table 9) is close to in-domain-trained SIGNET (72.1 vs. 76.6 AUROC on BM-MN). Tested scale is small: test sets of 188–2,000 graphs, average 14–430 nodes. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM (first formalization of generalist graph-level anomaly detection with few-shot cross-domain adaptation) plus NEW METHOD (GenGLAD). The genuinely new elements are the problem formulation applied to graph level and the coupling of cross-domain motif injection with multi-dimensional discrepancy-based linear adaptation. The individual ingredients are standard: memory networks for anomaly detection (Niu et al. 2023), Gumbel-Softmax subgraph selection, prototype-based few-shot scoring, Wasserstein-1 distance, and pseudo-anomaly generation — the contribution is their composition for a new setting, which is a competent combination rather than a fundamentally new mechanism. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative, covering every pre-training loss term, every discrepancy measure, and the scoring module, on all 10 datasets (Tables 6–7); results report mean±std over 5 runs (no significance tests, but margins on AIDS/DHFR/COX2 are far beyond the reported std). Code is released at https://github.com/CampanulaBells/Generalist-Graph-Level-Anomaly-Detection; datasets are public TUDataset benchmarks; full hyperparameters, algorithms, complexity analysis, and hardware (single RTX 4090, 24GB) are disclosed. The NeurIPS checklist is filled out with mostly "Yes" answers. Methodological concerns: (1) the evaluation protocol (train on the largest dataset per domain, test on the rest) is adapted from ARC/UB-GOLD, but the discrepancy features and hyperparameters were developed with knowledge of these same 10 benchmarks — no held-out benchmark family exists; (2) the "anomalies" in these datasets are minority-class labels (e.g., mutagenic compounds), not operational anomalies, so absolute AUROC values overstate real-world readiness; (3) hyperparameters were selected by random search, and although the authors state no per-dataset tuning is done, the search itself was performed against this benchmark suite; (4) the class-level and instance-level discrepancies use the few-shot normal set, and the same 10 shots also generate adaptation pseudo-anomalies — a small, reused support set with no analysis of leakage or variance across support-set draws. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a method trained and evaluated by the authors; no deployment). Practical: Yes — runs on one consumer GPU (RTX 4090, 24GB) with 32GB RAM; no large-scale infrastructure needed. Efficient: Adaptation is 0.42s on AIDS, 2.1×–13.5× faster than all baselines; pre-training totals ~326s for 10,288 graphs — cheap relative to the one-model-per-dataset alternative. Effective: The evidence shows strong performance on benchmark minority-class detection under 10-shot transfer, which is a proxy for the stated real-world goal (detecting operational anomalies in genuinely new domains); no real anomaly deployment or user-facing anomaly data is evaluated. Scalable: Untested beyond ~10K training graphs and ~2K-graph test sets; the complexity analysis (O(N(KV+E)) per epoch) suggests linear scaling, but graphs far larger than REDDIT-B's ~430 average nodes, or hundreds of domains, are only claimed, not shown. The work delivers a software artifact (public code repository) plus a reusable recipe (motif injection + discrepancy scoring); no pre-trained model weights are mentioned as released. Strengths: (1) First formalization of the generalist GLAD problem, with a clean two-challenge decomposition (C1: transferable pattern learning; C2: few-shot adaptation) that structures the method and would structure follow-up work. (2) The cross-domain motif injection trick is a genuinely clever way to manufacture labeled anomalies in a normal-only, multi-domain setting, and the node-level loss on injected nodes gives fine-grained supervision that the ablation shows matters most (up to 16 AUROC points). (3) The discrepancy-based adaptation is well-designed for the few-shot regime: freezing everything except a k-dimensional linear head avoids overfitting on 10 samples, and the ablation showing naive score aggregation (mean/max/min) collapses to near-random AUROC credibly demonstrates the learned weighting is doing real work. (4) Honest, fixed-hyperparameter cross-domain evaluation plus a full ablation grid on all 10 datasets — more transparent than typical for this area. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The conclusion states that GenGLAD still requires few-shot supervision for adaptation and cannot yet achieve fully zero-shot generalist GLAD, proposing expert/external knowledge as future work. This is the only stated limitation; the authors do not address benchmark scale, the synthetic nature of benchmark anomalies, or the risk that the pseudo-anomaly definition drives what the model detects. The limitation is acknowledged but minimized — a single sentence, with no analysis of how performance degrades in the zero-shot regime they name as the goal. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The pseudo-anomaly construction defines the anomaly concept: at pre-training, anomalies are graphs with foreign motifs attached, and at adaptation, edge-shuffled and bridge-merged graphs. TUDataset minority classes may or may not resemble these corruptions; the strong results could partly reflect the benchmarks' anomalies being structurally injectable/outlier-like, and there is no experiment with real anomaly distributions (e.g., truly emerging-domain data). Notably, the pre-training ablation against in-domain motif injection — the control that would show cross-domain injection specifically matters — is absent. (2) No comparison with any alternative transfer strategy: e.g., graph pre-training + linear probing, adapting node-level generalist detectors (ARC, AnomalyGFM), or simply a GNN classifier pre-trained on the three training datasets' labels — the reader cannot tell how much of the gain comes from the framework vs. any cross-dataset pre-training at all (Table 2 only varies GenGLAD's own pre-training data). (3) The instance-level discrepancy contributes almost nothing in the ablation (AIDS 95.84→95.77, REDDIT-B 73.63→72.16; on PROTEINS removing it slightly helps), yet it is presented as a core contribution. (4) The few-shot support set is reused as context, class prototype, negative-sample source, and scoring training data, with no variance analysis across support draws — a small-n fragility the error bars (over 5 runs) may understate. (5) Scale extrapolation is unsupported: the largest training corpus is 10K graphs / 27M edges, far from the "large-scale databases" motivating the work. Bottom Line: A practitioner in graph anomaly detection should read this paper — it opens a well-motivated new problem setting with a credible, well-ablated first method and released code — but should treat the benchmark numbers as evidence of transfer to structurally-injected pseudo-anomalies rather than proof of generalist detection on real anomaly distributions, and watch for follow-up work with stronger transfer baselines and real-world anomaly data.

SteerDistill: Quantizing LLM Agents via Closed-Loop Teacher Steering (31 ▲ )

Genming Cui, Xiangyu Li, Zixu Hao, Xin Ding, Yunxin Liu, Ting Cao · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 12 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces SteerDistill, a quantization-aware distillation method in which a full-precision teacher steers a quantized LLM agent to revise its own failed rollouts via closed-loop execution feedback, then internalizes those verified corrections for unguided inference. - Why it's important: Low-bit quantization cuts multi-turn agent inference cost but degrades task success, and neither offline distillation data nor unguided on-policy rollouts supply correct actions in exactly the contexts where the quantized agent fails (unguided retries yield a correct action at only 9.6% of divergent turns in their diagnostic). - How it does it: The core move is aligning failed student rollouts against successful teacher references by environment transitions, intervening at the first behavioral divergence with a structured teacher steering prompt, locally verifying each revised action against the reference transition, and then distilling with forward KL toward the steered student at corrected turns and reverse KL toward the teacher elsewhere. - The good: Across five agentic benchmarks and three models under W4A16, SteerDistill beats the strongest quantized baseline (QeRL) by 1.67–2.18 average points and lands within 1 point of BF16 (e.g., 53.18 vs. BF16's 53.54 on Qwen3-8B), with a five-question ablation that isolates every major design choice. - The missing: The method requires a successful teacher reference per failed task, restorable environment state, and reliable local verification — all assumptions the authors admit are untested outside their simulated, state-checkable environments — and ablations cover only BFCL V4 with one model at one precision. - Read it or not: Worth reading for anyone doing post-training of quantized agents or on-policy distillation of multi-turn agents; skippable if you only care about weight-reconstruction quantization (GPTQ/QuaRot-style), which this work does not touch.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (68) is the top dimension — the closed loop of divergence localization via environment-transition alignment, teacher steering, local verification, and asymmetric FKL/RKL internalization is a genuinely new integration, backed by a quantified supervision-gap diagnostic (9.6% → 82.3% Pass@4). Rigor (62) is pulled down by headline results without seed variance (error bars only on one benchmark's training curve), ablations confined to a single model/precision/benchmark, a proprietary user simulator in the loop, and preprint status. Resilience (60) is weakened by the untested comparison against teacher-guided decoding and unquantified dependence on reference availability; Completeness (70) benefits from a direct, non-minimizing limitations section. Weighted composite: 0.20*68 + 0.25*62 + 0.15*65 + 0.15*70 + 0.15*60 + 0.10*62 = 65.

Problem & Motivation: Operators deploying LLM agents face high inference cost from repeated multi-turn model calls, and low-bit weight quantization (W4A16 and below) is the standard remedy. The paper's diagnosis — supported by rollout inspection (Sections D.1–D.2) — is that quantized agents fail not through generic degradation but through behavioral divergence: they overlook task requirements or environmental conditions (booking a train ticket for an invented route, leaving files empty after creating them, reading a file before entering its directory), producing environment transitions that diverge from a successful full-precision reference. Existing fixes leave a coverage gap: offline distillation data (GPTQ, EfficientQAT, BitDistiller) does not include the student's specific failure contexts, while on-policy rollouts in those contexts rarely contain correct actions (turn-level Pass@4 of 9.6% for unguided retries on BFCL V4). Key Idea: Construct behavioral corrections that the student could not produce on its own, then internalize them. A frozen full-precision teacher does not replace the student's failed action (takeover) or merely let it retry; instead, it explains the overlooked requirement as a structured steering prompt (discrepancy, applicable conditions, corrective rule), the frozen quantized student snapshot generates the revision conditioned on that prompt, execution feedback verifies the resulting environment transition against the teacher reference, and the teacher refines the prompt on failure. The privileged guidance is then stripped out: the trainable student is distilled to match the steered snapshot's distribution at corrected turns (forward KL, target conditioned on G) and the full teacher elsewhere (reverse KL), so it acts correctly without any prompt at inference. Context distillation of teacher guidance is known; the combination with divergence localization by environment-transition alignment (not action-token mismatch, worth +1.83 points) and per-turn local verification is the distinctive part. Methodology: Each training cycle alternates two phases. (1) Teacher-steered trajectory revision (Algorithm 1): failed student rollouts from a frozen snapshot are aligned to a fixed successful teacher reference by matching environment-state transitions; at the first divergence t★, history and environment are restored, the teacher emits a structured prompt G from the aligned discrepancy plus a memory of the last accepted prompt, the snapshot samples a revised response and executes it, and a LocalVerify step compares the resulting transition (and returned information) with the reference; on rejection, the verification report feeds back into a refined prompt for up to R=4 attempts. Verified corrections replace the failed turn, the student continues unguided, and revision iterates to the next divergence; trajectories are retained for distillation even if the task remains unsolved. (2) Internalization: per-token objective (Eq. 3) averaging forward KL to the fake-quantized steered snapshot at corrected turns and reverse KL to the frozen BF16 teacher at all other turns, trained with straight-through estimation on BF16 master weights over two epochs, batch size 16 trajectories, LR 8e-6, on 8×A100. Critical design decisions, each ablated (Table 2): intervening at behavioral divergence rather than action mismatch (+1.83), teacher steering versus retry/takeover (+2.38/+1.78), local verification versus none (+4.66, and terminal-success filtering actually hurts slightly), and FKL/RKL routing (+1.55–2.56 over alternatives). The environment-transition-based localization is well justified (equivalent actions can differ textually); the reliance on reference availability is justified only by construction. Key Results: On Qwen3-8B under W4A16, five-benchmark averages (BFCL V4 Overall, τ²-Bench Pass@1, WebShop SR, ALFWorld SR, Search QA EM): SteerDistill 53.18 vs. QeRL 51.00, On-Policy QAD 50.38, BitDistiller 48.49, EfficientQAT 47.87, GPTQ 46.36, BF16 53.54 — a 0.36-point gap to BF16, with per-benchmark wins on all five. Gains hold on Qwen3.5-4B (60.95 vs. 59.24 QeRL; BF16 61.68) and Gemma 4 12B-it (64.31 vs. 62.64; BF16 65.13). Under harder settings on Qwen3-8B, margins widen: +1.93 over QeRL (W4A8) and +3.39 over On-Policy QAD (W2A16, 42.97 vs. 39.58). Efficiency: on τ²-Bench, a 32-GPU-hour checkpoint reaches 31.68% Pass@1, exceeding QeRL's converged 96-GPU-hour score (29.84%) by 1.84 points with 67% fewer GPU hours, ±1 std over four evaluation runs; successful tasks average 4.0K output tokens vs. 4.1–5.2K for quantized baselines and 3.9K for BF16, with fewer interaction steps (11.6) and tool calls (4.24). Baselines are current and reasonably strong (QeRL, 2025; NeMo-RL's on-policy QAD workflow), though both were re-adapted from NVFP4/Hopper configs to group-wise integer quantization on A100s. The paper also reports results without initial GRPO post-training (Table 5), where the ordering persists with smaller margins. An emergent, untrained behavior — recovery from mid-rollout execution errors at inference (Figures 13–14) — is reported qualitatively. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (with supporting NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING on where quantized agents fail). Genuinely novel: the closed loop that verifies student-generated corrections at the divergent turn against reference environment transitions and refines teacher guidance from execution feedback, plus the asymmetric FKL/RKL internalization of steered behavior. Standard components reused: quantization-aware distillation with KL objectives, context distillation of privileged guidance, structured feedback prompting (Self-Refine-style), and GRPO post-training for teacher checkpoints — the contribution is their integration and the divergence-localization mechanism, not any single ingredient. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are strong: five targeted intervention groups (Table 2) isolate localization, intervention strategy, steering format/source, retention policy, and loss routing, each with a plausible alternative and quantified deltas. Error bars (±1 std over four runs) appear only for τ²-Bench training curves; headline Table 1 results do not report seeds or significance tests, though four-run averaging is stated for τ². Code is released (github.com/air-embodied-brain/SteerDistill) with a project page. Concerns: (a) ablations are confined to BFCL V4 + Qwen3-8B + W4A16, so generality of the design insights is asserted, not shown; (b) the τ²-Bench user simulator is GPT-5.6 at temperature 0, a proprietary component in the evaluation loop; (c) all environments are simulated with programmatically checkable state, which is precisely the condition the method depends on; (d) baselines were re-implemented/adapted by the authors rather than taken from vendor reports, which is fair but self-administered. arXiv preprint, not yet peer-reviewed. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a training method run and measured on real pipelines, not a deployed system). - Practical: Runs on 8×A100 80GB with group-wise integer quantization — no exotic hardware; inference uses only the quantized student. - Efficient: 67% fewer training GPU hours than QeRL at higher accuracy on τ²-Bench, and shorter successful trajectories (4.0K vs. 4.1–5.2K output tokens), though total training still costs tens of GPU hours per task family. - Effective: Evidence supports the stated problem — near-BF16 task success across five benchmarks — but only in environments permitting reference-guided, state-verifiable revision, which is a proxy for open-ended agent deployment. - Scalable: Untested beyond 4B–12B models and W4; the per-failure teacher-steering loop with R=4 retries and environment restoration plausibly grows expensive with task horizon and fleet size, and the paper offers no claim or experiment at 10× scale. Deliverable: a software artifact (code repository and project page) plus a reusable training recipe; no released model weights are mentioned. Strengths: - The failure analysis is mechanistic, not anecdotal: divergences are defined operationally via environment-transition mismatch against references, and the 9.6% → 82.3% turn-level Pass@4 jump under steering quantifies exactly the supervision gap the method exploits. - The ablation suite (Table 2) is unusually decisive — e.g., removing local verification costs 4.66 points while adding terminal-success filtering costs 0.54, a non-obvious result the authors interpret honestly (verified corrections from failed trajectories are valuable). - Efficiency claims are paired with matched measurement: GPU-hour curves include steering overhead, and token-efficiency is computed per method over its own successful tasks, avoiding the common trap of comparing token counts across different success sets without disclosure. - Internalization is cleanly designed so the learner never sees steering prompts at training or inference time, making the deployed artifact genuinely unassisted rather than prompt-dependent. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: Section E states three prerequisites — successful teacher references, restoration of pre-error history and environment state, and reliable local verification — and admits applicability to environments lacking state restoration or reliable verification is untested. It also concedes that local verification of a single transition does not guarantee eventual task success or correctness of every reasoning step. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section; the authors correctly identify the assumptions that bind the method's scope. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No comparison against teacher-guided decoding at inference (e.g., speculative or assisted decoding from the BF16 teacher), which is the obvious alternative spend of the same teacher compute and may close the quantization gap without any training. - The GRPO-post-trained teacher and student share a checkpoint and task-specific training data, so the teacher reference is guaranteed strong on-distribution; behavior when the teacher itself is weak or references are rare (the paper's own fallback silently degrades to plain on-policy distillation) is unquantified — no experiment reports what fraction of rollouts actually receive corrections per benchmark. - Search QA mixes in-domain (NQ, HotpotQA) and five out-of-domain datasets, but the QA setting is single-turn relative to the multi-turn tool environments where the mechanism operates; evidence that divergence-localization matters for Search QA specifically is thin. - Statistical rigor is asymmetric: four-run error bars exist for one benchmark's training curve, but headline cross-benchmark deltas of 1.67–2.18 points carry no variance estimate. - Steering-prompt sensitivity is tested across format and source (Q3), but not robustness to verification noise (false accepts/rejects), which in noisier real environments is the likely failure point. Bottom Line: For practitioners post-training quantized agents in simulated, state-checkable environments, SteerDistill is the strongest documented recipe in its setting and the ablations alone justify reading it; for anything outside that envelope — live web agents, unrestorable state, or no verifiable references — its central mechanism is unproven, and QeRL or plain on-policy distillation remain the safer default.

Learning Heterogeneous Tactile Representation for General Dexterous Manipulation (92 ▲ )

Bing Han, Yichuan Peng, Haoyu Dong, Yuanmeng Hu, Yongyi Jia, Fangjing Wang, Kecheng Zheng, Yiming Zhang, Yanhong Zeng, Xiaoqing Zhang, Chen Song, Rundong Zou, Anqi Dong, Yuan Guan, Ka Leong Cheng, Xing Zhu, Yujun Shen, Nan Xue, Wei Ning · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 10 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces LingBot-Touch, a tactile foundation model and a 5,000-hour multi-sensor pretraining corpus that learns one frozen contact representation shared across piezoresistive, magnetic, and visuotactile sensors, transferable to unseen sensor models without retraining. - Why it's important: Tactile data are locked to the physics of the sensor that produced them, so no cross-sensor corpus can be pooled and every policy-building effort starts from scratch — this is the main bottleneck preventing touch from scaling the way vision and language did. - How it does it: Every sensor's taxels are mapped into a canonical geometric fingertip space addressed by 5D rotary position embeddings, and a shared Haptic Transformer is trained with a JEPA-style latent-prediction objective (Tactile-JEPA) plus layout randomization, so the model learns contact rather than transducer physics. - The good: The transfer evidence is strong and multi-level: on the XHand1 magnetic sensor absent from pretraining, the frozen encoder beats FTP-1 fitted with a sensor-specific adapter on all five probing tasks (e.g., 1.32 N vs. 3.72 N force error), and the same frozen tokens add 14–26 percentage points across four real-robot policy families on 26 tasks. - The missing: The paper trains and evaluates on two proprietary hands (one seen, one unseen in pretraining) and never compares against other cross-sensor tactile encoders such as AnyTouch, T3, or HTT — FTP-1 is the only external baseline, so the claimed generality is demonstrated against a single competitor. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on tactile representation learning, cross-embodiment robot learning, or VLA conditioning; skip it if you need a careful independent comparison of cross-sensor encoders, because the evaluation is confined to the authors' own ecosystem and one baseline.
