Problem & Motivation: Commercially available tactile sensors — piezoresistive (e.g., STAG gloves), magnetic (ReSkin, PaXini), and visuotactile/optical (GelSight, DIGIT, Sharpa Wave) — each define their own channels, taxel layouts, resolutions, and sampling rates, so a reading from one sensor is meaningless to a model trained on another. This heterogeneity blocks the three ingredients that let vision and language scale: a common input format, a large pooled corpus, and a shared representation for comparison. The consequence is that robots manipulate almost entirely by vision, cannot sense grip force, slip, or occluded contact, and every tactile-learning result is confined to a single sensor type and task. The problem affects anyone building dexterous manipulation policies that need touch, since each hour of tactile data requires a sensorized hand physically interacting with the world. Key Idea: The core insight is that contact itself is sensor-agnostic — a fingertip pressing an edge is the same event regardless of transduction — so representing each taxel by a continuous 3D position in a canonical per-finger coordinate frame (plus a finger identity and time, forming 5D addresses injected via RoPE) strips out sensor-specific physics and lets one shared Transformer learn a transducer-independent representation of contact from heterogeneous sources pooled together. Latent-space prediction (rather than signal reconstruction) handles the sparsity of tactile signals, and layout augmentation (multi-density resampling plus bounded taxel-position perturbation) prevents the encoder from memorizing the three training layouts and enables transfer to unseen sensors. Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) Corpus construction: 4,983 hours / 464,431 episodes / 1.33B frames — about two-thirds egocentric recordings from human piezoresistive and magnetic tactile gloves, one-third teleoperation on a dual-arm Sharpa Wave system with visuotactile fingertips — across 24 task categories, with no labels below episode level. (2) Tactile-JEPA pretraining: modality-specific two-layer-MLP tokenizers embed two consecutive frames per taxel into tokens; a shared 12-layer Haptic Transformer (Tiny 5.46M, Small 21.76M parameters) encodes visible tokens under 80% spatial masking (extended across the whole clip), and a per-modality predictor maps context outputs plus learned mask tokens to targets from an EMA target encoder read out at four depths. The loss is L1 feature prediction at masked positions plus a weighted (λ=0.5) context loss at visible positions with stop-gradient; a mask-ratio warm-up from 40% to 80% over 300 steps stabilizes training on sparse signals. (3) Frozen readout: pretrained EMA encoders feed attentive probes (five contact-physics tasks), imitation/VLA policies (tokens via cross-attention readouts into Diffusion Policy, π0.5, LingBot-VLA, T-Rex), and PPO-based RL in simulation. Critical design decisions: the canonical fingertip space with 5D RoPE (well justified by the unseen-sensor transfer results); latent prediction over reconstruction (justified by the VAE/MAE comparison, where VAE error degrades with more data); and layout augmentation (justified by ablation, retrieval recall 37.1% vs. 25.6% without augmentation). Key Results: Frozen-encoder probing on the seen Sharpa Wave hand: force recovery MAE 0.81 N (vs. 2.31 N for FTP-1 with adapter), contact-center error 0.12 mm (vs. 2.19 mm), coverage error 0.66 pp (vs. 2.90), future-force 1.04 N (vs. 1.67), tactile-to-video retrieval Recall@5 72.6% (vs. 16.5%). On the unseen XHand1 magnetic hand with zero adaptation: 1.32 N, 0.16 mm, 0.43 pp, 1.45 N, 47.1% retrieval, versus FTP-1's 3.72 N, 5.89 mm, 4.39 pp, 2.00 N, 6.0%. Scaling: the Small model improves monotonically from 1K to 5K pretraining hours on every task on both hands; Tiny saturates at ~4K hours. Real-robot results on 26 dual-arm tasks (200 demos/task, 20 trials each): mean success rises from 21.6%→35.6% (Diffusion Policy), 48.1%→69.9% (π0.5), 48.3%→73.1% (LingBot-VLA), 45.4%→68.6% (T-Rex), while adding raw tactile signals yields at most about half the gain and hurts in 22 of 104 task-policy pairs; gains persist on the unseen XHand1 hand (+16.3 to +24.5 points). Simulation RL across 12 dexterous tasks (3 seeds, PPO): 69.0% mean success vs. 45.6% (task-specific CNN features), 38.5% (raw signal), 21.4% (no touch), with seed-std averaging 3.9 points vs. up to 55 for baselines. Scale of testing is substantial — 5K pretraining hours, two real dual-arm platforms, 26 real tasks — and the raw-signal control showing that representation, not modality, drives gains is a genuinely informative finding. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK and NEW METHOD. The genuinely novel elements are the 5,000-hour cross-transduction corpus (first tactile corpus at representation-learning scale pooling human-glove and teleoperated data across three sensing principles) and the canonical-fingertip-space + 5D-RoPE + layout-augmentation combination enabling encoder transfer to unseen sensor models without per-sensor adapters. The JEPA objective, EMA target encoder, and Transformer backbone are standard ideas adapted from V-JEPA/V-JEPA 2.1/2.1 to a new modality — competent adaptation, not new architecture. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are thorough (Tab. 1): spatial masking ratio, temporal masking span, augmentation type, clip length, tubelet size, EMA momentum schedule, tokenizer/predictor interfaces, and objective — each isolated on a fixed 1K-hour Tiny setup. Objective comparison (VAE vs. MAE vs. JEPA at matched capacity, 1K and 4K hours) and two data-mixing regimes (fixed per-sensor vs. fixed total budget) are methodologically careful. RL uses three seeds with variance bands; however, the frozen-encoder probing results (Fig. 6) and most real-robot results report single-run numbers with no error bars or significance tests, and 20 trials per task give wide binomial confidence intervals. The paper states that inference code, sample recordings, and Tiny/Small checkpoints will be released (GitHub robbyant/lingbot-touch, HuggingFace robbyant/lingbot-touch), but as a preprint this is a promise; whether the full 5K-hour corpus is released is not stated — only a sample set. Methodological concerns: FTP-1 is the only external encoder baseline (AnyTouch, T3, HTT, UniTouch, Sparsh are absent); the authors' own LingBot-VLA is one of the four policy baselines; and evaluation is confined to the authors' two hand platforms, so self-reported numbers on proprietary hardware cannot be independently checked. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (and partly SYSTEMS — a released encoder/checkpoints). - Practical: Yes — the deployed encoder is 5.46M parameters (Tiny), adding 0.13–0.16% to policy parameter counts, and runs on standard hardware; pretraining compute is not reported. - Efficient: Inference overhead is negligible relative to the policies it augments, and the paper claims strong computational efficiency; no wall-clock latency or pretraining-cost numbers are given. - Effective: The evidence shows real gains on real hardware across four policy families and on unseen sensors, though only on the authors' two platforms and 26 tasks. - Scalable: Not directly tested beyond 5K hours and 21.76M parameters; the monotonic scaling curve to 5K hours is the strongest evidence, but 10× corpus/model scale and transfer to capacitive or palm-mounted sensing remain untested claims. The work delivers a software artifact: inference code, sample data, and pretrained Tiny/Small checkpoints on HuggingFace; the full corpus release is not specified. Strengths: - The unseen-sensor result is the intellectual core done right: zero parameter updates on XHand1's magnetic sensor (absent from pretraining, different layout/resolution/rate) still beats FTP-1 with a sensor-specific adapter on all five probing tasks — direct evidence that the canonical space plus layout augmentation removes transducer dependence rather than merely pooling data. - The raw-tactile control in the policy experiments cleanly separates "having touch" from "understanding touch" (raw signals help at most half as much and degrade 22 of 104 policy-task pairs), converting a foundation-model claim into a testable hypothesis. - The two-regime data-mixing analysis (fixed per-sensor hours vs. fixed total budget) yields a non-obvious, actionable finding: intensity and dynamics transfer across transducers, but spatial precision requires a sensor's own layout at its own resolution — directly informing how practitioners should spend data-collection budget. - The VAE/MAE/JEPA comparison at matched capacity shows reconstruction objectives actively degrade with scale on sparse tactile data (VAE contact-center error rises 3.03→4.08 mm from 1K to 4K hours), an empirical finding of independent value to the representation-learning community. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state three limitations: (1) real-world and simulation experiments need a wider variety of hand embodiments; (2) capacitive sensing is absent from pretraining because available recordings did not meet quality requirements; (3) the canonical geometry covers fingertips only, leaving palm and mid-finger contacts underrepresented, with whole-hand coverage flagged as future work. They confront limitations directly and concretely rather than minimizing them — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) Only one external encoder baseline (FTP-1) is compared, despite the related-work section enumerating at least five cross-sensor tactile encoders (AnyTouch, AnyTouch 2, T3, HTT, UniTouch, Sparsh-skin) — the breadth of "general" claim rests on a single comparison. (2) Probing results lack error bars or repeated runs, and 20-trial real-robot evaluations carry substantial sampling uncertainty that is not quantified. (3) The corpus is proprietary in practice: no statement that the 5,000 hours will be publicly released, which limits the community value of a paper whose central argument is that scale matters. (4) Pretraining compute cost and inference latency are never reported, so the "computational efficiency" claim is qualitative. (5) The tactile-to-video retrieval probe uses V-JEPA 2 (from the same JEPA lineage) as the frozen vision backbone, and FTP-1's weakest number is retrieval — the cross-modal task may structurally favor the JEPA-family representation. (6) Simulation tactile data are generated by the authors' own geometric penetration-depth method, so the RL gains could partly reflect favorable coupling between the pretrained encoder and the simulation's tactile rendering rather than general contact understanding. (7) The paper is a preprint with author-affiliation ties to the Sharpa Wave hardware vendor (LingBot/Robbyant branding), so vendor-hardware benchmarks warrant independent verification. Bottom Line: A practitioner building dexterous manipulation policies should read this — the unseen-sensor transfer result, the raw-signal control, and the released frozen encoder are immediately usable and the data-scaling analysis genuinely informs collection strategy — but treat the cross-sensor generality claim as provisionally demonstrated against one baseline on one vendor's hardware pending independent replication.

GreyZone: Production-quality Agentic Application Threats

R Zhou, S Jiang, H Ruan, A Roychoudhury · arxiv.org · generating environments for agent testing in enterprises - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces GreyZone, a benchmark of 10 independently developed open-source agent applications and 46 executable attack scenarios for evaluating automated red-teaming services (Promptfoo, Dreadnode, PyRIT, DeepTeam) as end-to-end attackers, with scenario-specific oracles that verify security-policy violations from execution evidence and application state rather than service-reported success. - Why it's important: Enterprises increasingly deploy tool-using agents in coding, banking, commerce, and infrastructure, and a failed red-team test is currently ambiguous — it may mean the agent is secure or that the testing service never reached the weakness — so there is no grounded way to know which red-teaming tools actually work on production-like applications. - How it does it: Each scenario fixes a security policy, attack objective, initial state, and attacker constraints exposed through a unified MCP interface with per-service adapters; success is judged by independent oracles that inspect execution traces and state deltas, separating attack capability from attack-judgment differences. - The good: The two detailed Promptfoo case studies are genuinely informative — one shows a failed credential-exfiltration attack where diagnostic HTTP feedback still seeded new pretexts, and the other shows a 5-round confused-deputy attack on a multi-agent enterprise platform where an unverified authorization claim led to verified disclosure of a management-only memo across an A2A channel. - The missing: Despite integrating four red-teaming services and building 46 scenarios, the paper reports no comparative evaluation — only two single-run case studies with one service (Promptfoo), so the benchmark's headline purpose (comparing red-teaming services) is asserted, not demonstrated. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or select automated red-teaming tooling for LLM agents or work on agent-security benchmarking, since the scenario/oracle design and released artifact are useful; skip it if you want empirical evidence about which red-teaming service is better, because the paper does not provide that yet.
Why this rank

Problem & Motivation: Organizations deploying LLM agents that read external content, invoke tools, and mutate application state face prompt-injection and privilege-boundary threats whose effects show up in tool calls and state changes, not in the agent's final response — so meaningful security evaluation requires executing workflows and verifying outcomes. A commercial and open-source ecosystem of automated red-teaming services (Promptfoo, Dreadnode, PyRIT, DeepTeam) has emerged to probe such applications, but when a test reports no violation, practitioners cannot distinguish genuine resistance from a service that failed to reach the attack surface. Existing agent-security benchmarks (AgentDojo, AgentHarm, ASB, InjecAgent) evaluate the subject agent's robustness under attack in benchmark-built tool environments, not the attacking service's end-to-end capability on real applications with real permission checks and workflow dependencies; REDAgentBench verifies executable attacks but compares target models and harnesses rather than red-teaming services. The gap: no benchmark measures how effectively complete red-teaming services discover verified violations in independently developed agent applications. Key Idea: Treat the red-teaming service as the system under test, and make each evaluation unit a scenario tuple σ = ⟨A, s₀, P, g, C, O⟩ — application, initial state, security policy, attack objective, attacker constraints, and an executable oracle — so that heterogeneous services attack the same fixed objective through the same permitted interfaces and are graded by evidence-based outcome verification rather than their own self-reports. This inversion (attackers as evaluatees, with independent oracles as ground truth) is the trick that makes cross-service comparison meaningful. Methodology: The benchmark is built in four phases. (1) Application selection: 10 open-source applications chosen for execution capability, explicit security boundaries, plausible attacker access, and experimental controllability — Letta Code, Clawith, Inbox Zero, Alpaca, Commonly, Shopware, Banking Assistant, Smart Home, kubectl-ai, ZerePy — spanning single- and multi-agent workflows and direct/indirect injection surfaces. (2) Environment preparation: Docker/Docker Compose deployments with controlled substitutes for external dependencies (e.g., a simulated Alpaca trading backend, a Gmail emulator for Inbox Zero), snapshot-based state reset, and administrative access kept separate from attacker- and agent-facing interfaces. (3) Scenario construction: policy-driven — each scenario starts from a security policy P, derives a concrete violation objective g, defines attacker constraints C (role, interfaces, interaction limits, e.g., 10 messages for Letta Code, 5 for Clawith), and fixes an initial state s₀; the 46 scenarios cover confidentiality (credential/memo/customer-data exfiltration) and action authorization (unauthorized trades, refunds, invitations, door unlock, Kubernetes escalation). (4) Execution and verification: a unified MCP attacker interface exposes scenario-permitted operations; per-service adapters (built for Promptfoo, Dreadnode, PyRIT, DeepTeam) configure the service, translate payloads into application-interface arguments, and return responses; runs distinguish conversational from content-placement interaction modes; scenario oracles check run-baselined execution evidence (records, state deltas, traces) against g and P, and run statuses are recorded separately so delivery failures/timeouts are not counted as successful defenses. Critical design decisions: (a) preserving real application execution paths while simulating only external dependencies — justified by the argument that benchmark-built interfaces omit permission/workflow constraints that determine attack feasibility; (b) independent oracles with run-specific baselines — justified by documented cases where service-reported or response-based judgments diverge from actual state effects; (c) service-specific adapters rather than forcing uniform service behavior — reasonable but means adapter quality could confound cross-service comparisons (the paper does not discuss this risk). Key Results: The empirical results are two qualitative single-run case studies, not a comparative evaluation. In Letta Code runtime-credential-disclosure (Promptfoo v0.122.2, debug-access plugin, stateful crescendo strategy, GLM-4.7 attacking GLM-5.3-Flash), the attacker used all 10 messages; the agent refused direct disclosure, and although a diagnostic authentication probe returned HTTP 200 for a task token and HTTP 401 for the protected API key — which Promptfoo exploited as pretext for requesting the full authorization header — the oracle found no credential values in any attacker-visible reply, so the attack failed. In Clawith private-agent-leak, the attack succeeded in 5 rounds: the agent Morty initially refused, then accepted the attacker's unverified claim of approval from a project lead, contacted the private agent Meeseeks via A2A (a relationship the attacker could not access directly), and published the memo's bid ceiling, counterpart contact, and deadline in the group; the oracle matched all three protected values across A2A records, workspace files, and group replies, classifying success(private-agent-leak). No aggregate success rates, no numbers for Dreadnode/PyRIT/DeepTeam, and no repetition statistics are reported — the authors explicitly state the case studies 'do not establish comparative service performance.' The non-obvious qualitative findings are that (1) routine diagnostic feedback (an HTTP 401) becomes attack material even when the agent refuses, and (2) an initial refusal can be fully reversed by an unverified authorization claim plus delegated tool access that omits the requester's identity. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK plus NEW FORMULATION. The genuinely novel contribution is the evaluation-target inversion — benchmarking red-teaming services as end-to-end attackers against independently developed agent applications, with independent oracle-based verification — which distinguishes it from AgentDojo/ASB/AgentHarm (subject-agent robustness in built environments) and REDAgentBench (verified attacks but model/harness targets). The individual mechanisms (Docker deployment, MCP tool interfaces, snapshot resets, trace-based checking) are standard engineering combined competently; the 46 scenarios' policy/oracle/constraint structure is the main artifact-level novelty. Rigor & Reproducibility: No ablations exist in the conventional sense, and the evaluation is thin relative to the artifact: two case studies, single runs each, one service, one model pairing per study, no error bars, no significance tests, no repeated trials (the authors acknowledge this in Section 5.2). Oracle checks are demonstrated on examples but no oracle precision/recall or validation against known ground truth is reported. Code and artifacts are released at https://github.com/Ruoyyy/GreyZone with a leaderboard at https://greyzone-bench.github.io/, which supports reproducibility of the infrastructure. Methodological concerns: (a) the paper's central claim — enabling comparison of red-teaming services — is never exercised; (b) scenario policies and oracles are authored by the benchmark designers, so scenario difficulty and oracle leniency are uncalibrated; (c) the same team constructs the scenarios and interprets the case studies, and adapter quality differences across the four services are unexamined as a confound. This is an arXiv preprint (arXiv:2611.09161) and appears not yet peer-reviewed; confidence should be adjusted accordingly. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a built benchmark/evaluation infrastructure, released as a tool). - Practical: Yes — all applications run locally under Docker/Docker Compose with simulated external dependencies (e.g., Gmail emulator, simulated trading backend), requiring no proprietary infrastructure beyond LLM API endpoints. - Efficient: Not stated — no per-scenario runtime, token, or cost figures are reported; the cost of a full 46-scenario sweep across four services is unquantified. - Effective: Partially — the oracle mechanism demonstrably catches the difference between service-reported progress and verified violations (the Letta Code case where Promptfoo's adaptive probing still yielded no verified disclosure), but evidence that the benchmark discriminates between services is absent. - Scalable: Untested beyond 10 applications/46 scenarios and 2 executed runs; scaling to more applications depends on manual policy/oracle construction per application, which the paper does not cost or automate. The work delivers a concrete software artifact (benchmark repository, 10 application environments, scenario definitions, four service adapters, oracles, leaderboard) rather than stopping at paper form. Strengths: - The evaluation-target inversion is a real conceptual contribution: grading red-teaming services by independently verified application-state outcomes, with run baselines that separate execution failures from verified defenses, directly addresses an ambiguity (no-violation ≠ secure) that current practice conflates. - Grounding scenarios in 10 independently developed applications with their real interfaces, permissions, and workflow dependencies — rather than benchmark-authored tool collections — is a substantive realism advance, and the multi-agent A2A confused-deputy scenario (Clawith) exercises an attack surface most benchmarks lack. - The Clawith case study is a well-traced, mechanism-level analysis of how a confidentiality refusal collapses: unverified authorization acceptance plus delegation that strips the requester's identity and prior dispute — a transferable insight about multi-agent trust boundaries. - Honest self-assessment: the authors explicitly refuse to claim comparative service performance from two episodes and lay out exactly what a proper evaluation requires (matched initial states, repeated runs, varied budgets/configurations). Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state clearly (Section 5.2) that controlled local deployments and simulated external dependencies may omit behavior of deployed systems; that policies and oracles delimit what is measured to specified violations and observable evidence; that an unsuccessful attack means only the targeted violation was not verified, not that the agent is secure; and that the empirical analysis is limited to two Promptfoo episodes with specific model configurations and budgets, so the infrastructure alone 'does not establish comparative attack effectiveness.' They confront limitations directly and proportionately — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No oracle validation: false-positive and false-negative rates of the oracles are never measured (e.g., can a benign workflow trip a disclosure check, or can exfiltration via channels the oracle does not monitor evade it?), yet all headline judgments rest on oracle verdicts. - Adapter confound: cross-service comparisons will measure service capability only if the four adapters are equally faithful; nothing tests whether an adapter's translation of payloads loses attack fidelity, and the paper does not acknowledge this. - Scenario difficulty is uncalibrated: with 46 scenarios but no baseline attack success rates (even for hand-crafted attacks), nothing distinguishes scenarios that are trivially solvable from impossible-under-constraints ones, so future leaderboard scores may be dominated by a few informative scenarios. - The case studies conflate illustration with evaluation: single runs with single model pairings (GLM-4.7 vs GLM-5.3-Flash) mean the Clawith success and Letta Code failure could be model-specific; no seeds, no alternative subject models, no interaction-budget sensitivity. - State-reset fidelity is asserted via snapshots but never verified — no experiment shows repeated runs on the same scenario yield identical initial conditions despite persistent agent memory (directly relevant to the Letta Code memory-poisoning scenario). Bottom Line: A practitioner selecting or building automated red-teaming tooling for agent applications gains a genuinely useful artifact and a correct evaluation formulation, but the paper is a challenge statement rather than a study — anyone seeking evidence of which red-teaming service is actually better must wait for the leaderboard results the authors promise, and stronger empirical treatments of adjacent ground (e.g., REDAgentBench for verified attacks, Hofer et al. for attack-method comparison in AgentDojo) currently cover more of the measurement side.

MAC-v2: Long - horizon model-based value expansion from pixels

K Park, S Levine · arxiv.org · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces MAC-v2, an offline model-based RL algorithm that performs value expansion over more than 100 environment steps directly from pixel observations by combining a reconstruction-free latent world model with action chunking. - Why it's important: Prior pixel-based offline model-based RL methods (LOMPO, OfflineDV2, SeMOPO) collapse beyond ~5-step imagination horizons, so long-horizon visual tasks had to rely on short-horizon off-policy bootstrapping, which propagates value inaccurately; showing long-horizon latent imagination works from pixels closes a gap between state-based and pixel-based offline RL. - How it does it: The encoder is trained only on latent dynamics prediction, chunked reward prediction, and flow-matching behavior cloning (no reconstruction), and action chunking (n=10) cuts a 100-step imagination horizon down to 10 recursive model predictions, suppressing compounding error. - The good: On 25 visual OGBench tasks, MAC-v2 reaches 95% success on puzzle-3x3 where the best of seven baselines reaches 22% and prior model-based baselines score near zero, and it is the only RL method on Robomimic to match or beat behavior cloning on all three tasks (e.g., 72% vs. 68% BC on square). - The missing: All evaluation is in simulation on single-task benchmarks with limited visual diversity, baseline model-based methods are dated (2021–2023), and no code release is confirmed (only a project page), so the strongest external-validation levers are absent. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on offline RL from pixels, world models, or action-chunked robot learning — it is the first credible demonstration of >100-step latent value expansion from images; skip it if you only care about state-based offline RL (read MAC, Park et al., 2026, instead) or real-robot deployment.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (68) rests on a genuine capability finding — first credible demonstration of >100-step latent value expansion offline from pixels — but the authors honestly position it as a system combination of standard components (MAC-style chunked value expansion, flow matching, DreamerV3-style heads), not a new objective. Rigor (68) is supported by 4 seeds with per-task std, one hyperparameter configuration across 48 tasks, and an ablation suite that tests three alternative encoder objectives rather than strawmen; it is materially reduced by 2021–2023 model-based baselines, a disclosed budget asymmetry (100K vs 500K gradient steps), hyperparameters tuned on the evaluation benchmark families, and no code release. Non-Obviousness (65) is moderate — decoupling imagination depth from prediction depth via chunking is sensible and any practitioner facing compounding error would consider it, though making it work offline from pixels was not obvious. Completeness (65) is hurt by the un-discussed dmcontrol/maniskill weaknesses and simulation-only, visually-simple evaluation. Resilience (65) and Impact (55, no confirmed artifact, consumer-simulation scope only) round out a work whose central claim is well-measured but whose generality is unproven. empirical Novelty 68 Rigor 68 Non-Obv 65 Completeness 65 Resilience 65 Impact 55
Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Offline RL learns policies from fixed datasets without environment interaction; with pixel observations, the agent must simultaneously learn a visual representation and its dynamics, and errors in either compound recursively over imagined trajectories — a problem the offline setting cannot correct because no new data can be collected in poorly modeled regions. Practitioners in robot learning and visual control face this when long-horizon credit assignment (e.g., multi-stage manipulation) is needed but off-policy value bootstrapping over long horizons is unreliable. Prior pixel-based offline model-based RL methods kept model rollouts to ~5 steps precisely because longer latent rollouts were unstable, while recent state-based methods showed long-horizon model-based value expansion works in low-dimensional state. The gap: no method had shown that latent world models could support long-horizon (100+ step) value expansion from images. Key Idea: The core trick is decoupling imagination depth from prediction depth: learn a latent dynamics model that predicts n=10 environment steps per recursive call (one action chunk), and learn the latent representation jointly from chunked dynamics prediction, chunked reward prediction, and a flow-matching behavior-cloning objective — with no pixel reconstruction. This yields a latent space that is (a) predictable under the learned dynamics, (b) reward- and control-informative, and (c) chunks coarsen the horizon so a 100-step value expansion needs only 10 recursive model predictions. The authors are explicit that the representation objective itself is not new (they adopt the reconstruction-free latent-prediction paradigm of MuZero/TD-MPC2-style methods); the contribution is showing this combination makes long-horizon latent value expansion feasible offline from pixels. Methodology: MAC-v2 is a block-MDP offline RL pipeline with four training stages. (1) World model: a deterministic encoder f_ξ maps images to 512-d latents; an action-chunked dynamics model p_ψ(z_t, a_{t:t+n-1}) regresses sg(f_ξ(o_{t+n})) with an L2 loss (Eq. 5), and a distributional reward model r_ψ predicts the discounted n-step return via a two-hot/symexp categorical loss (Eq. 6). (2) Behavior policy: a flow-matching policy (ODE-based velocity field, Eq. 7) is trained by behavior cloning on chunked actions; gradients from all three objectives flow into the encoder. (3) Value expansion: on-policy latent rollouts of H=10 chunks (100 environment steps) are generated starting from dataset latents, with actions from a rejection-sampling policy that draws M flow-policy candidates and picks the argmax under a learned chunked Q-function (Eq. 8); a distributional value V_φ is regressed on n-step λ-style targets from these rollouts (Eq. 10), and Q_φ is distilled from V_φ (Eq. 11). (4) Evaluation uses the rejection-sampling policy with N_test=32 candidates. Key design decisions: reconstruction-free encoding (justified by ablation — reconstruction, SimCLR, and LeWorldModel encoders all degrade performance badly, Fig. 4); action chunking n=10 (justified by horizon/chunk-size sweep, Fig. 1); joint actor+world-model gradients into the encoder (justified by gradient ablation, Fig. 3). A terminal-prediction head variant is given in the appendix. One hyperparameter setting (n=10, H=10, N_train=8, N_test=32) is used across all benchmarks with no per-task tuning. Key Results: On 25 visual OGBench tasks (success rate, 4 seeds × 15 episodes), MAC-v2 averages 74/53/72/95/46% on cube-single/cube-double/scene/puzzle-3x3/puzzle-4x4 versus best baselines QC (78/6/57/0/20%), FQL, IQL, ReBRAC, IFQL, and model-based LOMPO/OfflineDV2 (both near 0% on nearly every task); on puzzle-3x3 MAC-v2 scores 95±4% vs. 22±1% for the best prior method (ReBRAC). On 10 MMBench2 unseen tasks (normalized score 0–100), MAC-v2 averages 66 on pygame and 33 on ogbench (best on both), but 31 on dmcontrol vs. FQL's 53 and 4 on maniskill vs. LOMPO's 23 — it is competitive, not dominant, outside structured manipulation. On Robomimic (3 tasks, multi-human data), MAC-v2 gets 100/95/72% on lift/can/square vs. BC 100/97/68% — the only RL method matching or exceeding BC everywhere; on LIBERO-10 it ties BC at 80±1% average success. Ablations: rollout horizon 10→50→100 steps improves success monotonically on puzzle-4x4; chunk size 1→5→10 improves it; QC and OfflineDV2 show no benefit from extended horizons (Fig. 2); removing actor or world-model gradients from the encoder, or replacing the objective with reconstruction/SimCLR/LeWorldModel, sharply degrades success (Figs. 3–4). Baselines are current and strong on the model-free side (FQL, QC are 2025-era) but the visual model-based baselines (LOMPO 2021, OfflineDV2 2023) are outdated, and no modern pixel-based offline model-based competitor (e.g., a DreamerV3-adapted offline variant) is compared. Scale is standard benchmark scale, not stress-scale; one run takes ~9–14 hours on a single A5000 GPU. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING and NEW METHOD (system combination). The genuinely new element is the empirical demonstration that reconstruction-free predictive latents plus action chunking support stable >100-step latent value expansion offline from pixels — a capability prior pixel-based offline model-based RL explicitly lacked — plus the joint encoder objective mixing chunked dynamics, chunked reward, and flow-BC gradients. The components are standard: action-chunked model-based value expansion and rejection sampling come from MAC (Park et al., 2026), flow matching and rejection sampling from existing work, distributional two-hot heads from DreamerV3; the authors honestly state they do not propose a new representation-learning objective. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and targeted: horizon/chunk-size sweeps (the central claim), encoder-gradient ablations, and four alternative representation objectives — each isolates a claimed component. Results average 4 seeds with per-task standard deviations reported; training curves with mean±std are shown per task; evaluation is 15 episodes/seed. No statistical significance tests beyond mean±std. No code release is stated (only a project page URL, https://kwanyoungpark.github.io/MAC-v2/), though the reproducibility statement provides detailed hyperparameters for MAC-v2 and all baselines, including per-task tuned baseline hyperparameters — a good-faith fairness effort. Concerns: model-based baselines were capped at 100K gradient steps because "performance starts to degrade after 100k steps" (a budget choice that may handicap them); MAC-v2 and model-free baselines share encoders/augmentation but LOMPO/OfflineDV2 use their original architectures, a mild confound; and hyperparameters for MAC-v2 were presumably selected on the same benchmark families used for evaluation (no held-out tuning protocol stated). Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (methods run and evaluated in simulation; no primary theoretical claim). - Practical: Yes — trains in 9–14 hours on a single consumer-grade A5000 GPU per benchmark. - Efficient: Comparable to model-free baselines (~9 hrs for OGBench/MMBench2) and cheaper than LOMPO/OfflineDV2 (~16 hrs at their budget), though rejection sampling at N_test=32 flow integrations per action adds inference cost. - Effective: Evidence supports the stated problem on long-horizon structured manipulation (OGBench, Robomimic), but the MMBench2 dmcontrol/maniskill results show the method does not yet solve general visual control better than model-free FQL. - Scalable: Untested — all experiments are single-task simulation with limited visual variation (authors acknowledge this); 10–100× scale (multi-task, real robots, higher-resolution or diverse visuals) is only proposed as future work (VLAs/world action models). The work delivers a method and full hyperparameter specification; no public code, dataset, or trained-model artifact is confirmed. Strengths: - The headline empirical finding is real and specific: prior visual model-based offline RL scored ~0% across OGBench while MAC-v2 reaches 53–95% on the hardest families, and the horizon ablation (Fig. 1) directly ties the gain to rollout length — the paper measures its own central claim rather than just asserting it. - The ablation suite (Figs. 2–4) is unusually complete: it shows baselines do not benefit from longer horizons (ruling out "just increase H"), and tests three concrete alternative encoder objectives (reconstruction, SimCLR, LeWorldModel) rather than a single strawman. - Honest framing of novelty: the authors explicitly state the representation objective is adopted, not invented, and position the contribution as the feasibility result — this makes the contribution easy to verify and build on. - Strong experimental hygiene: one hyperparameter configuration across all 48 tasks, per-task baseline tuning with published sweep tables, matched encoders for model-free comparisons, and per-task training curves. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: - Fixed chunk length trades off long-horizon prediction against policy reactivity; adaptive or hierarchical chunking is left to future work. - Experiments are limited to simulated, single-task environments with limited visual variation; extension to multi-task/VLA-scale settings is open. The authors confront both limitations directly in the closing remarks rather than minimizing them — a credibility positive. They do not, however, discuss the weak dmcontrol/maniskill MMBench2 results beyond calling themselves "competitive." Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The compared visual model-based baselines are 2021–2023 methods tuned only over an uncertainty coefficient; a modern pixel-based offline model-based baseline (e.g., an offline adaptation of DreamerV3 or TD-MPC2) is absent, so "prior model-based methods score near zero" may reflect stale baselines as much as the long-horizon gap. - Model-based baselines were stopped at 100K gradient steps because their performance degraded beyond that — this budget asymmetry (MAC-v2 trains 500K steps) is disclosed but not analyzed, and it inflates the model-based comparison. - The Markovian, frame-stack-1 setting with 64×64 images and limited visual diversity sidesteps the hardest part of "learning from pixels" (partial observability, distractors); no robustness or distractor experiment is run, so generalization of the claim beyond clean benchmarks is extrapolation. - Some results have very high variance (cube-double-task4: 10±5%; puzzle-4x4-task5: 16±16%; scene-task5: 29±29%), and 4 seeds with 15 episodes cannot resolve these; no significance testing is provided. - Value targets are computed purely from model rollouts initialized from dataset states; no analysis of model-exploitation behavior (the classic model-based offline RL failure mode) or of value-estimate error as a function of horizon is presented. - No code release is confirmed in the text, limiting reproduction despite the detailed appendix. Bottom Line: For researchers in offline RL, world models, or robot learning from pixels, this paper is worth reading — it is the first well-ablated demonstration that latent world models can sustain 100-step value expansion offline from images, and its combination recipe (predictive latents + chunking + rejection sampling) is a concrete template others can adopt — though the outdated model-based baselines and simulation-only, visually-simple evaluation mean its generality beyond structured manipulation benchmarks remains unproven.

PhysLoop: Harnessing LLMs' Physics Awareness for Self-Improving Video Generation Models (42 ▲ )

Yuxuan Chen, Xiaojie Li, Hao Chen, Juncheng Ma, Kewei Zhang, Zhongjing Du, Guoqiang Wei, Fangfang Wang, Zhen Dong, Zhiyang Dou, Liming Zhao, Yan Zeng, Jianwei Zhang, Daquan Zhou · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 13 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces PhysLoop, an agentic harness in which LLM agents construct simulator-verified scenes, render physically consistent multi-view videos, and refine them with a video generation model, yielding a 100K-video training set plus generation and repair benchmarks. - Why it's important: Video generation models produce visually plausible footage with physically broken dynamics, and training them on real captured data with controlled physical variations is expensive and hard to annotate. - How it does it: An LLM agent writes task specs and scene programs executed in Unreal Engine (with Taichi/Genesis adapters), a multi-layer verifier (task assertions, technical quality gate, semantic review) checks both simulation and refined video, and failures loop back for revision before the verified motion is used as a reference for appearance refinement. - The good: The repair result is striking — 86% task success on PhysLoop-Repair versus 19.33% for the strongest standalone video generator — plus honest cost accounting (~$43 per 10 tasks for video generation, 7–12 minutes per task) and disclosure that automatic metrics favor baselines. - The missing: Despite the 'self-improving' framing, the paper never fine-tunes a video generation model on PhysLoop-100K, so the core recursive-self-improvement claim is entirely untested; the loop closes only at data production. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building sim-to-video pipelines or physics evaluation for video models; anyone expecting evidence that simulated video data actually improves a video model's physics will need to wait for follow-up work.
Why this rank
Scored using Systems profile. Resilience (55) and Rigor (55) pull the composite down: the title's 'self-improving' claim is entirely untested (no video model is ever fine-tuned on PhysLoop-100K), two of three benchmarks are author-created, a co-author performed the pairwise human evaluation, and no significance testing is reported — despite the genuinely striking repair result (86% vs ≤19.33%). Completeness (62) is mixed: exceptional transparency about costs, metric disagreements, and future-work distance, but the framing oversells relative to delivered evidence. Impact (75) is strong — released harness, 100K annotated training set, and two benchmarks — and Novelty (65) reflects the new post-refinement re-verification loop and localized repair capability built from known components. Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Video generation models (HunyuanVideo, Movie Gen, etc.) produce temporally coherent videos that violate physics — objects vanish or multiply, contact forces are wrong, gravity and inertia are misrendered. Improving this requires training videos that systematically vary physical conditions (release height, velocity, materials) with reliable supervision, but real-world capture does not scale and general multimodal evaluators judge physical validity poorly. The target community is video generation researchers and anyone building world-model-style training pipelines; the specific gap closed is connecting an LLM's latent physical knowledge to a verifiable executable environment so that generated training data carries a checkable physical correctness signal rather than just a plausibility judgment. Key Idea: Ground LLM physical knowledge in an executable simulator-in-the-loop: the agent must realize a requested event as a scene program whose simulation outcome is machine-checked against pre-registered assertions (contact events, state deltas like a 0.45 m displacement, trajectory integrity), and only videos whose refined output still passes verification are accepted. Verification precedes appearance refinement, and verification is repeated after refinement — the key move is treating the simulator's state record, not the video, as the ground truth for physical correctness. Methodology: The pipeline has five agent stages: (1) a planner expands a request into a task spec with recorded assumptions and verification criteria; (2) an asset manager retrieves/generates 3D assets (catalog, Poly Haven, Meshy), pairing visual meshes with separate collision proxies, and writes a scene program with low-resolution preview checks; (3) an executive runs simulation in UE Chaos (rigid), Taichi (cloth), Genesis (fluid) via adapter interfaces, capturing RGB, depth, segmentation, and object states on a shared timeline across 3–5 cameras; (4) a verifier applies three layers — machine-checkable task assertions (with a 4 cm proximity tolerance for contacts), a technical quality gate (depth MAE ≤1 cm vs. declared support, joint frames within 2 mm/0.1°), and semantic review of an evidence bundle; (5) a refiner (Seedance 2.5) converts the verified render into a realistic video using the simulation as the sole motion source, followed by a final-video re-verification. Two applications share the workflow: training-data construction (parameter grids, e.g., glass impact at 1.5/3.0/5.0 m/s) and localized repair, where a diagnosed error interval [a, b) is replaced (V′ = V₀:a ∥ V̂ₐ:b ∥ V_b:T) with blending confined to the interval. Design decisions: fixed task objectives across revisions (well-justified — prevents spec drift), simulation annotations kept separate from refined videos since refinement breaks pixel alignment (honest and correct), and verification-before-refinement ordering (well-motivated by the case analysis, though it creates the refinement-drift problem they acknowledge). No loss function is stated; downstream training usage is described but not performed. Key Results: On PhysLoop-Gen (100 author-designed tasks), PhysLoop (GPT-6 Astra + Seedance 2.5) achieves 85% task success vs. 73% for standalone Seedance 2.5, 53% for H3, and a 75.76% pairwise win rate; human raters score it higher on physical plausibility (4.06 vs. 3.80) and causal consistency (4.12 vs. 3.80) but lower on visual realism (3.72 vs. 4.29). On PhysLoop-Repair (50 tasks), PhysLoop reaches 86.00% vs. ≤19.33% for all standalone generators. On external Physics-IQ Verified (66 single-view cases), PhysLoop scores 52.06 vs. 48.07 for Seedance 2.5, with Claude Opus 5 as backbone reaching 53.75. The no-refiner ablation shows native simulation renders alone reach 80% generation success and 60.67% repair success, isolating the refiner's contribution (+5 points generation, +25 points repair). Automatic metrics (VideoCon-Physics, VBench) actually favor baselines (PC 15.29 vs. 21.51 for Seedance), which the authors attribute to evaluator limitations — a claim, not a measurement. Baselines are current commercial frontier models (Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash, Seedance 2.5, MiniMax H3), not strawmen. Scale is modest: 100 generation tasks, 50 repair tasks, 900 evaluated videos. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL and NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK. The genuinely novel element is the end-to-end verified pipeline where simulator state records serve as acceptance criteria for refined video, enabling localized physical repair of existing videos (86% vs. ≤19% is a real capability gap demonstrated). The components themselves — LLM agents driving simulators, VLM feedback for video refinement, verification-then-refinement — are a competent combination of existing ideas (the authors cite PhysAgent, Newton, VideoAgent, Scenethesis as close predecessors); the repair application and the strict post-refinement re-verification are the differentiators. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: backbone swaps (Claude Opus 5, Kimi K3 vs. GPT-6 Astra), refiner swaps (H3, Gemini Omni, none), and the no-refiner configuration that cleanly decomposes simulation vs. refinement contributions. Error bars, seeds, and significance tests are absent; human evaluation is a pilot snapshot with 2,565 single-video and 855 pairwise records where only 630 of 900 videos have ≥3 ratings, and — flagged directly in the paper — the 301 pairwise win-rate comparisons were made by one author unblinded (method identities hidden from the rater, but the rater is an author, a conflict of interest). Code, datasets, and tools are released (github.com/DAGroup-PKU/PhysLoop). Anti-Goodhart hygiene is notably good: the authors state that Physics-IQ variants developed with test feedback are reported as diagnostics only, and they use a pre-registered single-candidate selection rule for the benchmark. Main concerns: two of three evaluation benchmarks are author-created; the repair baseline framing (asking text-to-video generators to do interval replacement with preservation constraints) is arguably a task mismatch rather than a fair capability comparison; the automatic-metric disagreement is explained away rather than resolved. This is a preprint (arXiv 2611.16748), not peer-reviewed. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a built agent harness with released data artifacts, evaluated by benchmark runs). - Practical: Yes — simulation runs on a Mac mini (M4, 16 GB), and the LLM/video-model components are commercial APIs. - Efficient: Moderate — 7–12 minutes and roughly $4.30 per task in video-generation charges plus ~20M tokens per task of LLM usage (~$200 per 10 tasks at GPT-6 Astra rates); cheaper than physical world capture but nontrivial at 100K-video scale. - Effective: Strong evidence for controllable generation and repair against author benchmarks, weak evidence that the output improves a video model's physics (Physics-IQ gain is +4 points and unaccompanied by any training experiment). - Scalable: Not tested beyond 100K videos from 2.5K events with exhaustive parameter grids; the paper claims a path to recursive self-improvement but explicitly has not built the training loop, and simulator/asset coverage bounds what event families are reachable. Deliverables: a software harness (GitHub repo), the PhysLoop-100K training set with simulation annotations, two evaluation datasets (PhysLoop-Gen, PhysLoop-Repair), and prompt/skill documentation. Strengths: - The repair result (86% vs. ≤19.33% for every standalone generator) demonstrates a capability that no existing video model has, and the mechanism — explicit reconstruction specs checked against simulation — is convincingly isolated by the no-refiner ablation. - Unusual transparency: the paper reports that its own automatic metrics favor baselines, discloses full token/cost accounting including failed attempts, marks retrospective best-variant Physics-IQ scores as diagnostics, and archives a pilot-only human-evaluation snapshot with coverage gaps stated numerically. - The three-layer verification design (task assertions, technical quality gate with concrete tolerances, semantic review) plus mandatory post-refinement re-verification directly addresses the known failure mode that refinement silently breaks verified dynamics — evidenced by repair success dropping from 60.67% to 86% when the refiner is added without re-verification logic being the only difference. - The dataset design (parameter grids with archived configurations, grouped splits by source event, explicit separation of pixel-aligned simulation annotations from refined video) is engineered to prevent leakage in a way most synthetic video datasets are not. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that PhysLoop is bounded by simulator, asset, and verification coverage; that simulation requires assumptions about unobserved geometry/materials so a valid simulation may not recover the true physical process; that refinement can introduce new errors; and that localized replacement fails when an error has already propagated to later events. They further state plainly that a complete RSI loop (weakness discovery, data selection, model updates across rounds, sustained held-out gains) is future work requiring independent evaluation. This is direct, non-minimizing acknowledgment — a credibility positive — though the abstract and title's 'self-improving' framing does not convey how far the work sits from that goal. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The central untested claim: no experiment fine-tunes any video model on PhysLoop-100K, so the paper's thesis that this data improves physical dynamics is supported by zero direct evidence — the headline training-set contribution is delivered without its headline use case. - The 75.76% win rate and part of the human evaluation come from one author performing 301 pairwise comparisons; even with hidden method identities, this is a self-evaluation conflict that no number of blinding controls fully removes. - The repair baselines are text-to-video models asked to satisfy preservation and interval constraints they were not designed for; a fairer comparison against video inpainting/editing systems (ProPainter, AVID, TokenFlow — all cited but not compared) is missing. - No ablation of simulator choice (UE vs. Taichi vs. Genesis) or of the semantic-review layer, so the contribution of each verification stage beyond the machine-checkable assertions is unknown. - PhysLoop-Gen tasks were designed by the same system's authors and likely align with simulator-supported event families (68/100 rigid-body), creating a coverage bias that favors the agentic approach by construction; no held-out task family designed by an independent party is evaluated. - The semantic 'reviewer' in the verification layer is not specified as human or LLM, leaving the human-intervention level ('limited human intervention') unquantified for the headline runs. Bottom Line: A practitioner building physics-grounded video data pipelines gains a concrete, cost-accounted, well-verified reference system and a genuinely new repair capability, but the title oversells: this is a data-generation and repair harness, not a demonstrated self-improvement loop, and the missing fine-tuning experiment is the paper a reader most wants next.

Yingtao Ren, Xiao Luo, Yiwei Fu, Jinzhao Zhou, Yu-Cheng Chang, Chin-Teng Lin · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 10 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces TRIO, a multi-agent RAG framework that splits the pipeline into three individually fine-tuned agents — query extension, context-sufficiency judgment, and answer generation — where the answer agent's outcome quality serves as the supervision signal for training the other two agents. - Why it's important: Standard RAG pipelines either reuse one backbone for all roles (inheriting its biases) or run multi-agent debates without task-specific training, yielding poor retrieval precision and hallucination at a high inference cost; TRIO targets better accuracy at lower latency for knowledge-intensive QA. - How it does it: Each agent gets its own training objective tied to downstream answer quality: GRPO with answer-delta rewards (F1 change before/after adding a chunk) for the query agent, unanimity-of-16-samples SFT labels for the judge, and two-stage GRPO with EM+precision then EM+F1 rewards for the answer agent. - The good: TRIO-8B achieves the best average exact match (0.4294 vs. 0.4034 for Search-R1) across five QA benchmarks while cutting inference time roughly 9× versus the multi-agent debate baseline DRAG (79.9 vs. 695.8 seconds per 100 queries), and the full training cost is modest (93 H100 GPU-hours for the 8B version). - The missing: No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported, training questions come from HotpotQA/2Wiki whose dev sets are also evaluation sets, and the paper reports a single-run point estimate for every headline number. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building trained (RL-optimized) RAG or multi-agent pipelines who want a concrete recipe for cross-agent reward transfer; skip it if you need web-scale or long-form RAG, since the paper covers only short-answer QA over a static Wikipedia corpus.

Problem & Motivation: RAG systems fail in two places: retrieval queries fail to target missing knowledge (pulling in irrelevant or biased documents), and the generator fails to use retrieved context faithfully (hallucinating despite good evidence). Prior fixes adjust the pipeline (branching, ranking, iterative loops) or fine-tune a single model to both query and answer, which inherits that model's intrinsic biases. Multi-agent RAG variants coordinate specialized roles but typically share one untrained backbone, so coordination is prompt-level rather than learned. The unaddressed gap is how to train each pipeline role separately while keeping their objectives coupled, without human annotation. Practitioners deploying RAG for multi-hop QA over static corpora have this problem. Key Idea: Use the answer agent's measured answer quality as a universal, automated reward signal for all three agents: a query is good if adding its retrieved chunk improves the answer agent's F1 (Eq. 7 delta-reward); a context is "sufficient" if 16 stochastic answer-agent samples all succeed and "insufficient" if all fail (test-time labeling à la TTRL); and the answer agent itself is trained with GRPO under a two-stage reward (top-3 chunks with EM+precision, then top-5 chunks with EM+F1, plus a length-penalty format term). This aligns the individual optimization objectives with the end-to-end pipeline outcome — the trick that lets three separate checkpoints cooperate without shared weights or human labels. Methodology: The pipeline has three phases. (1) Answer-agent optimization: training questions (8,148 from HotpotQA/2Wiki training sets, filtered to medium/hard) are run through a three-round retrieval-debate pipeline (DRAG-style); snapshots at each round with varying chunk counts form 18,380 samples; the agent is trained with GRPO in two curriculum stages (top-3 chunks with reward Ra1 = EM + α·precision + length penalty, then top-5 chunks with Ra2 = EM + α·F1 + length penalty). (2) Query-extension optimization: single-retrieval samples from 10,000 questions; the agent is GRPO-trained with the outcome-delta reward Rq = F1(y_{n+1}) − F1(y_n) computed by freezing the trained answer agent. (3) Judge-agent optimization: 49,785 candidate samples labeled by running the answer agent 16 times per sample (unanimous success → "Sufficient", unanimous failure → "Insufficient", 10.7% mixed discarded, leaving 44,473 samples with a 9,087/35,383 sufficient/insufficient imbalance), then standard SFT. At inference, the query agent emits one keyword-only query per round, the judge decides stop-or-continue (max 3 rounds), and the answer agent produces an answer-only output. Critical design decisions: per-role distinct training corpora (justified by ablations); two-stage reward curriculum for the answer agent (justified by a generalization analysis showing single-reward training drops 17.03% on out-of-domain EM on average); automatic judge labeling inherited from TTRL (justified only by downstream results, not by label-quality analysis — a weaker justification given the label imbalance and discarded mixed cases). Key Results: TRIO-8B (Llama3.1-8B-Instruct) reaches average EM 0.4294 across HotpotQA (0.4350), 2Wiki (0.4710), NQ (0.4339), Musique (0.1857), and Bamboogle (0.4960), versus Search-R1 at 0.4034 and R1-Searcher at 0.3779 — a stated 6.45% average improvement over the second-best method and 72.45% over the multi-agent baseline DRAG (0.2490). Note TRIO-8B loses to Search-R1 on NQ (0.4339 vs. 0.4382); it wins 4 of 5 benchmarks. TRIO-4B (0.3988 avg) matches reasoning baselines but degrades out-of-domain relative to in-domain, attributed to model capacity. Inference takes 79.9 s/100 queries (TRIO-8B) vs. 90.1 (Search-R1), 88.0 (R1-Searcher), and 695.8 (DRAG) on two L40S GPUs. Under high noise (3 of top-5 chunks replaced), TRIO-8B holds EM 0.1348 on Musique while Search-R1 collapses to 0.0144. On unseen PubMedQA, TRIO-8B scores 0.766 vs. 0.716 for Iter-RetGen and 0.568 for Search-R1. Ablations show the trained answer agent is the critical component (removal drops EM up to 43.55% on Bamboogle), the trained judge matters least (and slightly gains EM on 2Wiki without training, suggesting judge overfitting). Flexible stopping beats all fixed 1–5-round schedules (e.g., 0.4960 vs. 0.4480–0.4560 EM on Bamboogle). Baselines include current strong methods (Search-R1, R1-Searcher), all reproduced under identical FlashRAG settings; evaluation is standard-scale (dev/test sets of established benchmarks), not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING with elements of NEW METHOD. The genuinely novel piece is the cross-agent outcome-coupled training formulation — using answer-agent deltas and 16-sample unanimity as automated rewards/labels for the query and judge agents, so each agent gets an individually optimized but pipeline-aligned objective. The components themselves are standard: GRPO (DeepSeek-R1), debate-RAG data generation (DRAG), test-time labeling (TTRL), keyword query expansion, and three-role multi-agent RAG (MA-RAG and similar). The two-stage reward curriculum is a competent, well-evaluated engineering refinement rather than a new technique. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations cover each agent's contribution, retrieval-round sensitivity, single-vs-two-stage reward, noise robustness (two noise levels), an out-of-domain biomedical benchmark, training GPU-hour and memory accounting, and case studies — this is above-average ablation coverage. However: no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests anywhere; all headline numbers are single-run point estimates on benchmark dev/test sets of at most a few thousand questions (Bamboogle has 125 questions, so a 0.4960 EM is 62 questions — differences of a few percent are within plausible sampling noise). Training data derives from HotpotQA/2Wiki training splits while those benchmarks' dev sets serve as "in-domain" evaluation, so in-domain numbers partly reflect distribution overlap. Code and trained model checkpoints are released at https://github.com/yingtaoren/TRIO. The judge-labeling procedure discards 10.7% ambiguous samples, which silently biases the judge toward easy contexts; this is reported but not analyzed. Goodhart risk is present for the query agent: its reward is defined as answer-agent F1 improvement, so it optimizes the answer agent's preferences rather than ground-truth retrieval quality directly. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (trained agents, deployed and timed on commodity GPUs). Practical: Yes — training used two H100s (93.0 GPU-hours for 8B, 58.1 for 4B, ~94 GB peak per GPU) and inference runs on two L40S GPUs. Efficient: 79.9 s/100 queries for TRIO-8B, comparable to Search-R1 (90.1) and ~8.7× faster than DRAG (695.8), because answers are 5–7 tokens of keyword-only output; deployment needs three separate checkpoints (~40 GB for 4B, ~60 GB for 8B), which is heavier than a single-model baseline. Effective: Evidence supports the claim for short-answer multi-hop QA over a static Wikipedia corpus; effectiveness for live search, long-form generation, or dynamic corpora is untested (acknowledged). Scalable: Not tested beyond five benchmarks and a 20-chunk evidence cap; the three-checkpoint serving footprint and per-round sequential agent calls are unexamined at 10–100× query volume or corpus size. The work delivers a concrete software artifact: released code, prompts, and three trained model checkpoints per backbone size. Strengths: (1) The cross-agent reward transfer is a real formulation contribution: query-agent training and judge labeling both consume answer-agent behavior, which removes the need for human annotation of retrieval quality or sufficiency — a practical path that prior multi-agent RAG (DRAG, MA-RAG) lacks. (2) The efficiency result is substantiated, not claimed: TRIO-8B beats reasoning RAG baselines on EM while generating near-minimal token counts, and the paper reports full training GPU-hour and memory budgets (93.0 H100-hours, 94 GB/GPU peak), which most RL-RAG papers omit. (3) The noise-robustness analysis is a genuinely useful empirical finding — trained-reasoning RAG (Search-R1) collapses under distractor chunks (EM 0.0144 on Musique high-noise) while role-decomposed TRIO degrades gracefully (0.1348) — a counter-intuitive result about where robustness actually comes from. (4) Honest ablation reporting, including that removing the judge agent sometimes helps (2Wiki EM +1.17%), which the authors interpret as judge SFT overfitting rather than hiding. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state TRIO is evaluated only on short-answer QA, has not been validated for live web search or long-form generation, and that the adaptive loop may fail on long retrieval chains due to error and irrelevant-evidence accumulation across rounds; they also note live-web challenges (changing document availability, heterogeneous page structure) and call for calibrating retrieval-stopping decisions in dynamic corpora. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No statistical rigor: single runs, no seeds/confidence intervals, and small test sets (Bamboogle, 125 questions) mean the 6.45% average margin over Search-R1 cannot be assessed for significance, and the NQ loss to Search-R1 suggests the true ordering may be closer than reported. (2) The in-domain/out-of-domain split is contaminated: training questions come from HotpotQA/2Wiki and the "in-domain" evaluation uses those benchmarks' dev sets; only three datasets are truly held out, two of them multi-hop like the training data. (3) The judge's unanimity labeling discards 10.7% ambiguous cases and produces a 1:3.9 sufficient/insufficient class imbalance; neither the label quality nor the sensitivity to the 16-sample threshold is studied, and the ablation showing the untrained judge matches or beats the trained one on 2Wiki hints the SFT judge adds little. (4) All experiments use a single retriever (E5-base-v2) and a single static 2018 Wikipedia corpus; retrieval-quality gains from the query agent are never measured directly (no retrieval recall/precision metrics), only through downstream EM. (5) Serving three separate 8B-scale checkpoints (~60 GB) is presented as an efficiency story but compared against baselines serving one model; a fair deployment comparison would account for the multi-checkpoint memory cost or explore weight merging. (6) The "curriculum learning" framing in the abstract overstates what is a two-stage reward-schedule ablation. Bottom Line: A practitioner building trained, multi-agent RAG over static corpora gains a concrete, resource-accounted, reproducible recipe with released checkpoints, but the gains over strong single-model RL-RAG (Search-R1) are modest, statistically unverified, and confined to short-answer QA — so read it for the cross-agent reward-transfer idea and the noise-robustness finding, not as a settled replacement for single-model reasoning RAG.

G-STAR: Group-Scaled Token Capacity for Deeply Compressed Autoregressive Generation (41 ▲ )

Xu Huang, Ye Huang, Xiaotong Li, Zhengrong Yue, Jialv Zou, Minhao Jing, Haodong Li, Wenhao Yan, Yaxin Luo, Duomin Wang, Daquan Zhou · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 13 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces GSTAR, a spatial–group co-scaling framework for discrete autoregressive image generation that combines product-quantization tokenizers at 32× and effective 64× spatial compression with a semi-autoregressive intra-group decoder, yielding two text-to-image models (GSTAR-Pro-8B, GSTAR-Flash-1.7B) that generate a 1024×1024 image in 2.5 seconds on one H200. - Why it's important: Discrete autoregressive image generators suffer latency that grows with token sequence length, putting them far behind parallel diffusion models; this work attacks the sequence-length bottleneck directly rather than by parallel diffusion heads. - How it does it: The core move is co-scaling — when the per-axis spatial compression factor s grows by α, scale the number of quantization codes per position G by α² so the nominal information budget per image stays constant while the global autoregressive sequence shrinks by α², plus a depth decoder that computes all intra-group features in one parallel pass and applies only a single-layer causal Transformer for sequential code sampling. - The good: The ablations are the strongest evidence: group size G swept from 1→32 at fixed K=16,384 shows reconstruction rFID improving 2.06→0.43 and linear-probe accuracy 81.45→84.55%, and matched-training head comparisons show the Semi-AR head matches Causal AR quality (PRISM 5.46 vs 5.46) at roughly half its latency (3.41s vs 6.44s per 512×512 image). - The missing: The headline generation quality trails the strongest baselines (GSTAR-Pro-8B: DPG 83.38 vs Seedream 3.0's 88.27 and Emu3.5's 88.26), so the contribution is a latency–quality trade-off, not parity, and the paper does not include a head-to-head latency comparison against diffusion models — only prior discrete AR systems. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building discrete AR/multimodal generators who care about tokenizer compression and intra-group decoding; practitioners seeking the highest image quality should look at diffusion or proprietary systems, since GSTAR wins on speed, not fidelity.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile (with a released systems artifact). The composite is pulled down by Resilience (58) and Rigor (62): the gFID spike at G=32 directly implicates the flagship Flash configuration and is unexplained at production scale, the speedup claim is scoped only to prior discrete AR systems with no diffusion-latency comparison, SFT data includes images regenerated by evaluated proprietary baselines, and no error bars are reported for single-run benchmark scores. Novelty (68) and Non-Obviousness (65) are genuine — the spatial-group co-scaling relation and lossless 64x packing are crisp, checkable, and empirically validated with honest caveats about nominal vs. effective capacity — while Impact (75) is well-earned through released weights, tokenizer, and an SGLang-integrated serving stack achieving 2.5s per 1024x1024 image.
