Problem & Motivation: LLM-based KGQA methods (ToG, PoG) assume the reasoning chain of graph edges exists, so accuracy collapses when the required triples are missing from the KG — the norm for real KGs like Freebase and Wikidata. Generation-based alternatives (GoG) fill missing links from LLM parametric knowledge, which risks inserting outdated or hallucinated facts. The authors target the middle ground: recover missing path elements from learned graph structure, keeping the LLM grounded in curated evidence. The intended audience is anyone deploying KGQA over production KGs where curation cannot guarantee completeness. Key Idea: Replace LLM hallucination as the recovery mechanism with graph-internal signals: (a) a type-level entity–relation co-occurrence matrix that proposes relations typical for the current entity's type even when the specific edge is missing, and (b) ComplEx link prediction that retrieves plausible tail entities from the embedding space, with the LLM demoted to a semantic pruner over these small, structure-derived candidate sets. Hierarchical bucketing of candidate relations keeps LLM pruning effective when candidate pools grow to ~98 relations. Methodology: XoG runs an iterative planning–exploration–reasoning loop, extending PoG's framework. (1) Planning: an LLM decomposes the question into sub-questions with tracked completion status. (2) Relation exploration: candidates = relations adjacent to the current entity e_c ∪ relations ranked by the normalized co-occurrence score ψ(r_j | e_c) = F[t_c, j]/Σ_k F[t_c, k]; if the pool exceeds a bucket size, a hierarchical strategy prompts the LLM to score buckets independently and merges survivors across rounds. (3) Entity exploration: for each (e_c, r), ComplEx scores ϕ(e_c, r, e) (or reversed) rank top-K candidate entities, optionally pre-filtered by DistilBERT question–entity similarity, then the LLM prunes the set. (4) Reasoning: the LLM updates sub-question status and either answers from the collected paths or loops back for more exploration. Design decisions of note: multi-retention per bucket (justified as protecting bridge relations), random bucket assignment (justified because the pool is pre-filtered), and ComplEx as the KGE (justified as efficient and swappable — but only weakly ablated against alternatives). Key Results: On WebQSP/CWQ with GPT-3.5-Turbo, XoG scores Hits@1 83.7/64.4 on complete graphs and 77.6/55.7 on IKG-40%, beating ToG (76.9/47.2; 63.4/37.9) and PoG (82.0/63.2; 69.7/53.7); with Claude Opus 4.8 it reaches 89.2 Hits@1 on WebQSP IKG-40% vs ToG's 78.6. Token consumption drops 27–33% versus PoG under IKG settings (e.g., WebQSP IKG-40%: 5,634 vs 8,409 total tokens); end-to-end latency is ~12 s/question with KGE scoring adding only ~0.3 s. On the Wikidata-based BRINK benchmark, XoG achieves F1 0.71 (complete) and 0.52 (incomplete), the best among training-free methods under incompleteness but behind fine-tuned GNN-RAG (0.68→0.79 complete; 0.68 incomplete). Ablations show link prediction is the critical component (−7.5 Hits@1 on CKG when removed) and that LLM pruning beats embedding-only top-1/top-3 selection. Error analysis attributes 84–93% of failures to retrieval gaps rather than LLM selection errors. Baselines are recent (2023–2025 methods) with GoG/PoG being the closest competitors; supervised fine-tuned methods still lead on complete graphs. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (partially) and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel piece is modest: substituting KGE link prediction plus type-level co-occurrence statistics for LLM generation as the missing-edge recovery mechanism inside a PoG-style loop, plus the hierarchical bucketing prompt strategy. The planning–exploration–reasoning loop, LLM-as-pruner pattern, and ComplEx scoring are all standard components; the contribution is their integration and the demonstrated finding that structure-grounded recovery beats LLM-grounded recovery as backbones get stronger. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations cover both recovery mechanisms and both LLM pruning modules across three sparsity levels; sensitivity analyses cover bucket size (best at 30: 80.40 vs 77.38 without hierarchy) and retrieval quality (LLM selection accuracy tracks KGE Hits@100). However, no seeds, error bars, or significance tests appear anywhere, and single-run differences as small as 0.7–2.3 Hits@1 (e.g., XoG 83.7 vs PoG 82.0 on WebQSP CKG) are presented without statistical support. Some baseline numbers are copied from the GoG paper rather than re-run, and PoG numbers under incompleteness were produced by the authors. Code, prompts, and setup are released at https://github.com/colab-nyuad/XoG. Main methodological concern: the synthetic incompleteness protocol (random removal of gold-path triples) is itself derived from a benchmark whose gold paths were used to construct the sparsity — a controlled but potentially unrepresentative evaluation, acknowledged by the authors. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a method evaluated through experiments, with a released system). - Practical: Yes — runs on commodity hardware plus API LLM calls; the only GPU need is a one-time ComplEx training (~5 h on one A100 for Freebase). - Efficient: 33% fewer tokens than PoG under incompleteness, ~12 s/question end-to-end, with recovery overhead negligible (~0.3 s KGE scoring) relative to LLM calls (~85% of latency). - Effective: Evidence supports the claim under the tested synthetic-sparsity protocol (beats all training-free baselines on IKG settings across six backbones), though effectiveness on naturally incomplete KGs is unverified. - Scalable: Not stress-tested — evaluation uses Freebase and Wikidata5m at standard KGQA scale; behavior on KGs an order of magnitude larger, or without usable entity-type annotations (a stated requirement), is only claimed, not measured. Delivers a released code artifact with prompts and configuration. Strengths: - The core design move — constraining the LLM to select from structure-derived candidates instead of asking it to generate missing facts — is a clean, defensible answer to the hallucination-vs-coverage trade-off, and the Fig. 1 motivating example makes it concrete. - The backbone study (six LLMs including GPT-3.5 through Claude Opus 4.8) substantiates a non-obvious finding: stronger parametric knowledge does not close the missing-evidence gap, since KG-grounded methods stay well above backbone-matched CoT under incompleteness. - Honest error analysis decomposing failures into selection errors vs retrieval gaps (84–93% retrieval) correctly locates the bottleneck in the embedding retriever, not the LLM — a useful, transferable insight for future work. - Efficiency analysis is measured, not asserted: per-component LLM call, token, and latency breakdowns versus the closest baseline at three sparsity levels. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that (1) ComplEx is a deliberately simple KGE whose quality caps the system (with a synthetic sensitivity study quantifying this), (2) incompleteness is synthetic (random crucial-triple removal, and BRINK's rule-mined removal) and may not match real-world coverage patterns like long-tail or class-uneven gaps, (3) generalization beyond Freebase/Wikidata5m is unestablished, and (4) the method requires accessible entity-type information, excluding KGs without type structure. This is a direct, credible limitations section that does not minimize — a clear credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No variance reporting: with no seeds or confidence intervals, several claimed wins (e.g., 83.7 vs 82.0 on WebQSP CKG; 64.4 vs 63.2 on CWQ CKG) are within plausible run-to-run noise. - The ablation non-monotonicity (w/o Link Prediction scores 62.0 at IKG-40% but 67.0 at IKG-80%) is hand-waved rather than explained, hinting the sparsity protocol's random removal interacts unpredictably with per-question gold paths. - The efficiency comparison is only against PoG; no token/latency comparison against GoG or ToG under incompleteness, so the "best accuracy–cost trade-off" claim is untested against the other main recovery baseline. - Because the synthetic protocol removes exactly the triples on gold paths, type-level co-occurrence statistics may effectively leak which relation types matter for benchmark questions (relation types appearing in test gold paths are the same ones the statistics rank highly) — no experiment separates this from genuine generalization. - The new-in-2026 backbones (GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.8) are evaluated only by the authors with no independent replication, and CoT with GPT-5.5 reaches 74.0 Hits@1 on CWQ IKG-40% — the margin of KG-grounded methods over a strong LLM-only baseline narrows substantially as backbones improve, which the narrative of "stronger LLMs don't solve incompleteness" underplays. Bottom Line: Practitioners building LLM-over-KG pipelines should read this: it is the strongest currently available training-free recipe for KGQA under missing edges, with honest analysis of where it breaks (retrieval quality) — but the gains are incremental over PoG/GoG, rest on single-run synthetic-sparsity numbers, and are unlikely to survive the next generation of LLM backbones unchallenged.

Bayesian Model Discovery with Language Models: Closing the Loop between Hypotheses and Experiments

JK Yuh, B Park, E Choi, J Baek, J Cho, KH Choi… · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Bayesian Model Discovery (BMD), a closed-loop framework in which an LLM proposes candidate model families (functional forms), a numerical engine fits their parameters via sequential Monte Carlo, weighs them by model evidence, and selects the next experiment by maximizing joint expected information gain over families and parameters. - Why it's important: LLM-based scientific agents either predict outcomes via in-context learning without explicit model evaluation, or use Bayesian inference restricted to a fixed candidate set; BMD addresses the cost of scientific experimentation by making each experiment maximally informative while allowing the hypothesis space itself to grow. - How it does it: The core move is a division of labor — the LLM generates symbolic functional forms guided by fed-back numerical beliefs and residual diagnostics, while Bayesian machinery (SMC posteriors, evidence-weighted Bayesian model averaging, joint model–parameter EIG) evaluates hypotheses and picks experiments the LLM cannot evaluate itself. - The good: A controlled fixed-pool ablation isolates each component: moving from direct ICL (A) to LLM-selected model (B) to Bayesian parameter fitting (C) to evidence-based selection (D) yields monotonically lower error, with D achieving a 4.7× reduction in cross-benchmark geometric-mean error over A and lifting pooled top-1 ground-truth identification from 79.3% to 84.8% across 217 runs. - The missing: All evaluation is on simulated benchmarks with noise-free targets, and the structural-recovery comparison against LLM-AutoSciLab is confounded by substantial missing-run exclusions (AutoSciLab contributes only 26/27 ChemBench and 8/15 BoxingGym predictive runs), with no significance testing reported. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building LLM-driven scientific discovery or autonomous experimentation agents — the component-wise ablation and honest accounting of evaluation targets are unusually careful — but practitioners seeking real-world validation will find only simulations here.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. The composite is pulled down by Practical Impact (40) and Rigor (55): no code, prompts, or run logs are released despite a multi-component pipeline depending on a proprietary frontier LLM; there are no significance tests anywhere (only seed-dispersion bands); the headline structural-recovery comparison is confounded by 30–50% missing baseline runs; and all evaluation is on noise-free simulated benchmarks that violate the paper's own likelihood assumptions. Completeness (75) is a genuine strength — the A–D fixed-pool ablation isolating each Bayesian ingredient is exemplary, and limitations are confronted quantitatively. Novelty (65) is moderate: a well-executed synthesis of standard SMC, evidence weighting, joint EIG, and LLM hypothesis generation, with close concurrent competition. Resilience (65) holds for the bounded design-pattern claims but would not survive questions about prior-sensitivity Goodhart risk or real-world noise. Weighted composite: 0.20*65 + 0.25*55 + 0.15*70 + 0.15*75 + 0.15*65 + 0.10*40 = 62.

Problem & Motivation: Scientists and automated-discovery systems face a dual problem: proposing candidate mathematical models of an unknown system and designing experiments that discriminate among them. In-context-learning (ICL) approaches let the LLM predict outcomes and pick experiments directly, but never commit to explicit fitted models or quantify which explanations remain plausible. Classical Bayesian approaches quantify model plausibility and guide experiment selection, but cannot escape a predefined candidate pool. The gap BMD targets is connecting family search, parameter inference, and experiment selection so each informs the others — the authors cite Gandhi et al. (2025) finding no consistent benefit from naively augmenting an LLM with a statistical model as evidence that the coupling, not the components, is the open problem. Key Idea: Treat the LLM as a hypothesis generator embedded inside a Bayesian loop: fit every LLM-proposed functional form with SMC, weight families by model evidence, predict via Bayesian model averaging, choose experiments by joint EIG over families and parameters (decomposed via the mutual-information chain rule into model-discrimination and parameter-refinement terms), and return posterior beliefs plus residual diagnostics to the LLM so its next proposals target what current models fail to explain. The insight is that LLMs and Bayesian inference have complementary strengths — broad domain priors for proposing forms versus principled evaluation of fits — and that the loop closes only when numerical feedback drives the next proposal round. Methodology: The pipeline per round: (1) an LLM (Claude Opus 5.5, medium reasoning, anonymized variable names, withheld task metadata on three of four benchmarks) proposes functional forms subject to a fixed operator grammar (≤6 coefficients, ≤15 operators; ±sin/cos on ForceBench), coefficient roles, and a fixed per-task likelihood family; (2) a numerical engine runs SMC tempering (500 particles × 2 chains, ESS target 0.5, PyMC or JAX) to produce parameter posteriors and evidence estimates Ẑ_m under role-based priors (e.g., N(0,1) signed, LogNormal(0,1) positive); (3) the pool retains the K=12 highest-evidence families and predictions use an evidence-weighted posterior-predictive mixture; (4) the next design maximizes joint EIG a_t(x) = I(Y_x; M, Θ_M | D_t), estimated by Monte Carlo log-likelihood ratios with 128 posterior draws and optimized by gradient ascent (Adam) or finite-difference/compass search depending on benchmark; (5) evidence weights, posterior summaries, one-step predictive log scores, and standardized residuals are fed back into the proposer prompt, with an archive-review mechanism that can revive retired candidates every fifth round. Critical design decisions: joint rather than model-only or parameter-only EIG (justified by ablation, Fig. 5); explicit belief + residual feedback (justified by 2×2 ablation, Fig. 6); fixed observation-likelihood family per task with role-based priors (partially justified — the supplied-form diagnostic in Table 11 shows posterior medians badly biased, 10.70–27.61 vs. truth 50, on a hard task, indicating prior/inference sensitivity the authors flag but do not resolve). Key Results: Across ChemBench, BoxingGym, ForceBench, and NewtonBench (90, 15, 15, 27 sequential runs respectively, 3 seeds each), BMD attains the lowest final prediction error on all four benchmarks against direct ICL, LLM-AutoSciLab, Box's Apprentice, and DP-Agent, e.g., final geometric-mean errors of 2.90×10⁻⁶ vs. ICL 2.72×10⁻⁴ (observation target, ChemBench EIG seed 31) and ForceBench trajectory nMSE down to ~10⁻⁵–10⁻⁸ range. In strict functional-form recovery, BMD recovers true forms on BoxingGym, ForceBench, and NewtonBench where AutoSciLab achieves zero strict recovery; on NewtonBench AutoSciLab often selects containing-but-not-equivalent families while BMD achieves high recovery under both criteria. The fixed-pool ablation (217 runs) shows relative error falling 1.000 (ICL) → 0.613 (LLM model) → 0.369 (Bayesian fit) → 0.214 (evidence selection), i.e., 4.7× overall reduction, and GT identification rising 79.3% → 84.8%. Joint EIG beats model-only, parameter-only, and random selection on both tested benchmarks. Baselines are recent (2025–2026 LLM agents) and run under a matched information interface, which is a strength; however, some baseline curves omit 30–50% of runs (AutoSciLab 8/15 BoxingGym, Box's Apprentice 10/15), and bands summarize seed dispersion rather than confidence intervals. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL with an EMPIRICAL FINDING component. The genuinely novel element is the specific closed-loop integration: joint model–parameter EIG computed from fitted SMC posteriors and evidence within an evolving LLM-proposed family pool, plus belief/diagnostic feedback into the proposer. Individually, each piece is standard — SMC posterior/evidence estimation, joint EIG criteria (Borth 1975; McGree 2017), LLM symbolic proposal (LLM-SR, BoxLM), and evidence-weighted model comparison (recent concurrent work) — so the contribution is a well-executed synthesis of known Bayesian design and LLM hypothesis generation, in a space with close concurrent work (Murphy 2026's Model Discovery Agent) that the authors discuss explicitly. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are a clear strength: the A–B–C–D fixed-pool study isolates explicit modeling, parameter inference, and model selection separately; the EIG ablation and 2×2 feedback ablation each change exactly one factor with shared initialization via replayed round-0 state. Evaluation is unusually careful — a deterministic versioned structural judge (symbolic canonicalization plus numerical spot checks), explicit strict-vs-containment criteria, disclosure of prediction-target subtleties (observation mean vs. primary law, with a decomposition and concrete counterexample in Appendix H), and full accounting of missing/terminated runs. No error bars or significance tests are reported (only seed-dispersion bands, explicitly disclaimed as not confidence intervals). No code, data, or artifact release URL is mentioned. Methodological concerns: development diagnostics (Appendix H) were run on the same benchmark family later used for headline results, though the authors segregate cohorts; priors and prompt scaffolding are hand-tuned per benchmark; the structural-recovery comparison is confounded by unequal run inclusion; and all targets are noise-free simulated quantities, so real experimental noise is never confronted. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a framework run on simulated benchmarks). - Practical: Yes in principle — it needs API access to a frontier LLM plus PyMC/JAX on commodity hardware, but depends on Claude Opus 5.5, so availability is gated by a proprietary model. - Efficient: Nontrivial per-run cost: 100–160 paid LLM calls, 500-particle × 2-chain SMC with 600–1800-second fit limits, and multi-start acquisition optimization per round; how this compares in cost to baselines is not stated. - Effective: The evidence shows it solves the proxy (prediction error and structural recovery on noise-free simulated laws), not real-world discovery; the supplied-form control showing biased posteriors even with the correct form suggests effectiveness can degrade on hard identification problems. - Scalable: Not tested beyond ~30-observation budgets and ~12-family pools; behavior with larger budgets, higher-dimensional design spaces, or less constrained grammars is claimed only implicitly. Deliverable form: paper only — no released library, dataset, or trained artifact is mentioned. Strengths: - The component-isolating fixed-pool ablation (A–D, 217 shared-candidate runs with the GT family inserted) is the cleanest demonstration in the paper: it separates hypothesis generation from model evaluation and shows each Bayesian ingredient adds measurable value, directly answering Gandhi et al.'s negative result about LLM-plus-statistical-model augmentation. - Honest evaluation infrastructure: the strict-recovery judge distinguishes structural equivalence from mere containment, discloses unresolved symbolic checks as failures, separates prediction-target ambiguity with an explicit error decomposition, and reports exact missing-run lists rather than silently dropping them. - The anonymization protocol (withheld variable names and task metadata on three benchmarks) strengthens the claim that discovery is driven by numerical feedback rather than semantic leakage from the LLM's priors about benchmark tasks. - The discovery-trajectory analysis (Fig. 4) demonstrates a property pure Bayesian methods cannot have — introducing a missing ground-truth family mid-run at n=9 after it was absent from the initial pool — which is the clearest qualitative evidence for the closed-loop design. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that (1) all experiments are on simulated tasks and real-world validation is future work; (2) uncertainty estimates are conditional on the finite current candidate pool, not the space of all laws; (3) discovery depends on the LLM generating a suitable family at all; and (4) structural-recovery evaluation covers only targets expressible in the modeling interface (e.g., Bessel functions and image sums on ForceBench, normal CDF on one BoxingGym task, trigonometric functions on NewtonBench Malus are excluded). They also disclose in appendices that posterior medians can be badly biased even with the correct form supplied (Table 11) and that calibration was not established across worlds. This is a credibility positive: limitations are confronted directly and quantitatively, not minimized. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No significance testing or paired statistical comparison anywhere; headline claims rest on geometric-mean curves whose bands are seed dispersion only, and some curves pool different task–seed sets due to baseline exclusions (AutoSciLab 8/15 BoxingGym, Box's Apprentice 10/15), so the recovery comparison in Fig. 3 is not apples-to-apples on identical denominators. - Evaluation targets are noise-free simulators, and several benchmarks return deterministic responses to repeated designs — directly contradicting the conditional-independence likelihood assumption used for fitting (the authors note this discrepancy in Appendix A but do not measure its effect). - Prior sensitivity is only probed via one supplied-form control; role-prior choices (e.g., wide vs. default) are benchmark-tuned, and the evidence-based model selection that drives everything depends on these priors, raising a Goodhart concern given development diagnostics ran on the same benchmark family. - Compute/cost comparisons between methods are absent — the paper cannot support any claim of efficiency relative to baselines. - Only joint-EIG vs. its components and Random are compared head-to-head; the EPIG comparison is relegated to an auxiliary study with an older configuration and different runs, so the acquisition-function recommendation rests on two benchmarks. - No release of code, prompts beyond the appendix text, or run logs is mentioned, which limits reproducibility of the multi-component pipeline. Bottom Line: A practitioner building autonomous scientific-discovery agents should read this: the division-of-labor thesis is convincingly validated by the best component ablation I have seen in this subfield, but the absence of real-experiment validation, statistical testing, released artifacts, and the close concurrent competition (Murphy's MDA) mean it establishes a strong design pattern rather than a settled or deployable solution.

DAISY: Fault-Guided Assertion Inference for Dafny

ÁF Silva, R Martins, A Mendes · sat-group.github.io · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds DAISY, a tool that repairs Dafny verification failures caused by missing helper assertions by localizing likely insertion points (via verifier diagnostics, LLM prediction, or their union), generating candidate assertions with retrieval-augmented LLM prompting, and validating candidates with the Dafny verifier. - Why it's important: Writing helper assertions dominates proof-engineering effort in industrial verification and is a documented barrier to adoption of verification-aware languages, so automating this step lowers the cost of formal verification for practitioners. - How it does it: The core move is a two-stage localization-then-generation pipeline that treats verifier error messages and LLM-predicted positions as complementary signals (union of both works best), then validates up to 10 ranked candidates per placeholder directly with the verifier rather than trusting LLM output. - The good: On a new 448-program benchmark derived from DafnyBench, the best configuration (Claude Opus 4.5 + combined localization) verifies 86.0% of programs with one missing assertion and 61.4% overall, with statistically significant improvements (McNemar's test, α=0.05) over diagnostic-only and LLM-only localization. - The missing: Each configuration is run only once with no error bars or repeated seeds, the w/o-all tier has just 28 instances, and the benchmark is synthetic (assertions removed from verified programs), which may not represent organically failing proofs. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers and tool-builders in LLM-assisted formal verification — the localization-strategy ablation, validity-based localization metric, and tiered difficulty benchmark are directly reusable — but practitioners wanting a drop-in Dafny assistant should also compare against Laurel, which this paper extends but does not head-to-head benchmark.

Novelty (55) is the main drag: the pipeline inherits Laurel's localize-generate-validate skeleton, and the contribution is extension to multi-assertion cases plus a union-localization trick — incremental over clear prior art, with no head-to-head against Laurel itself. Rigor (62) is mixed: McNemar's tests and an ExactFL upper-bound control are good practice, but single runs, a synthetic benchmark (assertions stripped from verified programs), and a mildly leaky pre-test temper confidence. Completeness (68) is a strength — the failure taxonomy, cost accounting, and bounded-pairing trade-off are confronted directly. Non-Obviousness (60) is saved by the inter-assertion-dependence finding (35.9% vs ~74% independence prediction). Impact (62) reflects a released tool and reusable tiered benchmark. Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Dafny programs rarely verify with specifications alone; developers must insert numerous helper assertions that guide the SMT solver without changing program behavior. Industrial reports cited in the paper (formal verification of cryptographic systems) and developer studies (Oliveira et al., ISSRE 2025) identify failing-proof repair — with missing assertions as the primary cause — as the majority of proof-engineering effort. The closest prior system, Laurel (OOPSLA 2025), handles mainly lemmas and single missing assertions; the gap is repairing failures in ordinary program code where one or more interdependent helper assertions may be needed. Key Idea: Combine verifier diagnostics and LLM-based fault localization as a union of candidate insertion points, then generate verifier-validated candidate assertions per point with retrieval-augmented prompting. Two sub-ideas matter: (1) verifier-diagnostic heuristics are precise but pattern-limited, LLM localization exploits broader context but is less reliable, and the union of both dominates either alone; (2) successful repair need not reconstruct the original proof — any assertion set that lets Dafny verify the original specification is acceptable, and the paper empirically shows inferred assertions often differ from ground truth. A key enabling decision is the bounded candidate-combination search: rather than the Cartesian product of ranked candidate lists across multiple placeholders, DAISY evaluates each candidate individually and rank-aligned combinations. Methodology: DAISY is a three-stage pipeline. (1) Fault localization consumes a failing method plus verifier diagnostics and produces insertion placeholders, using five strategies: DiagFL (Laurel-derived diagnostic rules), DiagFL+ (adds four new rule categories: LoopInvariants, TimeOut, SubsetConstraints, ElementNotInDomain), LLMFL (zero-shot LLM localization), ExLLMFL (few-shot with three retrieved examples), and BothFL (union of DiagFL+ and ExLLMFL positions). (2) Assertion inference consumes the localized program and prompts an LLM for up to 10 ranked candidates per placeholder; in-context examples are selected from a repair corpus by zero-shot, random, TF-IDF, code-embedding (jina-embeddings-v2-base-code), or hybrid embedding retrieval scored as α·sim_error + (1−α)·sim_code, with α ∈ {0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1}. (3) Verifier validation runs Dafny (fork of v4.10, Z3 4.15.4, 60s timeout) on each candidate individually and on rank-aligned combinations. There is no explicit loss function — the objective is verification success (pass@10 under a fixed budget). Critical design decisions: the union-based localization (justified by a localization-quality study showing 80% valid placements vs. 72% for DiagFL+ alone), the bounded pairing strategy for multi-assertion cases (acknowledged as a tractability trade-off that can miss correct combinations), and reporting only pass@10 since parallel validation of 10 candidates costs roughly the same latency as one. Key Results: On the 448-program benchmark (236 w/o-1, 184 w/o-2, 28 w/o-all, derived from DafnyBench's 782 verified programs by systematic assertion removal), with Claude Opus 4.5: BothFL verifies 86.0% of w/o-1, 35.9% of w/o-2, 21.4% of w/o-all (61.4% combined), versus ExLLMFL at 78.0%/33.2%/28.6% and DiagFL+ at 75.4%/6.0%/21.4%. With the cheaper Claude Haiku 4.5, BothFL reaches 67.4%/14.1%/21.4% (42.6% combined), and ExactFL (ground-truth positions) reaches 50.0% combined, bounding what generation alone can do. Localization quality: BothFL places assertions at verifier-valid positions in 80% of cases vs. 72% (DiagFL+), 61% (ExLLMFL), and 25% unsupported cases for DiagFL. Retrieval: MixEmb0.25 achieves 50.0% combined success with ExactFL vs. 40.6% zero-shot, but does not significantly outperform plain TF-IDF (48.7%), and random examples give no benefit. A counter-intuitive finding: the w/o-2 success rate (35.9%) is far below the ~74% independence prediction (0.86²), showing inter-assertion dependencies are the real bottleneck. Localization validity correlates with downstream success: valid positions are 60% more likely than partial positions to yield verified repairs. A full-response single-shot baseline (FullResponse) is less reliable and 5–10× more expensive ($20 vs. $2.8 per dataset pass with Haiku). Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (combined diagnostic+LLM fault localization for assertion placement; multi-assertion inference) and NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (448 verification-failing DafnyBench variants tiered by number of removed assertions) plus a reusable validity-based localization evaluation metric. The core skeleton — localize, retrieve, generate, verifier-validate — is Laurel's; the genuine novelty is extending it to multi-assertion failures in program code, the LLM-as-localizer component with union combination, and the controlled difficulty-tiered evaluation. The retrieval methods themselves are standard. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are systematic and well-designed: five localization strategies, nine retrieval strategies, two models (Haiku and Opus 4.5), plus ExactFL as a localization-upper-bound control. McNemar's tests (α=0.05) are applied to key comparisons. Toolchain versions are pinned; the tool and artifacts are stated to be on GitHub with a self-contained Zenodo artifact (no URLs given in the text). Methodological concerns: (1) each configuration runs once — the authors acknowledge sampling noise but provide no repeated-seed variance; (2) the benchmark is synthetic — assertion removal is not the same distribution as organically failing proofs, and the paper's benchmark construction filters to cases where removal actually breaks verification, which is honest but means results do not directly transfer to real developer failures; (3) the model pre-test used 30 instances with ground-truth positions, a mild form of selection on the evaluation data; (4) the retrieval corpus overlaps the benchmark domain (same-function examples excluded, but cross-program leakage is not analyzed); (5) the paper does not run Laurel itself as a baseline on the new benchmark, comparing only against its own strategy variants and a FullResponse baseline. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a built tool evaluated by experiments, not production deployment). - Practical: Yes — it needs only API access to an LLM (Bedrock/OpenAI), Dafny, and Z3, all commercially available; per-dataset evaluation costs are measured at $1.6–$2.8 with Haiku. - Efficient: The two-stage design is cheaper than one-shot full-response prompting ($2.8 vs. $20 for equivalent 10-candidate budget), and parallel candidate validation keeps latency near single-candidate cost. - Effective: Evidence shows it solves the stated problem on its own benchmark (86% single-assertion, 61.4% combined), but effectiveness on real-world failing proofs rather than synthetically stripped ones is unmeasured. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 448 programs; w/o-2 performance (36%) already degrades sharply with two interdependent assertions, and the bounded pairing search would grow combinatorially with more placeholders, so behavior at higher assertion counts is untested. The work delivers a software artifact (tool on GitHub, self-contained artifact on Zenodo) and a public benchmark dataset. Strengths: (1) The combined-localization finding (union of diagnostic and LLM-predicted positions) is a genuine, statistically supported insight with a mechanistic explanation — diagnostics are precise but pattern-bound, LLMs add positional diversity — and the paper demonstrates complementarity with concrete examples. (2) The validity-based localization metric, which classifies insertion points by whether the ground-truth assertion verifies there rather than by edit distance, is a real methodological contribution: the perturbation study showing up to 25 valid locations per assertion and 40+ line separations justifies it. (3) The tiered benchmark (w/o-1, w/o-2, w/o-all) turns synthetic corruption into a controlled difficulty axis and produced a non-obvious finding about assertion interdependence. (4) Honest cost accounting ($50 Haiku vs. $250 Opus for ablations) and explicit reporting of the bounded-pairing trade-off reflect unusually transparent engineering. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly. They note: single-run nondeterminism with no repeated seeds (deemed prohibitively expensive); potential pretraining data leakage, partially mitigated by showing that retrieved examples improve results and that inferred assertions often differ from ground truth; a 14% residual failure rate on w/o-1 even with perfect localization, with a manual failure taxonomy (missing by-proofs with reveal clauses, sequence slice/concatenation reasoning, context omissions, near-miss arithmetic errors); the small w/o-all tier (28 instances) treated as a stress test rather than a comparison basis; and the bounded pairing strategy potentially missing correct multi-assertion combinations. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No direct comparison with Laurel on the new benchmark — DAISY extends Laurel's rules but never measures whether it actually outperforms the prior system on comparable inputs, only that DiagFL+ (its Laurel-derived strategy) is dominated by BothFL. (2) The retrieval corpus construction is underspecified relative to the test set: excluding same-method examples prevents obvious leakage, but whether corpus programs overlap the DafnyBench test programs is not stated. (3) The synthetic benchmark may inflate practical relevance: removing one assertion from a verified program is a narrow failure mode, whereas real verification failures often involve wrong specifications or code bugs that DAISY explicitly does not touch. (4) The FullResponse baseline was observed to "sometimes modify unrelated code," but no systematic measurement of unsafe modifications is reported. (5) Validity of positions is measured using ground-truth assertions, which the authors note is not exhaustive, yet downstream claims lean on this metric without quantifying how often LLM-generated assertions succeed at positions the ground-truth assertion cannot. (6) The paper dates LLM evaluations to January 2026 with models like GPT-5.2 and Claude Opus 4.5 — given rapid model churn, the reported numbers are a moving target rather than a stable result. Bottom Line: A practitioner or researcher in LLM-assisted deductive verification gains concrete value from this paper — a reusable benchmark, a validated localization-combination strategy, and honest cost/effectiveness data — even though it incrementally extends Laurel rather than replacing it, and its synthetic benchmark leaves real-world generalization unproven.

Reframe: Observation-Aligned Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation for Agentic Visual Reasoning (38 ▲ )

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Reframe, a two-stage post-training framework — Ground-Drop-GRPO (GD-GRPO) for training spatial/temporal tool-use specialists, followed by Observation-Gated-MOPD (OG-MOPD) for repairing deficient tool actions mid-rollout during multi-teacher on-policy distillation — that unifies image and video agentic visual reasoning in a Qwen3.5-9B model without SFT cold start. - Why it's important: Agentic VLMs frequently invoke tools but ignore what the tools return ('observation neglect'), and unified image–video training via SFT-then-RL lags badly behind single-modality specialists; both failure modes cost real accuracy in perception-heavy applications. - How it does it: GD-GRPO couples grounding (IoU-based) rewards with stochastic dropping of the original visual input after the first tool call (with drop-conditioned advantage subgroups), forcing the policy to rely on tool-returned observations; checkpoint selection and reward thresholds are developed on the same benchmarks used for headline claims. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building tool-use VLM post-training pipelines — the observation-dropout and mid-rollout repair mechanisms are concrete, reusable ideas — but general readers can rely on Tables 2–4; the heavy reward-engineering appendix is only useful if replicating the setup.

Problem & Motivation: Agentic visual reasoning equips VLMs with tools (image cropping, frame selection) to acquire fine-grained evidence. Two gaps motivate this work. First, invoking a tool does not guarantee the model uses the returned observation — the authors cite prior causal audits showing tool outputs may have little effect on predictions ('observation neglect'). Second, models trained to handle both image and video tools via mixed-data SFT-then-RL end up significantly worse than single-modality specialists, which the authors attribute to off-policy SFT pattern conflict plus sparse RL credit assignment. Practitioners building vision agents need a post-training recipe that produces genuine tool reliance and consolidates modality specialists without sacrificing on-policy exploration. Key Idea: Treat the observation state — not just the output distribution — as an object of alignment, via two complementary mechanisms: (1) make the tool-returned observation necessary by stochastically deleting the original visual input mid-rollout after the first tool call (with advantages normalized within pre-sampled drop/keep subgroups so the dropout condition cannot confound credit assignment), and (2) keep the observation valid during distillation by surgically replacing only missing, invalid, or low-IoU tool actions with annotation-derived canonical actions before the teacher supervises the continuation. The repaired-action tokens get NLL loss; the student-generated continuation keeps standard MOPD reverse-KL supervision. Methodology: Stage 1 (GD-GRPO) trains a spatial specialist (CropImage) and a temporal specialist (SelectFrames) from Qwen3.5-9B on the image/video subsets of a new 100K-example corpus. The reward is R = R_ans + f(p)·R_call + λ_obs·R_obs − R_pen, where R_obs is IoU-based grounding quality (global one-to-one matching of crops for images; latest-attempt frame IoU with 0.85 discount for videos), R_call is a decaying exploration bonus, and grounding credit is not gated on answer correctness. Original-observation dropout (p=0.5 after first successful tool call) forces reliance on returned evidence, and advantages are normalized within subgroups sharing the pre-sampled drop flag. Stage 2 (OG-MOPD) consolidates the two specialists: an 'observation gate' checks each student tool action against annotated evidence (δ_crop=0.25, δ_select=0.15 IoU thresholds), replaces deficient actions with canonical ones, executes them, and resumes student sampling from the repaired observation; the loss is L_MOPD(student tokens) + λ_br·L_NLL(injected tokens). Data construction (Reframe-100K: 63K image + 37K video QA) uses a five-step cascade: text-shortcut removal via DeepSeek V4.1-Flash, full-input and evidence-only auditing with 8-sample pass-rate filters, and LLM-based final review. Key design decisions: restrict to two tools (justified for simplicity, though limiting), annotation-derived tool-applicability labels (justified as avoiding base-model prediction bias), and context expansion of boxes (1.5× spatial, ±1 frame temporal) — reasonable but heuristic choices. Key Results: On 14 benchmarks (7 image, 7 video) with Qwen3.5-9B base, Reframe reaches 69.48 image average and 53.10 video average, beating vanilla MOPD (68.19/52.32), Mix-RL (66.75/51.41), and both single-modality specialists (67.92 image / 52.78 video for Video-RL) — it surpasses its own teachers. Against external agentic models, it exceeds the strongest external image/video averages by 11.71 and 8.86 points, though those baselines appear to use weaker base models. GD-GRPO vs outcome-based GRPO: image average 67.92 vs 65.85, tool gain +3.82 vs +1.97, dependence 69.03 vs 52.59. OG-MOPD adds +1.29 (image) and +0.78 (video) over vanilla MOPD with the same teachers, with the largest gain on VisualProbe (+4.86). Tool gain is +5.23 vs at most +1.47 for DeepEyes/Thyme/Pixel-Reasoner and −2.45 for DeepEyesV2. Tests are at standard 9B scale, not stress-scale. A notable counter-intuitive finding: cross-modality transfer exists in both directions (image-RL improves video average 49.75→50.39; video-RL improves image average 63.46→66.35), suggesting grounding training improves general perception. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (aligning the observation state, not just outputs, during distillation) plus NEW METHOD (GD-GRPO dropout with drop-conditioned subgroups; OG-MOPD mid-rollout action repair with branch-aware losses) and NEW DATASET (Reframe-100K). The genuinely novel pieces are the original-observation dropout and the selective mid-rollout tool-action repair inside an OPD loop — both directly target a mechanism (conditioning of supervision on observation quality) that prior OPD/MOPD work explicitly leaves untouched. The MOPD backbone, GRPO, reverse-KL distillation, and NLL auxiliary losses are standard; the contribution is their composition with two intervention mechanisms rather than a new learning algorithm. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are substantive for the core claims: GD-GRPO is decomposed against outcome-based GRPO, paradigm comparison isolates Mix-RL vs MOPD vs OG-MOPD with the same teachers and data, and the observation-dependence probe is a controlled experiment (GT/random/blank injected observations with matched pre-continuation text). However: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere, despite evaluation differences of 1–2 points driving several conclusions; the dependence metric (Eq. 6) is a novel self-defined quantity computed on a single 191-question benchmark (V*); the external baselines (Pixel-Reasoner, Thyme, DeepEyes, DeepEyesV2) appear to be built on different, weaker base models, making the 11–12 point average gaps confounded by base-model capability; and the checkpoint is selected by benchmark performance ('select the best-performing checkpoints'), a Goodhart risk if the selection set overlaps the reported benchmarks. Scoring uses an LLM judge (Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite) for non-exact matches, adding judge variance that is unquantified. Code, dataset, and model are stated as open-sourced at https://github.com/EliYuan30/Reframe, with unusually complete training hyperparameters (Appendix B) and evaluation prompts (Appendix A) — a reproducibility positive. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (trained models and benchmark experiments; the framework is a training recipe, not a deployed system). - Practical: Yes — a 9B model trained on 32 GPUs for specialist RL and 8 GPUs for distillation with frozen vision encoder, well within commercial feasibility. - Efficient: Distillation is cheaper than joint RL (8 vs 32 GPUs) and the inference-time overhead is zero (no gate, no teachers at inference), which is a stated design win. - Effective: The controlled dependence probe and positive tool gain support the causal claim that the model uses tool evidence, but effectiveness is measured on multiple-choice-style benchmarks with an LLM judge rather than open-ended real-world tool use. - Scalable: Only claimed, not tested — no experiments beyond 9B parameters, two tools, and three assistant turns; behavior with richer toolsets or larger models is unexamined. The work delivers a software artifact (code, Reframe-100K dataset, trained checkpoints) plus a reusable training technique. Strengths: - The original-observation dropout with drop-conditioned advantage subgroups is a genuinely clever mechanism: it converts 'did the model use the observation' from a hope into a training constraint, while the pre-sampled subgroup normalization cleanly avoids confounding dropout condition with trajectory quality. - OG-MOPD's selective repair (only deficient actions replaced; NLL only on injected tokens) directly addresses a real structural blind spot of OPD — token-level feedback cannot retroactively fix an observation acquired by a bad earlier action — and the paper articulates the on-policy-vs-validity trade-off honestly. - The evaluation goes beyond accuracy to a controlled causal probe (GT/random/blank observations with ceiling-normalized dependence), which is the right instrument for the 'illusion of tool use' question and yields the paper's most persuasive numbers (75.53 vs ≤41.93 dependence; +5.23 vs ≤+1.47 tool gain). - The 100K dataset pipeline (text-shortcut removal, pass-rate auditing, evidence verification with a final reviewer) is a competent, model-bias-avoiding execution of known data-cleaning ideas, and hyperparameter disclosure is unusually complete. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly frame OG-MOPD as a trade-off between observation validity and on-policy fidelity (an externally supplied action changes the continuation history), and acknowledge that GD-GRPO yields only modest gains in general visual capability (+0.22 tool-free) with its benefit concentrated in tool-mediated reasoning. They note the observation-repair gain is confined to tool-applicable examples with deficient actions. They do not include a dedicated limitations section; limitations emerge implicitly from the analysis. The framing is direct rather than minimizing, which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No variance reporting at all; several headline conclusions (e.g., OG-MOPD's +1.29/+0.78 over MOPD, Mix-RL trailing specialists by ~1.2 points) rest on differences of 1–2 points with no seeds or significance tests. - The external-model comparison is confounded by base-model mismatch — the compared agents were not retrained on Qwen3.5-9B, so the 11–12 point average gaps conflate method with backbone; only the paradigm-internal comparison (Tables 2–3) is controlled. - The dependence metric is validated only on V* (191 questions) and its normalization can be gamed by a model that is simply accurate under GT; robustness of the metric to other choices is unexamined. - Only two tools, three assistant turns, and a single 9B base model; the framework's dependence on high-quality grounding annotations (IoU thresholds against ground truth for both rewards and repair) means it does not obviously extend to tasks lacking such annotations — a restriction the authors do not discuss. - Reward engineering is heavy (≈10 tuned coefficients in Table 5); sensitivity of results to λ_obs, δ thresholds, and the 0.5 dropout probability is not ablated. - Checkpoint selection by benchmark performance combined with evaluation on those same 14 benchmarks raises a selection-contamination concern the paper does not address. Bottom Line: Practitioners building tool-use VLM post-training should read this paper — the observation-dropout and mid-rollout repair mechanisms are concrete, well-motivated, and backed by a controlled probe — but the headline margins over external agents are inflated by base-model confounds, and replication-grade confidence requires waiting for independent runs with variance reporting.

Agentic Chip Design: A Survey of Architectures, Design Methodologies, and Evaluation

M Xing, B Dai, X Ye, B Zeng, Z Li, S Chen, B Li, H Shi… · preprints.org · specification to code with formal verifications - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper presents a survey of LLM-based agentic chip design that connects agent architectures, design tasks (digital through analog/RF), EDA tool development, and benchmark/evaluation methodology into a single analytical framework. - Why it's important: Chip design burns months of engineering per tapeout, and LLM agents are being deployed into this flow faster than the community can assess when their reported gains reflect real decision quality versus extra compute, reference leakage, or favorable evaluation settings. - How it does it: It formalizes agentic design as a policy over an EDA execution environment (Section 2.2) and then compares ~100 methods along three axes: the design representation being modified, the tool feedback used to select revisions, and the correctness/quality/cost procedures used to judge outcomes. - The good: The evaluation section (Section 6) is genuinely analytical — it dissects why the same benchmark result can mean different things under different reference access and budgets (e.g., VerilogCoder achieves 94.2% on VerilogEval v2 with ~13× the tokens of a single-shot GPT-4 Turbo baseline), a comparison most primary papers avoid making about themselves. - The missing: As a survey it runs no experiments, and its central claims (which agent mechanisms matter, when memory/planning help) rest on scattered ablations from primary papers with heterogeneous settings rather than any controlled cross-comparison. - Read it or not: Read it if you build or evaluate chip-design agents and need a map of the method landscape and evaluation pitfalls; skip it if you want new technical results, since it introduces no method, dataset, or measurement of its own.
Why this rank

Novelty (65) rests on the decision-theoretic abstraction and the coupled method-analysis/evaluation-critique structure — genuinely useful but reorganizational rather than inventive. Rigor (55) is the main drag: the survey never reports how many papers were screened or included, the quality-assessment rubric is stated but never applied per-paper, and general claims about which agent mechanisms matter rest on two ablations. Non-Obviousness (60) comes from the memory-vs-persistent-tool-state distinction and the insistence that single-generation pass rates and iterative agent success rates are different quantities — points primary papers routinely conflate. Problem & Motivation: Chip design requires coordinating specification, RTL implementation, verification, synthesis, and physical implementation, where decisions across stages are coupled (an RTL rewrite can worsen post-route timing). Existing ML-for-EDA methods optimize individual tasks with fixed representations and objectives, while three gaps block end-to-end automation: (1) task-specific optimizers don't compose into flows that implement high-level specifications, (2) EDA tool failures can originate in the design, testbench, or tool configuration, complicating diagnosis, and (3) stage-level improvements don't guarantee final implementation quality. The audience is EDA researchers, hardware engineers, and the LLM-agent community; the survey aims to close the gap of no systematic account of how agent decisions (planning, diagnosis, memory, tool use) interact with circuit correctness and implementation quality, and of how to evaluate such systems honestly. Key Idea: The unifying analytical move is to treat every agentic chip-design method as a decision policy π selecting operations in an EDA execution environment, and to classify and compare methods by what design representation they modify, what feedback they consume, and what verification/cost procedure gates acceptance — explicitly separating designing a circuit from developing the EDA software that designs circuits (Section 5), and agent memory from persistent tool state (Section 4.3/4.4). This last distinction — whether retained information is a reusable procedure, a measurement valid only under compatible evaluation conditions, or a loaded tool database — is the survey's most reconstructable insight. Methodology: The survey first gives a formal problem statement: at step t, an agent with policy π selects an action a_t ~ π(·|R, h_t) from interaction history, the environment transitions via (s_{t+1}, o_{t+1}) ~ P_E(·|s_t, a_t), and optimization tasks reduce to minimizing a declared objective q_E(d) over the feasible set F_E(R) under an execution budget (Eqs. 1–2). Literature was collected through October 2026 via structured searches of ACM DL, IEEE Xplore, DBLP, and arXiv with explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria and four quality-assessment questions. The body is organized in four themes: (1) design tasks — specification/architecture, RTL generation, verification/testbenches/assertions, RTL optimization, HLS, logic synthesis, physical design, plus analog/mixed-signal/RF; (2) agent architectures — domain models and training (e.g., PRO-V-R1's SFT-then-RL with verification rewards, VFlow's MCTS workflow search), planning and multi-agent orchestration, memory and stateful optimization, tool interfaces (MCP-based microservices, persistent backends); (3) EDA algorithm discovery and tool development (MappingEvolve, Self-Evolved ABC, EvoPlace, GR-Evolve, DRC-Coder, SpiceFuzz); (4) benchmarks and evaluation methods, with tables mapping each benchmark to its correctness checks, implementation stages, and cost measures. Critical design decisions: the deliberate coupling of methods analysis to evaluation critique (justified, and the survey's differentiator), the two-track treatment of design-vs-tool agents (well-justified via Fig. 5), and a five-level autonomy taxonomy (L1–L5) adopted from Synopsys/Cadence blog positions rather than derived from the literature (asserted, not independently grounded). Key Results: Not applicable in the experimental sense — the survey reports no new measurements. The quantitative content it synthesizes includes: VerilogCoder's component ablation on VerilogEval v2 specification-to-RTL tasks (baseline planner 66.7% pass rate, +waveform tracing 78.2%, planner replacement 74.4%, combined 94.2%) at ~13× the token cost of a GPT-4 Turbo single-shot baseline; MAGE's multi-agent vs merged single-agent comparison on VerilogEval v2 (93.6% vs 83.9% pass rate with Claude 3.5 Sonnet); and a structured comparison table of roughly a dozen benchmarks (VerilogEval v1/v2, RTLLM, RTLBench, CVDP, FVEval, TicTacBench, PDAGENT-BENCH, PostEDA-Bench, CLOSER-Bench, etc.) noting that many report no computational-cost dimension at all (marked with dashes in Table 3). Its headline finding is qualitative: broader agent control expands optimization opportunities but increases dependency-management and re-verification burden across the flow. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM framing (agentic chip design as a distinct synthesis of two literatures) plus a NEW FORMULATION in the sense of the Section 2.2 decision-theoretic abstraction and the evaluation taxonomy; it is NOT a new method, dataset, or empirical finding. The genuine novelty is the analytical framework connecting agent mechanisms to verification obligations and cost accounting — the constituent methods, the MDP-style formalism, and the autonomy levels are all existing ideas reorganized for a new setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: As a survey, it has no ablations, seeds, or error bars of its own, and the formalism in Section 2.2 is definitional rather than yielding theorems or bounds. Strengths: the search protocol, inclusion/exclusion criteria, and quality-assessment questions are stated explicitly (Section 2.3), and the evaluation section itself models the controlled-comparison discipline it preaches — e.g., insisting that reference access, implementation stage, and search budget be reported with every result. Weaknesses: the survey does not report how many papers were screened or included (a reproducibility gap for a systematic review), provides no quantitative meta-analysis of its quality-assessment rubric, and relies on a literature where most primary results come from a small set of industrial-adjacent groups (NVIDIA, NVIDIA-affiliated collaborations dominate VerilogEval, VerilogCoder, CVDP, FVEval citations), which the survey does not flag. No code or artifact is released; the deliverable is the paper and its tables. Deployability: Profile: THEORETICAL/survey — a synthesis with a formal frame, no primary experimental claim. - Sound: The formulation is internally consistent but only definitional; it yields no propositions, and the autonomy levels (L1–L5) are borrowed from vendor blogs without critical scrutiny. - General: The task/feedback/evaluation taxonomy applies across digital and analog/RF domains and appears broadly realistic for currently published work. - Tight: Not applicable — no bounds; the closest analog (the cost accounting framework in Table 4) is appropriately discriminating rather than vacuous. - Implementable: The evaluation checklist in Section 6.5 and the open problems in Section 7 (specification interpretation, failure attribution, cross-stage replanning, budget allocation, generalization testing) are directly actionable for benchmark builders and method authors. The work delivers no software artifact — it stops at paper form. Strengths: - The persistent coupling of method analysis to evaluation critique: nearly every surveyed method is re-read through what its benchmark actually measured (reference access, implementation stage, token budget), e.g., correctly noting that a single-generation pass rate and an iterative agent-run success rate are different quantities that primary papers conflate. - The clean separation of design-editing agents from EDA-software-editing agents (Section 5), including the point that a design-specialized evolved algorithm must report discovery cost and per-circuit runtime separately from reusable-algorithm quality — a distinction absent from most primary papers in this space. - The agent-memory vs. persistent-tool-state distinction (Sections 4.3–4.4), which clarifies when stored information remains valid (procedures transfer under compatible failure types; measurements require rechecking when design or evaluation conditions change). - Breadth with structure: coverage extends past the usual digital RTL-generation papers to verification agents, HLS, physical design, and analog/mixed-signal/RF, connected through one consistent analytical vocabulary. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge (Section 7) that specification interpretation remains unsolved, that failure diagnosis must distinguish design, testbench, and tool-configuration errors, that repository-level scaling requires deciding how much surrounding design to recheck, that cross-stage optimization lacks a principled choice of which abstraction level to modify, that early-stage proxies may rank candidates differently from final implementations, that public RTL training data is scarce, and that human-review placement in agent loops is unprincipled. They confront these limitations directly and trace each to specific surveyed methods — a credibility positive. They do not, however, discuss limitations of the survey itself (search completeness, single-team screening, no inter-rater process reported). Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The five-level autonomy taxonomy is sourced from Synopsys and Cadence marketing/blog positions (references 4–5) and adopted uncritically; a reviewer would ask whether vendor framings map onto any measurable capability axis. - The quality-assessment rubric (Section 2.3.3) is stated but no per-paper scores are reported, so the "assessment" is unverifiable and the selection cannot be audited; the count of included studies is never given. - The survey's comparative claims about which mechanisms matter (role separation, memory, planning) rest on two ablations (VerilogCoder, MAGE) at one benchmark and one model each; it does not acknowledge that this evidence base is too thin for the general statements it draws. - Dominance of a few industrial groups in both benchmarks and methods creates potential circularity (benchmarks built by the same organizations whose agents are evaluated on them), which the Goodhart-conscious Section 6 does not name. - Almost all surveyed primary works are 2024–2026 arXiv preprints or very recent venue papers; the survey does not weight evidentiary confidence by peer-review status of the works it synthesizes. - Analog/RF coverage is thin relative to digital (one subsection, ~7 methods), yet the abstract advertises it as co-equal coverage. Bottom Line: For anyone building or reviewing LLM-based EDA agents, this is currently the most useful map of the landscape and the best available evaluation-methodology checklist — read it as a rigor-enhancing survey, not as new science, and pair it with the primary benchmark papers (CVDP, VerilogEval v2, CLOSER-Bench) it critiques.

DensePath REINFORCE: Lightweight Policy Improvement from SFT-Induced Token-Level Reward Signals

J Li, TT Vu, E Abbasnejad, G Haffari · aclanthology.org · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Dense-Path REINFORCE (DPR), a post-SFT policy-improvement method that extracts a dense token-level reward from the log-probability gap between the final SFT model and an intermediate SFT checkpoint, then optimizes that frozen reward with a REINFORCE objective. - Why it's important: Teams that only have demonstrations (no preference data, no external teacher, no separately trained reward model) currently must either settle for vanilla SFT or run expensive adversarial/bilevel IRL pipelines; DPR offers a nearly-free reward signal from artifacts (checkpoints) that standard training already produces. - How it does it: The core trick is a baseline-relative reward r(s,a) = log π_SFT(a|s) − log π_CKPT(a|s), justified via a telescoping argument that SFT teacher-forced likelihood equals an inverse-soft-Q objective on a deterministic finite-horizon token MDP, so the log-probability acts as a shaped dense reward; the checkpoint subtraction cancels length/EOS and token-frequency biases of raw log-probabilities. - The good: The ablation isolating the checkpoint baseline is decisive — removing it drops win rates by 10–15 points (e.g., 60.6→49.8 on LLaMA-3.1-8B AlpacaEval), directly confirming the paper's central claim that relative likelihood gain, not absolute log-probability, is the useful signal. - The missing: No variance, error bars, or significance tests are reported (variance is merely asserted to be "small"), all results come from a single 100k Open-Orca dataset judged almost entirely by LLM-based evaluators (GPT-4o and Skywork reward models), and no code or checkpoints are stated to be released. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on demonstration-only or preference-free post-training and want a cheap dense-reward alternative to SPIN/AIRL-style pipelines; skip it if you need strong human-verified or downstream-task evidence, or if you already use RLVR with verifiable rewards as your primary signal.

Problem & Motivation: Practitioners post-training LLMs on expert demonstrations typically use SFT, which treats demonstrations purely as behavior-cloning supervision and discards everything else about the training process. Recent methods that squeeze more signal from demonstrations — self-play/self-imitation (SPIN, GSIL) and adversarial or bilevel inverse RL (AIRL-style) — do beat SFT, but require synthetic preference construction, separately trained reward models, external teachers, or max-min optimization. The gap the paper targets: can a reward signal good enough for further policy improvement be recovered from the SFT run itself, at near-zero marginal cost, in the strictly demonstration-only setting? Key Idea: The single core insight is that the trajectory of SFT is itself a reward annotation: tokens whose probability rose substantially between an intermediate checkpoint and the final SFT model are exactly the behaviors the demonstrations taught, so the per-token log-ratio between these two frozen models is a dense shaped reward. The theoretical backing is an SFT–inverse-soft-Q equivalence: on a deterministic finite-horizon token MDP with γ=1, the reduced IQ-Learn objective telescopes exactly to teacher-forced maximum likelihood, so SFT log-probabilities are shaped rewards up to a state-only potential term — and differencing two checkpoints keeps this property while canceling shared LM prior, token-frequency, and early-EOS biases. Methodology: DPR is a two-stage pipeline. Stage 1: standard SFT on demonstrations (cross-entropy, N steps), saving checkpoints; the checkpoint baseline π_CKPT is chosen by a signal-to-noise criterion (maximize μ(t)²/σ²(t) of the token log-ratio over a reference prompt set, Eq. 41 in App. A.8), which usually lands near mid-training. Stage 2: an actor initialized from π_SFT generates on-policy rollouts on the same prompt pool; each token gets reward r̂(s,a) = log π_SFT(a|s) − log π_CKPT(a|s); discounted token returns (γ=1 default) feed a REINFORCE policy-gradient loss (Eq. 3) plus a sampled-token KL penalty to π_SFT (λ_KL=1e-5), implemented on OpenRLHF's REINFORCE++ stack. Both reward scorers are frozen; gradients flow only through actor log-probabilities. Critical design decisions: (1) γ=1, justified because the SFT–IQL identity is exact only undiscounted, and empirically confirmed (performance peaks at γ=1.0 across all four backbones, Fig. 4) — well-justified; (2) skipping explicit value correction (the w/V ablation with a value-corrected reward underperforms by 2–7 win-rate points), argued via a telescoping identity showing the log-prob return differs from the unshaped return by a state-only baseline — well-justified both theoretically (App. A.5) and empirically; (3) SNR-based checkpoint selection rather than a fixed midpoint, supported by a unimodal curve in Fig. 5 — justified, though the SNR rule and midpoint perform similarly in practice. A dual-contraction theorem (App. A.6) motivates reward stability, and a generic proxy-reward bound (App. A.10) is included for completeness. Key Results: On 100k Open-Orca samples with four pretrained-only backbones (LLaMA-3.1-8B, Qwen-2.5-7B, Mistral-v0.1-7B, Gemma-3-4B) and four evaluations (AlpacaEval, Arena-Hard, LIMA win rates vs. SFT judged by GPT-4o; MT-Bench 1–10): DPR achieves 55.2–66.8% win rates over SFT and MT-Bench gains of +0.22–0.46 (e.g., Qwen-2.5-7B 6.83→7.29; LLaMA-3.1-8B 5.74→6.01). It beats or matches the best of five baselines (SPIN, GSIL, AIRL, sentence-level REINFORCE/SR, plus SFT) in 15 of 16 benchmark×backbone settings; notably SR collapses on Mistral (46.6 AlpacaEval vs DPR's 61.0), showing dense propagation matters most for weaker backbones. An independent Skywork-Reward-V2 4-model ensemble corroborates GPT-4o rankings (e.g., LLaMA-3.1-8B average 8.87 SFT → 10.81 DPR). Controls: continued SFT (SFT-2Epoch) stagnates or slightly degrades (~49–51% win rates), so gains are not just more optimization; DPR on disjoint unseen prompts performs comparably or slightly better (DPR† 57.6/56.0/59.6/7.32 on Qwen), suggesting the reward transfers within-distribution. A compatibility experiment grafts DPR's sequence-aggregated reward into GRPO with independently standardized group-relative advantages on Qwen2.5-3B math data, improving the four-benchmark average from 32.8 (GRPO) to 34.5 (GRPO+DPR) on AMC/Minerva/OlympiadBench/Math500. Baselines are recent and appropriate for the demonstration-only setting; scale is standard (4–8B models, 100k samples), not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD with an element of NEW FORMULATION: the genuinely novel piece is the checkpoint-relative dense reward — using the log-probability gap between two frozen checkpoints from one SFT run as a free token-level reward. The SFT–IRL/inverse-soft-Q connection is explicitly credited to prior work (Wulfmeier et al. 2024; Sun 2024) and is not claimed as new; the REINFORCE + KL machinery, OpenRLHF stack, and reward-shaping telescoping arguments are standard. The main novelty is therefore a clever reuse of existing training artifacts, not a new learning paradigm. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and targeted: the checkpoint baseline removal (10–15 point drops) and value-correction removal (2–7 point drops) directly test the two core design claims, and sensitivity analyses cover evaluation temperature, discount factor γ, checkpoint position, and per-length KL/reward profiles. However, results are averaged over three runs with variance "omitted due to its small magnitude" — no error bars, standard deviations, or significance tests are printed anywhere, so the narrow margins (e.g., DPR 57.3 vs SR 55.9 on Qwen AlpacaEval) cannot be statistically assessed. Two independent judge families (GPT-4o, Skywork-Reward-V2 ensemble) mitigate single-judge bias, but both are LLM-derived preference scorers, and Skywork reward models share a possible circularity with likelihood-based signals; no human evaluation is reported. All methods share the same 100k Open-Orca data and hyperparameters, which is fair, but the evaluation rests on a single training corpus. No code, data split, model weights, or repository URL is mentioned — reproducibility currently depends on the appendix's hyperparameter tables (Tables 5–6) alone. The method is developed and evaluated on the same prompt distribution, though the DPR† unseen-prompt control partially addresses within-distribution overfitting. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a secondary SYSTEMS flavor via the OpenRLHF implementation). - Practical: Yes — 4–8B open-weight backbones, two frozen scorers plus one actor, all runnable on commodity multi-GPU setups with a public RLHF framework. - Efficient: Moderate — no extra training of reward models, but every generated token requires a forward pass through two frozen 4–8B models, adding roughly 2× scorer inference cost during the RL stage; the authors acknowledge this. - Effective: The evidence (win rates over SFT, MT-Bench gains, reward-model ensemble corroboration, SFT-2Epoch control) supports improvement over SFT, but effectiveness is measured only by LLM-judge proxies, never by humans or downstream task accuracy outside the GRPO math appendix. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 8B/100k samples; the authors claim generality ("simple and scalable path") but provide no experiment at larger model or data scale, and the extra scorer cost grows linearly with model size. The work delivers a method and recipe (algorithm, SNR checkpoint rule, hyperparameters) but no released software artifact, dataset, or trained model is stated. Strengths: - The checkpoint-relative reward is a genuinely cheap and clever source of dense supervision: it requires no data the practitioner doesn't already have and turns discarded SFT checkpoints into reward annotators. - The theory is honest and well-scoped: the SFT–IQL telescoping identity (App. A.4), the shaped-reward identity (A.5), and the EOS/length pathology formalization (A.9) precisely delimit what is proven (undiscounted, deterministic, finite-horizon) versus what is heuristic, and the γ-sweep empirically confirms the γ=1 prediction. - The ablations map one-to-one onto the paper's central claims — removing the checkpoint baseline reproduces the predicted length pathology (win rates fall to 40–50%), and the sentence-level SR baseline cleanly isolates dense versus sparse credit assignment using the same reward source. - Evaluation triangulates across two judge families and includes controls (SFT-2Epoch saturation, unseen-prompt generalization) that many post-training papers omit. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The limitations section is candid and specific: (1) the strictly demonstration-only setup excludes preference data, verifiable rewards, and online interaction; (2) DPR assumes saved intermediate checkpoints, which is inconvenient when only a final SFT model is available, and the two-scorer reward adds RL-stage inference cost; (3) the recovered reward is a proxy inherited from demonstration coverage and quality, not a measure of human preference or correctness, with untested generalization to specialized domains, multilingual settings, and long-horizon tasks. The authors confront these directly rather than minimizing them — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the acknowledged limits, a reviewer would flag: (1) the absence of any reported variance or significance testing despite three-run averaging, which matters because several margins over AIRL/SR are within 1–2 points; (2) judge circularity — the Skywork "independent" verification models are themselves preference-trained LLM scorers, and GPT-4o win rates can favor responses that merely match judge stylistic priors; no human or task-grounded evaluation exists; (3) a single training corpus (Open-Orca) and four chat-style benchmarks, so the claim of broad applicability to "more specialized domains" is extrapolation; (4) no code release stated, which combined with the SNR checkpoint-selection rule and multiple unstated implementation details limits reproduction; (5) the GRPO+DPR math result (34.5 vs 32.8) uses one 3B model, one dataset, and no seed variance, and the λ=1 combination weight is not ablated, so the RLVR-extension claim is a compatibility check, not evidence at parity with the main setting; (6) compute/throughput numbers for the RL stage are absent, so the "lightweight" framing is not quantified against AIRL or SPIN training cost. Bottom Line: A practitioner doing demonstration-only post-training should read this: the checkpoint-relative dense reward is a cheap, well-motivated trick with the strongest ablation-backed evidence in the paper, but its gains are modest, judge-only, single-dataset, and unaccompanied by released code — so treat it as a promising recipe to replicate, not a validated drop-in replacement for stronger IRL pipelines.

WAM-Sim0. 1: World Anchored Memory Meets Online RL for Consistent and Realistic Driving Simulation

J Cui, J Li, W Zhang, Y Li, S Luan, Q Tang, J Han… · arxiv.org · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper builds WAM-Sim, a driving world model that combines a persistent three-tier memory (HD-map structural tokens, read-only geolocated scene tokens, write-once instance appearance tokens) with Drive DiffusionNFT, an online flow-matching RL post-training stage using hierarchy-aligned visual and VLM physical rewards, to suppress structural drift, identity drift, and quality decay in minute-scale autoregressive rollouts. - Why it's important: Long-horizon driving simulation is the bottleneck for closed-loop autonomous-vehicle testing, and existing autoregressive world models collapse beyond a few seconds because conditioning signals are transient and errors compound recursively. - How it does it: The core move is separating world state into three tiers matched to their persistence dynamics—trajectory-aligned map latents injected additively, pose-retrieved geolocated references injected via segment-masked cross-attention, and first-seen object crops locked in a track-keyed bank retrieved via instance-masked attention—then restoring the fidelity lost to dense conditioning via group-relative flow-matching RL on self-generated rollouts. - The good: The quality–horizon decay analysis (Appendix B.3) is the most credible evidence: over 10s→60s rollouts, memory conditioning holds FVD to 137.9 vs. 286.5 without it, and Scene Similarity to 0.828 vs. 0.697, with per-tier ablations (Tables 3, 5, 6) isolating each component's contribution. - The missing: The headline nuScenes results are obtained without scene memory (no geolocated database exists there), so the flagship public-benchmark numbers do not exercise the paper's central contribution; the strongest long-horizon claims rest entirely on a proprietary self-collected benchmark where the strongest baseline (OmniDreams) was fine-tuned by the authors. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building long-horizon video world models or driving simulators, since the write-once instance bank and memory-bounded-RL synergy observation are directly transferable; skippable for those seeking only open-benchmark driving generation numbers.

Rigor (65) is above-average for this area (per-tier ablations, statistically tested human study with honestly reported non-significance) but capped by a proprietary benchmark, no seeds, and a residual reward/eval-metric Goodhart overlap.
