Problem & Motivation: Sheaf neural networks assign each node and edge its own vector space (stalk) with learnable linear restriction maps, enabling feature comparison across heterophilic edges and mitigating oversmoothing — capabilities standard GNNs lack because they force neighbors into one shared feature space. Since Bodnar et al. (2022), a growing family of SNN variants (attention, second-order propagation, polynomial filters, bundle diffusion, Bayesian sheaves, heterogeneous and directed extensions) has emerged, but most implementations assemble the sheaf Laplacian as a global sparse nd×nd block matrix and apply it to stacked node states. For n nodes with d-dimensional stalks this is expensive in memory and computation, particularly for large graphs or large d, and forces researchers reimplementing variants to maintain separate, incompatible codebases. The gap: no unified, operator-free implementation framework exists for the SNN literature, and the field lacks a shared benchmarking protocol. Key Idea: The sheaf Laplacian action (L_F x)_u = Σ Fᵀ_{u⊴e}(F_{u⊴e}x_u − F_{v⊴e}x_v) is a sum of per-edge local operations, so it can be evaluated as message passing — transport both endpoints into the edge stalk, compute a message ψ_e, pull back through Fᵀ_{u⊴e}, aggregate — without constructing the nd×nd operator. Non-obvious cases are handled by two moves: augmenting node states to absorb higher-order recurrences (NSP's second-order update becomes first-order on a doubled stalk R^{2d}; PolyNSD's degree-K Chebyshev filter becomes K steps on a tripled stalk R^{3d} with a running accumulator), and treating graph pooling (SheafPool) as messages to a receive-only virtual node. Methodology: The paper defines a general SheafMPNN blueprint in five equations: (2) a stalk/channel transform z_u = W₁x_uW₂; (3) an edge-stalk message ψ_e between transported endpoint states; (4) pullback through Fᵀ_{u⊴e}, weighting ω_uv, and permutation-invariant aggregation; (5) a node-local update φ_u. The framework is a formal unification, not a new learning algorithm: Theorem 1 shows NSD, standard MPNNs (identity restrictions), SheafAN/Res-SheafAN/sheaf adjacency, and NSP (on an augmented sheaf) are instances; appendix theorems extend to PolyNSD via Chebyshev recurrences (Theorem 6), SheafPool via Procrustes-aligned messages to virtual nodes (Proposition 10), heterogeneous type-conditioned NSD/NSP (Theorems 13, 15), directed/cooperative/joint/bundle/Bayesian variants (Theorems 19–23). The library (three packages: sheaf_mpnn, hetsheaf_mpnn, exp) implements 15 homogeneous families with heterogeneous counterparts (29 model types), six restriction-map parameterizations (diagonal, general, orthogonal via Cayley/Householder, low-rank, and two attention variants), and a CLI with Optuna hyperparameter sweeps, split management, and SLURM-based benchmarking against the original NSD implementation (included as a git submodule). Critical design decisions: (a) normalization via N_u = (D_u + I)^{-1/2} instead of D^{-1/2}_u, justified because D_u + I stays positive definite even for singular restriction maps; (b) precomputing per-edge products S_ue = FᵀF and C_uve = Fᵀᶠ rather than applying maps per-message — a memory/latency trade-off; (c) numerical safeguards (jitter on the identity term, entrywise clipping of general-map products to [−1,1]) that break exactness during training — the paper honestly notes Equation (33) is exact at evaluation time only when clipping is inactive. The design decisions are justified, though the clipping caveat means train/eval dynamics can differ. Key Results: Not evaluated. The paper contains no experimental results tables. Its quantitative content is asymptotic: transport-and-aggregation costs O(|E|d²f) operations with O(|E|d² + |E|df + ndf) memory, versus the reference implementation's assembly of a sparse nd×nd operator with O(nd² + |E|d²) non-zeros; Remark 9 concedes that both approaches perform the same O(|E|d²f) arithmetic per step, so the saving is confined to avoiding assembly and storage of the global operator (and avoiding O((nd)³) eigendecomposition for spectral filters). The benchmarking suite covers 20+ datasets (heterophily benchmarks from Platonov et al. 2023, OGB node datasets, Pokec, Telegram, HGB heterogeneous datasets, TU graph datasets) with configurable comparisons of epoch time, peak GPU memory, and inference latency against the original Bodnar et al. implementation — but the paper reports none of these measurements. The main non-trivial findings are theoretical: exact equivalence of second-order and polynomial-filter propagation to single-step local message passing on augmented stalks, and the honest Remark 11 that SheafPool's gauge invariance is only partial (regularized whitening is not invariant to general linear stalk changes). Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL with a secondary NEW FORMULATION contribution. The genuinely novel elements are (1) a unified, Laplacian-free message-passing implementation of 15 SNN families under one PyG-compatible interface with equivalence proofs, and (2) the explicit derivations showing state augmentation tames second-order/polynomial recurrences. The locality observation itself is a modest insight — the authors correctly note that sparse matrix-vector products already exploit locality, so the arithmetic is identical and only operator assembly is saved — and the individual architectures are all pre-existing; the theorems are careful verification rather than deep new theory. Rigor & Reproducibility: The theory is internally rigorous: every equivalence claim has an explicit proof, and the paper is unusually candid about the boundaries of its claims (e.g., Remark 9's admission that per-step arithmetic is unchanged; the statement that practical efficiency "must be evaluated empirically"; the appendix admission that "this paper reports neither test coverage nor numerical parity with reference implementations"). No ablations, error bars, seeds, or significance tests appear because no experiments are reported. Code, documentation, ten tutorial notebooks, and a pinned environment (Python 3.13, PyTorch 2.8.0, CUDA 12.8) with CI are publicly released at https://github.com/alessioborgi/sheaf-mpnn under CC-BY 4.0. Methodological concern: the paper is a tooling paper whose central practical advantage is untested in the paper itself, and the equivalence theorems assume a normalization (D^{-1/2}) that the released code deliberately deviates from ((D+I)^{-1/2}) — the authors address this, but it means published results against other implementations require care. The benchmark harness comparing against the original NSD implementation as a git submodule is a good reproducibility practice, but its outputs are not shown. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a built library; the paper's contribution is infrastructure plus formal unification, evaluated by neither deployment nor reported experiments). - Practical: Yes — pure PyTorch/PyG with CPU and CUDA wheels on Linux/Windows/macOS; no exotic hardware required. - Efficient: Unmeasured; complexity bounds suggest memory savings from avoiding the nd×nd operator, but per-step FLOPs are identical to sparse multiplication, so any speedup depends on implementation details the paper does not quantify. - Effective: The equivalence theorems establish exactness of the reformulation analytically, but there is no empirical evidence that trained models match reference implementations in accuracy. - Scalable: Not tested; the argument for scalability (no global operator) is structural, and no experiments at 10×–100× graph sizes are reported. The work delivers a concrete software artifact (library, CLI, benchmark harness, tutorials) plus a reusable proof technique (the augmented-state SheafMPNN blueprint) — not just a paper. Strengths: - Genuine unification value: consolidating 15 architecturally divergent SNN families into one blueprint with per-architecture equivalence proofs is a real service to a fragmented subfield, and the derivations (augmented stalks for NSP and PolyNSD, receive-only virtual nodes for SheafPool, conditional SheafMPNNs for Bayesian SNNs) are non-trivial and reusable. - Exceptional intellectual honesty for a tooling paper: the authors repeatedly flag what their formulation does not buy (identical per-step FLOPs), where exactness breaks (clipping during training), and that SheafPool's gauge invariance is only partial (Remark 11). - Engineering maturity: pinned environments, CI with coverage, typed configs, Optuna sweeps, a benchmark harness against the original implementation as a submodule, and ten tutorials substantially lower the barrier to reproducible SNN research. - Honest complexity accounting (Remark 9) that correctly separates avoided assembly/storage costs from unchanged arithmetic — a distinction many library papers would blur. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that (1) the practical efficiency of the message-passing formulation "depends on the implementation and must be evaluated empirically"; (2) the paper reports neither test coverage nor numerical parity with reference implementations; (3) the per-step arithmetic cost is the same as sparse Laplacian multiplication, with savings only in assembly and storage; (4) SheafPool's whitening provides only partial (not full) gauge invariance; and (5) numerical safeguards mean exactness holds at evaluation only when clipping is inactive. This is a model of direct confrontation with limitations rather than minimization — a strong credibility signal. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The most serious gap is the absence of any reported measurements from the paper's own benchmarking harness — the tool to compare epoch time, peak memory, and latency against the original NSD implementation exists, is described in detail, and produces no numbers in the paper, leaving the motivating claim (Laplacian assembly is a real bottleneck worth eliminating) empirically unsupported. Second, the paper never characterizes when assembly overhead actually dominates: for small graphs or small d the O(nd²) storage may be negligible, and the library's precomputed dense d×d per-edge products (stored even for low-rank maps, as Table 3 notes) could erode the memory advantage. Third, the equivalence proofs cover forward-pass layer dynamics, but equivalence under SGD — where clipping, jitter, and the (D+I)^{-1/2} normalization shift gradients — is not analyzed, so "equivalent architectures" may train differently. Fourth, several recovered architectures (BuNN spectral solver, cooperative SNNs) are only conditionally or partially local, and the practical reach of the "never assemble a Laplacian" promise across all 15 families is not stress-tested. The authors do not acknowledge these specific gaps beyond the general efficiency caveat. Bottom Line: For researchers actively building or benchmarking sheaf neural networks this library and its equivalence derivations are immediately useful and likely the best available unified foundation; for readers seeking evidence that Laplacian-free sheaf propagation delivers measurable speed or memory wins, the paper's own admission that those numbers are not yet reported means a stronger alternative (measured comparisons) remains to be published — ideally by these authors using the harness they built.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces TOME-Math, a 380,292-record proof-supervision corpus extracted from 2,118 university mathematics textbooks that preserves chapter order, proposition–proof links, and dependency references, and shows that training on it — with a forward textbook-order, Gap-first curriculum — improves a Qwen3-30B-A3B base model's six-benchmark mean from 29.17% to 45.83%. - Why it's important: Mathematical SFT data is almost universally flattened into isolated problem→solution pairs, discarding the pedagogical organization of the source; if structure (not just volume) drives reasoning quality, this changes how math training data should be collected, organized, and scheduled. - How it does it: An LLM-driven pipeline (DeepSeek-OCR parsing → state-machine chapter recovery → proposition–proof extraction → LLM-detected proof gaps rewritten as self-contained sub-propositions) produces two supervision streams (Proof QA and Gap QA), and the retained chapter indices enable controlled curriculum-order experiments at matched token budgets. - The good: The curriculum study is genuinely controlled — identical QA sets, token budgets, and initialization across SHUFFLE/FORWARD–GAP/REVERSE–GAP/FORWARD–MIX schedules — and FORWARD–GAP wins in all 18 subject×scale cells, with macro-average pass@16 rising from 45.38% to 50.93% at the largest budget. - The missing: The headline comparison confounds corpus with data organization (acknowledged by the authors), two of six evaluation benchmarks are self-constructed from the same textbook distribution as the training data, and the LLM-judge verifier carries a measured 18.1% false-rejection and 8.7% false-acceptance rate that injects material noise into all long-form proof scores. - Read it or not: Read it if you build math SFT datasets or study data ordering/curricula for reasoning — it is the largest structure-preserving proof corpus with controlled organization experiments; skip it if you want a new training algorithm, since the method is SFT over a data asset.

Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (60) and Novelty (62) jointly define the paper: the matched-budget curriculum design, component ablations, and human-calibrated LLM judge (κ = 0.771, reported error rates) are above-average evaluation practice, and the Gap QA supervision unit is a genuinely new contribution — but single backbone, single seed, dated baselines (missing NuminaMath-CoT/OpenMathInstruct-2), and two self-built benchmarks cap both. Completeness (62) is helped by the authors' direct confrontation of the corpus-vs-organization confound, yet the sub-50% groundedness audit result is never connected to downstream risk. Resilience (60) is limited because the +16.7-point headline rests partly on self-referential evaluation, while the internally controlled curriculum finding would survive review better. Impact (65) reflects a promised 380K-record corpus and a cheap ($7/book) reusable pipeline, with no weights release stated. Problem & Motivation: Practitioners fine-tuning LLMs for mathematical reasoning rely on instruction corpora (MetaMathQA, OpenMathInstruct-2, NuminaMath-CoT) whose supervision unit is an isolated problem–solution pair. Textbooks, by contrast, encode prerequisite relations via chapter order, lemma→theorem dependency chains, and staged exercises, but prior textbook-derived resources (MathPile, CollegeMath, NaturalProofs) either use textbooks as raw text or cover only a handful of books. The open problem is how to scale natural-language proof supervision from textbooks while retaining chapter progression, proposition dependencies, provenance, and exercises in one framework, and whether that retained structure actually helps — at inference time (as an evidence index) and at training time (as a curriculum). Key Idea: Treat a textbook's native structure as trainable signal in three layers — hierarchical (chapter order as curriculum), dependency (references resolved into a retrieval index over propositions), and gap-based (implicit proof steps detected by an LLM and rewritten as self-contained Gap QA obligations) — so that the same corpus supports structure-guided retrieval, textbook-aligned curricula, and source-breadth scaling studies under matched budgets. The Gap QA construction (mining what the textbook proof left unstated and turning it into additional supervision) is the most distinctive ingredient; the rest is a competent, structure-preserving extraction pipeline. Methodology: Pipeline stages: (1) DeepSeek-OCR converts PDFs to multimodal Markdown; (2) gpt-oss-120b separates front matter/TOC/body and a state machine (INIT/READ/JUDGE/RETRY/UPDATE/PASS/NEXT) reconstructs chapter boundaries conditioned on the recovered hierarchical TOC; (3) a second pass separates expository content from exercises (exercises reserved for evaluation, excluded from training-data generation); (4) gemini-3.1-flash-lite extracts theorem/lemma/definition–proof units and resolves references against a book-level proposition library; (5) gemini-3-flash-preview with thinking audits proofs for gaps ("obviously"-style omissions, skipped transformations), and flash-lite rewrites each gap as a self-contained proposition with a completed proof; (6) a gpt-oss-120b judge audits candidates on five axes (completeness, accuracy, LaTeX, self-containment, atomicity), with accuracy failures (invented steps, altered relations) as hard rejects. Training is standard SFT (AdamW, lr 8e-5, 1 epoch, seq len 131k, 16×H200) on Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base. Key design decisions: (a) keeping exercises out of the training-data path to enable book-held-out evaluation — well justified; (b) the hybrid model allocation (~$7/book vs $40–50 for pro-thinking) — justified by a six-dimension model-quality trade-off analysis; (c) normalized chapter stages (i/Nb bucketed into 10 stages) for cross-book curricula — reasonable but imposes an assumption that all books' chapter progressions are pedagogically commensurable. Key Results: Full-corpus SFT on 364,631 records (after removing 15,661 held-out-book records): six-benchmark mean 45.83% vs 29.17% base; best on five of six benchmarks — TOME-LONGFORM 43.86 (base 13.25), TOME-OBJECTIVE 43.96 (32.93), MiniF2F 57.43 (34.45), ProofNet 42.98 (17.14), MATH-500 76.55 (68.80), AIME 2026 10.19 (8.44). Beats OpenMath1 (1.82M examples, ~4.8× larger) on all six benchmarks, MetaMath (395k), and MathInstruct (262k); the authors explicitly note this comparison is confounded and does not isolate structure causally. Training-free structure-guided retrieval on 300 held-out exercises: pass@1 rises 13.25% (closed-book) → 14.00 (random same-book) → 14.71 (local chapter) → 15.54 (propositions only) → 17.38 (propositions + Gap QA) under identical context budgets. Curriculum: FORWARD–GAP beats SHUFFLE by 4.34/6.46/7.72 points at 0.75M/1.8M/2.4M tokens; chapter direction (vs REVERSE–GAP) contributes 5.65–8.50 points, Gap-first ordering 1.53–2.37. Source breadth: spreading a 0.75M-token budget over 16 vs 8 books adds 1.6–4.8 pass@16 points (avg 3.3). Cross-subject transfer coefficient 0.92 (macro). Ablations: removing Gap QA costs 5.05–6.77 points on the four proof benchmarks. Scale tested: 30B-parameter MoE, ~171M training tokens — standard SFT scale, not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (the largest structure-preserving natural-language proof corpus at 380K records from 2,118 books) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (textbook-order curricula and Gap-first scheduling consistently beat shuffling at matched budgets; source breadth is a distinct scaling axis). The gap-mining idea (rewriting omitted proof obligations as Gap QA) is a genuinely new supervision unit; the training method itself is standard SFT, and retrieval over dependency graphs extends the NaturalProofs line of reference-grounded proving to a much larger, more structured corpus. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative (Gap QA removal, curriculum removal, Gap-first removal, each with per-benchmark numbers, Table 4). The curriculum studies are the methodological high point: identical QA IDs, realized token counts (matched to within 33 tokens), initialization, and optimization across schedules, with data-loader shuffling disabled to preserve prescribed order. Confidence intervals: 95% problem-clustered bootstrap CIs (2,000 resamples) for the full-corpus comparison; AIME-26 carries ±8.75 half-widths on 30 problems — that column is essentially noise. The eight-review pessimistic verifier is human-calibrated on 600 stratified responses (κ = 0.771 between two human annotators; 8.7% false-accept, 18.1% false-reject, 85.9% human–judge agreement), a level of evaluation transparency few dataset papers attempt. Concerns: single backbone (Qwen3-30B-A3B), single training run per condition with no multi-seed error bars on the headline table; two of six benchmarks are self-built; no comparison against NuminaMath-CoT or OpenMathInstruct-2 (the corpus's own related-work table lists them); corpus quality audits show groundedness/evidence-alignment passing below 50% of records with a "no verbatim evidence" flag on 48.4% — the authors report this but do not connect it to downstream risk. The corpus is promised for release (project page: https://tome-math.github.io/); no weights release is stated. Deployability: EMPIRICAL profile. Practical: Yes — extraction pipeline uses commercially available APIs plus open-weight models, and SFT runs on 16×H200, well within reach of mid-size labs. Efficient: Extraction costs ~$7/book via the hybrid model allocation (vs $40–50 for pro-only); SFT is one epoch of 171M tokens, cheap for a 30B MoE. Effective: Evidence supports improved proof generation on both textbook-derived and public benchmarks, but long-form scores flow through an LLM judge with ~18% false-rejection rate, so absolute proof-correctness numbers should be read as verifier-relative; the structure benefits (curriculum ordering, retrieval) are cleaner because they are internally controlled. Scalable: Not tested beyond ~2,118 books and 171M tokens; the claim that structure helps at 10–100× scale is extrapolation, though the monotonic gains from 0.75M→2.4M tokens and 8→16 books are consistent with it. Delivers a dataset artifact (corpus + evaluation suites, promised release) and a reusable extraction pipeline; no trained model weights are stated for release. Strengths: - The corpus-construction engineering is real and documented to an unusual depth: state-machine chapter recovery, a four-stage proposition pipeline with reference resolution, per-book cost accounting, and versioned model allocation — this is a reusable recipe, not just a data dump. - The matched-budget curriculum design (nested book/QA sets, token-matched cells, order-preserving loaders) is the cleanest test of "does organization matter" in the math-SFT literature the authors cite, and the forward-vs-reverse comparison cleanly attributes the effect to chapter direction rather than Gap placement. - Human calibration of the pessimistic verifier, with stratified sampling, inverse-probability weighting, double-coded 30% subset, and κ reporting, is a credibility positive most LLM-judged evaluations lack. - The Gap QA stream (19.00% yield from 918,235 candidates) converts textbook implicitness into explicit intermediate supervision, and the ablation confirms it is the largest single component (5–7 points on proof benchmarks). Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state directly that the full-corpus comparison "does not by itself isolate textbook structure as the causal factor" because the corpora differ in several respects, and they respond with controlled retrieval/curriculum studies — a direct confrontation of the main confound. They also note model-allocation changed during pipeline development (versioned per run), that intermediate retrieval conditions are not monotonically ordered within every subject, and that the corpus is concentrated (top ten subjects = 84.4% of records; analysis-heavy vs graph-theory concentration varies 216 vs 976 records/book). They do not dwell on verifier error rates in the main text, though the calibration table exposes them fully. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Baseline set is dated for the claim being made: MetaMath (2023), MathInstruct, and OpenMathInstruct-1 are compared, but NuminaMath-CoT and OpenMathInstruct-2 — listed in the paper's own Table 1 as the modern scale points — are absent, leaving the "structured beats flat" claim tested only against older flat corpora. - Two of the six headline benchmarks (TOME-LONGFORM, TOME-OBJECTIVE) are drawn from the same textbook distribution and construction pipeline as the training data, and even though books are held out, style/topic overlap plausibly favors TOME-Math over corpora built from competitions and web exams; the four public benchmarks show smaller, noisier margins. - The 18.1% false-rejection rate of the verifier means long-form pass@1 values (e.g., 43.86 vs 35.87 over MathInstruct) sit atop substantial measurement noise, and no significance test is reported on the headline Table 2 rankings despite CIs being computed. - Single backbone, single seed per condition: the curriculum result is impressive in its 18/18 consistency, but nothing establishes transfer of the finding to other model families or sizes. - Groundedness below 50% pass and a 48.4% "no verbatim evidence" flag rate in the corpus's own audits are reported as characterization, but their downstream effect on training-data reliability is never quantified. - License/copyright status of QA pairs extracted from copyrighted textbooks is not addressed. Bottom Line: For anyone building mathematical SFT data or studying data organization, this is worth reading for the corpus, the gap-mining idea, and the cleanest curriculum-order controls available in this space — but the headline "+16.7 points" should be discounted for the self-referential evaluation split, the dated baseline set, and the noisy LLM judge until independent replication on third-party benchmarks confirms the structure effect.

EvoWorld: Towards Out-of-Sight World Evolution in Generative Video Models (19 ▲ )

Yequan Bie, Dengyang Jiang, Zhixuan Chen, Xiaozhuan Liang, Haoxuan Che, Quande Liu, Xi Chen, Hao Chen · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 9 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Out-of-Sight Causal Evolution as a new task for video world models — the camera leaves a subject, an event occurs, and the model must render a causally plausible post-event state of the subject upon revisit — and delivers EvoWorld, a VLM-brain + segment-autoregressive-renderer framework with a ~12k-video training dataset and a 120-case benchmark that reaches 90.8% Core Task Success versus 21.7% for the best baseline. - Why it's important: Current generative video world models freeze or hallucinate off-screen entities, which blocks their use as long-horizon world simulators where the world must keep evolving coherently outside the camera's field of view. - How it does it: A VLM brain continuously records generated world state and converts the realized event into a concrete reasoning prompt, while an LTX-based renderer trained with Identity-Anchored Attention (a directional +β attention bias to retrieved entity latents on revisit windows) and two-stage online autoregressive rollout training realizes the inferred state visually. - The good: The ablations credibly decompose the gains — dropping the reasoning prompt falls to 58.3% Core, and transplanting the same reasoning prompts into Evoke-Turbo lifts it from 21.7% to 45.0% Core, showing the reasoning layer itself carries much of the improvement. - The missing: No code, dataset, or model weights are reported as released, and the headline 90.8% score on the authors' own benchmark comes from a renderer trained on data purpose-built for that exact task — the strong baselines were not given equivalent task-specific training, so the margin conflates method and data advantage. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers in video world models, world-state consistency, and agentic simulation who want a concrete new task formulation and a reference brain-renderer decomposition; skip if you only care about pixel-quality video generation advances.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (76) is strong — Out-of-Sight Causal Evolution is a genuinely new problem formulation, and the blind-revisit-prompt protocol cleanly forces inference rather than script-following; the ablation/transplant analysis honestly decomposes gains. But Rigor (55) and Resilience (55) are pulled down hard by train–eval distribution coupling (the renderer is trained on the exact five-beat rollout pattern the benchmark evaluates, with baselines receiving no equivalent task-specific training), judge circularity (Qwen-family VLM scores outputs prompted by a Qwen-family brain), and no seed variance on a 120-case benchmark. Completeness (60) benefits from candid scope limitations, and Non-Obviousness (70) from the finding that component metrics mask causal-chain collapse; Impact (40) suffers because no code, dataset, or weights are reported as released. Weighted composite: 0.20*76 + 0.25*55 + 0.15*70 + 0.15*60 + 0.15*55 + 0.10*40 = 61.

Problem & Motivation: Generative video models are increasingly positioned as world simulators, but they render plausible pixels without an explicit mechanism to reason about how the world should evolve — especially entities outside the current frame. The motivating failure is concrete: after a monster or collapsing facade appears off-screen, a model should show the revisited subject fleeing, taking cover, or bracing, but existing models (HY-World 1.5, Echo-WM, LingBot-World, SANA-WM) produce absent events, subjects that follow the camera or duplicate, appearance drift, or implausible reactions. The paper targets practitioners building interactive video world models and closes the gap between visual persistence (keeping what you saw) and causal evolution (inferring how unseen events change unseen entities), which prior out-of-sight work (ReMind, LiveWorld, Hybrid Memory) only tested as continuation of active motion through observation gaps rather than event-conditioned state change. Key Idea: Separate world-state reasoning from rendering: let a VLM observe each generated segment, maintain persistent world memory, and — conditioned on the event actually realized in pixels, not just the requested prompt — write a concrete generation prompt describing the causally plausible post-event state of the off-screen subject; then train the renderer to execute such revisit prompts while anchoring subject identity via retrieved entity latents plus a directional attention bias (IAA). The three-part rollout structure (initial / event / revisit with a blind revisit prompt that prescribes no reaction) is the evaluation trick that makes causal reasoning measurable: the model must invent the reaction itself. Methodology: The pipeline has three parts. (1) Data engine (EvoWorld-Data, ~12k videos ≥10s, 896×512 @ 24fps): structured tuples (subject, scene, event, compatible reaction, camera trajectory) are expanded by Gemini3.1-Pro into five-beat single-take scripts, rendered by Seedance 2.0/2.5, then verified — VLM checks for shot continuity, subject exit/re-entry, visible event and reaction; Lucas–Kanade + RANSAC affine-fit camera-flow estimation rejects bad trajectories; segment captions are audited for spoilers and overlap. Coverage: 19 event families/65 types, 16 scene families/63 types, 5 reaction families/14 types. (2) Renderer training on LTX-2.5 (rank-128 LoRA, effective batch 64, 8k steps): Stage 1 trains flow-matching (MSE on target-token velocity, Eq. 3) with a clean entity anchor (subject latents) and clean four-latent temporal anchor as zero-loss conditioning; IAA adds a +β (β=3.0) bias to attention scores between revisit-window queries and entity-anchor keys, active only on revisit samples (oversampled 3×). Stage 2 (200 steps, lr 2e-5) performs online one-hop autoregressive rollout: the model generates its own predecessor segment whose last four latents replace the ground-truth temporal anchor (75% online / 25% clean rehearsal), a Self-Forcing-style exposure-bias fix. (3) Inference: Qwen3.8-27B brain, served via vLLM, observes each generated segment, updates world memory, reasons over the realized event, and emits the revisit prompt ̂p plus retrieved entity evidence. Critical design decisions: anchors stay clean at timestep zero (justified by needing noise-free identity/continuity evidence); IAA only on revisit windows (justified by revisit-token dilution argument and ablation); one-hop rather than full-chain rollout in Stage 2 (justified for tractability, but untested for error accumulation over longer chains). Key Results: On EvoWorld-Bench (120 cases: 69 photorealistic, 51 game/virtual; 66 held-out frames + 54 GPT-Image-2 generated), EvoWorld achieves 90.8% Core Task Success (joint Revisit + Event + full Causal Plausibility), 100.0% Revisit, 97.5% Event, 94.2% Causal Plausibility, 85.0% Reaction Quality, and leads on Subject Consistency (99.2) and Background Consistency (98.3), vs. the next-best baseline Evoke-Turbo at 21.7% Core / 98.3% Revisit / 89.2% Event / 32.5% Causal — a +69.1pp Core gap over seven autoregressive baselines (LingBot-World v1/v2, YUME-1.5, SANA-WM, Echo-WM, Evoke, Evoke-Turbo), all run through their native interfaces with matched prompts. Ablations: IAA alone 82.5→84.2 Core; Stage 2 adds →90.8; removing the reasoning prompt (keeping the trained renderer) drops Core to 58.3; transplanting brain prompts into Evoke-Turbo lifts it 21.7→45.0. Auxiliary CLIP event–prompt alignment: EPA-TopK 0.3126 vs. 0.3043 for Evoke. One-shot models (LTX-2.5: 34.2 Core; MiniMax-H3: 21.7) trail badly. Baselines are recent and reasonably current (2025–2026 systems), though the tested scale is small (120 cases) and motion smoothness is saturated (~98–99.5 everywhere). The surprising finding is that baselines execute Revisit and Event individually at 60–98% but collapse to ~20–33% on the joint causal chain. Novelty Classification: NEW PROBLEM (Out-of-Sight Causal Evolution as a task coupling mid-rollout event realization, revisit consistency, and causal reaction — distinct from prior out-of-sight work on motion continuation), NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (EvoWorld-Data and EvoWorld-Bench with a careful train–test similarity screening protocol), and a NEW METHOD in the specific combination: VLM-brain reasoning over the realized event is a known agent-design pattern, IAA is a simple additive attention bias, and Stage 2 is adapted Self-Forcing — the genuinely non-obvious elements are the problem formulation and the finding that the joint causal-chain metric separates models that look strong on component metrics. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative (IAA, Stage 2, reasoning-prompt removal, prompt transfer to Evoke-Turbo, shared-prompt renderer comparison in Fig. 6). No error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported, despite a 120-case benchmark where each case is a binary-ish judgment. The training recipe is fully specified (LoRA rank, steps, learning rates, β, sampler, anchor layout, pseudocode in Algorithm 1). No code, dataset release, or model weights URL is mentioned in the paper text — a significant reproducibility gap for a paper whose central artifact is a dataset plus benchmark. Methodological concerns: (a) the renderer is trained on data purpose-generated for the exact three-beat rollout pattern the benchmark evaluates — the baselines received no such task-specific training, so the 69.1pp gap partly measures data-task alignment, not architecture; (b) the primary metrics are VLM-judged (Qwen3.8) by the same model family as the brain, with self-defined rubrics; the CLIP check is acknowledged by the authors as only a relative reference; (c) the data and benchmark are both synthetic products of the same VLM/generation stack, so judge and generation share stylistic priors; (d) the benchmark-train similarity screening is described carefully but is self-audited. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (systems-trained and benchmarked, not deployed). - Practical: Yes — built on a released open-weights backbone (LTX-2.5) with a rank-128 LoRA trained on 8 GPUs at 896×512/24fps, plus an off-the-shelf 27B VLM via vLLM; all commercially available components. - Efficient: Moderate — the brain calls a 27B VLM after every generated segment, adding latency and cost beyond pure video diffusion; inference uses an 8-step distilled sampler, keeping renderer cost low. - Effective: The evidence shows it solves the benchmark proxy convincingly; whether it generalizes to real footage, more complex camera paths, or multi-event worlds is untested (authors say so). - Scalable: Only claimed — the framework extends autoregressively, but training covered single-event/single-reaction chains and horizontal pan-away/pan-back trajectories; 10× longer or more complex rollouts are future work. The paper delivers a method and defines a dataset/benchmark but releases no artifact per the provided text (no repo URL stated). Strengths: - The problem formulation is genuinely new and well-motivated: prior out-of-sight evaluations test whether motion continues through an observation gap, whereas this couples mid-rollout prompt switching, off-screen causal inference, and revisit rendering into one measurable chain; the blind-revisit-prompt protocol (no prescribed reaction) is a clean device for forcing genuine inference rather than script-following. - The ablation/transplant analysis (Table 3, Fig. 5) cleanly attributes gains: reasoning prompts alone lift Evoke-Turbo by +23.3 Core, and the trained renderer without reasoning still beats all baselines — this decomposition is more honest than a single end-to-end number. - The data engine has real verification machinery beyond VLM vibes: optical-flow-based camera-trajectory rejection, spoiler/overlap caption audits, reaction-intensity calibration (strong vs. weak events), and a two-pass train–benchmark similarity screen with human adjudication. - IAA is a minimal, well-characterized intervention (one directional bias term, enabled only on revisit windows, with implementation details for LTX's mask path) rather than a heavy architectural change. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: In Appendix G the authors state: the work covers a single event and single subject reaction, not multi-event interacting worlds or multi-entity responses; camera trajectories are limited to horizontal move-away/move-back, with vertical, depth, orbital, and 6-DoF motion untested and likely harder for retrieval and revisit consistency. They also candidly report (Appendix F) that three recent systems (HY-World 1.5, Matrix-Game 3.0, AlayaWorld) were excluded from quantitative comparison because their released interfaces could not execute the protocol, and they caution against interpreting those trials as general capability assessments. This is direct, non-minimizing treatment of scope — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Train–eval distribution coupling: the renderer is trained on ~12k videos generated with the same five-beat script structure the benchmark uses; the fair comparison would fine-tune at least one strong baseline (e.g., Evoke) on EvoWorld-Data or evaluate EvoWorld zero-shot on externally sourced rollouts. - Judge circularity: the primary metrics (Event Success, Causal Plausibility, Reaction Quality, consistency) are all scored by a Qwen3.8 VLM — the same model family as the brain that generates EvoWorld's prompts — with no human evaluation study reported for the headline numbers; a human-agreement study on the 120 cases is needed to trust a 90.8 vs. 21.7 margin. - No error bars or seed variance on any metric, and binary success rates on 120 cases have ±~5pp confidence intervals; the gap is large enough to survive this, but the component-level ablation deltas (e.g., 82.5 vs. 84.2 from IAA) are within noise. - Subject-consistency asymmetry: the benchmark's I2V setup gives EvoWorld a one-step entity reference constructed so the target subject is clearly visible in the opening frame, while baselines receive no equivalent identity-conditioning mechanism. - The CLIP alignment table (Table 4) differences are tiny (0.3126 vs. 0.3043) and the authors themselves disclaim its diagnostic power; including it invites over-reading. - No qualitative failure analysis of EvoWorld itself — the paper shows baselines failing (Fig. 1) but no systematic account of when EvoWorld's brain mis-reasons or the renderer hallucinates. Bottom Line: A practitioner building reasoning-augmented video world models should read this for the sharpest available formulation of out-of-sight causal evolution and a well-ablated reference design, but should treat the 69-point benchmark margin as evidence of a task-aligned training pipeline plus brain-renderer decomposition rather than proof of a general world-evolution capability — and should demand the promised dataset/code release before building on it.

Problem & Motivation: LLMs reflect Western value profiles and fail on culturally situated behavior; prior Arabic cultural resources cover instruction-following (CIDAR, PALM) or evaluation (ARABCULTURE) but not preference-based alignment, and existing multilingual preference data (CARE) is too small and pan-Arab coverage is absent. A further gap the paper targets: treating Arabic speakers as homogeneous obscures country-specific norms (e.g., alcohol is prohibited in Saudi Arabia but liberal in Lebanon; public affection is disfavored in Egypt but acceptable in urban Tunisia). The intended beneficiaries are practitioners building Arabic-facing assistants and researchers studying within-language cultural heterogeneity. Key Idea: Country-conditioned contrastive preferences: for each (country, cultural aspect) pair, construct a preferred-vs-discouraged behavior pair plus MCQs whose distractors include the opposite behavior in-country and same-aspect behaviors from other countries — forcing models to distinguish norms within a cultural continuum rather than recognize generic Arab culture, with training/test splits at the country–aspect level to prevent leakage into the MCQ benchmark. Methodology: Four stages. (1) Data collection: manual curation of etiquette sources for 13 countries plus CultureBank entries; 16 categories expanded into 200 human-verified aspects. (2) Preference generation: Gemini-2.5-Flash paraphrases preferred/discouraged behaviors conditioned on source text; filters include language validation, MinHash dedup, and GemmaEmbedding cosine-similarity dedup (threshold 0.90). (3) HITL validation: two-stage protocol (cultural preference validation, then MSA verification) with 40 annotators, 2–3 experts per country, QC samples requiring ≥80% annotator accuracy, plus 10% secondary expert review; MCQ distractors are polarity-inverted or cross-country, semantically filtered at 0.80, and some MCQs were reduced to three options when multiple answers were defensible. (4) Alignment: LoRA post-training (rank 8, 3 epochs, 2×A100-80GB) of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct, and Jais-adapted-7B-Chat with SFT (NLL loss), DPO (β=0.1), and KTO, against CARE (Arabic portion) and PALM (MSA) baselines. Evaluation uses GPT-4o as LLM-as-judge on 1–5 Likert scales for Cultural Appropriateness, General Quality, and Literacy, plus exact-match MCQ accuracy via lm-evaluation-harness. Critical design decisions: country–aspect-level train/test splits (well justified, prevents leakage); the sampled ablation controlling for data volume (well justified, addresses the ARABPREF+CARE-vs-CARE confound); DPO/KTO hyperparameters (β=0.1, λ+=λ−=1.0) taken standard without tuning (not discussed). Key Results: The MCQ benchmark contains 992 questions per language; preferences total 15,530 train pairs per language and 3,300 filtered English test pairs. Best open-source MCQ results: Qwen-2.5-7B reaches 68.6% English (+5.3 over 63.3% vanilla) with ARABPREF+CARE DPO but only 58.7% Arabic (+1.1 over 57.6%); Jais improves from 49.6% to 53.7% English and 39.4% to 45.6% Arabic (largest gain from CARE DPO, +6.2 Arabic). Proprietary zero-shot references: Qwen3.6-Plus 80.5% En / 76.5% Ar; GPT-5.4 79.2 / 75.9. On generation (GPT-4o judging), Jais+SFT(ARABPREF+CARE) reaches 4.62 English average (from 3.74) and Qwen+KTO reaches 4.47 Arabic (from 3.98); Claude-Sonnet-4 tops English at 4.92 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash Arabic at 4.77. Scaling analysis: Qwen3-32B reaches 73.9% En / 71.4% Ar on MCQs; Jais 7B→13B improves Arabic (49.2→55.3) but not English. Notable negative/counter-intuitive results: no single alignment method wins across models and languages; SFT on ARABPREF+CARE degrades Qwen's Arabic Literacy to 2.60; head-to-head win rates favor ARABPREF+CARE over CARE-only in 5/6 DPO comparisons (Jais English 58.5% vs 30.3%) but not Jais-Arabic DPO; data-language sensitivity is architecture-dependent (Qwen does best with English-only training, Llama/Jais with the full dataset). Baselines (CARE, PALM) are recent and appropriate; the tested scale is standard (7–8B open models, proprietary API references). Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (first pan-Arab, country-conditioned behavioral preference resource with a matched MCQ benchmark) plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (alignment-method effects are inconsistent across architectures and languages, and Arabic gains lag English gains). The optimization machinery — SFT/DPO/KTO with LoRA, LLM-as-judge evaluation — is a standard combination of existing techniques applied to a new resource; the genuinely novel element is the fine-grained country-conditioning of preferences and the leakage-safe train/test split design. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and meaningful: a scale-controlled sampled-data ablation (30 pairs/country) isolating ARABPREF's contribution from data volume; sample-efficiency curves (10–100% data, 10–100 samples with DITTO); monolingual-vs-whole-dataset training; and scaling studies across three model families. Statistical treatment is above average: two-sided paired permutation tests (p<0.05) flag significant deltas, judge–human Spearman ρ per dimension per language (0.67–0.895 on 100 stratified samples), and judge self-consistency (Fleiss' κ 0.9503 over 1,800 scoring calls). No multiple-seed variance for the training runs themselves is reported. Full prompts, annotation guidelines, licenses, and hyperparameters are in appendices; the paper states the dataset and benchmark are released but no URL or repository is printed in the provided text. Methodological concerns: (a) the training preferences appear to be LLM-generated and filtered automatically, with HITL validation applied to test/MCQ data — training-pair quality rests on the 15.25% rejection-rate evidence from the annotation study; (b) MCQ distractors are country-labeled behaviors from other countries, so a model identifying the country from scenario cues could partially shortcut the cultural-reasoning task; (c) evaluation and benchmark were developed in-house, and the strongest claims about ARABPREF's value rest partly on the authors' own MCQ benchmark (though head-to-head win rates against CARE/PALM-trained models partially mitigate this). Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (dataset construction plus post-training experiments actually run; no new system infrastructure). Practical: Yes — LoRA post-training of 7–8B models on two 80GB A100s is commercially accessible. Efficient: Low cost relative to alternatives (3 epochs, LoRA rank 8, effective batch 16); inference at 2,048-token context. Effective: The evidence shows improved cultural appropriateness on the authors' own benchmark and judge protocol, with human–judge correlation supporting but not proving real-world alignment; Arabic improvements are the weakest link (+0.4 to +6.2 MCQ points depending on model). Scalable: Not directly tested — scaling claims rest on a separate observational study of pre-existing model sizes (up to 32B), not on scaling ARABPREF training itself; behavior beyond 32B is unexamined. Deliverable: a reusable dataset and benchmark artifact (bilingual preference pairs and MCQs), not a library or trained model checkpoint per the text. Strengths: - Genuine resource novelty: first country-level (as opposed to pan-Arab or pan-multicultural) behavioral preference dataset, with a taxonomy of 200 aspects across 16 categories and documented intra-Arab variation (Table 10's alcohol/dress/affection/greetings spectra), enabling a class of controlled experiments prior Arabic resources cannot support. - The leakage-safe design — splitting at the country–aspect level so no training prompt, chosen, or rejected response becomes an MCQ stem or option — is a methodological point most cultural-benchmark papers omit. - The validation protocol is unusually concrete: Native-In-Country policy (95% of annotators residing in-country), per-country expert assignment, QC-gated batches, and an explicit rejection rate (15.25%) showing humans reshaped rather than rubber-stamped the LLM-generated candidates. - Honest reporting of instability: the paper states plainly that no single alignment method consistently benefits all models and languages, and it quantifies the Qwen Arabic-Literacy degradation rather than burying it. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The Limitations section states that ARABPREF may not capture within-country regional/local diversity, that behavioral preferences omit other cultural dimensions (emotional expression, non-verbal communication), and that MCQ evaluation may not capture dynamic, open-ended, real-world cultural alignment. The Ethics section concedes the dataset represents only a portion of cultural practices and could reinforce stereotypes. The Conclusion adds future work on dialects, code-switching, within-country variation, temporal drift, and multi-turn contexts. The authors confront limitations directly rather than minimize them — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the authors' acknowledgments: (1) the asymmetry between validated test data and presumably unvalidated LLM-generated training preferences is not explicitly flagged, yet it directly conditions what the alignment experiments optimize; (2) the potential country-identification shortcut in MCQs (distractors from other countries) is not discussed or ablated (e.g., zero-context country-guessing baselines); (3) source data comes from travel blogs and Western government advisories (US State Dept, UK FCDO), a tourist-outsider perspective that may itself encode the stereotype-avoidance problem the paper targets — no analysis of this bias; (4) no evaluation on an external, non-author-built cultural benchmark (e.g., ARABCULTURE) to show the alignment gains transfer; (5) DPO/KTO hyperparameters appear untuned and no seeds are varied, so the cross-method inconsistencies that anchor the paper's empirical claims could partly reflect optimization noise; (6) the claimed release lacks a printed URL or archive identifier in the provided text. Bottom Line: For anyone building culturally conditioned preference datasets or working on Arabic LLM alignment, this is worth reading for the resource, the annotation protocol, and the honest cross-architecture negative results; for alignment-method research broadly, the algorithmic content is standard DPO/KTO/SFT and the published evaluation evidence for the Arabic side is thin enough that stronger domain alternatives (or this paper's own follow-ups) may soon cover the same ground.

HarnessFlow: MCTS-Guided Harness Optimization for LLM Agents

Z Hong, Q Wang, H Wei, A Wu, D Ying, M Kong, B Liu… · arxiv.org · automated generated environments for agent testing - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces HarnessFlow, a framework that automatically optimizes complete executable LLM agent harnesses by coupling Monte Carlo Tree Search over a tree of harness codebases with a coding agent that performs full-code refinements under a budget of 15 candidate evaluations per benchmark. - Why it's important: Harness design (context management, state tracking, tool interfacing, control flow) is currently manual and expertise-intensive, yet it materially changes agent performance without touching model weights — automating it makes agent quality cheaply adaptable across tasks. - How it does it: Each candidate is a full executable codebase stored as a tree node with its validation score; a mixture policy (score-softmax exploitation plus an inverse-expansion-count exploration term) selects which parent to refine, and a coding agent (Codex running GPT-5.5) edits the selected harness using an experience archive and a 21-module Harness Component Library. - The good: Under identical budgets, backbones, tool access, and evaluation protocols, it achieves the highest mean test score on all six benchmarks (69.48% average, +3.95 points over the strongest prior method Meta-Harness) while incurring the lowest average per-task execution cost ($0.232 vs. $0.398–$0.561 for hand-engineered harnesses). - The missing: One-time harness-search compute cost is explicitly excluded from the cost analysis and never quantified, and the method is only demonstrated with a per-benchmark search — no evidence that an optimized harness transfers across benchmarks or tasks. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building automated agent-design or self-improving-agent systems who need to compare search-organization strategies under evaluation budgets; practitioners who just want a good off-the-shelf harness can skip it and use Codex or Hermes directly.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (65) is solid — the fairest head-to-head protocol in this subfield, error bars over 5 runs, targeted ablations — but capped by ablations covering only 3 of 6 benchmarks, no significance tests on within-2-point margins, code promised but not released, and one-time search cost excluded from every cost claim. Novelty (62) is a well-motivated recombination (MCTS selection plus a coding-agent proposer over full harnesses) rather than a new formulation, and Non-Obviousness (60) rests mainly on the tree-preservation lineage finding. Resilience (60) and Completeness (60) are moderate: limitations are confronted honestly, but the absence of any transfer evaluation means the system is really six per-benchmark harnesses, and winner's-curse selection noise is unanalyzed. Practical Impact (55) is limited by per-benchmark specialization and an unreported search bill. Weighted composite: 0.20*62 + 0.25*65 + 0.15*60 + 0.15*60 + 0.15*60 + 0.10*55 = 61.

Problem & Motivation: LLM agent performance depends on the harness — the executable system governing context construction, state, tool access, and termination — as much as on the model itself. Harness design is manual and expertise-intensive, and existing automation either searches narrow spaces (fixed configurations, bounded edits, prompt-level changes: HARBOR, PRISM, Self-Harness) or, when it permits full-code modification, organizes refinement without explicit search over retained alternatives (Meta-Harness). The core problem is allocating a scarce budget of expensive end-to-end candidate evaluations across an open-ended design space: which harness to refine next, given that each evaluation costs multiple model and tool calls. The authors frame this as search over complete executable harnesses rather than prompts, configurations, or single workflow layers. Key Idea: Treat the population of evaluated harnesses as a refinement tree and use an MCTS-style selection policy to decide which parent to refine, while delegating how to refine to a coding agent with access to archived code, scores, execution traces, and a library of reusable harness mechanisms. Parent selection combines a temperature-softmax over validation scores (exploitation) with a (1+children)^(-α) term favoring under-expanded nodes (exploration), mixed with weight ε=0.35. Because every evaluated harness and its score are preserved in the tree, later rounds can return to and develop earlier designs rather than only the latest candidate — which the lineage analysis (e.g., SWE-bench Verified lineage 0→2→4→8→10, 67.60%→79.20%) shows is where late gains come from. Methodology: The setting fixes the model (GPT-5.4-mini at medium reasoning effort), environment, and evaluation protocol; a harness h is scored s(h|D) = E[r(Agent(m,h,x), y)] on a validation split D_v, and the optimizer maximizes this under N=15 refinement attempts, finally reporting the best-validation harness on a disjoint test set. The loop is: (1) Selection — shortlist up to K=5 highest-scoring nodes, sample a parent from π_n = (1−ε)·softmax(q/τ) + ε·(1+d)^(-α)-normalized, with τ set automatically to one standard error of the validation score (clipped to [0.005, 0.100]); (2) Expansion — the Refine step, a general-purpose coding agent that inspects the tree's experience archive A (code, edits, scores, task-level traces), a read-only snapshot of a 21-module Harness Component Library (context construction, memory/state, control-flow runners, tool interfacing, verification/recovery), and copies adopted modules into a self-contained candidate; (3) Evaluation — R=5 repeated runs on D_v; (4) Experience backpropagation — record the candidate, its edits, score, and parent-relative score change in A, add the tree edge, increment the parent's expansion count. The framework is explicitly a budgeted-search protocol rather than a learning method; there is no trained objective beyond the empirical validation score. Critical design decisions: representing candidates as whole codebases rather than configurations (justified as necessary for coordinated cross-mechanism edits, and supported by the ablation showing gains persist from a different initial harness); separating selection policy from the proposer (justified by the ε ablation showing the mixture beats pure exploit or pure explore by 5.4–5.7 points); and tree- rather than graph-structured search (acknowledged as a limitation — no cross-branch merging). Key Results: Across six benchmarks (TAU2-bench, AppWorld, WebShop, BrowseComp-Plus, SWE-bench Verified, BigCodeBench-Hard), HarnessFlow achieves the highest mean test score on every one, averaging 69.48% versus Vanilla 58.59%, Claude Code 61.71, OpenHands 62.61, Hermes 64.28, Codex 64.82, and Meta-Harness 65.53 — i.e., +10.89 over the starting harness and +3.95 over the strongest prior optimizer, with the largest per-benchmark gains over Vanilla on WebShop (+21.70) and TAU2-bench (+17.85). Search is sample-efficient: mean best-so-far validation score reaches 71.5% after 3 candidate evaluations and 74.2% by round 15. Execution cost is $0.101 per task (geometric mean across benchmarks), on the Pareto frontier with Meta-Harness ($0.092), while hand-engineered harnesses cost roughly 2–3× as much at lower scores. With a stronger executor (GPT-5.4) on three benchmarks, the gap persists: 83.58% vs. Meta-Harness 81.71 and Claude Code 80.85, at $0.21/task vs. $0.67 for Claude Code. Ablations: removing the component library drops the three-benchmark average from 65.03 to 63.39; starting search from the OpenHands harness instead of the benchmark reference still yields 62.61; and ε=0.35 beats both ε=0 (73.93) and ε=1 (73.65). All reported numbers are means over 5 runs with sample standard deviations. Baselines are current (fixed-version releases of Claude Code, Codex CLI, OpenHands, Hermes) and run under identical backbones, tool access, and limits — a fair comparison protocol. Test scale is modest (92–210 tasks per split), and the method is a per-benchmark optimization, not a single universal harness. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD with an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION component. The genuinely novel element is the explicit coupling of an MCTS-style parent-selection policy (with a noise-adaptive softmax temperature and expansion-count exploration term) to a full-codebase coding-agent proposer under a stated candidate-evaluation budget. The ingredients are individually known: MCTS over code-represented candidates is AFlow's move (the paper itself distinguishes HarnessFlow by searching the full harness rather than a fixed operator-workflow layer and by using an executing coding agent as proposer), archive-based self-improvement is SICA/Huxley–Gödel Machine territory, and component libraries for agent construction appear in HarnessX. The contribution is a well-motivated recombination targeting the full-harness layer plus a clean budgeted-optimization problem formulation. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and target the right questions — library removal, alternative initialization (OpenHands root), and the exploration coefficient ε — though the ablations cover only 3 of the 6 benchmarks. Error bars (±1 SD over 5 runs) are reported for all main tables, but no significance tests; several headline margins (e.g., 69.48 vs. 65.53 average) exceed the reported SDs, but per-benchmark gaps on AppWorld (80.76±1.33 vs. 76.76±2.94) and BCB-H are within roughly 1.5 SD. Validation/test splits are made once with a fixed seed and the test set is never seen by the optimizer — a Goodhart-respecting protocol, though with only 92–210 tasks per split and search selecting the max over 16 candidates, selection-on-validation noise is a live concern the paper mitigates (R=5 repetitions) but does not analyze. Code, scripts, and per-figure reproduction are promised ("will be released") but no URL or repository is given at submission time, and the component library itself is described but not released in this version. Baseline provenance is unusually well documented (exact releases, revisions, invocation details in Appendices C.2–C.3). One methodological flag: the one-time search cost (16 full harness evaluations × 5 repetitions × ~100–200 tasks, driven by a GPT-5.5 proposer) is excluded from all cost claims and never reported. Deployability: (EMPIRICAL profile):** The paper runs experiments end-to-end on real benchmarks with production baselines, so I apply the empirical check. - Practical: Yes — the optimized harness executes with a mid-tier commercial model (GPT-5.4-mini) in a sandboxed runtime; nothing requires exotic hardware, though search itself needs a frontier coding model (GPT-5.5) plus ~16 candidate evaluations. - Efficient: At inference, the most cost-efficient method evaluated ($0.232/task arithmetic average vs. $0.398–$0.561 for hand-engineered harnesses); at search time, cost is unreported and is a real one-time expense. - Effective: The evidence shows it solves the stated problem on benchmarks with automatic graders, at better-than-baseline cost — though "effectiveness" here is per-benchmark: each deployed harness is specialized to one benchmark's validation split. - Scalable: Not tested beyond N=15 attempts; the authors only claim, not demonstrate, that search compute amortizes over deployment, and behavior at larger budgets or with graph-structured search is unexplored. The work delivers a method and (promised) scripts; the reusable Harness Component Library is described in detail but is not itself released as a standalone artifact in this version. Strengths: - The fairest head-to-head comparison protocol I have seen in this subfield: identical backbone, tool access, per-task limits, sandbox, evaluation repetitions, and candidate budget across all methods including hand-engineered production agents, with exact baseline releases documented. - The tree-preservation insight is empirically substantive, not decorative: 4 of 6 benchmarks' final best candidates were first reached at round 10 or later by refining retained earlier harnesses, directly demonstrating why explicit search organization (vs. Meta-Harness's iterative refinement of the current proposal) matters under budget. - Honest lineage analysis — the paper explicitly states that lineage scores reflect cumulative harness designs, not isolated effects of individual edits, resisting the temptation to attribute gains to single "tricks." - The noise-adaptive temperature (τ set to one standard error of validation scores) is a small but thoughtful design choice that removes a per-benchmark hyperparameter. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state three: (1) the search requires an automatic grader, scoping the method to gradable tasks; (2) search consumes evaluation compute — a one-time but real cost that bounds the practical budget; (3) the tree structure forces single-parent descent, preventing candidates from combining mechanisms discovered on separate branches, which they flag as the natural next step (graph search). These are confronted directly and accurately, which strengthens credibility. They do not acknowledge the unreported magnitude of search cost or the per-benchmark specialization issue. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No transfer evaluation: the headline system is really six independently optimized harnesses; nothing shows an optimized harness (or the component library adoption patterns) helps on a benchmark it was not searched for. The practical claim "automating harness design" implies reusability that is never measured. - Search cost opacity: every cost claim excludes one-time search; a practitioner deciding whether to run this needs the (likely substantial, GPT-5.5-proposer) search bill, which is absent. - Selection-noise analysis missing: with ~100-task validation splits and best-of-16 selection, the expected winner's-curse inflation of the chosen harness's validation score is non-trivial; no analysis or correction (e.g., held-out confirmation within validation) is offered. - No significance testing despite multiple within-~2-point comparisons against Meta-Harness on individual benchmarks. - Prover-proposer upper bound: the coding agent is fixed at GPT-5.5 maximum reasoning effort; the paper does not ablate proposer capability, so the reader cannot tell how much of the gain depends on a frontier proposer rather than the search machinery. - The main-results ablations (library, initialization, ε) run on only 3 of 6 benchmarks; the ε ablation's large gaps on TAU2/SWE-V vs. near-tie on AppWorld suggest benchmark-dependent sensitivity that the 3-benchmark average may obscure. Bottom Line: For researchers working on automated agent design, this is the strongest and cleanest-evidenced entry in the fast-growing harness-optimization line and worth reading in full; for everyone else, the practical takeaway — that harness search buys ~4–11 points over both hand-engineered and iteratively-refined harnesses at lower inference cost, at the price of an unreported one-time search bill and no demonstrated cross-task transfer — is already covered by the abstract and tables.

Training-Free Residual-Guided Retrieval for Multi-hop KGQA with Single-Step LLM Inference

K Sei, SK Maurya, Y Kobashi, Y Matsuo · aclanthology.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a training-free residual-guided retrieval framework for knowledge-graph question answering that adapts the retrieval query at each hop via embedding-space vector arithmetic, using the LLM only once for final answer generation. - Why it's important: Iterative LLM-guided graph traversal (e.g., ToG, FiDeLiS) adapts retrieval but costs 10–15 LLM calls per question, while learned retrievers (GNN-RAG, SubgraphRAG) need ~28K–30K training examples; this method removes both costs, which matters for cheap deployment of KG-RAG over large graphs. - How it does it: At each hop it computes a residual vector r = norm(v_question − α_p·norm(v_path) − α_src·norm(v_source)) representing the question semantics not yet covered by the current reasoning path, and uses cosine similarity against this residual to score relations and edges for expansion. - The good: It achieves 86.0% Hit on WebQSP and 73.0% on CWQ with a single LLM call — beating FiDeLiS on CWQ (71.4%) while cutting calls from 15.2 to 1 — and the ablation isolates the residual's contribution (+4.5 Hit on CWQ), with gains reproduced across two embedding encoders. - The missing: The method over-generates answers badly — macro precision is 46.5 (WebQSP) and 30.4 (CWQ) versus recall of 75.1/69.0 — giving macro-F1 of 47.2/36.1, far below GNN-RAG's 71.3/59.4; the headline Hit metric masks this precision failure. - Read it or not: Worth reading if you build graph-RAG pipelines and care about inference cost or zero-training retrieval; skip if you need well-calibrated answer sets, since the precision problem is unresolved in the default configuration.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (60) rests on a simple but effective mechanism — a path-conditioned residual vector replacing hop-wise LLM re-planning — with a real, replicated single-call result on CWQ and a released code artifact (Impact 55). Rigor (58) is undermined by transcribed apples-to-oranges baseline numbers, no variance estimates, and — critically — a headline Hit metric that structurally rewards the over-generation the authors themselves document (macro precision 30-46); Resilience (55) suffers because the primary framing would not survive adversarial scrutiny of that metric choice, even though the limitations section is candid. Weighted composite: 0.20*60 + 0.25*58 + 0.15*62 + 0.15*70 + 0.15*55 + 0.10*55 = 60.

Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Multi-hop KGQA requires retrieving reasoning paths whose relevance shifts as reasoning progresses: the constraint needed at hop 2 differs from hop 1. Static retrieval with a fixed query embedding misses these changing constraints. Current solutions trade off two costs: iterative LLM-guided traversal (ToG, FiDeLiS, RoG, RJE) adapts at each hop but consumes 10–15 LLM calls per question, and learned graph retrievers (GNN-RAG, SubgraphRAG, GGR, D-RAG) achieve strong retrieval but require tens of thousands of task-specific training examples. Practitioners deploying KG-RAG over large KGs lack a method that is both adaptive across hops and cheap at inference with no supervision. Key Idea: State-dependent retrieval via linear residual subtraction in embedding space: after each hop, subtract the (normalized) current path embedding and source-entity embedding from the question embedding to obtain a residual vector that represents the remaining unresolved constraint, then rank next-hop relations and edges by cosine similarity to this residual. Because relation and entity ranking are cosine-based in one shared embedding space, changing the query vector directly changes the ranking direction — no LLM re-planning or learned retriever is needed. Methodology: The pipeline is beam-style breadth-first graph search with a running path-state embedding. (1) Encode the question into v_q with a dense encoder (Qwen3-Embedding-4B). (2) Initialize the frontier from topic entities. (3) At each hop and each frontier state, compute the residual r_z (Eq. 1) as the normalized difference of question, path, and source embeddings; the path state is updated incrementally by a weighted sum of relation and entity embeddings (w_rel=0.6, w_ent=0.4) rather than by serializing the path to text. (4) Score each outgoing relation with a weighted cosine combination of residual, question, and a rule-based answer-type anchor (λ_res/λ_q/λ_type = 0.3/0.5/0.2); keep top-3K relations, rerank using top-K_n neighbor evidence, score edges with an entity bonus (β_edge=0.2), extend the top-K paths, update the path state, and recompute the residual. (5) After a fixed maximum hop count T, one LLM call (Qwen3-8B) generates the answer from textualized paths. Critical design decisions: linear subtraction as a soft query update (justified in Appendix A as adequate because ranking is cosine-based in one space); a rule-based first-word answer-type anchor (well-justified — ablations show it contributes little, −0.5 WebQSP/+0.2 CWQ when removed); fixed hop budget with no adaptive stopping (weakly justified, acknowledged as a limitation). All eight hyperparameters were selected once on the 250-question WebQSP dev set and reused unchanged for CWQ, other encoders, and noisy-graph experiments. Key Results: On WebQSP (1,639 test questions) and CWQ (3,531 test questions), the method achieves 86.0% and 73.0% Hit with 1 LLM call, versus FiDeLiS at 84.1%/71.4% with 10.7/15.2 calls and ToG at 82.6%/67.6% with 11.2/14.3 calls. Against supervised retrievers, it scores 86.0/73.0 with zero training data versus GNN-RAG (85.7/66.8), RoG (85.7/62.6), and SubgraphRAG (89.4/68.6), each trained on 27.6K–30.5K examples — best on CWQ, competitive on WebQSP. Token cost is far below iterative baselines (CWQ: 1,731 input/61.9 output tokens vs. ToG's 8,183/1,486; ToG/PoG/RJE token numbers taken from the RJE paper, the authors' own numbers self-measured). Ablations: removing the residual term drops Hit by 1.9 (WebQSP) and 4.5 (CWQ) points, and the +4.5 CWQ gain replicates with BGE-large-en-v1.5 (66.2→70.7). An LLM-as-a-judge re-evaluation with GPT-4o-mini adds only +2.5/+2.7 Hit. Noisy-graph robustness testing (20–40% edge rewiring) degrades Hit by at most 0.1–0.8 points. Notably, a revised generator setup (Qwen3.8-27B + new prompt) raises macro-F1 by ~26 points on both datasets (73.4 WebQSP / 62.6 CWQ, exceeding GNN-RAG's 71.3/59.4) but lowers Hit by 2.0–2.7 points. Baseline Hit numbers are transcribed from the original papers rather than re-run. Error analysis on CWQ shows 69.2% of the 952 errors are retrieval failures (gold answer absent from retrieved paths). Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (residual-guided, training-free adaptive graph retrieval) plus an EMPIRICAL FINDING (adaptive multi-hop retrieval achievable with one LLM call). The residual/subtraction idea echoes vector-arithmetic tricks from prompt representation editing and query expansion, and the overall framework is a competent combination of dense retrieval, beam search over the KG, and single-call RAG — the genuine novelty is using a path-conditioned residual as the dynamic retrieval query in place of hop-wise LLM re-planning, and demonstrating it beats that paradigm at 1/10th the call count. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and targeted: they isolate the residual term, the type anchor, the prompt rules, the λ weightings, α/β sensitivity (all within 1.0 point of default), and embedding-model swaps. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere. Code is publicly released (github.com/SeiKdesu/Training-Free-Residual-Guided-Retrieval-for-Multi-hop-KGQA); no model weights or dataset artifacts beyond code. Methodological concerns: (1) all baseline Hit numbers are copied from the baselines' own papers under potentially different generators and prompts — an apples-to-oranges comparison the authors do not flag as such in the main table; (2) the metric of choice, string-match Hit (correct if any gold string appears in output), structurally rewards the observed answer over-generation, inflating Hit while macro-F1 collapses; (3) the token-cost comparison mixes figures taken from the RJE paper for baselines with self-measured figures for their method; (4) evaluation is confined to two English Freebase benchmarks. The hyperparameter protocol (tuned on WebQSP dev, reused unchanged on CWQ) is a credibility positive. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS artifact — released code). Practical: Yes — it runs on a 4B embedder plus an 8B generator (with a quantized 27B alternative tested), all commercially available hardware. Efficient: Strong — one LLM call and roughly 1/4 the input and 1/10–1/24 the output tokens of iterative baselines per question. Effective: Mixed — Hit evidence supports the retrieval claim, but macro precision 30.4–46.5 shows the end-to-end system returns bloated answer sets; the stated problem (accurate multi-hop QA) is only partially solved. Scalable: Not tested beyond these two benchmarks; behavior on larger KGs, deeper questions beyond 3 hops, or non-Freebase schemas is unexamined. Delivers a software artifact (public code repository); no trained model or dataset release. Strengths: (1) A crisp, inspectable mechanism — the residual vector is deterministic vector arithmetic, making multi-hop retrieval auditable in a way LLM-guided traversal is not, and the case studies (Tables 4, 19, 20) concretely show the residual redirecting search from covered to unresolved constraints. (2) A favorable point on a real trade-off curve: it beats LLM-guided baselines on the harder multi-hop benchmark (CWQ) at 1/10th–1/15th the LLM calls, which is the actual deployment-relevant quantity. (3) Disciplined hyperparameter hygiene — tuning once on 250 dev questions and freezing everything across datasets, encoders, and noise experiments — plus an unusually honest error analysis (69.2% of errors are retrieval-side, with three named failure patterns). (4) The residual effect replicates across two embedding families (+4.5 CWQ Hit on both Qwen3-Embedding-4B and BGE-large-en-v1.5), suggesting the mechanism is not encoder-specific. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state three limitations directly and confront them with data rather than minimizing: (1) the generator over-generates — macro precision 46.5/30.4 versus recall 75.1/69.0, macro-F1 47.2/36.1 far below GNN-RAG's 71.3/59.4, attributed to the un-finetuned generator being prompted to list all possible answers; (2) a fixed maximum hop length with no adaptive stopping criterion; (3) evaluation restricted to WebQSP and CWQ over Freebase, with no other KG structures or domains tested. They also note the type anchor is English-interrogative-word-specific and that hop-dependent weighting was not tested. This candor is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The headline Hit metric rewards the over-generation the authors themselves document — a prediction containing any gold string counts as correct, so a system that lists many candidates is structurally favored; presenting Hit as the primary result while the revised-prompt experiment (which trades Hit for F1) shows the tension is a framing choice reviewers should scrutinize. (2) All zero/few-shot baseline numbers are transcribed from other papers under different generator models and prompts; the paper runs no same-generator controlled comparison against ToG/FiDeLiS, so the Hit advantage may partially reflect the stronger answer generator (Qwen3-8B) rather than better retrieval. (3) The ToG diagnostic (Table 5) uses a compact quantized controller (Qwen3-8B-AWQ), a weak-man setting that flatters the deterministic approach; ToG with a frontier controller is not tested. (4) No statistical significance or variance estimates, and no latency/runtime numbers for the embedding-based traversal itself (embedding of large candidate relation sets could be non-trivial). (5) The claim of robustness rests on edge rewiring only; semantic noise (wrong-but-plausible relations) is untested. (6) The Qwen3.8-27B experiment changes generator and prompt simultaneously, so the paper's own best-F1 configuration is confounded — the authors note this but leave it unresolved. Bottom Line: A practitioner building cost-sensitive graph-RAG should read this: the residual mechanism is simple, code is released, and the single-call/zero-training result on CWQ is real, but treat the headline Hit numbers skeptically and plan to fix answer-set precision yourself, because the paper's own data shows the default system does not.
