Problem & Motivation: Hardware teams adopting AI-assisted design face a measurement and governance gap: agent benchmarks (VerilogEval, FIXME, HWE-Bench, CLOSER-Bench) score one-shot RTL generation or bounded cross-stage closure, while vendor announcements (Cadence ChipStack, Synopsys agentic verification, Siemens Questa One) report task-specific speedups with undisclosed baselines and acceptance criteria. Neither measures what actually costs time in chip development — revalidating evidence when a design changes — and the industry context is dire: the 2024 Wilson Research Group survey reports 14% first-silicon success for IC/ASIC projects and 75% schedule slippage. The paper argues the field lacks any longitudinal, complexity-normalized measure of accepted-change throughput, and that accelerating generation alone can even reduce accepted-change throughput by saturating scarce verification and review capacity. Key Idea: The core insight is revalidation locality: the operative question for hardware agility is not how fast candidates are produced but how much previously acquired evidence a change invalidates — a quantity distinct from textual diff size, since a one-line edit can globally invalidate timing evidence while a large rewrite may preserve a proven contract. Operationalizing this requires separating authority (the proposing agent cannot alter acceptance criteria), typing evidence by scope (a bounded model check is not an unbounded proof; a passing simulation is not a timing result), and measuring time-to-accepted-change rather than time-to-green-output. Methodology: The paper is a position/analysis paper with four components. (1) An architecture (Fig. 1) splitting an agent-controlled proposal workspace from an owner-governed acceptance path, formalized via an acceptance contract Γ = (R, A, P, M, U) over requirements, assumptions, constraints, obligations, and authority rules; evidence records e = (r, h, m, a, s, o, p, w) with Valid/Fresh/Authentic predicates; and an Accept(·) gate (Eq. 4) requiring all mandatory obligations to hold. Invalidation is a transitive closure I_G(Δ) over a dependency DAG (Eq. 3), with a conditional-preservation proposition whose premise — a complete semantic dependency model — is acknowledged as the hard engineering problem. (2) Analytical models: an Amdahl decomposition (a 20× generator with f=0.2 yields only 1.235× episode speedup), an invalidation-weighted cost model with break-even condition O < (1−Λ)V (Eq. 10), an amortization condition Σb_i > K, and a queueing-style admission-control condition ρ < 1. (3) A worked illustrative example: inserting an elastic stage into a ready–valid streaming buffer, enumerating which obligations (ordered transfers per reset epoch, stall safety, liveness under fairness, throughput, an independent decoder's proof, post-route timing) must be rechecked vs. conditionally retained. (4) A standard-library Python artifact testing the bookkeeping semantics (stale records rejected, bounded results not passing as proofs, protected-constraint tampering detected), plus reproducible scenario forecasts for 2027–2031 (Eq. 14) giving conditional 14–67% time savings across IP/FPGA/ASIC scopes. Critical design decisions — conservative invalidation before selective reuse, contract immutability within an episode, censored-episode reporting — are explicitly argued rather than merely asserted. Key Results: Not applicable in the experimental sense; the paper reports no measurements on real designs, tools, or engineers. Its quantitative content is analytical: the Amdahl ceiling (1.25× episode speedup for infinite generator acceleration at f=0.2); a synthetic serial episode showing 3.08× vs. 1.23× speedup from reuse vs. generator-only improvement (explicitly flagged as illustrative, not an experimental speedup); break-even sensitivity (reuse saves time only when overhead is below the (1−Λ)V diagonal); and scenario forecasts — central case: 45% elapsed-time saving for reusable IP (1.83×), 41% for integrated FPGA (1.69×), 32% for ASIC-to-qualified-die (1.47×) — all constructed inputs, not fitted models. Vendor figures are quoted only to be bounded in interpretation: 40–60× computational-lithography acceleration, ~12-week historical wafer fab lead times, 3–5% fab equipment throughput from AI use cases, and an NXP study removing 42–74% of test items (test items, not test time). The Python artifact passes unit tests for the acceptance semantics, which the authors state demonstrates hardware correctness "not at all." Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION plus a NEW METRIC (TTAC, revalidation locality as an organizing principle) and a NEW EVALUATION PROTOCOL (four falsifiable hypotheses, sequence-based evaluation, protected oracles, outcome vectors with censored episodes). The genuinely novel move is reframing agentic-hardware progress around evidence freshness and acceptance governance rather than generation quality. The constituent mechanisms — proof-carrying code/hardware (Necula 1997; Love et al. 2012), incremental build systems à la carte, continuous assurance via the Evidential Tool Bus, OpenTitan's staged development — are all existing ideas, and the paper says so explicitly; no new algorithm, theorem, or system is delivered. Rigor & Reproducibility: For a position paper, self-skeptical rigor is high: explicit non-claims, a source-audit appendix classifying every reference as observation/deduction/mechanism/hypothesis, vendor claims consistently labeled as unreplicated, and a falsifiability section (Table 5) that names disconfirming results. The Python artifact is reproducible (standard library, unittest commands given, arXiv ancillary files) and honestly scoped as testing bookkeeping semantics only. However: there are no error bars, seeds, or significance tests because there are no experiments; the Proposition is trivial (it follows directly from dependency completeness, as the authors concede); the scenario numbers are chosen inputs; and the manuscript discloses it "was drafted with generative-AI assistance" while noting "the actual authors must verify its content and provide their real names" — an unusual authorship posture for a single-named independent-researcher preprint that reviewers should weigh. No evaluation on the authors' own benchmark or benchmark gaming occurs, because no benchmark is run. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: THEORETICAL (analytical models and a formal proposal with no primary experimental claim; the artifact is a semantic illustration, not a deployed system). - Sound: The formalism is internally consistent and the one proposition's assumptions are stated, but its premise (complete, versioned semantic dependency models spanning RTL-to-netlist-to-physical evidence) is unproven and acknowledged as the open problem. - General: The argument spans RTL/FPGA/ASIC scopes and explicitly declines to cover analog, packaging, or board domains; applicability to small teams is conceded to be uncertain (overhead may exceed benefit). - Tight: N/A — no bounds are claimed; the closest analogue, the break-even condition, is exact within its serial toy model and the paper flags when the model is vacuous (global edits where Λ→1 force full revalidation). - Implementable: The contracts, records, and gate suggest a concrete build (secure tool wrappers, content-addressed logs, machine-readable evidence objects), and §8.5 sketches a feasible first study on open IP with an open toolchain, but nothing has been operationalized; no follow-up exists. The deliverable is a paper plus a small reproducible Python artifact (unit tests, analytical tables, forecast CSVs); no library, trained model, or production tool is released. Strengths: - The revalidation-locality framing and TTAC metric are a genuine conceptual contribution: they name a measurable quantity (how much evidence a change invalidates) that existing benchmarks and vendor claims ignore, and the Amdahl/break-even analyses give the framing quantitative teeth. - The four falsifiable hypotheses (H1–H4) with specified required evidence and disconfirming results are a model for how a position paper should expose itself to refutation; the four-configuration baseline design (human-led CI → AI-assisted → tool-closed agent → evidence-carrying agent) is directly usable by future benchmark authors. - The evidence-type taxonomy (Table 2) and the worked elastic-buffer example (Table 4) concretely demonstrate failure modes — stale timing reports, self-repairing tests, agent-shared oracles — that current agent benchmarks genuinely do not test. - Epistemic hygiene: the paper's relentless separation of vendor claims, illustrations, and findings, and its willingness to state that its own 3.08× figure "is not legitimate to advertise as an experimental speedup," are credibility positives. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: Extensive and direct: the paper states it is "a perspective with analytical illustrations, not a systematic survey, a new formal-verification algorithm, or an empirical claim"; the artifact's records come from a model, not real EDA tools, and it "must not be used as a production signoff gate"; the Proposition's dependency-completeness premise is "the engineering challenge"; the scenario forecasts are "not calibrated predictions"; the cost model is serial and ignores concurrency, license queues, and human availability; small teams may be overwhelmed by overhead; and a missing normalized historical speed series is flagged as a limitation of public evidence. The §10.3 objections section ("this is just good CI," "the contract cannot be complete," "reuse creates a single point of failure") confronts the strongest counterarguments head-on — a notable credibility strength. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The central empirical question — does sound evidence reuse lower amortized accepted-change cost on real revision sequences — is never instantiated even at toy scale on open IP (e.g., a parameterized FIFO family with a real simulator and Yosys/SBY), although the paper itself argues such a study is feasible without silicon. This is the dogs-not-barking omission: a two-week experiment would have materially strengthened the position. - No quantitative comparison against the closest existing prior art: the paper argues qualitatively that mature CI plus OpenTitan-style methodology is "a successful implementation of the principle" if cheaper, but never analyzes how far existing tools (Bazel-style content addressing, commerciale requirement-traceability tools, DO-254/ISO 26262 assurance-case practice) already provide Valid/Fresh/Authentic machinery. - The dependency model is manually declared in the artifact; the paper does not engage with the substantial existing literature on automated hardware dependency extraction or with the difficulty of fingerprinting tool-version semantics (mentioned but unaddressed). - The 2027–2031 scenario weights and multipliers, while labeled synthetic, risk anchoring effects precisely because they are presented with three decimal places of derived speedup; a reviewer could argue the forecast section adds length more than insight. - The generative-AI drafting disclosure combined with an "independent researcher" authorship and a note that "the actual authors must... provide their real names" raises uncustomary provenance questions the paper acknowledges but does not resolve. Bottom Line: A rigorously self-critical and genuinely useful position paper that gives the agentic-EDA field its missing evaluation vocabulary (TTAC, revalidation locality, acceptance integrity) and a ready-to-use protocol, but delivers no empirical demonstration — read it for the agenda and the honesty, and expect the first real evidence to come from whoever executes its §8 protocol.

Intelligent Security Agents : AI-Driven Security Logging Assessment for Specification-Driven Software Systems

E Orenstain · scholarscommons.fgcu.edu · automated generated environments for agent testing - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This Master's thesis builds and evaluates an LLM-based agent (built on Perplexity Sonar) that reads all 281 AUTOSAR R25-11 specification documents (~14,650 pages) and proposes design-time security logging requirements — 76 new security events plus no-event verdicts — which are validated by AUTOSAR security working-group experts and fed into a formal recommendation submitted to the AUTOSAR consortium. - Why it's important: Deciding what security events a system should log currently requires thousands of hours of manual expert review across specification corpora no individual can read, and logging gaps directly weaken attack detection, investigation, and response; the thesis also identifies an unoccupied position in the AI-security-agent literature — agents operating upstream of the logging decision rather than consuming pre-existing telemetry. - How it does it: A Python pipeline base64-encodes each AUTOSAR PDF into a Perplexity Sonar Chat Completions request with a fixed prompt (security-engineer persona plus a relevance constraint that suppresses low-precision proposals), collecting structured JSON outputs (event name, log context, rationale) at temperature 0.1. - The good: The core empirical finding is credible and well-characterized — the agent is dependable at surfacing security-relevant concerns (expert relevance 3.30/5, ICC = .66) but unreliable at architectural placement (accuracy 2.12/3, ICC = .18), with the dominant error mode being scope misattribution rather than conceptual invalidity. - The missing: There is no baseline — no comparison against a human-authored logging-requirement set, a naive single-prompt LLM pass, or any prior approach — and recall/coverage (how many genuine logging gaps the agent misses across the 235 documents where it proposed nothing) is never measured beyond a 10-item expert sample. - Read it or not: Worth reading if you work on security requirements engineering, automotive cybersecurity, or LLM agents for specification analysis, since it is the first empirical characterization of design-time logging derivation and includes an unusually candid failure analysis; skip it if you want generalizable LLM-agent techniques, because the method is a thin single-PDF-in/single-JSON-out prompting loop and the evaluation is confined to one standard with seven expert raters.

Problem & Motivation Large specification-driven software systems — exemplified by AUTOSAR, whose R25-11 release comprises 281 documents across Classic and Adaptive platforms — define security behavior across document volumes that no individual or team can comprehensively review. Deciding which security events should be logged, and what contextual data each log entry must contain, is a design-time task that today is manual, error-prone, and prone to omissions; poor logging undermines downstream detection and forensics, and AUTOSAR's existing security event definitions are scattered across documents with no consolidated view. The thesis's systematic literature review (6,608 records screened down to 47 papers) shows that every reviewed AI security agent category — IDS (72.3% of corpus), malware detection, security management, threat intelligence, penetration testing, fuzzing, and attack simulation — operates downstream of a logging schema that is treated as fixed, exogenous input; none participates in deciding what that schema should contain. The research question is therefore: how can AI agents automatically identify and generate security-relevant logging requirements from AUTOSAR specifications? Key Idea The core insight is positional: move the AI agent upstream of the logging decision. Instead of an agent that consumes logs (the universal pattern in the reviewed corpus), build an agent that reads raw specification text and proposes what the logging schema itself should contain — plus, critically, a conservative relevance constraint in the prompt that makes "no new event" a valid, first-class output. The thesis elevates this into a proposed ninth functional subcategory of cybersecurity AI agents, "design-time logging-requirement derivation," and its empirical punchline is that an agent in this position is a productive generator of candidate security concerns but an unreliable author of their architectural placement ("relevance without precision"). Methodology The method has four phases. (1) Specification acquisition: the 281 Classic/Adaptive AUTOSAR R25-11 PDFs are downloaded and organized in a metadata-encoding directory convention. (2) Agent design: a prompt-driven LLM agent on the Perplexity Sonar API, justified by the author against a definition of agency (goal-directed, reasoning over its environment, acting on that reasoning) as distinct from a fixed ML pipeline; a small 3-variant prompt ablation on two documents showed the relevance constraint was the only component with a clear precision effect (removing it produced six mostly safety-oriented false proposals) while the persona had little effect. (3) Results generation: a Python script (released at github.com/UdiOEagle/Security-Logging-AI-Agent) sends each base64-encoded PDF with a fixed system prompt (temperature 0.1, max_tokens 2048) and parses JSON outputs into CSVs; 34 of 281 documents yielded new events (18 Classic, 16 Adaptive), totaling 76 proposals. (4) Evaluation: author-scored accuracy (3-level) and relevance (5-point Likert) on all 76 outputs with non-parametric statistics (Mann-Whitney U, chi-square/Cramér's V); cross-model validation of a 20-case subset on GPT-5.4, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and Claude Sonnet 4.6 (95% unanimous agreement, framed explicitly as stability evidence, not validity); and an IRB-approved expert survey with 7 AUTOSAR security working-group members rating 20 randomly sampled outputs, analyzed with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, ICC(2,k) reliability, and Spearman correlation. Critical design decisions: the relevance constraint (well justified by the ablation), single-document processing scope (acknowledged as the main cause of scope misattributions), and Perplexity Sonar as the backbone (justified mainly by cost/accessibility, not by comparative model performance at generation time). Key Results Internal evaluation (author-rated, all 76 proposals): 39% correct, 53% partially correct, 8% incorrect; relevance median 4/5 on both platforms; Adaptive Platform accuracy trended higher (51% correct vs 28% Classic) but χ²(2)=5.65, p=.059 did not reach significance. Expert survey (N=7, 20 items): new-event accuracy mean 2.12/3.00 with no item rated fully incorrect; relevance mean 3.30/5.00; accuracy–relevance correlation weak and non-significant (ρ=.31, p=.39) — e.g., item NE1 scored 1.86 on accuracy (TLS event misattributed to Charging Manager instead of TcpIp) yet 4.14 on relevance. No-new-event accuracy was weaker on Adaptive (1.89 vs 2.31 Classic, p=.094, underpowered). Inter-rater reliability was ICC(2,7)=.18 (poor-to-fair) for accuracy versus .66 (moderate-to-good) for relevance. Cross-model validation: 19/20 (95%) unanimous agreement across four frontier models on the sampled cases. Tested scale: full 281-document corpus at generation, but expert evaluation only on a 20-item random sample. Baselines compared against: none — no competing method, human baseline, or unprompted-LLM baseline was evaluated. Novelty Classification NEW PROBLEM and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING: the design-time derivation of security logging requirements from specifications is a genuinely unoccupied agent role in the reviewed literature, and the accuracy–relevance divergence with its scope-misattribution failure mode is a real, non-obvious empirical characterization. The method itself is a standard combination — a prompted commercial LLM with a scripted document loop — and the taxonomy extension is a position argument rather than a new algorithm; the engineering is competent but conventional. Rigor & Reproducibility Strengths: a genuine prompt-component ablation (Appendix 4), a released pipeline repository, explicit use of non-parametric statistics with effect sizes, inter-rater reliability reporting, a cross-model stability check, and IRB approval with informed consent. Weaknesses: the full 76-output internal evaluation was single-rater, unblinded, and performed by the author who designed the agent — a direct confirmation-bias risk the author acknowledges; external validation covers only 20 of 76 proposals; N=7 experts makes all inferential tests underpowered (the author concedes p=.06–.09 results are directional only); there is no ground truth independent of expert opinion and no inter-coder reliability for the qualitative coding (single coder); and no recall/coverage measurement exists for the ~235 documents where the agent proposed nothing. The code repository is released, but the pipeline depends on a proprietary, version-drifting Perplexity API, which limits exact reproduction. This is an unrefereed Master's thesis (committee-approved), so confidence should be calibrated accordingly — the statistics are unusually careful for the format, but nothing has been externally peer reviewed. Deployability Profile: EMPIRICAL (a built agent pipeline with an executed evaluation). Practical: yes — it runs on a standard PC calling a commercially available API, with no training or GPU infrastructure. Efficient: per-document cost is one API call per PDF (~281 calls), far cheaper than the claimed thousands of expert-hours, though token/cost figures and runtime are not reported. Effective: partially — the evidence shows it solves the concern-surfacing proxy (relevance 3.30/5) but not the full stated problem of producing specification-correct logging requirements (accuracy 2.12/3, with misattributed architectural placement requiring expert rework); the authors themselves position it as a design-support aid, not an autonomous solution. Scalable: generation scales linearly with documents (demonstrated at 281), but single-document reasoning means quality may degrade further on even larger interdependent corpora, and the 10×–100× expert-validation regime needed to confirm quality at scale was not tested. Deliverable: a released Python pipeline and JSON/CSV output artifacts plus a recommendation report to AUTOSAR; no trained model, library, or reusable benchmark is delivered beyond the prompt and scripts. Strengths - Identifies and empirically occupies a real gap: the systematic review (6,608 → 47 papers, PRISMA-documented) credibly establishes that no reviewed AI security agent operates upstream of the logging decision, and the thesis is the first to characterize what an agent in that position can and cannot do. - The central finding — poor inter-rater agreement on accuracy (ICC = .18) but moderate-to-good agreement on relevance (ICC = .66), with scope misattribution rather than conceptual error as the dominant failure mode — is a genuinely useful, non-obvious result that also carries a methodological implication (evaluate coverage, not per-item placement accuracy). - Honest, specific failure analysis grounded in expert quotes ("SEVs ≠ Error codes", the watchdog-as-secure-boot-proxy miss) that converts evaluation errors into three concrete, addressable development targets: cross-document retrieval over the Security Events Specification, an explicit SEV-vs-error-code taxonomy, and encoded proxy-signal relationships. - Real-world transfer path: a formal recommendation was submitted to the AUTOSAR consortium, and expert recruitment came from the actual security working group — the population that governs the evaluated artifact. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors confront limitations directly and at length, which is a credibility positive: the N=7 expert panel (defended as reflecting a genuinely bounded expert population but acknowledged to limit statistical generalizability); underpowered inferential tests with directional p=.06–.09 results explicitly not claimed as effects; single-document reasoning scope causing cross-document blind spots (e.g., the TLS/Charging Manager misattribution); no empirical testing beyond AUTOSAR despite transferability claims about OpenAPI, ROS 2, and Kubernetes; single-reviewer literature screening with no inter-rater agreement; and the single unblinded author-rater for all 76 internal evaluations with acknowledged confirmation-bias risk. They also correctly frame the 95% cross-model agreement as evidence of stability, not validity. Analyst-Identified Gaps - No baseline of any kind: the field has no competing numbers, but even minimal comparators — a bare LLM call without the relevance constraint at full-corpus scale, or a small human expert deriving requirements for a few documents as a gold standard — are absent, so the agent's incremental value over naive prompting is unquantified beyond a 2-document prompt ablation. - Recall is never measured: 235 of 281 documents produced "no new event," and only 10 no-event items reached experts; the corpus-level rate at which the agent misses genuine logging gaps (the false-negative problem its conservative reasoning creates) is unknown, which weakens the "coverage" framing the thesis itself advocates. - Only 20 of 76 proposals (26%) received independent validation; the remaining 56 rest entirely on the author's unblinded ratings. - The 95% cross-model agreement is computed on cases selected partly because they were stable enough to serve as survey stimuli, and models agreeing on a concept says nothing about whether the concept is correct — the authors note this but the 95% figure still invites over-reading. - Model choice (Perplexity Sonar) was justified by cost and accessibility rather than any head-to-head generation-quality comparison, and API/model versioning is unaddressed for reproduction. - No cost, latency, or token-consumption figures are reported, so the "thousands of hours saved" motivation is asserted, not measured. - Expert panel familiarity with the Adaptive Platform was low (mean 2.43/5), yet Adaptive items were scored anyway; the authors flag this contextually but do not test whether it explains the weaker Adaptive no-event scores. Bottom Line A practitioner in security requirements engineering or automotive cybersecurity gains real value from this thesis — it names and empirically characterizes an agent role nobody else occupies, with a candid failure analysis worth more than its positive numbers — but readers seeking a deployable method or rigorous baselines should treat it as an honest proof of concept whose headline metrics (2.12/3 accuracy, 7 raters, no comparison condition) support only the modest design-support-aid conclusion the author ultimately claims.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces EvoML, a three-agent framework (Orchestrator, Executor, Curator) that synthesizes complete, executable ML pipelines from a dataset path and a one-line task description, using nnU-Net-grounded skill templates, phase-level validation gates, and post-run skill evolution, and reports full automation (EAC 1.0) and the best final model quality on all 8 evaluated medical-imaging datasets plus 3 general ML tasks. - Why it's important: Building correct medical-imaging ML pipelines currently costs 8–40 hours of expert labor ($800–$6,000 per pipeline by the authors' estimate), and a runnable pipeline can be silently wrong (e.g., wrong normalization for the modality), so reliable automation with correctness checks addresses a real, expensive failure mode. - How it does it: Each pipeline phase may advance only after passing structural, execution, and semantic validation gates (LLM-judged for semantics), and a post-run Curator converts validation/retry traces into validated skill-library patches, requiring a patch to pass its gate first-try before it is committed. - The good: The ablations are unusually informative: removing the gates drops FMQ from 0.9498 to 0.7116 on FastMRI, removing nnU-Net grounding drops FLARE22 FMQ from 0.9199 to 0.7150 and roughly doubles run-to-run variance, and disabling evolution increases retries from 27 to 13/51.9% fewer with evolution and cuts synthesis time ~41% — each component's contribution is isolated with numbers. - The missing: There is no baseline that simply runs nnU-Net natively (with a human configuration wrapper) on the same eight datasets, so the reader cannot separate the value of the agentic framework from the value of the nnU-Net procedure it encodes; the medical-segmentation FMQ numbers may be attributable almost entirely to nnU-Net. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building agentic AutoML or self-evolving agent systems who want a concrete validation-gate design and a template for component ablations; skippable for practitioners who just want automated segmentation pipelines, since installing nnU-Net directly remains the stronger, simpler option in its domain.

Problem & Motivation: Teams building ML pipelines — especially medical-imaging pipelines with heterogeneous formats, 2D/3D volumes, and modality-specific preprocessing — need end-to-end automation that does not silently propagate intermediate errors. Existing agentic AutoML systems either require user-supplied templates/skeletons (AutoML-Agent, M3Builder), validate only execution success rather than task correctness (MLZero, Codex, Claude Code), or discard execution-time experience at run end, so the same failure is re-discovered on every run. The paper targets autonomous pipeline synthesis from minimal input where errors are caught at phase boundaries and successful recoveries persist across runs. Key Idea: The core move is encoding an expert, self-configuring workflow (nnU-Net) as a library of agent-invocable skills with verifiable output contracts, then gating every phase transition on structural + execution + semantic checks — so free-form LLM code generation is confined to small, gate-verified template adaptations rather than whole-pipeline synthesis. The second half of the idea is that the same gate traces that drive in-run recovery also drive post-run evolution: the Curator consolidates the adapted script and a routing rule into the skill, and commits the patch only if the patched skill passes the gate on the previously failing input without retries (additive, monotone coverage). Methodology: Three GPT-5.5 agents coordinate four phases (Task Understanding, Planning, Training, Post-Train Processing) over nine skills. The Executor runs each skill by selecting a Python template or invoking Codex (via MCP) to adapt it, iterating until the skill's self-validation criteria pass. The Orchestrator evaluates each phase's artifacts against gate criteria Γ_k = Γ_str ∪ Γ_exe ∪ Γ_sem; failures produce a structured log returned to the Executor for bounded targeted recovery, with a minimal-safe fallback if the retry budget (R_max) is exhausted (never needed in experiments). HPO uses Optuna with a promotion threshold before five-fold cross-validated full training. The Curator post-run selects the skill with the highest accumulated retry count, diagnoses the failure from persisted traces, and patches the skill (new template + updated Markdown routing guidance), validated by re-execution on the triggering input (Eq. 6). Critical design decisions: (1) grounding in nnU-Net — well justified as resolving the flexibility/reliability tension, but it scopes the expert knowledge to medical imaging; (2) semantic checks judged by an LLM Orchestrator — reasonable, but the reliability of the LLM judge is not itself evaluated; (3) fixed nine-skill decomposition with additive-only evolution — simple and monotone, but limits structural adaptation. Key Results: On eight medical datasets (BTCV, ACDC, FLARE21, FLARE22, Promise12MSBench, OrganMNIST3D, FastMRI, IXI) against AutoML-Agent, MLZero, M3Builder, Codex (GPT-5.5 Medium), and Claude Code (Opus 4.7 Medium), EvoML reaches EAC 1.0 on all eight (3 runs each, mean ± std) and the best FMQ everywhere: up to 0.94 Dice on segmentation, 0.99 accuracy on OrganMNIST3D, 0.9498 SSIM on FastMRI (vs next-best Codex at 0.8579), and 0.7859 normalized PSNR on IXI (vs 0.7215). FMQ std stays below 0.013 for EvoML versus baselines up to ±0.2127 (AutoML-Agent on IXI). Ablations: gate removal drops EAC to 0.5333 on IXI and FMQ to 0.7116 on FastMRI; ungrounded skills drop FLARE22 FMQ to 0.7150; disabling evolution raises synthesis time from 290 to 490 minutes and tokens from 50M to 71M across the fixed dataset sequence, and lowers first-pass skill success from 79.4% to 57.1%. Against human leaderboard solutions, EvoML wins on FLARE21 (0.935 vs 0.909), FLARE22 (0.920 vs 0.910), Promise12 (0.920 vs 0.919) but loses on BTCV (0.837 vs 0.921), at 20–45 minutes and $10–$35 per pipeline versus 8–40 expert hours. Generalization: best FMQ on CIFAR-10 (0.9674), VOC2012 (0.7401), AG News (0.9548), with narrow margins. Backbone swap to Claude Opus 4.7 changes FMQ by <0.008 on three datasets. Baselines are recent and reasonably configured (skeletons supplied where required); scale is standard benchmarks, not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL with elements of NEW METHOD and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel pieces are (a) the patch-validation rule requiring first-try gate passage on the triggering input before committing a skill update, and (b) the empirical demonstration that gate-intercepted errors are largely silent semantic inconsistencies rather than crashes. The rest — multi-agent orchestration, skill/template libraries (Anthropic Agent Skills format), experience accumulation across runs, and nnU-Net as the expert substrate — is a competent combination of existing ideas applied to a new setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations cover all three headline components (gates, grounding, evolution) with per-dataset numbers. Each method is run three times per dataset with mean ± std reported; no significance tests. Backbone robustness is checked on only 3 of 8 datasets. Artifacts are released at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/EvoML-624B. Methodological concerns: (1) EAC is a self-defined metric with an arbitrary intervention budget of 3, constructed by the authors and used to crown their system; (2) the evolution ablation uses a single fixed dataset order, so cross-task reuse is demonstrated along one sequence, not randomized; (3) the semantic gate is an LLM judge whose false-positive/false-negative rates are unquantified; (4) the closest baseline — native nnU-Net with human configuration — appears only indirectly via leaderboard comparisons, and never as a controlled run under the identical protocol; (5) the FMQ advantage over other agents on medical segmentation conflates framework quality with nnU-Net's known strength. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a built system, evaluated by benchmark runs). - Practical: Runs on a 64-core Threadripper PRO with two RTX A6000 GPUs (48GB), i.e., commercially available hardware, though at the high end of the workstation range. - Efficient: $10–$35 and 20–45 minutes of synthesis per pipeline, but training is expensive — ~60 hours per segmentation task versus ~10 for baselines (nnU-Net's five-fold CV) and ~300 for native nnU-Net. - Effective: Evidence supports full automation and best FMQ on the tested datasets, but effectiveness on medical segmentation rests on encoded nnU-Net expertise, and the LLM semantic judge's reliability is unmeasured. - Scalable: Not tested at 10×–100× scale — eight small-to-moderate medical datasets and three toy general tasks; the evolution analysis covers one 8-dataset sequence, and whether the monotone-coverage skill library stays coherent over hundreds of tasks is unexamined. Delivers a software artifact (framework code and skills at the anonymous repository); no trained model weights or curated dataset are released beyond the code. Strengths: - The validation-gate design is concretely specified (structural/execution/semantic criteria per phase, structured failure logs, bounded retry, minimal-safe fallback) rather than described vaguely — a reviewer can reconstruct and reuse it. - The evolution mechanism has a genuine safety property: patches are accepted only if they pass the gate first-try on the exact input that failed, with additive-only commitment, which makes skill-library degradation structurally hard. - The ablations quantify each component separately, including process-level evolution metrics (first-pass success 57.1%→79.4%, retries 27→13, time −41%, tokens −30%) that go beyond end-task accuracy. - The FastMRI case study (Table I) traces quality differences to specific pipeline design errors (synthesized-from-target input pairing, sigmoid multi-channel heads on a regression task), giving an interpretable account of why baselines fail rather than only a scoreboard. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: dependence on the foundation model (mitigated by an Opus 4.7 rerun differing by <0.008 FMQ on 3 datasets); substantially longer model-training time (60h vs 10h baselines, framed as a deliberate trade-off); primary focus on medical imaging with only three general tasks as initial external-validity evidence; and that extension to broader software-engineering tasks requires adapting skill content and validation criteria. They confront limitations directly — the threats-to-validity section is specific and quantified, which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No controlled native-nnU-Net baseline under the identical protocol; on the six segmentation/classification datasets the FMQ result may reduce to "nnU-Net is good," leaving the framework's measured contribution as automation only. - The eight medical datasets are ones where nnU-Net and its design philosophy are known to excel — a favorable testbed selection that the paper does not discuss as such. - The LLM-performed semantic gate is the linchpin of the "silent error" claim, yet no experiment measures the judge's precision/recall; a gate that occasionally passes wrong semantics or blocks correct ones would undermine both RQ1 and RQ2 conclusions. - Evolution is evaluated on one fixed dataset order with n=1 sequence; ordering effects and the risk of over-fitting skills to the eight-dataset distribution are not addressed. - EAC is defined by the authors for this paper; its intervention-budget constant (3) and milestone weights are unjustified, and no external benchmark (e.g., MLE-bench, dismissed in one sentence) corroborates the automation claim. - The fallback path never fired in experiments, so the framework's behavior at the retry-limit boundary — arguably where reliability matters most — is untested. - Cost accounting omits the Curator's post-run LLM analysis cost and the token cost of retries within the $10–$35 figure's derivation. Bottom Line: A practitioner building agentic AutoML systems gains a concrete, well-ablated design pattern for validation-gated orchestration and validated skill evolution that is worth adopting, but anyone wanting automated medical-imaging pipelines should recognize that most of the measured quality comes from nnU-Net, and there is likely a stronger, simpler alternative (native nnU-Net) covering the same ground in-domain.

Hengyuan Cao, Biao Gong, Guoshan Lu, Qiyuan Zhang, Lin Liu, Yiding Tian, Yilei Jiang, Yuxin Ma, Chengzhang Wu, Kun Chen, Yiqian Xie, Ting Liu, Xin Zheng, Xijun Gu, Tianren Ma, Jiancheng Pan, Chi Zhang, Xuzhe Zheng, Siyi Li, Zhenzhong Lan · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 13 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces the Reciprocal World Model (RWM) framing and builds Duo v1, a full-duplex audiovisual system that continuously perceives streaming user audio/video while generating a speaking, visible assistant avatar in real time at 708 ms chunks, with released code and weights. - Why it's important: Interactive world models and video avatars today are either steered externally (keyboard/prompt) or unidirectional (talk-avatar or speech-duplex only); Problem & Motivation: Existing world models (Genie, Dreamer, Cosmos, video generators) simulate physical dynamics but keep intelligence outside the world: a user steers the simulation with prompts or controls, and nothing inside the world perceives the user in real time or decides how to respond. Conversely, full-duplex dialogue systems (Moshi, Qwen-Omni) handle speech turn-taking but not a visible, continuously generated body, and talk-avatar generators animate speech but do not decide participation timing. The paper targets the gap in between: a generated persona that simultaneously (a) perceives streaming user audio and video, (b) autonomously decides when to speak, wait, or be interrupted, and (c) produces synchronized assistant video and stereo audio causally, chunk by chunk. The audience is interactive-AI and world-model researchers, plus anyone building real-time multimodal agents. Key Idea: The core insight is the Intent/Realization split on a single causal timeline: an autoregressive multimodal LLM owns the decision to participate (emitting <speak> or <wait> per ~0.71 s chunk) and communicates that decision through its internal hidden states — not decoded text — to a joint audio-video diffusion transformer, with chunk-specific attention masks guaranteeing that neither module ever sees future user input and that noisy media tokens never see their own clean targets. The second key move is dual rollout distillation: DMD is run on rollouts where the intent LLM autoregressively generates the assistant turn and the diffusion model conditions on its own generated media history, closing the train/inference conditioning mismatch that causes drift in autoregressive video diffusion (Self Forcing, extended to the language side). Methodology: The system is chunk-wise full-duplex interaction: each chunk is 17 frames (~708 ms at 24 fps). Stage 1 (Intent) low-rank fine-tunes a pretrained multimodal LLM (Qwen3-VL) with a weighted next-token objective (Eq. 5) over ASR-aligned, causally assembled chunk views; critical design decisions include action-aware rebalancing to prevent collapse into perpetual <wait> (most chunks have no assistant speech), history corruption so the model recovers from imperfect earlier responses, and in-chunk temporal patch construction (last frame repeated, never paired with the next chunk's frame) so causality holds before attention. Stage 2 (Realization) trains a causal joint audio-video DiT (initialized from MiniMax-H3) with flow matching (velocity target z−ε), conditioning on the reference image, intent hidden states projected from layer 50, clean user audio/video latents, and previously generated assistant latents; a ½ causal + ½ bidirectional view mixture is used, and 3D-RoPE aligns audio (25 ms units) and video temporal positions to real playback time. Stage 3 distills to a 4-step generator via DMD (frozen real-score and trainable fake-score models, optional GAN head on middle-block features), with dual rollouts and a VGGT-estimated camera-rotation weighting that down-weights rotating windows (ρ between ρmin and ρmax) to suppress camera drift. Data combines screenplay-driven synthetic split-screen video calls (LLM-written JSON screenplays rendered block-by-block by MiniMax-H3 with a fixed block-0 quality/voice anchor to stop error accumulation) and ~3,000+ hours of recorded data across six categories (1,000 h each of single-stream, synchronous and asynchronous dual-stream; 100 h live streams; 83.3 h duplex audio; 3.14 h open datasets), processed with forced alignment, VAD, diarization, and four automated synthetic-data quality checks. The runtime runs on 8 GPUs with TP4 intent inference overlapping VAE decoding and DiT KV management with sliding-window eviction and periodic resets. The three-stage pipeline, masking scheme, and distillation design are each explicitly justified; the layer-50 hidden-state choice and the ½ causal/½ bidirectional mixture are stated but not empirically justified. Key Results: The headline evaluation is a human study on 30 real-time duplex interaction cases scored on six binary criteria (180 checks): 168 passed (93.3%). Language adherence, speech intelligibility, and visual identity stability each passed 30/30 (90/90); audio-visual emotional consistency passed 96.7% and lip-sync 90.0%; content responsiveness — whether the reply substantively addresses what the user said and showed — passed only 73.3% (22/30), with failures attributed to inferring intent from long-tail remarks and from speech-plus-video jointly. Systems measurements: intent inference 90–160 ms, joint latent generation 200–450 ms at 768×576, per-latent decoding ~30 ms against a 41.7 ms playback interval, end-to-end pipeline 330–650 ms against the 708 ms chunk budget on a single 8-GPU server. A synthetic-data ablation shows the block-0 anchor keeps mean luma at ~99 through block 9 of a 60 s rollout versus monotonic decline to 69.6 for the baseline chaining. There are no comparisons against Moshi, Qwen-Omni/Talker, Wan-Streamer, LiveTalk, OmniForcing, or CausForcing on any metric, no automated quality benchmarks, and no ablation tables isolating dual rollout, rotation weighting, or action rebalancing. The demonstrated scale is short scripted conversations (tens of seconds); long-session consistency is explicitly not established. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL. The RWM framing (intelligence and physical reality as co-fundamental, Intent + Realization on a unified causal timeline) is a genuinely new formulation for interactive world models, and the full-duplex joint audiovisual generation with autonomous participation timing is a new system capability. However, most component techniques are competent combinations of existing ideas: DMD and GAN distillation (Yin et al. 2024a/b), Self Forcing rollout training, CausVid/Diffusion Forcing causal adaptation, OmniForcing-style asymmetric block-causal alignment, and a Thinker-Talker-like modular split — applied together to a new setting (full-duplex audiovisual worlds with speak/wait decisions). Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are absent in quantitative form: the paper argues for action rebalancing, history corruption, dual rollout, and rotation weighting narratively but reports no before/after numbers for any of them (the only measured ablation is the synthetic-data luma-drift comparison). No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere; the human evaluation has no reported number of raters, no inter-rater agreement, and 30 cases is small. Code, weights, and a homepage are released (github.com/inclusionAI/Duo, huggingface.co/collections/inclusionAI/duo-v1, duo-v1.github.io), which is a strong reproducibility positive. Methodological concerns: the evaluation is entirely self-run on the authors' own showcase scenarios with binary pass/fail criteria the authors defined; the model is initialized from MiniMax-H3 and evaluated partly on data generated by the same family of model, raising train/eval entanglement for the synthetic-data pipeline; and the absence of any external baseline makes the 93.3% number uninterpretable as a quality claim. This is an arXiv technical report, not peer-reviewed. Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a built, running streaming system with reported deployment measurements; training is empirical). - Practical: No — sustained interaction requires a dedicated 8-GPU server (intent on GPU 0–3, DiT across all 8, VAE on 4–7), far beyond consumer or even single-GPU hardware. - Efficient: Within its own budget the pipeline is well-tuned (330–650 ms of compute per 708 ms chunk, with overlap scheduling), but the 8-GPU footprint per concurrent session is a high cost relative to speech-only duplex systems that run on far less. - Effective: The evidence (30-case binary human eval, no baselines) shows the system demonstrably works for basic audiovisual conversation but does not establish that it solves full-duplex interaction better than alternatives; content responsiveness at 73.3% is the honest weak point. - Scalable: Not tested — evaluation covers short, scripted-scale conversations; the authors themselves state that consistency over longer sessions, response timing, and misunderstanding recovery require broader evaluation, and the periodic KV-reset policy implies an untested memory/context trade-off at 10×–100× session length. The work delivers a real software artifact: released model weights, code, and a streaming runtime, not just a paper. Strengths: - The unified causal timeline is specified to an unusual level of rigor: per-modality RoPE alignment to real playback time (25 ms units), in-chunk temporal patch construction to keep the visual encoder itself causal, and a fully enumerated attention-visibility matrix — this is the kind of detail that determines whether such systems actually work and is rarely published. - Dual rollout distillation is a sensible and well-motivated extension of Self Forcing to the language side: distilling on intent-LLM-generated text and self-generated media history directly attacks the conditioning mismatch that causes autoregressive video drift. - The data construction is a real contribution: screenplay-controlled synthesis with diversity control cards, a fixed block-0 quality/voice anchor with measured luma stabilization, and a six-category recorded-data program with documented quality checks and timing-preserving causal alignment. - Honest self-reporting: the authors name content responsiveness (73.3%) as the weakest criterion, publish the failure taxonomy with a concrete example, and the conclusion plainly calls the system preliminary. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that Duo v1 remains preliminary and supports only basic audiovisual conversation; that response timing, consistency over longer sessions, and recovery from misunderstandings still require broader evaluation; and that content responsiveness (73.3%) is the main headroom, attributed to real-time intent inference from joint speech and video. They confront these directly rather than minimizing them, which is a credibility positive. They also acknowledge that intentional camera rotations and unreliable rotation estimates can distort the DMD loss weighting, and that the camera-rotation metric uses rotation alone. Analyst-Identified Gaps: Beyond the acknowledged limits, a reviewer would flag: (1) zero baseline comparison — the related work lists at least five directly comparable streaming systems, none evaluated, so all quality numbers are unanchored; (2) no ablation numbers for the three claimed technical contributions (autoregressive intent, dual rollout, rotation weighting), so it is impossible to tell which actually matter; (3) the human evaluation protocol, rater count, and case selection are author-defined and self-scored — 30 cases with binary checks cannot support the 93.3% framing as more than anecdote; (4) circularity between the synthetic training data generated by MiniMax-H3 and the Realization Module initialized from MiniMax-H3; (5) the Intent Module conditions on user video, yet the paper notes many training examples are solvable from text alone and visual grounding is handled by upweighting inspected turns — no measurement of how much the visual channel actually contributes to decisions; (6) the choice of layer-50 hidden states as the intent interface is unmotivated and untested; (7) the evaluation's replay format (pre-recorded user input paired with generated replies) does not test true closed-loop interactivity, where user behavior would adapt to the model — the hardest part of full-duplex evaluation. Bottom Line: A practitioner building real-time joint audiovisual generation or full-duplex multimodal agents gains a genuinely useful, unusually detailed engineering blueprint plus released weights, but anyone seeking evidence that this approach outperforms existing duplex or avatar systems will find no comparative or ablation support here — read it as a strong systems report, not a validated advance.

Reglos: A Self-Evolving Personal Memory Agent with Recursive Self - Improvement

S Yang, J Lin, Z Huang, W Liu · arxiv.org · recursive self-improvement - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Reglos, a training-free personal memory agent that pairs a per-user, append-only evolving memory with an offline recursive self-improvement loop in which a coding agent patches the context-building "harness" and a fixed evaluator accepts only patches that generalize to held-out validation personas. - Why it's important: Personal assistants must track changing and retracted user preferences, and naive harness auto-patching overfits to the failures it was shown; the paper targets whether memory-system improvements transfer to users whose failures nobody inspected. - How it does it: Two co-evolving loops: an inner loop writes an append-only fact record with validity/expiry times, supersession and retraction tombstones, and an outer loop has Claude Code propose harness patches from raw failure traces while a critic from a second model family (Codex/GPT-6.1 Sol) screens for benchmark gaming before a frozen evaluator with a pre-registered acceptance rule admits them. - The good: The strongest evidence is a set of honest controls: every baseline given Reglos's memory-use policy or harness still trails Reglos (best variant, EverOS+policy, 58.9% vs 61.3% on PersonaMem-v2), and raw retrieval inside the Reglos harness reaches 58.1%, showing precisely where the gains come from. - The missing: The harness was evolved on PersonaMem-v2 validation and the headline result is on PersonaMem-v2 test of the same benchmark, with the memory-use policy visibly tailored to that benchmark's category taxonomy (sensitive info, forgetting); no error bars, seeds, significance tests, or public code release are reported. - Read it or not: Read it if you build LLM memory systems or self-improving harnesses — the two-loop decomposition, the failure-attribution table (48% of failures need unstated facts), and the token-cost accounting are directly useful; skip it if you want a statistically rigorous comparison or a deployable open artifact.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Novelty (65) is solid — the two-time-scale split with a frozen, pre-registered evaluator and cross-family critic is a genuinely new combination, though the components are standard. Rigor (55) is pulled down by the complete absence of statistics, no released code or artifact, vendor self-reported numbers, and benchmark-development entanglement (harness, policy, and retraction mechanism all evolved on PersonaMem-v2, the same benchmark as the headline result), partially offset by unusually honest component-isolation controls. Resilience (50) is the weak point: the 2.5–3.2 point margins are within the authors' own conceded noise level and the sensitive-info gains likely reflect policy-benchmark alignment, so headline claims would not fully survive adversarial review. Completeness (65) benefits from direct, non-minimizing limitation acknowledgment. Weighted composite: 0.20*65 + 0.25*55 + 0.15*60 + 0.15*65 + 0.15*50 + 0.10*45 = 58.

Problem & Motivation: Personal agents serving a single user over months must store, update, and honor retraction of that user's preferences; benchmarks like PersonaMem-v2 show most memory systems underperform naive retrieval and that models often miss implied preferences or keep applying retracted ones. The paper's motivating observation is that harness code (what gets recalled and how it is shown to the reader) is where 31% of traced failures occur — evidence already in context but used wrongly — and that coding-agent patches to this harness, selected on the failures that prompted them, overfit: a GEPA-style prompt search gained 3.8 points on selection questions but only 1.1 on unseen questions. The gap addressed is how to let a harness improve itself without gaming the benchmark. Key Idea: Split self-improvement across two time scales with different owners and different verification: per-user memory evolves online under fixed write rules (supersede-but-keep, forget-as-retraction with tombstones), while the shared harness evolves offline through patches that must survive a cross-model-family critic and a frozen, pre-registered acceptance rule (gain on each of two persona-disjoint validation halves, cost a second reader at most one point). The append-only record with dual time axes (when a fact holds vs. when it was learned) is what makes conflicting preferences machine-interpretable at recall time. Methodology: The system is a Rust memory kernel over a single PostgreSQL 16 database (embeddings, trigram index, and entity graph as columns/tables beside facts; jobs leased by workers), a Python harness, and two loops. Inner loop: buffered messages are redacted, the frozen task model (Qwen3.8-27B, reasoning off) extracts facts/commitments/forget-requests in one batch adjudication call (new/duplicate/replacement/enrichment), facts keep source-message IDs, perspective, and validity/ingestion timestamps, a nightly "Dream" pass rewrites the profile, and recall fuses six routes (dense, keyword, entity graph, time, place, recency) by reciprocal rank fusion into an 8,100-token budget. Outer loop: Claude Code (Opus 5.5) reads raw failure traces and writes harness patches; Codex (GPT-6.1 Sol) independently clusters failures and rejects dataset-template-keyed patches; after freezing harness v3, a fixed evaluator applies the acceptance rule on 1,317 validation questions with GPT-5.6 Luna as a second reader. Five accepted steps built the final harness (54.2%→60.7% on validation). Critical design decisions: cross-family critic (plausible but unquantified), frozen evaluator with pre-registered rule (well-justified — the authors note the pre-freeze 3-point margin was close to run-to-run noise), and per-option recall on distinguishing words (justified by a mechanistic account: full-option text retrieves near-identical facts across options). Key Results: On PersonaMem-v2's official 5,000-question test set with Qwen3.8-27B writing memory for every system, Reglos reaches 61.3%, 7.5 points above the strongest baseline (MemOS 53.8%) and 12.0 above full context; with GPT-5.6 Luna answering, 57.5% vs 50.5% for the best baseline. On LongMemEval-S: 84.0% (Qwen) and 87.2% (Luna), 3.6 and 6.4 points above EverOS. On LoCoMo, Reglos leads memory systems (87.2%/89.5%) but full context with Luna reaches 90.0%, and the authors concede LoCoMo histories are short enough that Reglos passes the full dated history — that result measures the reader and prompt, not memory. On BEAM it ranks first at 500K tokens with Luna (65.0) but third at 100K with both readers. Largest per-type margins are exactly where the policy targets the benchmark: 91.4% on sensitive-information questions (baselines 42.9–47.6%) and 63.1% on asked-to-forget (Mem0 11.8%); preferences belonging to others sit below chance (~20%) for every system. Failure attribution over 159 traced development failures: 48% of failures require facts never stated in the conversation, 31% are reader errors with evidence in context, 16% extraction misses, 4% recall misses. Baselines (Mem0, MemOS, EverOS, Zep, raw retrieval, full context) are recent and mostly self-hosted, though MemOS/EverOS run under the OmniMemEval configuration which the authors note omits the persona description. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL with elements of NEW METHOD and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. Genuinely novel: the two-time-scale framing with a frozen, pre-registered evaluator gating post-freeze patches, and the cross-family critic screening for benchmark gaming — no prior system in the cited related work combines these. The components are otherwise standard: append-only temporal memory resembles Zep's temporal knowledge graph, harness evolution is MemPro/Self-Harness/Meta-Harness-style, and the failure-trace-driven proposer is GEPA-lineage; the failure-attribution finding (half of errors need unstated facts, capping a perfect reader near 80%) is a valuable empirical contribution but is measured on the authors' own development slices. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are unusually thorough on PersonaMem-v2 (Table 6: every baseline re-run with the authors' policy, the authors' harness, and persona cards, with Reglos still leading all variants), and the outer-loop trajectory is traced step by step (Table 5). However: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported, and the authors themselves admit the pre-freeze 3-point acceptance margin was "close to run-to-run noise"; the memory-write pipeline and results rest on single runs. No code, data, or weights are released — only a product website (https://reglos.ai); Appendix A's thresholds aid reimplementation but nothing is verifiable end-to-end. Methodological concerns: the outer loop was developed on PersonaMem-v2 and the flagship number is PersonaMem-v2 test of the same benchmark — the frozen-evaluator and held-out-persona rule mitigate but do not eliminate Goodhart risk, since question-type taxonomy is shared between validation and test and the memory-use policy is transparently written against that taxonomy; the 159-failure attribution audit is the authors' own tracing with a "stronger model checking each case," not an independent protocol; and the vendor context (all four authors at Reglos.ai, system serving their own product) makes self-reported numbers warrant reduced confidence. This is an arXiv preprint, apparently not peer-reviewed. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with SYSTEMS elements — the kernel is described as serving the company's production app, but no deployment evaluation is reported). - Practical: Yes — it runs on commercial APIs (DashScope, Claude Code, Codex) plus a Rust/PostgreSQL service; no special hardware. - Efficient: Costly on the write side — ingesting one persona's 32k-token history costs ~225k–260k task-model tokens (~7.5× the history) plus 40k embedding tokens, and judging one harness candidate on 1,317 questions with two readers takes ~16M prompt tokens; answering is ~6.0k prompt tokens per question. - Effective: On benchmarks, yes — it beats all tested baselines on two of three benchmarks with two readers, but no user study or production metric validates real-world effectiveness. - Scalable: Partially tested — accuracy holds from 25% to 100% history prefixes (59.1%→60.5% on early-history questions) and a 1M-token BEAM sample scores 67.6, but per-user fact counts of a few thousand and a 6-hour, 50M-token write for 200 test personas leave 10×–100× user-count scaling untested. The work delivers a commercial product (app + memory service) but no public library, dataset, or trained model; it stops at paper form for the research community. Strengths: - The control design is the paper's best feature: rather than only comparing to baselines as-is, the authors give every baseline their memory-use policy and their harness, isolating how much each component contributes (policy adds 3–6 points to baselines; the memory pipeline adds only 3.2 points over raw retrieval in their own harness) — a level of self-incriminating honesty most memory papers lack. - The failure-attribution analysis (Table 3) redirects the field: 48% of remaining failures require facts never stated in the conversation, so no memory system can fix them, and the reachable ceiling is near 80% — a concrete, falsifiable ceiling claim. - The frozen-evaluator-with-pre-registered-acceptance-rule design directly addresses the overfitting problem the paper opens with, and the authors report that the looser pre-freeze margin was noise-level, which motivated the stricter rule. - Mechanistically explained design choices (e.g., why full-option-text recall fails due to option templates, and why distinct-word per-option recall fixes it) make the harness changes interpretable rather than black-box search artifacts. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that one open 27B model writes memory for every system; that the published comparison number (57.2%, MemStack) uses a different reader (GPT-4.1-mini); that the LoCoMo result rests on reading short histories in full; and that BEAM systems sit within a few points of each other. They also identify the hardest unsolved slice — third-party preferences extracted as the user's own, below chance for every system, requiring write-path provenance — and note the reader model bounds most remaining reachable errors. This is direct, non-minimizing acknowledgment, a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Benchmark-development entanglement: the harness, policy, retraction mechanism, and per-option recall were all evolved and validated on PersonaMem-v2, and the policy's content (sensitive identifiers, forgetting, other-people's preferences, demographics) mirrors PersonaMem-v2's category list almost one-to-one; the 91.4% vs 42.9–47.6% sensitive-info gap is more plausibly policy-benchmark alignment than general memory skill, and only one other benchmark (LongMemEval-S) has no matching category where the margin shrinks to 3.6 points. - No statistical treatment anywhere: no seeds, no confidence intervals, no significance tests, and the authors concede noise was ~3 points on validation — the same magnitude as several claimed margins (e.g., +2.5 over EverOS+policy, +3.2 over raw retrieval in their harness). - No public code or artifact despite the two-loop pipeline being the contribution; results are not independently reproducible. - The cross-family critic's effectiveness is asserted, never measured — no ablation of how many gaming patches it caught, or whether a same-family critic would differ. - Only five accepted harness patches from one proposer run; the recursive self-improvement claim rests on a single, short trajectory with no variance estimate. - Cost is reported but not compared against baselines' memory-write costs, so the 7.5×-history token overhead cannot be placed in context; a cost-matched comparison is absent. - Deployment is claimed ("the same memory service serves our own app") but no production metrics, latency numbers beyond model-call timing, or user-facing evaluation appear. Bottom Line: A practitioner building agent memory systems should read this for its unusually honest component-isolation controls, its failure-attribution ceiling analysis, and its frozen-evaluator recipe for harness evolution — but should discount the headline margins as likely benchmark-policy alignment and wait for independent reproduction, since the artifact is closed and no statistics back the 2.5–3.2 point leads.

Recursively Self-Improving Electromagnetic Spectrum Agents: Architecture and Operation

B Chong, D Xu, Q Wang, F Zhou, Q Wu · arxiv.org · recursive self-improvement - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper proposes an architecture and operating process for LLM-based electromagnetic spectrum agents (RSI-ESAs) that diagnose capability gaps from operational feedback, generate and validate component modifications, and carry validated versions and diagnostic experience across improvement rounds. - Why it's important: Deployed spectrum agents face shifting environments (stale reports, delayed feedback) that can silently invalidate fixed task components, so long-lived autonomous wireless systems need mechanisms to repair and accumulate capabilities after deployment rather than requiring engineering intervention. - How it does it: An LLM reads task evidence and persisted diagnostic rules, proposes edits to a versioned configuration of task components from a defined search space, candidates are gate-checked and A/B-evaluated against the active version under matched seeds, and accepted versions plus modification records persist for the next round. - The good: The case study is unusually careful for this genre — frozen final versions evaluated on eight fresh held-out seeds, paired seeds across configurations, and an honest ablation showing the 8B model gains nothing from experience inheritance (69.62% vs. 69.13% vs. 69.13% critical delivery). - The missing: The 'recursive self-improvement' is in practice LLM-guided search over 864 predefined configuration combinations with predefined components; there is no open-ended capability construction, only two independent runs per condition (error bars = range of n=2), no code release, and no real-world or hardware validation. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers in LLM-agent self-improvement or cognitive/wireless networks who want a concrete, honestly-evaluated instantiation in spectrum management; skippable for those familiar with Darwin Gödel Machine/STOP-style work who only want the spectrum-domain translation.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. The composite is pulled down primarily by Novelty (45): despite the 'recursive self-improvement' framing, the method is LLM-guided search over a fixed 864-point configuration grid — a domain translation of Darwin Gödel Machine/STOP-style ideas, not open-ended capability construction. Practical Impact (40) also drags the score: no code, simulator, prompts, or any artifact released, and no real-world or hardware validation. The evaluation discipline is genuinely better than typical agentic papers (paired seeds, held-out final tests, the model-capability-dependent inheritance ablation supporting Non-Obviousness at 55 and Completeness at 70), but Rigor (60) is capped by n=2 runs with range-only error bars, the authors' own baseline, and a small reverse-engineered-looking simulator. Weighted composite: 0.20*45 + 0.25*60 + 0.15*55 + 0.15*70 + 0.15*65 + 0.10*40 = 57.
