Problem & Motivation: Teams adopting LLMs to write or modify RTL have no automated way to ensure that AI-driven edits preserve existing functionality. Prior assertion-generation approaches (GoldMine, HARM, A-TEAM, AutoSVA, and LLM-based AssertLLM/AssertionForge) either depend on simulation coverage, predefined templates, manual annotations, or specifications — which are often incomplete, ambiguous, or non-textual (waveforms, tables) — and none provide iterative repair of failing assertions or systematic maintenance of assertion suites across design evolution. The paper targets hardware verification engineers and, secondarily, maintainers of LLM-for-RTL benchmarks (RTLLM, VerilogEval, TuRTLe) whose binary pass/fail or simulation-based metrics miss corner cases. Key Idea: The central insight is the "snapshot" formulation: because the input RTL is assumed correct, formal verification results become an oracle — every counterexample (CEX) proves an assertion wrong, not the design — which licenses an autonomous LLM repair loop with FPV feedback and no human in the loop. Secondary supporting tricks are (a) CNF normalization (plus delay extraction) to detect logically equivalent assertions (e.g., a⇒b vs. ¬a∨b), which both avoids redundant FPV runs and provides a clean termination condition for set extension, and (b) a syntax-repair ladder from deterministic scripting (module-prefixing, name de-duplication) to LLM-based fixing with compiler logs, with graceful assertion pruning after 10 failed attempts. Methodology: The pipeline is EMPIRICAL and tool-centric, implemented in Python with LLM calls via the NVIDIA NIM API and Cadence JasperGold v2021.12 for FPV. Stage 1 scripts generate the formal testbench environment (directories, bind files, compile scripts). Stage 2 prompts an LLM with the golden RTL plus curated SVA writing rules (taken from AutoSVA2). Stage 3 repairs syntax via module-prefixing, name-collision fixing, then LLM correction with error messages (capped at 10 attempts, then progressive pruning). Stage 4 iteratively extends the assertion set: the LLM proposes new assertions given the RTL and existing properties, duplicates are removed via CNF comparison in a property database (equal CNF and equal delay ⇒ duplicate), and the loop terminates when the LLM produces only duplicates. Stage 5 runs FPV on all assertions; PROVEN ones enter the snapshot, CEX ones go through up to 5 LLM repair attempts (prompted with RTL, the failing assertion, the counterexample, and prior fixes). Critical design decisions: (1) the golden-reference assumption — well-argued as the enabling foundation, and honestly framed as assuming proofs are correct; (2) refusing automatic assumption synthesis — justified by citing the standard false-positive risk of underconstraining, leaving assumptions to engineers; (3) the 5-attempt repair cap — motivated empirically by observing most fixes succeed on the first attempt, though this is a convenience heuristic, not an optimized one. Key Results: Across 14 RTL modules (24–419 LOC, sequential and combinational, from internal projects and the open-source Sargantana core), with GPT-4.1-mini on all 14 and Llama 3.3 70B / Llama 3.1 405B on 6: checker coverage of proven assertions reached 100% on the alu, 98.9% on mul_unit (GPT-4.1-mini), 93.9% on popcount, 99.7% on div_unit_4bits (Llama 70B), but only 39.3% on tlb and 52.8% on ptw (GPT-4.1-mini) — showing control-heavy designs lag. Semantic repair (Stage 5) converted 43.3% of CEX assertions for GPT-4.1-mini (27% on the first attempt), 25.8% for Llama 3.3 70B, and 43.8% for Llama 3.1 405B. Notably, Llama 3.3 70B collapsed on mul_unit (1.76% final coverage vs. 98.9% for GPT-4.1-mini), a large model-dependent variance the authors do not deeply explain. Average runtime was ~66 minutes (77.4% in semantic repair; FPV alone was 69.4% of total time) at ~€0.50 per snapshot in LLM cost. Validation was limited to one manually injected bug (inst_d[2] vs. inst_d[1] in the scoreboard) caught by one assertion, and one Cursor/claude-4-sonnet refactor of ptw_arb that broke an IDLE-state assertion. Baselines: none compared against — coverage and pass rates are self-referential. Tested scale is small-to-standard for FPV (modules up to ~420 LOC, often split into submodules). Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (the snapshot toolflow: golden-reference-driven, fully automated generate–deduplicate–extend–repair loop with FPV feedback) plus a NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (differential behavior of LLMs on datapath vs. control logic, and the mul_unit collapse of Llama 70B). The genuinely novel element is the self-supervised repair/extension loop enabled by the golden-reference assumption and CNF-based dedup-as-termination; the individual components — LLM prompting for SVA, LLM syntax fixing, FPV proof, coverage measurement — are standard combinations, and the assertion-generation rules themselves are borrowed from AutoSVA2. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are partial: the paper dissects stage-wise runtime and the per-attempt success rate of semantic repair (justifying the 5-attempt cap), and shows initial-vs-final coverage per module, but there is no ablation removing components (e.g., extension without repair, repair without dedup) to show what drives coverage. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported, and temperature is fixed at 0.2 with no variance analysis. Artifacts: a repository named "dac-2026-artifacts" containing final assertion testbenches for six modules and a script to re-prove experiments with JasperGold and VC Formal is mentioned, but no URL is given; LLM configuration (temp 0.2, max_token 8192) and FPV version are stated, aiding reproduction. Methodological concerns: (1) the primary metric, "checker coverage," is the authors' own framing and is never compared to an independent quality measure or to assertions from any competing tool; (2) evaluation is entirely on the authors' internal modules plus one open-source core they co-develop; (3) the benchmarking use case (Section 2.3) is asserted but never evaluated — the paper explicitly defers it as "a paper on its own"; (4) bug detection is validated with n=2 anecdotes. This is a peer-reviewed-venue WIP poster (DAC 2026), and the evidence level matches that tier. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS component, as a working tool). Practical: Yes — needs only LLM API access and a commercial FPV tool (JasperGold; also validated on VC Formal), both commercially available. Efficient: Cheap in money (~€0.50/snapshot) but slow in time (~66 min average, 77% in repair; FPV is 69% of runtime) — a reduction to 2–3 repair attempts is proposed but untested. Effective: Evidence supports the stated goal of detecting functionality-breaking changes for the two demonstrated cases, but coverage is a proxy — the paper never measures recall of the snapshot over a systematic bug corpus, so effectiveness is shown, not quantified. Scalable: Untested beyond ~420 LOC; the authors themselves note state-space explosion may require the same divide-and-conquer partitioning standard FPV uses, and their own tlb/ptw results (39–53% coverage) suggest degradation at scale. The work delivers a software tool with a partial artifact release, not a packaged library. Strengths: - The golden-reference inversion is a genuinely useful framing: it converts FPV counterexamples from a debugging burden into a free oracle for fully autonomous assertion repair, removing the human from the loop in a way prior LLM assertion generators (AssertLLM, AssertionForge) do not attempt. - CNF-based duplicate detection doing double duty as a compute filter and a principled termination condition for set extension is a clean, well-motivated design point. - Honest cost/time dissection (per-stage breakdown, FPV = 69.4% of runtime, €0.50/snapshot) and the observation that most repairs succeed on attempt 1 give practitioners actionable tuning information. - The two validation cases are real and specific — the injected off-by-one bug and the actual claude-4-sonnet refactor breaking a concrete IDLE-state assertion — with the failing SVA shown, not just claimed. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state: (1) SVApshot does not verify the input RTL is correct — it only guards future modifications against breaking current behavior, and the entire method rests on trusting the golden reference; (2) the repair loop cannot fix CEXs requiring domain-specific input assumptions, and their single worked example (scoreboard flush-signal assumption) shows this leaves false-negative coverage on the table; (3) complex control logic resists semantic correction relative to datapath modules; (4) comprehensive LLM benchmarking via snapshots is deferred to future work. They also candidly report the Llama 3.3 70B mul_unit failure in their own results table. This is a credibility positive: limitations are confronted directly rather than minimized. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No baseline comparison of any kind: no head-to-head with AssertLLM, AutoSVA2's own original mode, template miners (HARM/A-TEAM), or even unmodified AutoSVA2 rules without the repair loop — so the contribution of the loop over plain AutoSVA2-style generation is unquantified. - Bug-detection capability is validated with n=2 hand-picked cases; a mutation-testing campaign (e.g., systematic injectable mutants per module, standard in assertion-mining papers) is absent, and detection rate/recall is never measured — the strongest missing experiment. - "Checker coverage" is defined only loosely; its relationship to standard FSM/architectural coverage or to mutation score is not established, making the headline numbers hard to compare across papers. - No seed variance or repeated runs: LLM outputs at temperature 0.2 still vary, and single-run coverage numbers may not be stable. - The mul_unit result for Llama 3.3 70B (0.7% initial coverage, 1.76% final) is a dramatic anomaly reported but never diagnosed; it may indicate fragility of the pipeline to a failure mode (e.g., syntax-pruning cascades) that could bite other models. - Internal (non-open) modules constitute most of the evaluation set, limiting external reproduction even with the released artifacts for six modules. - Incremental snapshots (Section 2.2, bullet 3) are described as a capability but never demonstrated. Bottom Line: A promising and honestly reported WIP tool paper whose snapshot-and-repair loop is worth adopting as an idea — and whose released testbench artifacts are useful — but a practitioner should not treat its coverage numbers as evidence of superiority, since no baseline comparison or systematic bug-detection evaluation exists yet; wait for the full version with mutation-based validation.

Where It Breaks: Diagnosing Perception, Memory, and Decision Failures of a Vision-Language Agent in Pac-Man

X Wang, E Wang, Y Zhang, Z Fan · arxiv.org · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper presents a provenance-audited empirical case study of a Qwen3.5-9B Pac-Man agent, decomposing its failures into perception, memory, and decision components and showing that a primitive-action RL policy improves from 0/96 to 77/96 (80.2%) normal-start clears on eight fixed held-out mazes while later checkpoints regress to 60/96, static screenshot transcription is near-perfect (24/24 greedy; 37,797/37,800 cells correct) yet closed-loop reading degrades (18/20 full-map, 131/138 actor queries exact), and further optimization in a separate lineage coincides with worse decisions (59/96 to 37/96 with replayed immediately lethal actions). - Why it's important: Teams post-training VLM agents routinely read a single training or validation score as evidence of whole-agent improvement, so misattributing a failure to the policy when the real fault is perception, or to mastery when training wins come from near-complete restart states, wastes expensive RL compute on the wrong fix. - How it does it: The core move is measurement-unit separation — the agent is functionally split into perception (V), state maintenance (U), and decision (π), and each is scored in its own unit (static image transcription, closed-loop observation audits, restart-batch wins vs. normal-start validation on a fixed 96-attempt panel), with training-start distribution audits (11 restart states from 2 maps/3 source episodes producing 192/192 batch wins) exposing what a training win actually exercises. - The good: The paired, seed- and layout-bound checkpoint comparison (0/96 to 77/96 on identical task/replica pairs, contract audited across 23 fields with zero mismatches) is a carefully verified descriptive result, and the restart-state source audit is a concrete, quantified demonstration of how a 100% training win rate can mask narrow experience. - The missing: The headline 0-to-270 improvement is selected and reported on the same repeatedly used eight-maze validation panel, with no independent layout sample, no training-seed replication, no confidence intervals on the main validation counts, and no measured unseen-layout generalization. - Read it or not: Read it if you are running RL post-training on game or embodied VLM agents and want a concrete checklist and failure taxonomy for interpreting learning curves; skip it if you want a new algorithm, a benchmark, or generalizable performance numbers, because it delivers none of these.

Problem & Motivation When a game-playing or embodied VLM agent trained with RL performs poorly or inconsistently, a developer cannot tell from a completion score alone whether the fault lies in reading the screen, in maintaining state, or in choosing actions over a long horizon — and each diagnosis implies a different (and costly) intervention. The problem is acute for post-training pipelines where a training win rate can be inflated by restart-based curricula, a strong validation checkpoint can coexist with later regression, and near-perfect static perception can coexist with in-loop reading errors. Prior interactive-agent benchmarks (BALROG, lmgame-Bench) rank agents across tasks and interfaces but do not follow a single development process to attribute which measured component failed; the authors position this work as evidence-grounded development experience rather than a benchmark or a new method. The audience is researchers and engineers running RLHF/PPO-style post-training on multimodal agents. Key Idea There is no single algorithmic trick; the identifiable core insight is that evaluation units must be kept separate and matched to intervention decisions: a screenshot transcription score, a closed-loop observation audit, a training-batch win rate, and a normal-start validation clear rate are different quantities that must never be pooled, and localizing a failure requires testing the suspect component in its own unit before attributing a game-level outcome to policy learning. The paper operationalizes this with a three-stage functional decomposition (perception zt = V(ot), memory mt = U(mt-1, zt, et), decision at = π(ot, mt, Ct)) and with audits of the training-start distribution (restart-state provenance, source coverage, filtering effects). Methodology The study aggregates retained development records from several lineages of a Qwen3.5-9B agent, explicitly not combined into one run. (1) ASCII primitive-policy post-training: a PPO-style clipped-surrogate objective (clip ε=0.05, zero KL/entropy coefficients, ClipCov modification, temperature 0.7, episode-level advantages with life/speed bonuses) trains a policy on spaced ASCII boards with open-action masking over a seven-tier curriculum (13×13/2 ghosts up to 21×25/4, i.e., sizes to 25×21), with 80% failure-state restarts and 18.75% earlier-tier rehearsal per 192-slot batch; validation is 12 samples × 8 held-out layouts = 96 attempts per stage with three extra lives and a 512-step cap, and the estimator is the mean clear indicator over the 96 task/replica pairs. (2) Perception audits: a frozen model with two-stage adaptation (vision encoder/merger full-parameter training, then language LoRA rank-16/α-32) is scored on 24 distinct screenshots (whole-board JSON transcription against visible-pixel labels) and, separately, in a closed-loop 64-action window (20 full-map queries, 138 actor queries). (3) A fixed-map action-head experiment trains a 2,019,328-parameter rank-8 residual at the output head (frozen base and perception) for 3 vs. 20 Adam updates, evaluated on 64 paired execution seeds per extra-life setting with McNemar tests and conservative Clopper-Pearson union-bound intervals. (4) Start-distribution and filtering audits quantify restart-state source coverage (e.g., 514 distinct state IDs across 520 sampled slots but only 2–5 maps and 4–12 source episodes per bank). Critical design decisions: separating restart training wins from normal-start validation (well-justified by the batch-333 audit showing 96/132 restart attempts began with ≤15 of 118 pellets); scoring perception against visible-pixel labels including occluded-unknown cells (well-justified — both interactive map errors replaced an occluded cell with asserted empty floor); and using a repeatedly reused validation panel for both checkpoint selection and reporting (acknowledged as a binding limitation, not independently justified). The paper is careful that the episode-grouping arithmetic diagnostic is a worked example, not an evaluated intervention. Key Results - Primary result: checkpoint 0 clears 0/96 and selected checkpoint 270 clears 77/96 (80.2%) on eight held-out normal-start mazes (3 extra lives, 512 steps, 12 samples/maze); the trajectory peaks at 78/96 at checkpoint 335 and the last complete check at 425 is 60/96, with mixed earlier-stage retention (T3 −4, T4 −2, T5 +8, T6 +6 clears between checks 249 and 425). - Restart-training pitfall: a 192/192 first-pass winning batch drew restart states from only 11 states on 2 maps and 3 source episodes, with 96/132 final-stage attempts starting with ≤15 of 118 pellets remaining; the same branch's last normal-start validation was 54/96. - Perception: static greedy transcription is exact on 24/24 images and 69/72 sampled outputs (37,797/37,800 cells correct, yet 3 complete maps wrong — a boundary wall read as empty, a ghost read as the house door), while in-loop audits give 18/20 exact full maps and 131/138 exact actor sets (Pac-Man exact on 138/138; errors concern ghosts and occluded cells). - Decision regression: a separate ASCII lineage falls from 59/96 to 37/96 validation clears, with 30 replayed regression cases including immediately lethal choices while an exit was available. - Action-head comparison: 20 vs. 3 Adam updates yields 14.1% vs. 28.1% clears (0 extra lives) and 78.1% vs. 85.9% (3 extra lives); paired discordance tests give p=0.0636 and p=0.3833 — no significant benefit from further RL. - External baselines (appendix): GPT-6 Luna clears 0/50 with primitive actions and 10/50 (image) / 14/50 (ASCII) with a Route-option harness on one fixed layout; a GPT-6.1 Sol single-game demonstration clears 1/1. - Baselines are thin and mostly in appendices; the Qwen agent's primary comparison is against its own pre-optimization checkpoint rather than competing methods. All testing is on one game with mazes up to 25×21 — a small-scale, single-domain study; the most counter-intuitive finding is that continued optimization and more RL updates each coincided with worse outcomes. Novelty Classification NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (primary), with a secondary claim as a diagnostic methodology/checklist; there is no new algorithm, benchmark, dataset, or system. The genuinely novel part is the provenance-verified quantification of specific post-training pitfalls (restart-state source concentration, static-vs-closed-loop perception divergence, RL-accompanied decision regression) in one documented agent lineage; the underlying phenomena — distribution shift from curriculum design, catastrophic forgetting under rehearsal, checkpoint regression, and VLM visual unreliability — are known, so the contribution is a rigorous instantiation of existing evaluation wisdom in a new setting rather than a new idea. Rigor & Reproducibility Ablations in the causal sense are absent — the paper explicitly declines to isolate the contribution of any curriculum technique, restart design, or ClipCov, which is honest but means no component-level attribution is established. Statistical treatment is uneven but unusually careful where present: McNemar tests and conservative Clopper-Pearson union-bound intervals accompany the action-head panel, and the paper repeatedly distinguishes correlated from independent samples; however, the headline validation counts (0/96 → 77/96) carry no intervals, no training-seed replication exists, and checkpoint 270 vs. 335 selection and reporting use the same eight-maze panel (Goodhart's-Law concern the authors acknowledge but do not resolve). No code, model weights, or full ledger release URL is stated in the main text beyond an anonymous companion site (https://where-it-breaks-review.vercel.app/); reproducibility notes describe retained ledgers with run IDs, seeds, and contract hashes, but complete per-slot map manifests and historical hyperparameters are admitted missing. Methodological flags: evaluation on the authors' own environment and panels, weak/appendix-only external baselines, a single domain (Pac-Man), and a legacy 55.17% headline the authors themselves flag as unverifiable — a transparency positive, but also evidence of how much of the original project record did not survive audit. This is an arXiv preprint (dated Nov 2026) and does not appear peer-reviewed. Deployability Profile: EMPIRICAL (the paper runs training and evaluation experiments; no artifact is released as a deployable tool). - Practical: Training used 8×H800 GPUs and inference one H800 per model, so it is reproducible only with datacenter-class hardware, though the evaluation harness itself is lightweight. - Efficient: The 430-update lineage logged ~175 hours of step time (up to ~31 minutes per update at stage T6), and perception-heavy closed-loop play costs ~6,300–11,000 perception calls per 64 episodes — far more expensive than non-VLM baselines, with no efficiency claim made. - Effective: The evidence supports a descriptive improvement on a fixed validation panel and concrete component-level diagnoses, but does not show unseen-layout generalization, full screenshot-driven end-to-end success, or that any intervention actually repaired a failure. - Scalable: Nothing is tested at 10×–100× scale (one game, ≤8 layouts per panel, ≤50-episode external baselines), and the paper makes no scalability claims. The work stops at paper form: no library, CLI, trained checkpoint, or dataset release is stated beyond an anonymous review companion; the reusable output is the diagnostic checklist and audit methodology. Strengths - The start-distribution audit is the sharpest contribution: tying a 192/192 training batch to 11 restart states, 2 maps, and 3 source episodes (96/132 attempts starting with ≤15 pellets) is a concrete, quantified demonstration of why training win rates mislead, which most RL-for-agents papers never measure. - The willingness to report unfavorable and null results — a regression from 80.2% to 60/96 under continued training, a non-significant or negative action-head comparison (−14.1 pp, p=0.0636), and the self-flagged unverifiable 55.17% legacy figure — is rare and raises confidence in the favorable numbers reported. - The static-vs-closed-loop perception dissociation (24/24 exact transcription vs. 18/20 in-loop maps with occluded-cell fabrication) isolates a specific, actionable failure mode (unknown cells asserted as empty) that a static VLM benchmark score would hide. - The evidence-unit discipline (never pooling restart wins with normal-start validation, never reading a fixed-map panel as layout generalization) is a genuinely transferable methodological contribution, executed consistently across the appendices. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors confront limitations directly and at length, which is a credibility positive: they state that (1) checkpoint selection and reporting share the same eight-maze panel, so results are descriptive rather than independent tests; (2) there is no training-seed replication and no complete per-slot map manifest, so train/validation separation cannot be fully proven; (3) the trajectory mixes curriculum changes, backplay, and restart continuations, so no single technique's causal contribution is identified; (4) the action-head panel shows no significant effect and establishes no general harm or benefit of RL; (5) logged time is not calendar duration or per-episode cost; and (6) no combined autonomous self-improvement gain has been measured. They also explicitly separate claims (e.g., "restart suffix improvement") from what would count as full-game mastery. No minimization pattern is apparent. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The paper never evaluates the complete screenshot-driven system end-to-end on the intended task — the headline improvement is ASCII-only, and the visual action-head result is null — so the motivating question ("why is my VLM agent bad at Pac-Man?") is answered for components but never closed at the system level, a gap the authors note only in passing. - No comparison against non-RL baselines for the ASCII policy (e.g., behavior cloning, DAgger with a programmatic teacher, or prompt-only chain-of-thought play by the same base model), making it impossible to judge whether the PPO machinery was the right tool. - The validation panel of eight fixed layouts with 12 samples each yields correlated, clustered data; the paper criticizes naive binomial reading in Appendix L but reports no cross-layout interval for its own headline result. - Single domain, single model family (Qwen3.5-9B), and one environment implementation: the transfer of the "checklist" lessons to other games, agents, or environments is asserted by implication but not evidenced. - Some provenance is unrecoverable (legacy denominators, missing hyperparameters, unlocated projector/serializer sources in Table 18), meaning parts of the development history rest on presentation-grade records the authors themselves downgrade — appropriate, but it caps the evidential weight of the historical panels. - The externally interesting result (GPT-6/GPT-6.1 with a Route-option harness reaching 10–28% vs. 0% primitive) is confined to one layout and 50 seeds and is not integrated into the main analysis. Bottom Line A practitioner running RL post-training on VLM agents gains a concrete, unusually well-audited set of cautionary measurements and a reusable diagnostic checklist from this paper, but should not expect an algorithm, benchmark, or transferable performance result — it is the best-documented negative-space case study in its niche rather than a must-read method paper.

Designing AI- Agent -Enabled Entrepreneurship Training Programs: An Experiential Learning Approach to Business Automation , Opportunity Recognition, and …

D Hayoshi · aijcst.org · automated generated environments for agent testing - new results
TL;DR:** - What it does: This paper introduces E-ACT, a theory-informed instructional design framework that integrates AI-agent workflows into entrepreneurship education through six competencies, three practice strands, an eight-week studio curriculum, a human-governed agent architecture, and a proposed evaluation protocol with four testable propositions. - Why it's important: Entrepreneurship programs are rapidly adopting generative AI, but prompting proficiency does not teach learners when to trust, test, or reject AI output, and successful automation can conceal whether a student understands the commercial assumptions behind a workflow. - How it does it: The core move is separating AI-mediated information retrieval and action proposal from human authorization and outcome verification, and grading learners on evidence quality, disconfirmation plans, and decision logs rather than on the polish of generated artifacts. - The good: The design is unusually disciplined about the claim/evidence boundary — it explicitly labels its 8-week duration, hour allocations, and competency structure as unvalidated design parameters and derives falsifiable propositions rather than claiming results. - The missing: There is no empirical data of any kind — no pilot, no participant, no rubric validation — so every pedagogical claim remains a hypothesis; the paper acknowledges this but the contribution is therefore entirely untested. - Read it or not: Worth reading for curriculum designers and education researchers building AI-agent coursework who need a scaffold for study design; skippable for anyone expecting evidence of effectiveness, since the paper itself concedes none exists.
Why this rank

Rigor (40) is the dominant drag — the paper contains zero empirical data, and while it honestly labels everything as unvalidated design parameters, 'rigorous design with no validation' still caps the contribution at hypothesis-stage. Novelty (55) is moderate: the proposal/authorization separation and criteria-before-ranking protocol are genuine pedagogical devices, but assembled from standard components (Kolb, EntreComp, NIST-style controls) for a new setting. Problem & Motivation: Entrepreneurship educators face a specific gap: AI-agent systems can plan multi-step business actions (drafting outreach, classifying customer feedback, proposing workflows), which creates (a) over-delegation risks — erroneous tool use, unauthorized communications, data leakage — and (b) an educational failure mode in which fluent agent output is mistaken for customer validation or commercial insight. Prior AI-entrepreneurship work either emphasizes idea generation (chatbot prompting) over disciplined hypothesis comparison, treats automation skills separately from opportunity-quality and managerial-responsibility learning objectives, or evaluates outcomes with subjective confidence/intention measures rather than observable decision quality (a critique grounded in Nabi et al.'s 2017 systematic review of 159 studies). The problem affects higher education, incubators, and professional entrepreneurship programs, all of which currently lack a replicable instructional design that connects agentic AI capability to entrepreneurial judgment under human accountability. Key Idea: The single core insight is that the agent's role in the learning environment must be structurally bounded at the point of consequential action: the agent retrieves information and proposes steps, but a human verifies assumptions and authorizes anything consequential, with outcome checks afterward. This 'proposal/authorization separation' is both a safety architecture and a pedagogical device — it forces every learner decision through an auditable artifact (evidence register, decision log, approval gate) so that judgment, not output fluency, is what gets assessed. Methodology: The paper uses a conceptual, design-science approach (Hevner et al., 2004) with four analytic steps: selecting foundational perspectives (experiential learning per Kolb, entrepreneurship-as-practice per Neck & Greene, effectuation per Sarasvathy, EntreComp competencies, AI literacy per Ng et al. and Long & Magerko, responsible-AI governance per UNESCO and NIST AI 600-1); consulting recent AI/agent literature; translating concepts into teachable competencies and supervised tasks; and constructing an evaluation protocol. The output artifact, E-ACT, has: (1) six competencies (problem framing, opportunity evaluation, workflow specification, agent supervision, traceable decision-making, reflection/transfer) each requiring a technical action plus entrepreneurial justification; (2) three practice strands — opportunity recognition (evidence inventories, competing problem explanations, disconfirmation criteria), business automation (bounded low-risk processes, mandatory failure cases, rollback procedures, agent-vs-rule-based comparison), and decision-making (criteria declared before viewing agent rankings, decision logs distinguishing predictions from commitments); (3) a human-governed agent configuration with least-privilege permissions, disabled external send functions, sandbox execution, and audit logs; (4) an eight-week, 48-hour curriculum with weekly deliverables; and (5) a proposed cluster-randomized or matched mixed-methods evaluation with blind-scored scenario tasks, pre/post/delayed measurement, and calibrated-reliance tests using deliberately erroneous agent suggestions. Critical design decisions: requiring criteria-before-ranking to prevent motivated reasoning (well-justified by automation-bias literature); mandating an agent-vs-deterministic-alternative comparison (well-justified); declaring the 8-week duration and hour split as design parameters rather than optimized values (honestly flagged as unvalidated). No participants, data collection, or statistical testing were undertaken — this is explicitly a design paper. Key Results: Not applicable — the paper reports no empirical results. The authors state plainly that "no scores, coefficient estimates or significance tests are presented because the programme has not yet been implemented as a study." The closest quantitative content is curriculum specification: 8 weekly 4-hour studios plus 16 independent hours (48 total), teams of 2–4, at least three realistic failure cases per prototype, and a four-level anchored rubric scale. The four propositions (P1–P4) — e.g., that integrated training yields greater gains on independently scored opportunity-evaluation tasks, and that source audits reduce acceptance of unsupported agent recommendations — are hypotheses for future preregistered testing, not findings. The only empirical numbers in the paper are cited from others: Renz et al. (2025), n=63, showing LLM-assisted opportunity-recognition gains largest for lower-baseline participants, and Vaccaro et al. (2024) meta-analytic evidence that human-AI combinations on average do not beat the stronger solo performer. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (an instructional design artifact), with the genuine novelty lying in the operational integration of human-in-the-loop agent governance into an experiential entrepreneurship curriculum — specifically the criteria-before-ranking protocol, mandatory agent-vs-rule comparison, and decision-log accountability structure. The underlying components are all standard: Kolb cycles, EntreComp competencies, AI-literacy frameworks, NIST-style risk controls, and human-approval gates are established ideas competently combined for a new setting (agentic AI in entrepreneurship education); the paper itself correctly labels its literature-to-design mapping as "an analytical synthesis, not a new empirical finding." Rigor & Reproducibility: As a conceptual design paper, rigor resides in internal consistency and claim discipline, both of which are strong: the paper scrupulously separates specification from result, labels figures as design values rather than data, and names limitations directly. There are no ablations, seeds, error bars, or significance tests (nothing to test yet), and no code, rubric instrument, dataset, or task materials are released — the paper only recommends that "publication of task materials, rubrics and deidentified protocols would support reproducibility." Methodological concerns: the literature synthesis is purposive and narrative, not systematic, with no screening strategy or exhaustive coverage (acknowledged); the framework was developed with no instructor or learner input whatsoever, so its usability, workload estimates (4-hour studios), and rubric anchoring are untested; and the proposed evaluation, while well-designed on paper (clustering, parallel forms, preregistration), has not been executed even at pilot scale. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS-adjacent EMPIRICAL-aspirational — the artifact is a curriculum design and governance architecture, evaluated by nothing yet (design only). - Practical: Yes — it assumes only institutionally approved LLM access and no-code tools, with paper-based and offline fallbacks specified for resource-constrained settings. - Efficient: 48 designed learner-hours per cohort plus a demanding instructor preparation rehearsal; the paper honestly flags that educator workload is unestimated and may be prohibitive in large cohorts. - Effective: Unknown — effectiveness is explicitly a proposition, and the paper warns that a sandbox demo "is not real-world reliability." - Scalable: Not tested; the design assumes instructors can inspect agent outputs and supervise judgment, which the authors admit may not hold at cohort scale without added support. The work delivers a paper-form instructional design; no reusable instrument, software artifact, or trained-material package is released. Strengths: - Exceptional claim discipline: the paper consistently distinguishes design specification from empirical claim (e.g., Figure 3 is labeled "design values, not observed data"; the illustrative scenario is labeled "not a real organization"), a level of honesty rare in education-design papers. - The 'do not automate' outcome as a legitimate success path — a student who rejects automation after comparing cost, uncertainty, and risk can meet the objectives better than one who builds an unnecessary agent — is a genuinely non-obvious pedagogical stance that counters tool-adopter bias. - The evaluation design is publishable in its own right: cluster-level assignment, blind scoring by two trained assessors, criteria-before-ranking to prevent retrofit justification, delayed transfer on unfamiliar cases, and calibrated-reliance testing with deliberately flawed agent suggestions. - Concrete safety engineering (Table 5) mapping each risk scenario to a preventive control and required response, grounded in NIST AI 600-1 and least-privilege principles rather than generic AI-ethics language. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly and extensively: no effectiveness demonstration; purposive rather than exhaustive literature synthesis; eight-week duration and competency structure unoptimized and un-validated; risk of higher-education bias in the design assumptions; platform churn outpacing curricula; instructor supervision infeasible in large cohorts without support; uneven benefits across prior domain knowledge; equity concerns (language, connectivity, subscription costs, disabilities); and self-generated risks including AI-centric capstones crowding out customer discovery, prompt homogenization of venture ideas, and team projects concealing unequal contribution. This candor is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The framework was developed with zero formative input from instructors, students, or incubator stakeholders; even a single expert review or cognitive walkthrough of the rubric would have substantially strengthened the design claim, and its absence means usability problems (e.g., the 4-hour studio feasibility, the decision-log burden) are undiscoverable from the paper. - The proposed evaluation's comparison condition ("conventional experiential entrepreneurship with an AI-literacy briefing") does not isolate the agent component from the added structure (decision logs, source audits, failure cases); a stronger design would include a structure-without-agent arm, which the paper does not consider. - The rubric's central construct — "decision quality" scored on a four-level anchored scale — is asserted but not developed; no sample anchors, no inter-rater pilot, and no treatment of the paper's own admission that "several choices may be defensible" at the anchor level. - No engagement with cost: platform subscription and per-token agent costs are mentioned only in passing, despite the framework targeting resource-constrained institutions. - Cited supporting evidence is thin and partly self-qualifying: Renz et al. (2025) had 63 participants, and Ahmad et al. (2026) explicitly failed to establish judgment improvements, so the empirical footing for the entire premise is two small, mixed studies — the paper reads this correctly but a reviewer may find the design under-motivated by evidence. Bottom Line: Education researchers and curriculum designers get a well-constructed, honestly scoped scaffold for studying agentic AI in entrepreneurship training — particularly the evaluation protocol and safety architecture — but anyone seeking evidence that such training works must wait for the empirical study this paper only proposes; there is currently no stronger alternative covering the same integration, which is both the paper's value and its exposure.

Fine-Grained Selective Refusal: Steering LLM Safety via Wasserstein-Informed Flow Matching

Z Liu, H Du, H Sun, H Tan · aclanthology.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces WassSteer, an activation-steering framework that detects unsafe activations with a lightweight SVM classifier and then uses flow matching with sliced-Wasserstein optimal-transport coupling to transport only those activations from harmful to refusal-safe distributions, leaving benign activations untouched. - Why it's important: Existing linear steering vectors (e.g., Refusal Direction) force a harsh safety-utility trade-off: they either miss sophisticated jailbreaks or collapse the model into over-refusing benign queries and losing reasoning ability, which is the central deployment blocker for inference-time safety control. - How it does it: It replaces a fixed linear shift (mean-difference vector) with a learned nonlinear velocity field trained via flow matching, using sliced-Wasserstein 1-D couplings to pair source and target activation distributions so the transport path minimizes displacement, plus a routing classifier that applies the flow only when unsafe content is detected at an early decision layer. - The good: The component ablation is convincing and well-targeted: sliced-OT coupling adds +5.0 average DSR over plain flow matching (94.1 vs 89.1 on Llama-3.1-8B), and the method holds utility essentially at base-model level (e.g., XSTest 90.7 vs 90.7 on Llama) while base DSR rises from ~60 to ~96.5. - The missing: The strongest baseline, Refusal Direction at α=0.4, scores 100% DSR on every attack and model, so WassSteer never wins on raw safety — its advantage rests entirely on the utility column, and no significance tests, seeds, or error bars are reported for any comparison. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers working on activation steering, refusal, or OT/flow methods for representation control, who will find a careful Pareto-framed evaluation and useful ablations; practitioners seeking a drop-in defense can skim the tables, and those outside safety steering can skip it.

Problem & Motivation: Operators of open-weight LLMs need defense against jailbreak prompts without retraining the model (SFT/RLHF are expensive, cause forgetting, and lag new attacks) and without the over-refusal that plagues aggressive safety interventions. Activation steering is the lightweight alternative, but the dominant approaches assume safety is encoded along a single linear direction (the Linear Representation Hypothesis). Recent evidence (concept cones, multi-dimensional refusal geometry) shows this assumption fails: linear shifts push activations out-of-distribution, yielding brittle defense and severe over-refusal. The paper targets the gap of achieving high defense success rate (DSR) against diverse jailbreaks while keeping false-refusal and general-capability metrics at base-model level — the safety-utility Pareto frontier. Key Idea: Reformulate safety steering as distribution-to-distribution transport rather than point-wise linear shifting: learn a flow-matching velocity field that moves the entire distribution of harmful activations onto the distribution of refusal-safe activations, using sliced-Wasserstein couplings so the transport path approximates an optimal-transport (minimal-displacement) route, thereby preserving semantic content; a decision-layer SVM routes interventions so only unsafe activations are transformed. Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) Layer Navigator: layer-wise t-SNE and per-layer DiffMean steering-effectiveness analysis select a decision layer ℓd (e.g., layer 11 for Gemma-2-9B, layer 4 for Qwen-2.5-7B) where harmful/harmless activations are most separable, and an intervention layer ℓi (e.g., layer 20/18) chosen via DSR probing and cross-layer cosine similarity. (2) Safety Routing: an SVM classifier gφ on activations at ℓd labels each prompt safe/unsafe; only unsafe activations proceed to steering. (3) Flow-matching steering: a network fθ(h,t) is trained with the flow-matching regression loss ‖fθ(ht,t) − (ν−µ)‖², where pairing of source µ (harmful/compliant activations) and target ν (refusal activations) is established per-batch by projecting onto L=100 random directions, sorting to get the optimal 1-D coupling (sliced-Wasserstein, Eq. 9), and using linear interpolants ht=(1−t)µ+tν. At inference, the ODE h1 = h0 + ∫₀¹ fθ dt is integrated with K steps and the steered activation replaces the residual-stream activation at ℓi. Critical design decisions: (a) sliced-OT coupling instead of independent coupling — justified by the +5.0 DSR ablation; (b) selective routing — justified since unconditional flow steering degrades XSTest (92.0 vs 90.7 with routing on Llama); (c) early-layer decision (ℓd ≪ ℓi) — motivated by layer-analysis figures but the choice of an SVM at a single early layer is less thoroughly justified against alternative classifiers or ensembles. Key Results: Evaluated on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-it, and Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct against seven jailbreaks (AIM, AutoDAN, GCG, Cipher, Jailbroken, PAIR, ReNeLLM), with baselines RD, Jailbreak Antidote, Surgical, AdaSteer, AlphaSteer, and Truthflow. Representative numbers: on Llama-3.1-8B, WassSteer achieves 100/99/100/96/94/99/97 DSR across the seven attacks versus base-model 92/48/61/15/74/45/28. Crucially, RD (α=0.4) attains 100 DSR on every attack and model — exceeding WassSteer (e.g., 72 on AIM for Gemma vs 100 for RD) — but RD collapses utility (0 on OKTest, XSTest, MMLU-Pro, GSM8K, MATH for Gemma). WassSteer preserves utility near base: Gemma XSTest 82.0 vs base 82.4; MMLU-Pro 35.5 vs base 35.5; Llama GSM8K 83 vs base 82. Against non-steering defenses on Llama-3.1-8B, WassSteer reaches 96.5 avg DSR / 90.7 XSTest versus CircuitBreaker 94.2/87.8, SmoothLLM 76.2/85.4, and SFT 87.6/90.0. Scale: 7–9B models in the main results, with an appendix test at Qwen-2.5-14B (95.6 DSR, 96.0 XSTest). Cross-judge checks with Llama-Guard-3-8B and exact-match scoring reproduce the GPT-4o-judged numbers. A surprising element is the explicit framing that the paper does not claim the best raw DSR — it claims a better Pareto position than RD's degenerate maximum-safety point. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (with an EMPIRICAL FINDING component). The genuinely novel element is the combination of sliced-Wasserstein-coupled flow matching with conditional safety routing for refusal steering, and the framing of steering as distributional alignment on the activation manifold. However, the ingredients are established: flow matching (Lipman et al.), sliced-Wasserstein distances, and OT-based activation manipulation already appear in TruthFlow (flow matching for hallucination correction), Linear-AcT (OT maps for toxicity), and SAKE (OT for knowledge editing); the contribution is a competent, well-evaluated transfer of that machinery to jailbreak defense with a routing layer, not a new formulation of transport itself. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are above average for this area: component ablation isolating routing vs. intervention vs. coupling (Table 3), layer-navigator ablation (+5.9 DSR over random layer pairs), cross-judge/exact-match robustness checks (Table 4), comparison with non-steering defenses (Table 5), a 14B-scale check, and a compute-cost analysis with measured training times (12.5–13.5 minutes on one A800). Concerns: no multiple seeds, error bars, or significance tests anywhere; DSR and false-refusal metrics depend on GPT-4o LLM-as-judge (partially mitigated by the Llama-Guard re-evaluation); the safety evaluation reuses attack benchmarks (JailbreakBench/AdvBench data also appear in the training mixture via JailbreakV-28K and related sets), so train/eval contamination risk deserves scrutiny — the paper does not state that evaluation attack sets are disjoint from training jailbreak data. No public code or model release URL is stated for WassSteer itself (baselines use public codebases; activations use EasyEdit2), which limits reproducibility. A methodological subtlety: sliced-Wasserstein couplings applied independently per random projection do not yield a true W₂ geodesic in d dimensions, so the "Wasserstein geodesic" claim is motivational rather than a proven property of the learned flow. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (inference-time method with trained components; no fine-tuning of the LLM). Practical: Yes — runs on a single 80GB A800; the steering network is an MLP on activation vectors. Efficient: Safe prompts pay only O(n_sv·d) for SVM classification at an early layer; unsafe prompts add O(K·d²) for ODE integration, independent of sequence length — heavier than a linear vector add but cheaper in training (under 14 minutes) than any fine-tuning defense. Effective: The evidence shows it solves the stated Pareto problem on 7–14B open models against seven benchmark attacks, but the safety claim is benchmark-judge-mediated and the routing classifier is a potential single point of failure against adversarial activations engineered to look benign at layer ℓd — an adaptive-attack evaluation is absent. Scalable: Claimed to scale favorably by complexity analysis, but empirically validated only to 14B; the authors themselves flag 70B+ validation as future work. Deliverable: method described in paper form with algorithms and hyperparameters; no released library, checkpoint, or steering-flow weights are mentioned. Strengths: - The Pareto framing is honest and unusual: the paper concedes RD wins on raw DSR and positions its contribution on utility preservation, with Table 2 making the RD utility collapse (0 across the board on Gemma) unambiguous. - The component ablation cleanly separates detection from intervention and shows the sliced-OT coupling — the paper's actual technical claim — carries real weight (+5.0 DSR over independent-coupling flow matching), rather than the gains coming from routing alone. - Evaluation hygiene beyond the field's norm: cross-judge consistency (Llama-Guard-3-8B), exact-match re-scoring for capability benchmarks, explicit judge prompts in the appendix, and measured wall-clock training times. - Comparison against non-steering defenses (CircuitBreaker, SmoothLLM, SFT, SelfDefend) situates the method in the broader defense landscape rather than only against steering cousins. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state three: (1) flow trajectories are hard to interpret in human-understandable semantic terms; (2) O(K·d²) inference overhead may strain latency-sensitive, high-volume deployments, with single-step parameterizations proposed as mitigation; (3) experiments cover only 7–9B models (14B in appendix), with 70B+ validation left as future work. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Train/evaluation contamination is unaddressed: the training mixture includes prompts from JailbreakV-28K, AdvBench, MaliciousInstruct, and JailbreakBench, and evaluation uses GCG (AdvBench-derived), Jailbroken, and other standard sets; no statement that evaluation attack instances are disjoint from training prompts. Given the routing classifier is trained on this data, DSR could be partly in-distribution detection rather than generalization. - No adaptive-attack evaluation: an adversary who knows the defense can craft prompts whose layer-ℓd activations evade the SVM; Cipher DSR on Qwen-2.5 (79, the method's weakest) hints at this fragility, but no evasion-aware attack is run. - The Wasserstein-geodesic story is asserted but never validated: no experiment measures transport cost of the learned flow versus linear or independent-coupling paths, so the central geometric claim connecting OT theory to the empirical gains is untested. - Single α/single-configuration comparisons: baselines appear at one fixed setting (RD α=0.4); a Pareto frontier is claimed, but the frontier is traced effectively at one operating point per method rather than sweeping steering intensities. - No variance reporting: every table is a point estimate; several Gemma margins (e.g., WassSteer 72 vs Adasteer 78 on AIM, where Adasteer actually wins) fall within plausible seed/judge noise. - The SVM router's own false-negative/false-positive rates on held-out adversarial data are not reported separately from end-task DSR. Bottom Line: A rigorously ablated and honestly framed contribution that credibly improves the safety-utility trade-off for activation steering at 7–14B scale, but whose headline geometric claim is unvalidated, whose evaluation leaves train/test contamination and adaptive attacks open, and whose novelty is a well-executed transfer of known flow/OT machinery — read it if you work on LLM safety steering; otherwise AlphaSteer or CircuitBreaker cover adjacent ground with released code.

Agent -R $^ 2$: Scaling Agents for Realistic Productivity Work via Real-Source Data Synthesis

T Pan, Z Wang, Y Yan, Q Wu, Y Chen, Y Qu, R Zhang… · arxiv.org · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Agent-R2, a three-stage data synthesis pipeline that mines occupational workflow blueprints from web corpora, retrieves authentic web-hosted office files as attachments, and synthesizes instructions with fine-grained rubrics, yielding 4k training instances from 10k candidates, and uses them to train Agent-R2-4B (SFT + rubric-reward GRPO) that reaches 51.0% Pass@1 on GDPval, beating the 235B-parameter Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507 (48.0%) despite a 4B backbone. - Why it's important: Real professional agent work (long workflows over messy heterogeneous files, graded deliverables) is bottlenecked by training data that is either hand-curated (does not scale) or LLM-fabricated (lacks realistic file structure), so a scalable pipeline grounded in real sources addresses the core data constraint for productivity agents. - How it does it: Ground every synthesis stage in real sources — O*NET occupational seeds + web-corpus workflow extraction, multi-turn web search-and-verify retrieval of genuine public files, then sandbox-verified instruction/rubric synthesis with Claude-Opus-4.5 expert trajectories — followed by SFT and GRPO where deliverables are scored by an MLLM-as-a-judge against the synthesized rubrics. - The good: The verification and controls are unusually thorough: a four-level decontamination audit (file hashes, URLs, MinHash 5-gram similarity avg 0.005 vs. GDPval, instruction embedding similarity 0.43), judge-stability analysis across two judges and three repeats, a 4k-SFT control isolating the RL gain (45.5 vs. 51.0), and rule-based behavioral metrics showing "writing despite an unfixed error" dropping from 55% to 11%. - The missing: The headline GDPval result is on a benchmark the authors themselves call in-domain (their pipeline targets exactly the occupational-workflow distribution GDPval tests), and the out-of-domain transfer to OfficeQA is only 1.0 point over the 235B baseline (14.8 vs. 13.8), with no seeds/error bars on the 1.9-point real-vs-synthetic-file ablation (43.3 vs. 41.4). - Read it or not: Read it if you build agent post-training data pipelines and need a concrete, well-audited recipe for grounding synthetic tasks in real files and rubric-scored RL; skip it if you want evidence of general capability gains beyond benchmark-matched distribution fit — Claude-Opus-4.5 still leads by 21.6 points.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Resilience (55) and Rigor (55) pull the composite down: the headline 4B-beats-235B claim is made on GDPval, which the paper itself designates as in-domain, OOD transfer is +1.0 point, and the central real-vs-synthetic-file ablation (1.9 points) sits inside the paper's own reported judge noise (~3.2 points) with no seeds or significance tests. Novelty (60) is moderate — grounding all three synthesis stages in real retrieved files with sandbox-verified rubric-reference revision is a real methodological contribution, but the SFT-plus-GRPO training recipe is standard. The four-level decontamination audit, cross-judge stability testing, and quantified behavioral shortcut metrics earn Completeness (65) some credit, but the quiet exclusion of the strongest open baseline (GLM-4.7, 61.1%) from the abstract's claim and an unevaluated same-family reward/synthesis loop cap it. Impact (62) reflects a released pipeline and a genuinely useful 4B recipe despite no stated weight release. Weighted composite: 0.20*60 + 0.25*55 + 0.15*55 + 0.15*65 + 0.15*55 + 0.10*62 = 56.

Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: Teams building LLM agents for economically valuable productivity work face a data bottleneck: success requires jointly (a) executing long-horizon professional workflows, (b) integrating evidence across heterogeneous, messy real files (PDF, DOCX, XLSX, PPTX), and (c) producing deliverables meeting fine-grained content and formatting standards. Existing training data covers these in isolation — instruction-following sets, document QA, single-deliverable generation (presentations, spreadsheets) — and provides no end-to-end supervision. Hand-authored workflows (as in GDPval) do not scale, while LLM-generated files lack realistic layouts, gaps, and cross-file dependencies. The intended beneficiaries are practitioners post-training small open models into useful work-completion agents. Key Idea: Treat the open web itself as the source of training task realism: instead of fabricating environments, mine file-oriented workflow blueprints from web-corpus evidence (seeds from occupational taxonomies like O*NET), retrieve and sandbox-verify the actual public files those workflows require, and derive both the instruction and a fine-grained rubric (15.3 items on average, 41.9% of rubric numbers appearing only in attachments) from the verified workflow-file pair — with Claude-Opus-4.5 solving each task in the sandbox to produce reference deliverables and expert trajectories, plus a rubric-vs-reference revision loop that filters or repairs unmet rubric items. Methodology: Three synthesis stages: (1) Workflow Extraction — Qwen3.6-Plus (πsyn) maps web-corpus segments (DLR-Web/FineFineWeb with discipline metadata) plus occupational seeds to workflow blueprints under workflow and file-oriented filtering filters; ~2.2k of 10k candidates discarded here. (2) Attachment Searching — a multi-turn search-and-verification loop generates queries, downloads candidates, inspects them via bash and view_image, and retains only files jointly satisfying the workflow's information needs (files >50 pages or >2 MB discarded); ~3.8k candidates lost here, leaving ~4k instances. (3) Task Synthesis — sandbox-embedded multi-turn design of instruction I, attachment set Fa, and rubric R (content vs. form categories), expert solving by Claude-Opus-4.5 to yield reference files Fr and trajectory τ, then verify-and-revise. Training: SFT of Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 on 3k filtered expert trajectories (2 epochs), then GRPO on 1k held-out tasks in a persistent sandbox (bash, web_search, web_fetch, view_image) with outcome-only reward r = Score(F̂d, Fr, R)/max_score against an MLLM-as-a-judge (Qwen3.6-Plus), group size 4, max 40 assistant turns, no KL-penalty-free intermediate shaping. Critical design decisions: outcome-only rewards (justified as avoiding tool-specific calling preferences, but untested — no shaping ablation), real-file grounding over synthetic files (justified by a 1.9-point ablation, weak evidence), and the same model family serving as both rubric synthesizer and RL judge (potential self-consistency bias, not discussed). Key Results: On the full 220-task GDPval set (agent-as-a-judge with Gemini-3.1-Pro, max 100 steps): Agent-R2-4B 51.0% Pass@1 vs. base Qwen3-4B-Thinking 32.4% (+18.6), surpassing Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507 (48.0%), Qwen3-VL-235B (49.7%), DeepSeek-v3.1 (48.8%), GLM-4.7 (61.1% — actually above Agent-R2-4B), GPT-4.1 (39.4%), and Gemini-2.5-Pro (57.9%); Claude-Opus-4.5 leads at 72.6%. On out-of-domain OfficeQA, 14.8% Pass@1 vs. 2.2% base and 13.8% for the 235B. Behavioral: SFT raises tool-call steps from 6.7 to 39.0; RL raises completion rate to 90.9% and cuts tool-call errors to 12.9; "writing despite an unfixed error" falls 55.0%→16.0% (SFT)→11.0% (RL); placeholder text falls to 5.7%, matching expert-written GDPval deliverables. Ablations: real-file SFT 43.3 vs. synthetic-file 41.4 GDPval Pass@1 (1k matched pairs, no significance test); rubric rewards 51.0 vs. 49.5 without; 4k-SFT control 45.5 confirms the +5.7 RL gain is not mere data exposure. Scaling SFT data 1k→4k shows held-out synthesized-task score rising (0.486→0.617) but GDPval saturating (43.3→45.5). Baselines are current and strong; the evaluation scale is standard (single 4B backbone, one benchmark-family focus). Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (a real-source-grounded data synthesis pipeline for deliverable-level productivity tasks) plus an EMPIRICAL FINDING (rubric-scored real-source data mitigates measurable shortcut behavior). The genuinely novel element is grounding all three synthesis stages in real occupational evidence and authentic retrieved files rather than LLM-fabricated environments, with the sandbox-verified rubric-reference revision loop. The training recipe (SFT → GRPO with rubric-as-reward, MLLM-as-judge) is a straightforward combination of established techniques (Gunjal et al. 2025; Huang et al. 2025) applied to this new data distribution. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and targeted (real vs. synthetic files, rubric vs. no-rubric reward, 4k-SFT data-vs-RL control, data scaling), which is above average for this area. However, no seeds, error bars, or significance tests are reported anywhere; the real-vs-synthetic gap (1.9 points) and rubric-reward gap (1.5 points) are within plausible seed/judge noise given the reported median per-task judge variance of 3.1–3.2 points. Judge stability is explicitly tested (Agent-R2-4B stays within 50.8–51.1 across three Gemini-3.1-Pro repeats and 51.7–52.3 under DeepSeek-v4-Flash; inter-judge Pearson 0.93) — a credibility positive. Code is released at https://github.com/ZJU-REAL/Agent-R2; the 4k dataset release is described in Appendix E but no URL is given for it. Methodological concerns: (1) GDPval is explicitly the in-domain benchmark, so the flagship comparison against the 235B model is on the distribution the pipeline was built to match — the 4-level decontamination audit addresses leakage but not distribution matching; (2) the RL reward model (Qwen3.6-Plus) is the same model family as the rubric synthesizer, creating a possible self-preference loop; (3) the OOD evidence (OfficeQA, +1.0 point) is thin relative to the in-domain claims. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a trained model produced by an executed pipeline). - Practical: Yes — a 4B backbone with the open AIO Sandbox and verl v0.6.x runs on commodity GPU hardware; API costs for synthesis (Claude-Opus-4.5 expert, Qwen3.6-Plus judge) are incurred once. - Efficient: Strong inference-side efficiency (4B vs. 235B baselines), but training requires sandboxed multi-turn RL rollouts (65,536-token responses, MLLM-judge scoring per rollout) — cost is moderate but non-trivial and not quantified. - Effective: Evidence supports solving benchmark-matched productivity tasks (51.0 GDPval Pass@1, 90.9% completion rate), but OOD gains on OfficeQA are marginal (+1.0 over the 235B), so the evidence for general productivity competence is a proxy backed mainly by in-domain results. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 4k instances; the authors' own scaling data (Table 9) shows GDPval saturation from 2k to 4k SFT tasks, so claims of further scaling producing proportional gains are unsupported. The work delivers a software artifact (code, synthesis prompts in the appendix) and presumably a dataset; it stops short of released model weights being stated in the text. Strengths: - The end-to-end grounding discipline — real web files, sandbox verification of rubric satisfaction against expert-generated references, and a revision loop for unmet rubric items — is a real methodological contribution over LLM-fabricated-file synthesis pipelines, not a re-skin of existing work. - The shortcut-behavior analysis is concretely operationalized with rule-based metrics (re-checking rate 0.5%→95.8%, bypass-on-error 55%→11%, traceable numbers 31.2%→38.8%) rather than asserted, and the effective-steps-vs-performance correlation (Figure 5) links mechanism to outcome across model scales. - Controls that most papers omit are included: the 4k-SFT control cleanly attributing the RL gain to optimization rather than data exposure, the decontamination audit at four granularity levels, and cross-judge stability testing. - The judge-noise honesty — reporting median per-task score variance of ~3.2 points under the same judge — calibrates how large a difference must be to matter, which appropriately contextualizes (and undermines) some of their own smaller ablation gaps. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge that SFT increases tool-call errors (16.3 vs. 2.88) and drops completion rate (86.8%→78.2%) due to limited model capacity; that RL reduces total effective steps, explained via a step-type decomposition showing the drop comes from redundant computation (11.9→7.3); that manual audits found 14% of tasks with only partial workflow-question alignment, 15% cross-file inconsistency, and 15% feasibility issues; and that non-office deliverable types (audio, video) are outside their focus. These limitations are confronted directly with quantified evidence rather than minimized — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - In-domain circularity: the headline claim (4B beats 235B) is made on GDPval, which the paper itself designates as in-domain; the paper never evaluates on a second held-out occupational-productivity benchmark to show the gain is not distribution fit. GTA-Workflow appears only in the appendix with a single number (4.52/10 vs. DeepSeek-v4-Flash's 5.15/10 — the model loses to a stronger baseline there). - The real-vs-synthetic-file ablation — the paper's central motivation — rests on a 1.9-point difference on a 1k-task subset with no seed replication or significance testing, and is contradicted in direction by the paper's own 1k data-scaling row (43.3 for 1k real files), making the effect size suspect. - Reward-hacking risk under rubric-based RL is never probed: rubrics are synthesized by Qwen3.6-Plus and scored by Qwen3.6-Plus during RL; the paper does not check whether the RL model inflates judge scores on rubric items the behavioral metrics do not cover (e.g., superficially satisfied form criteria). - No comparison against simply distilling Claude-Opus-4.5 trajectories at larger scale or against few-shot prompting of the 235B baseline, so the reader cannot tell how much of the gain is the pipeline versus any tuned 4B expert distillation. - Claude-Opus-4.5 and GLM-4.7 both exceed Agent-R2-4B on GDPval, and GLM-4.7 is open-source; the abstract's "surpasses several larger open-source baselines" quietly excludes GLM-4.7 (61.1%), the strongest open baseline reported. Bottom Line: Practitioners building agent training pipelines gain a concrete, unusually well-audited recipe for grounding synthetic productivity tasks in real files and rubric-scored RL, but the paper's headline result is an in-domain benchmark fit whose general-agent significance is unproven and whose own ablations sit inside measurement noise.
