LIQUID: Linking Data Quality Issues to Deviations in IoT-Enhanced Process Mining

C Imenkamp, Y Bertrand, L Malburg, A Maldonado… · wi2.uni-trier.de · business process mining or process mining - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces LIQUID, a quality-aware extension of the IoT process mining pipeline that preserves data quality metadata across preprocessing, abstraction, and case correlation, and applies probabilistic causal backtracking to trace conformance deviations back to sensor-level root causes, emitting template-based explanations. - Why it's important: In IoT-enhanced process mining, sensor faults propagate through abstraction layers and surface as unexplainable conformance deviations, so analysts cannot distinguish real process problems from data artifacts, undermining trust and root-cause diagnosis. - How it does it: The core move is Bayesian bookkeeping along the pipeline: issue-specific priors and evidence-function likelihoods are updated into posteriors at each transformation stage, propagated forward as 'issue signatures,' and traversed in reverse when conformance checking flags a deviation, with chain strength computed as the product of stage probabilities. - The good: On five public IoT datasets (up to 96.3M raw readings), LIQUID achieves mean detection precision 88.2%, recall 89.0%, and root-cause attribution accuracy 86.4% (e.g., 86.1% on documented Hydraulic Systems degradation, 95.2% on Smart Home drift), with a parameter sensitivity analysis isolating only 3 of 10 parameters as needing domain calibration. - The missing: There is no comparison against any alternative root-cause method (e.g., eRooMiner, which the authors themselves cite as the closest work), and the explainability claim is evaluated only through proxy metrics, with no human assessor study — a limitation the authors concede. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers in IoT-enhanced process mining, data quality management, or explainable BPM who want a concrete, open-source pattern for linking upstream sensor faults to downstream conformance results; practitioners seeking validated, competitively benchmarked root-cause tooling should look elsewhere.
Why this rank
Scored using the Empirical profile. Rigor (50) is the main drag: no comparison against any competing root-cause method including eRooMiner, which the paper itself names as the closest prior, a trivial 50% statistical baseline with N=5, lenient ±1-level attribution, and author-side expert annotations risking circularity. Novelty (60) and Non-Obviousness (58) reflect a genuinely useful architectural pattern — carrying quality metadata as first-class evidence through abstraction and backtracking deviations to sensor origins — built from standard Bayesian machinery. Open-source code and disciplined Sobol sensitivity analysis support Impact (55) and Completeness (60), making this a credible feasibility study rather than a validated advance. Weighted composite: 0.20*60 + 0.25*50 + 0.15*58 + 0.15*60 + 0.15*52 + 0.10*55 = 56.
empirical Novelty 60 Rigor 50 Non-Obv 58 Completeness 60 Resilience 52 Impact 55
Show full analysis
Problem & Motivation: IoT-enhanced process mining transforms raw sensor streams into event logs via preprocessing, event abstraction, and case correlation. Sensor faults (noise, drift, low sampling rates, range limits, packet loss) propagate through these transformations and typically manifest only downstream as missing events, wrong labels, or incorrect timestamps. Standard practice removes such anomalies during preprocessing, severing the contextual link between a detected conformance deviation and its sensor-level origin. The result: analysts see, e.g., fitness = 0.65 with no traceable explanation, cannot diagnose root causes, and lose trust in process mining results. The closest prior work (eRooMiner) operates retrospectively on event logs only and cannot see issues observable before abstraction. The target audience is BPM analysts and process owners in IoT-heavy industrial and smart-environment settings. Key Idea: Preserve data quality metadata (issue type, posterior confidence, affected entities, evidence values) as compact 'issue signatures' at every pipeline stage, so that when conformance checking flags a deviation, a reverse traversal of the pipeline — combining per-stage posteriors with a frequency-based backtracking probability and a multiplicative chain strength — can rank the most plausible sensor-level origin. Notably, the authors are explicit that this is probabilistic support along known pipeline structure, not formal causal inference. Methodology: The artifact follows Design Science Research across three iterations (requirements, method, explanation template). The method extends the four-stage pipeline of Koschmider et al. (preprocess → abstract → correlate to cases → mine) with five computational steps: (1) pattern-based quality detection with domain-informed priors P(C_i); (2) issue-specific evidence functions f_i: X_i → [0,1] mapping symptom vectors (sampling rates, gap counts, outlier/noise levels, clipping ratios) to likelihoods P(E|C_i); (3) Bayesian updates computing posteriors P(C_i|E) and propagating issue signatures forward; (4) conformance checking whose failure triggers backtracking; (5) reverse traversal computing P(i|c) as the normalized frequency of issue i among affected entities, with chain strength = product of per-stage probabilities × P(i|c). Explanations are rendered through a six-part template (header, context, action mapping, confidence/affect, narrative, references) driven by qualitative requirements R1–R5. Critical design decisions: hand-set, deployment-specific priors and thresholds (justified by sensor specs and expert knowledge, but a stated fragility); keeping the full posterior distribution rather than thresholding early (well-motivated); and the multiplicative chain-strength formula (an independence assumption across stages that is asserted, not justified). Key Results: Evaluated on five public IoT datasets: OPPORTUNITY (944,384 readings, 126 sensors), Hydraulic Systems (96.3M readings, 34.3% degradation states), Future Factory (168,001 readings, 30 hours), Intel Berkeley (2,313,682 readings, 54 nodes), and Open Smart Home IoT-IEQ (219,595 readings). Against ground truth from documented defects (GT1) and expert pattern-catalog annotation (GT2): mean precision 88.2% (t(4)=13.23, p<.001), recall 89.0%, attribution accuracy 86.4% (measured within ±1 abstraction level); per-dataset figures include 86.1% (31/36) on Hydraulic drift in pressure sensors PS1/PS2/PS5, 88.9% (24/27) on Future Factory, 78.5% on OPPORTUNITY, and 95.2% (40/42) on Smart Home drift. Sensitivity analysis (OAT sweeps + Sobol indices): 3 of 10 parameters are HIGH sensitivity (min acceptable rate: 24pp recall variation; outlier IQR multiplier: 30pp precision range; conformance threshold: 21.7pp), bootstrap CI of 16.3pp impact gap between critical and stable parameters. Explainability proxies: explanation completeness 89.4%, interpretability gain 0.648, actionability gain 0.566, semantic coverage 92.0%, chain strength 0.692 (r=0.96 with confidence). No injected synthetic anomalies were used. Importantly, there is no baseline system comparison — statistics test against a fixed 50% baseline, not against competing methods — so these numbers establish feasibility, not superiority. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (quality-metadata-preserving pipeline extension with probabilistic backtracking from process deviations to sensor origins) plus an ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION/template contribution for explainability. The genuinely new element is the pipeline-spanning linkage — prior uncertainty work (Pegoraro et al., Lepsien et al.) and root-cause work (eRooMiner) each operate on only one side. The Bayesian machinery itself is standard (Bayes' theorem with hand-set priors and heuristic evidence functions), and the explanation template synthesizes known explainability guidance; the paper honestly labels its 'causal chain' as probabilistic support rather than causal inference. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present in the form of a structured sensitivity analysis (10 parameters, OAT + Sobol classification, bootstrap CIs), though Sobol analysis did not converge for two parameters (N=1000 samples, flagged). Statistical testing is consistent (α=0.05, t-tests, binomial, Mann-Whitney U, bootstrap) but with only 5 datasets, degrees of freedom of 4, and a trivially low 50% baseline for the t-tests. Code is open source at github.com/chimenkamp/LIQUID with the template published. Methodological concerns: (1) no comparison baseline against eRooMiner or any competing attribution method despite citing it as the nearest prior; (2) ground truth GT2 relies on expert annotations that may be the authors' own (ambiguity acknowledged); (3) attribution accuracy counts matches within ±1 abstraction level, a lenient criterion; (4) the explainability evaluation uses author-defined proxy metrics (interpretability/actionability 'gains') with no user study — the numbers validate the artifact's internal consistency, not human understanding. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (implemented Python pipeline, evaluated on real datasets) with a SYSTEMS artifact component (open-source tool + explanation template). - Practical: Runs in Python on standard hardware with public datasets; the main deployment prerequisite is domain knowledge to set priors and calibrate evidence-function thresholds per sensor type. - Efficient: Not stated — no runtime, memory, or throughput figures are reported despite datasets up to 96.3M readings. - Effective: Evidence shows correct attribution to documented sensor faults on real data, but effectiveness for the human-facing goal (analysts acting on explanations) is unproven without a user study; only proxy metrics are measured. - Scalable: Only claimed implicitly — the largest dataset (Hydraulic Systems, 96.3M readings) was processed, but no scaling behavior, runtime curves, or cost analysis at 10×–100× scale is provided. The work delivers a real software artifact (open-source Python pipeline and reusable explanation template), not just a paper. Strengths: - The core reframing — treat data quality metadata as first-class evidence carried through the entire abstraction pipeline rather than cleaned away — is a genuinely useful architectural idea that connects two literatures (IoT data quality patterns and process mining uncertainty) that previously stopped at the pipeline boundary. - Evaluation on five heterogeneous, public, real-world IoT datasets (industrial, wearable, environmental, smart home) with no synthetic anomaly injection, and correctness anchored to externally documented defects in at least one dataset (Hydraulic degradation states), strengthens the feasibility claim. - The sensitivity analysis is unusually disciplined for this venue: parameter classification via Sobol indices, bootstrap CIs separating critical from stable parameters, and explicit identification of the three parameters requiring per-deployment calibration. - Intellectual honesty: the paper explicitly disclaims formal causality, reports non-converged Sobol analyses, and acknowledges the absence of human evaluation — rare candor. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly, which is a credibility positive. They state: expert annotations may be ambiguous; priors and evidence functions influence confidence values; LIQUID yields plausible explanatory chains, not experimental causality; no human assessors rated the explanations, so perceived interpretability/actionability is unestablished; the five datasets cannot represent all deployments; the method requires raw sensor access, a documented abstraction pipeline, and domain knowledge; evidence-function thresholds need sensor-specific calibration and are unverified on unseen sensor types; and the approach is unsuitable for event logs without raw data or deviations without observable sensor segments. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No head-to-head comparison with any alternative — including eRooMiner, which the paper itself positions as the nearest approach — so the reported accuracies cannot be interpreted as an advance over existing root-cause methods; the 50% statistical baseline is trivial. - The t-tests use dataset-level means (N=5) against a fixed baseline; with such a weak null and small N, the significance testing adds little discriminative power, and per-dataset variance (attribution 78.5% to 95.2%) is glossed over in the aggregate. - GT2 expert annotations risk circularity: the pattern catalog P1–P6 motivating the detection rules is from a co-author group (Bertrand et al.), and annotation provenance/independence is not stated. - The chain-strength independence assumption (multiplying per-stage probabilities) is presented without justification, and the reported chain-strength figures are inconsistent in magnitude across sections (0.81 in EG1, 0.53 mean in EG3, 0.692 in the statistical validation), which is never reconciled. - The '±1 abstraction level' attribution criterion could inflate accuracy by crediting near-miss locations as correct; sensitivity of results to this leniency is not tested. Bottom Line: A credible, well-executed, and honestly reported design-science contribution that establishes a new and useful pattern for tracing conformance deviations to sensor faults, but a practitioner should read it for the architectural idea and open-source artifact rather than as evidence of a validated advantage over existing root-cause analysis tools — no such comparison exists yet.

Protocode: Prototype-Driven Interpretability for Code Generation in LLMs

BK Vamshi, H Yang · aclanthology.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Protocode, a two-stage framework that selects in-context learning (ICL) demonstrations for LLM code generation via manifold-aware prototype sampling and evaluates retrieval quality through both pass@k correctness and AST-grounded interpretability alignment. - Why it's important: Poorly chosen ICL demonstrations can degrade code-generation performance below zero-shot levels, and existing retrieval and interpretability methods are evaluated in isolation from each other, so practitioners lack a way to pick demonstrations that improve both correctness and explainability. - How it does it: A small network is trained jointly with a Proxy-Anchor loss (learnable per-class proxies, momentum-updated) and a piecewise-linear manifold point-to-point loss on target-model embeddings; learned proxies are mapped to nearest training instances as prototypes, and token-level influence is computed as the gradient of cosine similarity between token representations and the averaged prototype representation, replacing token probabilities inside the ASTrust AST-analysis pipeline. - The good: Evaluation across 8 models (1B–14B) with a broad baseline set (zero-shot, KNN, clustering, MBPP-ICL, EPR, Ada-ICL, Random, BM25), a loss ablation isolating the manifold objective (+2–4 points), and a genuinely independent causal validation via AST mutation testing (AUC 0.52–0.68) that goes beyond correlational interpretability claims. - The missing: All functional-correctness evaluation is on a single benchmark pair (MBPP/MBPP+, Python-only, single-turn function completion), and the headline interpretation mechanism is only moderately faithful (mutation-testing AUC as low as 0.52), so the interpretability contribution rests on a weak signal. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers working on ICL demonstration selection or code-specific interpretability who want a template for coupling retrieval with attribution; practitioners building production coding assistants can skip it, since the method requires target-model hidden states and was not evaluated beyond MBPP.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (62) is the relative strength — the mutation-testing causal validation and 5-seed appendix ablations exceed area norms — but it is capped by MBPP/MBPP+-only evaluation, headline tables without error bars, no code release, and an unverified fine-tuning comparison. Novelty (55) is a competent recombination of Proxy-Anchor, manifold learning, and ASTrust rather than a new formulation, and Non-Obviousness (58) is moderate since coupling retrieval to attribution is a plausible next step, not a surprise. Completeness (58) benefits from the honest limitations section but is dragged by the single-benchmark evidence and the Goodhart-adjacent reliance on the paper's own AST-confidence metric. Practical Impact (42) is low: no artifact and a hard dependency on target-model hidden states. Weighted composite: 0.20*55 + 0.25*62 + 0.15*58 + 0.15*58 + 0.15*52 + 0.10*42 = 56.

Problem & Motivation: Teams relying on LLM code generation (the paper cites Cursor, Windsurf, and big-tech adoption) face suboptimal or insecure generated code, and two communities address this separately: ICL demonstration-selection methods optimize retrieval quality (or hurt performance when badly chosen, per Rodriguez-Cardenas et al.'s causal evidence of ±3–5% ATE), while code-interpretability methods like ASTrust analyze generated code in isolation from retrieval, at the cost of storing full vocabulary distributions at every decoding step. The gap is that no framework links the quality of retrieved demonstrations to syntax-grounded explanations of the generated code, so neither retrieval quality nor explanation quality can be assessed jointly. Key Idea: Replace token-probability confidence in AST-based code interpretability with prototype-conditioned attribution — the gradient magnitude of the cosine similarity between a generated token's latent representation and the average representation of the retrieved prototypes — and generate those prototypes themselves with a joint manifold-learning (piecewise-linear local PCA neighborhoods) plus metric-learning (Proxy-Anchor with momentum-updated proxies) objective so that retrieved demonstrations respect the target model's own representation geometry. Methodology: Stage 1 (offline, per target LLM): prompts from Magicoder-OSS-Instruct-75K (75K examples, 9 programming languages as classes) are embedded by the target LLM; a single-layer network hθ (Linear → InstanceNorm → ReLU) is trained 200 epochs minimizing L_total = L_PA + L_manifold. L_PA is a Proxy-Anchor loss with Euclidean distance, learnable proxies θ_q (backprop) and momentum proxies θ_m (θ_k ← γθ_k + (1−γ)θ_q, γ=0.99). L_manifold is a point-to-point regression loss matching learned Euclidean distances to manifold similarities s(z_i,z_j) built from orthogonal and projected distances to m-dimensional (m=3) local linear submanifolds fit by PCA with a 90% reconstruction threshold. After training, each momentum proxy is mapped to its nearest training instance, yielding one prototype per class (9 total). Stage 2: prototypes are used as ICL demonstrations for MBPP/MBPP+ completion; token confidence for AST analysis is ||∂cos(z_wi, z_a)/∂z_wi||₂, where z_a is the mean prototype representation; tokens are aligned to terminal AST nodes, aggregated to non-terminals, and grouped into 8 manually defined syntax categories. Critical design decisions: (1) one demonstration per class with fixed class-wise ordering across all methods — well-justified as confound control; (2) replacing full-vocabulary probability storage with gradient-based prototype attribution — motivated by ASTrust's memory scaling problem but validated only weakly (mutation AUC 0.52–0.68); (3) model-specific retriever training on target-model hidden states — central to why it works, but a deployment constraint the authors acknowledge. The claimed 'on par with fine-tuning' efficiency comparison (Appendix B.2) is not backed by any reported fine-tuning experiment. Key Results: On MBPP/MBPP+ (EvalPlus, unbiased P@k estimator) across 6 small models plus CodeLlama-13B and Qwen2.5-Coder-14B, Protocode wins every model/metric cell against zero-shot, Clustering, MBPP-ICL, KNN, EPR, and Ada-ICL. Representative numbers: CodeLlama-7B MBPP P@1 0.228 vs zero-shot 0.159, EPR 0.205, Ada-ICL 0.183 (P@10 0.526 vs 0.497); Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B MBPP P@1 0.308 vs 0.233 zero-shot; Qwen2.5-Coder-14B MBPP P@1 0.645 vs 0.564 zero-shot and 0.620 Ada-ICL. Appendix baselines with 5-seed error bars: on Qwen3-0.6B MBPP P@10, Random 0.346±0.022 and BM25 0.349±0.022 vs Ours 0.495±0.017. Protocode also achieves the highest mean AST confidence for all 6 models (e.g., 0.675 for CodeLlama-7B vs 0.644 Ada-ICL), tracking the P@10 ranking. Causal mutation validation: Protocode attribution predicts pass→fail flips with AUC 0.52–0.68 (vs 0.52–0.64 for ASTrust token probabilities), combined 0.62–0.73. Loss ablation (5 seeds): removing the manifold loss costs ~2–4 points on every model. Scale: 1B–14B models on a single RTX A6000 (~2h, 4.7 GB for selector training). Notably, distance-based ICL selection (KNN, MBPP-ICL) sometimes underperforms zero-shot, confirming prior causal findings that bad demonstrations hurt. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely new elements are (a) the prototype-conditioned attribution score that substitutes for token probabilities in the ASTrust pipeline, connecting retrieval to syntax-grounded explanation, and (b) the demonstration that retrieval quality correlates with AST-confidence alignment. The components themselves are standard: Proxy-Anchor loss, momentum updates (MoCo), local PCA manifolds, and the AST analysis framework are all borrowed; the joint manifold+metric objective and the 9-language class structure are competent recombinations applied to a new setting (ICL selection for code). Rigor & Reproducibility: Above average for this area. Ablations are present and informative: the manifold-objective ablation (Table 9, 5 seeds, mean±std), extensive hyperparameter sweeps (m, γ, N_α, N_β, T, δ, α, ε) on two models, Random/BM25 naive baselines with error bars, and an unusually rigorous causal validation via grammar-preserving mutation testing with coverage-traced nodes — this directly addresses the usual circularity of interpretability claims. Confound control (identical demonstration count, ordering, truncation across methods) is explicit, and the authors honestly flag that their zero-shot numbers differ from official technical reports, attributing it to decoding parameters. Concerns: Table 1 (the headline results) reports single numbers without seeds or significance tests; all functional evaluation is on MBPP/MBPP+ developed and evaluated in the same narrow setting; the interpretability claim is evaluated largely on the authors' own alignment metric; no code, data, or model release URL is mentioned; and the 'competitive with fine-tuning' claim has no supporting table. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: Yes — the entire selector trains on a single RTX A6000 (~4.7 GB peak), and inference uses only text demonstrations. Efficient: Selector training is ~2 hours parallelized per target model; at inference it adds no cost over any ICL method, and avoids ASTrust's per-step vocabulary-storage overhead. Effective: The evidence shows it improves P@1/P@10 and AST confidence on MBPP/MBPP+ — a single-turn, function-level, Python-only proxy for the code-assistant scenarios motivating the paper; effectiveness in repository-scale or multi-turn settings is untested. Scalable: Tested up to 14B parameters with consistent gains, but scaling requires retraining the selector per model on that model's hidden states, which is infeasible for API-only models (Codex, Claude Code) — the authors state this constraint directly. Deliverable status: paper only; no library, tool, dataset, or trained-model artifact is reported as released. Strengths: - The causal validation via mutation testing (Table 6) is the paper's standout: constructing pass/fail flip labels independent of both attribution mechanisms and reporting honest AUCs (0.52–0.68) rather than only correlational agreement is rare in interpretability-for-code work and strengthens the faithfulness claim beyond what most reviewers see. - The unified retrieval-plus-interpretability evaluation (Table 2) demonstrates an actual empirical finding — AST confidence tracks P@10 ranking across all six models — rather than merely asserting the connection. - Careful experimental hygiene: confound-controlled prompts across all ICL methods, naive Random/BM25 baselines with 5-seed error bars, a loss ablation showing the manifold objective contributes a consistent 2–4 points, and transparent discussion of why their zero-shot scores diverge from vendor reports. - The honest deployment analysis in the limitations section — explicitly noting the hidden-state requirement excludes API-only models and proposing (but not running) a cross-model transfer experiment — is a credibility positive. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that (1) prototypes come only from Magicoder, with cross-dataset ranking left to future work; (2) model instability is a real issue — Llama3.2 is highly hyperparameter-sensitive with inconsistent P@k results while Qwen2.5-Coder is stable; (3) the causal mutation validation covers only type/arity-compatible substitutions on test-executed nodes, with AUC 0.52–0.68 being 'far from a complete predictor'; (4) the method requires target-model internal representations and cannot apply to API-only systems (Codex, Claude Code) as-is; and (5) evaluation is single-turn, function-level MBPP/MBPP+, not the multi-file, multi-turn agentic setting. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — a strong credibility signal. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Single-benchmark evaluation: every headline number is MBPP/MBPP+ (Python-only, 378 test problems); no HumanEval, MultiPL-E, or cross-language test, despite the method being motivated by 9-language prototypes and the cross-language transfer claim (language-specific manifolds as carriers of 'broader program semantics') being asserted, not tested. - Headline Table 1 lacks error bars or seed counts (error bars appear only in appendix tables), so the margin over EPR/Ada-ICL on some rows (e.g., 0.526 vs 0.490 P@10) cannot be assessed for significance. - The fine-tuning comparison in Appendix B.2 ('performance on par with fine-tuning') is a claim with no reported experiment. - The interpretability contribution is validated against AST confidence — a metric the method directly optimizes proxies toward — creating mild Goodhart risk; the mutation-based AUC (as low as 0.52 for Llama3.2) suggests the attribution signal is weak in absolute terms, which the authors quantify but do not dwell on. - The 8 syntax categories are manually defined for Python only; no evidence the framework transfers to other languages' ASTs. - No code or artifact release is mentioned, limiting reproducibility of the multi-stage pipeline. Bottom Line: A rigorously validated but narrowly evaluated contribution — the retrieval-interpretable coupling and mutation-based validation are genuinely worth studying for ICL-selection and code-interpretability researchers, but the method's dependence on target-model hidden states and its MBPP-only, single-turn evidence mean practitioners building real coding assistants will find stronger, more generalizable alternatives elsewhere.

PyRUA-REAL: Robot Exploration and Adaptive Learning through RSI in the Real World

Q Wang, J Bi, S Jiang, R Si, W Huang, K Chen, J Li… · arxiv.org · recursive self-improvement - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces PyRUA-REAL, a dual-agent (researcher/engineer) coding framework in which LLM agents iteratively explore, diagnose, and refine robot manipulation programs on a physical dual-arm Franka platform, retaining experience in a three-level persistent repository (facts, memory, implementations) so that refined programs can be frozen and deployed without runtime LLM calls. - Why it's important: Online LLM-driven robot control is slow and expensive because agent inference dominates execution time (63–90% of recorded online run time here); converting exploration into agent-free executable programs targets the gap between capable-but-latent coding agents and deployable robot skills. - How it does it: A researcher agent selects objectives and stopping criteria while an engineer agent implements, tests, and revises code against live execution feedback, with all findings, failures, and reusable primitives persisted across tasks and improvement cycles while foundation-model parameters stay fixed. - The good: The paper traces full development histories (e.g., stacking placement error dropping from 2.69 to 0.44 mm and cycle time from 285 to 156 s across 33 revisions) and quantifies the deployment payoff honestly, including reporting that Ethernet insertion never reached agent-free execution after 240 hours. - The missing: Nearly every headline comparison is confounded or unreplicated — the RoboDojo baselines come from a leaderboard snapshot with unspecified seeds, key studies use a single development session per condition, and placement-precision numbers are visual estimates rather than physical measurements. - Read it or not: Worth reading for robotics and agentic-systems researchers building real-world self-improving systems, because its honest negative results (reviewer agents slow exploration, offline programs fail on contact-rich tasks, human input shapes acquired skills) are more useful than the headline success rates.
Why this rank

Rigor (42) is the binding weakness: single-session comparisons, confounded ablations, leaderboard numbers under unspecified seeds, a numeric inconsistency (84.4/84.82/84.42) for the headline result, and no code or data release. Novelty (50) is a competent combination of known ideas (memory hierarchies, code-as-policy, frozen deployment) rather than a new formulation. The paper's real value shows in Non-Obviousness (65) — the honest findings that reviewer agents slow exploration, that Ethernet insertion fails entirely after 240 hours, and that humans covertly shape acquired skills are genuinely informative — and in Completeness (75), which confronts limitations more directly than nearly any peer. Problem & Motivation: LLM coding agents can generate robot control code, but two open questions remain: (1) can agents turn physical interaction experience into capabilities that persist and improve across attempts (embodied recursive self-improvement, RSI), and (2) can the resulting programs run efficiently without repeated online LLM calls? Prior embodied-RSI work largely operates in simulation or uses the real robot only as a final validation step. Practitioners deploying robots face a tension: online agent control is flexible but introduces latency and cost, while frozen programs may not cover execution-time situations. The paper targets labs and engineers who want self-improving robot skills on real hardware without fine-tuning foundation models. Key Idea: The core move is structuring embodied RSI as a two-agent division of labor — a researcher agent that owns task-level strategy, experiment objectives, and stopping criteria, and an engineer agent that owns implementation, physical trials, and local diagnosis — connected through a three-level persistent experience repository (L0 environmental facts, L1 problem-solving memory, L2 reusable code) so that improvements persist as executable skills rather than model updates. Freezing the resulting program for agent-free deployment is the second half of the idea. Methodology: The system receives a human goal plus a task specification (objects, positions, orientations, variants). In the improvement loop, the researcher defines an experiment (objective, stopping criteria, relevant retrieved experience); the engineer generates/edits a task program (perceive/plan/control, optionally calling locally deployed SigLIP and SAM for perception), runs physical trials on the dual-arm Franka platform, diagnoses failures from frames, states, and logs, and returns a structured report. The researcher then either continues local refinement or redirects at task level. Execution is a frozen program using live observations with no runtime LLM calls. The formal objective (Eq. 3) maximizes expected task performance J(π) subject to interaction and compute budgets. Critical design decisions: (1) researcher/engineer split — motivated by observed deadlocks but the reviewer-agent ablation actually shows added coordination can hurt (median trial interval 16.9 vs 3.4 min), so the coordination design is only partially justified; (2) three-level experience hierarchy — plausible but its retrieval/adaptation policy is never ablated as a whole; (3) offline freezing of programs — justified by the deployment-time comparisons in Section 4.8. Key Results: Real-world: across eight dual-arm Franka tasks (tic-tac-toe, five-block stacking, Tower of Hanoi, Ethernet insertion, towel folding, Push T, block sorting, block storage), development success ranges 91.67–100% for the seven tasks solved agent-free (abstract average 91.1%); time to first success spans 1.5 h (block storage) to 45 h (Push T); Ethernet insertion got 0% agent-free after ~240 h and 58.82% with online assistance. Continued improvement: stacking cycle time 285.3→156.0 s, lateral error 2.69→0.44 mm (visual estimates), angular error 1.37°→0.25°; tic-tac-toe jumped 50%→100% after a motion-strategy change; Hanoi shifted from reliability (1402 s cycles at 60%) to speed (793 s at 100%). RoboDojo (42 tasks, 5 capability groups): 84.42% capability-averaged success vs 50.35% for PyRUA-Lean and 22.48% for GPT-6-Astra (leaderboard snapshot, seeds unspecified); Generalization is actually lower than PyRUA-Lean (41.17% vs 43.17%). Feedback study: video+joint feedback (BVJ) reaches 54.2% mean success vs 15.3% for outcome-only (B) at lower optimizer time (25.4 vs 31.8 min), but each condition uses a single session. Explicit variation specs: +11.4 to +36.6 pp on held-out layouts (confounded with extra exploration). Skill-library transfer: 40.0% vs 21.3% mean success on eight new tasks. Deployment: frozen programs are 4.6–5.0× faster than online coding (PyRUA-Lean) and 9.9–11.5× faster than direct online action inference (GPT-6-Astra); neither online baseline finished Hanoi within 120 minutes. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDINGS. The genuinely novel element is the end-to-end real-world RSI pipeline — exploration, improvement beyond first success, and deployment-efficiency analysis on physical hardware with persistent multi-level experience — rather than any single algorithmic component. The researcher/engineer split, experience memory, code-as-policy, and frozen-program deployment are each known ideas (Reflexion/ExpeL-style memory, STOP/ADAS-style code self-modification, Code as Policies); the contribution is their combination and the empirical characterization of when real-world RSI works, stalls, and fails. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper is unusually candid about confounds: it flags that reassessment timelines don't isolate the reviewer effect, that the variation-spec comparison includes extra exploration, that BS feedback has privileged ground-truth state access, and that placement errors are visual estimates. However: there is essentially no multi-seed replication — the feedback study uses one session per task–condition pair (authors state session variability 'remains unmeasured'); the RoboDojo comparison mixes their seed-0 self-run with reported leaderboard numbers whose seeds are unspecified and, for the baseline PyRUA-Lean, from its official evaluation — not matched conditions; success-rate trajectories aggregate development attempts, not independent tests of a fixed program; and there is a numeric inconsistency between 84.4% (abstract), 84.82% (Section 1), and 84.42% (figures/tables) for the same RoboDojo result. Ablations of sorts exist (feedback interface conditions, with/without reviewer, with/without skill library, with/without variation specs), but each is a small, partially confounded comparison. No code, data, or model release is stated; only a project page URL (https://dagroup-pku.github.io/PyRUA-Lean/real/). Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS with an EMPIRICAL evaluation program. - Practical: Yes — runs on commercially available hardware (two Franka Research 3 arms, Robotiq-85 grippers, ZED Mini and RealSense D405 cameras) with off-the-shelf perception models (SigLIP, SAM) deployable locally. - Efficient: At deployment the frozen programs are cheap and fast (e.g., 2.99-min stacking cycles, zero LLM calls), but the development cost is large — 1.5 to 45+ hours of physical exploration per task, and 240 hours without success on Ethernet insertion. - Effective: Effective on 7 of 8 real tasks and on precision/long-horizon RoboDojo groups, but the evidence is development-record success rather than controlled post-freeze reliability testing, and the precision numbers are visual estimates rather than measured accuracy. - Scalable: Not tested — a second task's experience repository, a different robot, or 100-task transfer is unexamined; the transfer study covers only 8 tasks with one comparison each. The work delivers a framework and extensive development records; no code library, dataset, or trained weights are stated as released. Strengths: - Honest negative results embedded in a systems paper: the reviewer-agent slowdown (16.9 vs 3.4 min per trial), the total failure of agent-free Ethernet insertion after 240 hours, and the documentation of human interventions (e.g., suggesting SigLIP) that the agents would not have found themselves — these directly challenge the narrative that RSI is uniformly autonomous and beneficial. - The deployment-time analysis cleanly decomposes online latency: agent thinking accounts for 63–90% of online execution time, and PyRUA-Lean's non-agent time on stacking (3.1 min) is close to the frozen program's 2.99-min cycle — a well-constructed attribution. - Development-history tracing (success, cycle time, and placement error across up to 33 program revisions, with regressions shown) is a genuine empirical contribution; most RSI papers report only before/after numbers. - The feedback-interface study (8 conditions, 576 test executions, cost accounting in optimizer time and tokens, including the OLS fit R²=0.691 between success and development cost) is a more careful protocol than typical agentic-robotics evaluations, despite its single-session limitation. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state that: Ethernet insertion requires online assistance and frozen programs can't cover every execution-time situation; the reviewer-effect insertion timeline doesn't isolate the reviewer's impact (sequential phases); the variation-spec gains are confounded with additional exploration; placement errors are visual estimates, not independent physical measurements; BS feedback uses privileged ground-truth diagnostics; the feedback study has one session per task–condition pair so session variability is unmeasured; RoboDojo comparisons are reported results with different/unspecified seeds; human assistance shaped acquired skills and 'reports of autonomous improvement should document what humans contributed'; and method selection can bottleneck self-improvement. This is a paper that confronts its limitations directly — a substantial credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The central claim — accumulated experience enables sustained improvement — is supported only by observational development histories on three tasks; there is no controlled with/without-memory run of the full real-world pipeline, so H1 rests on trajectory plots rather than an ablation. - The 91.1% headline 'development success' aggregates attempts across program revisions; the frozen-program reliability on the physical tasks is never characterized with a fixed-program test battery (contrast with the careful RoboDojo protocol), so real-world deployment reliability is essentially unevaluated. - The skill-library transfer study (H5) has no description of how the library was selected, no baseline for a generic prompt-only skill hint, and per-task gains from single comparisons with no variance estimates. - The RoboDojo leaderboard comparison compares a self-run against other teams' reported numbers under uncontrolled seeds and possibly different evaluation pipelines — the strongest headline number (84.42%) is the least controlled. - The arXiv preprint's numeric inconsistency (84.4% / 84.82% / 84.42% for the same result) was not caught in proofing, which matters for a paper whose value is empirical precision. - Compute cost of development (total tokens, wall-clock agent time across the full 8-task campaign) is reported per-study but never totaled, making the exploration budget for a new task hard to estimate. Bottom Line: A practitioner building real-robot self-improving agent systems gains a lot from the honest process-level findings and deployment-cost analysis here — this is one of the few papers that documents how embodied RSI stalls, what humans covertly contribute, and what frozen programs still cannot do — even though the headline benchmark numbers are weaker evidence than the case studies and no stronger alternative currently covers this ground in the real world.

Formalizing Patient-Set Semantics for OMOP CDM-Based Clinical Trial Feasibility Assessment: A Neuro- Symbolic Methodology for Traceable Site-Feasibility Patient …

S Jeon · arxiv.org · neural symbolic - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces NS-CoT, a neuro-symbolic framework that transforms natural-language clinical trial feasibility criteria into declared, executable patient-set semantics over OMOP CDM, and proposes an evaluation paradigm that measures semantic fidelity at the levels of counts, patient sets, failure localization, and downstream site-feasibility decisions rather than SQL executability alone. - Why it's important: Site-feasibility patient-count estimates drive site selection and recruitment planning, yet are often based on investigator guesswork because converting free-text eligibility criteria into trustworthy, reviewable cohort logic over standardized research data remains a major informatics bottleneck (prior work reports only ~51% of trial criteria fully implementable in ATLAS and 21-50% hallucination rates for GPT-4-generated OMOP SQL). - How it does it: The core move is an architectural separation — an LLM only performs typed semantic decomposition of criteria into an intermediate representation, while deterministic symbolic modules handle OMOP vocabulary grounding, descendant expansion, local executability filtering, single-anchor temporal predicates, anchor-bound exclusions, patient-set algebra, and CTE-chain SQL compilation, producing provenance traces for every count. - The good: The layered evaluation construct itself — verifying that equal counts denote equal person sets, that failures localize to specific transformation stages, and that site rankings and feasibility labels are preserved across OMOP schemas — is a genuinely reusable contribution, and person-set verification empirically confirms that count agreement tracks patient-set agreement. - The missing: Evaluation rests largely on author-constructed benchmark environments (SYN-SNUH synthetic data, CQ-Bench designed around the framework's emphasized semantics, COVIC simulation with reference-defined labels), and the provided text contains no comparison against the closest published systems (Criteria2Query 3.0, LeafAI), no reported error bars or multi-seed variance, and no public code release. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on OMOP cohort tooling, trial feasibility automation, or neuro-symbolic clinical NLP pipelines — the formalization and evaluation paradigm are transferable; skip it if you want end-to-end quantitative head-to-head results against state-of-the-art baselines, which the framework chapters only partially deliver.

Problem & Motivation: Sponsors and CROs assess candidate trial sites via questionnaires that ask for counts of potentially protocol-eligible patients; these estimates are typically produced from investigator experience because direct EHR querying faces privacy, governance, and heterogeneity barriers. Even where institutional OMOP CDM instances exist, the free-text inclusion/exclusion criteria behind feasibility questions cannot be executed directly: they require commitments about standard concepts, descendant expansion, domain-table routing, temporal anchors, observation windows, proxy variables, and exclusion scope. The paper argues that framing this as text-to-SQL is incomplete — a query may execute while encoding an unintended interpretation (unscoped negation instead of anchor-bound absence, wrong domain routing, missing hierarchy expansion), yielding a count that is not interpretable as feasibility evidence. The target users are clinical research informaticians, data teams at trial sites, and sponsors needing reproducible, evidence-based site counts. Key Idea: Treat a feasibility patient count not as a database output or a hidden true cohort, but as the cardinality of a declared executable patient-set semantics — an explicit, reviewable intermediate object (typed IR → grounded concept sets → patient-set algebra → deterministic SQL) to which the final count is accountable. Once clinical meaning is externalized as this computable object, fidelity can be measured in layers (count, person set, trace, decision impact), and the LLM is confined to interpretation while execution semantics are fixed symbolically. Methodology: The pipeline is formalized as q →(Φ) IR_q →(G) IR_g →(𝒜) h_q →(Compile_θ) SQL_q →(Exec_D) C_q(D), with count = |C_q(D)|. Φ is LLM-mediated: it decomposes criteria into typed facts (domain, mention, role, polarity, temporal cues, value/unit constraints) using reasoning-structured prompts; the author explicitly distinguishes this from free-form chain-of-thought. G performs OMOP standard-vocabulary grounding, descendant expansion, drug-mention subtype routing, and local CDM-aware executable concept filtering (separating vocabulary validity from local data availability). 𝒜 composes grounded facts through a patient-set algebra (REQUIRE, FORBID, GROUP_AND, GROUP_OR) over persons with valid observation periods; exclusions are anchor-bound temporal absences compiled to correlated NOT EXISTS rather than unscoped negation. Compile_θ is deterministic CTE-chain SQL generation parameterized by compiler version, dialect, and vocabulary snapshot. Output artifacts link each count to concept sets, temporal specs, exclusion logic, SQL, execution traces, and intermediate cohorts. Critical design decisions: (1) LLM restricted to the IR boundary — well-motivated by cited evidence of LLM hallucination in OMOP SQL; (2) anchor-bound (scoped) exclusion semantics — well-justified as the main failure mode of direct SQL generation; (3) restriction to single-anchor temporal predicates and primary Condition/Drug domains — stated as a deliberate scope boundary but limits coverage of multi-step temporal logic common in real protocols. Key Results: The provided text (abstract, introduction, related work, and part of Chapter 3) does not include the headline numeric tables from Chapter 5; quantitative claims available are directional. The abstract reports that NS-CoT shows higher count fidelity on temporal-inclusion and anchor-bound exclusion queries in CQ-Bench and comparable fidelity on template-derived FOEM queries; person-set verification confirmed exact count agreement corresponded to underlying patient-set agreement; and in the COVIC multi-schema simulation, intermediate artifacts enabled failure localization, targeted second-pass repair, and improved preservation of counts, patient sets, and site rankings, with comparisons against FastOMOP for criterion-site fidelity and site-ranking preservation (McNemar's test for paired comparisons, AUROC/AUPRC for site-feasibility discrimination, rank correlation for site ordering). Contextual baselines from related work: CriteriaMapper normalized only 57.3% of 640 unique criteria attributes; Blasini et al. found only 51% of 223 criteria fully implementable in ATLAS; GPT-4 OMOP SQL systems exhibit 21-50% hallucination rates. Benchmarks: CQ-Bench (semantic strata), FOEM (external template-derived queries), COVIC (multi-schema, multi-site simulation on SYN-SNUH-derived environments), plus protocol-derived case studies. Whether baselines are current and strong cannot be fully assessed from the provided text; FastOMOP is the only named empirical comparator, and LeafAI/Criteria2Query 3.0 are discussed as related work but not compared against empirically in the excerpt. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION and NEW SYSTEM/TOOL with a NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING component. The genuinely novel elements are (a) the reframing of feasibility counting as declared, reviewable patient-set semantics rather than SQL generation, and (b) the layered decision-preservation evaluation construct (count → person-set → trace → site ranking). The neuro-symbolic split (LLM parsing into a typed IR, symbolic compilation to SQL) is a known architectural pattern applied to a new domain; the patient-set algebra, anchor-bound exclusion compilation, and OMOP grounding machinery are competent combinations of established OMOP/cohort-definition concepts. Rigor & Reproducibility: The evaluation design is unusually structured: paired query-level comparisons with McNemar's test, person-set exactness checks beyond count agreement, ablation-style stratification of CQ-Bench by semantic complexity, first-pass vs. second-pass repair comparison (Table 24), and multi-schema robustness in COVIC. The provided excerpt does not state error bars, multiple LLM seeds, or code/data availability (a reference implementation and runtime configuration are described in Sections 3.9-3.10, but no repository URL appears in the provided pages). Methodological concerns: (1) the primary benchmarks (CQ-Bench) are constructed around the semantic components the framework is designed to emphasize, creating a potential Goodhart/circularity risk partially mitigated by the external FOEM benchmark; (2) the evaluation environment is synthetic (SYN-SNUH), so local-data-realism effects are simulated rather than observed; (3) semantic fidelity is defined relative to author-declared executable references, not chart-reviewed clinical truth — the authors acknowledge this explicitly, which is honest but means the evaluation target is functional fidelity, not clinical validity. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a built framework with system-level evaluation; SYSTEMS elements via trace artifacts). - Practical: Requires an institutional OMOP CDM instance plus an LLM backend, both commercially available, though local governance constraints apply. - Efficient: Not stated — no compute, latency, or cost comparison against direct text-to-SQL or manual curation appears in the provided text. - Effective: Evidence shows fidelity to declared executable reference semantics and preservation of reference-defined feasibility labels in simulation; it does not show chart-reviewed clinical validity or prospective recruitment utility, which the authors explicitly exclude. - Scalable: Tested across multiple OMOP schemas and a multi-site simulation; behavior at 10-100× scale (many sites, full protocol criterion sets, real multi-institution networks) is claimed as motivation but not tested. Deliverable: a described reference implementation and methodology paper; no public artifact URL is stated in the provided text, so it effectively stops at paper form plus internal tooling. Strengths: - The conceptual reframing — a feasibility count is the cardinality of a declared patient-set semantics, not a discovered truth — cleanly resolves why count accuracy is ill-defined without prior interpretive commitment, and this argument is well-supported by concrete OMOP examples ("diabetes on insulin therapy" admitting distinct executable interpretations). - Person-set verification is a real methodological advance over count-only evaluation: it exposes that identical counts can denote different cohorts, and the paper operationalizes this rather than merely asserting it. - The scoped/anchor-bound exclusion semantics (correlated NOT EXISTS vs. unscoped negation) addresses a documented, concrete failure mode of LLM-generated OMOP SQL rather than a strawman. - The decision-preservation evaluation (site-feasibility label AUROC/AUPRC, rank correlation) connects cohort fidelity to the actual operational use of the count, a transferable measurement construct independent of this particular system. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors are unusually direct: the framework supports only OMOP-expressible criteria representable in structured fields, with primary empirical scope on Condition and Drug domains; temporal semantics are limited to single-anchor predicates (no multi-anchor sequential chains); criteria requiring unstructured notes, imaging, subjective judgment, or unavailable local data are out of scope; proxy selection is made explicit but not solved; semantic fidelity is not chart-reviewed clinical validity; no regulatory compliance (FDA 21 CFR Part 11) is claimed — trace artifacts are research provenance, not legal audit trails; and no claim is made that NS-CoT is universally more accurate than existing systems. This candid boundary-drawing is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Evaluation environment circularity: SYN-SNUH is synthetic and CQ-Bench strata emphasize exactly the semantics (temporal anchoring, anchor-bound exclusion, drug exposure) the architecture is built to preserve; the external check (FOEM) is template-derived, so performance on genuinely unstructured, real-protocol free text is shown only through qualitative case studies. - The provided text shows no empirical comparison against the closest published systems (Criteria2Query 3.0, LeafAI, Lee et al.'s GPT-4 OMOP SQL system); FastOMOP is the only named comparator, limiting the ability to attribute gains to the neuro-symbolic design versus generic IR-mediated prompting. - No sensitivity analysis over the LLM backend is visible: since Φ is LLM-mediated, results may be brittle to model choice, prompt version, or vocabulary snapshot, and reproducibility claims about determinism apply only downstream of the LLM boundary. - The COVIC "multi-site" result is a simulation against reference-defined labels, not evidence from real federated sites with heterogeneous ETL quality — the setting where the computability gap is claimed to matter most. - Single-author work with no stated code release in the provided pages makes independent verification of the trace/fidelity pipeline difficult. Bottom Line: For OMOP-facing informaticians and anyone building trial-feasibility or cohort-generation tooling, this is worth reading for its patient-set-semantics framing and layered evaluation construct, which are more durable than the NS-CoT system itself; for readers seeking a proven, benchmarked drop-in replacement for text-to-SQL cohort tools, stronger empirical head-to-head evidence against current systems will be needed first.

#170 — Moderately Innovative (54)

Video-Coder: Reinforcing Agentic Coding for Video Generation (16 ▲ )

Chaoyang Wang, Sicheng Gao, Junan Hu, Kunyang Li, Dongyang Chen, Yiyang Zhou, Huaxiu Yao, Yong Jae Lee, Radu Timofte, Yuzhang Shang · arxiv.org · Daily papers of 9 Nov 2026
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Video-Coder, a 9B multimodal coding agent trained with SFT and harness-native agentic RL (GRPO) that autonomously writes and iteratively revises Blender Python programs rendering untextured 3D "draft videos," which are then used as structure-and-motion conditioning for a downstream video generator. - Why it's important: End-to-end video diffusion models persistently violate object counts, spatial relations, and physical laws, and users cannot precisely control or reproduce scenes through prompt rewriting alone; providing an executable, verifiable 3D scene representation addresses controllability and physical plausibility at the source. - How it does it: The core move is decoupling structure/motion from appearance — the agent programs a gray-clay "white-model" render that pins geometry, layout, motion, and camera, while a frozen video generator adds appearance — trained with a dual reward (binary execution reward + VLM-judged video reward) under a time-based annealing schedule R = α·R_video + e^(−steps/T)·R_exe. - The good: The ablation study on PhyGenBench isolates every component (SFT alone 0.63, RL to 0.67, each reward removal and annealing removal degrades to 0.63–0.65), and the system transfers to an unseen backbone, lifting OmniWeaving from 0.48 to 0.51. - The missing: No error bars, seeds, or significance tests on any number; evaluation is entirely MLLM-judge-based on two physics benchmarks; the paper reports mutually inconsistent dataset sizes (SFT-6k/RL-2k in the abstract vs. SFT-10k/RL-4k in Section 4 and the conclusion) and an internally inconsistent OmniWeaving gain (0.48→0.51 described as "16.28 points"). - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building agentic RL environments with visual feedback loops or working on controllable video generation; skippable if you only need better physics in video output and can use existing conditioning pipelines like Video-CoCo or physics-simulation guidance.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (45) is the primary drag: no error bars or seeds anywhere, all evaluation is MLLM-judge-based with the RL reward judge entangled with the evaluation backbone, model-generated 'ground truth', and internal reporting inconsistencies (6k/2k vs 10k/4k dataset sizes; an OmniWeaving gain of 0.03 described as '16.28 points') that undermine reporting hygiene. Resilience (48) suffers because the value of RL training over simple test-time prompting is never established — the SFT-only baseline (0.63) already captures most of the gain over the bare generator (0.61). The white-model interface is genuinely clever (Non-Obviousness 65) and the released weights/data/code lift Impact (70), but the headline contribution rests on unverified judge scores. Problem & Motivation: Video generation models (diffusion and autoregressive) fit pixel/latent distributions without modeling 3D structure, so prompts requiring precise spatial relationships, object counts, multi-object interactions, or physically governed motion yield wrong counts, occlusion failures, implausible trajectories, and vanishing objects; generated videos are also hard to edit or reproduce. Prior code-driven approaches (3D-GPT, SceneCraft, GPT4Motion, Video-CoCo) prompt frozen LLMs in single-turn or fixed pipelines and never optimize the coding model against final video quality. The gap closed is training an agent, end-to-end through RL, whose multi-turn Blender code is optimized for the physics fidelity of the final video, not just code executability. Key Idea: Treat video generation as an agentic programming task where the verifiable intermediate representation is a standardized "white-model" render (Blender Workbench, single gray color, fixed resolution/fps) that carries only structure and motion; because this draft is cheap to render and checkable by the harness (execution feedback, content checks, sampled frames), it supplies dense RL-relevant feedback, and a dual reward with exponential annealing shifts the optimization target from "does the code run" to "does the final video match the prompt" as training proceeds. Methodology: Four-stage data pipeline: (1) LLM-rewritten scene-centric prompts filtered to exclude appearance-heavy content; (2) agentic trajectory generation where Gemini 3.8 Flash iterates write–run–revise Blender code in the harness up to T_max turns; (3) ground-truth video synthesis by feeding prompt + draft video into MiniMax-H3; (4) three-level filtering (execution validity, draft quality, prompt–video consistency judged by Seed2.0). The Video-Coder Harness provides two tools (check_script static check, run_blender execution+render), three feedback types (execution errors, content checks, visual frames), and a clean-room re-execution of the final script for acceptance. Training initializes Qwen3.5-9B, SFTs on ~6k trajectories, then runs GRPO (group size 8, up to 100 turns, 120K context, unfinished rollouts masked) with the annealed dual reward; the video generator stays frozen throughout. Critical design decisions: (a) standardized untextured rendering — well justified, since it isolates the signal the draft should convey; (b) reward annealing — supported by the ablation (fixed-weight variant drops 0.67→0.65), though the mechanistic explanation (execution reward "masking" video-reward differences) is post-hoc; (c) harness re-execution acceptance — sound engineering that guarantees reproducibility of every accepted episode. Key Results: On PhyGenBench (MLLM-judge protocol, [0,1] scale), Video-Coder-9B + MiniMax-H3 scores 0.67 average (Mechanics 0.68, Optics 0.79, Thermal 0.60, Material 0.61) vs. MiniMax-H3 alone at 0.61, Wan2.2-TI2V-5B at 0.54, Gen-3 at 0.51, Kling at 0.49, and Video-CoCo at 0.51 — first place in all four categories. On the physical dimensions of VBench-2.0, it scores 78.19% average vs. CogVideoX-1.5 at 77.04% and MiniMax-H3 at 54.58% (+23.61 points), reaching 88.67% on Mechanics but losing to CogVideoX-1.5 on Material (75.02% vs. 83.19%), a failure mode the authors attribute to the white-model discarding appearance information. Baselines are current and include both commercial systems and recent open-source models, though the strongest comparison is the paper's own backbone with and without the agent. Cross-backbone transfer is tested once (OmniWeaving 0.48→0.51). Ablations on PhyGenBench: SFT-only 0.63, full RL 0.67, −video reward 0.64, −execution reward 0.63, fixed-weight rewards 0.65. α sensitivity shows stable performance for α∈[0.5, 0.6] with slight drops at 0.4 and 0.7. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (first trained multimodal coding agent optimized via agentic RL for final video quality) combined with NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (Video-Coder Harness with visual-feedback RL environment) and NEW DATASET (two curated trajectory/video datasets). The genuinely novel elements are the harness-native RL with video-quality reward and the annealing between executable-code and video rewards; the components themselves — Blender scene programming, GRPO, VLM-judge rewards, draft-then-generate conditioning — are standard ideas recombined in a new setting, with GPT4Motion and Video-CoCo as close untrained precursors. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and well-structured, isolating SFT, each reward, and the annealing schedule, plus an α sensitivity sweep — this is a genuine strength. However, no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere, and headline gaps like 0.63→0.65 (fixed-weight vs. annealed) rest on single runs. Code, data, and models are claimed fully open-source (GitHub CYWang735/Video-Coder, HuggingFace Video-Coder). Methodological concerns: (1) all evaluation is MLLM-judge-based (GPT-4o for PhyGenBench, benchmark-native protocol for VBench-2.0), with no human study; (2) the video reward during RL is computed by Qwen3.8-omni-flash judging against a reference video generated by the same MiniMax-H3 used at test time, creating a closed loop between training signal and evaluation backbone; (3) the "ground-truth" reference videos are themselves model-generated, not real footage; (4) the paper contains internal inconsistencies — dataset sizes (6k/2k vs. 10k/4k), the abstract's "~7 points" vs. the table's 6-point PhyGenBench gain, and the OmniWeaving improvement described as both 0.48→0.51 and "16.28 points". Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: Yes — the agent runs on a single 9B model and Blender on CPU at inference, though it requires a hosted or open video generator for the final render. Efficient: RL training is expensive (8 H100s for the agent plus 16 H100s dedicated to MiniMax-H3 rollout video generation, ~3 days total), and each RL step requires full video generation, making training roughly an order of magnitude costlier than code-only agentic RL; inference adds Blender render time (20–120s per run) plus video generation latency. Effective: The evidence shows improved judge-scored physical plausibility on two benchmarks, not verified real-world physical correctness or human preference. Scalable: Only claimed, not tested — no experiments at larger agent scale, longer videos, more complex multi-object scenes, or larger training sets beyond the ~6k/2k regime. The work delivers a real software artifact: open-sourced model weights, datasets, harness, and code. Strengths: (1) The white-model rendering convention is a smart, well-motivated interface: it standardizes what the draft conveys (structure/motion only), makes visual feedback interpretable for the agent, and cleanly delegates appearance to the generator. (2) The harness-native RL setup with a graded VLM video reward plus binary execution reward, and the annealing between them, is a concrete, ablation-supported answer to the real problem that early RL rollouts rarely produce executable code, let alone good video. (3) The acceptance protocol (independent clean-directory re-execution of the final script) guarantees every accepted trajectory is reproducible from code alone — a detail many agent papers omit. (4) The cross-backbone result (OmniWeaving improvement) supports the claim that the learned skill is generator-agnostic rather than backbone-tuned. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly note the Material-dimension deficit on VBench-2.0 (75.02% vs. CogVideoX-1.5's 83.19%) and correctly attribute it to the white-model design discarding appearance and material response — a direct, non-defensive confrontation of a real failure mode. They also acknowledge prompts requiring fine-grained appearance, human facial expressions, or non-geometric content are filtered out of training data, implicitly bounding the method's applicable domain, though they do not quantify what fraction of real-world prompts falls outside this envelope. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) No human evaluation anywhere — all headline numbers come from MLLM judges, and the video reward's judge (Qwen3.8-omni-flash) plus PhyGenBench's GPT-4o judge introduce unquantified judge bias; since the RL objective is a VLM judge score, Goodhart-style optimization of the judge rather than of physics is a live risk that no off-judge metric probes. (2) The ground-truth reference videos are MiniMax-H3 outputs conditioned on the agent's own drafts, so the training target and the deployed system share a generator; a real-video-grounded dataset would substantially strengthen the claim. (3) The transfer experiment covers exactly one alternative backbone (OmniWeaving, +0.03 absolute), and the reported "16.28 points" for that gain is arithmetically inconsistent with the table, suggesting the number was not checked. (4) No comparison against training-free baselines under matched compute, e.g., prompting a frozen LLM with the same harness in a test-time loop, which would separate the value of RL training from the value of the draft-video conditioning itself; the 0.61→0.67 RL delta over the 0.63 SFT point suggests the draft conditioning, not RL, does most of the work. (5) Dataset-size discrepancies (6k/2k vs. 10k/4k) between the abstract and Sections 4/5 are unexplained and undermine confidence in reporting hygiene. (6) No evaluation on non-physics dimensions or general video quality, so possible regressions in aesthetics or temporal smoothness from draft conditioning are unmeasured. Bottom Line: A practitioner working on controllable or physics-aware video generation should read this paper for its harness design and dual-reward annealing recipe, which are reusable and ablation-backed, but should treat the headline gains cautiously given the judge-only evaluation, model-generated ground truth, single-seed numbers, and internal reporting inconsistencies; Video-CoCo and GPT4Motion cover adjacent ground and the marginal evidence for RL training over strong test-time prompting remains unestablished.

#171 — Moderately Innovative (54)

, at an Effectuation Boundary, That an Operation Proposed by an Autonomous or AI Agent Matches Currently Valid Authority Before Producing an External Effect

SK Das · tdcommons.org · generating environments for agent testing in enterprises - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper proposes an architectural model, "execution finality," in which the last non-bypassable component that produces an external consequence (the "effectuation boundary") must reconstruct the actual pending operation and verify it against currently valid, bound, single-use authority before allowing the effect — packaged as 14 normative requirements, a 13-item threat model, and a mapping onto existing IETF work (OAuth/RAR, DPoP, Transaction Tokens, WIMSE, RATS, AgentProto). - Why it's important: AI agents are starting to trigger real-world actions (payments, writes, transmissions, actuator commands) within milliseconds, so human-speed review is impossible and an action that was authorized at workflow start may be substituted, redirected, or stale by the time it executes — a gap current platform guardrails and credentials do not close. - How it does it: The core move is a TOCTOU-style separation: upstream computation produces only a NON-EFFECTIVE proposed action plus a canonical authorized descriptor (D_A), and the sink independently derives a descriptor of what is actually about to happen (D_S); effect requires Match(D_A, D_S, CurrentState), freshness, correct boundary, and atomic consumption of authority, failing closed otherwise. - The good: The document is unusually self-critical for a patent-derived disclosure — it rigorously distinguishes its proposal from existing mechanisms (e.g., DPoP proves possession, not that this exact operation is authorized; attestation proves the platform, not the action), and its 18-point canonicalization/semantic-equivalence analysis (UNKNOWN ≠ AUTHORIZED, duplicate-key rejection, URI and unit binding) is a genuinely useful contribution to descriptor-based authorization design. - The missing: There is no implementation, prototype, experiment, measurement, or worked attack demonstration whatsoever — every claim about feasibility, latency, and composability with OAuth/WIMSE/RATS is asserted, not tested, and the central open question (whether existing IETF mechanisms already compose to satisfy the property) is left entirely to the community. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on agentic-AI authorization, tool-call security, or IETF standards for agents (OAuth, WIMSE, MCP/AgentProto) and want a sharp problem statement and requirements checklist; skip it if you need evidence-backed mechanisms, since it is an unvalidated, patent-encumbered position document.
