Problem & Motivation: Modern AI systems orchestrate multiple LLM calls, dynamically generated code, and tool invocations, producing traces whose opacity and non-determinism undermine trust, accountability, and debugging. Current observability tools operate at service-span or per-agent level and lack cross-component semantic provenance. On the retrieval side, RAG over induced graph structures and LLM-generated SPARQL suffer from invalid queries, entity mismatches, and memorization-driven gains. The gap addressed: how to semantically represent multi-stage workflow executions and query them so explanations are faithful, traceable, and auditable — targeting practitioners deploying LLM systems in critical domains. Key Idea: The core move is inverting inference-time query generation: because workflow traces conform to a known ontology, the schema is exhaustively traversed offline to enumerate valid semantic paths, and each path is compiled into a parameterized, pre-validated SPARQL query paired with an LLM-generated natural-language question. Explanation answering then becomes selection and composition over a constrained, verified function library plus iterative question refinement with an LLM judge, rather than open-ended retrieval or free text-to-SPARQL. This shifts the hallucination-prone step (query construction) to a filtering-verifiable offline phase. Methodology: Three setup stages plus a QA stage. (1) Workflow graph annotation: Python/R libraries record each program/agent step as provone:Program, each invocation as provone:Execution, and artifacts (prompts, generated responses, dataframe rows) as provone:Data/Collection, with EO/SIO extensions (workflow:Generative_Task, workflow:LLMOutput via sio:contains to provone:Program) linking LLM usage into PROV-O structure; serialized as Turtle. (2) Synthetic question (SQ) generation: BFS over the ontology schema (14 classes, 385 raw paths, depth Lmax=5), each path yielding forward and reverse parameterized SPARQL templates; a 1-shot LLM generates the NL question; queries returning empty results on the graph are filtered (ChatBS-NexGen keeps 252/314, Biomni 208/270). (3) QA loop: given user question q0, the system grounds entities/classes, restricts the SQ library, an LLM selects one SQ, executes its SPARQL, a summarizer produces an intermediate answer, and an LLM judge decides sufficiency or supplies feedback to rewrite the question; the loop runs at most 3 steps, with embedding-based entity-linking fallback (initial step) and class-level fallback (post-loop). The accumulated step records {(q_i, SQ_i, a_i, e_i)} form a chained-evidence report. Key design decisions: precomputed constrained query set (justified by cited evidence on constrained-query reliability, but coverage depends on filtering — a soft spot); fixed 3-step loop (a hyperparameter, no ablation on its value); LLM-judge sufficiency check (subject to judge bias, acknowledged). No explicit objective/loss — it is a pipeline, not a trained model. Key Results: Tested on two workflows: ChatBS-NexGen (4-step LLM pipeline, R-instrumented, 103 questions: 38 T/F, 49 entity, 16 numeric) and Biomni (12-step free-form agentic execution, Python-instrumented, 106 questions: 39 T/F, 46 entity, 21 numeric). Baselines: GWB (symbolic heuristics), VSB (embedding top-k), GRASP (iterative LLM-generated SPARQL), HippoRAG-KG, HyperGraphRAG-KG — a reasonable spread across paradigms, though all were re-implemented/adapted by the authors on their own graphs. Headline numbers: on ChatBS-NexGen the method scores 69.24% completeness, 65.44% reference agreement, 91.97% relevance, 71.05% boolean accuracy, 43.75% numeric accuracy, 38.37% final-step entity recall, versus best-baseline values of 38.68/48.20/69.09/52.63/25.00/34.55 (HippoRAG/HyperGRAG). On Biomni: 68.45/65.47/93.75/76.92/52.38/46.81. HippoRAG beats the method on total entity recall (64.79% and 66.58% vs. 49.42% and 55.68%) but not on explanation quality. Pairwise win rates range 65.4–92.8% (ChatBS) and 64.3–91.1% (Biomni). Cost: the method is slowest — 39.98s (ChatBS) and 146.06s (Biomni) average latency, ~7–9.3 LLM calls per question. The class-level fallback fires in 16.5%/27.4% of questions — a non-trivial indicator that the SQ library misses coverage in a quarter of Biomni cases. Instrumentation cost: ~30 annotation calls and 870–1,172 LOC per system. Notably, all semantic scores are LLM-judged (three judges: Gemma 4 31B, Qwen 3.6 35B A3B, GPT-5.4 mini) rather than human-verified. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (ontology-constrained precomputed question-SPARQL library as a constrained retrieval function space for explanation QA over workflow provenance graphs) plus NEW SYSTEM/TOOL (annotation libraries, SQ generator, QA pipeline in the released repo). The individual ingredients — ProvONE/PROV-O provenance modeling, schema-aware text-to-SPARQL, LLM-as-judge iterative retrieval — are established; the novelty is the composition into a schema-enumerated, pre-validated query library with iterative selection/judge refinement applied to AI-workflow explanation, which is a genuine but incremental formulation rather than a fundamentally new technique. Rigor & Reproducibility: Code, baselines, benchmarks, and raw results are released (https://github.com/DevinDeSilva/LLM-Workflow-Explorer), and an explicit appendix defends evaluation/SQ separation — positives for reproducibility. Ablations are effectively absent: no ablation over loop depth (3), judge model, SQ-library size, or the contribution of filtering vs. fallback mechanisms. No error bars over retrieval seeds; the ±values reported are cross-judge disagreement, not run-to-run variance. Entity recall and exact-answer metrics provide grounding beyond LLM judges, but all semantic metrics are LLM-as-a-judge, and judges share the same model lineage as the answering LLM (gpt-oss-20b); Krippendorff's α of 0.656–0.771 for relevance/RA shows moderate judge divergence. Both benchmarks are the authors' own instrumented workflows evaluated against their own ontology — a self-referential setup where the backing ontology is co-designed with the evaluation questions' SPARQL templates; GRASP and HippoRAG were applied out of their native domain, and no baseline was tested under tuned, graph-specific configurations. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (systems with a built artifact and experiments). Practical: Yes — self-hosted gpt-oss-20b via LM Studio on an NVIDIA DGX plus a BGE-large embedder; no exotic hardware beyond one GPU server. Efficient: Poorly — highest latency of all methods (146.06s/question on Biomni, ~9.3 LLM calls), and ~870–1,172 LOC of manual instrumentation per system is a real adoption cost the authors concede. Effective: Evidence supports better explanations than baselines on these two workflows, but "explanation quality" is measured by LLM judges against template-derived ground truths, not by the developers/users who would actually consume the explanations. Scalable: Untested — both graphs are small (895 and 2,022 triples, single executions), single workflow per system; behavior on graphs orders of magnitude larger, or with many executions per graph, is unclaimed experimentally (SQ-library size may grow combinatorially with schema depth). Delivers a software artifact: GitHub repository with source code, benchmark data, and raw results; the annotation libraries and QA pipeline are reusable. Strengths: - The constrained-retrieval formulation is a clean, well-motivated response to known text-to-SPARQL failure modes (invalid queries, entity mismatches, memorization), backed by a filtering step that verifies every query returns results before deployment. - Dual evaluation on contrasting workflow types (fixed LLM-function-generation pipeline vs. free-form agentic loop) demonstrates the annotation libraries and pipeline generalize across instrumentation styles. - Honest error analysis: the paper reports that its own method has the worst latency, that the fallback fires in 16.5–27.4% of questions, and pinpoints numeric-accuracy failures (ontology-class grounding errors and LLM counting errors) — including the anomaly that HippoRAG wins total entity recall while losing explanation quality. - The evidence-chained report structure (every claim traceable to a step's executed query and entities) is a real, verifiable mechanism for reducing hallucinated explanations, not just a claim. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly concede: developer-driven instrumentation overhead; latency from the multi-step LLM pipeline; restriction to trace-based/data explanations; dependence of completeness on SQ-library coverage; and the absence of user-centered evaluation of interpretability/utility. They confront limitations directly rather than minimizing them — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Evaluation is entirely self-referential: one workflow per system, one or a few executions each, benchmarks built from 13 and 22 string templates with manually authored SPARQL against the authors' own ontology — the method and its evaluation instrument share design lineage, and no external or public KGQA benchmark is touched. - Judge and answerer share the gpt-oss family; circularity risk in pairwise and absolute LLM-judged scores is not discussed, and moderate inter-judge agreement (α as low as 0.656) is reported without sensitivity analysis per judge. - The fallback firing on 27.4% of Biomni questions suggests SQ-library coverage is the binding constraint, yet no ablation isolates how much performance the precomputed library vs. the fallback class-level retrieval contributes. - GRASP and HippoRAG/HyperGraphRAG were adapted onto a domain (tiny workflow graphs) far from their intended operating regime; no tuning of baseline parameters (e.g., top-k for VSB) is reported, so margin-of-victory figures may be inflated. - Scalability of BFS path enumeration and SQ-library size on larger schemas (depth > 5, hundreds of classes) is unexamined. - Ground-truth explanations are template-derived and manually authored by the same group; no inter-annotator agreement on the gold answers is reported. Bottom Line: A solid, honestly-reported workshop paper whose constrained query-library idea is a practical and verifiable design pattern for provenance-grounded explanation of agent workflows — practitioners building auditable LLM systems gain real value from the released code and evaluation design, but the tiny self-authored benchmarks and LLM-judge-only quality scores cap confidence, and anyone needing provenance-based explanation should read it alongside stronger independent benchmarks before treating the reported margins as general.

A generative adversarial network-augmented dual-stream Mamba-transformer framework for advanced intrusion detection and cyber threat mitigation in smart …

P Kumar, S Kumar, I Mukherjee · nature.com · cyber model training - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces GAN-MambaFormer-IDS, an intrusion detection framework that routes network-flow features into four protocol-aware tokens, encodes them in parallel with a Mamba state-space stream and a Transformer attention stream, and augments minority attack classes with CTGAN, achieving 97.71% accuracy and 0.7901 macro-F1 on the 19-class CICIoMT2024 test set. - Why it's important: IoMT networks in hospitals carry life-critical traffic (healthcare breach costs averaged USD 10.93M in 2023, and ransomware has been linked to excess patient deaths), so IDS that miss rare-but-critical attacks under severe class imbalance (up to 2212:1) have real clinical cost. - How it does it: The core trick is a Protocol-Aware Feature Router (PAFR) that splits 45 flow features into four semantically coherent groups (flow, flag, transport, application), converts them into 4 tokens, and fuses two complementary inductive biases — selective state-space recurrence and self-attention — over those tokens, with CTGAN-generated samples (276,520 synthetic records) for seven minority classes. - The good: The evaluation is unusually complete for this subfield: per-class F1, a component-wise ablation (each component contributes 0.04–0.17 macro-F1), a five-seed stability check (macro-F1 0.7901 ± 0.0025), significance tests against both single-stream baselines (p < 0.001), SMOTE/ADASYN comparison, and an honest per-epoch convergence analysis that dissects an epoch-6 training instability. - The missing: The two-stream machinery operates on only G=4 tokens, so the claimed sequential/global dependency modeling is over a trivially short sequence — the paper never tests whether the dual streams beat a simple 4-token MLP or permutation-invariant pooling over the same tokens, which is the ablation that would validate the central architectural claim. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building IoMT/IoT IDS on CICIoMT2024 or similar tabular flow benchmarks, since the pipeline details, ablations, and minority-class analysis are reusable; skippable for anyone seeking architectural novelty in sequence modeling, because Mamba and Transformer are applied in a setting where neither operates on real sequences.

Problem & Motivation: Healthcare providers deploying IoMT device fleets face DDoS, DoS, spoofing, reconnaissance, and MQTT-specific attacks over heterogeneous protocols (Wi-Fi, MQTT, Bluetooth), while conventional IDS struggle with three compounding difficulties: protocol-heterogeneous high-dimensional traffic features, long-range temporal dependencies that LSTM/CNN models handle poorly, and extreme class imbalance that biases learning toward benign/majority traffic. Prior IoMT IDS work addresses these problems one at a time — Mamba-based models (IDS-GraphMamba), federated TabTransformer, CGAN augmentation in general IoT — but, per the authors' literature synthesis, no framework simultaneously handles post-LSTM temporal modeling, global feature interaction, protocol-specific routing, healthcare-specific generative augmentation, and cross-dataset validation. The domain stakes are concrete: the paper cites 531 major healthcare hacking incidents in 2023 compromising 70M+ patient records, and evidence tying ransomware to 42–67 excess Medicare patient deaths over five years. Key Idea: Convert the flat 45-dimensional flow vector into a short sequence of four protocol-group tokens via learned group encoders with soft gating, then apply two complementary encoders — a gated selective state-space recurrence (Mamba-style, d_s=64, 2 layers) and multi-head self-attention (4 heads, 2 layers) — over those same tokens, concatenate both pooled outputs with a global projection, and train with inverse-frequency-weighted cross-entropy plus CTGAN-augmented minority samples. The dual-inductive-bias framing (state-transition prior vs. content-adaptive relational prior) is the paper's stated conceptual contribution rather than a new learning primitive. Methodology: The pipeline has four stages. (1) Preprocessing: 8.77M CICIoMT2024 records from 40 IoMT devices are label-normalized from 57 variants to 19 classes via regex, imputed (median), z-scored, and split per the official CIC train/val/test directories (6,086,706 / 1,074,125 / 1,614,182). (2) PAFR: four binary masks isolate feature groups (17 flow, 11 flag, 9 transport, 8 application); each group is projected to a 64-d token by a group-specific encoder, scaled by a learned soft gate, yielding a 4×64 token matrix. (3) Dual-stream encoding: the Mamba stream runs input-dependent gated state updates (update/decay/candidate gates, sigmoid activations, residual + FFN) over the 4-token sequence; the Transformer stream runs pre-norm multi-head self-attention + FFN over the identical tokens; both are mean-pooled, concatenated with a global bypass projection, fused to d_fuse=128, and classified into 19 logits via weighted cross-entropy (weight exponent 1.0). (4) CTGAN augmentation: classes at or below the 35th count percentile (7 classes) each get an independently trained CTGAN (3 epochs, batch 512, pac=10), capped at 40,000 synthetic samples/class. Training uses Adam (lr 8e-4, weight decay 5e-7), batch 512, ≤8 epochs, gradient clip 1.0, early stopping on validation macro-F1. Critical design decisions: (a) routing to G=4 tokens makes attention cost O(4²) — well-justified for efficiency, but it also collapses the "long-range temporal dependency" motivation, since the model never sees an actual traffic sequence; (b) CTGAN vs. SMOTE is empirically justified (Minority F1 0.6477 vs. 0.5627); (c) the global-bypass projection in the fusion layer is introduced without ablation, so part of the "PAFR matters" gain could come from the bypass path. Key Results: On the CICIoMT2024 test set, the full model reaches 0.9771 accuracy, 0.7901 macro-F1, 0.9763 weighted-F1, and 0.9842 ROC-AUC, versus Transformer-only (0.9594 / 0.6985), Mamba-only (0.9621 / 0.7062), BiLSTM (0.9487 / 0.6648), 1D-CNN (0.9412 / 0.6319), MLP (0.9308 / 0.5931), plus CNN-Transformer, GNN-IDS, federated, and attention-based IDS baselines (macro-F1 0.7415–0.7589). Inference is 0.43 ms/flow on GPU and 6.8 ms/flow on a Raspberry Pi 4B, with 1.21M parameters, 24.6M FLOPs, and 9.4 MB memory. CTGAN lifts minority-class macro-F1 by up to +0.2109 (recon_ping_sweep: 0.3245 → 0.5354, from only 629 training samples) and beats SMOTE (Minority F1 0.5627) and ADASYN (0.5794). Ablations: removing PAFR drops macro-F1 to 0.7389, removing the Mamba stream to 0.7245, removing the Transformer stream to 0.7312, removing CTGAN to 0.7156 (Minority F1 0.4812). Cross-dataset (retrained from scratch, shared hyperparameters): macro-F1 of 0.7589 (CICIoT2023), 0.7369 (UNSW-NB15), 0.7522 (Edge-IIoTset), 0.7436 (WUSTL-EHMS-2020). The rarest classes remain weak (recon_ping_sweep recall ≈51.08%, recon_vulscan ≈58.91%). Notably, the accuracy–macro-F1 gap (~0.19) on all datasets shows accuracy is inflated by imbalance; the paper reports both, which is to its credit. Scale: standard benchmark scale (~8.8M flows), not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (weak) + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING + ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The genuinely new element is narrow: applying CTGAN augmentation to healthcare-protocol-specific IoMT attack classes on CICIoMT2024 and pairing it with protocol-grouped token routing. Each component — selective state-space modeling (Gu & Dao), multi-head self-attention, CTGAN (Xu et al. 2019), soft-gated feature grouping — is standard; the dual-stream Mamba-Transformer combination has appeared in other domains, and the PAFR is essentially learned feature-group embeddings. The "theoretically motivated dual-stream" section is a design rationale, not a formal result. This is a competent domain-specific integration, not a new primitive. Rigor & Reproducibility: Above average for applied IDS papers. Ablations isolate all four claimed components; five random seeds with mean ± SD are reported (macro-F1 0.7901 ± 0.0025); significance tests against both single-stream baselines (p=0.0004 and 0.0008) are included; CTGAN output quality is validated quantitatively (JSD 0.037, Wasserstein 0.081, KS 0.064) and visually (t-SNE); a code package with preprocessing, model, and evaluation scripts is stated as deposited at Zenodo (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21293017), though verification at review time was not possible. Concerns: (i) the four non-core baselines (CNN-Transformer, GNN-IDS, Federated IDS, Attention-Based IDS) are compared without citation or implementation provenance, so their tuning quality is unverifiable; (ii) the paper reports a peer-reviewed venue (Scientific Reports), lending moderate confidence, but the epoch-6 collapse (validation accuracy 91.56% → 41.43% → 97.67%) is diagnosed post-hoc rather than prevented, and the epoch-7 checkpoint selection means the headline number comes from the single best-validation epoch of an unstable run; (iii) no comparison against the strongest published CICIoMT2024 numbers cited in its own literature review (e.g., FedMedSecure at 99.9% accuracy on CICIoMT2024, stacking ensembles at 98%), making the "outperforms baselines" claim partially relative to self-implemented models. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (with a SYSTEMS flavor — latency benchmarks on edge hardware). - Practical: Yes — 1.21M parameters, 9.4 MB, PyTorch 2.1, demonstrated on a Raspberry Pi 4B at 6.8 ms/flow, well under a 100 ms/flow budget. - Efficient: 24.6M FLOPs and 0.43 ms/flow GPU versus 0.19 ms/flow for Mamba-only — the dual stream costs +0.12 ms/flow for +0.084 macro-F1, a favorable trade. - Effective: Partially — it clearly solves the benchmark task (97.71% accuracy) and materially improves minority-class detection, but rarest-class F1 of 0.54–0.61 means it detects, not reliably catches, the rarest attacks; no false-positive-rate-per-day analysis for operational use. - Scalable: Claimed but not tested — the fixed G=4-token design keeps cost constant per flow, but 100× traffic-scale behavior, throughput under concurrent flows, and CTGAN training cost (47 min for 7 classes) at larger class counts are extrapolations. Deliverable: a stated reproducibility package (code + configs + checkpoints) at Zenodo; datasets are public; the artifact exists at paper form plus claimed repository deposit. Strengths: - The evaluation protocol is genuinely rigorous: seed-variance reporting, paired significance tests, an augmentation-method comparison (SMOTE/ADASYN/CTGAN), and per-class confusion analysis that localizes failure to genuinely data-scarce classes rather than hiding it. - The PAFR-to-token design is a defensible efficiency insight: by fixing the token count at 4, the architecture sidesteps quadratic attention and long-sequence Mamba scans entirely, and the latency numbers (0.43 ms GPU, 6.8 ms Pi 4B) back the real-time claim empirically on both platforms. - The convergence analysis is a credibility positive: instead of smoothing over the epoch-6 validation collapse (91.56% → 41.43%), the authors derive the effective weighted-gradient for rare-class batches, attribute the instability to class weighting × synthetic-sample variance × fusion-layer misalignment, and show checkpointing mitigated it. - Cross-dataset validation across five benchmarks with frozen hyperparameters (only the classification head re-sized) is a fair generalization test that most single-dataset IDS papers skip. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that (i) the rarest classes (recon_ping_sweep, recon_vulscan) still underperform due to limited original samples; (ii) excessive synthetic samples may induce overfitting; (iii) the epoch-6 instability exists, is explained mechanistically, and motivates future use of warm-up, cosine decay, focal loss, class-weight annealing, or curriculum introduction of CTGAN samples; (iv) the Mamba stream is a simplified gated formulation, not the full hardware-aware selective scan of Gu & Dao. They confront limitations directly rather than minimize them, which strengthens confidence in the reported numbers. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The central claim — that dual streams provide complementary inductive biases — is never tested against the strongest trivial control: a single-stream model over the same 4 PAFR tokens with more layers, or simple concatenation of the four group embeddings into one MLP. Given G=4, a permutation of group order could change Mamba-stream behavior; no order-perturbation or ablation of the sequence assumption exists. "Sequential dependency" over 4 tokens is a category stretch relative to the long-sequence motivation in the introduction. - The introduction motivates long-range temporal modeling of traffic, but the method consumes only static per-flow feature vectors — no windowed or packet-level sequences are modeled anywhere. The motivation and mechanism are misaligned. - Baseline provenance is missing for the four strongest competitors (CNN-Transformer, GNN-IDS, Federated IDS, Attention-Based IDS): no hyperparameters, no citations, no indication they were tuned with equal effort. Meanwhile, published CICIoMT2024 results cited in the paper's own related work (99.9% FedMedSecure, 98% stacking ensemble) are not included in the comparison table. - The 0.9745 accuracy without CTGAN vs. 0.9771 with it means CTGAN buys +0.0026 accuracy for +0.17 macro-F1 — the paper could state more plainly that augmentation trades majority-class headroom for minority-class recall; downstream operators may care about the resulting false-positive shift, which is not analyzed. - No adversarial-robustness, drift, or concept-shift evaluation despite deployment framing; the cross-dataset test retrains from scratch, so it measures transferability of architecture, not of a deployed model. Bottom Line: A practitioner deploying tabular-flow IDS on IoMT benchmarks gains a well-validated, edge-deployable recipe (protocol-grouped tokens + CTGAN minority augmentation is the transferable part), but a researcher seeking architectural novelty will find the dual-stream Mamba-Transformer core to be a known-parts integration over a 4-token sequence, and there are stronger published CICIoMT2024 numbers it declines to compare against.

M Li, B Li, W Zhao, C Zhang, B Zhang, J Xu, Z Zang… · arxiv.org · recursive self-improvement - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces WeightLoop, a framework in which an LLM (GPT-6 Astra) writes a fixed, bounded "editor" program once, and that program then converts incoming experimental assay measurements into persistent, targeted parameter edits of a deployed predictor — with no further LLM calls and no gradient retraining. - Why it's important: In experimental science (e.g., cellular perturbation screens), predictors must rank thousands of candidates from only ~25–100 measurements, and each new assay batch reveals task-specific prediction errors that currently require manual retraining pipelines to exploit. - How it does it: The key mechanism is that the LLM-written editor exploits model structure — for the neural predictor, only the 128 linear functional-output weights are mutable, so each candidate edit's effect on the ranking loss is exactly computable from cached activations without backpropagation, and edits are validated on a held-out support split before being written to the checkpoint. - The good: The experimental design uses matched permutation controls (same number and norm of weight changes, permuted across coordinates) and paired gene folds, showing targeted edits beat permuted-edit controls in all 8 single-round settings and improve mean D100 discovery in all 3 sequential tasks. - The missing: There is no comparison against the obvious alternative of gradient fine-tuning the same 128 readout weights (or affine calibration) on the same feedback labels for the neural model, leaving the claim that weight-space programming beats cheap classical adaptation untested. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on LLM-driven scientific agents, model editing, or active-learning loops and want a concrete, well-controlled (if small-scale) demonstration of closing the measurement-to-model-update loop; skip it if you need large-scale or general-architecture evidence, since everything here is biology-specific with tiny edit counts.

Problem & Motivation: In experimental decision-making, a predictor ranks candidate interventions (e.g., genes to perturb), but true effects are known only after costly measurement, and a new objective may start with only a few dozen labels. Model-editing research produces one-off parameter corrections, and recursive-self-improvement systems (STOP) revise code, but neither connects an accumulating stream of real experimental outcomes to a deployed predictor's weights. The paper targets practitioners running sequential biological screens (DepMap Chronos fitness effects, HL60 proliferation/migration, LC3/NBR1 autophagic flux, HuH7 LDL uptake) who need each returned assay batch to improve the next batch's decisions. Key Idea: The core trick is to freeze the improvement loop's intelligence at program-construction time: the LLM writes an editor that exposes a task-appropriate mutable parameter interface (the 128 linear readout weights of a ReLU-MLP predictor, ridge coefficients, or XGBoost leaf values), after which purely numerical, deterministic logic — diagnose high-contributing coordinates against measured ranking errors, probe each candidate edit exactly using cached activations, validate on a support split, write back to the checkpoint — converts feedback into model updates with zero additional LLM calls, no gradients, and non-compounding patches (each Δt is reconstructed from the original θ0). Methodology: The pipeline has two phases. (1) One-time editor construction: GPT-6 Astra receives the task objective, model implementation, and parameter structure, and emits a bounded editing program specifying mutable parameters, candidate updates, validation rules, and checkpoint saving. (2) Repeated execution: given accumulated support St = {(gi, xi, yi)} of measured outcomes, the editor computes Δt = EI(θ0, St) and θt = θ0 + Δt, then the decision rule D applies budget constraints to select the next assay batch. For the neural model, the validation objective is a normalized weighted pairwise logistic ranking loss (Eq. 3) plus top-budget utility (BU@10); candidate edits halve individual output weights (w'_j = w_j(1 − α) for j in top-k gain set, k ∈ {4, 8, 16}, α ∈ {0.25, 0.5}), with three identity-based support folds selecting the accepted update. Ridge edits solve a closed-form ridge residual correction; XGBoost edits add shrunken residual means to supported leaves, selected by support MSE. Critical design decisions: (a) edits always start from θ0 so patches don't compound — justified for stability but untested for the alternative; (b) only output weights are editable while the encoder stays fixed — justified because this makes edits exactly computable without backpropagation, though it caps expressivity; (c) a no-op guard (no qualifying improvement → Δt = 0) — well justified, and 19/75 sequential updates indeed no-op'd. Key Results: Single-round ranking (HepG2/Jurkat growth via DepMap 24Q4, HL60 proliferation and migration; 5 folds × 2 seeds, 40 initial n=25 models): edited updates exceed random-edit controls in all 8 endpoint–budget settings and beat the original model in 7 of 8 (e.g., HepG2 B=50: BU 0.5208 → 0.5421). Sequential discovery (LC3, NBR1 autophagic flux; HuH7 LDL uptake; 5 folds, 1 seed, five 20-gene batches): edited policies improve mean D100 over both original and permuted-edit controls in all three tasks (LC3 +0.0334, NBR1 +0.0207, HuH7 +0.0147), with 4/5, 4/5, 3/5 positive paired folds. Ridge coefficient edits cut query MSE by 10.0–13.0%; XGBoost leaf edits by 2.4–2.6%. Persistence: a 16-weight edit (0.00044% of 3,604,535 parameters) reproduces all 914 edited predictions exactly after native checkpoint reload. Notably, the full n=100 retrained reference beats the edited n=25 model in most settings (e.g., HepG2 growth B=20: 0.6254 vs 0.5419), so editing improves the low-label model but does not close the gap to full-data fitting. Effect sizes are modest and the tested scale is small (25–100 labels, 128 editable weights, 5 batches of 20 genes). Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel element is the fixed-editor/evolving-predictor loop — an LLM writes a reusable weight-editing program once, and deterministic execution turns real experimental feedback into persistent checkpoint edits, connecting weight-space programming (Takehi et al., a non-peer-reviewed blog post) with RSI-style loops in a concrete scientific setting. The individual components — pairwise ranking losses, ridge regression, XGBoost, active-learning-style batch selection — are standard; the contribution is their orchestration and the demonstrated persistence mechanism, not new algorithms. Rigor & Reproducibility: The control design is a strength: matched permutation controls preserve the number and norm of changes, receive the same six-setting validation budget, and no-op rounds are reported (19/75 updates changed nothing). Ablations over k and α exist via the six-setting validation, and paired fold-level results are shown (HepG2 improves in all 5 paired folds at both budgets). However, no error bars, significance tests, or confidence intervals are reported; seeds are limited (2 for single-round, 1 for sequential). No code, data pipeline, or editor prompts are stated as released. A methodological concern the paper only partially addresses: "Editor design used DepMap experiments" while two DepMap cell lines (HepG2, Jurkat) are the primary single-round evaluation — the authors state rules were "fixed for HL60 and sequential evaluation" but the neural editor's diagnostic and loss were developed on the same data distribution it is evaluated on (Goodhart risk). The permuted-edit control mitigates but does not eliminate this. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL. Practical: Yes — edits require cached activations, a closed-form ranking-loss probe, and checkpoint write/reload; no specialized hardware or backpropagation. Efficient: Extremely — a deployed 3.6M-parameter model is updated by changing 16 weights (0.00044%) with zero gradient computation and zero LLM calls per feedback batch. Effective: The evidence supports improved ranking and acquisition on public screen data (BU and D100 gains over matched controls), but gains are modest (ΔBU typically 0.01–0.02; D100 +0.02–0.03) and measured on proxy utilities, not actual wet-lab success. Scalable: Untested — the mechanism depends on a 128-dimensional linear readout and small support sets; behavior when the mutable interface, the number of feedback batches, or model size grow 10–100× is only claimed, not shown. The work stops at paper form: no released library, tool, or checkpoint is mentioned. Strengths: - The permutation-control design is the strongest element: comparing targeted edits against same-norm, same-count permuted edits under an identical validation budget isolates the value of choosing which weights to change, not just that weights changed. - The exactly-computable edit trick (halving a readout weight changes standardized predictions by −0.5·w_j·h_ij, so diagnostics need no backpropagation) is a clean, correct use of the linear-readout structure. - The persistence evaluation (exact reproduction of 914 predictions after native checkpoint reload, reordered-query score checks, single-gene inference check) directly tests a claim most editing papers leave implicit. - Honest reporting of the full grid, including the two settings where editing loses to the original model (HL60 migration B=20/50 relative to the n=100 reference) and of no-op update rounds. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper acknowledges that "biological efficacy requires validation in the intended setting" (i.e., results are on recorded measurements, not live assays), that edits are restricted to a bounded parameter interface whose expressivity is tied to model structure, that no qualifying improvement yields Δt = 0, and that editor rules were designed on DepMap data. It does not include a dedicated limitations section; the Ethical Considerations note is brief (reversibility, traceability, public data) and does not confront evaluation weaknesses directly. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Missing baseline: gradient fine-tuning of the same 128 readout weights on the 75 feedback labels with the same ranking loss — cheap, structure-aware, and directly comparable — would test whether LLM-authored editing rules add anything over one line of PyTorch. - Editor-design data overlaps the single-round evaluation distribution (DepMap), a benchmark-development coupling the authors mention only obliquely. - Only 1 seed for all sequential-discovery results, the headline D100 gains (~0.02–0.03) are small, and no variance or significance is reported for them. - The comparison to the full n=100 retrained model shows editing is strictly worse than simply retraining with all labels; the practical niche (no gradients, fixed code) is asserted rather than shown to matter for retraining cost at this scale, where retraining a linear readout is trivial. - Reliance on GPT-6 Astra (a 2026 commercial model, cited only via API documentation) and on a blog post for the foundational WSP concept makes the pipeline's key component unreproducible from the paper. - The neural architecture is unusually favorable (a 128-dim linear readout atop a frozen encoder); generalization to end-to-end or larger models is unexamined. Bottom Line: A rigorously controlled but small-scale proof of concept that a fixed LLM-authored editing program can turn real assay feedback into persistent, verifiable weight updates; practitioners in LLM-for-science and model editing will find the loop design and controls instructive, but the absence of a gradient-fine-tuning baseline and the reliance on a proprietary unreleased LLM mean stronger, reproducible alternatives for closed-loop model adaptation likely exist or will soon.

From Universal Prediction to Universal Workflows: A Survey of Foundation Models for Tabular and Time Series Data

HR Cai, JP Jiang, SY Liu, HJ Ye · lamda.nju.edu.cn · 10 new citations to your articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper presents a survey that unifies foundation-model research for tabular data and time series under a single taxonomy organized around Input Encoding, Model Architecture, Pre-training Strategies, and Adaptation Techniques, and extends the review from model-level prediction to agentic end-to-end workflows. - Why it's important: Tabular and time-series communities have developed nearly identical solutions to shared structural problems (schema heterogeneity, tokenization of continuous values, distribution shift) in isolation, so a cross-domain map saves researchers from rediscovering ideas across the modality boundary. - How it does it: The organizing insight is a design-question-driven taxonomy: methods are grouped by how they solve shared challenges (patching vs. feature grouping, synthetic priors vs. real-data scaling, in-context vs. generative vs. parameter-generating prediction interfaces) rather than by modality. - The good: The cross-modality parallels are drawn concretely — e.g., Chronos's quantization ↔ TP-BERTa's tree-based binning, time-series patching ↔ TabPFN's feature grouping, and the explicit contrast between the tabular "Synthetic Prior Hypothesis" and the time-series "Empirical Scaling Hypothesis" — giving readers a genuine transferable framework, backed by a curated paper list (github.com/LAMDA-Tabular/Awesome-FMSD). - The missing: As a survey it reports no experiments; there is no quantitative cross-model comparison, no stated systematic paper-selection methodology (search strings, inclusion criteria), and the agentic-workflows section describes systems narratively without consolidated benchmark numbers. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers or practitioners entering structured-data foundation models who want a current, cross-modality map and open-problem list; specialists who already follow TabPFN-line and TSFM literature will find little they have not seen.

Problem & Motivation: Practitioners in finance, healthcare, and industrial IoT rely on structured data (tables and time series), where foundation models lag behind their NLP/CV counterparts. The two dominant structured modalities are usually studied by separate communities using separate vocabularies, even though time series are often stored as tabular panel data and tabular rows are often temporal snapshots. Prior surveys treat tabular learning or time-series learning in isolation, so the structural overlap — and the fact that both fields independently converge on patching/grouping, in-context inference, and synthetic priors — is left unexploited. The survey's stated aim is to close this gap with a unified perspective tracing a progression "from universal prediction to universal workflows." Key Idea: The core intellectual move is the unified challenge-based taxonomy: for each design question (encoding, architecture, pre-training, adaptation), the survey first states the shared challenge (e.g., the tokenization bottleneck, heterogeneity/vocabulary mismatch formalized via a risk-over-tasks objective in Eq. 1) and then shows that the two communities' answers are structurally parallel. This is a synthesis contribution, not a new algorithm; the key idea is the mapping itself, e.g., synthetic-prior pre-training (TabPFN's BNN/SCM priors) as the tabular analogue of what is only beginning to appear in time-series classification (TiCT, Cauker). Methodology: The survey is organized in four taxonomy sections plus one on agents. (1) Input encoding: three paradigms — patch/group aggregation (TimesFM, TabPFN v2's stochastic feature grouping), point/cell-level tokenization (Lag-Llama, Time-MoE, TabICL, Mitra), and structure-aware transformation (Chronos quantization, TOTEM VQ-VAE, TP-BERTa binning, random projection in HyperFast/iLTM, TabPFN-TS's reframing of forecasting as tabular regression). (2) Architecture: four prediction interfaces — contextual representation backbones (Moirai, MOMENT, TabDPT, LimiX), support-query in-context predictors (TabPFN family, TabICL, TiCT, TimEE), generative conditional predictors (TimesFM, Chronos-2, TimeDiT diffusion), and parameter-generating architectures (HyperFast, MotherNet, TabPTM) — each with named cost profiles (context-length scaling, autoregressive decoding, context-compression loss). (3) Pre-training: data source (synthetic priors vs. real-world corpora like Time-300B and TabLib) crossed with objectives (next-patch regression, prior-data fitting cross-entropy, context-conditional masked modeling in UniTS/LimiX). (4) Adaptation: cross-modal alignment (Time-LLM reprogramming, TabuLa-8B's row-causal masking, VisionTS image conversion) and tuning (context optimization via TuneTables' super-context maximization in Eq. 3, PEFT). Section 4 taxonomizes LLM agents by scope of autonomy into task-specific specialists (cleaning, feature engineering, HPO, inference refinement) and end-to-end generalists (AIDE, MLMaster, AutoKaggle, TabAgent). The scope is explicitly bounded: native TFMs/TSFMs plus cross-modal predictors and structured-data agents, excluding single-dataset models and generic agents, covering public work through September 2026. Key Results: Not applicable in the experimental sense — the paper reports no measurements. Its "results" are taxonomic coverage: it catalogs on the order of 100+ methods across the four dimensions plus ~25 agentic systems, and surfaces empirical observations from the literature it cites, e.g., TabFM's claim that scaling model size and synthetic pre-training data yields strong zero-shot tabular performance; recent evaluations [100] that PEFT versus full fine-tuning outcomes are model- and data-dependent and full fine-tuning can hurt calibration; and the observation that time-series classification is emerging as a testbed for whether synthetic priors can substitute for real-world scaling. No benchmark tables, accuracy figures, or head-to-head comparisons are consolidated in the survey itself. Novelty Classification: This is primarily a synthesis: a NEW FORMULATION (unified cross-modality taxonomy for structured-data foundation models) plus, in a minor key, a survey of an emerging area (agentic workflows for structured data). The genuinely novel element is the systematic tabular↔time-series correspondence at each design layer and the claim that the field is transitioning from model-level prediction to workflow-level agent composition. The individual methods covered are, by construction, standard prior work; the survey itself runs no experiments and introduces no new technique. Rigor & Reproducibility: As a survey, there are no ablations, seeds, or significance tests to assess, and no quantitative synthesis is attempted. The companion repository (https://github.com/LAMDA-Tabular/Awesome-FMSD) provides a curated paper list, which is the reproducible artifact. Methodological concerns for a survey: the paper-selection procedure is not described (no search protocol, inclusion/exclusion criteria beyond the informal scope statement, or coverage statistics), so completeness and potential selection bias toward the authors' own research line cannot be verified — the authors and their group (Cai, Jiang, Liu, Ye) author or co-author a noticeable fraction of cited works (e.g., refs 2, 3, 4, 14, 15, 16, 76, 93, 98, 117, 135, 136), which is a citable self-citation concentration a critical reader should weigh. Method placement is admittedly "representative rather than exhaustive," and assignments of a model to one taxonomy cell (when several apply, e.g., Chronos as both quantization and generative predictor) involve judgment calls that are discussed but not validated against model authors' own characterizations systematically. The scope statement's "through September 2026" combined with numerous 2026-dated citations means much of the covered literature is contemporaneous or, from the vantage of a reader today, unverifiable preprint material; confidence in specific claims about very recent systems (TabPFN-3.5, LimiX-2, Timer-S1) rests on self-reported vendor/technical-report numbers the survey does not independently verify. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: THEORETICAL (a survey/position synthesis with no primary experimental claim). - Sound: The taxonomy's assumptions (shared challenges across modalities) are argued through worked correspondences rather than proven, but the framework is internally consistent and its scope is stated. - General: The framework holds for the two covered modalities; the authors themselves flag graphs/relational data as a third structured modality the current taxonomy does not fully absorb. - Tight: Not applicable to bounds; the closest analogue is whether the four-dimension taxonomy is exhaustive, and the authors concede placement is by "primary role," so the partition is loose. - Implementable: The deliverable is a decision aid, not code: the per-paradigm cost discussion (e.g., parameter-generating models suit repeated queries on one dataset; support-query predictors suit immediate few-shot adaptation) is directly usable for architecture selection, and the repo operationalizes the bibliography. The work delivers a paper plus a public paper list; no software artifact, dataset, or trained model. Strengths: - The cross-modality mapping is substantive, not cosmetic: the Synthetic Prior (tabular) vs. Empirical Scaling (time series) dichotomy, and the observation that time-series classification is where these philosophies are beginning to collide, is an original and falsifiable framing a reader can act on. - The architecture section's organization by prediction interface (representation, support-query, generative, parameter-generating) rather than by task or modality cuts across the literature cleanly, and each paradigm is assigned a concrete cost profile. - Coverage is genuinely current, including 2025–2026 systems (TabPFN v2.5/3/3.5, Chronos-2, Moirai 2.0, LimiX, MantisV2), which most prior surveys predate. - The explicit scope statement (what is included and excluded) and the honest discussion of agent trade-offs (latency, stochasticity, reproducibility) are credibility positives. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that cited methods are "representative rather than exhaustive" and placed by primary role; that the survey centers on predictive modeling for two modalities while acknowledging other tasks (e.g., anomaly detection) are omitted; that many current agentic systems "still rely mainly on general LLMs and conventional tools" rather than native TFMs/TSFMs, so the model-agent convergence is early; and that agentic workflows suffer latency, overhead, and reproducibility problems versus static pipelines. They confront limitations directly in the Discussion paragraphs, which strengthens the survey's credibility. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No stated systematic literature-search methodology, making coverage claims unauditable and selection bias (including the high self-citation rate) unverifiable. - No quantitative synthesis anywhere: even where head-to-head benchmark results exist in the cited literature (e.g., TabArena for tabular models), the survey does not aggregate, tabulate, or reconcile them, so a reader cannot see which paradigm actually wins under which conditions. - The "universal workflows" framing is largely aspirational: the surveyed agents mostly wrap generic LLMs plus code execution, and the survey provides no evidence — only argument — that native TFMs/TSFMs compose well as agent primitives; this gap is acknowledged but its magnitude is minimized in the framing. - The unified risk-over-tasks objective (Eq. 1) is presented as a formulation but is never used to derive predictions, distinctions, or analysis; it is decorative formalism. - Tension between paradigms is described but not adjudicated: the survey does not commit to when synthetic priors beat real-data scaling beyond qualitative conditional statements, which is precisely the question a practitioner wants answered. - Confidence caveat: the text cites a large volume of 2026-dated technical reports and preprints (TabPFN-3/3.5, LimiX-2, Timer-S1, Xiaomi-TabLDM), including vendor blog and vendor technical-report numbers, none independently verified — treat those specific claims as provisional. Bottom Line: For anyone entering or bridging structured-data foundation-model research, this is currently the best single map of the tabular/TSFM landscape and worth a careful read; specialists seeking quantitative guidance on which paradigm to deploy will need to supplement it with the primary benchmarks it cites rather than relying on the survey alone.

Fairness-Aware Multi- Agent Planning Under Resource Constraints Using Column Generation and Lagrangian Relaxation

P Dewez · pure.tue.nl · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This master's thesis introduces a multi-agent planning framework that combines column generation with Lagrangian relaxation to enforce tunable fairness in capacity-constrained sequential resource allocation, where a centralized linear program coordinates decentralized agent-generated candidate policies. - Why it's important: Reward-only planners under shared-capacity constraints systematically starve low-reward agents (a high-reward agent captured nearly all resource claim in the motivating experiment), a problem relevant to recommender systems, ride-sharing, and compute allocation where long-term trust and equity matter. - How it does it: Fairness (variance of expected resource claims, per-timestep or cumulative scope) is added as a convex soft penalty to the master LP, its gradient is pushed into each agent's reduced-cost subproblem, and the fairness weight λ is either fixed by hand or adapted online via a dual update λ ← λ + α·sign(βf − f)·(e^(k|βf−f|) − 1). - The good: The fairness-reward sweep is thorough and reproducible (5 seeds, 100 Monte Carlo samples, code released at github.com/PaulD153/EquiAgents), showing Jain's index rising from 0.247 to 0.994 while total reward falls from 1918.81 to 864.86 in the high-complexity setting — a clean, quantified trade-off curve. - The missing: There are no external baselines — no comparison against existing fair MDP planning (e.g., Tu et al. 2024's generalized Gini approach), fair multi-agent RL, or hard-constraint LP formulations, so it is impossible to tell whether the method is better or merely different from prior fairness enforcement. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers in fair sequential decision-making who want a worked LP-based alternative to constrained RL and a template for tracing fairness-efficiency frontiers; skip it if you need proven fairness guarantees, realistic-scale evaluation, or comparative evidence, since this is an unpublished master's thesis on a synthetic environment with at most 10 agents.

Problem & Motivation: In centralized multi-agent planning over shared, capacity-limited resources (tourist recommendation, ride-sharing, compute sharing), maximizing total reward under capacity constraints produces persistent resource starvation of some agents — early decisions constrain future options, and prior work either evaluates fairness only post-hoc, uses static penalties that are hard to calibrate, or addresses local fairness without global capacity coordination. The targeted gap, as stated by the author, is that no prior work integrates an online Lagrange multiplier update inside a column-generation planning loop to actively enforce fairness over time, nor charts how standard fairness metrics (Jain, Gini, Nash welfare, minimum share, variance) respond across a continuum of fairness weights in such a framework. Key Idea: Treat fairness as a convex soft penalty in the master LP and decompose its gradient (2/N·(yi,t − ȳt) for stepwise variance) into the agents' reduced-cost objective, so the same column-generation machinery that prices congestion (duals µt from capacity constraints) also prices unfairness — with λ either fixed to sweep the fairness-efficiency frontier or updated online as a dual variable against a target fairness level βf. The stepwise-vs-cumulative fairness scope distinction (penalizing per-timestep imbalance vs. imbalance of horizon-total claims) is the second organizing idea. Methodology: The framework is a column-generation loop over a multi-agent CMDP. Each agent i is represented by candidate policies characterized by expected discounted reward r_i^π, a time-indexed claim vector u_i^π ∈ [0,1]^T, and a state-dependent cost. (1) Master LP (LP1) maximizes Σ x_i^π(r_i^π − Cost_i^π) minus a fairness penalty (stepwise variance Σ_t Var_t or cumulative variance Var_cum, both convex in x) subject to per-timestep capacity constraints on expected claims and normalization Σ_π x_i^π = 1; capacity uncertainty from an exogenous 3-state Markov chain is handled by averaging K sampled capacity trajectories (K = 100 at evaluation). (2) Agent subproblem (LP2) maximizes r_i^π − Cost_i^π − Σ_t µt·u_i,t^π − λΣ_t g_i,t·u_i,t^π over a relaxed claim-profile feasible set F_i (any u ∈ [0,1]^T), adding columns with negative reduced cost. (3) After column generation converges (no negative reduced cost below −10⁻⁵, max 75 iterations), the fairness score is computed and λ is updated via an exponential-form dual update. Critical design decisions: (a) fairness applied as soft penalty rather than hard constraint — justified as enabling frontier exploration but sacrifices guarantees; (b) claims rather than rewards chosen as the fairness quantity — argued for but never ablated against reward-based fairness; (c) the abstracted claim-profile subproblem (policies are arbitrary usage vectors) means the "policies" are far less structured than full MDP policies, a simplification the paper acknowledges only implicitly. Key Results: Experiments span Low (5 agents, T=10), Medium (8 agents, T=15), High (10 agents, T=20) complexity with stochastic capacity (3-state Markov chain), 5 seeds, and λ swept over 0–1000. Under reward-only optimization, Agent 3 (reward scale 100 vs. 5 for others) monopolizes claims (Jain's index 0.733 cumulative, minimum share 0.306). Sweeping λ: in the High/timestep setting, Jain's index rises 0.247→0.994 and inverse Gini 0.233→0.981 while total reward falls 1918.81→864.86; cumulative scope achieves equity at lower λ (Jain ≈ 1.0 at λ=200) and converges in fewer column-generation iterations (High: 19.71 vs. 28.71 mean; Low: 5.67 vs. 9.04). A surprising finding: at small-to-moderate λ, reward can increase (High/timestep reward rises 1918.81→1957.77 at λ=5) before degrading, and timestep scope achieves higher reward than cumulative at moderate λ while incurring higher cost. Monte Carlo rollouts with 95% CIs confirm the same trends with tighter variance at high λ. The online primal–dual loop drives Jain's index to its target (0.95) without manual λ selection, with λ stabilizing once the target is met. Baselines: none — the only comparison is against the authors' own reward-only (λ=0) configuration, so baseline strength is not assessable. Scale is toy-to-small (≤10 agents, ≤20 steps, LP-based). Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely new element is the integration of online Lagrangian dual updates for fairness inside a column-generation planning loop, plus the systematic sweep of fairness weight against five fairness metrics under two scopes — the author's gap analysis (Chapter 3.8) supports that this combination is unreported. The constituent techniques (column generation, Lagrangian relaxation, primal-dual constraint enforcement, variance/Jain/Gini fairness metrics) are all standard; the empirical demonstrations are competent applications of known optimization machinery to a new combination. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are partial: the stepwise-vs-cumulative scope comparison and fixed-vs-adaptive λ comparison are genuine ablations, but the choice of variance as the enforced penalty (versus other metrics listed) and of claims (versus rewards) as the fairness quantity is not ablated. Error reporting is mixed: standard deviations and standard errors are reported for iteration counts, 95% CIs for Monte Carlo results, but no significance tests for the trade-off comparisons. Code is public (https://github.com/PaulD153/EquiAgents) with fixed seeds and configuration files — a strong reproducibility signal. Methodological concerns: (a) no external baselines, so the method is only evaluated against its own unregularized variant (mild Goodhart risk since the fairness penalty and headline fairness measurement both center on variance); (b) all evaluation is on the authors' own synthetic environment; (c) fairness is enforced and measured on expected claims, not realized trajectories — the author acknowledges this; (d) this is an unrefereed master's thesis, so claims have not withstood peer review. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a built planning system run in simulation; no real deployment). - Practical: Yes — the method needs only LP solvers, running on commodity hardware; no GPU or specialized infrastructure is implied. - Efficient: Column generation converges in roughly 5–30 iterations on these instances, but iteration counts and variance grow with agent count and horizon, and no runtime numbers (seconds) are reported, so cost relative to alternatives is unknown. - Effective: The evidence shows the system reshapes expected allocations toward fairness targets in simulation; whether it solves fairness in real allocation problems (realized per-trajectory equity, strategic agent behavior) is untested — the author concedes fairness holds only in expectation. - Scalable: Not tested — the largest configuration is 10 agents over 20 steps; the claim of "promising prospects in larger-scale systems" is asserted, not demonstrated, and the LP master could grow badly since columns are full-horizon claim vectors. The work delivers a software artifact (code repository, EquiAgents) but no trained models, library packaging, or dataset. Strengths: - The fairness-gradient decomposition into the reduced-cost subproblem is a clean technical move: it reuses column generation's existing dual-price interface to transmit fairness pressure to decentralized agents without new machinery, and the convexity argument for the variance penalties in the master variables is correct. - The dual-scope evaluation design (optimize under one scope, measure under both) is an unusually careful empirical setup that exposes a real finding: fairness enforcement does not trivially generalize across scopes, and cumulative scope is a better default (faster convergence, comparable or better net value in Medium/High settings). - The demonstration that online primal-dual λ adaptation reaches a 0.95 Jain target without manual tuning is a concrete, useful result for practitioners who cannot grid-search fairness weights. - Honest, specific limitation discussion (expectation-only fairness, centralized synchronization, stationarity assumptions) that accurately maps the method's boundaries. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The author states: (1) column generation plans in expectation without optimizing over stochastic outcomes or belief states, limiting robustness under risk; (2) fairness holds in expectation over expected claims, insufficient for per-sample fairness domains like healthcare; (3) coordination assumes full observability and global synchronization via a centralized LP, ruling out distributed or partially connected deployments; (4) fixed population and stationary rewards — no nonstationarity in goals, reward drift, or evolving capacity; (5) standard fairness indices may not capture domain-specific ethical norms. This is a direct, non-defensive treatment of limitations — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No comparison against any prior fairness-enforcement method: Tu et al. (2024) generalized-Gini planning, Jiang & Lu (2019) FEN, Wen et al. (2021) fairness-constrained MDPs, or even a hard-fairness-constraint LP baseline. Without these, the paper cannot support its implicit claim that the soft-Lagrangian route is preferable. - Only variance is actually implemented as the enforced penalty despite five metrics being evaluated; whether the framework "can accommodate various fairness metrics" (a stated contribution) is demonstrated for exactly one, and non-differentiable metrics (Jain, NSW, min-share, Gini) would require different machinery. - The agent subproblem operates over abstract claim profiles (any u ∈ [0,1]^T) rather than policies executable in an MDP — the connection back to actual sequential decision-making policies, and whether generated claim profiles are realizable, is never validated. - The reported reward increase at small λ (e.g., 1918.81→1957.77) is unexplained and unexamined; if fairness regularization acts as a useful regularizer, this deserves analysis, and if it is seed noise, error bars on the reward sweep are missing. - Only one reward-asymmetry pattern (single dominant agent) is tested; fairness behavior under multiple competing high-reward agents, correlated preferences, or strategic manipulation of the planner is unexplored. - No wall-clock runtimes, LP sizes, or memory figures are reported anywhere, making the scalability claims unverifiable. Bottom Line: A solid, honestly reported thesis that delivers a usable LP-based template for tracing fairness-efficiency frontiers in capacity-constrained multi-agent planning, but with no external baselines and toy-scale synthetic evaluation it reads as a promising proof of concept rather than evidence that this beats existing fair-MDP methods — practitioners in fair sequential decision-making will find the scope analysis and adaptive-λ result worth borrowing; anyone seeking validated state-of-the-art fairness enforcement should look to the peer-reviewed fair-RL and fair-MDP literature first.

S Das, S Mittal, R Singhal · aclanthology.org · neural symbolic - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces ReThink, a training-free four-stage pipeline that reformulates adversarial arithmetic word-problem solving as Weighted MaxSAT/MaxSMT optimization over confidence-weighted Z3 soft constraints, cross-verified against a parallel Chain-of-Thought path. - Why it's important: LLM arithmetic reasoning is brittle to distractor insertion and contradictory facts — perturbations that a deployed tutor or question-answering system will realistically encounter — and adversarial training or intrinsic self-correction have not solved this. - How it does it: The LLM first classifies each statement as core/structural/distractor/contradiction and strips noise, then the cleaned facts are encoded as weighted Z3 soft constraints (structural facts at w=100, core numerics w∈[95,100], suspicious statements w∈[5,15]) so the solver can sacrifice low-weight adversarial statements, and disagreements with a parallel CoT run are adjudicated by a cross-verification LLM call. - The good: The ablation and per-component flip analysis are unusually honest: soft constraints helped 41 samples and hurt 0, replacing them with hard constraints costs 1.71 pp of adversarial accuracy, and removing Z3 entirely costs 1.83 pp — the authors do not over-attribute gains to a single component. - The missing: The closest related system, SatLM (declarative Z3 translation without the decomposition/weighting machinery), is cited but never run as a baseline, so the paper cannot show that the weighting and dual-path additions — not just solver use — cause the +3.29 pp gain; no significance tests, seeds, or released code are reported. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers working on LLM robustness or neuro-symbolic defenses who want a careful, self-critical evaluation template; skimmable if you only want a large effect — the headline gain is 3.29 pp at 3–6× the LLM call cost.

Problem & Motivation: LLMs solving arithmetic word problems lose accuracy when problems contain irrelevant distractor sentences, contradictory restatements of a fact, or a reversed queried quantity — the GSM-Plus setting shows degradation of roughly 17 pp for GPT-4.1 CoT (95.62% clean → 78.33% adversarial). Practitioners deploying math-assistant systems need defenses against such semantic noise. The paper argues prior options each fail: adversarial training is expensive and generalizes poorly; intrinsic self-correction often does not help (Huang et al. 2023) and CoT can rationalize biased answers (Turpin et al. 2023); PAL delegates arithmetic but still trusts the model's translation; strict solver-based methods (SatLM) break when the parsed specification is wrong. The gap is a defense that tolerates conflicting extractions rather than failing on them. Key Idea: Encode extracted facts not as hard constraints but as confidence-weighted soft constraints in a Weighted MaxSAT/MaxSMT objective (σ̂ = argmax Σ wⱼ·𝟙(σ ⊨ cⱼ)), so that if an adversarial statement slips through as a low-weight constraint conflicting with high-weight core relations, the Z3 Optimize engine sacrifices it — the solver itself performs conflict rejection. This is combined with an upstream LLM decomposition stage (strip distractors/contradictions using a primacy heuristic: first occurrence of a fact wins) and a downstream dual-path check (CoT on the original text vs. solver on the cleaned text), with disagreement (≈5% of cases) sent to a cross-verification LLM call. Methodology: Four-stage pipeline (training-free, prompting only, temperature 0.0): (1) Adversarial Decomposition — LLM classifies statements into CORE / STRUCTURAL / DISTRACTOR / CONTRADICTION and produces a cleaned problem; falls back to original text on failure. (2) Symbolic Translation and Solving — a semantic prompt maps the cleaned text to Z3 (v4.12.2, 15 s timeout) soft constraints via add_soft, with typed variables (Int vs Real to avoid integer division), a fixed weight hierarchy (structural = 100, explicit numerics 95–100, ambiguous 40–60, suspicious 5–15), and up to 3 translation-retry attempts on syntax/runtime/timeout errors. (3) Neural Verification — standard CoT on the original adversarial problem, deliberately a different representation. (4) Agreement-Based Decision — return agreed answers, fall back to the successful path on partial failure, otherwise a cross-verification call receives the problem, Z3 code/output, and CoT trace and adjudicates. The objective is the weighted-maximum-satisfaction sum in Equation 1. Critical design decisions: the primacy heuristic for contradictions (plausible but unvalidated, and risky when a perturbation legitimately changes a value); running CoT on the raw text to decorrelate path errors (well-motivated, though the paper concedes both paths share the backbone LLM); and the specific weight ranges (not ablated). Key Results: On a balanced 2,400-example GSM-Plus subset (8 attack types × 300) with GPT-4.1: ReThink 81.62% adversarial / 96.31% clean / 14.69 pp gap vs. CoT 78.33%/95.62%/17.29, PAL 78.00%, Self-Verification 77.79% — a +3.29 pp adversarial gain over the strongest baseline. Per-attack gains: reversing operation +7.33 pp, distraction insertion +4.33 pp, numerical substitution and adding operation +4.00 pp each, but only +1.00 pp on format conversion and problem understanding, and 0% on critical thinking for all methods (300 cases requiring detection of missing premises). Z3–CoT paths agree on 95% of adversarial examples; the 79 net corrected answers come from the 5% disagreement slice. Ablations (n=2400): remove Z3 → 79.79% (−1.83), hard constraints → 79.92% (−1.71), remove cross-verification → 80.54% (−1.08), remove decomposition → 81.00% (−0.62). Component flip counts: soft constraints +41/0, cross-verification +27/1, decomposition +22/7. Small-model transfer: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B (n=200) 63.00% vs CoT 54.50% (+8.50) but PAL reaches 62.50%; Llama-3-8B (n=300) 54.67% vs 52.00% (+2.67) with PAL at 53.67%. Cost: 3–6 LLM calls per sample vs 1 (CoT/PAL) and 2 (Self-Verification); latency not measured. Baselines are current prompting paradigms but omit solver-based competitors; scale is a standard benchmark, not stress-scale. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (weighted-soft-constraint MaxSAT/MaxSMT formulation for adversarial robustness) combined with competent engineering of known pieces (SatLM-style declarative Z3 translation, GSM-Plus-style decomposition, verifier-style adjudication). The genuinely new element is the soft/weighted formulation so the solver can discard conflicting low-weight adversarial facts — the hard-constraint ablation (−1.71 pp) substantiates this. The four-stage pipeline itself is a straightforward composition; the paper's framing of "conflict tolerance" as the mechanism is its main conceptual contribution. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations exist for all four stages and are complemented by sample-level flip analysis (helped/hurt counts, Appendix Table 8), which is above average for this venue; the authors explicitly note non-additivity of component gains and the limits of aggregate counts. However: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests — a +3.29 pp difference on 2,400 examples (~79 answers) is plausibly within prompt-variance noise; the weight ranges [95,100]/[40,60]/[5,15] and the primacy heuristic are not ablated; fixed evaluation is on the same benchmark family the design was motivated by, which is fine, but there is no second benchmark to test generalization. No code, prompts, or logs are stated as released. Methodological concerns: missing SatLM/Logic-LM baselines (the closest solver-based competitors), unequal sample sizes for the SLM analysis (200 vs 300) with no explanation, and per-attack tables for small models lacking the ReThink-∆ column that the GPT-4.1 table has. The honest treatment of the gap metric (Self-Verification has a smaller gap but lower absolute accuracy) is a credibility positive. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a prompted pipeline with an external solver, run on commercial APIs and open-weight models). - Practical: Yes — GPT-4.1 via Azure API, Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3-8B locally, Z3 v4.12.2; nothing exotic. - Efficient: Expensive relative to alternatives — 3–6 LLM calls per sample (3–6× CoT) for +3.29 pp on GPT-4.1; solver timeouts at 15 s add latency that was not measured. - Effective: Partially — evidence shows gains on seven determinable-answer perturbation types, but 0% on critical-thinking (missing-premise) cases and only +1.00 pp on two categories, so it solves noise rejection, not full adversarial robustness. - Scalable: Untested beyond 2,400 examples and 8B-parameter open models; cost scales linearly in calls and the paper only claims, not demonstrates, broader applicability. Delivers a paper-form method with described prompts; no artifact (library, dataset, or weights) is reported as released. Strengths: - The soft-constraint weighting idea is a real, defensible mechanism, and the paper isolates it: the hard-constraint ablation (−1.71 pp) and the 41-helped/0-hurt flip count link the formulation to specific corrected samples rather than relying on aggregate accuracy alone. - The agreement analysis is unusually candid: the authors state upfront that 95% path agreement cannot certify correctness and that residual failures are cases where both paths are jointly wrong — they do not oversell the dual-path design. - Component-level attribution across four ablations plus per-attack breakdowns lets a reader see exactly where the method helps (reversing operation, +7.33 pp; distraction insertion, +4.33 pp) and where it does not (format conversion, +1.00 pp; critical thinking, 0%). - Honest cost accounting: the paper reports the 3–6 call overhead and quantifies the cheaper decomposition-only variant (+1.46 pp at 2 calls), giving practitioners a real trade-off curve. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The limitations section is direct and substantive: (1) dependence on accurate NL→constraint translation, with failure modes including confidently wrong symbolic answers; (2) solver overhead and timeouts, with the concession that only call counts, not latency, were measured; (3) 0% on critical thinking because soft constraints cannot supply missing premises, and the pipeline stage causing the failure is not isolated; (4) the 95% agreement rate is not a correctness certificate; (5) evaluation restricted to GSM-Plus arithmetic, leaving generalization to other reasoning domains open. This is a model of confronting limitations rather than minimizing them. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No SatLM baseline despite SatLM being the cited closest system; without it, the reader cannot separate "using a solver helps" from "our weighting/decomposition/cross-verification helps." - The primacy heuristic (first fact wins) is unsafe for answer-changing perturbations such as numerical substitution, where the later value is the correct one; the +4.00 pp there suggests it mostly works, but no analysis of when it backfires is given, even though decomposition hurt 7 samples. - No statistical significance or seed variance for a headline margin of +3.29 pp (~79/2,400 answers) built on prompt-engineered, temperature-0 GPT-4.1 calls. - The critical-thinking failure (300/2,400 examples at 0% for every method) compresses all methods' aggregate scores by ~12.5 pp; a per-determinable-category comparison would show materially larger relative differences, but also that the benchmark is partly measuring a capability (premise-adequacy detection) the method explicitly lacks. - Weight ranges, decomposition prompt, and cross-verification prompt are not ablated or released; results may be prompt-sensitive. - Small-model evaluations (n=200, n=300) have wide per-attack cells (e.g., 8–23 examples per cell in Table 7) — per-attack conclusions there are not statistically meaningful. Bottom Line: A practitioner building robustness into LLM math pipelines gains a concrete, well-ablated recipe — weighted soft constraints in Z3 plus decomposition and disagreement-triggered verification — but should weigh the 3–6× call cost against modest margins (+3.29 pp), the missing SatLM comparison, and the absence of significance testing before adopting it over simply running a declarative solver baseline.

TSE-Bridge: Connecting Industrial Time-Series Events with Semantic Maintenance Evidence through Traceable Graph Relations

Y Peng, X Xie · ceur-ws.org · karypis - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces TSE-Bridge, a pipeline and typed-graph schema that materializes explicit, provenance-bearing Bridge relations between time-series-derived industrial events and semantic maintenance records (measurements, fault cases, work orders, documents), and evaluates ranking over those relations. - Why it's important: Industrial maintenance question-answering requires connecting sensor events to maintenance evidence that uses different identifiers, time scales, and record types; flattening both into text destroys the asset/time/type/scope context needed to judge whether retrieved evidence is usable. - How it does it: Hard admissibility gates (evidence type, exact-asset or declared family scope, non-empty provenance) create first-class Bridge relation records before any ranking; ranking is then a transparent weighted feature fusion over already-admissible candidates. - The good: A one-component-at-a-time ablation with confidence intervals identifies exact-device alignment as the dominant positive component (removal costs 0.1009 nDCG@10, 95% CI [0.0425, 0.1647], p<0.001), and 88.33% of the 377 events obtain a source-bearing relation — the connection stage is genuinely executed end to end. - The missing: The evaluation labels are generated by the same deterministic feature rules as the scorer (a metadata-derived target, not human relevance), and the proposed ranker (0.7266 nDCG@10) is beaten by its own GraphRAG analogue (0.7903) and by dropping its Bridge-prior term (0.8065) — so no configuration in the paper demonstrates the ranker's value under an independent target. - Read it or not: Worth reading if you build industrial graph-RAG or provenance-aware retrieval systems and want a concrete, honest case study of the connection-then-rank decomposition; skip it if you need evidence of retrieval quality against independent relevance judgments or at production scale.
