Problem & Motivation Teams building unified multimodal models (understanding + generation + editing + interleaved outputs) must handle ever-longer visual token sequences: 2K-resolution images and multi-image chains inflate the quadratic cost of full attention. Prior unified models either use full attention throughout (BAGEL, SenseNova-U1, Transfusion) or shared discrete visual tokenizers for context reuse (UniAR); the latter does not extend to continuous visual generation, where an in-progress image exists only as a noisy latent that must not leak into later predictions. The gap the paper targets is how to combine linear-cost recurrent attention with continuous flow-matching generation in one model while preserving a clean separation between reusable visual context and transient denoising state. Key Idea The single core insight is the public-context/private-target rule applied consistently across two attention operators: a noisy visual block may read the public prefix but its contributions — attention keys/values in full-attention layers, recurrent-state and convolution-history updates in GatedDeltaNet layers — are discarded, and only clean visual representations (t=0 latents or teacher-forced ground-truth encodings) update the shared state. Once this rule is stated, the rest of the system (MoT expert routing, flow matching, packing) reconstructs from standard components. Methodology The pipeline is: (1) Unified representation — text via language embeddings, understanding images via a Qwen3.5 vision encoder, generation targets/clean context via a frozen Wan2.2 VAE with patchification and a latent adapter, plus noise-level and positional embeddings. (2) Hybrid MoT backbone — token-type expert routing (text/semantic tokens to an understanding expert, VAE latents to a generation expert) with expert-specific normalization, attention projections, and FFNs, over layers that alternate full attention and GatedDeltaNet recurrence (state update S_i = alpha_i S_{i-1} + beta_i k_i(v_i - S_{i-1}^T k_i)^T); experts share the recurrent state, so expert switching does not reset context. (3) Joint objective — L = lambda_text L_text + lambda_vis L_vis, with autoregressive cross-entropy on assistant text and conditional flow matching (z_t = (1-t)z_0 + t*epsilon, velocity target u_t = epsilon - z_0, MSE loss). (4) Interleaved generation — sequence factorized over blocks p(B_1..B_K) = prod p(B_k | B_<k); training uses Eq. (9)-style sequences [T1, N1(t1), C1, T2, N2] with public state update S^pub_{b+1} = R(B_b, S^pub_b) for public blocks and unchanged state for private blocks. (5) Data — 159.66M generation samples, 213.39M understanding samples (99.98M captioning, 97.90M visual QA, 9.99M OCR, 4.51M grounding, 1.00M GUI), 0.50M editing, 624.8K interleaved sequences, 97.90M text-only, assembled by task adapters and online token-budget packing with cross-sample isolation; video interleaved data built from event-driven keyframe annotation of 24.24M source clips. (6) Training — four stages (Joint Multimodal Foundation at 256-scale, Progressive Resolution Scaling at 512, High-Resolution Refinement to 2K, SFT), AdamW, LR 1e-4 constant, bfloat16, FSDP hybrid sharding; then exploratory post-SFT video adaptation (5e-5 LR, frozen understanding branch) on 24.24M generation and 3.29M editing clips. Critical design decisions: the blockwise state-retention rule (well-motivated and clearly formalized, but never ablated), starting from the pre-trained Qwen3.5 hybrid backbone (justified by cost, but confounds attribution), and teacher-forced clean context during training versus re-encoded outputs at inference (a train/test mismatch the paper does not analyze). Key Results Understanding: MME-P 1766.0, MME-S 2470.3, MMBench 86.7, MMVP 72.0, MM-Vet 73.4, MathVista 77.2 — highest among listed unified models and above Qwen3.5-9B on MME-S, MMBench, and MMVP; MMMU-Val 56.7 trails MetaQuery-XL (58.6) and BAGEL (55.3 is close). Generation: GenEval 0.83 overall (counting 0.68, position 0.67, attribute binding 0.73 are weak), below LLaDA2.0-Uni (0.89) and Lumina-DiMOO (0.88); DPG-Bench 80.54, below BAGEL (85.07) and LLaDA2.0-Uni (87.76), and well below specialists Qwen-Image (88.32) and Seedream 3.0 (88.27). Editing: ImgEdit overall 3.13 with a different judge (Qwen3-VL-235B), explicitly flagged as not directly comparable; weakest categories are extraction (1.68) and hybrid editing (1.62). Efficiency (H20-3e GPU, BF16, batch 1): image generation median latency 7.27s at 512x512 and 14.16s at 1024x1024 versus BAGEL's 11.76s and 45.80s (1.62x and 3.23x speedups); at 2048x2048 UniSpark (51.48s, 79.56 tokens/s) beats SenseNova-U1 (58.34s) but uses 62.74 GB versus 37.39 GB peak memory. Understanding latency sits between baselines (6.02s at 1,024 visual tokens versus BAGEL's 3.76s and SenseNova-U1's 7.32s). Interleaved generation, sequence editing, video generation, and video editing are shown only as qualitative examples. Baselines are current (2025-2026 models), but several understanding scores are inherited from BAGEL's comparison and generation/editing baselines follow LLaDA2.0-Uni's numbers rather than re-evaluation. Scale is genuinely large on data (hundreds of millions of samples) and resolution (2K), tested on a ~9B-per-branch model. Novelty Classification NEW METHOD (partial) plus ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. The genuinely non-obvious element is the blockwise public/private information-flow protocol — specifically the rule that noisy flow-matching targets read but do not update the shared linear-attention recurrent state and full-attention context — applied to continuous visual generation in a hybrid backbone. Everything else is a competent combination of existing ideas: the MoT formulation from BAGEL, the GatedDeltaNet hybrid backbone from Qwen3.5, flow matching from Lipman et al., and Transfusion-style joint objectives; the paper is candid that it 'investigates' and 'characterizes' rather than invents the hybrid-attention machinery. Rigor & Reproducibility The report is unusually transparent about protocol caveats (MMBench answer-extraction differences, ImgEdit judge mismatch, configured sampling weights versus consumed tokens, per-branch parameter conventions, preliminary SFT settings). However: no ablations are presented — not for hybrid versus full attention, not for the state-retention rule, not for the packing scheme, not for expert routing; no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported; interleaved and video results are qualitative only, self-selected from 12 paired runs with the authors admitting failures ('flame direction and bell contraction remain imperfect'). No code, model weights, or data release is stated; only a project page (https://lucaria-academy.github.io/UniSpark/) is given. Baseline scores are largely imported from other papers' tables rather than re-run, and the paper correctly attributes this as a limitation. No Goodhart-style benchmark development issue is evident, but the headline efficiency gains are measured against only two unified baselines at batch size 1 on a single H20 GPU. Deployability: (4-property check) Profile: EMPIRICAL (a trained system with measured benchmarks and latency). - Practical: Runs on a single H20-3e GPU in BF16 at batch size 1, though 62.74 GB peak allocated memory at 2048x2048 generation exceeds most commodity accelerators. - Efficient: Generation is 1.62x-3.23x faster than BAGEL at 512-1024 resolutions and faster than SenseNova-U1 at 2048, at the cost of higher memory (62.74 GB vs 37.39 GB at 2048); understanding is slower and more memory-hungry than BAGEL. - Effective: Evidence shows competitive understanding and mid-tier generation/editing (GenEval 0.83, DPG 80.54, ImgEdit 3.13 reference-only), so it solves unification and latency but does not match specialist generators on prompt adherence or unified diffusion peers on composition. - Scalable: Tested to 2K resolution and hundreds of millions of training samples; linear-attention cost suggests further scaling headroom, but the paper only claims this, and no >2K or longer-sequence stress test is reported. Deliverable status: paper plus project page only; no software artifact, weights, or dataset release is mentioned. Strengths - The public-context/private-target state-retention rule (Eq. 3 and Fig. 5) is a clean, reusable technical contribution that solves a real problem — reusing continuous visual outputs as context without propagating transient denoising noise — and is enforced consistently across both attention operators. - The engineering infrastructure is genuinely non-trivial and well documented: online token-budget packing that preserves sample isolation, block structure, and per-operator attention metadata across heterogeneous multimodal tasks is a hard systems problem, and the paper describes it at implementable depth (Tables 3-4, Sec. 4.7, 5.7). - Evaluation honesty: the authors proactively flag every comparison caveat (judge mismatch on ImgEdit, inherited baseline scores, protocol differences, weight-versus-token mixture ambiguity), which raises confidence in the numbers that are reported. - Breadth at scale: a single model covering understanding, 2K generation, editing, interleaved prediction, and exploratory video adaptation, with data curation (including grounded keyframe-annotated interleaved data from video) described in reproducible detail. Author-Acknowledged Limitations The authors explicitly state: MMMU and some reasoning gaps (56.7 vs MetaQuery-XL's 58.6; Qwen3.5-9B higher on MM-Vet and MathVista) and that size/data/protocol differences prevent attributing results to hybrid attention; weak compositional control (counting 0.68, position 0.67, attribute binding 0.73 on GenEval; DPG Attribute/Relation/Other categories lowest); ImgEdit scores are reference-only due to a different judge; interleaved cases are hand-selected and imperfect; video work is 'exploratory'; efficiency measurements 'do not isolate the effect of hybrid attention'; data-source counts are registered pools, not deduplicated training counts; SFT settings are preliminary. This is a credibility positive — limitations are confronted directly and in detail rather than minimized. Analyst-Identified Gaps - The central hypothesis — that hybrid attention benefits unified multimodal modeling — is never tested: there is no full-attention-only control trained on the same data, so all results are confounded by the choice of the pre-trained Qwen3.5 backbone, the 373M+ sample data mixture, and the four-stage curriculum. - The train/inference mismatch for clean context (teacher-forced ground-truth encodings during training versus re-encoded model outputs at inference) is described but never quantified; exposure bias in interleaved chains could be substantial and is unmeasured. - No interleaved or sequence-editing quantitative benchmark exists in the paper — the capability that most directly motivates the context-handling design is validated only by cherry-picked examples from 12 runs. - The efficiency comparison covers only two baselines at batch size 1 on one GPU type; throughput at realistic batch sizes, on other accelerators, and against stronger generation-speed baselines is absent. - The GatedDeltaNet state-retention rule's interaction with long interleaved chains (how much context the fixed-size recurrent state actually retains across multiple images) is unanalyzed; linear-attention state compression could silently degrade editing consistency over many turns. - No release of code, weights, or data is stated, which limits verification of the packing and state-rule implementations, the paper's most intricate parts. Bottom Line A practitioner building unified multimodal systems should read this for the blockwise public/private state-retention protocol and the unusually honest, well-documented training infrastructure, but should not expect evidence that hybrid attention itself — rather than scale, data, or the inherited backbone — drives the results, and there is no released artifact to build on.

#189 — Moderately Innovative (50)

Extracting System Prompt of LLM Services in Complex (Agentic) Settings: Hierarchical Optimization and Reliable Evaluation Metrics

S Li, C Lin, X Yang, C Shen, Y Chen, Z Zhao · arxiv.org · Recommended articles
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces ExtraHerO, a black-box system-prompt extraction attack that decomposes extraction into a hierarchical, template-guided reconstruction loop driven by LLM-generated text gradients, and pairs it with a new three-dimensional evaluation framework (fidelity, functionality, adversarial utility) for complex/agentic LLM services. - Why it's important: System prompts now embed tool schemas, execution logic, and safety guardrails that constitute commercial intellectual property, but prior extraction attacks and token-overlap metrics were built for short, linear chatbot prompts and degrade or mislead on modern agentic services where only post-processed outputs (e.g., discrete UI actions) are observable. - How it does it: The core move is Decompose-then-Optimize: a pre-defined structural prompt template splits extraction into per-anchor sub-tasks, each optimized via an attacker LLM loop (probing agent + analyst) whose 'textual gradient' is the semantic residual between the current hypothesis and observed feedback, with a dual-track information-gain/cosine-stability monitor triggering early stop or restart. - The good: The evaluation is the strongest part — a five-tier complexity taxonomy (L1 persona to L5 production PaaS prompts of ~4,000 tokens), six real GUI agents across mobile/web/PC, and a demonstrated pilot showing all baselines collapse under post-processed outputs (e.g., SentenceSim drops from 62.46 to 42.85), which credibly motivates the new threat model. - The missing: The victim chatbot is only GPT-4o, the L1–L3 evaluation prompts are synthesized by GPT-4o itself (the same model family as the victim and likely the attacker LLM), and query budgets/costs for ExtraHerO versus baselines are not reported — so the efficiency claim and generality across victim models rest on thin evidence. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on LLM/agent security (prompt leakage, red-teaming, or defense design), because the threat-model analysis and the adversarial-utility metric are genuinely useful; skip it if you want a validated, efficiently implemented attack, since the artifact and cost analysis are incomplete.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (42) is the primary weakness: the victim is only GPT-4o, L1–L3 prompts are synthesized by the same model, the headline SKM metric is an unvalidated LLM-scored measure, query budgets are absent, some agent cells rest on 1–2 trials, and it is an unrevised preprint. Completeness (50) and Resilience (45) suffer because the single-victim circularity and metric validation gaps are never confronted, and Impact (35) is low with no released artifact. The threat-model formulation and adversarial-utility metric keep Novelty (68) respectable, but the evidence base cannot carry the claims. Weighted composite: 0.20*68 + 0.25*42 + 0.15*55 + 0.15*50 + 0.15*45 + 0.10*35 = 50.

Problem & Motivation: Operators of Prompt-as-a-Service platforms and agent vendors face a concrete economic threat: an adversary who recovers the system prompt can replicate a service's functionality, including its internal security architecture, at near-zero cost. Existing extraction attacks assume (1) short, unstructured prompts and (2) full visibility of the model's raw textual response. The authors show both assumptions now fail: production prompts are 4,000+ token modular programs with role, formatting, tool, reasoning, and safety components (their L1–L5 taxonomy), and agentic services expose only post-processed outputs such as UI actions. A secondary problem is evaluation validity: token-level metrics like BLEU/ROUGE-L reward recovering non-functional filler and even inverted/refusal phrasing (their Table 2 example: a refusal paraphrase scores ROUGE-L 84.00 versus 27.27 for a structurally correct extraction), so reported attack success has been partly an artifact of the metrics. Key Idea: The key idea is to exploit the LLM's drive toward contextual consistency by seeding each query with previously recovered prompt segments as 'semantic anchors': once a template skeleton is partially filled, the victim model treats follow-up extraction probes as coherent extensions of its own established persona and leaks the next component. This hierarchical anchoring, combined with treating the attacker LLM's feedback as an approximate gradient over a discrete prompt space (the OPRO/TextGrad insight applied to extraction rather than instruction tuning), is the reconstructable trick. Methodology: ExtraHerO has three modules. (1) Hierarchical Multi-Stage Decomposition: a pre-defined template (role, input format, workflow, output format, tool schemas, constraints) defines semantic anchors; each recovered segment is aggregated into the cumulative state, which conditions subsequent probes. (2) Iterative Refinement via Text Gradients (ExtractOpt): a Probing Agent P generates adversarial queries from a fixed 6-action space (components, number, details, usage, process, orthogonal break), the victim's response y_t is the only observation, and an Analyst G jointly outputs the current stage hypothesis and a text gradient capturing the semantic residual; the loop runs for up to T steps per stage. (3) Dual-Track Convergence Control: a sliding-window monitor computes incremental lexical gain IG_i = |T_i \ T_{i-1}|/|T_{i-1}| on the prompt track and cosine similarity between successive gradients on the gradient track; joint stagnation triggers early stop (Eq. 12) and the pathological pattern of stable gradients with abnormal token gain triggers a restart via an injected 'orthogonal break' meta-instruction (Eq. 13). Evaluation introduces sentence-level similarity, Structural Keyword Matching (SKM, an LLM-extracted keyword-recall metric), functionality via response similarity and action recall, and adversarial utility as the ASR delta of a downstream indirect prompt-injection attack with versus without the extracted prompt. Critical design decisions: the fixed template is justified only by appeal to common agentic prompt structure; the restart trigger thresholds (ε_ig = 0.15, ε_sim = 0.90) are tuned empirically on the same setup they are evaluated on; and the attack's reliance on GPT-4o-grade instruction following is acknowledged but not ablated. Key Results: On the chatbot setting (GPT-4o victim, 150 prompts across five complexity levels), ExtraHerO achieves 75.07 SentenceSim and 30.89 SKM versus the best baselines PRSA (62.57) and RTS (19.96), and reaches 76.67% downstream prompt-injection ASR versus 13.33% without an extracted prompt — average improvements of 12.5% fidelity, 2.3% functionality, and 6.0% adversarial utility. On six GUI agents (MobileAgent, AppAgent, BrowserUse, SeeAct, Agent-S, UFO), baselines essentially fail (SKM 0.00 for O2P/PRSA on most agents) while ExtraHerO reaches SKM of 76.92 (MobileAgent), 33.33 (AppAgent), 26.67 (BrowserUse), 34.62 (Agent-S), and 17.07 (UFO), with action recall up to 82.02 (BrowserUse) where most baselines score 0. Notable findings: token-level metrics rank baselines differently than structural metrics, confirming the metric-inflation argument; SeeAct's verbose tool descriptions cap SKM despite high semantic similarity; an ablation shows adding HMSD to IRTG alone decreases SKM (17.08 → 13.55), with the full configuration (21.47) needed for HMSD to help via DTCC as a regulator. Under an instruction-based defense, ExtraHerO's SKM drops from 49.90 to 14.60. Baselines (Naive, RTS, output2prompt, PRSA, T-GPS) are recent and reasonably strong, though the chatbot victim is a single model and agent results carry no variance estimates. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION + NEW METHOD + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel elements are the agentic threat model (post-processed-only observability), the hierarchical anchor-based decomposition of the extraction task, the adversarial-utility metric, and the empirical demonstration that existing attacks collapse under these conditions. The text-gradient optimizer itself is a direct application of known LLM-as-optimizer techniques (OPRO, TextGrad, ProTeGi) to a new objective, and the template scaffolding is a competent engineering choice rather than a new algorithmic primitive. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations exist and are informative — they show each component's contribution and honestly surface that HMSD alone hurts SKM, an unusual and credible result. Standard deviations are reported for chatbot fidelity (e.g., 75.07 ± 10.49), but agent tables show single-run point estimates with no seeds or significance tests, and the adversarial-utility agent experiments appear to use very few trials (counts as low as 1–2 in Figure 8). No code, data, or artifact release URL is mentioned. Methodological concerns: (1) the L1–L3 evaluation prompts are synthesized by GPT-4o, the same model serving as victim, creating a self-referential setup; (2) the SKM metric is itself computed by an LLM with an author-written extraction prompt, so the headline structural-fidelity numbers depend on an unvalidated, potentially circular metric; (3) ε_ig and ε_sim are tuned on the evaluated setup (Goodhart risk); (4) query-cost comparisons between methods are absent, so the claimed efficiency advantage of early stopping is unsubstantiated relative to baselines. The paper is an arXiv preprint (2611.04803), not peer-reviewed. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (an attack framework with experiments; no deployed system). Practical: Yes — the attack needs only public API access to a victim and a capable attacker LLM, so it runs on commercially available services. Efficient: Unclear — dual-track convergence control is designed to save queries, but no query counts or dollar costs per successful extraction are reported for any method. Effective: The evidence supports extraction of structural logic on the tested agents (SKM up to 76.92, action recall up to 82.02), but effectiveness collapses under even a simple instruction-based defense (SKM 49.90 → 14.60), so the real-world threat is conditional on absent defenses. Scalable: Not tested — L5 production prompts (~4,000 tokens) yield the weakest relative performance and SeeAct-style verbose prompts already degrade SKM to 4.00, suggesting scaling to larger prompt spaces is an open failure mode. The work delivers no reusable software artifact; it stops at paper form plus appendix prompts. Strengths: - The threat-model revision is well-executed and empirically grounded: the five-tier prompt-complexity taxonomy and the raw-versus-post-processed output pilot (Figure 3) constitute the paper's most transferable contribution and cleanly motivate the method. - The adversarial-utility metric reframes extraction risk in terms a defender cares about (does the leak enable downstream attacks?), and the measured ASR lift (13.33% → 76.67% on chatbots) is a persuasive risk quantification. - The ablation is unusually honest: reporting that HMSD alone reduces SKM by ~21% relative, and explaining DTCC as a necessary regulator, indicates the authors ran controls that could have falsified their design. - The metric-inflation analysis (Table 2) is a concrete, reproducible demonstration that BLEU/ROUGE-style fidelity scores reward semantically inverted extractions. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that none of the tested attacks, including ExtraHerO, were designed to bypass defenses, and show all attacks degrade substantially under an instruction-based defense. They acknowledge SeeAct's low SKM stems from verbose, redundant target prompts (an information-bottleneck limit), and the conclusion flags query-cost reduction and evaluation on tool-augmented/multimodal systems as open problems. They confront the defense limitation directly, which is credible; however, they do not address single-victim-model narrowness or the synthetic-prompt circularity anywhere. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The attacker LLM identity is never explicitly specified; if it is GPT-4o (as the victim-model choice rationale implies), the attack and victim share a model, and cross-model transfer of the attack is untested. - L1–L3 evaluation prompts are generated by GPT-4o from templates, so the attack's measured advantage may partly reflect exploiting its own generator's stylistic regularities rather than a general extraction capability. - SKM is LLM-scored with an author-written prompt; no human agreement study or validation against expert judgment is provided, yet SKM carries the headline claims. - Query budgets are absent for all methods, so the efficiency contribution of DTCC (one of three headline modules) is asserted, not measured. - Adversarial-utility agent experiments appear to run on single-digit trial counts for some cells, which cannot support the reported percentage differences. - Only one, weak, inference-time defense is tested; prompt-hardening and fine-tuning defenses are cited but not evaluated, so the defensive outlook is incomplete. - The paper contains a duplicated Conclusion section (Sections 7 and 8 are identical), indicating weak final review; small typos in equations/tables ('W~e', 'ExtractOpt' labels) further suggest a rushed preprint. Bottom Line: A practitioner in LLM/agent security gains real value from the threat-model analysis, the L1–L5 complexity taxonomy, and the adversarial-utility metric, but should treat the attack's headline numbers as preliminary given the GPT-4o self-referential setup, unvalidated LLM-scored SKM metric, and missing query-cost accounting — read it for the problem framing and evaluation framework, not as a deployable attack toolkit.

#190 — Moderately Innovative (49)

An examination of the financial reporting quality of public-private partnerships and emerging growth companies .

ID Harr · minds.wisc.edu · generating environments for agent testing in enterprises - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This doctoral dissertation (two essays) empirically tests whether emerging growth company (EGC) status under the JOBS Act and participation in public–private partnership (PPP)-like government contracting are associated with financial reporting quality (FRQ) in U.S. public firms, using standard accrual-quality and earnings-management measures on 2011–2024 panel data. - Why it's important: Regulators, auditors, and contracting agencies need to know whether scaled disclosure relief (EGC) and government contractual oversight (PPP) weaken or strengthen reporting discipline, since both regimes alter managers' reporting incentives at scale. - How it does it: It regresses discretionary accruals (Kothari et al. 2005; Jones 1991), Dechow–Dichev accrual quality, and Roychowdhury real earnings management proxies on EGC status, a PPP indicator constructed by matching FPDS/SAM.gov federal contract records to Compustat firms, and their interaction, with industry/year fixed effects and firm-clustered standard errors. - The good: The PPP result is consistent and statistically robust across four alternative discretionary-accrual models (PPP coefficient roughly −0.56 to −0.65 on |DA|×100, p < 0.01, ~9–10% of the sample mean), a meaningful large-sample association. - The missing: Causal identification is weak — the instrumental-variable check (industry-year PPP rate) loses significance, and the "PPP" construct is federal contracting broadly rather than formal PPP arrangements, so the headline finding is an association in a noisily proxied setting. - Read it or not: Worth reading for accounting researchers studying JOBS Act disclosure relief or government-contracting monitoring effects; practitioners in corporate reporting policy will find the 404(b)-exemption result more actionable than the EGC null, but methodologists will find nothing new.
Why this rank

This is the most methodologically serious paper in the cluster: Rigor (55) benefits from four alternative accrual models, high-dimensional fixed effects, and honest reporting of nulls and a failing IV, though the internally contradictory REM results narrative, no code release, and dissertation status hold it down. Novelty (50) rests on real but modest contributions — first large-sample U.S. accrual evidence on PPP-like contracting and the sharp decomposition of the EGC bundle from its 404(b) component — using otherwise standard accounting methods. Problem & Motivation: Two institutional settings in U.S. public markets plausibly shape managers' reporting incentives but lack firm-level accounting evidence. First, EGCs (post-2012 JOBS Act, modified by the 2015 FAST Act) receive bundled disclosure relief — including SOX Section 404(b) auditor-attestation exemption — and it is unknown whether this relief degrades reporting quality or is offset by capital-market scrutiny. Second, U.S. PPP research has focused on cost efficiency and value-for-money, not financial reporting, and is hampered by the absence of a national PPP registry; whether government contractual monitoring constrains or complicates reporting is an open empirical question. The dissertation closes both gaps with one empirical framework and adds a third question: does PPP oversight moderate any EGC effect? Key Idea: There is no new methodological trick. The operational move is (a) treating EGC status and SOX 404(b) exemption as separable regulatory variables within the same regression to isolate which provision matters, and (b) constructing a PPP-participation indicator by filtering 453,142 federal contracting entities from FPDS/SAM.gov down to listed firms and applying contract classification and duration thresholds (detailed in Appendix B) as a proxy for PPP-like arrangements. The intellectual frame is agency theory: disclosure relief (EGC) and contractual monitoring (PPP) are distinct oversight channels whose joint effect on FRQ is testable via an interaction term. Methodology: Both essays use the same panel framework (2011–2024, firm-year unit). FRQ is proxied three ways: absolute discretionary accruals from the performance-matched modified Jones model (primary, ×100 for interpretability), Dechow–Dichev/McNichols accrual quality (rolling five-year residual standard deviation), and a Roychowdhury composite real earnings management index (−AB_CFO + AB_PROD − AB_DISEXP, estimated by FF-48 industry-year groups with ≥10 firms). Essay 1 (up to 35,459 firm-years) regresses each proxy on EGC status plus controls (size, ROA, leverage, loss, volatility, Big 4, auditor specialization, EXEMPT_404B, litigation, intangibles) with industry/year fixed effects and firm-clustered SEs. Essay 2 (85,452 firm-year full sample; ~53,000–59,000 in regressions; 15,243 PPP firm-years, ~17.8%) adds the PPP indicator and then a PPP×EGC interaction (Equation 9), with robustness covering alternative DA models, log audit fees as an audit proxy, log market equity as size, one-year-lagged PPP, and an industry-year leave-one-out IV. Critical design decisions: (1) separating EGC status from 404(b) exemption — well-justified and the essay's most valuable move; (2) using federal contracting as a PPP proxy — acknowledged as coarse but the only feasible U.S. option; (3) deferring audit-fee controls to supplemental analysis in Essay 1 (inclusion would cut the sample >95%) — reasonable but reduces comparability across essays. Key Results: Essay 1: EGC status is not significantly associated with any FRQ proxy once controls are included (Table 3: |DA|×100 coefficient −0.086; accrual quality −0.002; the text inconsistently reports the signed-REM coefficient as +0.031, p < 0.05 in one passage and −0.010, insignificant in another — see Gaps). In contrast, SOX 404(b) exemption is significantly associated with higher discretionary accruals (+0.721, p < 0.01) and lower accrual quality (+0.003), indicating that the specific assurance mechanism, not the EGC bundle, tracks reporting quality. Essay 2: PPP participation is negatively and significantly associated with |DA|×100 across four DA models (−0.627, −0.563, −0.601, −0.652; n ≈ 53,200; R² 0.19–0.21), a ~9–10% reduction relative to the ~6.3 sample mean, supporting the monitoring hypothesis (H2). Robustness is mixed: the association survives lagged PPP (−1.065**) and alternative size measurement, but becomes insignificant with log audit fees as the audit control (−0.092) and under the industry-level IV (−1.499, insignificant). Per the abstract, the PPP×EGC interaction is not statistically significant (Table 13 is beyond the truncated text; the interaction cell contains only 192 EGC-PPP firm-years), and real-earnings-management evidence is "mixed" with no systematic substitution pattern. Baselines/comparators are the standard earnings-management literature rather than alternative methods; the scale is a full-sample panel of all listed non-financial U.S. firms, not a toy setting. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING in two under-studied settings; ENGINEERING of a new firm-level PPP indicator from FPDS/SAM.gov procurement data. The measures (Kothari, Dechow–Dichev, Roychowdhury), the fixed-effects panel design, and the agency-theoretic framing are entirely standard; the genuine novelty is (a) the first large-sample U.S. accrual-based evidence on PPP-like contracting and FRQ, and (b) disentangling the EGC bundle from its 404(b) component, which is a modest but real conceptual contribution. The EGC null partly replicates known logic from prior JOBS Act work (Barth et al. 2017; Dambra et al. 2015) in a new outcome domain. Rigor & Reproducibility: Strengths: multiple FRQ proxies per hypothesis, four alternative discretionary-accrual models, winsorization, VIF diagnostics, firm-clustered SEs, high-dimensional fixed effects, and an honest endogeneity section that reports the IV losing significance rather than burying it. Weaknesses: no multiple seeds concern (not applicable), but no code or data release is mentioned; the PPP construct is validated only by distributional tables, not by any manual audit of sampled contracts; the IV's exclusion restriction (industry PPP rates affect firm accruals only via own participation) is dubious and the author concedes it; and the Essay 1 narrative is internally contradictory on whether EGC firms show significantly higher real earnings management (the results narrative asserts β = +0.031**, p < 0.05, driven by discretionary-expense cuts, while the summary/interpretation passages claim the EGC coefficient is insignificant across all three proxies, and the abstract says "mixed"). No significance tests or effect-size comparisons for the interaction tests are visible in the provided text. This is a dissertation, not a peer-reviewed publication; confidence should be calibrated accordingly. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (archival panel regressions; no artifact beyond the paper). - Practical: Fully replicable from public sources (FPDS, SAM.gov, Compustat, ExecuComp, Audit Analytics) with standard statistical software, though the firm-name matching pipeline is nontrivial to rebuild. - Efficient: Standard OLS on ~35,000–59,000 firm-years; negligible compute cost. - Effective: The evidence supports an association between PPP-like contracting and lower accrual-based earnings management, not a causal effect, and the PPP proxy captures federal contracting broadly rather than formal PPPs — so the practical claim "PPP oversight improves reporting" is only proxy-supported. - Scalable: Already population-scale for listed U.S. non-financial firms; extending to private PPP entities or international registries is claimed as future work, not tested. The work delivers no software artifact, dataset release, or tool; it stops at paper form. Strengths: - The decomposition of the EGC regulatory bundle — including EGC status and SOX 404(b) exemption as separate regressors — is the sharpest idea in the dissertation, and it pays off: 404(b) exemption is significantly associated with worse accrual-based measures while the EGC label is not, a finding directly relevant to how regulators evaluate scaled disclosure regimes. - The FPDS/SAM.gov-to-Compustat matching (453,142 contracting entities filtered to listed firms; 15,243 PPP firm-years) is a substantive data-engineering contribution in a domain the author correctly identifies as lacking any U.S. registry, and the mapping rules are documented in Appendix B. - Honest reporting of null and fragile results: the EGC null (H1 rejected), the insignificant interaction (H3), and the IV that loses significance are all reported plainly rather than spun. - Consistent measurement across both essays enables the within-dissertation comparison the framing depends on. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that (1) FRQ proxies are indirect and omit disclosure clarity and internal-control effectiveness; (2) the observational design does not permit causal inference; (3) the PPP measure captures broad federal contracting rather than formally identified PPP arrangements; (4) results apply to U.S. listed firms in federal-procurement settings and may not generalize to private PPP entities or international regimes; and (5) audit-fee data availability forces supplemental rather than primary treatment in Essay 1. The limitations are confronted directly rather than minimized — a credibility positive, particularly the explicit concession that the IV "did not establish definitive causal effects." Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Internal inconsistency in Essay 1's results narrative: the text simultaneously claims EGC is significant for real earnings management (β = +0.031**, driven by discretionary-expense cuts) and insignificant across all proxies (β = −0.010). Table 3 column (3) is labeled "Signed" REM while other passages refer to the absolute-value REM used in primary analyses; which result is the paper's actual finding is unrecoverable from the provided text, and the discussion builds on the significant version. - Selection into PPP participation is treated only with lagged specifications and a weak industry-level IV; no matched-sample or difference-in-differences design around contract initiation is attempted, despite the panel structure supporting one. - The interaction test (H3) has only 192 EGC-PPP firm-years — the author shows the joint distribution (Table 7) but the text does not confront the power limitation this imposes on the null interaction result. - No validation that the FPDS-derived "PPP" indicator corresponds to infrastructure/service-concession PPPs as defined in the PPP literature it cites (Grimsey & Lewis; Andon); concentration in Business Services and Pharmaceuticals (Table 6) suggests the proxy captures generic government contracting, and the PPP framing may be largely rhetorical. - The PPP result may partly reflect firm maturity or political-cost dynamics (which the paper cites but does not test) rather than monitoring; no mechanism test distinguishes these. - No code, data, or replication package is mentioned. Bottom Line: A competent, honestly reported dissertation that usefully documents that federal-contracting firms show ~9–10% lower discretionary accruals and that 404(b) exemption — not EGC status — tracks reporting quality, but its causal claims are soft, its PPP construct is a proxy stretched beyond the literature's definition, and accounting researchers would likely get more from the underlying JOBS Act and government-contracting papers it builds on; read it for the 404(b) result and the procurement-data pipeline, not for new methods.

AI Agent Safety: One Company Cannot Appoint a Supervisor for Another

SK Das · tdcommons.org · generating environments for agent testing in enterprises - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper (a patent-style defensive publication with a licensing solicitation) introduces a protocol and reference implementation by which two independent organizations can jointly and revocably appoint a bounded AI "supervisor" agent, such that neither organization's agent can unilaterally create, authorize, or extend a shared coordinator's authority. - Why it's important: As AI agents increasingly cross organizational boundaries (scheduling, payments, actuation), a coordinator created by one party could otherwise claim—or be tricked into claiming—authority over the other party's resources; this targets that authority-escalation gap. - How it does it: The core trick is separating nomination from authorization: a canonical, digest-bound appointment proposal must receive authenticated consent from every mandatory resource-owning principal, be independently installed at each domain's local gate, and then pass a per-call admission predicate (epoch, expiry, scope, nonce, budget) — with coordination authority never implying native effect authority. - The good: The author is unusually candid about scope, explicitly listing what the prototype does not prove (no cross-organization revocation, no non-bypassability, no distributed consensus), and ships an executable reference implementation with 91 passing tests and a 25-event executed trace. - The missing: There is no distributed implementation or external evaluation whatsoever — all tests run in one Python process with one SQLite file and locally generated keys — and no comparison against any existing delegation, federation, or leader-election protocol. - Read it or not: Read it if you design multi-agent authorization or cross-org agent governance and want a thorough, self-critical design checklist; skip it if you want empirical evidence, baselines, or peer-reviewed validation — it provides none.

Problem & Motivation: When agents A and B belong to mutually independent companies, today's identity and transport layers (A2A, SPIFFE, OpenID Federation, OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange) can authenticate messages and workloads but do not establish that both resource owners have consented to a shared project manager, nor bound that manager's scope, lifetime, or revocation. The failure modes the author enumerates are concrete: a service starting a supervisor process without authority, an initiator impersonating both owners, a supervisor overrunning its appointment, a stale token surviving one party's withdrawal, and a coordination role quietly acquiring payment or actuation rights. The intended audience is agent-platform, telecom, cloud, and industrial-control engineers building cross-organization agent workflows. Key Idea: The single core insight is that manager creation is not manager authorization, and coordination is not effectuation: a supervisor appointment must be a typed, immutable, digest-bound object that (a) is approved by an authority roster derived from a protected resource-dependency registry rather than the proposer's declaration, (b) is installed independently at each affected domain's local gate, and (c) is revalidated on every call against live epoch, policy, instance identity, nonce, and quota state — with a separate resource-side "finality gate" required for any real-world effect. Once understood, the whole system follows from unanimous-digest approval plus per-domain installation convergence plus fail-closed per-call admission. Methodology: The specification is a state-machine protocol: PROPOSED → CONSENT_PENDING → AUTHORIZED_TO_INSTALL/AUTHORIZED_TO_HOST → INSTALLING → ACTIVE → EXPIRED/REVOKED/COMPLETED, with HOLD/DISPUTED/UNKNOWN_CONVERGENCE branch states. It is specified through 24 functional components, a 100-stage workflow (Phases A–J), a 36-stage authority-formation procedure, 40 enforcement invariants, 40 adversarial scenarios, and formal predicates: A(h,e) = ∧_d [Approved(d,h,e) ∧ Eligible(d,m,p_d)]; installation I(h,e) = A ∧ ∧_d Installed(d,h,e,p_d); and a per-call admission predicate requiring Active ∧ CallerMatches ∧ LivePolicy ∧ ScopeMatch ∧ ¬Revoked ∧ t<T ∧ c<q ∧ Unused(u). A derived-roster function computes mandatory approvers from a task-resource dependency graph, so omitting owner C fails roster completeness even with A and B's valid signatures. The reference implementation (Python 3.11, Ed25519, SQLite with BEGIN IMMEDIATE serialization for nonce/budget consumption) is included in the PDF with a second disclosed variant using non-cryptographic protected-local identity. Critical design decisions: (1) digest-binding every approval to one canonical proposal — well justified against substitution/replay; (2) deriving the mandatory roster from a provisioned owner registry rather than proposer input — justified, but the registry's own trust basis is assumed; (3) restricting the coordinator to coordination-only verbs with effects gated separately — justified, and the most distinctive move. Key Results: The measured results are entirely local: the E20 test suite reports 91 passing tests in one process; an executed bilateral worked example reports 25 asserted outcomes (successful admission, rejection of replay, out-of-scope actuation, quota exhaustion, forged signatures, roster mismatch, withdrawal, expiry, and refusal); the companion E19 excerpt reports 84 passing tests and a local benchmark of median 4.776 ms (p95 5.854 ms) for a signed effect-plus-close operation. No external systems, no real cross-organization deployment, no distributed revocation, and no comparison baselines were exercised — and the author says so explicitly. There are no baselines to assess as strong or weak, because none are compared. The only mildly notable empirical observation is the denial-trace itself: each negative test produced the expected typed rejection code (REPLAY, OUT_OF_SCOPE, QUOTA_EXHAUSTED, NOT_ACTIVE, ROSTER_MISMATCH, DECLINED). Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (cross-organizational multi-agent supervisory appointment with derived mandatory rosters and per-domain installation convergence) plus ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION of known primitives. The genuinely distinctive element is the combination of proposal-digest unanimity, independently derived authority rosters, per-domain installation acknowledgements, and coordination/effect separation into one fail-closed admission protocol for agent supervisors. The author himself states the building blocks — federated identity, delegation, leases, quorum, leader election, runtime attestation — are known, that no claim-level prior-art review has been done, and that "this disclosure alone does not establish novelty or patentability." As a research contribution, it is largely a competent composition of standard distributed-authorization ideas applied to the emerging agent-supervisor setting. Rigor & Reproducibility: The reproducibility posture is unusually strong for this genre: full Python source is embedded in the PDF, a demonstration script with a SHA-256 hash (e6bc2236…) is attached, and both test suites are claimed executable with a single dependency (python cryptography). There are no ablations in the research sense (no component-removal study), no error bars or multiple seeds, and no significance testing; the 91/84 test counts are functional conformance checks, not statistical evidence. Methodological concerns: (1) the evaluation is entirely on the author's own artifact against the author's own adversarial scenario list — a self-referential conformance exercise with no external red team; (2) the benchmark measures only local serialized crypto-and-SQLite overhead, which the author concedes is not a distributed latency or scaling result; (3) there is no survey or comparison against existing delegation/federation/leader-election protocols, so the protocol's differential value is unmeasured. No peer review has occurred; this is a self-published defensive publication dated November 2026. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a built reference implementation, evaluated by local execution only). Practical: Yes — it runs on commodity hardware with Python 3.11 and one pip package; the cryptographic profile needs only Ed25519 and SQLite. Efficient: Sub-5 ms per signed operation locally, but no distributed cost is characterized, and every call requires full predicate re-check plus serialization. Effective: The evidence shows the local controller admits and denies correctly per its own specification — a proxy only; the stated problem (cross-organization supervisory authority) is by definition not solved by a single-process demo, and the author admits revocation propagation, non-bypassability, and consensus are unimplemented. Scalable: Not tested beyond one process and one database; at 10×–100× scale (more domains, real networks, distributed nonce stores), the paper offers design guidance (leases, fail-closed partitions, freshness proofs) but no measurements. Deliverable: a software artifact (four Python files, an executable demonstration script, schemas, flowcharts) distributed as PDF attachments under CC BY-NC 4.0, with commercial implementation explicitly gated behind a separate patent license. Strengths: - The discipline of separating four identity layers (organization, hosting authority, supervisor instance, resource owner/evaluator) and deriving the mandatory approver roster from a protected dependency graph — directly closing the "propose-and-self-approve" and "clone-agent quorum" attack classes with a roster-completeness predicate rather than ad-hoc checks. - Exceptional intellectual honesty: the author pre-emptively concedes nearly every limitation a reviewer would raise (single-host prototype, no distributed revocation, signatures ≠ truth, registry trust assumed, no patentability claim), which makes the document unusually trustworthy about its own boundary. - The adversarial scenario catalog (40 failure modes, 12 targeted attacks, 11 conformance tests) is a genuinely reusable design checklist for anyone building agent delegation systems, independent of adopting this protocol. - Executable, hash-verified reference code with typed denial outcomes, which is more reproducibility than most defensive publications or position papers provide. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The author explicitly states: the reference implementation uses process-local keys and one shared SQLite file and does not implement distributed consensus, privileged administrative isolation, instantaneous cross-organization revocation, trusted time, or rollback protection; signatures authenticate key holders but not ownership truth; the owner registry is a pre-provisioned trust assumption; an unrestricted alternate channel defeats universal enforcement; the 91 tests "should not be interpreted as production qualification"; and no patentability or novelty is established. The limitations section (E20.5) and the repeated "non-claim" statements confront limitations directly — a strong credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No distributed prototype at all: the entire value proposition is cross-organization, yet every test is intra-process; the gap between the formal multi-domain predicates and the single-host realization is acknowledged but never bridged even at toy scale (e.g., two processes on two machines). - No comparative evaluation: the paper does not measure or even enumerate how the protocol differs operationally from OAuth token exchange chains, SPIFFE federation plus OPA-style policy, or classic leader-election with leases — so a reader cannot assess added value over existing stacks. - The protected owner registry is the load-bearing assumption; a compromised or stale registry breaks the roster-completeness guarantee, and the paper offers no mechanism (beyond stating the requirement) for registry integrity, freshness, or dispute resolution. - Scalability of unanimous per-domain approval and installation convergence is unanalyzed: for N domains or frequently changing policies, the renegotiation cost (every material change invalidates all prior approvals) could be prohibitive, and no liveness/availability analysis or quorum alternative is evaluated. - The benchmark methodology is a single local run of 30 samples with no variance reporting — immaterial to the thesis but presented as "measured verification." Bottom Line: A practitioner building cross-organization agent governance gains a rigorous, executable design reference and an excellent attack checklist from this disclosure, but anyone seeking evidence that the approach works — or beats existing delegation/federation machinery — will find nothing beyond one author's self-validated prototype, so it should be read as a design artifact, not a research result.

Plug-and-Play Verifier for Decoupling Process Reward in Stabilizing Long - Horizon Agentic Reasoning

M Xu, J Pei, B Tu, H Fang · arxiv.org · long-horizon RL for agents - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a plug-and-play verifier framework that decouples process verification from reward composition and policy optimization in agentic RL, allowing domain-specific deterministic verifiers to be swapped in and out through a unified interface that passes bounded verification scores assigned to source interaction steps. - Why it's important: Outcome-only rewards in RL cannot distinguish trajectories that made genuine intermediate progress from those that did not, and in long-horizon agentic tasks an erroneous early step propagates to later decisions, degrading reliability as the interaction horizon grows. - How it does it: The core trick is a unified contract — each verifier extracts explicit artifacts (citations, code executions, arithmetic equalities, image crops), checks them against recorded evidence with deterministic rules, and returns weighted sums of verification scores assigned to source steps; because a group-shared outcome-process weight causes the common outcome reward to cancel under GRPO group normalization, differences in remaining process returns yield nonzero advantages even when all rollouts share identical outcome rewards (the "last-mile" signal). - The good: Consistent improvements across four domains and two model scales — e.g., Qwen3.5-4B average accuracy of 48.02% vs. 44.95% for outcome-only GRPO — plus an ablation showing the deterministic verifier (60.18% on HotpotQA) outperforms an LLM-as-a-judge baseline (58.28%) while approaching a gold-evidence upper bound (61.40%). - The missing: No error bars, no multiple seeds, no significance tests (single seed 42), no comparison against the closest competing methods (GiGPO, IGPO), and training caps at 3–5 interaction steps, which undermines the "long-horizon" framing. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers designing process supervision in agentic RL who want a modular alternative to learned reward models, but skip if you need evidence on genuinely long-horizon tasks (SWE-Bench, WebArena-scale) or statistical confidence in reported gains.

Problem & Motivation: Language-model agents trained with RL on multi-turn tasks face a credit-assignment gap: binary outcome rewards assign identical feedback to all rollouts in a group when they all succeed or all fail, producing zero group-relative advantages under GRPO and leaving partially useful failed trajectories indistinguishable from entirely unproductive ones. As interaction horizons grow, hallucinated claims, arithmetic errors, or misread tool outputs compound across steps, degrading trajectory stability. Existing solutions have drawbacks: learned critics estimate returns but do not verify artifact validity; LLM-as-a-judge process rewards are black-box and potentially gameable; human step annotations do not scale. The paper targets researchers and practitioners training agentic LLMs with RL who need dense, trustworthy intermediate supervision without gold evidence or expensive judge models. Key Idea: The single core insight is that verification of intermediate artifacts is independent of reward composition and policy optimization, so it can be externalized behind a minimal contract: verifiers return bounded weighted sums of scores assigned to source steps, and nothing else. Downstream training consumes only these (step, score) pairs. Combined with a group-shared weight w < 1 mixing outcome and process rewards, the common outcome term cancels in GRPO's group-mean subtraction, leaving differences in verified process returns as the sole nonzero advantage signal in all-correct or all-incorrect groups — providing a "last-mile" refinement signal precisely where outcome-only GRPO is blind. Methodology: The framework operates in three phases. (1) Artifact extraction: domain-specific parsers identify m explicit artifacts from the trajectory, such as arithmetic equalities, citation certificates, code-execution records, or image-crop references, along with their source interaction steps. (2) Local verification: each artifact is scored by a deterministic check V_d(c_j; ξ_j) ∈ [0,1] against task conditions and recorded evidence; the verifier does not access policy internals, sample continuations, or estimate eventual success. Domain-specific implementations include source-span grounding for QA, developer-test replay for code, crop provenance for visual reasoning, and numeric-equality checking for mathematics. (3) Reward composition and optimization: scores within each step are aggregated as bounded weighted sums q_ℓ with Σq_ℓ ≤ 1; step rewards follow r_t = w·1{t=T}·E_d + (1−w)·p_{d,t}, where w is drawn from U(0,1) per prompt group after a 50-update outcome-only warmup. These composed rewards feed standard GRPO (group-relative normalization) or PPO (GAE with a learned critic). Critical design decisions: (a) bounding process rewards to [0,1] keeps the composed reward in a fixed range — justified by stability, but the specific normalization scheme is not ablated; (b) group-shared w ensures the outcome term cancels in GRPO normalization — mathematically derived in Eq. (7)/(12), a clean and well-justified choice; (c) deterministic rules rather than learned verifiers — justified by avoiding Goodhart risk, but limits coverage to explicitly checkable properties, which the authors acknowledge hurts MATH-Vision performance. Key Results: Across five benchmarks (AIME 2025, AIME 2026, HotpotQA, LiveCodeBench, MATH-Vision) with Qwen3.5-4B, the method achieves 48.02% average accuracy vs. 44.95% for outcome-only GRPO, 46.44% for GRPO+LLM-as-a-judge, and 38.81% for ReAct prompting. With Qwen3.5-9B (LoRA rank 64), the method achieves 53.66% average vs. 51.36% for GRPO, improving on all five benchmarks individually. On HotpotQA, the largest single-domain gain is 60.18% vs. 57.73% (+2.45 pp); on AIME 2025, 40.00% vs. 33.33% (+6.67 pp). The framework transfers to PPO (57.60% vs. 55.10% outcome-only on HotpotQA, +2.50 pp). Ablations on HotpotQA with Qwen3.5-4B show outcome+process (gold evidence) at 61.40%, outcome-only at 57.73%, and process-only at 47.27%, confirming process rewards are complementary rather than a replacement for outcome supervision. Training uses 10,000 examples per domain, 500 updates, 4 rollouts per prompt, on 8× A40 GPUs (~80–94 hours per run). AIME 2025/2026 contain 30 problems each, making single-run differences of a few percentage points statistically fragile. All results use a single random seed (42); no error bars or significance tests are reported. Baselines are current (GRPO, LLM-as-a-judge on the same backbone) but omit recent step-level credit-assignment methods (GiGPO, IGPO) that the paper itself cites. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD + NEW SYSTEM/TOOL. The genuinely novel element is the unified interface contract — bounded weighted sums of verification scores assigned to source steps — that decouples verification from training and enables plug-and-play verifier replacement across agents and RL algorithms. The individual components (deterministic artifact checking, reward mixing, GRPO/PPO) are established; the combination and the architectural decoupling applied across four domains with a shared abstraction is the contribution. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and informative: they isolate the contribution of process rewards (Table 2a), compare three verification mechanisms against a gold-evidence upper bound (Table 2b), and test transfer across GRPO and PPO (Table 3). However, no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported; a single seed (42) is stated in the hyperparameter tables. Code is available at https://github.com/momo1443/plug-and-play-verification. Hyperparameters, training details, and dataset specifications are documented in appendices. Methodological concerns: (a) the paper claims to address "long-horizon" reasoning but trains and evaluates at maximum 5 interaction steps; (b) AIME 2025 and AIME 2026 contain 30 problems each, so reported differences (e.g., 40.00 vs. 33.33) carry high variance; (c) missing comparisons against GiGPO and IGPO, the two closest cited competitors; (d) potential contamination — DeepScaleR training data includes AIME problems from 1984–2023, and AIME 2025 is used as a held-out benchmark without an explicit contamination check. Deployability: (4-property check):** Profile: EMPIRICAL. - Practical: Runs on 8× NVIDIA A40 GPUs (48 GB each), commercially available hardware, using standard vLLM + FSDP infrastructure. - Efficient: ~80 hours for 500 updates on Qwen3.5-4B and ~94 hours on Qwen3.5-9B; comparable to standard GRPO fine-tuning plus the verifier's extraction and replay overhead, which is deterministic and therefore cheap relative to LLM-judge inference. - Effective: Evidence shows consistent accuracy improvements on four benchmark families, but only for short-horizon tasks (≤5 steps); whether the last-mile signal materializes on genuinely long-horizon tasks is untested. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 9B parameters or 5 interaction steps; the authors claim extensibility to production agentic post-training but provide no experiment supporting that claim. Delivers: a code repository on GitHub with the verifier framework and training pipeline; no trained model weights are mentioned as released. Strengths: - The decoupled interface is a clean architectural abstraction that makes process verification modular and reusable across agents, domains, and RL algorithms — demonstrated empirically by reusing the same verifier contract across GRPO and PPO without modification. - The mathematical derivation (Eq. 7/12) showing that a group-shared outcome-process weight preserves nonzero advantages in all-correct/all-incorrect GRPO groups is a genuine, actionable insight for reward design that goes beyond heuristic reward shaping. - Deterministic verifiers sidestep Goodhart risk from learned or LLM-based reward models and match within 1.22 percentage points of the gold-evidence upper bound on HotpotQA, providing strong evidence that simple rule-based checks capture most of the useful signal in that domain. - Cross-domain evaluation spanning QA, code, multimodal, and mathematical reasoning with four distinct verifier implementations demonstrates the framework's breadth beyond a single-domain proof of concept. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: - Verification is limited to per-turn reasoning steps (evidence grounding, execution replay) rather than multi-turn semantic correctness; the authors state this directly and note it explains the MATH-Vision underperformance relative to LLM-as-a-judge. - Agents operate on short interaction horizons on public benchmarks; the authors acknowledge the need to extend to longer-horizon environments (WebArena, SWE-Bench) for production use. - The authors confront these limitations directly and name concrete future work, which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No comparison against GiGPO or IGPO, which the paper cites as addressing similar step-level credit assignment for agentic RL; these are the closest competitors and their omission makes the reported improvements difficult to contextualize. - No statistical uncertainty quantification despite benchmark sizes (e.g., 30-problem AIME sets) where single-seed differences of 3–7 percentage points are within plausible sampling noise. - The theoretical claims of "verification-privileged self-consistency" and "verifier-induced self-reflection" (Section 3.3) are asserted but never measured — no experiment quantifies revision frequency, error-correction rate, or trajectory consistency before vs. after training, so the causal mechanism linking process rewards to the claimed behavioral changes is unvalidated. - The weight schedule w ~ U(0,1) per prompt group is not ablated; no comparison against fixed weights, annealed weights, or adaptive schedules, leaving the sensitivity of results to this design choice unknown. - No contamination analysis: DeepScaleR training data includes AIME problems (1984–2023) while AIME 2025 serves as a held-out evaluation benchmark; the paper does not verify disjointness. Bottom Line: A researcher building agentic RL training pipelines gains a concrete modular pattern and useful evidence that deterministic process verification outperforms LLM-as-a-judge rewards, but the short evaluation horizons and missing head-to-head comparisons with GiGPO/IGPO mean this is a promising framework paper rather than a definitive solution, and practitioners should treat the "long-horizon" claim as unvalidated.

Problem & Motivation: After Facebook's October 2021 renaming to Meta, Indonesian firms and state-owned enterprises launched metaverse initiatives during 2022–2023; several years later public attention has cooled, leaving documented entry decisions whose revenue logic can be reconstructed and compared. The problem is that existing literature offers no guidance for this comparison: metaverse scholarship is rich on definitions, technology components, and sectoral possibilities but thin on revenue mechanics, rarely engages Southeast Asian evidence, and business model frameworks predate immersive platforms. Indonesian firms deciding where metaverse investment is commercially defensible, and regulators deciding what to enable, currently lack a grounded viability assessment. The paper targets three questions: what revenue models are documented for metaverse platforms, how they map onto Indonesian initiatives since 2022, and which are commercially viable under Indonesian conditions. Key Idea: The central insight is a cost-shape matching test applied through the Business Model Canvas: because metaverse world operation carries a permanent, semi-fixed operating cost base (moderation, identity, payment trust, continuous world operation), only revenue models with a temporally matching recurring stream (service contracts, subscriptions, commissions, marketing fees) are viable, while one-time asset sales matched to permanent costs signal a model with a "missing revenue block." Combined with two-sided market theory (users as the subsidised side, brands/enterprises as payers), this lets the authors sort all seven revenue mechanisms — and all four Indonesian cases — into durable versus speculative categories. The trick is simple but genuinely diagnostic: asking "who pays, from which budget, since when?" Methodology: The study is a structured literature review plus qualitative, document-based case analysis. The review draws on peer-reviewed metaverse, virtual world, platform economics, and business model literature from major publishers (Elsevier, Springer Nature, Wiley, Taylor & Francis, SAGE, Oxford), with metaverse-specific sources concentrated post-2021 and supplemented by pre-2021 virtual world research (Second Life, free-to-play games). Two analytical frames structure the synthesis: the Business Model Canvas (nine blocks) for comparing value creation/delivery/capture configuration, and revenue model typologies (product sales, asset sales, advertising, subscription, usage fees, brokerage/commission, licensing). Four Indonesian cases met inclusion criteria (publicly launched, attributable to an identifiable organisation, documented by more than one public source): Telkom's metaNesia (July 2022), WIR Group's Nusameta ecosystem with the B20/G20 pavilion, the March 2022 BRI/BNI metaverse banking memoranda, and Jagat's virtual Nusantara (October 2022). Promotional-only initiatives were excluded. No proprietary data, interviews, or financial disclosures were used; the analysis is entirely inferential from public documents. Critical design decisions: (1) public-source-only evidence, justified by the exploratory stage of the field but capping evidential strength; (2) the three-layer ecosystem view (platform owner / orchestrator / complementor) borrowed from Schobel and Leimeister, well-justified because it disambiguates where revenue is earned; (3) the viability ordering derived from cost-revenue temporal matching plus Indonesian readiness factors (devices, willingness to pay, regulation) — internally consistent but never validated against actual revenue outcomes. Key Results: The paper's headline output is a viability ordering: (1) most viable — B2B services (training, simulation, digital twins) monetising measurable organisational savings under existing procurement and regulation; (2) advertising and brand experience production services paid from marketing budgets; (3) conventional free-entry game/social models with cosmetic and convenience purchases in mobile-first products; (4) platform commissions — viable only for operators with existing large transaction flows, which no domestic platform has; (5) least viable — virtual land and token sales to retail buyers, dependent on speculative appreciation and legally classified as commodity trading rather than property in Indonesia. Supporting evidence: 221.56 million Indonesian internet users in 2024 (79.5% penetration, APJII) and approximately US$90 billion GMV digital economy in 2024 (e-Conomy SEA 2024), the largest in Southeast Asia; video commerce at roughly one-fifth of Southeast Asian e-commerce GMV, a more-than-fourfold share increase since 2022. Case-level findings: metaNesia required no headset or wallet, with revenue logic closest to advertising/brand experiences plus enterprise services; the bank initiatives were explicitly channel experiments and brand positioning financed from innovation budgets, not transaction revenue; Jagat's Koin Jagat drew official regulatory warnings in early 2025 after crowd incidents. There are no accuracy, F1, or speed metrics — this is a qualitative study, and the "results" are the ordering and the diagnosis of why initiatives stalled (announced ecosystems before revenue blocks were specified, no domestic critical mass against incumbent global platforms, imported token volatility, regulatory absence keeping banks in demonstration mode, and Meta's own pivot to AI removing fear-of-missing-out pressure). Baselines here are prior scholarly framings (e.g., Kraus et al.'s finding that Meta's transformation was incremental) rather than competing empirical assessments of Indonesia. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (contextual) plus a modest NEW FORMULATION. Genuinely novel is the mapping of seven global metaverse revenue mechanisms onto documented Indonesian cases and readiness factors, yielding a viability ordering grounded in a non-Western, mobile-first market that the metaverse literature has not covered; the comparative canvas diagnosis of why the three cases diverged is a real, if small, empirical contribution. Everything else — the Business Model Canvas, two-sided market theory, revenue typologies, the meta-ecosystem layering — is a standard combination of existing frameworks applied to a new setting; the seven-mechanism taxonomy itself is a synthesis of prior literature, not a new classification. Rigor & Reproducibility: This is a qualitative study with no ablations, error bars, seeds, or significance tests, which is appropriate to its design but means claims cannot be statistically stress-tested. Case selection criteria are explicit and transparent (public launch, identifiable owner, multi-source documentation), and the exclusion of promotion-only initiatives is a genuine methodological strength. All evidence comes from public documents — official statistics, company announcements, press coverage — with citations to identifiable sources; no code, data, or artifacts are released (none would be expected). Methodological concerns a reviewer should flag: (1) the study evaluates commercial durability using the same press sources that amplified the launch hype, creating a survivorship and salience bias the authors partially acknowledge; (2) the viability ordering is derived from theory and case narrative, never validated against actual revenue or shutdown data — the ordering is an argument, not a measurement; (3) the journal itself (Journal of Business and Digital Strategy, Vol. 1, No. 1, October 2026) is a first-issue outlet, so peer-review depth is unverified; (4) the conclusions about "stalled" initiatives rest partly on absence of press coverage, which the authors concede is asymmetric. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (qualitative, document-based empirical analysis; no system is built). Practical: Not applicable in the hardware sense — the output is an analytical framework and ordering usable immediately by managers and policymakers at zero cost. Efficient: The framework costs only analyst effort and public data, a genuine advantage over proprietary market studies. Effective: The evidence shows the framework correctly retro-diagnoses the divergent trajectories of 2022-era initiatives, but it has not been tested prospectively on new ventures, so it solves the descriptive problem, not yet the predictive one. Scalable: Not tested — the analysis covers exactly four cases in one country over roughly three years; extending it to other Southeast Asian markets or the post-2024 period is claimed implicitly but not demonstrated. The work delivers no software artifact, dataset, or reusable tool — it stops at paper form, with the framework itself as the only reusable output. Strengths: - The cost-shape matching argument (recurring revenue must match permanent operating cost) is a crisp, transferable analytical lens that converts a vague "hype vs. substance" debate into a checkable design question about revenue blocks. - The three-case canvas comparison is the paper's best execution: identifying who pays, from which budget, since launch day cleanly separates contractual revenue (metaNesia, WIR/banks) from circular in-world revenue (Jagat) and explains outcomes better than any technology-based account. - Honest evidential scoping: the authors explicitly confine claims to what public documentation supports and exclude promotion-only initiatives, an unusual discipline in this genre. - The policy translation is concrete and non-generic — interoperable identity/payment standards, virtual-asset consumer protection, and government procurement demand target the viable end of the ordering without subsidising the speculative end. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that (1) the analysis relies on public documentation because Indonesian firms do not publish metaverse segment revenue, so it evaluates revenue logic and documented activity rather than audited financial outcomes; (2) press coverage of launches exceeds coverage of quiet discontinuations, which may flatter the durability of the cases; and (3) the literature base reflects a field whose empirical record is still short. They directly recommend follow-up interview and financial-disclosure research. This is a candid, non-minimising limitations section — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The viability ordering is the central result but is never tested against any outcome data: no revenue figures, user counts, shutdown confirmations, or post-2023 status checks for any of the four cases. "Stalled" is asserted from narrative inference, not measured. - Four cases, all launched within a five-month window in 2022, is a thin evidential base for a country-level viability ranking; a single additional failure or success in a different configuration could reorder the ranking. - No comparison against actual current state of the cases: the paper cites a January 2025 report on Jagat but does not report metaNesia's or Nusameta's status as of writing, leaving the durability claim for enterprise-financed models unsupported by the cases' own endpoints. - The claimed structural demand for B2B digital twins and training ("a large manufacturing base, state-owned enterprises with dispersed operations") is asserted without a single documented Indonesian procurement of metaverse-based training or twin services — the top-ranked model has the weakest case evidence in the paper. - The regulatory analysis relies on a "study-first posture" from early 2022; no evidence is offered on whether the regulator's position changed through 2024–2026. - Publication venue is a first-volume journal with unverified review standards, warranting lower confidence than indexed peer-reviewed work. Bottom Line: An Indonesia-focused manager or policymaker gains a genuinely useful, honestly scoped sorting of metaverse revenue models that justifies reading, but scholars seeking validated business-model findings will find a thin four-case inferential study whose central viability ordering remains an argument rather than an empirically demonstrated result.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces Compounding Physical RSI, a three-stage self-evolving policy loop (Diagnosis–Remedy–Retention) that turns a robot policy's own execution failures into inherited capability, and delivers CSU-AI-07, the first-place entry (Overall Score 26.15, Success Rate 20.70%) on the 42-task RoboDojo-Sim leaderboard. - Why it's important: Generalist VLA policies hit their real capability limits only during closed-loop physical execution, where staged task structure hides downstream failures until earlier stages pass — so improvement requires an iterative loop, and regressions from naive fine-tuning compound as fast as gains do. - How it does it: Each generation localizes the failing task stage (capability frontier), curates validated stage-relevant experience into an objective-conditioned behavior-regularized offline RL update, then selects a weight-space interpolation between the old and new policies via full-benchmark evaluation before promoting it. - The good: The policy wins the public leaderboard on both metrics by large margins (5.92 points / 29% relative over the next-best Overall Score; 5.82 pp / 39% over next-best Success Rate among 13 public generalist policies), with three-seed means and narrow seed variance (1.07 points, 0.74 pp). - The missing: No ablations or generation-wise improvement curves are reported, so the paper never empirically demonstrates the compounding (multiplicative cross-generation gains) it takes as its central thesis; the loop's contribution over simple fine-tune-and-evaluate is unmeasured. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on VLA policy post-training, benchmark-driven policy iteration, or robot self-improvement loops and want a concrete challenge-winning recipe; skip it if you want rigorous evidence that recursive self-improvement actually compounds — the framework is described but not dissected.
