Problem & Motivation: Generalist robot manipulation policies are trained on static offline datasets, but physical manipulation unfolds through stage-gated sequences (approach, grasp, transport, place, verify). A failure in a downstream stage is unobservable until all earlier stages pass, so each fix moves the "capability frontier" and exposes a new, previously unseen failure mode whose character depends on the policy's own closed-loop state distribution. A fixed dataset or single training run therefore cannot anticipate or fix these latent failures. The authors argue the central open problem is not whether a policy can improve once, but whether improvements compound across recursive generations — because task success is a product of stage pass rates, stage-level gains (and cross-task regressions) multiply. Three bottlenecks are identified: terminal failure feedback does not localize the failing stage; failed trajectories contain no corrective action; and updating shared weights to fix one failure can silently erase previously mastered skills. Practitioners building generalist robot policies face exactly this multi-task brittleness. Key Idea: The core insight is to make each recursive generation's update traceable to a structured "improvement objective" g_k that (i) is extracted by diagnosing where closed-loop rollouts diverge from expected stage progression, (ii) conditions both experience curation and an offline RL update anchored to the reference policy, and (iii) hands the decision of what gets inherited to evaluation-guided weight-space consolidation rather than to the raw fine-tuned checkpoint. The retention trick — promoting only the best linear interpolation between the inherited reference and the refined policy, justified via linear mode connectivity — is the concrete mechanism that converts a fragile fine-tune into a heritable, verified capability state. Methodology: The framework formalizes one generation as a policy transition with five operators: A (diagnosis), F (validation), C (curation), U_off (offline RL), and S (selection). (1) Diagnosis: the current policy π_k is rolled out in RoboDojo-Sim with per-trajectory logging of task-stage boundaries, states, actions, and terminal conditions; a stage-level capability-gap assessment compares observed progression against expected stages and compiles the failing context, bottleneck stage, and capability dimension into a structured objective g_k. (2) Remedy: all experience is normalized into a unified "Episode" schema (task, instruction, time-synchronized observation–state–action, stage boundaries, outcome flags, provenance); a five-stage validation pipeline (normalization, temporal alignment, stage association, consistency check, versioned release) filters which traces become actionable supervision; curation retrieves validated Episodes matching the diagnosed stage/object/transition pattern; the update maximizes an objective-conditioned value E[Q(s,a|g_k)] minus λ·D(π, π_k) — behavior-regularized, conservative offline RL with g_k acting as a universal-value-function goal, deliberately avoiding per-step online rollouts. (3) Retention: compatible checkpoints are merged into a reference state via model-soup averaging and interference-aware merging (TIES-style); candidates θ_i = (1−α_i)θ_k + α_iθ'_k are sampled along the linear interpolation path, each evaluated on the full 42-task suite under the standard protocol, and the best candidate is promoted as π_{k+1} with archived lineage (model identity, experience version, evaluation logs). Critical design decisions: offline optimization over accumulated experience (justified by physical rollout cost), behavioral (not loss-based) promotion gating (justified by poor correlation between proxy losses and closed-loop contact-rich success), and on-policy execution evidence inclusion (justified by the distribution-shift argument for offline RL). All three are reasonable but justified narratively rather than experimentally. Key Results: On all 42 RoboDojo-Sim tasks, CSU-AI-07 achieves a three-seed mean Overall Score of 26.15 (seeds: 26.53, 25.46, 26.45) and mean Success Rate of 20.70% (seeds: 21.05%, 20.31%, 20.75%). It ranks first against 13 public generalist policies: GalaxeaVLA/G0.5 (20.23, 14.88%), Xiaomi-Robotics-1 (20.07, 13.93%), Hy-Embodied-0.5-VLA (13.07, 8.80%), SimpleMemVLA, Spatial Forcing, π0.5 (11.44, 6.93%), InternVLA-A1.5, VLAct, X-VLA, X-WAM, StarVLA, π0 (3.48, 1.53%), and GR00T-N1.7 (2.85, 1.31%). Relative margins are 29.3% on Overall Score and 39.1% on Success Rate; versus π0.5, nearly 3× the completion rate. The benchmark is acknowledged as hard (best baseline SR is 14.88%). Baselines are recent (2025–2026 VLA models evaluated under a shared public protocol via XPolicyLab), so the comparison set is current and credible. Scale is a full benchmark suite at 3 seeds — standard for a challenge, not a stress test. Notably, Seed 0 was used for candidate selection during iteration; Seeds 1 and 2 align closely, which the authors present as evidence of cross-seed generalization. Nothing is reported about how many RSI generations were run, what the generation-by-generation gains were, or how much each of the three stages contributed. No counter-intuitive findings are reported. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION plus NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (a leaderboard result), with the machinery being a competent combination of existing techniques: stage-level failure diagnosis echoes prior embodied self-improvement work; objective-conditioned offline RL is standard behavior-regularized/conservative offline RL with a goal conditioning (universal value functions); weight-space consolidation is model soups plus linear interpolation between two endpoints. What is genuinely new is the framing — defining compounding as the central objective of Physical RSI and structuring a closed-loop pipeline (diagnose frontier → cure against it → verify inheritance) around the multiplicative stage-pass-rate argument — plus the demonstration that this recipe wins a current public benchmark. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations: none; the authors explicitly concede that fine-grained ablations isolating diagnosis, experience selection, and weight consolidation are future work. Seeds: three evaluation seeds with per-seed numbers reported and narrow variance, though Seed 0 doubled as the selection seed (a mild selection-bias concern the authors address only by pointing to agreement on held-out seeds). No significance tests. Code, data, checkpoints, and the RSI-loop implementation are not stated as released; no URL is given for the artifact, only the leaderboard context. The evaluation uses the public RoboDojo-Sim protocol and a third-party leaderboard rather than the authors' own metric, which mitigates benchmark-gaming risk; however, this is a challenge technical report with self-authored system descriptions, is a preprint (not peer reviewed), and the diagnostic/curation operators are described at the level of a pipeline diagram without algorithmic detail, hyperparameters, model backbone, or offline RL algorithm specification — reproduction from this text alone would not be possible. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a simulation benchmark system; no physical-hardware deployment is reported). - Practical: The final policy is a standard VLA checkpoint (weight interpolation adds zero inference overhead), so it runs wherever comparable VLA policies run, though hardware/compute requirements are not stated. - Efficient: Inference cost is unchanged versus the underlying policy; the loop's cost driver — full-benchmark evaluation of multiple interpolated candidates per generation — is not quantified in wall-clock or rollout counts. - Effective: The evidence (first place, both metrics, three seeds) shows it solves the stated problem on the benchmark proxy; real-robot transfer is claimed as future work, not measured. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 42 tasks and 3 seeds; the multiplicative-compounding benefit across many generations is asserted structurally, never demonstrated empirically at any scale. The work delivers a trained policy checkpoint and a described pipeline; no library, dataset release, or reusable tool is stated. Strengths: - The compounding framing is a genuine conceptual contribution: grounding the necessity of recursive improvement in the stage-gated, multiplicative structure of manipulation success is a crisp, falsifiable argument that clarifies why single-shot fine-tuning plateaus. - The retention stage is the most technically substantive piece: separating "what the update produces" from "what the next generation inherits" via evaluation-guided linear weight interpolation, grounded in linear mode connectivity, is a practical mechanism that keeps candidates as standalone zero-overhead policies. - The empirical result is real and current: first place on both metrics of a demanding public benchmark against 13 recent (2025–2026) VLA policies under a shared third-party protocol, with multi-seed means rather than a single cherry-picked run. - The formalization of a generation as an explicit operator sequence (A, F, C, U_off, S) with archived lineage makes the loop auditable in principle — an unusually disciplined structure for a challenge report. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state three: (1) missing fine-grained ablations isolating the contributions of diagnosis, experience selection, and weight consolidation; (2) the improvement operators themselves remain fixed — only policy capability evolves, not the improvement procedure, which they call the "higher bar" set by prior Physical RSI formulations; (3) the framework has been validated only in simulation, and transfer to physical hardware where trials are costlier is future work. They confront these limitations directly rather than minimizing them, which is a credibility positive; they do not, however, acknowledge the absence of generation-level evidence for the compounding claim itself. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The central thesis — that gains compound across generations — is never shown: no figure or table reports Overall Score/SR as a function of generation k, how many generations were run, or the gain attributable to the loop versus the initial reference policy. The paper argues compounding is possible; it does not measure it. - No comparison against the obvious cheaper baseline: fine-tune π_k on the curated data and evaluate directly (α = 1 with no retention search), or simple full-suite-evaluate-and-keep-if-better without interpolation. Without these, the value of diagnosis and retention specifically is unknown. - The capability-gap assessment operator A is described only narratively; whether it is rule-based, LLM-assisted, or human-in-the-loop is unstated, which matters enormously for whether the "automated" diagnosis claim holds. - The offline RL instantiation (algorithm, λ, Q-learning variant, action head, backbone of π_k, training compute) is absent, blocking reproduction. - Seed 0 was used for selection; although held-out seeds agree, the paper does not report how many candidate checkpoints or generations were screened on Seed 0, so promotion-based selection bias cannot be ruled out. - The 20.70% success rate leaves ~79% failure — the paper spins this as fuel for future generations, but it also means the promoted policy fails most tasks, and per-dimension (generalization, memory, long-horizon, precision, open-specification) breakdowns are not reported. Bottom Line: A practitioner in VLA post-training or robot self-improvement gains a concrete, current, winning recipe — diagnose the stage frontier, cure it with anchored offline RL, inherit only verified weight interpolations — but should treat the "compounding" claim as an untested hypothesis, since this report shows a strong endpoint and not the multi-generation growth curve that would validate its own thesis.

Inverse Reinforcement Learning for Resource Preference Modeling in Business Processes

L Kirchdorfer, SAP Signavio, H van der Aa, T Kampik… · hanvanderaa.com · business process mining or process mining - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces an Inverse Reinforcement Learning (MaxEnt IRL) approach that learns per-resource preference models (linear reward functions) from business process event logs, instantiated for the case-prioritization decision problem. - Why it's important: Resource prioritization choices drive waiting times, cycle times, and SLA risk, yet process mining has no established way to learn these choice preferences; realistic resource behavior would improve simulation and predictive process monitoring. - How it does it: It reconstructs each resource's decision points from event logs (queues of available cases as states, selected case as action), then fits a linear Boltzmann-choice model via maximum-entropy IRL, recovering interpretable feature weights per resource. - The good: On eight synthetic logs generated under known prioritization strategies, the IRL model recovers the intended preference signal and averages 46% top-1 / 67% top-3 accuracy versus 37% / 61% for the best supervised baseline (LR). - The missing: On the two real-life logs (BPIC2012W, BPIC2013), supervised tree ensembles (XGB, DT) outperform IRL, so the claimed advantage holds only on synthetic, fully-observed preference patterns; no error bars or significance tests are reported. - Read it or not: Worth reading for process-mining researchers working on the resource perspective or simulation realism — it is the first IRL application in the field — but ML researchers will find the method a direct application of Ziebart's 2008 MaxEnt IRL to a new domain.

Problem & Motivation: In business processes, human resources autonomously choose which case to work on next (case prioritization), and these choices reflect individual preferences — e.g., favoring high-value customers over FIFO order — that shape cycle times and outcomes. Process mining has traditionally focused on control flow; resource preference learning from event logs is underexplored. The closest prior work (Bidar et al., 2019) treats next-task selection as supervised classification, which the authors argue is the wrong inductive frame: a choice is only meaningful relative to the set of alternatives available at that moment, and the reward function (not the label mapping) is the transferable description of behavior. The stakeholders are process analysts and simulation model builders who currently default to FIFO assumptions. The paper targets both retrospective analysis (detecting systematic deviation from intended prioritization rules) and prediction (anticipating which case a resource picks next). Key Idea: Treat the event log as demonstration data from multiple agents and recover each resource's reward function with MaxEnt IRL — a linear utility over queue features with a Boltzmann policy — so that preferences are modeled as choice-among-alternatives rather than label prediction. The enabling move is reducing the classical MDP formulation of IRL to independent, myopic single-shot decisions, which matches the assumed short-sightedness of queue selection and collapses learning to maximum-likelihood estimation of feature weights via the standard gradient (empirical minus model-expected feature sums). Methodology: The pipeline has two stages. (1) Trajectory extraction: events are sorted by start timestamp; at each start time, the state is a feature-based representation of the available queue (case-level availability: case arrived and not currently being processed), and the action is the selected case ID, yielding per-resource state–action trajectories. Features must be observable at decision time to avoid leakage; the feature set is process-specific (e.g., loan amount, waiting time for BPIC2012W; product, impact, previous resource for BPIC2013). (2) Reward learning: MaxEnt IRL with reward R_r(s,a) = θ_r^T φ(s,a), selection probability π(a|s) = exp(θ^T φ(s,a))/Z_s, optimized by gradient ascent on the log-likelihood (Eq. 5), 100 epochs, learning rate grid {0.001–0.1}. Prediction ranks available cases by the learned policy. Critical design decisions: (a) the myopic, static-decision simplification instead of full MDP IRL — motivated but not empirically validated against an MDP variant; (b) case-level rather than work-item-level availability — acknowledged simplification for processes with concurrent enabled activities; (c) MaxEnt over max-margin/Bayesian/GAIL alternatives — justified via interpretability, efficiency, and noise robustness. The code and synthetic logs are public (github.com/lukaskirchdorfer/IRL4PM). Key Results: Evaluated on 10 logs: eight synthetic loan-application variants (1000 cases each, avg. queue size 32, three resources, eight ground-truth strategies: EDD, FCFS, SPT, Random, Value, Platinum, Mix-1, Mix-2) plus BPIC2012W (9,270 decision points, avg. queue 14) and BPIC2013 (11,497 points, avg. queue 329). Baselines: Random, FIFO, Decision Tree, SVM, Logistic Regression, XGBoost, feed-forward NN, all tuned by grid search with temporal 64/16/20 split. IRL is best or second-best on 8/10 logs; across all logs it averages 0.46 top-1 / 0.67 top-3 accuracy vs. 0.37 / 0.61 for second-best LR. On synthetic EDD, SPT, and Mix-2, IRL reaches 0.69, 0.68, and 0.86 top-1. Exceptions: FIFO attains 1.00 on the FCFS log (trivially), and all methods fail on Random (~0.07–0.09 top-1), as expected. On the real logs, IRL does not win: XGB leads on BPIC2012W (0.36/0.62 vs. IRL 0.28/0.53) and DT on BPIC2013 (0.36/0.36 vs. IRL 0.16/0.28). Learned weights on synthetic logs match the generating strategies (e.g., large positive TSA weight for FCFS, large negative TUDD weight for EDD), demonstrating interpretability. Scale is modest — synthetic logs are toy-sized; real logs are standard BPIC benchmarks. Baselines are reasonable but tabular; no deep sequence models are compared. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (domain-first) and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel element is the framing of resource preference learning in process mining as IRL — the first such application per the authors and, checking against the related work (Bidar et al. 2019's SVM approach, organizational/decision/user-behavior mining), this claim is credible. The IRL machinery itself is a direct, competent application of Ziebart et al. (2008) MaxEnt IRL with a hand-rolled myopic simplification; the trajectory reconstruction from event logs is sensible engineering rather than a technical contribution. Rigor & Reproducibility: The evaluation is reasonably structured: eight controlled synthetic conditions with known ground truth, two public real logs, seven baselines, temporal train/validation/test split, hyperparameter tuning via validation set for all methods, and top-k accuracy as the metric. Ablation-style evidence exists in the form of weight inspection (Figure 2) confirming the recovered reward aligns with generating strategies. Weaknesses: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests (with ~1000–11,000 decision points, several top-1 gaps are within plausible noise, especially on real logs); no ablation of the myopic simplification or of feature-set choices; code and synthetic data are released (GitHub link in paper), but derived queue reconstructions for the real logs are not explicitly stated as released. A methodological caution: synthetic performance is measured on data generated under exactly the linear-reward assumption MaxEnt IRL encodes, so the synthetic results partly test assumption-matching rather than general advantage; the real-log results, where the assumption does not hold, are the more honest signal and there IRL loses to tree ensembles. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a method run on logs, plus a released implementation). - Practical: Yes — Python implementation, gradient-based training on tabular features; runs on commodity hardware (no GPU implied). - Efficient: Very — the myopic simplification makes training a small logistic-regression-style fit (100 epochs, one tuned hyperparameter), far cheaper than MDP-based or adversarial IRL. - Effective: Partially — it predicts choices better than heuristics and most supervised baselines on synthetic data, but on the real logs it is outperformed by XGB/DT, so effectiveness in the wild is not yet demonstrated. - Scalable: Not tested — BPIC2013's avg. queue of 329 is the largest choice set; behavior under much longer queues, many more resources, or drifting preferences is claimed (via future work) but unmeasured. The work ships a software artifact (Python code + synthetic log generator) in a public repository; no trained models or downstream integration (e.g., into a simulator) is delivered. Strengths: - Correct problem framing: recasting resource choice as preference-among-available-alternatives (IRL) rather than label classification is a genuine conceptual contribution to process mining and is well argued against the Bidar et al. supervised baseline. - Interpretability by construction: the linear reward yields per-feature weights, and the paper validates them against known ground-truth strategies on synthetic logs — a check most applied-ML papers omit. - Honest baseline coverage and tuning discipline: seven baselines including gradient boosting and a neural net, all tuned on a validation set, evaluated on identical reconstructed decision points. - The myopic simplification of MaxEnt IRL is a pragmatic, well-motivated adaptation that makes the method essentially as cheap as logistic regression while retaining the choice-set semantics supervised models lack. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The conclusion is candid: evaluation is limited in scope (only case prioritization; other decision types like handover untested); synthetic logs simplify real behavior (no competing or changing preferences); the myopic IRL formulation excludes strategic, history-dependent decisions; the approach assumes the log captures all decision-relevant attributes (unobserved factors appear only via proxy correlations); preferences are assumed static; and privacy concerns for individual employees are flagged with a recommendation to abstract to process-level statements. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The headline average accuracy (46% top-1) is dominated by synthetic logs where the data generator satisfies the linear-reward/Boltzmann assumption exactly; the paper's framing of "often outperforming supervised baselines" leans on these favorable conditions while the real-log results (IRL behind XGB by 8 points top-1 on BPI12W and behind DT by 20 on BPI13) receive softer treatment. - No statistical uncertainty: with per-resource models and single runs, differences of 1–3 points between IRL and LR in the averages may not be meaningful. - No sequence-aware baselines (e.g., LSTM/transformer over the queue or case history) despite the sequential nature of the data; the NN baseline is a small feed-forward net. - Queue reconstruction relies on start-timestamp ordering and case-level availability; sensitivity of results to this reconstruction (e.g., timestamp noise, concurrent work items) is unexamined, and the derivation assumes life-cycle timestamps exist — many real logs lack them. - The choice-set dependence claim is not isolated: a per-alternative pairwise comparison (e.g., learning on case pairs) could capture some of the same benefit; no ablation distinguishes IRL's contribution from merely conditioning on the queue. - Per-resource sample sizes on real logs are not reported; with few decisions per resource, individual reward functions may be under-fit or over-fit, and no pooling/shrinkage across resources is explored. Bottom Line: For process-mining researchers, this is a worthwhile and credible first step that establishes IRL as a viable paradigm for resource preference modeling and provides reusable code, but practitioners seeking maximum predictive accuracy on real logs today should still use gradient-boosted trees, and the field needs follow-up work with MDP structure, drifting preferences, and stronger sequential baselines before the IRL advantage is proven outside synthetic conditions.

Recursive Self - Improvement for Long-Horizon Role-Playing Dialogue

YL Li, YH Wu · arxiv.org · recursive self-improvement - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a bounded recursive self-improvement (RSI) framework that iteratively repairs an original-character role-playing agent's memory, stable persona instructions, and prompt-construction policy, and additionally evolves the repair policy itself (the 'updater') from accumulated repair history. - Why it's important: Long-horizon role-play agents fail through inconsistent identity, forgotten events, and speaking for the user, and these failures are hard to localize across memory retrieval, persona instructions, and dynamically assembled prompts; Problem & Motivation: Role-playing conversational agents must maintain character identity, memory, and context-sensitive interaction over hundreds of turns. A locally fluent reply can contradict established world state, reverse a relationship, repeat a plot beat, or act on the user's behalf, and diagnosing which component is at fault (memory storage, retrieval, stable persona instructions, or the dynamic prompt policy) is difficult because the final response depends on all of them. Practitioners building original-character (OC) agents — implicitly commercial role-play product teams — need a mechanism that both localizes failures to the responsible component and accumulates corrections across iterations without corrupting episode-specific state or drifting into degenerate self-generated data. Prior work (RoleLLM, CharacterEval, EmoCharacter, MiniMax's Role-Play Bench) evaluates or tunes role-play quality but does not treat the diagnostic-and-repair procedure itself as an editable, versioned object. Key Idea: The core insight is a two-level feedback loop: the standard inner loop (diagnose failure → propose localized character edit → validate against parent) is wrapped in an outer loop in which the repair history itself drives revisions to the updater's diagnostic, routing, and selection rules. Separating 'what was changed for this character' from 'what procedure produces future repairs' — with the updater represented as structured, versioned, permission-bounded rule records — is the trick that distinguishes this from Self-Refine/Reflexion-style output refinement applied once. Methodology: The system fixes an immutable character canon and base model weights, and exposes three editable surfaces per character: memory items (with source spans, story time, character/episode IDs, revision status), stable persona instructions, and a dynamic policy that assembles turn-level prompts. Each RSI iteration runs four steps. (1) Diagnose: an optimization trajectory plus canon and current configuration are passed to the updater, which emits a failure record (turn, category, supporting span, responsible component) under diagnostic rules that require evidence or abstain — distinguishing, e.g., an event never stored versus a retrieval miss versus ignored retrieved evidence. (2) Propose: routing rules map diagnoses to edit surfaces and operators within a bounded candidate budget, always including a no-change control, with candidates checked against both the triggering scene and contrasting scenes where the prior behavior was legitimate. (3) Validate: a candidate character configuration is accepted only if it improves the target bad-response rate by a configured minimum on validation scenarios and passes hard canon constraints; accepted and rejected repairs are logged with full provenance. (4) Update the updater: a fixed meta-update instruction prompts an LLM to propose a minimal atomic rule diff (with cited repair pattern, expected effect, and a counterexample where the rule should not apply), which is validated by having candidate and parent updaters perform repairs on the same fresh validation failures under the same budget. The framework is explicit about data hygiene: optimization, validation, and final-test scenarios are grouped by template family before partitioning, validation feedback is logged as potential selection data, and the updater cannot self-expand permissions, thresholds, or budgets — enforced by an orchestration layer. No formal objective function is given; the implicit objective is minimizing a binary 'bad-response' rate under protected constraints. Key Results: On an internal test of 50 OCs × 5 base models × 2 conversations × 100 rounds (49,824 baseline and 49,793 RSI scored replies, pooled), the bad-response rate falls from 14.00% to 4.94% — a 9.06-point absolute, 64.71% relative reduction. In 600 blinded pairwise human comparisons, RSI wins 294 (49.00%), ties 187 (31.17%), loses 119 (19.83%); among the 413 decisive judgments the win rate is 71.19%, and the half-credit preference score is 64.58%. The bad-response rubric adapts MiniMax's Worlds/Stories/User-Preferences taxonomy with a confirmed-violation threshold. The baseline is the same underlying system without the RSI loop, using identical base models per pairing — an appropriate ablation-style control, though the comparison contains no external benchmark, no third-party system, no per-model breakdown, and no significance testing or confidence intervals (the authors state uncertainty estimation would require conversation-level records and evaluator-agreement data). Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (partially) and ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. Genuinely novel is the explicit two-level formulation: the repair policy itself as a structured, versioned, permission-bounded editable object validated by downstream repair performance. The individual ingredients — diagnose-propose-validate cycles, memory correction, prompt-policy revision, protected test sets — are competent combinations of existing ideas (Self-Refine, Reflexion, Generative Agents, standard data-partition hygiene), and the paper honestly acknowledges that isolating the updater-evolution contribution requires a component-level comparison it does not run. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are absent: the paper measures only the complete framework against the baseline and explicitly notes that isolating updater evolution 'requires a component-level comparison' that is not provided. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported; the authors flag this as future work dependent on conversation-level records. No code, data, or model artifacts are released, and the evaluation is entirely on an internal test distribution with AI-generated interlocutors — self-reported vendor-style numbers throughout. Mitigating factors: the data-partition protocol (template-grouped splits, protected final test, logged validation queries) is unusually well-specified for a company report, and the bad-response definition (confirmed contextual violation, not stylistic preference) is operationalized. A methodological concern: the diagnostic labels that define the primary metric appear to be produced under the same rubric ecosystem the system optimizes, so the 64.71% reduction is partly on the optimizer's own terms; the human evaluation partially offsets this but is small (600 judgments) and its inter-annotator agreement is not reported. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (an internal system pipeline with measured outcomes; no deployment evidence). - Practical: Yes in principle — it operates via LLM calls and orchestration over existing role-play stacks, but no hardware requirements or artifact are published. - Efficient: Not stated; each iteration consumes diagnosis, repair, and validation LLM calls, and the paper only says candidate budgets bound the search without reporting per-character iteration counts or total compute cost. - Effective: The evidence (large defect-rate reduction plus favorable human preference on an internal distribution) supports effectiveness on the proxy metric, but production transfer is explicitly unevaluated. - Scalable: Untested beyond 50 characters and 5 models; whether updater-rule revisions learned from 50 characters generalize to hundreds — or whether rule accumulation bloats or overfits — is only claimed, not measured. The work delivers a paper only; no library, tool, dataset, or trained model is released. Strengths: - The two-level formulation is a real conceptual contribution: representing the updater as versioned diagnostic/routing/selection rules with explicit permission boundaries, rollback targets, and atomic rule diffs makes 'recursive self-improvement' concrete and auditable rather than rhetorical — a sharper design than the Self-Refine/Reflexion lineage it cites. - Data-hygiene discipline is a standout: grouped scenario splits to defeat paraphrase leakage, treating repeated validation feedback as selection data, frozen rubric/model/simulator configs before final evaluation, and rejection of checkpoint selection on the final test set. Most industrial self-improvement papers skip this entirely. - The evaluation design (5 models × 50 characters × 100-round conversations, ~100k scored replies pooled, plus blinded human comparison) is substantially larger and more multi-model than typical role-play papers, and the design honestly anticipates model-collapse concerns from recursive data by citing and guarding against distributional narrowing. - The diagnostic taxonomy correctly refuses a single ideal answer per scene and requires evidenced violations before authorizing durable edits, which guards against overwriting legitimate character behavior — the no-change control in every candidate set is a sensible, uncommon touch. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: AI-generated interlocutors may concentrate tests around simulator style; findings concern internal dialogue quality and production transfer requires separate evaluation; pooled results mask per-model/per-character/per-turn variation; uncertainty estimates require conversation-level records and evaluator-agreement data; and repeated validation feedback risks overfitting selection scenarios (motivating the protected final test). This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations section — a credibility positive — though it stops short of the missing ablation, which is conceded only obliquely in the interpretation section ('Isolating the additional contribution of updater evolution requires a component-level comparison'). Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No ablation of the outer loop. The headline result could be explained almost entirely by a single-pass diagnose-repair-validate loop; without a 'fixed updater vs. evolving updater' condition, the paper's titular claim (recursion improving the improvement process) is unsupported by evidence. - No external benchmark (CharacterEval, EmoCharacter, Role-Play Bench are cited but not run), so results cannot be situated against any published number, and the internal 'bad-response' metric is defined and scored by the same organization that built the system — a self-grading loop even with the human spot-check. - The human evaluation omits inter-annotator agreement, number of annotators, and instruction details; 600 judgments across presumably many character–model pairs may be thinly spread, and the 'decisive win rate' (71.19%) framing downplays the 49.00% raw win rate against a baseline that includes no self-improvement at all. - The five base models are never named, and per-model results are absent — readers cannot tell whether the gain is uniform or driven by one weak model, nor reproduce any pairing. - Cost is undisclosed: an RSI cycle involving optimization dialogues, diagnosis, candidate generation, validation, and meta-updates could be orders of magnitude more expensive than the baseline per point of quality, and no token/call accounting is provided. - The updater-gate comparison (candidate vs. parent updater repairing the same fresh failures) has an unexamined variance problem: with fixed candidate budgets, small validation samples could make acceptance noisy, and no analysis of accepted-versus-rejected updater revisions is reported (how many rule revisions were actually accepted across the run?). - References include items dated 2026 (MiniMax, Memory-Driven Role-Playing, PersonaForge), and the paper reads as a company technical report; no peer-review status is indicated. Bottom Line: A practitioner building role-play agents will gain a genuinely useful design template — particularly the versioned, permission-bounded updater and the data-partition protocol — but should treat the quantitative claims as internal, unaudited vendor results on the system's own metric, and look elsewhere for externally validated evidence that the recursive (rather than merely iterative) part of the loop pays for itself.

Leakage aware gated non local fusion network for calibrated IIoT SCADA cyberattack detection supporting cyber risk management and operational resilience

Z Doha, AA Mojumder, K Hossain, MS Ahammed… · link.springer.com · cyber model training - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces the Gated Non-local Fusion Network (GNF), a compact tabular deep-learning model (~1.4M parameters) that performs five-class intrusion detection (Backdoor, Command Injection, DoS, Reconnaissance, Normal) on the cleaned WUSTL-IIoT-2021 dataset with explicit leakage-aware preprocessing, semantic feature-group tokenization, and post-hoc probability calibration. - Why it's important: Published IIoT/SCADA intrusion-detection results are often inflated by preprocessing leakage and dominated by majority-class accuracy, so operators and researchers lack trustworthy, calibrated signals for prioritizing rare but high-consequence attack alerts. - How it does it: GNF groups 41 flow predictors into 7 semantic feature-group tokens, applies depthwise Conv1D for local token interactions plus gated non-local attention for global token mixing, trains with class-balanced focal loss, and fits a scalar temperature (T = 1.37) on validation logits. - The good: The evaluation is unusually thorough for this literature — ablations isolating every major component, five-seed variability (macro-F1 0.9393 ± 0.0057), bootstrap CIs, McNemar testing, IP-disjoint and temporal splits, and an honest confusion-matrix analysis showing Backdoor recall of only 0.7000 despite 0.9998 accuracy. - The missing: All evidence comes from a single cleaned benchmark; there is no cross-dataset validation, no code release, and the macro-F1 gain over the closest published comparator (DeepNonLocalNN, 0.93 vs. 0.9399 under different protocols) is small and not established under a shared evaluation. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on network-intrusion detection evaluation methodology (leakage audits, calibration, minority-class reporting on WUSTL-IIoT-2021 specifically); skip it if you want a genuinely new architecture, since GNF is a competent recombination of known tabular and non-local attention components.

Problem & Motivation: Operators of IIoT/SCADA systems face cyberattacks that threaten data integrity, availability, and physical process continuity, and they need network-flow intrusion detectors whose reported performance is trustworthy. The paper argues that much of the ML/DL intrusion-detection literature suffers from three defects: preprocessing leakage (scalers/encoders fitted on all data before splitting), severe class imbalance that lets accuracy and weighted-F1 mask weak minority-attack detection, and poorly calibrated confidences that undermine alert triage. The affected audiences are industrial security teams and the researchers who benchmark detectors on public IIoT datasets. The gap addressed is methodological: demonstrate a detector evaluated under leakage-aware, class-aware, calibration-aware protocol on WUSTL-IIoT-2021 rather than introduce a fundamentally new learning problem. Key Idea: The core move is to represent each network flow not as a flat vector or arbitrary column sequence but as a short sequence of 7 semantically meaningful feature-group tokens (endpoint/port, packet count, byte volume, load/rate, timing, jitter/loss, protocol/TCP state), then process this token sequence with complementary local (depthwise Conv1D) and global (gated non-local attention) operators, trained with class-balanced focal loss and calibrated by temperature scaling. The semantic grouping is the paper's distinctive assumption: it lets convolution operate along an imposed but domain-justified ordering of feature families rather than raw column positions. Methodology: The pipeline has three stages. (1) Leakage-aware data preparation: label isolation, 60/20/20 split before any stateful transformation, scalers/encoders fitted on the training partition only, deduplication of 3,436 corrupted/duplicate flows (1,194,464 → 1,191,028 records), plus leakage audits reporting 0.0% train–test IP overlap and zero test-before-train flows. (2) Representation and fusion: 41 predictors are partitioned into 7 disjoint semantic groups (sizes 2, 3, 6, 6, 9, 8, 7), each projected to a common embedding dimension; depthwise Conv1D with GELU, dropout, and residual addition models neighboring-token interactions; a gated non-local module computes row-normalized query–key affinities across all 7 tokens, aggregates values, and modulates the contextual update with a learnable gate before residual fusion; a token-wise Transformer FFN with residual and layer normalization refines tokens; attention pooling and mean pooling are concatenated into a 2d-dimensional flow embedding feeding a 5-logit head. (3) Training and calibration: class-balanced focal loss (weights ~995.9 for Backdoor, ~796.8 for Command Injection, reflecting inverse-frequency weighting) handles imbalance; temperature scaling is fitted by L-BFGS on validation NLL with network weights frozen. Critical design decisions: the semantic grouping (justified by domain reasoning but acknowledged as not provably optimal); the imposed token ordering that the Conv1D depends on (acknowledged as imposed, not chronological); the gated fusion, whose rationale (different flows need different degrees of global mixing) is plausible but only supported indirectly by the ablation. Key Results: On the WUSTL-IIoT-2021 test set (238,205 records; test supports of 40 Backdoor, 50 Command Injection, 15,540 DoS, 1,632 Reconnaissance, 220,943 Normal), GNF achieved 0.9998 accuracy, 0.9999 ROC-AUC, 0.9399 macro-F1, 0.9998 weighted-F1, and 0.0042 ECE after temperature scaling (down from 0.0210), with ~1.4M parameters and 1318.4 s training time. Against FT-Transformer (macro-F1 0.7070), SAINT (0.6662), XGBoost (0.6276), TabNet (0.5864), TabTransformer (0.5289), and 1D-CNN-BiGRU (0.4596), GNF led on every reported metric. Crucially, the confusion matrix shows recall of 0.7000 (28/40) for Backdoor and 0.8600 (43/50) for Command Injection versus ≥0.999 for the large classes. Ablations attribute the largest macro-F1 drops to removing focal loss (−0.1420), gated non-local attention (−0.0949), and semantic grouping (−0.0700). Under stricter splits, macro-F1 fell to 0.9203 (temporal) and 0.9156 (IP-disjoint); FGSM ε=0.05 degraded macro-F1 to 0.8967, worse than Gaussian noise or feature dropout. Five-seed macro-F1 was 0.9393 ± 0.0057 with Backdoor recall varying 0.65–0.75 (26–30 of 40 correct). Against published WUSTL-IIoT-2021 results under non-identical protocols, DeepNonLocalNN reported 0.9999 accuracy / 0.93 macro-F1 — essentially comparable to GNF's 0.9998 / 0.9399. The baselines are representative and reasonably current (FT-Transformer, SAINT), and the paper is careful to present cross-study comparisons as contextual, not shared-protocol results. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (partially) plus ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION: the genuinely novel element is thin — the gated non-local fusion applied to semantic feature-group tokens for flow classification is a specific integration of known components (non-local attention from Yilmaz et al.'s DeepNonLocalNN lineage, depthwise Conv1D, focal loss, temperature scaling, leakage-safe splitting as in XNFT). The most defensible novelty is the disciplined, leakage-audited, calibration-focused evaluation protocol on this dataset, which is more a rigorous synthesis than a new formulation. Rigor & Reproducibility: The paper is above-average in rigor for this venue: component-wise ablations exist and every component shows a measurable contribution; five random seeds with means and sample SDs are reported; 1,000× bootstrap CI (macro-F1 0.9399 ± 0.0102) and a McNemar test vs. FT-Transformer (χ² = 14.7, p < 0.001) are provided; alternative splits and adversarial perturbations are tested. Concerns: no code release is mentioned (only the Kaggle-hosted dataset); Backdoor and Command Injection test supports of 40 and 50 make class-wise metrics extremely noisy (one flipped prediction = 2.5 points of Backdoor recall — the authors acknowledge this); the semantic grouping was designed on the same dataset it is evaluated on, so its ablation advantage may partly reflect benchmark-specific fitting; baseline hyperparameter tuning protocols are not detailed. The authors are commendably explicit that cross-study comparisons are not shared-protocol evaluations. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (benchmark experiments; no deployment). - Practical: Yes — a 1.4M-parameter model trained in ~22 minutes is trivially runnable on commodity hardware; no GPU requirements are stated, but the scale implies modest needs. - Efficient: Moderate — GNF trains faster than SAINT (2050.7 s) but ~4× slower than XGBoost (305.6 s); no inference latency, throughput, or memory figures are reported, which the authors flag as future work. - Effective: Partially — it solves the benchmark classification task with strong aggregate and macro metrics, but 30% of Backdoor test flows are missed, and effectiveness on the stated real problem (risk-relevant alerting in operational OT networks) is explicitly not demonstrated. - Scalable: Untested — 10×–100× scale behavior (larger datasets, streaming, concept drift) is only claimed as future work; the temporal and IP-disjoint splits already show ~2–3 point macro-F1 degradation, hinting that generalization narrows under shift. The work delivers no software artifact (no library, CLI, or released weights); it stops at paper form plus a dataset pointer. Strengths: - The evaluation discipline is the real contribution: split-before-scaling preprocessing, a quantified leakage audit (IP overlap, temporal ordering), and insistence on macro-F1/class-wise recall over accuracy directly address documented pathologies in the IDS-benchmarking literature. - Honest minority-class reporting: the paper foregrounds that 0.9998 accuracy coexists with 0.7000 Backdoor recall and analyzes the discreteness of the 40-sample support across seeds rather than hiding it. - Ablations covering every architectural and training component, with the calibration ablation correctly isolating that temperature scaling changes ECE (0.0210 → 0.0042) but not hard predictions. - The robustness matrix (Gaussian noise, feature dropout, FGSM, three split protocols) gives a realistic picture of where the model degrades, with adversarial perturbation correctly identified as the weakest axis. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly and at length (a credibility positive): single-benchmark evaluation with no cross-dataset generalization; severe imbalance with persistent Backdoor/Command Injection weakness despite focal loss; distribution-shift sensitivity shown by the temporal (0.9203) and IP-disjoint (0.9156) splits; adversarial fragility under FGSM; calibration and attention-based explanations not being causal; and no deployment readiness (no latency, streaming, SIEM integration, or edge-hardware testing). The abstract itself cautions that results 'should not be interpreted as uniform detection across attack categories.' Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The headline architecture comparison may be confounded: baseline hyperparameters, tuning budgets, and whether baselines received the same class-balancing and calibration treatment are not reported, so the large macro-F1 gaps (0.9399 vs. 0.7070 for FT-Transformer) could partly reflect implementation effort rather than architecture. - The semantic grouping is engineered with knowledge of WUSTL-IIoT-2021's 41 predictors; the ablation showing its value is therefore evaluated on the same distribution that shaped it, with no transfer test of the grouping to another flow dataset. - No comparison against SMOTE/cost-sensitive or oversampling-augmented baselines despite the related-work section citing SMOTE-based studies as the standard imbalance remedy; focal loss is only compared against plain cross-entropy. - Backdoor/Command Injection support (200/250 records total) is so small that the model's minority-class conclusions are statistically fragile; no stratified resampling or per-class CIs are given for these cells (only recall ranges across seeds). - The framing tying the detector to 'cyber risk management and operational resilience' in the title is not experimentally supported — appropriately disclaimed in the abstract, but the title overpromises relative to the evidence. - Inference-time cost, the metric that matters for operational alerting, is never measured. Bottom Line: A methodologically careful single-benchmark study whose evaluation protocol (leakage audit, calibration, minority-class honesty) is worth emulating, but whose architecture is a competent recombination of existing ideas with only marginal macro-F1 advantage over the closest prior model — practitioners seeking a deployable or cross-dataset-validated IIoT IDS will find better-grounded alternatives, while benchmark methodologists will find the protocol instructive.

Benchmarking Fine-Grained Visual Reasoning for Remote Sensing in Urban Management

TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces UMBench, a 2,733-question multiple-choice benchmark built from 583 UAV images for evaluating fine-grained visual reasoning in urban management, and proposes a training-free evidence-first chain-of-thought prompting method that improves MLLM accuracy on it. - Why it's important: Urban management decisions (traffic violations, road damage, water pollution, disaster warning) require reading small local visual evidence, yet existing RS benchmarks (RSVQA, FloodNet, VRSBench) mostly test scene-level classification, so MLLMs can score well by exploiting scene priors while missing the details that matter operationally. - How it does it: A three-stage prompt template (Visual Grounding → Prior Suppression → standardized output letter) forces the model to cite concrete local image evidence before choosing an option, requiring no fine-tuning or weight access. - The good: The paper controls for prompt length with a zero-shot CoT baseline, showing evidence-first CoT beats generic "Let's think step by step" (e.g., InternVL3.5-8B: 46.62 vs 44.31 vs 42.47 direct), which isolates the value of evidence orientation rather than mere longer reasoning. - The missing: No inter-annotator agreement, no significance testing or seeds, no released code/data link, and images are downscaled to 800 px on the long side — an odd choice for a benchmark whose entire premise is fine-grained small-object inspection. - Read it or not: Worth reading for researchers building RS-specific MLLM evaluations or applying MLLMs to urban operations; skippable for prompting-method researchers, since the method is a straightforward prompt template with modest, model-dependent gains.
Why this rank
Scored using Empirical profile. Rigor (40) is the primary drag: single-run accuracies with no seeds or significance tests on gaps as small as 0.99–1.4 points, no inter-annotator agreement, no chance-level/guessing analysis, no code or data release, and a clear Goodhart circularity — the evidence-first CoT template was designed for UMBench's distractor structure and validated only on UMBench. Novelty (50) is split: the anti-prior distractor design is a checkable and somewhat clever mechanism, but the prompting contribution is a thin reordering of known CoT and grounding ideas. Non-Obviousness (48) is low for the method — forcing a model to ground evidence before answering is what any competent practitioner would try given prior-suppression intuition. Completeness (55) gets partial credit for honest acknowledgment that gains are model-dependent and prompting alone does not solve fine-grained reasoning, but the 800 px image downscaling directly undermines the benchmark's fine-grained premise and is merely disclaimed, not investigated. Resilience (48) and Impact (45, unreleased dataset and no reusable artifact) complete a paper whose benchmark idea outstrips its execution. Problem & Motivation: Urban management agencies use remote sensing to monitor traffic, construction, environmental quality, and disasters, but these tasks need answers that hinge on small, ambiguous targets embedded in complex backgrounds (a vehicle crossing a lane line, local pavement cracks, inundation cues) rather than global scene category. Existing MLLM benchmarks for remote sensing test scene-level understanding or generic VQA, where many answers are inferable from scene priors — a failure mode related to object hallucination in vision-language models. The gap: no benchmark tests whether an MLLM grounds answers in fine-grained visual evidence versus guessing from scene-level priors in an urban-management context. Key Idea: The core insight is two-fold: (1) design benchmark questions whose scene-compatible distractors are plausible at the scene level but contradicted by small visual details, so scene-prior guessing fails by construction; (2) at inference time, impose an "evidence bottleneck" via prompt ordering — force the model to ground local cues and suppress priors before it commits to an answer. The second part is prompt engineering, not a new algorithmic mechanism. Methodology: UMBench construction: 583 UAV images (PNG, long side resized to 800 px, quality-controlled to remove blur/ambiguity/near-duplicates), 2,733 expert-curated multiple-choice QA pairs across four task groups — Traffic Monitoring (1,129 tags), Urban Construction (755), Environmental Quality (992), Disaster Warning (429) — with 3,305 cumulative tag assignments. Annotators identified a visually verifiable evidence region, wrote a question depending on that region, and built scene-compatible distractors; consensus review replaced an inter-annotator agreement score. Evaluation: zero-shot top-1 accuracy, identical images/questions/decoding across six models (Qwen3-VL-8B, InternVL3.5-8B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B locally; Gemini-3-Flash, Grok-4.20, GPT-4o via API); invalid outputs scored as incorrect. Three prompting conditions compared: direct answering, zero-shot CoT ("Let's think step by step"), and evidence-first CoT (Visual Grounding → Prior Suppression → Final Answer: <Option Letter>). Critical design decisions: (1) scene-compatible distractors — well-justified as the anti-prior mechanism; (2) replacing agreement statistics with a described consensus protocol — weaker justification, unquantified label reliability; (3) 800 px image resizing — explicitly disclaimed ("GSD metadata was not available") but poorly justified given the fine-grained premise. Key Results: Direct answering is weak across the board: Qwen3-VL-8B 47.35%, InternVL3.5-8B 42.47%, Qwen2.5-VL-7B 43.13%, GPT-4o 46.03%, Grok-4.20 44.97%, Gemini-3-Flash 51.58% (best). Evidence-first CoT improves all six models: +2.69 points for Qwen3-VL-8B (50.04), +4.15 for InternVL3.5-8B (46.62), +1.43 for Qwen2.5-VL-7B (44.56), +1.39 for Gemini-3-Flash (52.97), +3.60 for Grok-4.20 (48.57), +3.24 for GPT-4o (49.27). Against the ZS-CoT control, evidence-first CoT wins on all three open-source models (e.g., InternVL3.5-8B 46.62 vs 44.31; Qwen2.5-VL-7B 44.56 vs 43.57; Qwen3-VL-8B 50.04 vs 46.51), though gains over ZS-CoT are small (0.99–3.53 points). Notably, even the best model sits at ~53% on a multiple-choice benchmark, and per-task gains are inconsistent (Qwen2.5-VL-7B evidence-first CoT drops EQ from 50.10 to 47.28), confirming gains are model- and task-dependent. Baselines are current-generation models (2024–2026), which is appropriate; scale is modest (583 images, single benchmark, no stress-scale testing). Novelty Classification: NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK (first urban-management-focused fine-grained RS reasoning benchmark with scene-pair distractor design) plus a minor methodological contribution (evidence-first CoT is a lightweight reordering of known prompting ideas — CoT, visual grounding prompts, output-format constraints — applied in a new setting). The benchmark's distractor construction against scene priors is the genuinely new element; the prompting method is a competent combination of existing techniques. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present in one useful form: the ZS-CoT control separates evidence-orientation from generic longer reasoning, which many prompt papers omit. Missing: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests (single-run accuracies on a 2,733-item benchmark — several reported gaps of 1–2 points may not be significant); no inter-annotator agreement, acknowledged as replaced by consensus curation; no code, data, or model weights release URL stated. Methodological concerns: the prompting method is developed and evaluated on the same benchmark whose distractor structure it was explicitly designed for (the template's Prior Suppression stage is "designed for UMBench"), creating a Goodhart-style circularity; only the authors' own benchmark is evaluated, with no cross-benchmark evidence (e.g., does evidence-first CoT help on VRSBench or RSVQA?); commercial API results are vendor-system-dependent and version-sensitive. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (benchmark + prompting experiments actually run). - Practical: Yes — the method is a text prompt; open-source models run on standard GPUs, commercial models via public APIs. - Efficient: Negligible marginal cost; adds short prompt text and possibly some generated reasoning tokens, with no training, no extra images, no weight access needed. - Effective: Partially — it improves accuracy on its own benchmark by 1.4–4.2 points, but absolute performance stays near 50%, so it mitigates rather than solves fine-grained reasoning failures, and per-task results show it can hurt (EQ for Qwen2.5-VL-7B). - Scalable: Untested and not claimed beyond UMBench; 10× scale would require more images and would raise questions about expert curation cost, which the paper does not discuss. Delivers a dataset/benchmark (release mechanism not stated) and a reusable prompt template; no trained model or software library. Strengths: - The anti-prior distractor design is a concrete, checkable mechanism: questions are constructed so scene-level priors point to wrong answers, directly operationalizing the difference between scene recognition and evidence-based reasoning. - The three-way prompting comparison (direct vs. ZS-CoT vs. evidence-first) is a proper control that many prompt-engineering papers lack, and it supports the specific claim that evidence orientation, not reasoning length, drives the gain. - Evaluation covers both weight-accessible open models and black-box commercial APIs under identical decoding and preprocessing, demonstrating the prompt intervention transfers across access settings. - Honest framing of negative/nuanced results: the authors state gains "remain model- and task-dependent" and that "prompting alone cannot fully solve fine-grained visual reasoning." Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge that (1) gains from evidence-first CoT are model- and task-dependent with some per-task regressions visible in their own tables; (2) prompting alone cannot fully solve fine-grained visual reasoning; (3) no inter-annotator agreement score was computed, with consensus curation offered as the substitute protocol; (4) GSD metadata was unavailable for the processed images. They confront these reasonably directly rather than minimizing them, which is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The 800 px long-side resize and absent GSD metadata sit awkwardly against the paper's core claim of testing "fine-grained" inspection; small-object evidence (cracks, lane lines) may be partially destroyed by resizing, and the paper does not report what native resolution the UAV images had or test resolution sensitivity. - No missing-value/guessing-rate analysis: with ~50% accuracy on multiple-choice questions, the number of options per question and chance level are unreported, making absolute scores hard to interpret. - No comparison against other training-free visual-grounding interventions (visual cropping/zooming, Set-of-Mark, V*-style prompting) that plausibly target the same failure mode — the evidence-first prompt may underperform simple image cropping for small objects. - Single-run, no-variance reporting on gaps as small as 0.99–1.4 points (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL-7B over ZS-CoT) risks overstating differences. - The benchmark and the method are co-designed, so headline improvements may partly reflect prompt-benchmark fit rather than a general intervention; no held-out task family or external benchmark transfer is shown. - No release URL or licensing statement for UMBench, which limits community reuse — the main value of a benchmark paper. - "Expert team" composition and annotation guidelines are not described, so the curation protocol cannot be audited. Bottom Line: The benchmark's scene-prior-resistant distractor design is a genuinely useful evaluation tool for RS-MLLM researchers, but the evidence-first CoT method is thin prompt engineering with single-digit gains validated only on the benchmark it was designed for — read it for the dataset and evaluation protocol, and look elsewhere for prompting techniques.

Model -based graph reinforcement learning for robust cyber -attack defense in active distribution systems with high DER penetration

L Mou, Z Wang, L Wang, X Li · link.springer.com · cyber model training - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces MBGRL, a model-based graph reinforcement learning framework that combines a learned power-flow surrogate model with a GNN policy, adversarial training, and safe action masking to defend DER-rich active distribution systems against false data injection attacks (FDIAs). - Why it's important: Distribution grids with high DER penetration have a growing cyber-attack surface, and existing model-free RL defenses need excessive simulator interactions, generalize poorly across grid configurations, and ignore network topology, limiting real-world deployment for grid operators. - How it does it: The core move is training an SAC-style agent on a graph-structured MDP whose dynamics are captured by a learned neural surrogate (used for imagined rollouts to cut simulator calls), with adversarially poisoned observations mixed into training and a one-step surrogate-based filter that masks actions violating hard operational constraints. - The good: A controlled ablation replacing the GNN encoder with a fully connected encoder increases voltage violations by 32–47% and losses by up to 12%, directly evidencing that topology modeling—not just RL machinery—drives the gains; headline results (e.g., 5 vs. 12/18 voltage violations under load attacks) are averages over 20 Monte Carlo trials with randomized attack timing and targets. - The missing: All experiments are on a single IEEE-123 bus system, so the paper's claims of scaling with network size and generalizing to unseen attack patterns are never actually tested, and there is no comparison against other model-based RL or graph-RL baselines (e.g., MBPO-style or the graph-DRL methods the paper cites as closest work). - Read it or not: Worth reading for power-systems researchers building learning-based grid defense controllers who want a template for combining model-based RL with GNNs and safety masking; skip it if you need evidence of scalability or generalization, which is asserted but not demonstrated.

Problem & Motivation: Utilities and distribution system operators face stealthy false data injection attacks that corrupt sensor readings or DER control commands without triggering alarms, potentially causing unsafe voltage excursions, overloaded DERs, or unnecessary load shedding. The paper identifies two gaps in prior DRL-based defenses: (1) model-free RL requires many simulator interactions and does not generalize to large or dynamically changing grids; (2) prior agents treat grid state as a flat vector, discarding topology that determines how attacks and voltage violations propagate spatially. It also argues that detection-oriented works dominate the literature while control-oriented defense over coordinated multi-vector attacks (load alteration + DER setpoint tampering simultaneously) is underexplored. The motivating users are distribution operators of DER-rich feeders who need real-time, interpretable, safety-constrained mitigation. Key Idea: Reformulate FDIA defense as an MDP whose state is a graph (bus features = voltage magnitudes, DER P/Q, storage SoC, violation flags; edges from the admittance matrix) and train a model-based SAC variant: a learned dynamics surrogate generates imagined rollouts to reduce real simulator calls, a GNN policy/critic exploits topology, and a surrogate-based one-step predictor masks infeasible actions. The surrogate-in-the-loop is the load-bearing trick—it simultaneously enables sample-efficient model rollouts and fast (0.4 ms) safety filtering. Methodology: The framework has four components. (1) MDP formulation: graph-structured state per bus, hybrid action space (continuous DER setpoints, binary load shedding, switch configuration encoded as a decimal index from a binary vector), and a reward penalizing active-power losses, load shedding, voltage violations (±5% band), and SoC deviation with weighting coefficients. (2) Model-based learning: a neural network trained by MSE on replay-buffer transitions predicts next states; imagined rollouts supplement real OpenDSS interactions. (3) GNN policy and twin critics in the SAC structure, with a stochastic Gaussian actor (reparameterization trick) for exploration robustness; adversarial training mixes poisoned observations using the additive FDIA perturbation model with random perturbation magnitudes. (4) Safe action masking: a lightweight surrogate predicts one-step transitions and filters actions violating voltage limits, inverter ratings, or radiality/feasibility of switch states. Training co-simulates with OpenDSS in an OpenAI Gym wrapper (PyTorch, custom GNN layers, AMD Ryzen 9, 64 GB RAM). Critical design decisions: hybrid discrete/continuous actions with a single decimal index for switch configurations (justified only implicitly—this encoding assumes the agent can distinguish semantically unrelated topologies that map to nearby indices); adversarial perturbations sampled to be "modest" (justified by appeal to prior FDIA studies and NIST guidance for magnitudes, though the training-vs-eval perturbation distributions are not fully specified); and one-step lookahead for masking (justified by the 0.4 ms inference time fitting the 5-minute control cycle). Equations for the objective, constraints, and FDIA model are given, though the rendered math in the text is partially corrupted. Key Results: On the IEEE-123 bus system (60 DERs: 30 PV + 30 storage at 1200 kW each, 8 tie switches, 320 control steps of 5 min), averaged over 20 Monte Carlo trials: Scenario 1 (load-altering FDIA, 20 buses, 130–160% scaling) — MBGRL 5 voltage violations / 89 kW losses vs. SAC 12/102, MPC 18/111, Volt-VAR 51/129, Volt-Watt 47/133. Scenario 2 (DER setpoint attacks, 10 DERs, 25–40% drops during 11:30–13:30 solar peak) — MBGRL 6/91 vs. SAC 15/107, MPC 24/113. Scenario 3 (combined attacks, 15 loads overreported 50–70% + 8 DERs cut 40%, evening peak) — MBGRL 9/92 vs. SAC 19/109, MPC 30/121, Volt-VAR/Volt-Watt >60 violations. Scenario 4 (200% overload demanding load shedding) — MBGRL sheds 41% of load on ≤13 buses with 7 violations vs. SAC 53%/13 and MPC 60%/21. Efficiency: 54% fewer simulator interactions and >60% less training time than model-free SAC. Latency: GNN forward pass 0.7 ms, surrogate one-step prediction 0.4 ms. Variation across trials is reported as ±1 violation and ±3–4 kW losses. Baselines include a tuned SAC (matched hyperparameters), a CVXPY/OSQP MPC, and OpenDSS Volt-VAR/Volt-Watt — the MPC and SAC baselines are reasonable, but no model-based RL or GNN-based RL competitor is included, and the rule-based Volt-VAR/Volt-Watt baselines serve mainly as lower bounds. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (integration) and NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING. The genuinely novel element is the joint integration of a learned power-flow surrogate, GNN policy, adversarial training, and surrogate-based action masking within one cyber-defense framework—each ingredient (model-based RL, GCN/GAT policies, domain randomization, action masking) is standard in isolation, and the paper itself concedes novelty arises from the combination, not the components. The empirical finding that topology-aware encoding reduces violations by 32–47% versus a flat encoder on identical RL machinery is the most transferable insight. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are partially present: a fully connected encoder replacement (GNN ablation) and a tie-switch loss heatmap, but no ablation isolates the surrogate model's contribution to the 54%/60% efficiency claims, nor the adversarial training's contribution to robustness. Statistical treatment is limited to 20 Monte Carlo trials with reported variation ranges (±1 violation, ±3–4 kW); no confidence intervals, seeds analysis, or significance tests are given. No code, data, or trained weights are released ("data can be shared upon request"). Methodological concerns: (1) the claim of scaling with network size is evaluated only on one 123-bus feeder; (2) robustness to "unseen attack patterns" is claimed but no held-out attack type is tested—evaluation scenarios overlap the adversarial training distribution; (3) the abstract describes an "attention-based GNN" for interpretability while the implementation section specifies a GCN + 2-layer MLP, an internal inconsistency that undercuts the interpretability claim; (4) surrogate model accuracy (prediction error) is never reported, though the framework's performance is stated to depend on it; (5) reference [11] is cited both as Jacob et al. (Nat. Commun.) and as "Edeh" for a GCN+DQN detection model, a citation error. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (co-simulation study; no field or hardware deployment). - Practical: Yes in principle—a single AMD Ryzen 9 workstation with 64 GB RAM suffices; no GPU is reported as required, and per-step inference (1.1 ms total) fits a 5-minute control cycle. - Efficient: 54% fewer simulator interactions and >60% less training time than model-free SAC, with low inference latency; absolute training compute is not stated. - Effective: The evidence shows it outperforms SAC, MPC, and static controls on four synthetic FDIA scenarios in OpenDSS simulation—a proxy for real-world defense; no hardware-in-the-loop or field validation. - Scalable: Claimed but untested—at 10–100× scale (larger feeders, thousands of DERs), GNN message-passing cost, switch-configuration action encoding (exponential in switch count), and centralized MPC-free training all become open questions the paper acknowledges only qualitatively. The work delivers no software artifact; it stops at paper form with a described PyTorch/OpenDSS pipeline. Strengths: - The controlled GNN-vs-FC-encoder ablation is the paper's most credible contribution: it isolates topology modeling as the causal factor behind a 32–47% reduction in voltage violations, not just the overall framework. - The dual use of the learned surrogate—both for sample-efficient imagined rollouts and for sub-millisecond safety masking—is a clean design that ties sample efficiency to operational feasibility within one component. - Evaluation covers a meaningful threat taxonomy (load alteration, DER setpoint tampering, coordinated multi-vector attacks, forced load shedding) with attack magnitudes grounded in NIST guidance rather than arbitrary choices. - Honest reporting of Monte Carlo variation ranges (±1 violation, ±3–4 kW) rather than presenting noisy means as deterministic, and an explicitly acknowledged dependency of performance on surrogate accuracy. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that MBGRL's performance depends on the accuracy of the learned surrogate model, which may degrade under highly nonlinear or previously unseen conditions; that scaling to very large networks may increase GNN computational overhead; and they flag real-time deployment constraints, continual learning for online surrogate updates, and distributed/multi-agent extensions as future work. They confront the surrogate-accuracy limitation directly, which is a credibility positive, though they do not quantify how accurate the surrogate actually is. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Single-test-system evaluation: all results are on IEEE-123; the abstract's claim that MBGRL "scales effectively with network size" is never tested on any larger feeder (e.g., IEEE-8500). - No held-out attack generalization test: adversarial training uses the same FDIA model family as the evaluation scenarios, so "robustness to unseen attack patterns" is asserted, not measured (e.g., no test against attack types excluded from training). - Missing the most relevant baselines: no model-based RL competitor (MBPO/Dreamer-style) to substantiate the efficiency claims, and none of the graph-DRL methods cited as closest prior work (e.g., the capsule-GNN outage management of ref. [11]) are empirically compared. - The interpretability claim rests on an "attention-based GNN," but the architecture is described as GCN + MLP with no attention visualization or interpretability experiment shown. - The decimal-index encoding of switch configurations conflates combinatorially distinct topologies and grows exponentially with switch count; its learnability and scalability are not analyzed. - Surrogate model prediction error is never reported despite the framework's stated dependence on it. Bottom Line: A practitioner in grid cyber-defense gains a useful, well-motivated design template (surrogate + GNN + masking) and a credible topology ablation, but should look to stronger-validated work (e.g., graph-DRL outage management studies with broader feeder testing) before trusting the scalability and robustness claims as evidence.

J Krogstie · link.springer.com · simulation environments for business processes - new results
TL;DR:** - What it does: This paper (Chapter 1 of a Springer book on model quality) articulates a conceptual position that the quality of models must be evaluated for two audiences simultaneously — humans and machines — and sketches how the author's semiotic SEQUAL framework for visual conceptual model quality should be extended to sub-symbolic machine learning models. - Why it's important: As AI agents become both producers and consumers of models in enterprises and digital ecosystems, practitioners lack a shared vocabulary for judging whether a model is 'good' when its audience is no longer only human; unexamined model quality directly affects system quality, sustainability, and who holds epistemic control ('model power'). - How it does it: The core move is mapping Stachowiak's three criteria of a model (representation, simplification, pragmatic orientation) and Stamper's semiotic layers onto machine learning artifacts, arguing ML models only partially qualify as models and coining the Machine Learning Result (MLR) for what an ML model outputs when classifying unseen data. - The good: The Stachowiak-based argument that an ML model lacks transparent intentionality (its pragmatic orientation is not articulated, so goal alignment cannot be verified) is a genuinely crisp conceptual contribution that motivates the MLR distinction and the book's agenda. - The missing: There is no empirical evaluation whatsoever — no cases where the extended framework is applied and shown to yield different or better quality judgments than existing ML-quality frameworks (e.g., Siebert et al. 2022, which the chapter reproduces as a table); the promised integration is deferred to later chapters. - Read it or not: Read it if you work on conceptual modeling, enterprise modeling, or model quality and need a bridge-vocabulary toward ML/LLM artifacts; skip it if you want technical depth on XAI, neuro-symbolic methods, or ML data quality, which the chapter only lists and defers to Chapters 2–6.
