Problem & Motivation: The chapter addresses a conceptual gap in information systems research: the frameworks for assessing model quality (the author's SEQUAL, grounded in Stachowiak's general model theory and Peirce/Stamper semiotics) were built for visual models made by and for humans, while models are increasingly produced and consumed by digital actors (ML models, LLM-based agents). The motivating stakes are broad — business processes, digital business ecosystems (illustrated throughout with a Norwegian EV-charging ecosystem around Deftpower), and societal sustainability — all mediated by models whose quality dimensions (time, cost, quality, flexibility, resource use, compliance, etc.) trade off against each other and now include machine audiences. The chapter also raises a governance concern: AI systems act as 'model-strong' agents that can dominate 'model-weak' humans via model power/monopoly (Bråten), so keeping humans meaningfully in the loop requires models that remain understandable to people. Key Idea: The single core insight is that model quality is audience-relative and the audience now includes machines: the author applies Stachowiak's three model criteria to ML models and concludes that, because an ML model's pragmatic orientation (its training intention) is not transparently articulated, an ML model is not a model in the traditional sense — what it produces on unseen data is instead termed an MLR (Machine Learning Result). This reframing is intended to justify extending SEQUAL's seven quality layers (physical, empirical, syntactic, semantic, pragmatic, social, deontic) to cover data-as-models, ML models, and hybrid neuro-symbolic systems, with human judgment remaining indispensable at the higher semiotic layers. Methodology: This is a conceptual/position chapter, not an algorithmic one. Its method is framework synthesis: it assembles (1) Stachowiak's model theory and Stamper's/FRISCO's semiotic layers as the philosophical foundation; (2) the author's prior SEQUAL quality framework, defined via the tuple (G, L, D, M, A, K, I, T) — goals, language extension, domain, model, audience access, knowledge, social and technical interpretation — with quality types from physical through deontic; (3) a typology of modelling perspectives (behavioural, functional, structural, goal/rule, object, communication, actor/role, topological); (4) a knowledge-maturing process model (individual idea → organisational institutionalisation) and social-construction epistemology (Berger & Luckmann, Sølvberg) to argue models are subjective, socially constructed interpretations rather than objective depictions; and (5) catalogues of modelling goals (model mapping, communication, quality assurance, twinning, deployment/activation, context of change, implementation), model types by temporality (as-is, to-be, ideal, burning platform, etc.), and data-quality dimension tables. Critical design decisions: treating data itself as a model (argued via representation/simplification/pragmatic-orientation analogy), applying model-power theory to LLM chatbots (rule 3 updated so conversations with a model-strong tool can further train it), and classifying ML models as not-quite-models. None of these are empirically justified within the chapter; the social-construction stance is argued philosophically against Chen's objectivistic ontology, drawing on Sølvberg (1980). Key Results: No empirical results are reported — this is a conceptual chapter, and no measurements, benchmarks, or case outcomes are evaluated in it. The 'results' are the artefacts described: the SEQUAL tuple and quality typology (from prior work, Krogstie 2012/2016), reproduced tables of business-process value dimensions, data-quality dimensions (Batini & Scannapieco 2006), the Siebert et al. (2022) ML-quality meta-model spanning model/data/system/infrastructure/environment views, and the MLR/Stachowiak classification. Supporting empirical claims (e.g., LLM hallucination inconsistency per Krügel et al. 2023; model collapse from recursive training per Shumailov et al. 2024; overreliance on ChatGPT health advice per Sun et al. 2024) are cited from other literature, not tested here. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (partial) and position/survey content; the genuine novelty is the audience-extension of a human-centric model-quality framework to machine audiences and the Stachowiak-based argument that ML models fail the pragmatic-orientation criterion, yielding the MLR construct and the re-casting of model-power theory for AI agents. Everything else — semiotic layers, SEQUAL, business-process value dimensions, SusAF sustainability dimensions, Big Data V's, CRISP-DM, ML algorithm taxonomy, XAI surrogate/intrinsic/extrinsic categories — is standard prior work restated as groundwork for later chapters. Rigor & Reproducibility: Not applicable in the experimental sense: no ablations, seeds, or statistics exist here; no code, data, or artifacts are released. As a scholarly synthesis, the framework definitions are internally coherent and well-cited, but the chapter evaluates nothing — not even a worked application of the extended SEQUAL to a single ML model (the EV-charging and metro-map examples are described, not analysed). Two methodological concerns: (1) the central claim that ML models are 'not models' in Stachowiak's sense is asserted rather than stress-tested against counterarguments (e.g., alignment tuning arguably does articulate intent); (2) the quality-of-ML content is largely imported from Siebert et al. (2022) and Sancricca et al. (2025) rather than contributed. Peer-review status: it is a book chapter in a Springer volume (© 2027), presumably editorially reviewed rather than peer-reviewed as a conference paper. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: THEORETICAL (a conceptual framework/position chapter with no primary experiments and no software). - Sound: The framework is internally consistent and its assumptions (social construction of models, subjectivity of quality judgment) are stated explicitly, though the pivotal 'ML models are not models' argument has unexamined objections. - General: The claim is pitched broadly — all of traditional modelling plus data-as-models plus ML — which is a strength of scope but means the framework's applicability is illustrated, not delimited, with testable conditions. - Tight: Not a bound-bearing result; the closest analogue is that the framework's higher layers (semantic, pragmatic, social, deontic) are deliberately left to human judgment rather than formalised, so the framework is loose by design. - Implementable: Partially — SEQUAL is already used in practice for visual model quality, and the chapter promises a 'rejuvenated SEQUAL' integrating machine-audience aspects in Chapter 3; nothing operational is delivered in this chapter itself. The work delivers no software artifact, dataset, or trained model; it stops at paper (book-chapter) form, functioning as a reusable conceptual vocabulary. Strengths: - The Stachowiak-criterion analysis of ML models, and the derived MLR distinction, give conceptual modeling researchers a precise, arguable thesis about what kind of artifact an ML model is — a sharper move than the usual 'models for machines' rhetoric. - The extension of Bråten's model-power/model-monopoly theory to LLM-based agents (a model-strong tool whose answers a model-weak human internalises, potentially reinforced by retraining on that conversation) is a genuinely non-obvious transfer of 1970s systems-theory to current AI-governance concerns, connecting automation bias, RAG trust, and epistemic control. - The systematic unification of three previously separate literatures — conceptual model quality (SEQUAL), data quality (Batini/Scannapieco, Price & Shanks), and ML-system quality (Siebert et al.) — under one semiotic umbrella is a real synthesis contribution, even if the components are borrowed. - Honest epistemological positioning: the chapter explicitly rejects the objectivistic 'the world consists of entities and relations' stance of Chen-style modeling and states the social-construction alternative clearly, including its implications (multiple coexisting models, Sapir-Whorf-style language bias, premature closure). Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge that (1) quality of models is always a trade-off across dimensions that cannot be simultaneously optimised; (2) ML models trained on past data are 'models of the past' and not necessarily suited to predicting the future; (3) ML models' intentionality is opaque, so goal alignment of ML models cannot be verified — the stated reason for demoting them from full model status; (4) machine-learning data requirements partially conflict with traditional data-quality characteristics (e.g., balanced data is not inherently 'better'); (5) AI is not yet capable of abstraction across untrained domains or of creating new knowledge-representation mechanisms (citing Yadlowsky et al. 2023); and (6) some machine-relevant SEQUAL aspects (secondary notation, affective quality) are 'apparently less relevant' for machines and are deferred to Chapter 3. The chapter is candid about deferring technical depth to later chapters, which is appropriate for an opening chapter but means the framework integration claimed in the abstract is promised, not delivered. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The headline claim — extending model quality to machines — is never demonstrated: no worked example applies even the current SEQUAL to an ML model, MLR, or XAI output, so the reader cannot judge whether the extension is meaningful or vacuous. - The 'ML models are not models' argument ignores the strongest counterexample: alignment/RLHF pipelines are explicit, documented pragmatic orientations, and the author's own framing that 'the intention is often not clearly articulated' is an empirical claim about practices with no evidence cited. - The model-power analysis of LLMs assumes the human is model-weak, but offers no account of when or how to measure model strength asymmetry, nor of the reverse configuration the author himself gestures at ('keeping the human as the model-strong' via RAG control). - The chapter treats 'data as models' by analogy to Stachowiak's criteria, but does not confront the disanalogy that dataset curation lacks the intersubjective agreement processes (knowledge maturing, negotiation) that ground social quality for human models. - Claims about sustainability, neuro-symbolic computing, and agentic AI are forward-looking surveys of related work; a critical reader should treat all forward statements in the chapter as research agenda, not findings. Bottom Line: For conceptual- and enterprise-modeling researchers and practitioners confronting LLM-era 'models', this chapter is a useful, opinionated grounding document that earns its keep through the MLR and model-power arguments — but it is a program-setting opener whose actual framework extension is deferred to later chapters, so ML-focused readers will find better coverage elsewhere.

TL;DR - What it does: This paper reports a small, domain-specific empirical evaluation of OpenAI's Codex agent (configured with gpt-5.6-Sol) selecting among GraphDB MCP-server tools to answer managerially phrased natural-language questions over RDF-serialized BPMN and Working Environment models, scored with precision/recall/F1 against a hand-built gold standard. - Why it's important: Business users who cannot write SPARQL or formal process query languages need reliable natural-language access to annotated process model repositories, and prior LLM approaches failed on ordering, decision-point, and cross-pool questions. - How it does it: A single-agent MCP loop connects Codex to one GraphDB server exposing eight tools (SPARQL, retrieval search backed by a Weaviate/embedding pipeline, similarity search, full-text search, etc.), with tool selection left entirely to the agent and answers constrained to a JSON schema. - The good: The per-question analysis of tool calls vs. final answers isolates two concrete failure mechanisms — queries that exclude nested tasks, and relevant facts retrieved by tools but dropped from the final answer — which is more diagnostic than a headline score alone. - The missing: There is no baseline at all (no unaided LLM, no LLM-plus-RAG without MCP, no other model), and everything is evaluated on one synthetic repository authored by the same researcher who wrote the gold standard. - Read it or not: Read it if you work at the intersection of BPM knowledge graphs and MCP-mediated LLM agents and want a concrete error taxonomy and reusable protocol; skip it if you need statistically grounded benchmark results or model comparisons.

Problem & Motivation: Owners of business process model repositories annotated with execution-related information (responsibilities, durations, costs) face an accessibility gap: formal process query languages (BP-QL, APQL, BPMN-Q, PQL) and SPARQL require expertise business users lack, while LLM-based process question answering has shown uneven reliability — earlier studies reported misinterpreted dependencies, omitted activities, and poor handling of task order and decision points. The paper targets the question of whether a single LLM agent, given a standardized tool interface (MCP) to a graph database, can reliably answer multi-step, cross-model questions about process structure, routing, resource allocation, and organizational communication — question types that previously challenged LLM approaches. Key Idea: The core move is to let a general-purpose coding agent (Codex) autonomously orchestrate heterogeneous graph-repository tools exposed through a single MCP server — combining SPARQL with semantic retrieval (a GraphDB retrieval connector feeding an embedding pipeline into Weaviate) and a Lucene-based similarity index over SPARQL-generated element descriptions — so the agent itself decides when to use structured querying versus fuzzy retrieval, rather than the system designer fixing a retrieval strategy. There is no new algorithm; the contribution is the configuration and its empirical interrogation. Methodology: The pipeline has four stages. (1) Modeling: a synthetic judicial-collaboration scenario (client, law firm, court) is built in Bee-Up 1.7 — one BPMN collaboration with six subprocesses (52 tasks, 26 events, 13 gateways, 6 data objects) plus two Working Environment organizational models with RACI assignments over 50 tasks and time/cost attributes on all 52 tasks. (2) Serialization: a TriG export preserves one named graph per model plus a metadata graph, imported into a local GraphDB 11.4 repository with a cleanup SPARQL delete; a retrieval connector verbalizes property chains (e.g., responsible-actor relations) into text for text-embedding-3-large indexing in Weaviate, and a similarity index represents each element as a document assembled from name, type, model, cost, duration, and predecessor/successor labels. (3) Querying: 63 questions across six managerially oriented categories (element identification/containment, ordering/routes, resource allocation/performance, document use, participant communication, process weaknesses), adapted from prior query-framework taxonomies, are each posed in three fresh Codex chats with a read-only sandbox, high reasoning effort, and a JSON answer schema; the agent freely selects among eight MCP tools. (4) Evaluation: a Python evaluator scores answers against a manually constructed gold standard (with documented alternative acceptances) using precision, recall, and F1, and the exported transcripts are analyzed for tool selection and error sources. Critical design decisions: fresh chats per question to prevent cross-contamination (well justified); gold standards with explicit alternative answers for ambiguous scope (well justified, and honestly documented); only three runs per question at a single reasoning-effort setting (thin — the paper itself notes run-to-run variation is not statistically characterized). Key Results: Aggregate performance is high but reported mostly per representative question rather than as a single headline. Per category over three runs: element identification — 23/27 structured answers exact, 14/15 binary correct; ordering/routes — 13/18 structured exact, 9/9 binary correct; resource allocation — 60/69 exact; documents — 20/24 exact; communication — 15/15 exact; weaknesses — 10/12 exact. Figure 3 reports macro-averaged P/R/F1 per run in the 92.7–97.7% range. Specific failure patterns recur: all three runs conflated subprocess activation with internal start events; all runs omitted law-firm tasks when enumerating steps between two process points (F1 0.82); two runs returned a 34-hour "longest route" that silently dropped all court activities despite those facts appearing in tool results (run 3 with ontology-schema use reached the accepted 39h10m, F1 0.96); one run dropped two of four cross-pool outcome dependencies after a final filtering query (recall 0.50). Tool use is dominated by SPARQL calls, with retrieval_search present in most runs; more tool calls did not produce more complete answers. No baselines are compared — the evaluation is against a gold standard only, so these numbers describe absolute accuracy, not improvement over alternatives. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (modest) plus ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. What is genuinely novel is the setting and the evidence: this is, to the author's knowledge, the first quantitative evaluation of MCP-mediated tool selection by an agent over RDF-serialized BPMN knowledge, extending prior binary question evaluations to multi-step, cross-subprocess, cross-pool relations. Every component — Codex, MCP, GraphDB, Bee-Up RDF export, RAG over embeddings, similarity search — is an existing, standard technology; the paper is a competent, well-instrumented combination of known tools applied to a new domain configuration, not a new method or formulation. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations in the classic sense are absent, but the paper substitutes something arguably more informative for this setting: a trace-level analysis correlating tool calls, retrieved facts, and final-answer content to localize information loss. Error bars, seeds, and significance tests are not reported; the three repetitions per question are acknowledged as insufficient to characterize stochastic variation. Reproducibility is strong for the artifact layer: the complete query set, gold answers, raw Codex transcripts, reports, and evaluator are released on GitHub (github.com/DamarisDd/MCP-Codex-GraphDB-experiments), and the deployment configuration (model, reasoning effort, sandbox settings, connector/index definitions with SPARQL excerpts) is documented in detail. Methodological concerns: (1) the gold standard and the repository were constructed by the same author, so gold interpretation ambiguities (e.g., what "initiated" means) are resolved by the evaluator's own conventions — the paper mitigates this with documented alternative golds but a second annotator or inter-annotator agreement is absent; (2) no baseline condition exists, so the central claim that MCP-mediated access helps rests on comparison with qualitatively cited prior work, not measurement; (3) evaluation is entirely on the author's own single synthetic repository, developed in the same intellectual environment as the questions. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a built and run evaluation environment with a small systems component). - Practical: Yes — the entire stack (Codex client, GraphDB, Dockerized retrieval plugin and Weaviate) ran on one Windows workstation, all commercially available. - Efficient: Not measured; the paper reports tool-call counts per question (e.g., 4–23 calls) but no token, latency, or cost figures relative to alternatives. - Effective: Partially — the agent answers most questions correctly on this repository, but the evidence covers one small synthetic model set, and the residual errors on cross-pool scope and nested subprocesses show the stated problem is not fully solved even there. - Scalable: Only claimed, not tested; the author explicitly states the single small repository limits conclusions about larger repositories or other domains, and scaling to public BPMN collections would require extensive RDF re-serialization work the paper does not perform. The work delivers a software artifact: the experiment configuration, gold standard, and evaluator on GitHub, plus a reusable (if single-repository) experimental protocol; it stops short of a general-purpose tool or benchmark, which is deferred to future work. Strengths: - The diagnostic depth is the paper's real contribution: by comparing tool-retrieved facts against final answers, it identifies two distinct information-loss mechanisms (queries excluding nested tasks; answer-stage omission of retrieved facts) and shows that additional tool calls do not monotonically improve completeness — a finding that generalizes beyond BPM querying. - The question catalog is grounded in prior BPM query-framework taxonomies and deliberately targets question types (ordering, decision points, cross-pool dependencies) where earlier LLM evaluations documented failures, making the empirical coverage purposeful rather than arbitrary. - Unusually transparent error reporting: run-by-run discrepancies are enumerated, gold-standard interpretation decisions and their rationale are documented in the tables, and the gold alternatives concede where the question, not the agent, was ambiguous. - Full artifact release (queries, gold answers, raw transcripts, evaluator) makes the evaluation inspectable and re-runnable. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The paper states plainly that the experiments are "bounded by one synthetic repository, one agent and three repetitions per question, limiting conclusions about larger repositories or other domains"; that run-to-run differences reflect stochastic variation rather than learning; that category comparisons are descriptive because question counts and difficulty were uncontrolled; and that whether more detailed guidance improves answers remains untested. These limitations are confronted directly rather than minimized, which strengthens the paper's credibility. The planned follow-up — a reusable NL-querying benchmark over BPMN patterns and public model collections (Camunda, BPM Academic Initiative) — is a sensible remediation, with the RDF-serialization bottleneck honestly flagged. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No baseline condition. The most significant omission: nothing here measures whether MCP tool access outperforms (a) the same model answering from a serialized model dump, (b) a plain RAG pipeline without tool selection, or (c) direct SPARQL generation. The motivation rests on qualitative citations of prior LLM failures, so the central design choice is never validated against its alternatives. - Single-model, single-agent evaluation. gpt-5.6-Sol is the only model tested, at one reasoning-effort level, with no ablation over reasoning effort, temperature, or agent framework — yet the paper's conclusions about tool-selection behavior are model-specific. - Question–repository–gold co-design. The questions were instantiated on a repository built by the same author who wrote the gold standard, so the apparent difficulty profile (which categories are hard) may partly reflect how the questions and models were authored rather than intrinsic task difficulty. Inter-annotator agreement on the gold is absent. - Uncontrolled scoring discretion. Several golds accept alternative answers shaped after seeing agent outputs (e.g., the five-document alternative in Category 4, the assumption-guided withdrawal interpretation); while documented, this post-hoc flexibility risks inflating scores in ways a pre-registered gold would not. - The process-weakness category is the least validated. Questions about "where the process lacks a fallback" or "repeats work" have the most interpretation-dependent golds and the fewest questions (four examined), yet they are presented as a peer category alongside structural questions with objectively checkable answers. Bottom Line: A practitioner building natural-language interfaces over process knowledge graphs gains a concrete, honest error taxonomy and a replicable evaluation protocol worth borrowing, but will need to look elsewhere (or run their own baselines) for evidence that the MCP-mediated design actually beats simpler alternatives — this is a well-executed preliminary study, not yet a benchmark or a validated method.

Problem & Motivation: EdTech startups operate with small teams and tight budgets while facing investor-driven expectations of rapid scaling. AI agents — software performing multi-step tasks with limited supervision — are widely promoted as the way to reconcile this tension, yet the academic literature covers either AI in education from a pedagogical angle (OECD, UNESCO) or AI adoption in large enterprises, leaving the operational use of AI agents by early-stage EdTech companies almost unstudied. The dissertation also identifies secondary gaps: the literature treats AI adoption as binary rather than graded, reports cost savings without baselines, ignores upfront implementation costs, and exhibits survivorship bias toward success stories. Key Idea: The core move is not a technical insight but an empirical one: collect structured self-reported data directly from startup practitioners (founders, engineers, managers) in ecosystems (Ghana, Germany, and 8 other countries) that the dominant literature ignores, and read the results through four adoption frameworks (TAM, RBV, Diffusion of Innovation, Dynamic Capabilities) plus the Empowerment–Entrapment lens. There is no methodological trick; the contribution is the dataset and its descriptive patterns. Methodology: A quantitative, cross-sectional, positivist survey design. An 18-item structured questionnaire (5 sections: demographics, adoption, impact, barriers, outlook) was administered via Microsoft Forms and distributed through email, LinkedIn, and a startup community over roughly two weeks; 45 responses were received. Sampling was non-probability (purposive plus snowball), targeting professionals with direct AI experience in startups. Analysis was purely descriptive: frequency distributions, percentages, and Likert means (e.g., cost reduction and growth items), plus informal content analysis of one optional open-ended question. Three critical design decisions: (1) defining "AI agents" broadly to span ChatGPT-assisted drafting through fully autonomous workflows — practical for a niche population but one that dilutes construct validity; (2) sampling cross-sector because EdTech respondents were too scarce, interpreting EdTech findings from a 24.4% subset — a transparent but consequential compromise; (3) rejecting qualitative interviews after scheduling failures, acknowledged as pragmatic rather than principled. Justification for each decision is stated candidly. Key Results: Adoption was near-universal: 75.6% actively using and 15.6% piloting (91.1% combined). Top deployment areas: customer support/chatbots (62.2%), administrative automation (55.6%), content generation/personalisation (53.3%), software development (46.7%). Platforms: OpenAI 71.1%, Anthropic 64.4%, Google 46.7%; custom models only 15.6%. Cost reduction as motivation: 73.3%. Perceived cost reduction mean 3.82/5 (31.1% transformative, 31.1% significant); growth contribution mean 3.82/5. Largest savings reported in content creation (62.2%), customer support (51.1%), marketing (48.9%). Most common single experience: scaling without proportional headcount increase (26.7%); notably, 20.0% found implementation more complex than expected. Top barriers: data privacy/regulatory compliance (46.7%), high implementation costs (42.2%), data quality (37.8%), skills gap (31.1%). Team resistance was low (8.9%), diverging from SME literature. Investor expectations as motivation: only 6.7%. There is no comparison group, no baseline cost data, and no inferential statistics — all numbers are self-reported perceptions. Sample scale is small (n = 45, 10 countries, concentrated in Ghana 37.8% and Germany 28.9%); the EdTech subset is n = 11. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (modest). The genuinely new element is primary descriptive data on AI agent adoption from practitioners in understudied African and European startup ecosystems, plus the low-resistance and investor-motivation findings that diverge from SME literature. Everything else — the survey instrument, descriptive statistics, and the four-theory framing — is a standard application of established social-science methods to a new setting. No method, system, or benchmark contribution. Rigor & Reproducibility: No ablations, error bars, seeds, or significance tests (none expected for a descriptive MSc survey, but no inferential analysis is attempted). The full questionnaire is reproduced in Appendix A and summary tables in Appendix B, which supports replication of the instrument, but the raw dataset and code are not stated as publicly released. The limitations section (§3.8, §5.4) is unusually honest: it flags the n = 45 ceiling, possible duplicate firms within the anonymous sample, selection bias toward AI-favorable respondents from the researcher's network, geographic concentration, social desirability bias, and the fact that results describe AI-enabled automation generally rather than autonomous agents specifically. Methodological concern: the study's perceptions-based measures cannot distinguish recouped investment from net ongoing cost, and the survey was fielded to a sample likely predisposed toward AI — so the uniformly positive impact scores may be inflated. No Goodhart-style benchmark gaming applies, since there is no benchmark. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (a survey study, not a system). - Practical: Trivially reproducible — the instrument and analysis require only Microsoft Forms and spreadsheet-level statistics; no hardware constraints. - Efficient: The entire study cost roughly 45 respondents and two weeks of fieldwork; the recommendations (prioritize content/support/marketing, budget for complexity, avoid single-vendor lock-in) are actionable without capital. - Effective: Evidence is perception-based, not measured — respondents rated cost reduction on a 1–5 Likert scale rather than reporting actual figures, so the paper shows perceived benefit, not verified cost reduction. - Scalable: Not tested and not claimable; the authors correctly state the design cannot support generalization, and a 10× sample with EdTech-specific targeting is named as future work. The deliverable is paper form plus a reusable questionnaire; no dataset release, tool, or trained model is stated. Strengths: - Genuinely scarce primary data: the study delivers practitioner-level adoption statistics (e.g., 91.1% adoption, platform shares, barrier frequencies) where the prior literature offered only conceptual models and platform case studies. - A critical literature review that does real work: it interrogates survivorship bias (Byju's counter-example), flags the missing cost baselines and upfront-cost underreporting in the AI-cost literature, and questions whether commoditized AI satisfies RBV's inimitability criterion — this is above-average for the genre. - Honest accounting of the EdTech sample weakness: the paper repeatedly and explicitly reframes its claims as cross-sector with an indicative n = 11 EdTech subset rather than overstating them. - Concrete empirical nuances that challenge prior work: low team resistance (8.9%) versus SME findings, internally-driven rather than investor-driven adoption (6.7%), and implementation complexity reported by 20%. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors directly acknowledge: small sample precluding inferential statistics; non-probability sampling with selection bias toward AI-favorable, network-adjacent respondents; geographic concentration (Ghana, Germany); the EdTech subset forming only 24.4% of the sample; the unit of analysis being individuals who may share firms; self-reported data with social desirability risk; a broad AI-agent definition spanning assisted tools to autonomous agents; cross-sectional design unable to capture cost-benefit timing; and the loss of the planned interview component. This is a credibility positive — limitations are confronted directly and at length rather than minimized. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The title and research question center on EdTech startups, but the evidence base for that population is 11 self-selected respondents; the paper acknowledges this but still titles and frames the work as an EdTech study, an extrapolation beyond the data's strength. - Survivorship bias operates within the sample itself: failed startups and abandoned AI initiatives are unlikely to be represented among survey respondents recruited via founder communities, further inflating the positive impact means. - The uniformly positive Likert outcomes (means of 3.82 for both cost and growth, one "no reduction" out of 45) invite acquiescence-bias and common-method-variance concerns that a forced-comparison or behavioral-item design would mitigate; the paper does not address these. - No objective corroboration of any claim: a single item asking for approximate cost savings in percentage or currency terms would have materially strengthened the cost-reduction finding, and its absence is not explained. - The barrier "interconnection" analysis (§4.2.4) is acknowledged as speculative, yet the barrier co-occurrence data exist in the dataset and cross-tabulation was feasible; this is a missed analysis rather than a data limitation. - The regional comparison (Ghana vs. Germany) is set up as a motivation but essentially abandoned in analysis due to sample size — stated, but the framing still implies regional insight that the data cannot deliver. Bottom Line: A competently executed, honestly reported MSc survey that supplies the first small empirical snapshot of AI agent adoption in startups — worth a practitioner's or EdTech researcher's time for its descriptive data and critical literature review, but its EdTech-specific conclusions rest on 11 self-reported responses, so anyone needing rigorous EdTech evidence should treat this as a hypothesis-generating starting point, not a foundation.

Problem & Motivation: Organizations serving and training LLMs on cloud accelerators face volatile TCO: hardware depreciation is stable, but electricity rates, cooling, idle capacity, and regional pricing fluctuate across datacenters (the paper maps TPU service-rate variation by region as of 2026). Exploiting this via workload mobility — migrating a model from, e.g., TPU v5p to v6e — is blocked by three concrete hurdles: (1) HBM disparities (v7x offers 192 GiB/chip vs. 32 GiB on v6e) causing compiler OOM unless sharding is recalculated; (2) topology shifts (3D Torus v5p vs. 2D mesh v6e) invalidating collective-operation cost models and prior logical-axis mappings; (3) strict sharding divisibility rules (e.g., model_kv axis must divide attention head count) whose violation yields silent errors or compiler rejection. Existing cluster schedulers (Sia, Nexus, Frenzy) treat workloads as black boxes, and sharding compilers (GSPMD, Alpa, TAPAS) are hardware-agnostic — neither couples internal workload bottleneck analysis with real-time fleet economics, which is the gap ATLAS targets. Key Idea: Treat hardware migration as a closed-loop agentic pipeline rather than a search problem: the core move is an MCP-connected empirical feedback loop in which candidate sharding configurations are cross-compiled and executed on a cycle-accurate simulator before provisioning, so the Coordinator can parse compiler stack traces, persist failures in state, and roll back the Migration Agent to synthesize alternatives — turning the error-prone human iteration loop into an automated one, with cost selection driven by a work-normalized Normalized Cost per 1000 Steps metric rather than raw hourly chip rates. Methodology: The system runs on Google's Agent Development Kit with Gemini 3.1 Pro as the reasoning engine, orchestrated as five sub-agents: (1) a Coordinator maintaining persistent JSON state (session_id, source_metadata, target_platform, active_proposals, compilation_history) with a retry-and-rollback handler; (2) an Analyzer that parses XProf traces and classifies the workload as compute-, memory-, or communication-bound via a Roofline model; (3) a Selector computing Compute Parity (N_target = ⌈N_source × TC_source / TC_target⌉) and Memory Feasibility (N_mem = next_power_of_2(⌈M_total / HBM_target⌉)), taking N_final = max(N_target, N_mem), rounded to valid slice sizes, and reconciling against regional availability and on-demand/spot pricing; (4) a Migration Agent doing cosine-similarity RAG (1000-char chunks, 200-char overlap, gemini-embedding-001 into a 3072-dim vector store, top-3 retrieval injected as few-shot demonstrations) over spec sheets and historical code changes, followed by a symbolic constraint engine validating attention-head divisibility and embedding sharding dimensions; (5) a Validator executing XLA cross-compilation and the compiled HLO graph on the HybridSim simulator via MCP, returning estimated step times. The explicit objective is Equation (4): Normalized Cost per 1000 Steps = Step Time (ms) × Normalized Total Cost per Hour / 3600, with source-platform hourly cost normalized to 1.0. Critical design decisions: (a) work-normalized costing rather than hourly rates — well-justified, since a cheaper-but-slower platform can raise total cost to completion; (b) simulation-based validation instead of physical hardware — convenient but unvalidated against real chips (see gaps); (c) restricting synthesized configurations to standard ici_mesh axes — acknowledged as a scope limit. Key Results: Six production LLM migration scenarios across TPU v5p, v6e (Trillium), v5e, and v7x (Ironwood): Case 1 (v5p→v6e, 128→512 chips): -44.85% cost, -39.33% step time (7406.1 ms → 4493.0 ms), +64.84% throughput, with two default configurations failing OOM while ATLAS's (seq:4, model:4) sharding compiled. Case 2 (v6e→v5p, 256→128): best proposal -50.80% cost, +58.26% throughput, though the paper notes human experts can beat it with weeks of secondary tuning. Case 3.1 (v5e→v7x, 256→32): -21.41% cost, +59.06% throughput. Case 3.2 (v5e→v6e): modest -7.52% cost, +21.66% throughput. Case 3.3, a forced migration to the Selector's least-recommended target (v5p), shows +18.20% cost / +35.07% step-time regression at the recommended proposal — used as evidence the Selector ranks correctly — though one of three tested proposals on that platform actually achieved -28.37% cost. Case 4 (simulated v6e price surge → v5e, 16→32 chips): -32.80% cost at the price of +123.63% step time, demonstrating the economic guardrail trades latency for budget. Lifecycle: average 1.19 hours versus stated 91.7–510.16 hours of manual engineering (up to 428× Time-to-Value speedup); averages across recommended optimizations: -31.48% cost, -32.77% step time, +50.96% throughput. Scale: standard production workloads and chip counts up to 512; no stress-scale or toy-model sweep. Baselines are the source-platform default configurations — no comparison against any automated sharding compiler or human-optimized configuration at equal time budget. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL with a secondary NEW PROBLEM framing (automating the full migration lifecycle, not just sharding search). The genuinely new element is the coupling of fleet economics (regional pricing, compute parity, price-surge guardrails) with an agentic diagnostic-synthesis-validation loop; the individual mechanisms — RAG few-shot synthesis, symbolic constraint checking, simulator-in-the-loop validation, coordinator state machines — are standard combinations of existing ideas (ADK patterns, retrieval augmentation, constraint validation) applied to this new setting. The related-work positioning against black-box schedulers and hardware-agnostic sharding compilers is accurate but the bridge is largely orchestration of known components. Rigor & Reproducibility: No ablations isolate which components matter (e.g., does RAG retrieval outperform prompting the LLM with spec sheets alone? Does the symbolic engine matter given the Validator would catch violations anyway?). No error bars, seeds, or significance tests; several scenarios report only one to three point configurations each. The clearest control — Case 3.3 as a suboptimal-target ablation — is undermined by its own Table 6, where proposal P3 on the 'least-recommended' platform achieves -28.37% cost, contradicting the ranking-validation narrative. No code, data, vector-store contents, prompts, or model weights are released (no URL given); the simulator (HybridSim) is not described in enough detail to reproduce. All performance claims rest on the authors' own simulator rather than hardware counters or physical runs — a self-reported, unverifiable evidence base. Manual-baseline times (91.7–510.16 hours) are asserted without methodology. This is an anonymous NeurIPS 2026 submission (preprint, not yet peer-reviewed). Deployability: Profile: SYSTEMS (a built agentic tool evaluated via deployment in simulation). Practical: The agent stack runs on commercially available LLM APIs and standard tooling, but depends on internal-adjacent artifacts (XProf traces, XLA cross-compilers, MCP server, HybridSim simulator) whose availability outside Google's ecosystem is unstated. Efficient: ~1.19 hours and a handful of Gemini 3.1 Pro calls plus simulated compilations per migration — cheap relative to weeks of engineer time, though LLM token and simulation costs are not itemized. Effective: Evidence shows the system produces valid, cost-improving configurations in simulation; it does not show a single physical-hardware run, so real-world effectiveness is a proxy claim only. Scalable: Untested beyond 512 chips and six scenarios; the deterministic Selector formulas (Equations 1–3) are crude first-order models (raw TensorCore ratios, power-of-two chip counts) whose accuracy at much larger slices or with multi-job interference is unknown. The work delivers no public software artifact — it stops at paper form; the reusable takeaway is the architectural pattern, not a library. Strengths: (1) A genuinely well-chosen problem formulation: reframing sharding/hardware selection as an economic (work-normalized cost) optimization over live pricing rather than a pure performance search — the Normalized Cost per 1000 Steps metric is a real conceptual contribution that fixes a common naive-costing error. (2) The closed-loop validation design is architecturally sound: the rollback-on-failure state machine that feeds compiler stack traces back into the Migration Agent's context is a concrete, transferable mechanism for agentic systems operating against compilers. (3) The OOM-avoidance result in Case 1 — where two default sharding configurations fail compilation but ATLAS's memory-aware (seq:4, model:4) scheme passes — is the paper's most credible evidence that knowledge-augmented synthesis adds value over naive retargeting. (4) Including a deliberately suboptimal-target control (Case 3.3) and a price-surge guardrail scenario (Case 4) shows the authors designed experiments to test decision quality, not just headline wins. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state the system relies on high-fidelity post-run profiling traces (requiring an already-profiled workload) and focuses only on standard ici_mesh variables, deferring compiler-specific kernel flags and dynamic batch sizing to future work. They also concede that human experts can achieve deeper peak optimizations with weeks of tuning (e.g., Case 2), positioning ATLAS as producing a fast baseline rather than a global optimum. They confront limitations briefly but do not engage the simulation-versus-hardware gap, which is the more serious caveat. Analyst-Identified Gaps: (1) The elephant: every performance and cost number derives from a cycle-accurate simulator validated nowhere in the paper against physical TPU measurements — the '50.8% TCO reduction' claim is entirely a simulation artifact, and the paper never reports a single physical run. (2) 'TCO' is a misnomer: the metric is normalized chip-hour cost × step time; cooling, depreciation, and idle-capacity factors motivating the introduction are never modeled. (3) No baselines from the automated-sharding literature the paper itself cites (GSPMD, Alpa, TAPAS) — the only comparison is against default/naive configurations, the weakest possible control. (4) The Case 3.3 'validation' contradicts its own data (P3 achieves -28.37% cost on the supposedly worst platform), and the write-up does not address this. (5) Only one region pair per case, one workload per case (models unnamed), three proposals per scenario — far too few samples to support reliability claims like 'reliably preventing compilation and runtime failures.' (6) The manual-baseline time figures (91.7–510.16 hours) underpin the headline 428× speedup but have no stated provenance. (7) The Compute Parity formula ignores memory-bandwidth and interconnect differences that the paper's own topology discussion says dominate collective-heavy workloads. Bottom Line: A credible and timely systems-vision paper with a genuinely useful economic framing (work-normalized cost) and a sensible agentic architecture, but with headline numbers resting entirely on unvalidated simulation, no external baselines, and no released artifact — practitioners should read it for the design pattern and cost metric, while treating every percentage claim as unproven until someone runs it on real hardware.

An Intelligent Multi-objective Decision Support Model for Sustainable Remanufacturing

MS Amjad, H Charkhgard, N Diaz-Elsayed · link.springer.com · simulation environments for business processes - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper introduces a tri-objective integer linear assignment model that allocates remanufacturing jobs to machines to simultaneously minimize cost per part, GHG emissions per part, and process noise per part, solved exactly with the quadrant shrinking method, and packages it into a DMAIC-based implementation framework for SMEs pursuing circular economy adoption. - Why it's important: SMEs make up 90% of businesses and dominate manufacturing employment, yet they lack accessible decision tools that balance economic, environmental, and social sustainability tradeoffs when adopting remanufacturing; prior work relies on heuristics that give no optimality guarantee and ignores the social dimension. - How it does it: The core move is formulating remanufacturing task assignment as a balanced binary assignment program with three objective functions (cost, kg-CO2-eq, and noise converted from logarithmic decibels to the linear sone scale and integer-scaled by 100), then enumerating the entire nondominated frontier with the exact quadrant shrinking scalarization algorithm rather than a metaheuristic. - The good: The exact method generates all 33 nondominated solutions for the 5×5 instance in under 4 seconds on commodity hardware (8 GB RAM, 6-core i5), demonstrating that full Pareto-frontier enumeration is computationally tractable enough for re-runnable, dynamic decision support. - The missing: The evaluation is a single 5×5 toy instance with randomly sampled simulated coefficients — no real factory data, no scaling study beyond 25 machine-job pairs, no comparison against the heuristic baselines (NSGA-II, MOEA/D) the paper criticizes, and the DMAIC framework is presented but never deployed or validated. - Read it or not: Worth reading for sustainability-manufacturing researchers and SME practitioners who need a concrete template for exact tri-objective remanufacturing optimization and a DMAIC adoption roadmap; optimization researchers will find the methodological content is a direct application of Boland et al. (2017) and can skip it.

Problem & Motivation: Small- and medium-sized manufacturing enterprises considering remanufacturing — a value-retention circular economy practice where remanufactured goods sell at 60–70% of original price at 35–60% of original production cost — lack tools to understand whether remanufacturing is actually beneficial across all three sustainability dimensions simultaneously. Existing multi-objective optimization work in remanufacturing targets buffer allocation, supply chains, facility location, and lot sizing, but is dominated by hybrid metaheuristics (NSGA-II, MOEA/D, MOGA) that optimize only economic and environmental objectives, offer no guarantee of global optimality or even feasibility, and collapse tradeoffs into weighted aggregates that bias results. The social dimension is poorly captured because standard indicators (employee satisfaction, health) are qualitative; the authors argue a directly measurable physical proxy is needed. The gap the paper closes is an SME-focused, exact, tri-objective formulation that includes a quantifiable social indicator — a claim supported by the authors' literature review assertion that no prior method applies exact multi-objective optimization to all three sustainability dimensions in remanufacturing. Key Idea: The core insight is that the social sustainability dimension — usually qualitative and excluded from optimization — can be operationalized as process noise exposure (a directly measurable, OSHA-regulated physical parameter), enabling a standard three-objective assignment integer program to represent the full triple bottom line; solving it with the exact quadrant shrinking method guarantees every returned point is nondominated, unlike heuristic alternatives. A secondary technical trick is handling the logarithmic decibel scale by converting to the linear sone scale (via Stevens' formula) and scaling by 100 to satisfy the algorithm's integer-coefficient requirement. Methodology: The model is a binary balanced assignment program: decision variable x[i][j] = 1 if job j is assigned to machine i; constraints (5)–(6) force each machine to exactly one job and each job to exactly one machine. Three objectives are minimized: total cost per part (USD), total GHG emissions per part (kg-CO2-eq), and total sound pressure per part (dB, optimized on the sone scale). The pipeline is: (1) generate coefficient matrices by random sampling within representative ranges (cost [1,100] USD, emissions [1,100] kg-CO2-eq, noise [60,100] dB); (2) convert noise to sones and integer-scale; (3) solve with the quadrant shrinking method (Boland et al. 2017) implemented in Python 3.9 with Gurobi 11.0 — the method first minimizes the third objective to obtain a weakly efficient solution, then optimizes the sum of objectives subject to lower bounds, iteratively shrinking unexplored regions of the criterion space until the full nondominated set is certified; (4) translate the Pareto front into a four-phase DMAIC framework (Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve/Control) for circular economy adoption. Critical design decisions: (a) noise as the social proxy — justified by measurability and OSHA relevance, though it is a narrow reading of "social" sustainability (worker health hazard only, not wages, satisfaction, or community impact); (b) an exact algorithm over heuristics — justified by optimality guarantees and the sub-4-second runtime; (c) equal weighting across objectives with post-hoc decision-maker selection from the frontier — reasonable, but the paper offers only pointers to selection methods (TOPSIS, VIKOR, Nash-welfare multiplicative programming) rather than implementing one. Key Results: On a single 5×5 simulated instance (5 machines, 5 jobs), the quadrant shrinking method generated 33 nondominated solutions in under 4 seconds on average, on a desktop-class machine (Intel i5-10500, 8 GB RAM, Gurobi 11.0). The frontier exhibits the expected tradeoffs: the minimum-cost assignment has the highest noise, and the minimum-emissions assignment has the highest cost. No baseline comparisons (heuristic or exact) were run; no performance metrics beyond the 33-point frontier and runtime are reported. The scale tested is explicitly toy — the authors state the 5×5 instance is illustrative. There are no surprising findings; the paper's empirical claim is that full exact frontier enumeration is fast enough for interactive, re-runnable decision support, which the sub-4-second runtime supports at this scale only. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (an exact tri-objective assignment model combining cost, emissions, and noise-as-social-proxy for remanufacturing) plus a conceptual framework contribution. The genuinely new element is the claim — plausible per the literature review — that this is the first exact multi-objective optimization of all three sustainability dimensions for remanufacturing; however, the optimization machinery is a direct, unmodified application of the existing quadrant shrinking method, the DMAIC framing is a well-known lean six sigma construct re-contextualized for circular economy, and the noise-for-social-sustainability indicator idea is borrowed from Guarnaccia et al. (2014) and Golinska-Dawson et al. (2018). This is a competent combination of known techniques in a new application setting, not a new method. Rigor & Reproducibility: There are no ablations (there is essentially one component to ablate, the exact algorithm, but no sensitivity analysis on coefficient ranges or instance structure), no error bars, seeds, or statistical treatment — a single random 5×5 instance is reported, with the full coefficient table given in Table 1, which aids reproduction. No code or data repository is released; the Data Availability statement says contributions are included in the article and directs inquiries to the corresponding author. The formulation is simple enough that reproduction would be straightforward for anyone with Gurobi. Methodological concerns: (1) evaluation exclusively on the authors' own randomly generated instance — no standard benchmark, no real factory data; (2) the paper argues exact methods are necessary because heuristics cannot guarantee optimality, yet never actually compares runtime or solution quality against NSGA-II/MOEA/D on any instance, so the claimed advantage is asserted, not measured; (3) the word "intelligent" in the framing (contrasting with FIFO/manual scheduling) is marketing-adjacent relative to what is demonstrated. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a small optimization study with simulated data), with a systems-flavored framework component that is not deployed. - Practical: Yes — the model runs in Python with Gurobi on an 8 GB desktop, hardware any SME owns, though Gurobi's commercial licensing cost is not discussed. - Efficient: Under 4 seconds for the 5×5 instance; efficiency at industrially relevant sizes (hundreds of machines/jobs) is untested, and the authors themselves acknowledge combinatorial scaling concerns. - Effective: The evidence shows the model produces a certified Pareto front for a synthetic toy problem — it demonstrates solvability, not that it improves any real remanufacturing decision; the DMAIC framework's effectiveness is entirely unevaluated. - Scalable: Not tested beyond 25 assignments; quadrant shrinking methods are known to scale poorly on tri-objective problems with large fronts, and the paper only asserts that AI/RL enhancements could address large-scale cases. The work delivers no software artifact, library, or trained model — it stops at paper form, with the model "designed with future application to real-world data." Strengths: - The quantification of the social sustainability dimension as measurable, OSHA-bounded process noise (with the psychophysical decibel→sone conversion handled correctly for linear aggregation) is a genuinely useful modeling move that makes the triple bottom line tractable in a single optimization framework. - The choice of an exact scalarization method with a certified termination condition (the unexplored-region set is exhausted) is well-motivated against the heuristic-dominated remanufacturing literature and gives decision-makers defensible, nondominated options. - The DMAIC-based framework is concretely phased with named indicators per dimension (cost per part, kg-CO2-eq per part, noise/sones per part) and mapped to specific stakeholder groups, making it more actionable than the purely conceptual circular economy frameworks the paper critiques. - Honest scoping: the authors repeatedly and explicitly state the data are simulated, the instance is illustrative, and practical implementation "remains to be seen." Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors confront limitations directly and at length: the optimization was tested only on a 5×5 instance and computational effort will grow with problem size (a known challenge in combinatorial optimization); all data are simulated and the practical implementation of the DMAIC framework is unvalidated; the model requires integer objective coefficients; and future work is needed for full job sequencing/scheduling with machine states (on/off/standby/idle), supply-chain-level 6R scope, and net-zero factory objectives. This candor is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No head-to-head comparison with the heuristic baselines (NSGA-II, MOEA/D, SPEA) the paper criticizes — the central argument for exact methods rests on a claimed, not measured, advantage, and heuristics often find the full frontier on small instances at trivial cost. - Noise as the sole social indicator ignores wage fairness, job security, ergonomics, and community impact — dimensions the paper's own literature review identifies as part of social sustainability; the proxy choice is narrowed without discussion of what is lost. - Random uniform coefficient sampling assumes machine-job cost/emission/noise independence and uniform spreads; real factories exhibit correlated structure (an old machine is likely both costly and loud), which would reshape the frontier and possibly the tractability. - The claim that the model supports "dynamic decision making" is not tested — no re-solve under changed conditions, no stochastic or uncertainty treatment (return quality and discard rate variability, cited as core remanufacturing characteristics, are absent from the model). - Noise aggregation by simple summation of sones assumes negligible auditory interaction between sources, an assumption stated but not tested even in the toy instance, and cumulative worker noise exposure over a shift (the actual OSHA metric) is not modeled. - The 5×5 balanced case (equal machines and jobs) is the easiest possible assignment variant; unbalanced, capacitated, or precedence-constrained variants that occur in practice are not explored. Bottom Line: A practitioner in sustainable manufacturing or circular economy operations gains a usable formulation template and a sensible DMAIC adoption checklist, but an OR researcher will find nothing beyond a clean application of Boland et al.'s (2017) quadrant shrinking method to a toy instance — stronger, larger-scale, data-backed alternatives exist in the remanufacturing scheduling literature this paper itself cites.

Problem & Motivation: Researchers building learning-augmented combinatorial solvers face two gaps the authors target: (1) the ML/RL machinery (GNNs, PPO, actor–critic, bandits, differentiable logic, attention) is typically assumed known, yet solver researchers come from symbolic/OR backgrounds; and (2) learning components appear in the literature attached to different solver stages without a common formal skeleton, making architectures hard to compare. The supplement addresses who-needs-what by providing the shared mathematical specification (MDP tuples, message-passing equations, policy-gradient theorem, CVaR risk objectives, differentiable neural logic operators) that the main paper's taxonomy presumes. It also documents the classical baseline landscape — AC-3, backtracking, branch-and-bound, A*, LCG, CDCL, and solvers from Chuffed and Gecode to Kissat, Z3, and Yices — so that learned enhancements can be situated against the systems they would replace or augment. Key Idea: The single organizing insight is that learning-augmented solvers are best understood phase-wise: rather than treating ML as an end-to-end replacement for search, the document embeds a learnable policy or predictor into each of the three canonical LCG/CDCL phases — propagation (ML backbone prediction + RL-guided pruning, Algorithm 11), heuristic decision (instance classification, auto-tuning, bandit/Transformer branching, Algorithm 12), and conflict analysis (learned clause-utility regression over size/LBD/age/activity features, RL restart scheduling, neural prioritization via NeuroGIFT, Algorithm 13) — all sharing one MDP/PPO formalism and reward-shaping scheme (reward = reduction in working-clause count or conflict rate). Differentiable neural logic (smooth conjunction/disjunction with sigmoid-tempered weights, Eqs. 9–10) supplies the continuous bridge for disjunctive (DisP) constraints. Beyond this framing, the content is competent assembly of known techniques; the supplement itself concedes the relational/FOL module is 'an optional supplementary extension rather than a separate unified pipeline.' Methodology: As supplemental material for a survey, the methodology is formal exposition rather than experiment. The document proceeds in layers: (1) ML/RL foundations — MDP M = (S, A, Pr, R, γ), policy-gradient theorem, tabular Q-learning and DQN temporal-difference loss, A2C (Algorithm 1) and PPO with the clipped objective LCLIP (Algorithm 2), distributional RL with CVaRα(Z) = E[Z | Z ≤ F⁻¹_Z(α)]; (2) neural machinery — feedforward networks, GNN message passing h⁽ᵏ⁺¹⁾_v = ϕ_upd(h⁽ᵏ⁾_v, Σ ϕ_msg(h⁽ᵏ⁾_u, e_uv)), node2vec, scaled dot-product and pointer attention, logistic polarity prediction, and UCB bandits underlying LRB branching; (3) classical CSP/SAT — AC-3 (Alg. 3), BTS (Alg. 4), BB (Alg. 5), BFS/DFS (Algs. 6–7), A* (Alg. 8), generic LCG (Alg. 9) and CDCL (Alg. 10) with explicit conflict-analysis/backjump pseudocode, VSIDS (Alg. 15) and CHB (Alg. 16); (4) direct solution learning — a solution operator Φ: I → S trained by supervised loss with constraint-violation penalty, self-supervised satisfaction maximization with sigmoid-temperature binarization, and gradient projection refinement; (5) formulations of six network-design and six graph-optimization problems as MILP/MINLPs, with GNN decoders for shortest path, MST, max-flow/min-cut, and attention-RL TSP construction; (6) DisP case studies (job-shop with GNN+PPO, attention-based deep RL, CVaR distributional RL, neuro-symbolic ILP+RL) and an Algorithm 18 for neural-assisted grounding of first-order relational constraints into propositional form. Critical design choices: the reward-shaping convention r_t = |C^{t-1}_working| − |C^t_working| is reused consistently across propagation, restart, and direct-solving MDPs (well-justified for comparability); PPO is repeatedly chosen as the training objective without justification over alternatives (unjustified but conventional); the differentiable-logic temperature c is introduced with clear semantics (larger c → closer to crisp Boolean behavior) but no guidance on tuning. Key Results: The document reports no experiments of its own; 'Key Results' are literature summaries in Section 9 and Table 3, all second-hand: GNN+RL dispatching policies achieve 10–25% makespan reduction on job-shop scheduling (Park et al., 2021); deep RL with GNN features gives 20–35% runtime improvement on dynamic JSSP (Liu et al., 2023); attention-based RL with disjunctive-graph embeddings reduces tardiness by 30% (Chen et al., 2023); ML-guided branching (LRB, Liang et al., 2016) speeds SAT solving on industrial benchmarks; NeuroSAT (Selsam et al., 2018) achieves competitive satisfiability prediction accuracy on SATLIB and handcrafted datasets; an ML+SAT hybrid reduces timetabling runtime and raises feasibility rates (Matos et al., 2021); binarized physics-inspired GNNs reach comparable accuracy at lower compute cost (Krutský et al., 2025). The baselines in the cited works are a mix of metaheuristics and domain-specific solvers — for the SAT entries the baselines are strong (MapleSAT-lineage solvers), for scheduling they are heuristic/metaheuristic rather than exact. The scale is 'standard benchmark' throughout; no stress-scale or large-instance results are claimed. The only counter-intuitive-adjacent observation the authors volunteer is that reported gains 'remain benchmark- and implementation-dependent.' Novelty Classification: This is a synthesis artifact supporting a NEW TAXONOMY/NEW FORMULATION claim in the parent paper: the genuinely novel element is the uniform phase-wise formalization that plugs a shared MDP/PPO/reward-shaping interface into each LCG/CDCL stage, plus the differentiable-logic treatment of DisP disjunctions. Everything else — GNN message passing, PPO, VSIDS/CHB, AC-3, LBD, NeuroSAT, CVaR RL, MILP formulations of TSP/MST/max-flow — is standard material restated with the authors' notation. No new method, dataset, system, or empirical finding originates here. Rigor & Reproducibility: There are no ablations, seeds, error bars, or significance tests — none are possible, since no experiments are run. The empirical table (Table 3) reports point ranges (e.g., '10–25%', '20–35%') from prior publications without confidence measures or unified evaluation protocols. Reproducibility assets: the supplement itself is hosted at github.com/GS1400/suppMat_ML_CSP, and the pseudocode is detailed enough to re-implement, but no code implementing Algorithms 11–18 is provided. Methodological concerns: (1) all quantitative claims are self-compiled from heterogeneous literature with varying benchmarks, hardware, and baselines — a practitioner cannot treat Table 3 as comparable evidence; (2) the parent e-print is an Optimization Online preprint (ID 32520), not peer-reviewed, and reference [27] carries a future-dated access stamp ('accessed: 2026-10-05'), suggesting citation-metadata sloppiness; (3) several 'algorithms' (VSIDS, CHB, BFS, DFS) are textbook procedures whose inclusion inflates the algorithm count without adding technical content. Deployability: Profile: this is neither an EMPIRICAL nor THEORETICAL paper in the strict sense — it is a survey supplement; I apply the EMPIRICAL check to the workflows it specifies, judged against the evidence it cites, not against its own runs. - Practical: The specified components (PPO, small GNN encoders, logistic heads) run on commodity hardware; nothing here demands accelerators beyond what the cited works used. - Efficient: Not evaluated — the document offers no cost measurements; the closest signal is the cited Krutský et al. binarized-GNN result of comparable accuracy at reduced model size. - Effective: The cited evidence shows improvements on specific benchmark families (industrial SAT, job-shop, timetabling), not that the phase-wise architecture generalizes; the document itself flags gains as benchmark-dependent. - Scalable: Only claimed via the cited GNN-for-TSP statement that tours are 'competitive with classical heuristics (e.g., Lin–Kernighan) on moderate-size instances' — no 10×–100× scaling test is presented anywhere. The deliverable is a PDF supplement plus a public repository mirror of it; no trained models, solver code, or dataset artifacts are released. The reusable contribution is the formal notation and pseudocode templates, not software. Strengths: - The phase-wise mapping (learning component ↔ specific LCG/CDCL step, e.g., Algorithm 13's clause-utility regression over [LBD, size, age, activity] feeding retention decisions) is a real organizational contribution that makes heterogeneous literature comparable — this is the survey's intellectual core, not mere compilation. - Algorithm 9 and 10 give unusually precise conflict-analysis/backjump pseudocode, including the UIP subtlety in computing d_backjump (the text correctly notes that the simplified max-level formula must exclude the UIP literal in practice), which many surveys gloss over. - The differentiable neural logic operators (Eqs. 9–10) with a temperature-controlled bridge from soft to crisp logic, and the L_logic loss that is zero exactly when all clauses are satisfied, provide a clean, implementable neuro-symbolic interface for DisP. - Section 9 is honest: it explicitly qualifies every reported improvement as benchmark- and implementation-dependent rather than presenting second-hand numbers as settled fact. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that RL/ML gains 'remain benchmark- and implementation-dependent' (Section 9.1), that the relational/FOL-CSP material is 'an optional supplementary extension rather than a separate unified constraint-solving pipeline' (Section 8.4), and that community-structure ML analysis applies to structured (not random) SAT instances. These are stated directly, which is a credibility positive; however, the document does not confront the larger limitation that it contains no original evaluation of the workflows it formalizes — the acknowledgment is implicit, not explicit. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No unifying experiment: a taxonomy whose stated purpose is comparing solver architectures would be far more valuable with even one shared-benchmark comparison of, say, PPO-guided restarts versus CHB on identical instances; none is attempted here or cited. - PPO is adopted as the training objective for propagation pruning, restart scheduling, and direct solving without any ablation or argument against cheaper alternatives (bandits, contextual bandits), despite the document itself introducing UCB bandits as the lighter-weight mechanism for exactly these decision problems. - The future-dated self-citation dates in references [26]–[27] (an e-print 'updated: 2026-10-05' and a supplement 'accessed: 2026-10-05') and minor formulation errors (the GCP objective rendered as 'min k s.t. ...' with a dangling objective) suggest the document was not carefully proofread — a flag for the parent paper's overall polish. - Table 3 mixes effect types (makespan %, runtime %, tardiness %, qualitative 'accurate prediction') into one table, inviting apples-to-oranges reading; the '10–25%' style ranges carry no variance or instance-count context. - Several of the 18 algorithms (BFS, DFS, VSIDS, CHB, A*) are classical textbook content; counting them alongside the genuinely integration-specific algorithms (11–14, 17–18) overstates the supplement's technical density. Bottom Line: As a tutorial companion that turns a fragmented neuro-symbolic solver literature into one consistent formal skeleton with implementable pseudocode, this supplement earns its place on a graduate student's desk — but it contains no new science, and anyone seeking evidence or a critical empirical comparison of learning-augmented solver architectures should go to the primary papers it cites rather than rely on its second-hand Table 3.

Integrating Business Process Reengineering (BPR) and Lean in the Industry 5.0 Era: A Systematic Literature Review

M Jonatan, I Hapsari · sostech.greenvest.co.id · simulation environments for business processes - new results
TL;DR - What it does: This paper presents a PRISMA-guided systematic literature review of 30 peer-reviewed articles (screened from 2,127 records) that synthesizes how Business Process Reengineering (BPR) and Lean management are integrated, and maps the reported approaches against the Industry 5.0 pillars of human-centricity, sustainability, and resilience. - Why it's important: Organizations pursuing both radical process redesign and continuous improvement face high failure rates (the paper cites 70–80% for standalone BPR), and the Industry 5.0 agenda adds human and environmental criteria that neither methodology was originally designed to serve. - How it does it: It thematically clusters 30 articles into six groups (BPR frameworks, Lean/TQM tools, Lean Six Sigma hybrids, healthcare applications, Industry 4.0/digital tools, and knowledge management) and derives integration approaches and organizational enablers from the clustered evidence. - The good: The review is honest about its central evidentiary weakness — it explicitly states that reported operational-performance gains should not be conflated with measured human well-being, sustainability, or resilience outcomes, and that the literature provides almost no direct empirical evidence on the Industry 5.0 pillars. - The missing: There is no formal quality appraisal of the 30 included studies, no inter-rater reliability for screening/synthesis, and the Industry 5.0 framing is largely imposed retrospectively on papers that were mostly written about BPR, Lean, or Industry 4.0 — not about Industry 5.0. - Read it or not: Worth reading for operations-management researchers or practitioners wanting a compact annotated map of BPR–Lean integration methods (DMAIC, TQM–BPR–TQM, PRISM, BPR-LC, dynamic VSM) and a research agenda; skip it if you seek validated Industry 5.0 guidance, which the review itself concedes does not yet exist.
Why this rank

Novelty (30) is the primary drag — the authors themselves disclaim originality in combining the methods, and the six-cluster synthesis is a competent reorganization of known operations ideas with the Industry 5.0 framing imposed largely retroactively. Rigor (35) suffers from no formal quality appraisal, a single narrow search string, citation-count-based exclusion biasing against precisely the recent work the framing needs, and a weak venue. Completeness (55) is a genuine strength — the evidentiary honesty about what the literature does and does not measure is exemplary — but a review with no new method, no validation, and no artifact (Impact 35) cannot clear the Innovative band.
