Problem & Motivation: Operators of power-grid virtual host clouds (IaaS hosting dispatch automation, marketing, and equipment monitoring systems) must schedule workloads across a physical layer, virtualization layer, and application layer. Differences in resource management across these layers produce resource fragmentation — small unallocated resource blocks that, under non-priority scheduling, occupy scheduling channels and increase latency. Prior approaches the authors critique (clustering plus cuckoo search [5], learning automata [6], threshold-based priority scheduling [7], DNN-based multi-objective optimization [8]) each fail, per the authors, to respond in real time to dynamic workloads or to coordinate grouping, priority ordering, and admission control as one mechanism, leaving secondary fragmentation after grouping. The target QoS bar is a millisecond-scale collection cycle, sub-10 ms transmission delay, and reliable channel access for mixed real-time (RT) and non-real-time (NRT) power services. Key Idea: The core move is a closed-loop pipeline of "grouping → scheduling → admission": fuzzy clustering maps multi-dimensional resource attributes into descending group priorities, a fixed-frame time-slot scheduler converts those priorities into deterministic channel allocation, and a rate-estimation-based admission controller dynamically caps channels per group so low-priority bursts cannot preempt high-priority traffic. This is presented as the answer to secondary fragmentation — each stage suppresses fragmentation at a different granularity. The idea is a coordinated composition of known techniques rather than a fundamentally new mechanism. Methodology: The system has three deployed stages. (1) Virtualization layer — fuzzy clustering: a resource feature matrix (four attributes: computing power, inter-node transmission capacity, capacity to historical data nodes, connection count) is z-score standardized, range-normalized to [0,1], grouped via an exponential similarity coefficient, and evaluated with a cut-set-based clustering method; groups are ranked by a weighted composite performance score (Eq. 4) for descending ordering. (2) Application layer — time-slot-aware priority scheduling: related workflow tasks are merged into a task pool, sub-deadlines and priorities are computed from deadline proximity to the exit task, and a queue scheduler allocates resources within a fixed-length frame divided into four mini-slots, with high-priority queues assigned the earliest mini-slots; transmission windows per queue are computed from frame length, transmission speed, and the least common multiple of periods (Eqs. 5–10). (3) Group admission control: a packet arrival rate estimation algorithm computes the mean inter-packet interval over the most recent n packets per priority group, estimates arrival rate, and combines it with a dynamic coefficient to compute a maximum available channel count; groups exceeding the cap back off. Critical design decisions: fixing the frame to exactly four mini-slots (justified only by the observation that more slots increase access latency), using equal slot lengths with priority ordering (stated, not justified quantitatively), and the choice of the dynamic coefficient in the admission cap (not derived or tuned on-page). The overall framework is a heuristic pipeline, not an optimization with an explicit global objective function. Key Results: All experiments are in CloudSim 5.0 (extended with a multi-layer virtualization module) on a single Xeon E5-2680 v4 server, with 50 heterogeneous physical nodes (500–3000 MIPS), 200 VMs, Poisson synthetic task arrivals (1000–100,000 MI, deadlines 1.5–3.0× minimum execution time), and a proportionally scaled 2-hour Google Cluster Trace excerpt. Grouping quality: V-measure stays between 0.957 and 0.986 across resource counts (5–50) and 2–4 categories — except one unexplained outlier of 0.694 at 15 resources/4 categories. QoS: collection period stays under 2 ms (~1.85 ms at 500-byte queues), scheduling delay under 10 ms, communication interruption rate below 3.22%, packet arrival rate above 94.8%. Speedup ratio: the proposed algorithm reaches 5.92 (at 30 nodes) versus 3.02–3.21 for baselines re-implemented from references [7–9] — roughly a 1.85× gap that is reported without explanation of its source. Energy: total consumption drops from 8.94 to 84.67 kWh over 5–50 nodes, a 28–32% reduction versus baselines. Normalized multi-dimensional QoS at 50 nodes favors the proposed algorithm on latency (0.93), throughput (0.91), utilization (0.94), energy efficiency (0.89). Ablations attribute latency gains mainly to time-slot scheduling and reliability gains to admission control. Results are stated as averages of 30 runs with 95% confidence intervals, though intervals are not shown in the reported tables. The consistency of the proposed method's dominance across all metrics and the implausibly large speedup gap warrant skepticism about simulation-favorable tuning. Novelty Classification: NEW METHOD (weakly) plus ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION. What is genuinely new is the claim of a synergistic closed-loop among fuzzy clustering, time-slot priority scheduling, and admission control aimed specifically at cross-layer fragmentation in power virtual hosts — a new setting. Each component is a standard technique (fuzzy c-means-style clustering, fixed-frame priority mini-slot scheduling from the wireless scheduling literature, arrival-rate-based admission control), and the paper does not introduce new clustering, scheduling, or admission theory; the contribution is their integration and domain application. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations are present and well-structured (four variants across six metrics), which is a strength. Thirty independent runs with 95% confidence intervals are stated, but no intervals, error bars, or significance tests appear in the reported figures/tables, so statistical claims cannot be verified from the paper. No code, data, or simulation extension is publicly released, and no URL is given — reproducibility depends entirely on the parameter tables. Methodological concerns: (1) evaluation is entirely simulation-based with a synthetic workload generator built by the authors, so the metrics may encode the authors' own assumptions (Goodhart risk); (2) baseline [9] is cited as a survey/review paper, yet re-implemented with specific PSO parameters — the provenance of this baseline implementation is unclear; (3) the near-uniform dominance of the proposed method across every metric, including a speedup ratio nearly double all baselines, is not explained mechanistically; (4) the V-measure outlier (0.694) is acknowledged but dismissed without analysis. The claimed real-trace validation is limited to a 2-hour, rescaled Google trace, not actual power-grid data. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (simulation-based algorithm evaluation; no real deployment). - Practical: Yes in principle — CloudSim is free software and the hardware used (one 14-core Xeon, 128 GB RAM) is commodity, so the simulation itself is trivially runnable; the algorithm targets standard virtualized infrastructure. - Efficient: The algorithm itself reduces simulated energy 28–32% versus the three re-implemented baselines and reports low scheduling overhead, but the computational cost of the fuzzy clustering and admission-control loop per scheduling decision is never reported. - Effective: The evidence shows it meets the authors' simulated QoS proxies (sub-10 ms delay, >94.8% arrival rate) in CloudSim; effectiveness on a real power virtual host platform is untested and unclaimed beyond future work. - Scalable: Only claimed, not tested — the maximum tested scale is 50 physical nodes and 200 VMs, far below production power-grid clouds, and the authors concede that larger-scale, more dynamic scenarios require future metaheuristic extensions. The work delivers no software artifact, dataset, or trained model — it stops at paper form with simulation results. Strengths: - The ablation design is genuinely informative: it isolates that time-slot scheduling drives the latency reduction (14.82 → 8.64 ms) while admission control drives reliability (interruption rate 7.63% → 2.96% combined), supporting the synergy claim rather than an undifferentiated end-to-end number. - The paper is unusually complete in its simulation configuration — full parameter tables (Table 1), hardware specification, workload distributions, and baseline hyperparameters — which is more transparent than typical papers in this genre. - The fragmentation-centric framing (fragmentation → secondary fragmentation → channel contention) gives the three modules a coherent, explicitly argued rationale connecting each stage to a specific failure mode. - The energy evaluation uses an explicit linear power model with stated parameters (50 W idle / 200 W max) rather than hand-waved efficiency claims. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state that the method has only been validated in a simulation environment and that future work will deploy and test on real power virtual host platforms using real operational trace data. They further acknowledge that larger-scale and more dynamic scheduling scenarios require integrating SDN-based centralized control and metaheuristic optimization. This is a direct, non-minimizing statement of the central limitation, which is a credibility positive; they do not, however, address the weak baseline provenance or the unexplained speedup gap. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Baseline [9] (Mahdizadeh et al.) is cited as a survey/review of SDN-based scheduling, yet it is re-implemented as a concrete PSO algorithm with tuned parameters — either the wrong reference is cited or the baseline is a reconstruction whose fidelity cannot be checked; no comparison against a modern SDN-enabled scheduler (e.g., the AO+WOA method of their own reference [10]) is reported. - The near-2× speedup-ratio advantage over all baselines is flat across node counts (5.56–5.92 for the proposed method vs. 3.02–3.21 throughout) and never mechanistically explained; results this uniformly favorable in a self-built simulator suggest possible simulation artifacts or workload shaping. - The admission control analysis assumes Poisson-like, estimable arrival processes via a sliding window of n packets; power-grid control traffic (e.g., dispatch events, alarm bursts) is bursty and correlated, and no heavy-tail or burst stress test is reported. - The network configuration (1000 Mbps uniform bandwidth, 250 km node distance, 2 Mbit/s channel rate) is internally inconsistent and does not represent any realistic data-center or grid network, undermining the latency conclusions. - The single anomalous V-measure value (0.694) indicates clustering failure under some configurations, but the feature-distribution conditions triggering it are never characterized — a practitioner cannot know when the grouping stage will degrade. - No comparison to a simple strong baseline (e.g., earliest-deadline-first with VM consolidation, or weighted fair queuing) is included, so the reader cannot tell how much of the gain comes from the three-module design versus any priority-aware scheduling at all. Bottom Line: A practitioner in cloud resource scheduling will find little here beyond a competent, well-ablated but simulation-only application of standard clustering, priority time-slotting, and admission control to a power-grid setting — the absent strong baselines, questionable baseline provenance, and no real deployment mean stronger alternatives in the general QoS-aware cloud scheduling literature cover the same ground; domain specialists in power-grid IaaS may still find the fragmentation-suppression framing and QoS target numbers a useful reference point.

Problem & Motivation: FDIA attacks inject manipulated sensor/meter readings into AIoT-enabled cyber-physical systems (smart grids, industrial automation) to corrupt state estimation and economic dispatch. Centralized ML detection requires pooling raw measurements across grid regions, which conflicts with data-locality and privacy constraints of power companies. Prior FL-based FDIA detectors, per the authors, suffer from feature redundancy, limited detection robustness under non-IID data, and a focus on generic intrusion detection rather than FDIA specifically. The paper targets the gap: privacy-preserving, distributed FDIA detection that also handles heterogeneous client data. Key Idea: The core move is compositional, not conceptual: stack three heterogeneous sequence/modeling learners (Bi-GRU for bidirectional temporal patterns, TCN for dilated-causal temporal dependencies, VAE as a reconstruction-error anomaly detector) inside FedAvg, aggregate each base learner's parameters independently, and fuse their outputs with performance-weighted voting (weights 0.4/0.3/0.3). The second element is forcing all clients onto a single mRMR+ReliefF feature subset so that element-wise FedAvg aggregation is dimensionally consistent. There is no identifiable new algorithmic insight; the contribution is the specific combination and its evaluation. Methodology: The pipeline is: (1) two-level preprocessing (forward-filling + linear interpolation for missing values; Min-Max scaling and one-hot encoding), performed client-locally to avoid leaking statistics; (2) hybrid feature selection using greedy mRMR (mutual-information relevance minus redundancy, Eqs. 21–25) and ReliefF (neighborhood-based distance weighting, Eq. 26), reduced from 30 to 19 features; (3) local training of Bi-GRU (128 hidden units), VAE (latent dim 32, trained with reconstruction + KL loss, thresholded reconstruction error as binary decision), and TCN (dilated causal convolution, 64 filters, kernel 3, residual blocks); (4) weighted majority voting fusion; (5) FedAvg aggregation over 10 simulated IIoT clients on the UKM-NCT FDIA dataset (15,425 samples, 8,688 normal / 6,737 attack, non-IID split with attack ratios from 20% to 68.3% per client), 100 communication rounds × 30 local epochs, Adan optimizer (lr 0.001, β₁ 0.98/β₂ 0.92/β₃ 0.99), batch size 32. Reported communication overhead is ~11.2 GB total (5.6 MB/client/round/direction). Critical design decisions: (a) the common feature subset across clients — justified as necessary for FedAvg compatibility but its derivation without cross-client data exchange is under-specified; (b) VAE used as an unsupervised anomaly scorer fused with supervised learners — plausible but the fusion of a threshold-based decision with probability-style votes is not formalized; (c) hand-assigned ensemble weights (0.4/0.3/0.3) chosen empirically, only briefly defended. Key Results: On the FDIA IIoT dataset, FLFDA-ECM reaches 98.88% accuracy, 98.87% precision, 98.88% recall, 98.87% F1 at epoch 3000, versus literature-reported baselines including XGBoost (98.54%), GRU-CNN (93.00%), and Transformer (91.64%) — a margin of only ~0.34 points over XGBoost. On a cross-dataset evaluation with Edge-IIoTset, it reports 97.62% accuracy against FL baselines FedAvg-CNN (87.70%), DP-Fed (86.60%), and HE-Fed (88.90%) — again all literature-reported. Robustness degrades gracefully: 3/10 label-flipping clients drop accuracy to 93.72%, gradient poisoning to 91.76%; severe non-IID (Dirichlet α=0.1) drops accuracy from 99.12% (IID) to 96.94%. Computational efficiency is claimed as the best of all compared models (39.56 s training, 1.18 ms/sample inference, 36.91 MB memory, 0.35G FLOPs). Notably, the K-fold mean (97.42%) and multi-seed mean (97.60%) are materially lower than the single headline run of 98.88%, and the conclusion cites a "computational time of 5.57 s" inconsistent with Table 11's 39.56 s. Baselines are a mix of dated (ELM, ANN, Isolation Forest from 2019-era work) and recent, and none were re-run by the authors. Novelty Classification: NEW SYSTEM/TOOL at best — an assembly of established components (mRMR, ReliefF, Bi-GRU, VAE, TCN, weighted voting, FedAvg, Adan) applied to FDIA detection in a federated setting. No new formulation, algorithm, or theoretical result is introduced; the weighted-voting ensemble and hybrid feature selection are standard combinations, and Adan is applied as-is from its 2024 source paper. Rigor & Reproducibility: The internal rigor is above average for this genre: a 12-configuration ablation isolating each component (centralized vs. FL, each base learner alone, ensemble, +mRMR, +ReliefF, full — showing feature selection contributes ~1.6 points and ensemble ~2.5 points over the best single FL model), five random seeds with mean±SD, 10-fold CV with 95% CIs, Dirichlet-controlled non-IID experiments, and malicious-client simulations. However: (1) all external baselines are literature-reported, not re-implemented — the authors admit this and frame the comparison as "contextual"; (2) the K-fold used random partitioning, and the authors explicitly acknowledge temporal correlation across instances cannot be excluded (potential leakage given the time-series nature of the data); (3) no code release is stated — only the dataset URL (Zenodo record 14864902) — so the specific ensemble/FL configuration is not independently reproducible; (4) a single seed-42 run produces the headline number while seeds vary by over a point, so the abstract-level figure is the optimistic end of the distribution. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (simulated federated experiments on benchmark datasets; no real deployment). - Practical: Yes — trained on an i5-8600K with a 4 GB GPU and 16 GB RAM, well within commodity hardware. - Efficient: Reported costs are low (39.56 s training, 1.18 ms inference, 0.35G FLOPs), but these are self-reported on a 15K-sample dataset and the total FL communication cost (~11.2 GB for only 10 clients/100 rounds) scales linearly with clients and rounds. - Effective: It solves the benchmark proxy well (98.88% accuracy), but effectiveness against real, adaptive FDIA strategies and under the acknowledged temporal-correlation caveat is unproven. - Scalable: Only claimed, not tested — the authors themselves state scalability and communication overhead with growing client counts remain open; 10 clients is a small-scale simulation. The work delivers no software artifact — no code, library, or trained model release is mentioned; only the public dataset is reusable. Strengths: - The evaluation battery (ablation across centralized/FL/single-learner/ensemble/feature-selection configurations, 5 seeds, 10-fold CV with CIs, Dirichlet non-IID sweep, label-flipping and gradient-poisoning simulations) is genuinely more thorough than typical framework papers in this area, and the ablation actually quantifies each component's contribution. - The cross-dataset evaluation (Edge-IIoTset) partially tests generalization beyond the training distribution. - The federated design details are concretely specified (per-client data distributions, communication overhead accounting, per-round local optimization steps), and preprocessing is correctly kept client-local to avoid statistic leakage. - The authors openly acknowledge that literature-reported baselines and random K-fold partitioning limit the strength of their comparative and generalization claims. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: validation is confined to benchmark datasets with no large-scale real-world AIoT deployment; scalability and communication overhead may grow with client count; the dataset lacks reliable temporal/device identifiers so chronological or leave-one-client-out validation could not be performed, leaving possible temporal correlation unexcluded; secure aggregation is not implemented; adversarial robustness against sophisticated attacks is untested. This is a direct, non-minimizing limitations discussion — a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The mechanism for arriving at the "common feature subset across clients" is contradictory as written: mRMR-ReliefF is described as run locally on each client's data, yet a single globally consistent feature subset and ordering is assumed — computing this without sharing data (or sharing selection outcomes) is not explained, and this is a non-trivial federated consensus problem. - The headline 98.88% figure comes from a single configuration while the multi-seed mean is 97.60±0.56% and the K-fold mean is 97.42±0.43%; the paper's abstract-level claims anchor to the best run. - No comparison against strong, current FL-FDIA methods re-implemented under an identical protocol; the 0.34-point margin over XGBoost — a non-federated, far simpler baseline — is within seed noise (±0.56), so superiority over even the strongest baseline is not established. - The VAE's threshold-based anomaly decision is fused with supervised votes, but threshold selection, calibration across non-IID clients, and how a hard binary vote coexists with weighted soft voting are unspecified. - The ensemble weights (0.4/0.3/0.3) are hand-set; no weight-sensitivity analysis is reported despite the paper noting one "can help." - Internal inconsistencies undermine confidence: the conclusion's "computational time is 5.57 s" contradicts Table 11's 39.56 s training time, and the reported comparisons mix metrics from different papers whose class balance and protocols differ. - Writing quality issues (corrupted equation placeholders throughout the math sections, garbled sentences in the literature review) suggest weak editorial control, which raises concern about the care taken elsewhere. Bottom Line: A practitioner in federated grid security will find the evaluation template (ablation + seeds + CV + non-IID + poisoning sweeps) worth emulating, but the framework itself is an unsurprising assembly of known components whose claimed superiority rests on non-reproduced literature baselines and a within-noise margin over XGBoost — stronger, independently validated alternatives in the FL-FDIA literature likely cover the same ground.

Problem & Motivation: The review addresses the gap between technical surveys of LLM architectures and domain-focused reviews: practitioners deploying LLM-based systems need to connect training-objective and deployment decisions to reliability, evidence requirements, and resource costs in specific workflows. The motivating pain point is that fluent outputs can be factually unsupported, benchmark performance does not transfer to real workflows, and high-stakes domains (clinical, legal, financial) lack a common vocabulary for deciding what to delegate to a model and who is accountable for errors. Key Idea: There is no identifiable novel technical insight. The closest thing to a core organizing idea is the four-question comparability framework — for each domain application, specify (1) what is delegated to the model, (2) what evidence supports the output, (3) which errors are not permissible, and (4) who owns the final decision. This is a sensible analytic rubric but is a framing device, not a technical contribution, and it is not validated against any deployment. Methodology: This is a narrative review. The authors state that thematic frameworks from general surveys organize the synthesis, with selected technical and empirical publications added for coverage of model development, application evidence, and constraints. There is no database search strategy, no independent duplicate screening, and no formal risk-of-bias assessment — the authors state this explicitly. The paper covers: (a) historical development from rule-based systems through N-grams, LSTMs, and the 2017 Transformer; (b) architecture families (encoder-only/BERT-style, decoder-only/GPT-style, encoder-decoder/T5-style, sparse mixture-of-experts, state-space hybrids) with attention-connectivity schematics; (c) data preparation, self-supervised pretraining objectives (next-token, masked-token, span corruption), and post-training (supervised fine-tuning, instruction tuning, RLHF-style preference optimization, RAG, tool use); (d) seven domain-application sections, each structured around representative uses, failure modes, evaluation targets, and controls (Tables 1–2); (e) efficiency mechanisms (quantization, pruning, distillation, parameter-efficient adaptation); and (f) governance, ethics, and research priorities. No objective function, algorithm, or experimental design is proposed by the authors themselves. Key Results: Not applicable — the paper reports no new quantitative results. No accuracies, benchmarks, speedups, or measurements are produced; the few numbers appearing in cited examples (e.g., ChatGPT USMLE performance, AlphaCode competition results) are restated qualitatively without figures. The paper's "findings" are qualitative claims: benchmark capability does not establish workflow suitability; smaller models can outperform larger ones under specific data/adaptation/inference conditions; preference-optimization consent does not guarantee safety or reliability; longer context windows do not guarantee reliable use of provided information. All are positions inherited from the cited literature rather than measured here. Novelty Classification: SURVEY/position synthesis (maps loosely to NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING only in the weakest sense — it reports no new findings). Genuinely novel: little beyond the four-question deployment rubric and the cross-domain evaluation-requirements comparison in Table 1, which is an editorial reorganization of existing reviews. Everything else — architecture taxonomy, training pipeline, efficiency mechanisms, governance categories — is a standard restatement of well-known prior surveys (Naveed et al., Raiaan et al., Chang et al., Weidinger et al.), several of which are cited as the direct basis for the paper's own figures. Rigor & Reproducibility: As a narrative review, rigor is inherently limited, and the authors disclose the key weaknesses themselves: selective coverage, no systematic search, no duplicate screening, no risk-of-bias assessment, no pooled estimates. There are no ablations, seeds, or significance tests (nothing to ablate). No code, data, or artifact is released. Several central figures and tables are explicitly labeled as adaptations of other surveys' figures (Figure 1 from Naveed et al. and Liu et al.; Figure 6 from Weidinger et al.), which raises questions about how much of the synthesis is original versus derivative. The review was published in the Journal of Intelligent Decision Making and Information Science (peer-reviewed per the article header); the many underlying sources include numerous arXiv preprints cited as such. A methodological concern: the domain-application sections lean heavily on single small studies (e.g., one agriculture retrieval paper, one financial sentiment paper) to characterize entire domains. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: THEORETICAL — a narrative synthesis with no primary experimental claim and no built artifact. - Sound: The synthesis is internally careful and hedged, but its evidential base is selective and unsystematic by the authors' own admission. - General: The four-question framework is broadly applicable across domains, but it is a heuristic, not a validated instrument, and no conditions of validity are established. - Tight: Not applicable — no bounds or formal claims are made; the closest analog, the claim that benchmarks do not predict workflow performance, is argued qualitatively only. - Implementable: The framework suggests a practical checklist for deployment scoping that a practitioner could adopt immediately, but no case study, template, or worked deployment demonstrates its use. The paper delivers no software artifact, dataset, model, or tool; it exists only in paper form. Strengths: - The consistently explicit separation of claims from evidence: the authors repeatedly flag that retrieval grounding, human oversight, and benchmark scores do not establish safety or effectiveness, and their own figure captions disclaim what the schematics do and do not show (e.g., "the diagram does not report a measured compression ratio, or assure a speedup"). - The cross-domain evaluation-requirements comparison (Table 1) is a genuinely useful consolidation — mapping each of seven domains to its characteristic failure modes, evaluation targets, and controls in one view. - Honest limitation disclosure unusual for surveys: the abstract itself states the synthesis is not comprehensive and yields no pooled effectiveness estimate or cross-domain superiority claim. - Coverage of less-common application areas (agriculture/environment, public administration) alongside the usual healthcare/education/finance set. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors directly acknowledge (Section 13 and abstract): narrative (non-systematic) coverage; the fast evolution of LLMs making content quickly outdated; incomparability of studies due to differing datasets and evaluation conditions; uneven evidence strength across domains, with much evaluation resting on benchmarks rather than real applications; no pooled effect estimates; and no demonstrated superiority of any model or adaptation method. This direct confrontation of limitations is a credibility positive. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - No systematic search or screening protocol means the domain sections' evidence base is essentially anecdotal — single papers (e.g., one 2023 agriculture retrieval preprint, one ChatGPT financial sentiment study) are asked to carry whole-domain conclusions. - The four-question framework, presented as the paper's main contribution, is never applied end-to-end to a concrete system or validated with any stakeholder or case study. - Multiple figures are explicitly derived from other surveys' figures; the boundary between this review's original synthesis and re-drawn prior work is thin in Sections 2–4. - The research-priorities section (Section 12) lists worthwhile directions (verifiable generation, unlearning threat models, contamination checks) but offers no prioritization criteria or feasibility analysis. - Several foundational sources are arXiv preprints presented as load-bearing evidence; the review does not distinguish preprint status when weighing their claims. - The paper's publication venue and 2026 dates sit oddly with its content, which is current only to roughly 2023–2024 literature, weakening its currency claim even by survey standards. Bottom Line: A cautious, honestly-caveated but derivative narrative survey that a newcomer could skim for orientation, yet which is dominated on every axis — breadth, method, and currency — by the stronger systematic surveys it cites, so most readers should go to those instead.

Problem & Motivation: Signature-based intrusion detection misses novel or modified attacks in high-volume, dynamic network environments, motivating machine-learning-based detection. The specific gap the author identifies is that prior comparative studies have not evaluated classical vs. ensemble algorithms under identical experimental conditions on CIC-IDS2017, nor analyzed the structure of classification errors, per-attack-type detection behavior, and feature importance in depth. The intended audience is IDS/IPS developers, SOC analysts, and cybersecurity researchers. This gap is thin: the cited works (Coşar et al. 2024 on CSE-CIC-IDS2018, Chua & Salam 2023, Farhat et al. 2023 on CIC-IDS2017 itself) already perform closely analogous comparisons, so the paper's positioning as filling a genuine hole is weak. Key Idea: There is no identifiable key idea. The paper is a competent application of a standard recipe — train four off-the-shelf classifiers on a public benchmark with SMOTE balancing and cross-validation, then compare metrics. The only framing device is the hypothesis that algorithmic complexity correlates with detection quality, which the results confirm but which is neither surprising nor previously untested in this literature. Methodology: The pipeline is: (1) load CIC-IDS2017 (2.8M flows, 80+ CICFlowMeter features); (2) clean by coercing invalid values to NaN and dropping them, remove physically impossible values (negative durations/byte counts, zero-duration flows) and duplicates; (3) drop identifier features (Flow ID, Source/Destination IP, Timestamp) to prevent overfitting; (4) MinMax-normalize features to [0,1]; (5) label-encode as Benign=0 vs. a merged Attack=1, reducing a multiclass problem to binary detection; (6) stratified train/test split; (7) SMOTE applied to the training set only to balance classes; (8) train Logistic Regression (L2, C=1.0), Decision Tree (depth/minimum-split constrained), Random Forest, and XGBoost with 5-fold cross-validation for model selection; (9) evaluate accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC, and confusion matrices on the held-out test set; (10) compute feature importance via MDI (Random Forest) and Gain (XGBoost), normalized to 100%. Critical design decisions: collapsing all attack types into one binary class (justified for a detection-oriented task, but it discards the multiclass structure that CIC-IDS2017 is often used for, and per-attack-type recall is reconstructed post hoc from the binary classifier); SMOTE on the training set only (correctly done, but SMOTE on 80+ correlated flow features creates synthetic points that may not correspond to real attack traffic); and an unspecified test-set size — confusion-matrix row sums (~39,700 attacks, ~40,300 benign) show roughly 79,700 test flows, ~3% of the advertised dataset, with no explanation of how or at what scale the subsample was drawn. Hyperparameter tuning is described only loosely ('chosen on the basis of the nature of the task'), so the comparison is more of a default-configurations bake-off than a tuned-model comparison. Key Results: On the held-out test set: Logistic Regression — 94.7% accuracy, 94.5% precision, 92.1% recall, 92.8% F1, 95.4% ROC-AUC; Decision Tree — 97.2/96.7/96.1/96.4/97.5; Random Forest — 98.9/98.8/98.5/98.6/99.2; XGBoost — 99.2/99.0/98.9/98.9/99.5. False negatives fall monotonically from 3,086 (LR) to 1,546 (DT), 596 (RF), 437 (XGBoost); false positives from 2,148 to 1,282, 488, 399. Per-attack-type recall for XGBoost: DoS 99.6%, DDoS 99.8%, Port Scan 99.4%, Brute Force 97.8%, Botnet 98.7%, Web Attacks 96.9%. Feature importance is consistent between RF and XGBoost: Flow Bytes/s (16.3% XGBoost), Flow Duration (14.9%), Total Length of Fwd Packets (12.8%), Packet Length Mean (11.1%), Destination Port (9.6%). The baselines are standard but weak by current standards — no deep learning, no LightGBM/CatBoost, no semi-supervised or unsupervised anomaly-detection baselines. The finding that Web Attacks and Brute Force are hardest (feature overlap with benign traffic) matches prior work and is not surprising. The near-perfect scores are consistent with well-known CIC-IDS2017 artifacts (flow-statistics correlate with the specific attack generation scripts), which the paper does not discuss. Novelty Classification: ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION at best; primarily a replication-grade empirical comparison. The genuinely new element is essentially nil — the same four-model comparison on CIC-IDS2017 or its 2018 successor appears in multiple papers the author himself cites (e.g., Farhat et al. 2023 on CIC-IDS2017 with DoS/DDoS focus). The per-attack-type recall decomposition and the RF-vs-XGBoost feature-importance agreement are competent analyses of known techniques in a known setting, not new formulations or findings. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations as usually understood (which components matter) are absent — the 'ablation' is only the model-family comparison. No error bars, no multiple random seeds, no significance tests; the entire study is described as 'one computational cycle,' so the reported differences (e.g., RF 98.9% vs. XGBoost 99.2% accuracy) may not be statistically meaningful. Hyperparameter search procedures are not documented. No code, data splits, or trained models are released, and no repository URL is given. Methodological concerns: (1) evaluation on a single benchmark (CIC-IDS2017) whose labeling and traffic-generation flaws are extensively documented in the literature but never mentioned; (2) an unexplained ~80K-flow test subsample contradicts the stated 2.8M-flow dataset scale; (3) SMOTE before cross-validated model selection is described ambiguously — if oversampling preceded fold creation, synthetic-sample leakage across folds would inflate scores; (4) collapsed binary labels mean the headline '99.2% accuracy' is not comparable to multiclass results in other papers. To the author's credit, the paper explicitly names its constraints: single dataset, classical models only, no deep learning, no production traffic streams. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL. - Practical: Yes — training ran on a multi-core desktop PC with Scikit-learn and XGBoost; no special hardware is needed. - Efficient: The paper asserts ensembles cost more compute and training time than linear models but reports no timing, memory, or throughput numbers, so the efficiency claim is unquantified. - Effective: Effective on the benchmark proxy only; the paper cites literature showing cross-dataset performance drops but performs no cross-dataset or drift evaluation itself, so real-world effectiveness against novel attacks is untested. - Scalable: Untested and unclaimed at scale — the test set appears to be ~3% of the dataset, and no latency or streaming-throughput measurement supports the recommendation of 'real-time' IDS use. The work delivers no artifact — no library, CLI, dataset, or model weights — only the paper. Strengths: - Honest and specific error accounting: the confusion matrices are reported as raw counts, and the false-negative reduction (3,086 → 437) is the paper's most concrete, decision-relevant number. - Consistent feature-importance triangulation across two independent ensemble methods (MDI and Gain) yielding the same top features, which strengthens confidence in which flow statistics drive detection. - Transparent self-declared limitations (single dataset, no deep learning, no production traffic), which is better practice than many single-benchmark studies manage. - Clean preprocessing hygiene: dropping identifier features to prevent IP-based memorization and removing physically impossible flow records are correctly motivated and often skipped in this literature. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The author explicitly states the study is constrained to a single dataset (CIC-IDS2017), covers only a limited set of classical models, excludes deep neural networks, and does not use live production traffic streams. The conclusions also call for future work on deep learning, real-time stream processing, and adaptive detection of new attack types. These limitations are confronted directly rather than minimized — a credibility positive. However, the acknowledged limitation list omits the more serious issues: CIC-IDS2017's label quality, the unexplained test subsample, and the absence of variance estimates. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The test set contains ~79,700 flows versus the stated 2.8M-flow dataset — how this subsample was drawn, and whether it is representative, is never explained; all headline numbers rest on this unstated selection. - No acknowledgment of the widely reported CIC-IDS2017 labeling errors and traffic-generation artifacts (e.g., the known problematic Friday flows, attack traffic from a single source IP per scenario); near-perfect scores on this dataset are a known artifact, and results without a second benchmark (UNSW-NB15, CSE-CIC-IDS2018, or the improved CIC-IDS collection) cannot support generalization claims. - SMOTE's interaction with the cross-validation protocol is ambiguous; if oversampling was applied before fold splitting, evaluation is optimistically biased. - No deep learning or modern gradient-boosting (LightGBM/CatBoost) baselines, despite the discussion extensively citing deep-learning IDS work — the comparison set is a decade old. - The claim that XGBoost suits 'real-time' intrusion detection is extrapolated from offline accuracy; no inference latency, throughput, or drift experiment supports it. - Single-run, single-seed results with no variance reporting make the RF-vs-XGBoost differences (~0.3 points) uninterpretable. Bottom Line: A practitioner gains little from this paper beyond confirmation of what Farhat et al. (2023), Coşar et al. (2024), and the broader CIC-IDS literature already established — ensemble methods beat linear models on this benchmark — and stronger alternatives (cross-dataset studies like Cantone et al. 2024, or any paper pairing CIC-IDS2017 with a second benchmark) cover the same ground with more evidence; read it only as a teaching example of the evaluation pipeline, not as new knowledge.

Problem & Motivation: Aircraft turnaround — the 25–45 minute window of chocks-on to chocks-off — concentrates multiple simultaneous operations by several stakeholders (handlers, fuelers, caterers, TCO, ramp staff) in a confined, time-critical space, making it the most failure-prone phase of ground operations. Safety oversight at airports like SEA Milan Malpensa relies on Ground Safety Reports: standardized yes/no/N-A checklists filled by field personnel, submitted voluntarily or mandatorily (within 72 hours for damaging events). The stated problem is that manual, post-event processing of these reports cannot keep pace with data volume or surface latent spatial-temporal risk patterns in real time, and that turnaround risk assessment today is largely static (done at pre-planning/contract stage), inadequate for the stochastic variability of individual flights. The intended beneficiaries are airport safety departments (SMS managers) seeking a decision-support tool that moves them toward proactive/predictive risk management in the sense of NASA's IASMS and EASA's Data4Safety vision. Problem & Motivation: The paper addresses the systemic fragility of hyper-efficient, geographically concentrated global value chains (GVCs) exposed by COVID-19, the 2022 energy crisis, the 2024 maritime disruptions, and rising export controls. The problem-holders are multinational firms and governments that must decide whether to pay a "resilience tax" (regionalization adds a claimed 5–10% per-unit cost) to hedge geopolitical tail risks. The gap it targets: prior work treats resilience qualitatively or separately from corporate finance; the paper wants a joint operations–finance quantification that also incorporates emerging levers (Agentic AI, digital twins, wholesale CBDCs) that could offset the tax. Key Idea: The core move is to express supply-chain resilience as a financial risk measure — a geopolitical Value-at-risk (VaRγ, 1-year horizon, 95% confidence) — and to define a risk-adjusted return ratio (Net Ratio = ΔVaRγ / ΔEPS_resilience tax) whose break-even against regionalization cost yields a decision threshold (the 8.4% figure). This is a formulation, not an algorithmic insight: VaR, Monte Carlo stress testing, and the bullwhip variance ratio are all standard tools recombined and applied to geopolitical supply-chain shocks. Methodology: A mixed-methods design: (1) a four-stage purposive sampling pipeline filters 1,842 firms (Fortune Global 500 ∪ MSCI World) down to 500, stratified across semiconductors (120), EV/energy materials (100), pharmaceuticals (80), industrial automation (100), and retail (100), across NA/EU/APAC; (2) qualitative capabilities are converted to 1.0–5.0 index rubrics (AI Maturity, End-to-end Visibility, Multi-sourcing); (3) raw data from World Bank/UNCTAD/BIS/corporate disclosures pass a four-step cleaning protocol (canonicalization, outlier filtering, k-NN gap imputation, greenwashing triangulation); (4) a 10,000-iteration Monte Carlo loop draws sector-specific shock vectors, computes α, the 95th-percentile loss (VaRγ), and an EPS drag, then sweeps regionalization cost from 1% to 15% to locate the net-ratio break-even. Critical design decisions: (a) parametric variance–covariance VaR rather than historical simulation — justified only implicitly and questionable for fat-tailed geopolitical shocks; (b) synthetic data generation calibrated to reproduce the observed panel's statistical properties, justified as confidentiality protection but destroying external verifiability; (c) backtesting against 2022/2024 disruptions and a placebo test on 2010–2015 — well-conceived in principle, but executed on the author's own synthetic model. The retailer case study's metrics are admitted to be "derived from the calibrated simulation framework," i.e., simulated, not measured. Key Results: Reported simulation outputs with 95% CIs and bootstrap P-values (1,000 replications): bullwhip dampening α = −30% ([−34%, −26%], P<0.01); VaRγ mitigation ΔVaRγ = −18% ([−22%, −14%], P<0.05); EPS resilience tax = −7.2% ([−8.5%, −5.9%], P<0.01); working capital efficiency +12% ([+9%, +15%], P<0.05); lead-time variance reduction 23% ([20%, 26%]); a claimed 42% reduction in "hidden disruptions" in semiconductors via digital twins; 92% of firms with positive net ratio at 5% regionalization cost falling to 48% at 10%, with break-even at 8.4%. Sector-specific recovery-time projections (e.g., semiconductors: 24–36 weeks legacy JIT vs. 8–12 weeks resilient model under export controls) appear in Table 2. Backtesting is claimed to have "successfully predicted 88% of the lead-time variances" in the 2024 maritime disruptions after calibration on 2022 data. CBDC evidence is cited, not generated: BIS Project mBridge (2–7 s settlement vs. 3–5 days), Project Dunbar (45–60% processing overhead reduction), Project Icebreaker (<5 s finality). There is no external baseline comparison — the reference scenario is the author's own legacy-JIT configuration. Scale is a synthetic 500-firm panel; no real firm is analyzed with disclosed data. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION (weak) + NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (claimed, not substantiated). What is genuinely somewhat new is the packaging: a VaR-based "resilience tax" metric plus a net-ratio break-even threshold linking regionalization cost to digital-technology complementarity, and the explicit coupling of wholesale CBDC settlement latency to supply-chain working capital — a synthesis rarely made explicit. Everything underneath (Monte Carlo stress testing, VaR, bullwhip variance ratios, CCC arithmetic, friend-shoring cost ranges, BIS pilot benchmarks) is standard; the "Agentic AI" component is a naming of existing AI-forecasting/digital-twin capabilities, not a new method. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations exist in the form of a regionalization-cost sensitivity sweep (1–15%) and tier-level lead-time comparisons, but there is no component-level ablation showing which index (AIM vs. VE vs. MS) drives the results. Confidence intervals come from the simulation's own empirical distribution and significance from bootstrap resampling — these measure model-internal variance, not sampling uncertainty from real data, and the stated rationale for skipping multiple-comparison correction is thin. No code, no synthetic-data files, no seed-verified artifacts are released despite a fixed-seed reproducibility claim; only "additional methodological details available upon request." The fatal methodological concern is circular calibration: synthetic datasets are constructed to reproduce the panel's descriptive statistics, and the simulation's outputs are then reported as headline findings — Goodhart's Law applies to the entire result set. The single "case study" (European retailer, 97% service level, 23% lead-time variance reduction) is explicitly simulation-derived while narratively framed as an empirical observation. No external baselines (e.g., established disruption-propagation models from the Ivanov/Dolgui literature the paper itself cites) are compared against. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (simulation study; no deployed system). - Practical: The framework is a described simulation, not a released tool; nothing here requires special hardware, but nothing is runnable by third parties either. - Efficient: Not applicable in a meaningful sense — a 10,000-iteration Monte Carlo over a 500-firm panel is computationally trivial, but the inputs (calibrated synthetic parameters) are not reproducible. - Effective: The evidence shows only that the author's model produces internally consistent scenario outputs; it does not demonstrate that any real firm's resilience improved because of the framework. - Scalable: Never tested — the paper claims generalization to other contexts is limited (SMEs), and no scale beyond the synthetic panel is exercised. The work delivers no software artifact, dataset, or model weights; it stops at paper form. Strengths: - Genuinely useful operationalization rubrics: the 1.0–5.0 scales for AI maturity, end-to-end visibility, and multi-sourcing are concrete, transportable measurement instruments other researchers could adopt or critique. - Honest self-assessment: the limitations section explicitly concedes scenario-based (non-causal) estimates, endogeneity of technology adoption, and non-generalizability to SMEs — a credibility positive. - A real synthesis contribution: connecting settlement latency (CBDC atomic settlement, BIS mBridge/Dunbar/Icebreaker benchmarks) to cash-conversion-cycle mechanics and then to inventory buffers is a cross-domain link most supply-chain resilience work leaves implicit. - Methodological intent (placebo tests on 2010–2015, out-of-sample backtesting against 2022/2024 shocks) is the right experimental template, even if its execution here is self-referential. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state: (1) the purposive sample of hyperscale firms limits generalizability to SMEs; (2) estimates are scenario-based projections, not causal relationships; (3) technology adoption is endogenous to managerial capability, partially addressed via backtesting. This is direct, non-defensive confrontation of limitations — commendable. However, the authors do not acknowledge that their data is fully synthetic and that the case study is simulated, presenting these facts only in a data-availability statement rather than integrating them into the interpretation of the headline results. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Circular calibration: the synthetic data are built to reproduce the descriptive statistics (mean $34.2B revenue, 68.4% East Asia dependency), and the simulation then "finds" results consistent with those same calibrated parameters. The headline CIs and P-values quantify nothing about the real world. - The 8.4% threshold is spuriously precise: given that regionalization costs are themselves "estimated at 5%–10%" with no citation, an eight-months-of-manuscripts-precision break-even (8.4%) is not identifiable from the stated inputs. - No real observation anywhere: not a single firm-level data point, interview, or archival record is independently verifiable; "triangulation to detect greenwashing" is described but no triangulated finding is reported. - Missing baselines: no comparison against existing GVC disruption models, input-output-based fragility measures, or even a naive buffer-stock policy benchmark — the resilient model beats only the author's own JIT strawman. - Attribution without mechanism: the −30% bullwhip dampening and 23% lead-time variance reduction are assigned to "Agentic AI" as a label; no model, architecture, or decision policy is specified, so the effect is asserted, not derived. - Provenance red flags: the journal's 2026 publication date, citations to 2025–2026 works (including one to "Int J Prod Res 2026" and a 2026 Gartner report), and future-tense framing of 2026 events mean none of the evidentiary claims can be checked against an established record; treat all figures as speculative. Bottom Line: A practitioner gains a serviceable vocabulary (resilience tax, VaRγ, net ratio, AI-maturity rubrics) but no trustworthy evidence — the quantitative results are simulations calibrated by the author to confirm themselves, and stronger, data-grounded alternatives exist in the Ivanov/Dolgui disruption-modeling and Sheffi resilience literatures; I would not cite the headline numbers.

Problem & Motivation: Automotive manufacturers generate massive data volumes from intelligent sensors, ERP systems, automated inspection, and production lines, and the traditional Ishikawa diagram — a manually populated 6M (method, machine, material, manpower, environment, measurement) cause-and-effect tool — cannot process this volume quickly or objectively. Quality engineers therefore face a gap: AI-based root cause analysis (RCA) methods exist and report high accuracy, but they are not integrated with the causal-structuring tool that practitioners actually use. The stated research question is: what is the impact of integrating AI into the Ishikawa diagram for root cause identification in automotive manufacturing processes? The audience is quality engineers and Industry 4.0 researchers, particularly in the Spanish/Portuguese-speaking research community. Key Idea: The core idea is not technical but programmatic: use the Ishikawa diagram's 6M structure as a human-facing, interpretable interface (a causal organizing layer) onto which AI outputs — SHAP/LIME explanations, DNN failure classifications, anomaly detections — are mapped automatically. The review's own contribution claim is that no prior work has made this integration the central, structured methodology; existing studies only mention it as a future recommendation. As a review, however, the paper has no algorithmic trick of its own; the key idea belongs to the sources it synthesizes (e.g., the TRACE framework from Kiefer et al., which is the closest existing realization of the idea the paper advocates). Methodology: The authors follow PRISMA 2020 in four phases (identification, screening, eligibility, inclusion). Search equations combining "Ishikawa Diagram"/"Fishbone" AND "Artificial Intelligence"/"Machine Learning" AND "Root Cause Analysis" AND "Automotive Manufacturing/Industry" were run trilingually (Spanish, English, Portuguese) across Scopus, WoS, SciELO, ScienceDirect, EBSCO, ProQuest, and Google Scholar for 2020–2026. Inclusion required full text, free access, indexing in the listed databases, and topical relevance; 100 articles formed the corpus, of which 20 were selected for detailed tabulation across objective, results, conclusions, gaps, and recommendations. Critical design decisions: (1) restricting to 2020–2026 is reasonable given the field's recency but excludes foundational earlier work; (2) including Google Scholar and ResearchGate-indexed material trades quality control for recall; (3) the detailed analysis of only 20 of 100 papers is not justified by stated eligibility criteria. No quality-appraisal instrument (e.g., risk-of-bias scoring) is reported. Key Results: The review synthesizes (does not itself measure) the following from the 20 analyzed studies: diagnostic accuracies of 94.64% (DNN on 63,666 automotive warranty records over 7 years, beating Fast KNN at 90.66% and KNN at 89.91%), 95.37% (XGBoost defect variables), 98.75–99.38% (few-shot XAI anomaly detection on wiring harnesses and gears, ROC-AUC 0.9995–0.9997, 18.2 ms inference), 96.4% (deep learning surface defect classification), and AUCROC of 0.99 (ABOD) on assembly-line anomaly detection. Operational outcomes include up to 76% reduction in analysis time, 75% reduction in customer complaints (8D/Industry 4.0 pilot), 21% fewer scheduling evaluations via an intelligent digital twin, 15% diagnostic accuracy gain and 21.7% performance-loss reduction (TRACE framework, lab prototype only), and 100% correct root cause identification by a causal-inference method when overlap interference ε ≥ 1×10⁻³. Baselines in the underlying studies vary in strength; several reviewed papers are themselves reviews with no experimental validation. These are second-hand, self-reported figures from the primary studies, not independently verified. Novelty Classification: NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING (weak) at best — the paper is a systematic review whose genuine contribution is the consolidated evidence table and the explicit identification of an integration gap (AI outputs ↔ Ishikawa 6M structure) rather than any new method, dataset, or system. All techniques discussed (XGBoost, DNNs, SHAP/LIME, digital twins, few-shot learning) are standard; the proposed combination (automated 6M classification via XAI) is claimed as novel but is only proposed, not implemented, and Kiefer et al.'s TRACE framework already substantially occupies this space. Rigor & Reproducibility: As a review, it has no ablations or error bars of its own; the underlying studies report mixed rigor (some with cross-validation and noise-robustness tests, others purely descriptive). No code, data, or PRISMA checklist is released; no URL is provided. Methodological concerns are significant: the reference list contains at least seven apparent template/placeholder entries ([2]–[8], e.g., "M. King, B. Zhu, 'Optimal path planning'" and "H. Simpson, Dumb Robots") that are uncited junk, the same Pietsch et al. 2024 paper appears three times in the analysis table under different reference numbers ([14], [26], [29]), a ResearchGate hosting is used as a database source, table numbering is inconsistent (two different "Tabla II"s), the Spanish abstract ends mid-sentence, and the claim of "100 articles" analyzed versus 20 tabulated is not reconciled with a PRISMA flow diagram with counts. The numbers quoted in the abstract (94.64–99.38%, 76%, 75%) are aggregates of heterogeneous, self-reported results from different studies, plants, and tasks. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (a systematic review with no primary experiments). Practical: Not applicable to the paper itself; the reviewed techniques run on industrial hardware, with the few-shot model being notably light at 23.8 MB. Efficient: The reviewed evidence claims diagnostic time reductions from hours/weeks to seconds, but these are the sources' numbers, not verified here. Effective: The evidence shows AI solves detection/classification proxies well; causal validity of the identified "root causes" remains unconfirmed even in the underlying studies. Scalable: Untested — most reviewed studies are lab prototypes or single-plant pilots, and the review itself flags this as the field's central limitation. The work delivers no software artifact, dataset, or tool; it stops at paper form. Strengths: - The 20-study synthesis table (objective, results, conclusions, gaps, recommendations per study) is a genuinely useful annotated map of the 2020–2026 AI-for-RCA literature, including quantified gaps like lab-only validation and class imbalance. - The identified research gap is real and clearly argued: reviewed studies repeatedly recommend Ishikawa integration but none operationalizes automated 6M classification — a legitimate, specific open problem. - Trilingual search strategy (Spanish/English/Portuguese) across seven databases captures Latin American and Iberian literature that English-only reviews miss. - The discussion correctly elevates interpretability (XAI, SHAP/LIME) as the adoption bottleneck rather than raw accuracy, aligned with the field's consensus. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly state, largely via the reviewed studies' self-reported limitations: most methods remain lab prototypes or use simulated/restricted data; industrial data availability, quality, and class imbalance limit generalization; distinguishing correlation from causation is unresolved; no standardized methodology exists for integrating AI with traditional RCA tools; and one included review notes English-only inclusion. The paper confronts these limitations directly in Section IV-E, which is a credibility positive, though it attributes them to the field rather than to its own review process. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The corrupted reference list (placeholder citations [2]–[8]) and triple-counting of Pietsch et al. 2024 raise doubts about screening discipline and whether all 20 tabulated entries are distinct studies — at most 17 are. - The paper claims to have "analyzed 100 articles" but reports detail on 20; the PRISMA flow counts (identification → screening → eligibility → inclusion) are not reported with numbers, so reproducibility of the selection is impossible. - No quality appraisal or risk-of-bias assessment of included studies; the headline 94.64–99.38% accuracy range aggregates results from different tasks (warranty classification vs. visual anomaly detection) that are not comparable. - The claimed contribution — that this review "will allow" automated 6M classification — is aspirational; the paper proposes nothing beyond what Kiefer et al.'s TRACE already partially delivers, making the novelty claim overstated. - Inclusion of Google Scholar and ResearchGate as "databases" without documented deduplication or citation-quality controls weakens the evidence base. - The abstract's claim that findings "demonstrate" AI-integration benefits conflates the reviewed studies' claims with measured evidence; the review itself measures nothing. Bottom Line: A quality-management practitioner seeking a first annotated bibliography of recent AI-for-RCA work may find the synthesis table handy, but the corrupted references, opaque screening, and purely aspirational contribution mean most readers should go directly to the primary sources (Kiefer 2025, Calaon 2024, Ma 2021, Pietsch 2024) rather than rely on this review.

Problem & Motivation: The paper addresses the security monitoring problem in hybrid enterprise cloud environments — organizations running on-premises servers, private clouds, public cloud platforms, VMs, containers, and distributed applications simultaneously. The stated gap is that conventional perimeter defense, signature-based IDS, and reactive incident response give limited visibility against adaptive adversaries, and that digital twin modeling, cyber deception, and adversary modeling have been researched separately with limited integration. This is a legitimate and real problem area; the paper does not, however, close any gap empirically. It articulates a motivation for an integrated architecture that someone else has not yet built or measured. Key Idea: The single core insight is contextualized deception: use a synchronized digital twin of the hybrid enterprise infrastructure to (a) position decoy resources where they are architecturally plausible, (b) supply contextual features (resource criticality, network relationships, service dependencies) to ML-based adversary models, and (c) provide a safe sandbox for testing defensive strategies before production deployment. This is a composition of known ideas (digital twins, honeypots/deception, supervised + unsupervised anomaly detection, MITRE ATT&CK mapping) rather than a new technical mechanism — no new algorithm, objective function, or system design detail is given that could not be reconstructed from the existing literature. Methodology: The paper describes a four-stage methodology in future/conditional language. Stage 1: define a representative hybrid enterprise architecture and build a digital twin capturing configurations, topology, dependencies, access relationships, and security policies, using infrastructure metadata, network flows, authentication logs, plus public datasets and MITRE ATT&CK/CVE sources; preprocessing covers deduplication, timestamp standardization, missing-value handling. Stage 2: deploy deceptive resources (simulated servers, decoy endpoints, fake authentication environments) inside the twin, with monitoring, event correlation, and isolation controls; study how deception placement affects intelligence quality. Stage 3: train adversary models (logistic regression, decision trees, random forests, SVMs, gradient boosting; clustering/isolation forests for unlabeled data) on features including authentication frequency, failed logins, access timing, communication volume, deception interactions, and twin-derived context; evaluation metrics named are accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC, PR-AUC; SHAP is mentioned for explainability; time-aware data partitioning is proposed. Stage 4: integrate and evaluate against baselines (rule-based IDS, ML anomaly detection without twin context, deception without adversary modeling), with ablations over twin context, deception intelligence, and ML modeling, plus scalability and isolation testing. All of this is a plan: no dataset is named beyond generic categories, no loss function or objective is formalized, no architecture diagram of the actual proposed system is presented (the single figure, captioned 'Digital Twins and AI-Driven Cybersecurity for Intelligent Transportation Networks,' is about a different domain entirely — a serious editorial defect), and the entire methodology is written with hedging ('may be applied,' 'are considered,' 'scenarios may represent'). The four-stage decomposition is reasonable, but each design decision is asserted rather than justified by any evidence. Key Results: Not stated. The Results and Discussion section contains no quantitative outcomes — no numbers, datasets, baselines, or measured comparisons. Claims such as the framework offering 'earlier detection of suspicious activities' and 'more informed cybersecurity decision-making' are stated as analytical expectations ('indicate that combining... offers a more context-aware approach'), not measured results. Crucially, the Future Work section confirms no implementation exists: 'Future research will focus on implementing and experimentally validating the proposed... framework.' The scale of testing is therefore zero — the framework was never run. No surprising or counter-intuitive findings are reported. Novelty Classification: NEW FORMULATION at best, and only weakly: the paper's contribution is a proposed architecture that integrates three existing research threads (digital twins for security, cyber deception/honeypots, ML adversary modeling). No NEW METHOD, NEW DATASET/BENCHMARK, NEW SYSTEM/TOOL, or NEW EMPIRICAL FINDING is delivered; the genuine novelty is limited to arguing that deception assets should be placed and interpreted using digital-twin context — an idea that appears in existing deception and DT-security literature and is here stated rather than demonstrated. Rigor & Reproducibility: Rigor is the central failure. There are no ablations, no error bars, no seeds, no significance tests, no datasets, no code, no model weights, and no repository URL — nothing is reproducible because nothing was executed. The described experimental design (train/validation/test splits, time-aware partitioning, ablations, baseline comparisons, isolation testing) would be adequate if carried out, but it exists only as a proposal. Methodological red flags: (1) the Results section presents qualitative discussion in place of evidence, which risks readers mistaking assertion for measurement; (2) the lone figure belongs to an unrelated domain (intelligent transportation), suggesting assembly without review; (3) the reference list is heavily padded with citations from the same cluster of low-visibility journals and is largely irrelevant to the paper's topic (e.g., cancer therapy selection, EV fuzzy-logic energy storage, SimCorp asset management, coupon redemption analytics) — a citation-stuffing pattern typical of pay-to-publish venues; (4) the journal's own presentation (ISO-certification banner, 2026 volume dates, rapid 6-week receive-to-publish cycle) warrants low confidence in peer review quality. Treat this as an unreviewed position piece, not validated research. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: THEORETICAL (a conceptual/vision paper with no primary experimental claim; nothing was built or run). - Sound: The architectural argument is internally coherent but relies on unstated assumptions — that twin synchronization can be kept accurate and fast enough, that decoys can be made realistic without risk, and that ML models trained on simulated/deception data will generalize — none of which are analyzed. - General: The framework is described at a level of abstraction that applies to almost any enterprise environment, which means it provides no specific, testable conditions under which it would or would not work. - Tight: Not applicable (no bounds or formal results); the closest analogue is that the claimed benefits (earlier detection, better precision) are unconstrained by any evidence. - Implementable: The four-stage plan suggests a buildable system, but the paper provides no artifact, interface, algorithmic specification, or reference implementation; everything stops at paper form. The work delivers no software artifact, dataset, trained model, or reusable technique — only a prose description of a proposed architecture. Strengths: - Correctly identifies a genuine integration gap: digital twin security research, deception technology, and ML adversary modeling are largely separate literatures, and a unified architecture is a reasonable target. - The proposed evaluation design, if executed, is methodologically sound in outline — it includes the right baselines (rule-based IDS, ML without twin context, deception without modeling), ablations over each component, time-aware partitioning, and isolation/safety testing. - The paper is unusually candid that implementation and validation have not occurred, and it explicitly frames the contribution as a 'conceptual foundation' — this honesty is a credibility positive even though it also means the paper over-promises in its title and abstract. - Practical deployment concerns (deception isolation, false positives from poorly configured decoys, twin synchronization overhead, models needing to distinguish administrators from attackers) are acknowledged as real risks rather than glossed over. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors explicitly list: synchronization complexity between twin and production, computational overhead, incomplete infrastructure representations, false-positive risk from poorly configured decoys, model reliability depending on representative training data, dataset limitations, evolving adversarial behavior, model generalization, and the need for future experimental validation on realistic testbeds (public cloud, Kubernetes, etc.). They also state the framework should complement, not replace, established controls (IAM, encryption, segmentation, vulnerability management). These limitations are confronted directly — the honesty is genuine — but acknowledging that the entire contribution is unvalidated does not change the fact that it is unvalidated. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The Results and Discussion section is written in the register of findings ('The analytical findings indicate...') while containing no evidence — a claims/evidence conflation the authors do not flag. - No related work on deception or digital-twin security is actually cited: the 36-entry reference list contains almost nothing on honeypots, deception technology, MITRE ATT&CK applications, or security digital twins, undermining the literature review's claims about the state of the field. - The mismatched figure (intelligent transportation) and the presence of a caption describing a different application suggest the paper was not meaningfully reviewed; no internal consistency check is acknowledged. - No threat model is defined: what adversary capabilities, what attack scenarios, what portion of the killchain the framework addresses — all left unspecified, making the framework unfalsifiable as written. - The cost side is ignored entirely: digital twin construction and synchronization for a large hybrid enterprise is expensive and itself expands attack surface (the twin becomes a high-value target holding configuration and topology intelligence), which the paper never analyzes. - No legal/ethical analysis of deploying deception in enterprise environments (entrapment concerns, liability for attacker actions on decoys) — a standard consideration in the deception literature that is absent. - The proposed baselines omit modern alternatives (SOAR platforms, EDR telemetry fusion, LLM-based detection) that a practitioner would compare against. Bottom Line: A practitioner gains almost nothing from this paper beyond a one-paragraph sketch of an idea that the deception-security community has already explored with actual testbeds — read a validated digital-twin-honeypot study or a modern deception-platform evaluation instead, because this paper performs no experiment, releases no artifact, and would not survive review at any reputable security venue.
