Problem & Motivation: Systematic Literature Review (SLR) and bibliometric analysis require verified Scopus metadata, but open-access search engines (Google Scholar, Semantic Scholar) cannot strictly filter for Scopus-indexed publications, forcing researchers to manually cross-reference results. Existing automation tools — BiblioMerge and BibFusion (Python packages that merge and deduplicate Scopus/Web of Science exports) and R-based automated frameworks — demand programming skill from end users, and commercial screening software strains institutional budgets. The target gap is a lightweight, no-code, web-based extraction tool that avoids server-side storage costs, aimed at non-technical researchers at resource-constrained institutions (the author's context: Universitas Graha Karya Muara Bulian, Indonesia). Key Idea: The identifiable core idea is the stateless BYOK proxy pattern: the institutional server never persists data and holds no shared credentials — each researcher supplies their own Elsevier API key, the PHP Model layer forwards the query via cURL, and the raw JSON is shipped to the client where JavaScript maps JSON nodes to RIS tags (dc:title→TI, dc:creator→AU, prism:doi→DO, etc.) and instantiates a downloadable Blob. There is no algorithmic novelty beyond competent application of known web-engineering patterns (MVC separation, client-side Blob export, header-based API key authentication). Methodology: The paper describes a five-phase systems-engineering lifecycle: (1) requirement analysis of data noise in generalized search engines; (2) architectural design as a three-layer PHP-native MVC (Tailwind CSS View, query-sanitizing Controller, cURL-based API Model); (3) BYOK API integration against the Elsevier /content/search/scopus endpoint after sandbox validation of TITLE-ABS-KEY query parameters; (4) client-side implementation where JavaScript asynchronously maps the JSON payload to RIS tags and constructs a Blob with MIME type application/x-research-info-systems; (5) evaluation on a live campus server (mitrautamateknologi.xyz) validating RIS fields (DOIs, authors) against Mendeley. No formal objective function, algorithm, or optimization is defined — this is a software construction report, not an algorithmic method. Critical design decisions: statelessness for privacy/server load (defensible but asserted rather than measured), BYOK to bypass shared rate limits (reasonable), and client-side transformation to offload compute (justified by intent, not by benchmark). Notably, the title's "AI Enhanced Soft Computing" framing is not instantiated anywhere in the methods — no AI/ML component exists in the described system. Key Results: The paper reports no quantitative outcomes in the conventional sense. The claimed results are: (a) database inspection via phpMyAdmin showing 0 rows in both jurnal_tersimpan and riwayat_pencarian after "high-volume" retrieval queries, taken as proof of the stateless design; (b) a repeatedly asserted "100% Scopus-verified metadata" retrieval rate, which is trivially guaranteed by construction (the tool queries Scopus directly) rather than measured; (c) successful import of generated RIS files into Mendeley; and (d) a qualitative feature-comparison table (Table 2) against BiblioMerge-style Python frameworks and R-based frameworks, scoring the proposed tool as requiring no programming skill and zero server storage. No precision/recall, latency, throughput, query volume, record counts, or error rates are reported. Baselines are described but never actually run or benchmarked — the comparison is rhetorical, not experimental. Testing was at an unquantified, presumably small scale on a single live server. Novelty Classification: ENGINEERING OPTIMIZATION (and arguably NEW SYSTEM/TOOL in a narrow sense). What is genuinely novel: essentially nothing at the technique level — PHP MVC, BYOK API-key forwarding, and client-side Blob export are all standard, well-documented web engineering. The contribution is the application of these known patterns to the SLR metadata-extraction niche, plus open-source release. The comparison to BiblioMerge/R frameworks is a combination of existing ideas packaged for a no-code audience. Notably, the "AI Enhanced Soft Computing" in the title is unbacked by any AI component in the system. Rigor & Reproducibility: Weak. There are no ablations (the system is monolithic engineering, so none are strictly expected), no error bars, no multiple seeds, no significance tests, and no measurement of any performance metric. The "evaluation" consists of screenshots (API portal configuration, phpMyAdmin showing 0 rows, GitHub interface) and a qualitative comparison table authored by the system's creator. Source code is publicly released at https://github.com/mfurqanhakim139/ScopusMUT, which is a genuine reproducibility positive. Methodological concerns: (1) the sole empirical claim (0-row statelessness) is verified by the author's own inspection rather than instrumented measurement; (2) Table 2's superiority claims over Python/R frameworks were not validated by running those frameworks; (3) the "100% verified" claim is circular; (4) a live-looking Elsevier API key (4188bb25bc8937fec456570d455285ce) is printed in plaintext in the paper — a credential-hygiene failure that also undermines the paper's own security framing; (5) no load, concurrency, or scale testing despite claims of "highly scalable" architecture. The venue (ICTACT Journal on Soft Computing) is a lower-tier outlet; the October 2026 issue date suggests limited external scrutiny relative to major software-engineering or digital-libraries venues. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: SYSTEMS (a built, deployed web tool evaluated by observation of its deployment, with a released artifact). - Practical: Yes — it runs on commodity PHP/MySQL shared hosting with a browser client, and the Elsevier API key is free for eligible institutions. - Efficient: Very low server cost by design (proxy-only, zero persistence), but client-side cost was never measured for large result sets (Scopus queries can return thousands of records), so browser memory/CPU behavior is unverified. - Effective: The evidence shows only that the pipeline works end-to-end for the author's own queries; effectiveness relative to alternatives was never measured, and the stated "100% verified" proxy is satisfied by construction rather than demonstrating solved screening needs. - Scalable: Only claimed, never tested — no stress tests, no concurrent users, no large-result-set experiments; the client-side transformation path is precisely where scale limits (browser memory) would appear. The work delivers a real software artifact (open-source GitHub repository with the full MVC application); no dataset, benchmark, or reusable technique is contributed beyond the tool itself. Strengths: - Genuine open-source release of a working, deployed tool with a low barrier to entry (no-code GUI) — this fills a real accessibility gap between scraping tools and script-based bibliometric pipelines for non-technical researchers. - The stateless BYOK design is a sensible privacy posture: no query histories or extracted datasets persist on the institutional server, and per-user API keys sidestep shared rate limits legitimately. - The JSON→RIS mapping protocol is documented at field level (Table 1), making the transformation auditable and reusable. - Honest operational detail in one respect: the paper explicitly shows the empty database rather than hiding that no data is stored. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors acknowledge that the local database is "currently maintained as stateless (0 rows)" and that future work will "activate asynchronous storage features to support broader research team collaboration" — i.e., the tool currently cannot support shared team workflows. This is the only stated limitation. The authors do not confront the absence of any quantitative evaluation, do not qualify the "100% verified" claim, and do not note that the comparative superiority over Python/R frameworks is asserted rather than tested — a credibility-negative pattern of minimization rather than direct confrontation. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - The title promises "AI Enhanced Soft Computing" but the paper contains no AI or soft-computing component of any kind — a title-content mismatch a reviewer should flag outright. - No measurement of export correctness beyond eyeballing Mendeley imports: no field-level error rate, no record counts, no comparison against a ground-truth export from the Scopus web interface. - Security claims ("secure," "strict user data privacy") are asserted without any threat model; meanwhile the paper itself leaks an API key in plaintext. Client-side BYOK also means the key transits the author's server and could be logged or intercepted — the threat surface of the proxy is never analyzed. - No load or concurrency testing despite "high-volume" and "highly scalable" language; the term "high-volume" is never quantified. - The comparison to BiblioMerge is misleading on one axis: BiblioMerge consumes already-verified publisher exports, so claiming "100% verified vs. merged from multiple databases" conflates pipeline position with data quality. - Single-author, single-institution evaluation with no independent users — the accessibility claim (usable by non-technical researchers) is never tested with actual non-technical participants. Bottom Line: The underlying open-source tool may be genuinely useful to budget-constrained, non-technical researchers who need clean Scopus exports, but the paper itself is a thinly evaluated engineering report with a misleading AI-branded title and no quantitative evidence — read the GitHub repo, not this paper.

Problem & Motivation: Higher education students face growing exposure to cyber threats (phishing, malware, ransomware, password attacks, social engineering, data breaches) as they adopt online learning platforms, cloud services, and AI tools, yet the cited literature consistently identifies human factors and insufficient awareness — not technical weaknesses — as the dominant vulnerability. The authors, education-faculty researchers at Banaras Hindu University, target the gap that cybersecurity in universities is treated as a technical problem rather than an educational/behavioral one, and that existing reviews cover threats or awareness separately without an integrated conceptual structure linking threat types, causes, and prevention for students. Key Idea: The core move is a WHAT–WHY–HOW conceptual scaffold — students first learn what attacks exist, then why attacks occur, then how to prevent and respond — instantiated as three conceptual SEMs built on Protection Motivation Theory, where threat appraisal (severity, vulnerability) and coping appraisal (response efficacy, self-efficacy, response cost) mediate from awareness to protective behavior. The framework itself is the contribution; there is no estimation, algorithm, or empirical test behind it. Methodology: The paper uses an explicitly review-based methodology with secondary sources only — "does not involve the collection of primary data." The pipeline is: (1) thematic review of scholarly articles, review papers, books, and reports organized around four objectives; (2) construction of three conceptual SEM diagrams (WHAT: attack types/target/vulnerability/consequences/characteristics; WHY: financial motivation, information value, technological opportunities, human factors, strategic motives; HOW: six dimensions of cyber-safety behavior from education/awareness through responsible digital behavior); (3) integration into a single WHAT-WHY-HOW model with expected outcomes. The mathematical framing is SEM with latent constructs and indicator loadings, but no estimation procedure, sample, software, fit indices (CFI, RMSEA, etc.), or identification strategy is reported — the loadings are asserted, not computed. Critical design decisions: the PMT theoretical grounding is well-justified by cited empirical support; the decision to attach numeric path coefficients to a conceptual (non-estimated) model is not justified and is methodologically indefensible; the inclusion of India-specific government initiatives is a useful localization but narrows generalizability. The authors disclose that ChatGPT was used for "development of conceptual frameworks and diagrams." Key Results: As a review, the paper reports no primary outcomes. Synthesized findings include: 27.2% phishing victimization among 202 university students (Ruzaili et al., 2026); a 3,030-student Chinese study showing perceived threat influenced information security behavior with response efficacy the strongest predictor; a 1,027-participant 2025 study combining SEM and machine learning identifying self-efficacy and response efficacy as top predictors; a 154-student quasi-experimental PMT-based training improving knowledge and behavioral intention; and a 255-student PMT+TPB integration study. The "results" section presents asserted SEM loadings (path coefficients 0.65–0.86; e.g., consequences 0.86, financial motivation 0.84, education/awareness 0.85) that are labeled "conceptual" representations rather than estimated from any dataset. No baselines, benchmarks, or effect comparisons are applicable. The paper's only quasi-quantitative claim — that phishing knowledge alone did not significantly predict preventive behavior — comes from the cited literature, not from this study. Novelty Classification: ENGINEERING-OPTIMIZATION-LEVEL contribution at best: this is a NEW FORMULATION only in the weak sense of repackaging PMT plus a didactic WHAT/WHY/HOW taxonomy for an Indian higher-education audience. Every substantive element — PMT constructs, threat taxonomies, MFA/password/backup recommendations, the knowledge-does-not-equal-behavior distinction — is standard in the cited literature; the genuinely new artifacts are the three conceptual diagrams and their integration with Indian government awareness programs, which is competent synthesis rather than new science. Rigor & Reproducibility: Rigor is low. No ablations, error bars, seeds, or significance tests exist (nothing was estimated); no code, data, or artifacts are released (none were generated; "No primary data were collected"). The central methodological concern is severe: the paper presents SEM path coefficients and factor loadings for a model it explicitly states was never fitted to data — presenting invented numbers in the visual language of empirical SEM invites readers to treat them as evidence, which is a form of benchmark-adjacent misrepresentation. The review does not state inclusion/exclusion criteria, databases searched, search strings, or study counts (no PRISMA flow), so the synthesis is not reproducible. The reference list contains incomplete entries (two citations lacking author names) and one duplicated reference (Ruzaili et al. appears twice), consistent with weak editorial control. The AI-use disclosure is commendably explicit but confirms the frameworks and diagrams were AI-assisted. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: THEORETICAL/CONCEPTUAL (a conceptual framework paper with no primary experimental claim). - Sound: The PMT grounding is sound and well-cited, but the numerical "SEM" results are unsound — asserted coefficients without data violate the method they invoke. - General: The framework is broadly applicable to student populations but is illustrated only through cited studies (China, Indonesia, Malaysia, elsewhere) and Indian institutional context; no conditions of applicability are analyzed. - Tight: Not applicable — no bounds or estimates exist; the loadings have no uncertainty attached. - Implementable: The framework is directly implementable as a curriculum skeleton (Know–Recognize–Protect–Respond), which is its main practical value. The deliverable is paper-form only: no tool, dataset, instrument, validated survey, or training program is released. Strengths: - The WHAT/WHY/HOW scaffold is a genuinely useful pedagogical compression: it converts a diffuse literature into a teachable three-step structure that practitioners (instructors, student-affairs staff) can adopt directly for orientation modules or digital-literacy courses. - The theoretical grounding in PMT is well-chosen and honestly motivated — the paper correctly elevates the literature's most robust finding (coping appraisal, especially self-efficacy and response efficacy, predicts protective behavior better than knowledge alone) into the framework's backbone. - The localization to Indian government resources (Cyber Jaagrookta Diwas, Cyber Swachhta Kendra, CERT-In, I4C, helpline 1930) fills a concrete gap for Indian HEIs that generic international reviews do not address. - The AI-use disclosure is unusually explicit, naming ChatGPT and its role in framework/diagram development. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: The authors state only that the study is review-based, relies entirely on secondary sources, and collected no primary data. They do not discuss the implications of this for the SEM figures, the non-systematic nature of the review, or generalizability limits — the limitations are acknowledged minimally rather than confronted directly. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Fabricated-looking statistics: The path coefficients and factor loadings in Figures 3–9 have no data source; presenting them under the heading of "SEM" findings, with interpretations like "the path coefficient of 0.86 represents the strongest relationship in the model," is the single most serious flaw and is not acknowledged anywhere. - Non-systematic review: No search strategy, database list, inclusion criteria, or study-count accounting — the thematic selection is unreproducible and potentially cherry-picked, in contrast to the PRISMA-based reviews it cites. - Circular validation: The framework's "support" comes from the same PMT studies used to build it; no independent evaluation (e.g., expert review, pilot curriculum deployment, pre/post student assessment) is attempted. - Missing critical lens: The paper does not engage with measurement validity of the cited awareness studies or with contradictory findings in the phishing-susceptibility literature it cites (Jalali et al., 2026) beyond selective agreement. - Editorial quality signals: duplicated references, unnamed references, and a 2026-dated volume suggest weak peer review; claims (e.g., DDoS as a major student-facing threat) sometimes exceed what the cited student-level evidence supports. Bottom Line: A practitioner building a student cybersecurity-awareness program — particularly in India — could skim the Figures 2 and 6 framework and the government-initiative list for free curricular scaffolding, but anyone seeking validated models, systematic evidence, or methodological trustworthiness should go directly to the underlying reviews (Al-Hawawreh et al. 2021; Salam et al. 2026; Jampen et al. 2023) that this paper merely repackages, and should treat its SEM numbers as illustrative fiction rather than findings.

Problem & Motivation: Manufacturing enterprises — particularly serial mechanical-engineering firms — must choose among CMM technologies whose trade-offs in accuracy, speed, and cost differ sharply by industry and part mix. The authors argue that the shift toward Industry 4.0 and smart factories makes integrated, automated quality assurance a structural requirement, and that conventional absolute-coordinate CMMs are ill-suited to high-throughput shop-floor control because they are slow and expensive to operate at production rates. The stated gap is the absence of a principled framework positioning comparative gauging systems (exemplified by Renishaw Equator) as a distinct control tier rather than a cheaper CMM substitute. Key Idea: The central insight is that a comparative-gauging system operating in relative coordinates against a master artifact calibrated on a high-precision laboratory CMM converts systematic error compensation into a periodic re-mastering (differential) procedure, letting a low-cost parallel-kinematics device inherit much of the reference machine's accuracy. This is a known property of comparison gauging; the paper's putative extension is treating such systems as a structural element of a "hybrid metrological ecosystem" integrated with SPC/MES and digital twins. Methodology: The paper is a one-page extended abstract, so no algorithmic pipeline is specified. As described: (1) a generalized mathematical model of total error for comparative CMMs is claimed, incorporating reduced inertial components via light parallel kinematics and differential compensation via periodic re-mastering; (2) a criterion for optimal equipment selection is proposed (the criterion itself is never stated); (3) an implementation analysis for a serial-manufacturing enterprise covers critical-parameter control, CNC program adjustment, statistical database formation, and digital-twin integration. No objective function, model equations, or validation procedure is presented. The single explicit methodological reference point is calibration per ISO 10360. Critical design decisions — how re-mastering frequency trades against drift, how the error model is parameterized, how the selection criterion weights cost versus uncertainty — are asserted without justification. Key Results: No quantitative results are reported. The "main results" are four qualitative claims: substantiation of a hybrid metrology model with comparative systems as an independent control level; development of a generalized error model (no coefficients, uncertainty values, or validation data given); proposal of an equipment-selection criterion (not defined); and introduction of a "Metrology 4.0" concept (not operationalized). The conclusions assert that Equator is highly efficient for serial comparative control, reduces load on laboratory CMMs, and achieves economic efficiency in medium- and large-scale production — none supported by numbers, benchmarks, or case measurements. No baselines, datasets, or test scales are given because no evaluation is reported. Novelty Classification: At most NEW FORMULATION (the "hybrid metrology ecosystem" framing and "Metrology 4.0" label); the underlying technology — comparison gauging against a calibrated master with periodic re-mastering — is standard practice well documented in Renishaw's own materials and NPL guidance (which the paper cites). The error-model and selection-criterion claims would constitute NEW METHOD only if the mathematics were actually presented, which it is not. Rigor & Reproducibility: Not evaluated in any meaningful sense — there are no experiments, no ablations, no error bars, no seeds, no significance tests, and no quantitative evidence to reproduce. No code, data, or model weights are released (none could exist given the abstract form). Methodological concerns: the work effectively self-reports vendor-style qualitative claims about a commercial product (Renishaw Equator), names an industrial partner (UA Company KODA Ltd) whose deployment data is not shown, and the proposed selection criterion cannot be assessed because it is never defined. The three references include a master's thesis, an NPL good-practice guide, and a vendor-adjacent web resource — no peer-reviewed technical literature. Deployability (4-property check): Profile: EMPIRICAL (claimed) / SYSTEMS-adjacent — though the paper is actually a position abstract with no run experiments. - Practical: The Equator hardware it discusses is commercially available and shop-floor deployable, but the paper itself delivers no runnable artifact. - Efficient: Not stated — no cycle times, throughput, or cost figures are provided despite the efficiency claim being central. - Effective: Only a proxy — the claim that comparative control reduces laboratory CMM load is plausible but entirely unevidenced. - Scalable: Only claimed for "medium and large-scale production"; no data at any scale is presented. The work stops at paper (abstract) form; no software, dataset, model, or reusable technique is delivered beyond the "Metrology 4.0" concept. Strengths: - Correct and clearly articulated technical distinction between absolute-coordinate CMM measurement and master-referenced comparison gauging, including why re-mastering provides differential compensation of systematic errors. - The framing of comparative gauging as a distinct tier in an enterprise metrology architecture (feeding SPC, MES, digital twins) is a useful systems-level lens for production engineers planning quality-assurance layouts. - Grounding in an actual industrial context (serial mechanical engineering, with a named company use case) gives the motivation concrete stake, even if the evidence is absent. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: None stated. The abstract does not acknowledge any scope boundaries, failure modes (e.g., sensitivity to master-artifact wear, thermal drift between re-mastering cycles, applicability limited to parts with a well-defined master), or validation gaps. The absence of any limitation statement is a credibility negative. Analyst-Identified Gaps: The authors do not acknowledge: (1) that comparison gauging inherits the master's errors and only transfers uncertainty to the reference CMM — it does not eliminate it, and the claimed total-error model is never shown to quantify this; (2) the selection "criterion" is announced but never defined, making the paper's titular promise (optimal CMM selection) unfulfilled; (3) no comparison against alternative shop-floor solutions (in-process gauging, portable arms, vision systems) — the Equator system appears to have no competing baselines; (4) the industrial partner's use case is invoked but no deployment data, measurement studies, or cost analysis from it is reported; (5) "Metrology 4.0" is introduced as a term without definition or differentiation from existing Industry 4.0 quality literature; (6) the three-item reference list contains no peer-reviewed research, and the work is an unreviewed conference abstract (MicroCAD-2026). Bottom Line: A practitioner gains nothing from this abstract that Renishaw's application notes and NPL's measurement-uncertainty guidance do not already provide with real data; it should be treated as a position statement requiring substantial mathematical and experimental development before its claims about error models, selection criteria, or economic efficiency can be taken seriously.

Problem & Motivation: Digital advertisers need to know whether personalized recommendation relevance translates into consumer conversion, and which models best predict that conversion. The paper addresses the gap between predictive modeling (CTR/conversion prediction with feature-interaction architectures like DeepFM) and economic interpretation (is personalization itself associated with conversion?). The intended audience is marketing analytics researchers and practitioners using behavioral advertising data. The specific gap claimed is that prior work treats these as separate strands (recommender-system modeling vs. causal/statistical evaluation), and this study combines an interpretable logistic baseline with a nonlinear predictor on commercial data. Key Idea: There is no identifiable new technical insight. The core move is a standard combination: construct a cosine-similarity "Match" score between user and product feature vectors, regress a binary conversion outcome on it with controls, and benchmark DeepFM against conventional classifiers. This is a known model (DeepFM, Guo et al. 2017) applied to a known dataset with a standard association analysis — not a new formulation, architecture, or identification strategy. Methodology: The pipeline has four stages: (1) descriptive statistics and Pearson correlation on a described sample of 100,000 observations with 13 continuous and 26 categorical variables; (2) a baseline logistic regression, P(Convert=1) = Λ(α + β·Match + θ·Activity + δ′Z), with Z containing ad position, device type, and visit time; (3) a supervised model comparison of DeepFM, logistic regression, random forest, KNN, and Naive Bayes on a 62,234-train / 15,559-test split, evaluated by AUC, accuracy, and log loss; (4) robustness analyses — replacing Match with a CTR measure, a mobile-user subsample, Probit estimation, and propensity-score matching reporting ATT with covariate-balance checks. Critical design decisions: (a) defining Match as cosine similarity between user and product vectors — this is the linchpin of the causal-adjacent claim, yet the paper never explains what the underlying feature vectors are or how they were derived from Criteo's anonymized features, which is unjustified; (b) using PSM to make a causal-flavored claim from observational data — weakly justified, as unobserved confounding in ad targeting is severe; (c) treating the mobile-subsample sign flip as "scenario adaptability" rather than evidence against H1 — not justified. Key Results: The paper reports an 11.6% conversion rate; a Match coefficient of 0.0431 (SE 0.0087, p < .01), i.e., ~4.4% higher conversion odds per unit; a pseudo-R² of 0.386. DeepFM achieves AUC = 0.8471, accuracy = 0.8842, LogLoss = 0.3102, versus logistic regression (AUC 0.6269, LogLoss 0.3495), random forest (AUC 0.7249, LogLoss 0.5731), KNN (AUC 0.7089, accuracy 0.8854), and Naive Bayes (AUC 0.6201). Robustness: CTR-replacement coefficient 0.0452 (p < .001, with Activity flipping to −0.1917); Probit Match coefficient 0.0235, pseudo-R² 0.381; PSM ATT = 0.0427 (p < .01) with 38,621 observations per matched group and standardized balance differences below 5%. The DeepFM AUC of 0.8471 is broadly in line with published Criteo results, but the baselines (KNN, Naive Bayes) are dated for 2014-era Criteo benchmarks where gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost/LightGBM, cited but not run) are the standard strong comparison. The counter-intuitive finding — mobile-subsample coefficients for Match (−0.0504) and Activity (−0.1957) flip sign and are significant — is reported but not confronted. Novelty Classification: At most an application paper (standard empirical analysis in a new pairing); no NEW PROBLEM, NEW METHOD, NEW FORMULATION, or NEW DATASET. The genuinely mundane parts are everything: DeepFM is from 2017, the Criteo dataset from 2014, logistic regression, random forest, and PSM are off-the-shelf. The only marginally distinctive element — the Match cosine-similarity construct as a regressor — is poorly specified, and no new benchmark, tool, or system is delivered. Rigor & Reproducibility: Ablations exist only as robustness re-specifications (alternative predictor, Probit, subgroup), not component-level ablations of DeepFM (no comparison to FM-only or DNN-only arms). No error bars, no multiple seeds, no significance tests for the DeepFM-vs-baseline gaps are reported, despite the paper's own Table 2 listing "Architecture, seed, tuning" as required reporting for the nonlinear model — the paper then does not report these. No code or data are released ("available upon reasonable request"); no hyperparameters, preprocessing details, or split methodology are given. Serious methodological concerns: (1) the described variable set is inconsistent with the cited public Criteo dataset, which has anonymized hashed features and a click label — the Match, Activity, Position, Device, Time, and Convert variables cannot be straightforwardly constructed from it, and the paper provides no construction recipe; (2) the 100,000-observation sample with a "conversion" label and an 11.6% conversion rate does not match any documented public Criteo release; (3) a causal-flavor interpretation ("personalized recommendation contributes to higher conversion") is drawn from observational PSM despite acknowledgment of confounding literature. The keyword list ("AIGC; Traditional culture") is unrelated to the content, indicating manuscript assembly problems. Deployability: Profile: EMPIRICAL (regression and supervised learning on tabular data; no system is built). Practical: All methods (logistic regression, DeepFM, PSM) run on commodity hardware, assuming the data exist. Efficient: Cost is trivial relative to production advertising systems; DeepFM on ~100K rows is minutes of compute. Effective: The evidence shows association between a self-constructed Match score and conversion in a sample whose provenance is unclear; it does not demonstrate that deploying personalization raises conversion — no experiment or online test is run. Scalable: Not tested beyond ~100K rows; the paper only asserts that findings "motivate" deployment strategies, with no evidence at production scale (Criteo's full dataset is ~45M rows). The work delivers no software artifact, dataset, or trained model — it stops at paper form. Strengths: - The multi-pronged robustness template (alternative predictor, alternative link function, subgroup analysis, PSM with balance diagnostics) is more disciplined than typical applied papers in low-tier venues, and the PSM balance reporting (standardized differences < 5%, matched-group sizes) is a genuine execution detail. - The paper is internally transparent about its numbers: all coefficients, standard errors, and AUCs are tabulated, and the awkward mobile-subsample result is printed rather than hidden. - The model-comparison framing (interpretable baseline vs. nonlinear feature-interaction model on identical splits, per its Table 2 protocol) is methodologically sensible as a design principle, even though execution falls short of it. Author-Acknowledged Limitations: There is no explicit limitations section. The mobile-user subsample result (Match = −0.0504, p < .01), which contradicts the headline positive-association claim, is acknowledged as data but framed euphemistically as a "scenario-specific robustness analysis" and a discussion of "scenario adaptability" — a minimization rather than a confrontation. No scope boundaries (single dataset, no causal claim caveats, no temporal validity concerns) are stated by the authors. Analyst-Identified Gaps: - Data provenance is the fatal gap: the Criteo public dataset (cited as the source) contains 13 anonymized numeric and 26 anonymized categorical features with a click label; it contains no Match, Activity, ad position, device type, visit-time, or conversion variables. The paper never explains how its variable set was derived, making the study unreproducible and the construct validity of "Match" unverifiable. - Internal contradiction ignored: Activity is +0.1648 in the baseline, −0.1917 in the CTR-replacement model, and −0.1957 in the mobile subsample — three significant estimates with inconsistent signs that the narrative never reconciles. - Construct problem: Match is cosine similarity on a [0,1] scale, so a "one-unit increase" spans the entire range of the variable; the 4.4% odds interpretation conflates the full-range effect with a marginal effect. - Missing strong baselines: XGBoost/LightGBM are cited but not run, despite being the accepted strong benchmarks on Criteo; no FM-only or DNN-only ablation of DeepFM. - Causal overreach: the ATT from PSM is interpreted as personalized recommendation "contributing" to conversion, but matching on observables cannot address targeting-induced confounding, and no sensitivity analysis (e.g., Rosenbaum bounds) is reported. - No SHAP/attribution results despite the introduction promising model-attribution analysis. - Venue/quality signals: future-dated grant number (2026...), unrelated keywords, and generic governance boilerplate suggest weak editorial scrutiny; no peer-review confidence can be assumed. Bottom Line: A practitioner gains little: the paper applies a 2017 model to a dataset whose described variables cannot be reconstructed from the cited public source, reports internally contradictory results without reconciliation, and offers no artifact — stronger, reproducible alternatives on the same Criteo benchmark abound in the CTR-prediction literature.

Thematic Comparisons

LLM Routing and Serving Infrastructure — avg: 71 (Innovative)

These papers share a focus on making LLM systems more efficient at the infrastructure level, whether during inference, serving, or training. Several tackle routing directly but at different granularities: UNITOR routes individual tokens between small and large models with a zero-shot transferable router, PISA routes whole prompts to models or ensembles using cost-aware predictors, and Routed Continual Learning routes agent runs to appropriate memory systems. On the systems side, ROCm InferaSim replaces exhaustive GPU trials with analytical performance prediction, Evolving Infra redesigns prefill-decode disaggregation for agentic workloads, and Flide accelerates decision-model inference through exact state forking. InfraRSI extends the optimization scope to training throughput via verified agentic search, while Hyper-Connections reduces residual-architecture overhead during training. Collectively, the trend shows the field moving from hand-tuned, static configurations toward adaptive, learned, or agent-driven resource allocation, with routing emerging as a central lever for trading quality against cost across the LLM lifecycle.

LLM-Augmented Time Series Forecasting — avg: 68 (Innovative)

These papers share a common goal of improving time series forecasting by injecting external knowledge—whether from LLM reasoning, textual context, or retrieval—into time series foundation models (TSFMs). "Learning Evidence-Grounded Reasoning" and "TSFM Meets LLM: Context as Covariates" both build on Chronos-2 and use GRPO post-training, but differ in interface: the former has an LLM reason over context to revise prior forecasts, while the latter distills textual context into covariate channels consumed directly by the TSFM. In contrast, "LLMs Don't Know What They Know" serves as a cautionary evaluation, showing that LLM knowledge of historical events introduces hindsight leakage in financial backtesting. Collectively, the cluster reflects a trend toward hybridizing TSFMs with LLM-derived knowledge, alongside growing awareness that such knowledge must be grounded and leakage-audited rather than trusted at face value.

Safety-Targeted LLM Post-Training Interventions — avg: 67 (Innovative)

These papers share a common goal: fixing specific, well-diagnosed failure modes of large language models (toxicity, prompt injection, weakened refusals, reward hacking, degraded memory) through targeted post-training or inference-time interventions rather than full retraining. They differ sharply in where they intervene: LLM Detoxification via Transition-Aware Reward-Guided Representation Sampling and Fine-Grained Selective Refusal operate at inference/activation time, steering representations to preserve general capability; Post-Training Large Language Models with LLMON and PBPO modify training itself, using structured data formats or token-level PPO-style objectives; and SafeStart addresses safety purely as a systems-level serving problem. Several works isolate a narrow root cause — the item-mean term hacked in collaborative rewards, the intermediate-checkpoint log-probability gap repurposed as a dense reward, or the expert reduction that silently erodes refusals — and propose minimal corrections rather than wholesale pipeline changes. Collectively, the cluster reflects a maturing trend away from expensive end-to-end preference-data pipelines (RLHF/DPO at scale) and toward cheap, surgical, mechanism-aware fixes that repair one measured failure with minimal collateral damage to model capability.

Closed-Loop AI-Driven Scientific Discovery — avg: 67 (Innovative)

These papers share a focus on machine learning methods that accelerate closed-loop experimental science, where models select which experiments or candidates to evaluate next under tight measurement budgets. 'Out-of-the-Box Tabular Foundation Models for Bayesian Optimization in Materials Discovery' and 'Quantitative Assessment of Crystal Structure Prediction' target materials science, but differ in emphasis: the former shows off-the-shelf tabular foundation models can replace Gaussian-process surrogates in pool-based optimization, while the latter builds a benchmark exposing flaws in how structure prediction methods are evaluated. 'Bayesian Model Discovery with Language Models: Closing the Loop between Hypotheses and Experiments' and 'WeightLoop: Weight-Space Programming with Experimental Feedback' both use LLMs to translate incoming experimental data into improved models, but one performs principled Bayesian model selection over proposed functional forms, whereas the other compiles measurements into direct parameter edits via a one-time 'editor' program without retraining. 'ProTEUS: A mutation-resolved world model for closed-loop protein evolution' and 'Screen Before You Add: Reducing Candidate Inference in Model Ensembles' address efficiency in candidate selection—one through a pretrained protein-fitness world model enabling >10-fold enzyme gains in ~100 variants, the other through certified screening that avoids costly inference when deciding whether candidates should join ensembles. Collectively, the trend points toward replacing hand-tuned modeling choices (kernels, full screening runs, retraining loops) with automated, data-efficient surrogates that make each experimental query maximally informative.

Efficient Decoding and Inference for Generative Models — avg: 66 (Innovative)

These papers share a focus on reducing the latency, memory, and computational cost of running large generative models at inference time, spanning text diffusion, autoregressive image generation, speech synthesis, streaming ASR, and quantization. "Signals from the Future" and "G-STAR" both speed up decoding by extracting more useful output per forward pass—FUSA reuses discarded future-block logits in masked diffusion LMs, while GSTAR compresses token sequences via aggressive quantization-based tokenizers for images. "Precision on Demand" and "MACaQ" attack the memory-bandwidth bottleneck through adaptive low-precision computation, escalating weight bits only when uncertainty demands it or using calibrated MXFP4 quantization, whereas "Tree-Ising" takes an orthogonal route, casting weight repair as a discrete bit-level optimization problem. On the generative side, "Few-Step Streaming" and "WaveGen" cut multi-stage or multi-step pipelines down to fewer denoising calls or a single end-to-end model, and "Confucius4-R2T2" guarantees stable streaming output for real-time transcription. Collectively, the trend shows the field shifting from simply scaling models toward squeezing maximum throughput and quality per byte and per step, using decoding algorithms, quantization, distillation, and pipeline simplification as complementary levers.

Recursive Self-Improvement of AI Agents — avg: 66 (Innovative)

These papers collectively examine recursive self-improvement (RSI) in weight-frozen LLM agents, where systems modify their own harnesses, prompts, pipelines, or coordination protocols rather than model weights. Several contribute concrete systems or benchmarks in specific domains: Flex-RSI offers a 24-task vision and robotics benchmark with hidden test splits, SciMARS targets closed-loop scientific discovery through multi-agent role and memory editing, EnzymeRSI applies a dual-loop design to enzyme engineering with a cloud-lab feedback path, and the spectrum-agents paper addresses post-deployment adaptation in wireless environments. In contrast, the more analytical papers interrogate the paradigm itself: the Darwinian/Lamarckian/agent-directed framework proves a formal ranking of adaptation speeds while warning that faster search also accelerates convergence to misspecified objectives, and the agent-evolution empirical study shows aggregate benchmark gains can conceal regressions, deployment costs, and selective transfer. Together, the trend reveals a field maturing from proof-of-concept RSI systems toward rigorous measurement, domain-specific deployment, and critical scrutiny of whether self-improvement delivers genuine, transferable capability gains.

Collectively, the cluster signals a trend toward treating verification artifacts—assertions, certificates, evidence records—as first-class, machine-checkable currencies of trust in an era of AI-accelerated software and hardware development.

Collectively, these works reflect a shift from prompt-level safety mitigations toward structural, fail-closed governance — verifying authorization, bounding privileges, and preserving auditability at the system and protocol level rather than relying on model behavior itself.

The papers on BPR and Lean integration and global supply chain resilience both address operational transformation under disruption, but the former synthesizes literature on combining radical redesign with continuous improvement through an Industry 5.0 lens, while the latter quantifies the financial trade-offs of shifting from Just-in-Time to Just-in-Case models using simulation. In contrast, the metaverse business models paper emphasizes new digital revenue mechanisms in an emerging Southeast Asian market, and the financial reporting quality dissertation empirically examines how regulatory regimes and government contracting shape disclosure quality in U.S. firms. Collectively, the cluster reflects a broad trend of applying management, finance, and strategy scholarship to contemporary challenges such as digitalization, geopolitical uncertainty, and evolving regulatory oversight, spanning qualitative reviews, quantitative modeling, and econometric panel analysis.
  • An Examination of the Financial Reporting Quality of Public–Private Partnerships and Emerging Growth Companies [#190, Moderately Innovative]
  • Business and Revenue Models of the Metaverse in Indonesia's Digital Economy [#193, Moderately Innovative]
  • Integrating Business Process Reengineering (BPR) and Lean in the Industry 5.0 Era: A Systematic Literature Review [#206, Moderately Innovative]
  • Global Supply Chain Resilience—Economic Vulnerabilities, Geopolitical Shifts, and the Quest for Stability [#217, Incremental]

Optimized Computational Methods in Engineering — avg: 39 (Incremental)

These papers share a focus on improving the efficiency and precision of computational modeling and measurement tools used in large-scale engineering and scientific applications. FESOM2.8 in single precision optimizes a climate-scale ocean model through reduced numerical precision, achieving major performance gains while preserving fidelity over multi-decade simulations, whereas Optimization of Digital Modeling Methods in Mining takes a qualitative review approach, arguing that combined GIS, geostatistical, and machine learning workflows improve deposit modeling in an industrial context. Selection of the Optimal Coordinate Measuring Machine (CMM) addresses a complementary hardware dimension, offering a selection framework and error model to optimize measurement accuracy and cost in Industry 4.0 production environments. The papers differ in scope—rigorous numerical implementation versus methodological review versus equipment-selection criteria—but all target the trade-off between accuracy and resource efficiency. Collectively, they reflect a trend toward practical, application-driven optimization of modeling, simulation, and metrology infrastructure to maximize throughput and reliability in expensive industrial and scientific workflows.
  • FESOM2.8 in single precision: climate fidelity over six decades and performance on CPUs and GPUs [#1, Highly Innovative]

  • OPTIMIZATION OF DIGITAL MODELING METHODS IN MINING BASED ON GEOSTATISTICAL AND GIS APPROACHES [#224, Routine]
